The Federal Administrative Court of Switzerland has rejected the asylum application of Iranian refugee and Jewish conversion candidate Behnam Vali Heydarian, also known as Ben Vali, putting him at risk of deportation to Georgia and potentially Iran, Vali told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Vali previously spoke with the Post in August, describing the violent transnational aggression he said Iran had directed against him while he was in Georgia. A convert to Christianity at the time and a prominent figure in the refugee community, Vali drew the regime’s attention after initially being targeted for distributing Bibles in Iran and later for his pro-Israel advocacy following the October 7 attacks.
After being assaulted multiple times, Vali said he was threatened over his continued pro-Israel advocacy, had his bank accounts repeatedly frozen without warning, and was threatened with deportation by a person he believed was a member of Georgia’s security services.
'He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person'
Mikheil Grishashvili, a Jewish community leader and representative of the Peace Synagogue in Georgia, told the Post that Vali has been an active member of the community since 2023.
“He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person, and he very quickly became part of our community,” Grishashvili said, adding that Vali became increasingly involved in Judaism.
Returning to Iran would likely lead to Vali's execution
Aware that returning to Iran would likely lead to his execution due to his open support for Israel, his conversion and his proselytizing, Vali fled to Switzerland, where he had been granted a business visa.
Though Vali entered Switzerland legally, the country rejected his asylum application, stating that he had entered the country illegally and fled from a “safe” country, despite evidence he provided demonstrating what he described as a clear and present threat in Georgia. Offers from Swiss nationals to provide Vali with employment and housing, so he would not burden the system, also went unanswered.
Ibrahim Alvac, the representative of a Swiss lawyers’ bureau representing Vali, told the Post, “The Swiss authorities have ordered his removal to Georgia because he holds refugee status there and Georgia has agreed to readmit him. His Swiss asylum application was not examined on its merits as a claim concerning persecution in Iran. We challenged the decision to return him to Georgia and sought reconsideration, but we have been unable to persuade the Swiss asylum authorities that his personal circumstances make that return unsafe. The negative judgment of 17 September 2026 has made his situation still more troubling.
“Mr Vali Heydarian is living with the uncertainty of a removal order while trying to make his concerns heard through the legal procedures available to him. He has not hidden from the authorities. He has presented his identity, his history and his objections openly.”
“We appealed the reapplication, arguing that based on my individual risks and the problems I faced, they had to assess, analyze, and examine my individual case and circumstances. But they didn’t,” Vali said. “The final answer was that the State Secretariat for Migration had already done its job and that Georgia is a safe country. You can go back to the safe country and stay there. That’s it. That was the final hope that we had.”
Vali said that the entry ban now in place, preventing him from returning to Switzerland, would stop him from seeking refuge throughout the European Union. He said he has also been attempting to contact Israeli authorities, hoping his pro-Israel advocacy and position as a student of Judaism would encourage some protection, but did not receive a response.

NYT shareholders file lawsuit against paper's parent org. over biased Israel reporting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:19 UTC
02:35:19 KST

Shareholders of The New York Times filed a lawsuit against the paper’s parent company Wednesday morning, arguing the paper has failed to follow its own editorial standards.
The suit, filed by the State Board of Administration of Florida (SBA) and the National Center for Public Policy Research (NCPPR) in New York County Supreme Court, requests the Times board of directors to release internal records.
The company has refused to produce the records for four months, the majority of which pertain to the paper’s coverage of the Israel-Hamas war.
Requests were first made by the National Jewish Advocacy Center (NJAC), representing NCPPR, on May 29 following the May 11 Nicholas Kristof column titled “The Silence That Meets the Rape of Palestinians," but the NYT has not complied.
Lawsuit alleges that board failed to establish adequate oversight
The new lawsuit, as reported by The Jerusalem Post, notes that the Times’ reputation for independent journalism is "its most valuable" asset and alleges that the board failed to establish adequate oversight mechanisms to ensure compliance with the company’s own editorial standards.
It cites examples of corrections and disputed reporting, including the October 2023 Al-Ahli hospital explosion coverage, claims about Gaza war reporting errors, and concerns raised by a purported newsroom whistleblower who said internal reporting channels did not resolve her complaints.
The whistleblower, who is not named in the suit but who is said to be a Jewish former New York Times newsroom employee with about a decade’s tenure, said that that in the immediate aftermath of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, staffers spent weeks searching for evidence that Hamas did not use the tunnels beneath al-Shifa Hospital, even after the Israeli military released its own footage of the tunnels in November 2023.
Whistleblower claimed she raised concerns internally
On November 20, 2023, the head of the video department reportedly referred to the tunnels as "alleged tunnels" in the desk’s morning meeting.
The whistleblower claimed she raised concerns internally about what she believed were violations of the Times’ own editorial standards through internal channels, including EthicsPoint, the Standards desk, Employee Relations, and Human Resources, on at least 15 occasions beginning in 2019.
The filing says the whistleblower’s records include allegations that complaints about newsroom standards were not properly escalated, concerns about bias in coverage were not addressed, and senior leadership was aware of some complaints but did not take corrective action.
According to the filing, the whistleblower alleged that the internal complaint system failed to address her concerns and instead turned against her.
The petitioners argue they are not seeking to direct editorial decisions, but want records showing whether the board monitors compliance with the Times’ own standards and manages reputational risks.

Russia’s Supreme Court proposes cutting juries to four members and allowing judges into jury deliberations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:31:26 UTC
02:31:26 KST

Russia’s Supreme Court proposes cutting juries to four members and allowing judges into jury deliberations
Russia’s Supreme Court has drafted a plan to reform jury trials, according to RBC, Kommersant, and Vedomosti.
The proposal would create a panel comprising both jurors and a professional judge. The judge could join the jurors in the deliberation room to clarify issues that arise during voting.
Supreme Court Judge Sergei Zelenin said this would “considerably streamline the proceedings” and reduce the time needed to hear cases.
The proposal would also reduce the number of jurors to four. Until 2018, juries had 12 members. They now have eight members in regional courts and six in district courts and garrison military courts.
The plan would also allow people over 65 to serve as jurors if they are willing and healthy enough. It would simplify jury selection, particularly by ending the practice of disbanding a jury panel deemed incapable of producing an objective verdict.
Zelenin, who presented the proposal, said the current model was an artificial import from the Anglo-American system. “The separation of jurors and the professional judge, including the division of their powers, is primarily a feature of the Anglo-Saxon legal system and alien to the continental tradition,” he said.
Defendants may request a jury trial during court proceedings. RBC says juries most often hear cases involving murder, intentional infliction of serious bodily injury resulting in death through negligence, and armed gang activity.
Researchers at the Institute for the Rule of Law have repeatedly said the acquittal rate in jury trials is roughly 10 times as high as in nonjury trials, where it is below 1%.

The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:30:08 UTC
02:30:08 KST

In November 2020, Barack Obama warned of an “epistemological crisis” facing western democracies. Polarisation and radicalisation were corroding trust in established information sources. “If we do not have the capacity to distinguish what’s true from what’s false, then by definition the marketplace of ideas doesn’t work,” the former US president said.
That vulnerability has grown since then. Democracy’s enemies have become more determined to exploit it. This is the threat that Andy Burnham highlighted in a speech at the United Nations this week. The prime minister accused Russia of waging an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK’s information environment using bot armies and fake websites to spread falsehoods, interfere in elections, foment discord and poison inter-community relations.
The prime minister announced the creation of a National Centre for Information Defence to thwart campaigns of epistemological sabotage by hostile actors. It is an overdue enhancement of Britain’s civil defence capabilities.
Mr Burnham is right to highlight the threat, but he told only part of the story. The Kremlin would be wasting its money pumping out disinformation if large US tech platforms didn’t provide convenient channels for the toxin to spread, if there weren’t a complicit audience in Britain sharing the offending material and if the market for spreading pernicious propaganda weren’t so lucrative. Information warfare is only effective when it exploits structural vulnerabilities in the target society. Far-right material sowing hatred against migrants is most fruitful where the terrain has been fertilised by domestic politics.
Earlier this year, analysis by the Guardian found that more than half of accounts on X that were posting about racially aggravated riots in Belfast and civil disorder in Southampton were based outside the UK. Seven of the most-read tweets originated in the US, including one posted by X’s proprietor, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man.
Mr Musk has been assiduous in promoting a warped, dystopian idea of Britain as a failed state whose culture is being corroded by mass migration. His platform has been invaluable to far-right activists who have mustered gangs of masked men into mobs that obstruct roads, intimidate people and threaten asylum claimants at British ports. Last year, Mr Musk addressed a rally organised by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, where he called for the Labour government to be removed. Earlier this year, Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, travelled to Moscow on a trip funded by the Musk Foundation. He said the purpose of the trip was to “see the beauty of a civilised society”.
Mr Burnham did not address that side of the anti‑democracy equation in his speech, perhaps because he felt that it would be impolitic to impugn US big tech under the president’s nose. Mr Trump is also an originator and disseminator of falsehoods online, but the nature of transatlantic diplomacy prevents a UK prime minister confronting him with that record.
Under the circumstances, it made sense for Mr Burnham to concentrate his remarks on the threat from the Kremlin, but that must not signal the limit of his policy focus. British democracy is indeed under attack from Russia, but an effective campaign to build resilience has to recognise also the complicity of domestic extremists and the digital privileges they enjoy thanks to US technology companies.

The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:28:51 UTC
02:28:51 KST

The United Nations was created, its charter states, to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran, another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles.
The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking as he is in Washington to meet the US president. India’s Narendra Modi is not present; nor are Cyril Ramaphosa, Bola Tinubu or Abdel Fatah al-Sisi – the leaders of Africa’s three giants, South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt. While their reasons are various, the gaps speak collectively to Mr Trump’s wrecking capability and the broader challenges faced by the UN.
In a world where “cracks have become canyons”, to quote António Guterres, the body is more necessary than ever, and under greater strain. The outgoing secretary general has struggled with a “might is right” world: an authoritarian resurgence, the rising tide of conflict and a deadlocked security council. Mr Trump sought to supplant the UN with his “Board of Peace” for Gaza before largely losing interest. Even the biggest champions of multilateralism, such as Canada’s Mark Carney, are looking primarily to other mechanisms rather than UN reform.
With extremely limited powers, secretary generals usually fall into mediator or activist roles. Critics argue that Mr Guterres should have been more hands-on in diplomacy, in conflicts such as Sudan, as he was in brokering a Black Sea grain deal in 2022. But he has been a powerful voice of conscience: early to raise the threats posed by AI, passionate in calling for climate action and heartfelt on the suffering in Gaza, Ukraine and beyond. He has also kept the organisation on its feet – no mean feat given the disappearance of essential US funding (though Washington is now paying some of its debt).
The first female secretary general is long overdue and the informal regional rotation would suggest that a Latin American or Caribbean figure may succeed him; Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana have been frontrunners. But major powers may be biding their time, with serious contenders still to emerge. Observers think that there is a real possibility that a successor may not be agreed before Mr Guterres’s departure date of 31 December, underlining the UN’s challenges.
Yet it remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign – resulting in important action on issues from landmines to global heating and its consequences. And major powers will eventually have to recognise that the case for security council reform, stressed again by Mr Guterres, cannot be ignored for ever. The charter reminds us that the UN was born from the desperation engendered by two world wars rather than a utopian dream. It endures not because of glorious successes, nor because it has avoided glaring failures, but because a world without it would be far worse. The troubles it faces are all the more reason to defend it.

Iran sets conditions for resuming diplomacy with US in Qatar-mediated NY meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:28:21 UTC
02:28:21 KST

Iran sets conditions for resuming diplomacy with US in Qatar-mediated NY meeting
TEHRAN — Iran has laid out its conditions for resuming diplomatic engagement with the United States during a meeting between Iranian and American representatives in New York that was held through Qatari mediation, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said.
Speaking to IRNA late Tuesday in New York, Baqaei said the interaction between the two sides took place through Qatar, with the Iranian delegation clearly and explicitly conveying Tehran’s views and conditions to the US side through the mediators.
“The interaction that took place was through Qatari mediation. In fact, the Iranian delegation conveyed its views and conditions to the American side very clearly and explicitly through the mediators,” Baqaei said.
The meeting was held on Tuesday on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where senior officials and diplomatic delegations from around the world have gathered for high-level discussions on international and regional developments.
Iran outlines conditions for renewed diplomacy
According to Baqaei, Iran’s conditions for resuming diplomacy include an end to fighting on all fronts, a halt to US acts of aggression against Iran, an end to the US naval blockade and economic war against the country, and the release of Iranian assets.
The Iranian spokesman said Tehran had also communicated its conditions for diplomacy through various channels in recent weeks, including its position on issues related to the security of the Strait of Hormuz.
He said the presence of the Iranian delegation in New York provided an opportunity to reiterate these positions and convey them clearly to the American side through the Qatari mediators.
The remarks indicate that Tehran views any potential diplomatic process in the broader context of developments on the ground and the measures taken by Washington. From Iran’s perspective, the continuation of diplomacy is linked to the removal of military and economic pressure against the country.
Araghchi holds bilateral meetings on sidelines of UNGA
Baqaei also said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held separate meetings with officials from several countries on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
According to the spokesman, bilateral relations as well as developments in West Asia and other international issues were among the main topics discussed during the meetings.
The diplomatic activity comes as regional security developments, including issues surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the broader situation in West Asia, remain prominent topics in international discussions and diplomatic consultations taking place alongside the UN General Assembly.
Tehran responds to Trump’s remarks at UN
Baqaei also responded to remarks made by US President Donald Trump during his address to the UN General Assembly, saying that the comments amounted to “repeated claims and allegations” against the Islamic Republic.
He said the impression shared by diplomats and delegations from several countries present in New York was that the remarks did not reflect strength but rather desperation.
Baqaei further criticized the use of the UN General Assembly — the world’s largest international gathering — as a platform for remarks that are 'unlawful and contrary to diplomatic norms.'
He also criticized threats of military action against Iran, arguing that such threats are incompatible with accepted principles governing international relations.
Iranian delegation walks out during Trump’s speech
According to Baqaei, the Iranian delegation, headed by Foreign Minister Araghchi, left the venue in protest as Trump delivered his remarks.
However, one Iranian diplomat from the Islamic Republic’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations remained in the chamber to follow the proceedings, in line with established diplomatic practice, the spokesman said.
Addressing questions over why the entire Iranian delegation did not leave, Baqaei emphasized the importance Tehran attaches to maintaining its presence at the United Nations.
“Iran’s seat in a forum like the United Nations General Assembly is our stronghold,” he said, adding that leaving that position in response to hostile or offensive remarks would mean failing to fulfill the country’s diplomatic responsibilities.
Iran emphasizes active diplomatic presence
Baqaei’s remarks underscore Tehran’s stated intention to maintain an active diplomatic presence in international institutions while simultaneously challenging US military, economic and political pressure.
The Qatar-mediated meeting between Iranian and American representatives, alongside Araghchi’s bilateral consultations with foreign officials, forms part of Iran’s diplomatic activity on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Former Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years for sexual assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:26:39 UTC
02:26:39 KST

Beril Çanakcı
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
A court in New York sentenced Harvey Weinstein, a former Hollywood film producer whose case sparked a worldwide movement against sexual abuse, to 15 years in prison on Wednesday, according to a report by NBC News.
Weinstein, 74, was found guilty last year of sexually assaulting Miriam Haley, a former production assistant on a US television show, at his New York apartment in 2006.
Judge Curtis Farber told Weinstein that he had used force against the victim and had never accepted responsibility for his actions. After serving his prison term, Weinstein will be monitored by authorities for five years and must register as a sex offender.
Haley spoke in court and said the assault had seriously harmed her life. Weinstein, who attended the hearing in a wheelchair, again denied the accusations but apologized to anyone he may have hurt, according to the report.
For decades, Weinstein was one of the most influential figures in Hollywood. His companies produced and distributed well-known films such as "Pulp Fiction," "The King's Speech" and "The Artist." He won an Academy Award, the film industry's top prize, as a producer of "Shakespeare in Love."
His career collapsed in 2017, when The New York Times and The New Yorker magazine published investigations into allegations that he had sexually harassed and assaulted women for years. More than 80 women, including actresses and former employees, have since accused him of sexual misconduct.
The reports led to the #MeToo movement, in which women around the world shared their experiences of sexual harassment and abuse, often by powerful men in business, politics and entertainment. The movement led to investigations and firings in many countries.
Weinstein said all his sexual relationships were consensual. 
Long legal battle
Weinstein was arrested in 2018 and has since remained in custody.
A New York jury first convicted him in 2020, and he was sentenced to 23 years in prison. In 2024, however, New York's highest court overturned the conviction and ordered a new trial.
In the 2025 retrial, the jury again found him guilty in Haley's case but acquitted him of a second criminal sexual act charge involving former model Kaja Sokola. Jurors could not agree on a rape charge involving former actress Jessica Mann. A third trial on that charge also ended without a verdict, and prosecutors decided in June not to pursue the case again.
Weinstein faces a separate case in the state of California. A Los Angeles court convicted him in 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault and sentenced him to 16 years in prison. A California appeals court upheld his convictions but ordered him to be resentenced, overturning the original sentence.

No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:26:00 UTC
02:26:00 KST

The Chagos Islands deal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president.
After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during a meeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea.
But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.”
The UK signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year.
Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the deal could not go ahead without US support.
“This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme. “So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.”
The US had supported the plan, but Trump changed his mind amid a wider deterioration of relations with Keir Starmer over the lack of UK support for the US attacks on Iran.
Speaking after their first in-person meeting at the UN in New York on Tuesday, Trump praised Burnham but gave no ground on his scepticism about the Chagos deal.
“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible,” Trump told reporters. “It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before, after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.”
Burnham later said he had “inherited the situation” and had told Trump “that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides”. He added: “It was clear that we need to come to that agreement, but I’m confident we can find it working with our US partners.”
Given Trump’s objections appear based on the core element of the deal – the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius – there appears to be no immediate way forward. The UK government has previously made clear that Washington’s approval is a prerequisite for the plan.
UK officials stress, however, that while Burnham inherited the impasse from Starmer, there is no intention to deprioritise a plan, begun under Rishi Sunak, that the government says is vital to ensure the future of the strategically vital Diego Garcia base, given Mauritian claims to sovereignty of the archipelago.
“It’s not back to the drawing board, as we do need to find a diplomatic solution to this,” another UK official said. “Everyone agrees something has to be done, which is why several prime ministers and even more foreign secretaries have tried to get it over the line.”
Streeting stressed the same point to the BBC, saying: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”

France, UK, Denmark urge Russia at UN Security Council to end war on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:21:27 UTC
02:21:27 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The foreign ministers of France, the UK and Denmark on Wednesday urged Russia to end its war on Ukraine, warning that Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and airspace violations are creating wider security risks across Europe.
Speaking at a high-level UN Security Council session on Ukraine, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, who is chairing the council this month, said Russia is “using winter, the cold, and denial of the most basic needs as weapons of mass destruction, targeting civilian population.”
He said Russia is “lashing out at Europe in its entirety” through alleged targeted killings, sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation, adding that repeated airspace violations involving Romania, Poland, Moldova, Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Finland mean “there is not one state who is not now ill at ease” because of Russian aggression. He also pointed to a recent incident in Leipzig, Germany.
Barrot warned that Russia, “trampled upon by a permanent member of the Security Council,” is weakening the UN’s authority, and said Ukraine “is ready for peace” but has met only “Moscow’s stubbornness.”
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territory are “a blatant violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty,” warning that “we cannot accept the changing of borders by force.”
He said NATO “is and always will be a defensive alliance” and pledged to “continue to call out and act against Russia’s hostile activity.” Miliband, whose parents fled Poland and Belgium as refugees during World War II, said “it is time ministers told President Putin the truth,” adding that “the Russian people can feel” Russia is “failing” in the war.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said “if Russia stops fighting, the war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, it will be the very end of Ukraine.”
He said Denmark “strongly condemns all attacks in violation of international humanitarian law,” warning of a “dangerous spiral of escalation” as civilian infrastructure and energy facilities come under attack ahead of winter.
Rasmussen said attacks on Ukrainian ports and grain infrastructure “threatened trade, livelihoods, and global food supplies,” and cited Germany’s attribution of a “failed hybrid attack” at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia as one of several “reckless and dangerous acts” affecting Europe.
He said Denmark “will continue to provide financial and security assistance” to Ukraine, pledging support for reconstruction, humanitarian aid and increased pressure on Russia “through tough EU sanctions.”
All three foreign ministers linked the war in Ukraine to broader security risks across Europe and called for sustained diplomatic and economic pressure on Moscow to bring it to the negotiating table.

Emine Erdogan calls for new systems to address environmental crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:17:21 UTC
02:17:21 KST

Türkiye's First Lady and chair of the UN Advisory Board of Eminent Persons on Zero Waste, Emine Erdogan, has highlighted the global environmental crisis in a video message at the opening of the Sustainable Development Impact Meetings, organised by the World Economic Forum in New York.
“Our planet resembles a ravaged mine, the oceans cannot breathe, and cities are struggling to cope with their waste. Therefore, a circular economy is not one of the options before us; it is a necessity for our future,” she said in the video on Wednesday.
The first lady expressed her regret at being unable to attend the gathering and said that current production and consumption systems are not capable of carrying humanity into the future.
'We see zero waste as a key'
Emine Erdogan noted that achieving a transition to a circular economy means strengthening sustainable development, expanding recycling, improving waste management and turning towards renewable energy sources.
“We see zero waste as a key to achieving all of this. Because zero waste is not merely a waste-management approach that individuals incorporate into their daily lives. Zero waste means redesigning our production and consumption models and redefining our relationship with nature,” she said, stressing the need for new economic models to transform the entire system from production to consumption.
“We must establish an order in which people who adopt zero waste in their lives are supported by the right systems, and in which the production of durable, repairable products whose materials can be reused is encouraged,” she added.
“Indeed, we still have a window of opportunity to combat the climate crisis and build a sustainable future. I believe that Zero Waste, which we launched in Türkiye in 2017 and which has now become a global movement, is a transformative force in making the most of this opportunity,” she said.
“With the right steps we take together, I hope we can make a new beginning — one in which we protect our resources rather than consume them, and create value instead of waste,” she added.
Thanking the World Economic Forum for organising the meeting, Emine Erdogan expressed her hope of meeting the participants at COP31, which will be held in Antalya.

Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for Gaza's child amputees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:16:44 UTC
02:16:44 KST

Breadcrumb
'Calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life': Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for amputee children in Gaza
More than 900 wheelchairs donated by two Australian charities for wounded and amputee children in Gaza have been blocked by Israel from entering the enclave, with the shipments stuck in storage in Jordan since 2025.
Mohammad Helmy, a Melbourne-based pro-Palestine activist, told The New Arab that Israel's refusal to allow the wheelchairs into Gaza was intentional, accusing authorities of seeking to make life in the devastated enclave "impossible".
“Israel’s blockade of over 900 custom, all-terrain wheelchairs—hand-built by Australian volunteers to help amputee children navigate destroyed streets—exposes a calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life and render life in Gaza impossible,” Helmy said.
“By undertaking non-stop bombardment and then systematically denying the basic medical aid needed to survive it, Israel is actively executing an ongoing genocide. Trapping mobility gear in warehouses while children crawl through rubble is not a security measure—it is a deliberate policy of collective punishment and total destruction directed against the Palestinian people,” he continued.
The restrictions come as the UN has said Gaza has the largest group of child amputees in modern history as a result of Israel's attacks on the territory.
The charity Kids on Wheels Alliance sent two shipments that arrived in Jordan in February 2025, while another shipment from Wheelchairs for Kids arrived in October that year.
The wheelchairs remain at a storage facility managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organisation (JHCO), which said COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees the entry of humanitarian aid into Gaza, had blocked their delivery.
JHCO said it filed an application in late February 2025 for the Kids on Wheels Alliance shipments to enter Gaza as part of an aid convoy, but COGAT rejected the request. Israeli authorities said medical equipment and medicines had not been approved for inclusion in that convoy.
JHCO said its application has since remained "pending", with no further updates, leaving the organisation unable to submit a new application for the other shipments.
COGAT has not responded to media requests concerning the Australian donations. However, the Israeli agency has previously said that thousands of wheelchairs have been allowed into Gaza.
The wheelchairs donated by Wheelchairs for Kids are designed to withstand difficult terrain, including the rubble that now covers large parts of Gaza, and can be adjusted as children grow older and taller.
"The sooner they come out of there and get to the kids, the better, and the little kids can get a much better life," Brother Olly Pickett, co-founder of the charity, said in a statement.
"I think there's a lot of children waiting for them who have had amputations, and so they won't be able to walk around or get around. Once they get a wheelchair, they can get out and about, which would be wonderful,” he added.
Australian media reports, citing an informed source outside the region, said Israeli authorities had denied the wheelchairs entry because they considered them potentially "dual use", a classification applied to goods that authorities say could also have military applications.
Israeli rights group Gisha earlier this year published a report saying Israel had arbitrarily classified essential items, household goods and medical supplies as "dual use" since the start of the war on Gaza.
Items subjected to such restrictions have included flashlights, sleeping bags and portable toilets.
Rights groups have warned that restrictions on such goods have serious consequences for civilians, including tens of thousands of Palestinians attempting to recover from injuries and rebuild their lives amid the widespread destruction in Gaza.

UN says Russia’s war against Ukraine threatens global food security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:12:41 UTC
02:12:41 KST

UN says Russia’s war against Ukraine threatens global food security
UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo said this at the start of a UN Security Council meeting in New York on “Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine,” according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“The cascading effects of this war extend far beyond Ukraine, including through growing risks to global food security,” DiCarlo said, stressing that attacks on grain infrastructure, civilian vessels and ports, as well as serious disruptions to commercial shipping in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, have complicated agricultural exports.
She recalled that in August, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations Food Price Index rose again, reaching its highest level since late 2022.
“The consequences of prolonged disruptions will be felt most acutely by developing countries that depend on imports and are already facing high levels of food insecurity,” she said, reiterating the UN Secretary-General’s call to ensure freedom of navigation in accordance with international law and protect civilian ports and maritime infrastructure.
“The United Nations supports all efforts that contribute to the safe and predictable supply of food and fertilizers to global markets,” DiCarlo said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo said that the escalation of Russia’s war against Ukraine means an escalation of military risks for the wider region.

Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:11:02 UTC
02:11:02 KST

The EU Industry Commissioner warned that the EU will consider using punitive trade measures if Beijing does not rebalance the trade deficit, which costs the bloc thousands of jobs every week.
The European Union "urgently" needs to act quickly to rebalance its "unsustainable" trade relationship with China, Commission Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, Stéphane Séjourné, told Euronews, stressing that significant job losses are at stake.
Recent customs data showed the gap between the bloc's imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1 billion a day in July.
"This trade rebalancing is becoming existential for Europeans," Séjourné said on Euronews' interview programme The Europe Conversation.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," he noted, adding that the EU already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year. These were particularly concentrated in energy-intensive sectors and automotive supply chains. "It's urgent that we act, and urgent that we rebalance."
The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June this year, and has set a looming October deadline for concrete, "credible" outcomes. This will culminate in a high-stakes visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to Beijing on 8 and 9 October, where Brussels is hoping to secure commitments from China that it will curb exports to the EU.
"The European Commission has put forward a proposal to the Chinese side to discuss this sector by sector and look at how we can rebalance things," Séjourné said. "This imbalance isn't sustainable, not for China or for the EU."
However, so far, Beijing has been resisting calls from the Europeans, pushing back against calls for voluntary export curbs.
The EU Industry Commissioner said that negotiation and discussion will be "given a chance," but that the Commission has been clear on the consequences of talks not producing the results.
"Trade defence tools are on the table," he warned. "Today we need credibility in how we use these tools, and we won't hesitate to use them to rebalance things."
Tools currently on the table include anti-dumping duties and tariffs against unfair subsidies (in industries such as electric vehicles and solar panels).
But Brussels is walking a tightrope when it comes to defending the EU market, as Chinese retaliation could see the country restrict exports of rare earths, essential to several of the EU's key industries, including defence.
Watching US-China talks
The EU will also be keeping its eye on talks between Washington and Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping is landing in the United States for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, which is set to cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths.
The outcome of these talks between the two economic superpowers could directly affect Europe's economic interests, Séjourné explained.
"We need a constructive dialogue between China and the United States. As we saw last year, the trade escalation between Washington and Beijing on these issues could spark a trade war, one that could even affect the European economy."
Last year, an explosive tit-for-tat trade war saw the US and China hike tariffs on each other’s goods to dizzying heights. At the peak of this battle, the US imposed 145% tariffs on Chinese imports, while Beijing’s retaliatory duties reached 125%.
For Europe, a trade war between the US and China hits hard, as astronomical tariffs on China inevitably lead to the diversion of Chinese goods from the US to the EU.
On the agenda this week in the US will be the looming expiration of the trade truce, due to expire on 10 November.
"I hope this dialogue can be constructive, that an agreement can be reached, and that the situation can be stabilised," Séjourné concluded.

51 Countries Issue Joint UN Statement Urging Russia to Accept Immediate Ceasefire as Sybiha Condemns Latest Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:10:19 UTC
02:10:19 KST

Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement on Wednesday, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations as large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine continue in the fifth year of war.
The statement was delivered during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York by Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, alongside Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, according to Democrata.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the decision in a statement on Telegram.
“We stand with Ukraine and support it in confronting Russian aggression,” the statement by the 51 UN member states read. “As early as March 2025, Ukraine agreed to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire. We call on Russia to finally do the same,” it continued.
Call for civilian returns
Russia was also urged to ensure the immediate, safe and unconditional return of Ukrainian civilians who have been illegally detained, forcibly transferred or deported.
Children have been particularly singled out.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale war in February 2022, Russian forces have killed at least 707 Ukrainian children and injured 2,548 others, while more than 2,318 minors remain officially classified as missing, according to official statistics released by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.
More Range, More Payload: Ukraine’s Race to Build Better Drone Batteries
The number of casualties and unlawful adoptions is believed to be much higher than the released information shows. However, verifying the true extent remains impossible due to lack of access to Russian-occupied territories.
Independent experts appointed under the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Moscow Mechanism presented their assessment to the OSCE Permanent Council in July, concluding that Russia has systematically militarized and indoctrinated Ukrainian children in violation of international humanitarian law using intimidation, coercion and other forms of violence.
Ukrainian authorities and international war crimes prosecutors continue gathering evidence on Russia’s crimes, with Kyiv repeatedly stating that the unconditional return of all displaced children must be a core part of any possible settlement.
Sybiha condemns latest strikes
The diplomatic support came as Ukraine faced renewed Russian attacks overnight and Wednesday morning.
At least two people were killed and more than 40 injured, while Russian strikes also targeted major Ukrainian data centers and a college building in Kyiv where students were present.
“While the 81st session of the UN General Assembly is focused on peace efforts and diplomacy to end the war, Ukraine is once again under a massive Russian attack,” Sybiha said, calling for stronger sanctions and more missile interceptors.
“These attacks must not become the new normal,” he added.
His remarks came as the EU extended sanctions on Russia for three years on Tuesday, after Latvia dropped its opposition to the new version that would delist two Russian oligarchs.
Black Sea crisis continues
The 51 states accused Russia of trying to impede Ukrainian grain exports, warning again that continued disruption in the Black Sea threatens global food security.
They endorsed efforts to safeguard freedom of navigation and protect commercial maritime traffic and infrastructure tied to shipping routes.
The concern follows months of intense reciprocal strikes between the two countries at war.
Civilian vessels, export terminals and other shipping infrastructure have been targeted, constraining shipments of grain, oil, fertilizers and other crucial commodities, creating a large disruption to the Black Sea trade.
Speaking during the sixth International Crimea Platform Summit earlier on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to support a safe-passage regime for vessels in the Black Sea, provided Russia took genuine and reciprocal steps toward de-escalation.
On Tuesday, during a meeting with US President Donald Trump, Zelensky offered Russia a truce on energy strikes.

Badrinath Dham sees record 17.79 lakh pilgrims so far this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:09:14 UTC
02:09:14 KST

People visit the Badrinath Temple amid the ongoing 'Char Dham Yatra', in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. (PTI Photo)
More than 17.79 lakh pilgrims have visited Badrinath Dham so far this year, surpassing the shrine's previous annual footfall record.A total of 1,779,805 devotees had visited the shrine as of September 22, 153 days after the Badrinath Yatra began on April 23. The shrine's portals are expected to remain open for another one-and-a-half to nearly two months before closing for the winter.The latest footfall has exceeded the previous record of 1,780,429 visitors recorded in 2023 when comparing the current figure with the year-to-date data provided by the government. The 2025 figure stood at 1,778,298.
Footfall rises after pandemic disruption
According to the Tourism Department data, 695,332 pilgrims visited Badrinath in 2000, the year Uttarakhand was established.The number rose to 768,107 in 2007 and crossed the one-million mark in 2008 and 2010.The 2014 disaster led to a sharp decline in pilgrimage numbers, with footfall falling to 159,575.Visitor numbers subsequently recovered, with 1,048,051 pilgrims visiting Badrinath in 2018 and 1,244,993 in 2019. The Covid-19 pandemic again resulted in a steep decline, with 155,055 visitors recorded in 2020 and 199,409 in 2021.Footfall increased significantly from 2022 onwards. The shrine recorded 1,763,578 visitors in 2022, followed by 1,780,429 in 2023, 1,774,264 in 2024 and 1,778,298 in 2025.
On September 22, 6,685 devotees visited Badrinath, according to the data released by the state government.
Government focuses on pilgrim facilities
The government said arrangements for pilgrims had been strengthened in view of the increased footfall during the second phase of the Char Dham Yatra, including health and safety measures and facilities at the shrines and along the pilgrimage route.
The government also said work was underway to improve facilities at Badrinath Dham.“Keeping in view the increasing number of pilgrims during the second phase of the Char Dham Yatra, special focus has been placed on strengthening pilgrim facilities at the dhams and en-route halts. Health and safety arrangements have also been strengthened. Under the guidance of Hon’ble Prime Minister Narendra Modi ji, work is being carried out at a rapid pace to give Shri Badrinath Dham a grand, divine and well-organised form in keeping with its religious and mythological significance. This will provide better facilities and a more comfortable experience to devotees”, said Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami.

‘She was an incredible feminist’: Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi collection inspired by Italian pop legend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:09:05 UTC
02:09:05 KST

Maria Grazia Chiuri has been having more fun with clothes since she decamped from Paris back to her native Rome to work at Fendi. “I have less of a uniform these days. I think it is because being back here makes me feel young again. I’m not sure my daughter appreciates [this attitude]! But I don’t care,” she said at a preview before her Milan fashion week show.
Not that Chiuri doesn’t approach her work as a designer seriously. She described her second ready-to-wear season at Fendi not as a show, or a collection, but as “the second part of the project I am working on for them”.
She is continuing the protocol she developed as the designer of Dior of using each event as a platform to celebrate women’s creativity. But instead of a ceramicist or a philosopher, her muse for this season is the Italian pop legend Raffaella Carrà.
Carrà, once described as a “one-woman Abba”, had a Lady Gaga bob and a taste for sequined catsuits. She caused a sensation with her raunchy outfits – the first bare midriff ever seen on Italian TV, in 1970 – and her sex-positive lyrics (her song A Far L’Amore Comincia Tu translates as “Take the lead when making love”).
“She was an incredible feminist, and her relationship with her clothes was so free,” said Chiuri of Carrà, who died aged 78 in 2021.
On the catwalk, Carrà’s influence became diaphanous 1970s dresses with trailing hems, visible lace bras, embroidered waistcoats and vintage fur stoles, while men’s shirts were unbuttoned to the navel.
The biggest and starriest show of this Milan fashion week belonged not to any designer, but to Vogue. Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, Milan’s glass-domed cathedral to retail, became a catwalk for a line-up that included Jennifer Lopez in Dolce & Gabbana and Cardi B in vintage Versace, with the singer Alicia Keys and the ballet dancer Roberto Bolle performing live.
Vogue is leaning into live events to amplify its brand and strengthen its coffers as print income declines. Vogue World Milano follows last year’s Vogue World: Hollywood in LA, which generated $30m (£23m) in revenue.
Billed as a celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the human touch in fashion, the event highlighted the stark reality of an increasing dependence on benefactors from Silicon Valley.
Sponsors of the event included Meta Glasses and OpenAI, and the finale included two dancing robots, who were greeted with notably less enthusiasm by the stellar line-up of Italian designers in the front row than the rest of the show.
“The landlords have entered the chat,” read one comment beneath a video of the robots circulating on social media.

Drone and suspected explosives found near Bundeswehr base are  possibly linked to Leipzig airport incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:08:08 UTC
02:08:08 KST

A suspicious substance that investigators believe is likely explosive material was found just a few meters from the wreckage of a drone that was discovered near the Bundeswehr’s Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony late last week. As Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR report, Germany’s Federal Prosecutor General’s Office and the Federal Criminal Police Office are examining a possible link between the find and the early August attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which the German government has blamed on Russia.
In the latest incident, a farmer discovered a drone broken into several pieces near the Wunstorf military airfield. A few days later, police discovered a suspicious substance just a few meters away. According to German journalists, investigators are operating on the assumption that they are dealing with explosive material; however, forensic analysis of the substance has not yet been completed.
The drone found at Wunstorf is similar in design to those used in the attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. At least one of its components was made on a 3D printer. Investigators also suspect that the drone may have been lying near the base for an extended period of time — potentially as long as two years.
Wunstorf is a key base for Germany’s military transport aviation, hosting the 62nd Air Transport Wing and all 53 of the German Air Force’s Airbus A400M aircraft, according to Bundeswehr data. Germany received its 53rd and final A400M in April 2026. The Bundeswehr itself describes the A400M as the backbone of Germany’s military transport aviation.
It remains to be determined whether the two drone incidents are connected. Overnight into Aug. 5, a drone carrying explosives and a detonator was discovered in Leipzig. Investigators believe the target may have been Ukrainian cargo planes. In early September, the German government officially blamed Russia for the attempted attack, citing the results of a police investigation and intelligence data. Moscow denied any involvement.
Investigators have identified two suspects in the Leipzig case. One of them, Oleg L., a Latvian citizen with a Russian passport, had maintained contact with Russian military intelligence for years, including with Colonel Denis Smolyaninov of the Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), according to reporting by Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR.
A spokesperson for the Federal Prosecutor General’s Office declined to comment on details of the investigation into the more recent Wunstorf incident. Nevertheless, the drone discovered there was discussed on Tuesday at the weekly meeting of the heads of Germany’s security services at the Federal Chancellery.

Ukraine Turns to Formula 1 Engineers for Its Next Generation of MAGURA Naval Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:07:15 UTC
02:07:15 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Turns to Formula 1 Engineers for Its Next Generation of MAGURA Naval Drones
Ukraine’s defense technology company UFORCE, whose portfolio includes the MAGURA naval drone, is recruiting engineers with Formula 1 experience to apply technologies developed for high-performance motorsport to Ukrainian unmanned systems.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an interview with UFORCE CEO Oleg Rogynskyy published by DOU on September 23, specialists from Formula 1 have increasingly joined the company, bringing expertise in composites, carbon fiber, sensors, engine optimization, and reducing weight without sacrificing reliability.
“Formula 1 specialists have started coming to us en masse,” Rogynskyy said.
He said their experience is particularly relevant because Formula 1 engineers routinely work to remove unnecessary weight while maintaining reliability and rapidly redesigning systems—a combination that translates directly into requirements for unmanned platforms.
UFORCE pairs the Formula 1 specialists with Ukrainian engineers to work jointly on development projects. According to Rogynskyy, the company is particularly interested in their ability to optimize electric and conventional engines, work with advanced composite materials, and balance weight against energy consumption, computing power, and operational range.
The recruitment effort comes as UFORCE expands its engineering operations both inside and outside Ukraine. The company employs more than 1,000 people and operates R&D capabilities in several countries, while most of its workforce remains in Ukraine, Rogynskyy told DOU.
UFORCE has R&D operations in the UK and the US, where it has announced cooperation with ReconCraft on development and manufacturing. Rogynskyy said overseas engineering teams allow the company to develop systems for operating conditions that differ significantly from those in Ukraine, including larger waves in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
Such requirements involve larger vessels, Kevlar reinforcement, and different approaches to autonomy, with some of the resulting engineering methods later applicable to systems developed for Ukraine.
The company is also looking beyond motorsport for specialists. Rogynskyy said UFORCE recently searched for Ukrainian engineers working at major Western technology and defense companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Anduril, and Palantir.
The company says its overseas structure allows Ukrainian specialists abroad to contribute to defense projects without relocating their families to Ukraine.
Software is a central part of UFORCE’s development strategy. According to Rogynskyy, the company’s different unmanned platforms operate on a common software layer, requiring engineers to integrate hardware, autonomy, sensors, and computing systems across multiple types of equipment.
UFORCE’s portfolio includes the MAGURA naval drone family, Nemesis and R18 aerial systems, and ground robotic platforms. DOU reported that the company’s systems have collectively conducted more than 150,000 combat missions, while MAGURA naval drones have damaged or destroyed more than a dozen Russian vessels.
Rogynskyy said the company ultimately intends to integrate unmanned platforms operating on land, at sea, in the air, and in counter-drone roles through a common software architecture.
MAGURA naval drones have also been adapted for air-defense missions. In May 2025, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said MAGURA V7 drones armed with US-made AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles shot down two Russian Su-30SM fighter jets over the Black Sea—the first documented case of a sea drone downing manned combat aircraft with such weapons.

Russia’s industrial output flat in January-August 2026 — statistics service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:07:11 UTC
02:07:11 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Russia's industrial output remained unchanged year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026, while declining by 0.6% in August compared to the same month last year, according to the federal statistics service (Rosstat).
Month-on-month, industrial production also fell by 0.6% in August.
In the reporting period, mining output fell by 1% year-on-year, while manufacturing grew by 0.4%. Utilities (electricity, gas, and steam supply) rose by 0.5%, whereas the water supply, sewerage, and waste management sector saw a 2% decline.
In January-August 2026, the highest year-on-year growth rates were recorded in the manufacture of other transport equipment, including aircraft and shipbuilding (+18.6%); pharmaceuticals and medical/veterinary supplies (+11.5%); fabricated metal products, except machinery and equipment (+11%); computer, electronic, and optical products (+4.8%); motor vehicles, trailers, and semi-trailers (+4.7%); metal ore mining (+4.1%); other finished products (+2.6%); coal mining (+1.6%); furniture (+1.3%); food products (+0.7%); leather and leather products (+0.4%); and rubber and plastic products (+0.3%).
At the same time, output contracted in the following sectors: coke and refined petroleum products (-10.3%); paper (-8.2%); basic metals (-5.2%); other non-metallic mineral products (construction materials) (-4.7%); beverages (-4.4%); wearing apparel (-4.2%); other mining and quarrying (-3.8%); wood processing and wood/cork products (-3.8%); machinery and equipment not elsewhere classified (-3.4%); chemicals and chemical products (-3%); machinery and equipment repair (-2.7%); textiles (-2.2%); tobacco products (-1.8%); and electrical equipment (-1.5%).

He swore to defend Ukraine, then switched to Russia when it seized Crimea. Twelve years later, Ukrainian FPV drone found him commanding Russian regiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:06:50 UTC
02:06:50 KST

Ukraine has taken out a Russian artillery regiment commander in Kherson who was once a Ukrainian naval officer and who betrayed his country in 2014. Colonel Oleksandr Isaiev, a Mykolaiv native who defected to Russia during the seizure of Crimea and rose to command Russia's 8th Artillery Regiment, was killed by a Ukrainian FPV drone on 19 September, the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian government project documenting Russian war crimes, said.
Isaiev's death, if confirmed, closes a decade-long arc of betrayal. The Ukrainian citizen, who served in Ukraine's military from 1992, defected while serving as a senior officer in Ukraine's coastal artillery, joined Russia's Black Sea Fleet, and by 2024 was commanding a Russian regiment that shelled the country he had sworn to defend.
A drone finds the commander
The regiment Isaiev led, military unit 87714, operated on the coastal tactical axis in southern Ukraine as part of Russia's "Dnepr" grouping, the project said. An FPV drone, the small first-person-view aircraft that now dominates the front, struck him in Kherson Oblast on 19 September. The project provided no further details on the location, time, or circumstances of the strike.
The betrayal dates to Crimea
Isaiev was by 2014 chief of staff and first deputy commander of the 406th Separate Coastal Artillery Brigade in Ukraine's navy.
When Russia seized Crimea that year, he switched sides, in what Ukraine calls high treason, and took a post as chief of staff and deputy commander of the same 8th Artillery Regiment on the Russian side.
Discharged to the reserve in 2015, he returned to Russian service in October 2022 to join the war against Ukraine, and in September 2024 was made the regiment's commander and promoted to colonel.
A database keeps the list
The Book of Executioners is Ukraine's public register of those it accuses of crimes against the country, and it closed its report on Isaiev with a standing vow: every war crime will be investigated, every war criminal identified, found, and, in time, punished.

Seriously wounded West Bank ramming victim identified as Israeli ambassador’s son
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:06:36 UTC
02:06:36 KST

The man seriously wounded Wednesday in a terrorist ramming attack near the Maccabim checkpoint in the West Bank was identified as Neriya Leiter, the son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States, Yechiel Leiter.
Neriya is also the brother of Major (res.) Moshe Yedidyah Leiter, who was killed fighting in Gaza during the war.
Leiter, a member of a police patrol crew, was seriously wounded when a 29-year-old terrorist drove toward a police vehicle at the Bell checkpoint on Route 443 and struck him, police said.
He was evacuated unconscious to Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem, where he underwent lifesaving treatment before being transferred for further examinations while sedated and ventilated.
The terrorist was killed by forces at the scene.
Terrorist accelerated toward police crew
An initial investigation found that the terrorist had been driving from west to east on a road used by Palestinian traffic when he suddenly veered left, accelerated and attempted to hit a police officer and another patrol crew member standing outside their vehicle.
A soldier stationed at the checkpoint moved toward the terrorist and attempted to neutralize him. According to the initial investigation, the terrorist then tried to strike the soldier as well, after which other troops opened fire and killed him.
The vehicle used in the attack had previously been ordered off the road.
Police said: “A short time ago, a terrorist drove his vehicle toward a police patrol car from the Judea and Samaria District and ran over one of the crew members, who was seriously wounded. Forces at the scene killed the terrorist. Additional police forces are on their way to the scene and an investigation has begun.”
Official Palestinian sources identified the terrorist as Mahmoud Sliman, 29, from the village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah.
Shaare Zedek Medical Center said Leiter arrived at its trauma unit unconscious after suffering severe injuries in the ramming.
“He underwent lifesaving treatment in the trauma room and was transferred in serious condition for further examinations while sedated and ventilated,” the hospital said.
Magen David Adom said it received the first report of the attack at 4:54 p.m. after a man was struck by a vehicle on Route 443, west of Beit Horon.
MDA paramedic Yishai Mor and medics Yechiel Frankenhaus and Avraham Lavi said: “We saw a great deal of commotion and a man in his 40s who was unconscious and suffering from severe injuries after being run over. Together with IDF medical forces, we provided lifesaving treatment and evacuated him by MDA ambulance to the hospital in serious condition.”
IDF deploys 98th Division headquarters
Against the backdrop of the latest attacks, the IDF announced an unusual reinforcement of its forces in the West Bank.
The headquarters of the 98th Division will be deployed in the southern West Bank and take command of the Etzion Brigade, a significant move that military officials said has not been carried out in the area in recent years.
The deployment is intended to strengthen command and control in the sector following the recent attacks.
Wednesday’s ramming came three days after Netanel Shukrun, 48, of Alei Zahav, was killed in a shooting attack at the Ein Raya spring in the Binyamin area.
Shukrun had arrived at the spring with his 16-year-old eldest son. When the terrorist opened fire, Shukrun spotted him and shouted a warning to his son, allowing the teenager to escape unharmed.
Shukrun was shot and later pronounced dead at Beilinson Hospital.
The terrorist in that attack was wounded by an IDF tracker at the scene and captured several hours later at a hospital in Ramallah.

 Johann Georg Hamann (1730 – 1788) lived and worked in Prussia, in the context of the late German Enlightenment. Although he remained outside ‘professional’ philosophical circles, in that he never held a University post, he was respected in his time for his scholarship and breadth of learning. His writings were notorious even in his own time for the challenges they threw down to the reader. These challenges to interpretation and understanding are only heightened today….

The former Polish leader expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
The war may end, but the level of hatred, pain, tragedy and suffering it has caused will not disappear quickly, he said.
“Even if some wonderful leaders come to power in Russia, the reconciliation process will still take many, many years, because something like this is not easily forgiven,” the Polish politician emphasized.
Kwaśniewski believes that Putin is making a fundamental mistake by calling Ukrainians “brothers and sisters,” as these words contradict Russia’s actions.
“And from the Ukrainian side comes the question: if we are your brothers and sisters, why are you killing us? Why are you taking our children and Russifying them? Why are you setting fire to and attacking our cities and villages? Why are you forcing us to freeze to death by shelling power plants?” Kwaśniewski said.
According to him, such rhetoric is unacceptable to Ukrainians because it does not correspond to the reality of the war.
“If we are brothers and sisters, you have no right to treat us this way. You may love us more or less, but you cannot treat us this way. And this problem of ‘murdered brothers and sisters’ will last for generations. You cannot resolve it with one, two or three gestures. This will remain a difficult issue in Ukrainian-Russian relations for a long time,” the former Polish leader said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow sees no conditions for resuming dialogue on ending the war with Ukraine.
U.S. President Donald Trump said in his address to the UN General Assembly that the United States hopes to achieve peace between Ukraine and Russia. “This will happen sooner than expected,” he said.

Trump says he will 'control' Greenland after deal is reached, is he right?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:03:51 UTC
02:03:51 KST

After ten months of talks, the governments of Copenhagen, Washington and Nuuk have signed a deal settling the fate of Greenland. Trump claims it gives him "permanent control" over the Arctic island.
US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed a deal on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, putting an end to the political battle for control of Greenland.
The new agreement reaffirms Washington's right of access to Greenland but crucially does not grant it ownership. It also sets out plans for the US to reopen two more bases – at Narsarsuaq, a former Cold War-era installation in southern Greenland, and Mestersvig on the east coast.
The agreement comes after a sustained campaign by the White House accusing Denmark of not doing enough to defend Greenland from the growing threat of Chinese and Russian presence in the region, and demanded Denmark give the island to the United States.
The deal signed earlier this week shows that while Trump succeeded in ramping up America's military presence in Greenland, he compromised significantly on this maximalist demand to take over the strategically located island — the largest in the world.
As expected, negotiations over the deal were based on the pre-existing 1951 Defense of Greenland Agreement, which already allowed the US considerable rights to set up military bases and infrastructure.
The US military maintained 17 bases and around 10,000 military personnel at the height of its presence during the Cold War. This gradually whittled down to just one lone base – the Pituffik Space Base on the northwest coast.
Trump used his speech at the UN General Assembly to say the arrangement gives Washington "permanent control over security and all other needs" in Greenland.
"No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland anymore, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval," he said.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte also welcomed the new deal, posting on social media platform X, "This agreement, along with NATO’s growing role in securing this vital region, enhances our collective security and supports a safer and more stable future for us all."
What has the US gained?
The biggest gain for the US comes under Article 10, which effectively gives the US veto rights over foreign investment from any country that isn't an EU or NATO member.
"The Parties agree that states or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence.... unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order," the agreement reads.
Commenting on Washington's newly-won veto right, former US Judge James E. Baker told Euronews that overall the agreement should be taken in good faith.
"Trust is the coin of the realm with alliances. And trust is built through diplomacy, process, and the identification of shared interests and values, not threats," he said in an interview with the Syracuse University Institute for Security Policy and Law, which he directs.
"The agreement should put the US relationship with Denmark and Greenland and NATO back on a path that recognises and respects our longstanding friendship, alliance, and mutual security interests, including in the Arctic," said Baker.
Another provision under the agreement prohibits non-NATO states from establishing military installations in Greenland. But these provisions were already part of the previous deal.
Crucially, under the agreement, NATO will remain central to Greenland's security and defence and an "essential" part of its future.
A 'permanent' solution
The preamble of the agreement expressly recognises the "sovereignty and territorial integrity" of Denmark as well as the right to self-determination of the People of Greenland.
The deal is also deemed "permanent", so it will apply even if the Greenlandic people vote to separate from Denmark.
Greenland is politically attached to Europe through Denmark, but is also regarded as a strategic asset for North America by the Trump administration.
Its vast, sparsely populated territory is ideal for regional defensive military installations such as radar and warning systems. It sits amid critical North Atlantic and Arctic flight and missile paths — making it a militarily strategic island.
It's also rich with rare earth elements, and critical raw materials, although accessing and extracting these would require significant infrastructural commitment.
The island's shrinking icesheets are opening new sea lanes allowing for increased lucrative commercial activity, meaning we probably haven't heard the last on this issue.

Nicholas Galanin "interrupts sightline" of Gateway Arch with animal-hide sculpture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:00:46 UTC
02:00:46 KST

Nicholas Galanin "interrupts sightline" of Gateway Arch with animal-hide sculpture
Alaska-based artist Nicholas Galanin has created a metal sculpture resembling a stretched animal hide in front of the St Louis Gateway Arch to challenge "narratives of westward expansion" for art festival Counterpublic.
Land is Never a Gateway (Sightline/Lifeline) is located in front of the Eero Saarinen-designed monument, on a small sidewalk plot. From there, visitors can crouch down and look up at the piece, which is meant to create an optical illusion with the gateway.
When viewed from below, the sculpture resembles animal hide stretched across the arch, transforming it visually from a monument into a hide-processing frame.
Galanin created the piece to challenge the narratives surrounding the ideologies of Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny, movements under which colonial settlers, ranchers and the US government began to migrate past the Mississippi River and into the western United States beginning in the early 1800s.
Eero Saarinen's Gateway Arch, a grand, 630-foot-tall ( 94-metre-tall) swooping structure located on the banks of the Mississippi River, was designed as a monument to Westward expansion and is referred to as "The Gateway to the West" in popular culture.
"The work developed through thinking about the Gateway Arch and the narratives of westward expansion it monumentalizes," Galanin told Dezeen. "I wanted to interrupt that sightline."
"That alignment is both a sightline and a lifeline: a reminder that perspective determines which histories are visible and which have been obscured."
Galanin, who is based in Sitka, Alaska and is of local Lingit and Unangax̂ descent, was informed by visits to St Louis for the piece, where he researched local history as part of the commission for Counterpublic.
Specifically, he examined "the histories held in the land itself" and "Indigenous dispossession, racial capitalism, segregation, and extraction," he told Dezeen.
Processing a hide, or animal skin, is a traditional art practised by many Native American and First Nations people. One step in the lengthy process involves tying the hide to a frame to stretch and cure it, which is pictured in Galanin's sculpture.
Galanin often explores "adaptation, resilience, survival, active cultural amnesia, dream, memory, cultural resurgence, connection to and disconnection from the land" through his work, according to his artist statement.
The third edition of the Counterpublic brings together local and global artists to create commissioned pieces and works around the city.
This year's festival, Coyote Time, invited artists to explore the history, present and future of St Louis, and included installations by artists such as Oglála Lakȟóta artist Kite and Los Angeles-based artist Alice Bucknell among fifty others.
It is led by executive director James McAnally and assistant curator Charlie Farrell, with guest curation by Jordan Carterm, Rapheal Fonesca, Stefanie Hessler, Nora N Khan and Wanda Nandibush.
In 2023, New York artist Torkwase Dyson designed a monolithic black structure that highlighted the ragtime music of American composer Scott Joplin for the event.
The photography is by Jon Gitchoff, courtesy of Counterpublic
Counterpublic runs from 10 September to 12 December. For more architecture, design and art events across the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's lead envoy for Gaza, said the process had achieved what once seemed unlikely.
"Over the last year, we've had politically significant milestones. The 20-point plan, endorsed by the Security Council Resolution 2803, gave us the framework. Later, the roadmap we negotiated with Hamas, and I want to personally thank our mediating team from Türkiye, Egypt, and Qatar -- achieved what many, if not all, thought was impossible: a commitment to give up weapons," he said.
UN Resolution 2803 stipulated the establishment of a Board of Peace, an International Stabilization Force (ISF), and an administrative committee in the enclave.
"NCAG's (National Committee for the Administration of Gaza) authority in Gaza will grow, with step by step, and it will increase with every weapon that is accounted for, and every Israeli force that moves back to the perimeter. Our aim is to have Gaza under a unified transitional administration of the National Committee. And I want to be very clear that we're not bound by a calendar or dates; we're bound by verification," he said.

There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists.
