Board member and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair called Resolution 2803 a "remarkable achievement," noting it was the fourth Gaza conflict in less than two decades.
"What was remarkable, however, about 2803 was not only that it ended the formal conflict, but that there was unanimity around a coherent architecture for Gaza's future, one which would end the cycle of conflict and not perpetuate it," he said.
Blair said the coming year would mark a shift from planning to execution. "So, for the next year, we move from preparation to implementation," he said, adding that Gaza "must live in peace with its neighbors and with itself."
Ali Shaath, chief commissioner of the NCAG, said his body was working to bring order to a chaotic environment on the ground.
"We have started our planning process because the current situation on the ground is chaotic," he said. "We are building a lean, slim governance body, not over 120,000."
He said recovery plans span dozens of sectors. "The projects we have developed by the early recovery plan has really about 71 programs starting from humanitarian development to infrastructure, economic revivification, and security, as we are following one principle: one authority, one law, and one weapon will not allow things to go back," said Shaath.

Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks protests in Madrid
September 23, 2026
The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.
Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.
"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.
Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"
The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.
With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.
An 8-year-long battle
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.
The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.
The company has not made any public statements on the matter.
Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.
She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.
Spain's housing crisis
Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.
The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.
Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.
The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).

The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:57:00 UTC
01:57:00 KST

The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
The inaugural summit of the new Carpathian Eight (C8) cooperation format, initiated by Ukraine with EU support, took place on September 18-20. Leaders and representatives from eight countries in the Carpathian region were invited to discuss security, energy, logistics, and cross-border cooperation. The initiative – intended to unite nations, some of which do not officially supply weapons to Ukraine but wish to foster “good-neighborly relations” – has turned into a zero-sum game. Yielding no significant economic benefits and failing to address real economic challenges, it only serves to isolate the region from pan-continental logistics corridors.
Is the Carpathian Initiative a Ukrainian or European project?
The foundation for the Carpathian Initiative was laid by Ukraine back in 2001-2003, when it acted as the primary initiator and depositary of the Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians. Initially, the format was strictly environmental and conservation-oriented. Countries of the Visegrad Group, and primarily Poland, breathed geopolitical life and economic scale into the concept. For years, Warsaw actively advocated for the creation of a full-fledged EU Macro-Regional Strategy for the Carpathian Region (EUSCARP), aiming to transform the shared mountain range into a major logistics and infrastructure hub.
Over time, the EU fully took over this regional initiative, turning it into a systemic tool for the “soft integration” of Ukraine. After developing a strategic vision for the region in 2009 and adopting the Carpathian Roadmap in 2019, Brussels institutionalized the project in line with its own bureaucratic standards. What began as a modest environmental initiative has, through the efforts of European neighbors, transformed into a large-scale EU geopolitical project aimed at drawing Ukraine into the European orbit via infrastructure grants.
The September summit marked the latest stage of this project. Ukraine (backed by EU funding) attempted to reclaim its role as the primary “driving force” of the whole initiative by shifting the focus from environmental issues to matters essential for bolstering Ukraine’s influence on NATO’s eastern flank.
Ukraine’s autonomy is illusory, however. For the European Commission, the Carpathian region serves as a convenient geographic ‘sandbox’; the supranational bureaucracy seeks to bind the EU’s eastern fringes together through mutual dependency. Brussels’ ultimate goal is to dilute the agency and curb the independence of countries like Hungary and Slovakia, whose ‘Eastern’ initiatives – such as linking Central and Eastern Europe with Greater Eurasia – are gaining momentum. Ultimately, this measure would allow regional financial and other flows to be fully contained within the EU.
What’s wrong with the project, and why is it a zero-sum game?
Beneath the facade of discussions on “cross-border cooperation” set against the picturesque backdrop of the Ukrainian Carpathians lie pragmatic objectives that turn the Carpathian Eight into a classic zero-sum game. This is confirmed by the project’s geography: countries with the greatest interest in the initiative find themselves subordinate to those countries for whom the project is not a key priority. Ukraine’s actual geographic weight in the project is minimal; despite Kiev’s ambition to act as the main engine of regional integration, the Carpathians account for a mere 3.6% of Ukraine’s total territory. Ukraine possesses only 10% of the total area of the mountain range, yet it attempts to dictate the agenda to Romania and Slovakia, where the Carpathians form the backbone of national geography, covering 47% and 72% of the territory, respectively. Such evident disparity between Ukraine’s actual geographical “contribution” and its political ambitions sows the seeds of conflict within the project.
Moreover, the Carpathian macroregion is considered depressed and heterogeneous. Unlike the economically developed, navigable, and homogeneous Danube region – which served as a model for this project conceived by the Visegrad Group – the Carpathians are a patchwork of isolated mountainous areas. For centuries, this 190,000 sq km area has remained a remote periphery. Due to the highly underdeveloped infrastructure – the lack of modern roads, tunnels, and logistics hubs – the border regions of these eight countries have been trapped in a state of deprivation. In the past 25 years, no amount of targeted European funding has been able to rectify this situation. This should have compelled Brussels to step out of its comfort zone and realistically assess the physical boundaries of the region. This also explains why the Visegrad Group supports eastern initiatives in Greater Eurasia. However, instead of this, along with the economically unfeasible Three Seas Initiative and the “frontline zones” project, the Carpathians are being turned into another logistical dead end resembling an artificial buffer zone.
This perspective reveals the true purpose of the revived format: to serve as a covert logistical corridor for NATO. The projected budget of €9.4 billion ($10.7 billion) for 90 infrastructure projects is specifically aimed at modernizing narrow-gauge railways, bridges, and tunnels in the Carpathian Mountains. Under the guise of Euro-integration, Brussels is aggressively attempting to create a secure alternative route through the complex mountainous terrain for rapid deployment of heavy equipment, weapons, and NATO reserves, bypassing vulnerable border logistics nodes. Consequently, supranational strategists get to fully benefit from this venture while Central European countries bear all the attendant military and strategic risks.
Intrigues, scandals, and investigations
For the countries physically located in the Carpathians and those interested in developing the region, the hidden agenda of the initiative is apparent. Citing a sudden illness, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico canceled his visit to Bukovel and expressed his outright opposition to turning the region into a frontline zone and dragging Bratislava into the conflict under the guise of NATO obligations. As a result, Slovakia was represented at the summit only by the state secretary for foreign and European affairs. Local experts openly stated that Bratislava guessed the proposed zero-sum game: under the guise of cross-border corridors, Brussels and Kiev are attempting to establish a rear hub for supplying NATO’s eastern flank. For Slovakia, participating in such “road modernization” carries direct military risks, not security benefits. This forces the country to navigate a precarious line – seeking economic grants while sabotaging the military-political agenda of the proposed C8.
Following Slovakia, the Czech Republic demonstrated passive resistance to the project by adopting a stance of cautious pragmatism. Unlike Warsaw, Prague notably refrained from sending top officials to Bukovel, opting instead to send the vice-president of the senate. Czech economic analysts expressed doubt about the €40 billion investment portfolio announced by Kiev. The most important indicator of the failure of the “unified front” was that the Czech Republic effectively refused to sign the summit’s final declaration. As regional analysts point out, the country has “cooled” towards Ukraine’s ambitions. Moreover, unlike Ukraine, the Czech Republic has a realistic grasp of its geography; possessing only 8.5% of Carpathian territory, Prague saw no tangible economic benefit in a project burdened with militarization issues rather than cross-border development. Consequently, it chose to remain on the sidelines, unwilling to endorse someone else’s frontline agenda.
Predictably, only Poland and Romania expressed full and unconditional support for the project, emerging as the principal political beneficiaries of the initiative. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Romanian President Nicusor Dan signed the final declaration, explicitly linking it to military-strategic objectives. For Warsaw, the Carpathian Eight provided a convenient platform for lobbying an anti-ballistic missile defense coalition on NATO’s eastern flank, while for Bucharest, it offered a means to logistically connect the Ukrainian border with NATO’s largest European base, which is being constructed on Romanian territory. As a result, the document was signed only by those players intending to gain direct benefits from the region’s militarization, firmly establishing the C8 as a frontline coalition.
Hungary’s reaction is particularly noteworthy. On X, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar compared Kiev’s actions to village sports: “Hi, we have formed a football team in the next village. We don’t know each other, but you are in it, and you have to bring the ball.” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrey Sibiga, expressed surprise over Hungary’s attitude, but the situation is very clear and leaves no room for doubt.
Budapest was expected to sign the memorandum between its oil and gas company MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz to establish joint strategic fuel reserves along the border. However, Magyar firmly blocked this initiative, fully aware of the risks involved in turning Hungary’s bordering territories with oil depots into targets for someone else’s military needs. Apparently, even Euro-Atlantic solidarity has its physical boundaries.
Moreover, Budapest’s negative stance is reinforced by the situation in Transcarpathia. From 2014, the Hungarian population in the region has decreased from 150,000 people to around 70,000-80,000 due to stringent Ukrainianization policies in schools. The remaining population is facing selective forced conscription, with military recruitment offices compiling lists of Hungarian students and workers to send to the front lines, resulting in several widely reported casualties, including the death of 45-year-old Jozsef Sebestyen. Notably, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry is closely monitoring these developments: mobilized residents of Transcarpathia occasionally end up as prisoners of war, and Russian diplomatic agencies, in coordination with intelligence services, work on their direct transfer to Hungary, bypassing Ukraine. Aware that Brussels and Kiev are attempting to exploit Hungarian resources and territory, Magyar chose to flip the script. Budapest refused to fund this military version of ‘Carpathian soccer’ which is too costly for it, and vetoed Ukraine’s integration efforts.
In summary, we must note that despite the ambitions of European supranational entities to create artificial buffer zones (essentially ‘sandboxes’) in Central and Eastern Europe, their era is coming to an end. Attempts to impose a zero-sum game on other countries only exacerbate the internal rift which is becoming inevitable, considering the region’s actual geography and the projects gaining momentum across Greater Eurasia.

HRW urges Myanmar to free women political prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:55:56 UTC
01:55:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Human Rights Watch urges Myanmar to free women political prisoners after torture, abuse allegations
Women political prisoners in Myanmar have faced torture, sexual violence, unsanitary conditions, and life-threatening denials of medical care, Human Rights Watch said Wednesday, calling for their immediate release.
Myanmar suffers a civil war, affecting most of the country, following the military seizure of power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021.
The New York-based rights group interviewed 17 former female political prisoners—including activists, journalists, health workers, and aid workers who were held in 11 interrogation centers and prisons — as well as three family members and four lawyers and advocates in 2025 and 2026.
The women described beatings with sticks, chains, metal pipes, and slingshots, and said they were subjected to electric shocks, sexual violence, cigarette burns, prolonged stress positions, and weeks or months in solitary confinement, according to the report.
HRW also cited the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners — a group that keeps detailed records of arrests and casualties perpetrated by the authorities — noting that nearly 6,600 women and 640 children have been detained for political reasons since the takeover.
The rights group also said 43 women political prisoners and their children were among 290 political prisoners who died between 2021 and 2026, according to Myanmar Prison Witness, a watchdog group.
“Women who have been detained as political prisoners in Myanmar paint a deeply disturbing picture of a prison system in which suffering and neglect are both deliberate and routine,” Bryony Lau, HRW's deputy Asia director, said in the report. “The women face layers of injustice, from arbitrary arrest to torture and mistreatment in detention, to unrelenting fear and trauma following release.”
The report said one woman who was arrested in 2021 when she was three months pregnant was beaten and subjected to electric shocks during interrogation, despite authorities knowing she was pregnant, leaving her with chronic pain. She was held in a storage room with nine other pregnant women, where they slept on a concrete floor among used medical masks and gowns, the report said.
“There was no ultrasound, so there was no way to estimate the due date,” she told Human Rights Watch. “My water broke at midnight, but the (hospital) referral letter only arrived at 10 a.m. Chains were put back on my feet right after the delivery.”
The group said about 125 women political prisoners were detained while pregnant or with their children, citing the Women’s Organization of Political Prisoners.
The report said women prisoners had faced sexual humiliation or assault, including invasive body searches conducted in a manner and at a frequency that indicated an intent to humiliate rather than serving any legitimate security purpose.
One former prisoner held in the notorious Insein prison in the northern part of Yangon, the country’s largest city, and Daik-U prison in the lower-central Bago region, told HRW that guards coerced some women into sexual activity in exchange for medicine or other necessities, according to the report.
In Wednesday’s report, Human Rights Watch called on Myanmar’s military authorities to release all women political prisoners, including Suu Kyi, and their children, and to end torture and other mistreatment in detention.
The allegations could not be independently verified. A spokesperson for the military-backed government was not immediately available for comment on the report.
Rights groups have documented allegations of torture and sexual violence in Myanmar detention facilities since the military takeover.
In August last year, a U.N.-backed investigator said his team had turned up significant evidence of “systemic torture” in Myanmar’s detention centers, including electric shocks, strangulations, gang rape, and burning of sexual body parts over a one-year period between 2024 and 2025.

Gaza Board of Peace unveils $2.45B rebuilding push: ‘Hamas ready to disarm’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:55:47 UTC
01:55:47 KST

Despite continuing difficulties with both Israel and Hamas over implementation of U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza, members of the Gaza Board of Peace voiced optimism Wednesday that the project will move into a major implementation phase over the coming year.
Tony Blair, a senior founding member of the Board of Peace, told a gathering held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that Hamas had agreed to the destruction of its military infrastructure.
“Beneath Gaza City there are hundreds of kilometers of tunnels containing weapons stockpiles and weapons factories,” Blair said. “The new government cannot govern unless that infrastructure is systematically destroyed. Hamas has agreed that this will happen, and that is a milestone. Our challenge now is to turn it into an agreement.”
Blair said Gaza had been “liberated from Hamas control” and that Israel had agreed to a framework involving the full demilitarization of Gaza, a new security mechanism, an international stabilization force and a policing force.
“The question of a Palestinian state will not be resolved now, but the option will remain open, subject to Israel’s security and the legitimate desire of Palestinians to govern themselves,” he said.
Blair said the past year had involved intensive preparations by the Board of Peace to bridge outstanding gaps.
“Seventy percent of Gaza is destroyed,” he said. “There has been significant humanitarian improvement, but for many people the situation remains severe. In the coming year, we are moving toward implementation of the plan.”
‘Commitment to hand over weapons’
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, said the process had progressed further than he expected a year ago.
“If I look back one year, I did not think we would be here talking about the challenges we face in implementing the plan,” Mladenov said. “I did not think there would be a plan for disarmament and the transfer of civilian government, a reconstruction plan and a plan for an Israeli withdrawal.”
“The road map we reached with Hamas through Qatari and Turkish mediation includes a commitment to hand over weapons,” he said. “We want to give Gaza a chance, and we want the residents of the Israeli communities near Gaza to leave behind their sense of fear.”
Mladenov said the Palestinian technocratic committee established in early 2026 to manage civilian life and public services in Gaza already has a presence inside the Strip.
He also acknowledged that Israel’s election campaign has complicated negotiations.
“There are talks with Israel, and they are not easy because of the elections there,” he said. “Everything is more emotional and politically sensitive. We have had good talks and reached agreement on the final objective: disarmament, the demilitarization of Gaza and civilian governance that will allow Gaza to be rebuilt.”
More than 24 countries prepared to join effort
Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, said more than two dozen countries were prepared to contribute resources and personnel.
“More than 24 countries are ready to take part in the effort, with resources and a willingness to work side by side,” Witkoff said. “A year ago at the UN General Assembly, the situation looked different. Today you can point to real progress.”
“All the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, even if it is not perfect, but it still exists,” he said. “The humanitarian effort has achieved historic results, with billions of dollars in donations to meet urgent needs and reconstruction requirements.”
“The people involved in the Board of Peace are our secret weapon,” Witkoff added. “Everyone is working together under Trump’s leadership.”
Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and another senior member of the Board of Peace, said the initiative was designed to move beyond years of unsuccessful diplomatic meetings.
“Over the past decade there have been so many meetings about Gaza, and we tried to do something different,” Kushner said. “We did not want to blame anyone. We wanted to advance solutions rather than slogans and political statements.”
He said aid could now be delivered more efficiently and directly to Gaza residents than a year ago.
“I think we are building something more important than a company,” Kushner said. “We are building a platform that will allow the people of Gaza to focus on improving their lives and give those who want to live in peace the opportunity to do so.”
“Our goal is clear. We want Gaza to be able to prosper and fulfill its potential, and for that to happen it must be demilitarized,” he said.
Kushner said Trump’s plan had reduced tensions but had not yet solved the underlying problem.
“It solved only the first phase involving the hostages,” he said. “We need to stick with it and remain committed to it.”
‘The situation on the ground is chaotic’
Dr. Ali Shaath, head of the Palestinian technocratic committee, said his body would be responsible for providing services and rebuilding Gaza.
“We are a body that will provide services to the people of Gaza and rebuild it, for the children of Gaza who have been denied that right for far too long,” Shaath said. “For three years they have not gone to school.”
“The current situation on the ground is chaotic. This fragility will not serve the goal of rebuilding Gaza,” he said. “Winter is coming to Gaza and money is urgently needed. If we all implement one plan, together with the World Bank and aid organizations, we will all succeed.”
Gen. Jasper Jeffers, commander of the International Stabilization Force in Gaza, said a 500-member force drawn from Morocco and Kosovo had already been trained, while forces from Albania, Kazakhstan and other countries were also undergoing training.
“For the disarmament project, we are working on a military plan that can be implemented sector by sector,” the U.S. general said.
“There are hundreds of kilometers of tunnels and tens of thousands of weapons. We will dismantle or neutralize the tunnels and the weapons, follow the technocratic committee as it takes responsibility for the territory, and that will later lead to the IDF’s withdrawal.”
Jeffers said a weapons-neutralization team from Kosovo was already with him on the ground.
“Gaza will be rebuilt by Gazans,” he said.
66 projects worth $2.45 billion
The Board of Peace is also considering turning Gaza into a tax-free zone so that money donated to the Strip can be directed entirely toward reconstruction.
At the New York gathering, officials presented plans for 66 projects to be implemented in Gaza over the next six months at a total cost of $2.45 billion.
Some are intended to begin immediately and focus on humanitarian needs, sanitation, temporary housing and preparations for Palestinian police and international security forces.
For the Board of Peace, the coming year is intended to turn months of planning into implementation: disarming Hamas, transferring civilian control, rebuilding Gaza and creating the conditions for a gradual Israeli withdrawal.

6 people killed in bear attacks in Siberia, as official warns one town is "under siege"
At least six people have been killed in bear attacks in Russia's vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk in a month, prosecutors said Wednesday, as an official in a neighboring region reported bears had put one town "under siege."
Prosecutors said they opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia's brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia's natural resources ministry.
While the number of bear attacks across Russia has remained constant at around 20 to 30 a year, according to the ministry, local media and officials have expressed alarm about the rising numbers. At least 14 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since the start of the year, according to a tally by The Moscow Times.
Despite numerous warnings, local officials "failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people," the Investigative Committee of Russia's sparsely populated Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia regions said on its website.
The bodies of two pensioners were found mauled in a forest near the remote town of Podtyosovo earlier this month, followed by the death of a 40-year-old factory worker who walked through the forest on Sept. 6, according to local media.
Earlier this month, two people were killed while foraging for wild berries in a remote forest on the banks of the Lena River, the Moscow Times reported.
"One person managed to escape and report the incident," the regional branch of Russia's Interior Ministry said, according to the outlet.
A 39-year-old logger guarding machinery was killed by a bear in the forest early Wednesday, investigators said.
The deputy head of the neighboring Khakassia region, Dmitry Buchenik, said Wednesday that the forest town of Abaza — home to around 10,000 people — was surrounded by bears "on all sides."
"It was an alarming night in Abaza. The taiga town is effectively under siege by bears," he said.
"Some of the animals were chased off, but three were killed (one of them was huge)," he added.
Unverified social media videos purported to show a bear swimming across a river beside the town, while another showed a group of three bears leaping across a road in front of cars.
Russia's emergency ministry says bears flee in the vast majority of encounters with humans.
Earlier this year, officials said three members of a family, including a child, were injured by a polar bear in a rare attack in the far north of Siberia.

Finland and Ukraine sign drone production deal
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:54:52 EEST
01:54:52 KST

Finland and Ukraine have signed a defence cooperation agreement that sets the framework for producing drones and other weapons systems in Finland, as Kyiv seeks more production capacity and Helsinki expands cooperation between the two countries’ defence industries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the agreement in New York on Wednesday during the United Nations General Assembly. Stubb had travelled to New York for the UN’s high-level week, which runs from 20 to 24 September.
The agreement covers joint production of defence equipment, transfers of technology and expertise, and industrial projects between Finnish and Ukrainian companies.
Most drones produced in Finland under future projects are expected to go to Ukraine. Stubb said during an August visit to Kyiv that about 90 per cent of drones manufactured in Finland under the planned cooperation would go to Ukraine, while the remainder would stay in Finland or go to other customers.
The agreement itself does not transfer funding. Instead, it provides a framework for companies to negotiate production projects and other contracts.
“Ukraine needs all our support in its fight,” Stubb wrote on X after the signing. He said Finland would also use lessons from Ukraine to develop its own defence capabilities.
Stubb told Finnish media in New York that the speed of implementation would depend on cooperation between Finnish and Ukrainian companies. He said some Ukrainian drone models could be produced in Finland.
The two countries had worked on the agreement for several months. Finland and other Nordic and Baltic countries had already committed in August to expanding joint defence production with Ukraine, including drones, air defence equipment, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
Finland has also started building company-level links with Ukraine. Stubb travelled to Kyiv in August with representatives from Insta, Boomeranger, Patria, Nokia, ICEYE, Sensofusion and NestAI. Insta, Boomeranger and Patria signed letters of intent with Ukrainian partners during the visit, according to the Finnish president’s office.
The projects under discussion extend beyond aerial drones. Cooperation also covers unmanned ground vehicles and maritime systems.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the two countries’ defence ministries had negotiated the framework for months. He said it would create opportunities for Finnish defence companies and support Ukraine’s defence capacity.

Aysu Biçer
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The UK said Wednesday that it launch a new Royal Air Force squadron to protect satellites and counter hostile activity in space.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Britain must “keep pace in the new space race,” according to a statement by the government.
The new unit, No III Space Effects Squadron, will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to defend satellites that provide services, including missile warnings, communications and navigation for ships.
Two existing RAF units, No I Space Operations Squadron and No II Space Warning Squadron, already monitor and warn of threats in space.
The Ministry of Defense (MoD) said the new squadron would focus on acting against those threats. It will use technologies including electronic warfare to “disrupt, degrade and deny hostile actions.”
The unit is also intended to support offensive and defensive space operations, with its capabilities expected to expand as new technology enters service.
“Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th-century deterrence," said Streeting.
“That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space,” he added.
The MoD said the squadron would help protect space-based systems that people on Earth rely on every day, while strengthening the UK's ability to respond to threats in orbit.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to disqualify the Joint List from the Oct. 27 election, awaiting final decision at High Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:51:49 UTC
01:51:49 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Israel’s election panel bars Ra’am and Joint List; Supreme Court fight looms
Israel’s election panel bars Ra’am and Joint List; Supreme Court fight looms
The Arab-led alliance can appeal to the Supreme Court, which will have the final say on whether it appears on the ballot
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar both Ra’am and the Joint List from the October 27 parliamentary election, setting up a Supreme Court fight over whether the two Arab-led slates can appear on the ballot.
The challenge to Ra’am came from three petitioners: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party, and the Choosing Life forum of bereaved families and victims of terrorism.
They alleged that Ra’am supported armed struggle by a terrorist organization and rejected Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state. The committee voted 18–5 to disqualify the party.
The petitioners pointed to alleged connections between Ra’am, the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement and charities they claimed had assisted bodies linked to Hamas. Ra’am denies that the evidence connects the party to support for terrorism. Its leader, Mansour Abbas, called the committee’s decision political and said the party would challenge it in court. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara also opposed barring Ra’am, finding that the evidence did not establish grounds for disqualification.
The committee separately voted to disqualify the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad. Likud’s challenge to the alliance cited party positions and statements that it argued justified excluding the list. The panel also voted to bar two Joint List candidates individually: Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh. Those are separate decisions from the vote against the alliance as a whole.
The bans are not the final word. Ra’am and the Joint List can appeal the decisions against their full slates to the Supreme Court. The decisions against Cassif and Abu Shehadeh must receive Supreme Court approval before those candidates can be excluded. The court is expected to hear election disqualification cases next week.
The legal test is demanding. Israeli law permits disqualification for rejecting the state’s existence as Jewish and democratic, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle against Israel by a terrorist organization or enemy state.
The Supreme Court has required clear evidence that a prohibited position is central to a list’s or candidate’s activity, and it has overturned earlier committee bans on Arab parties. Its rulings will determine whether Wednesday’s votes change the October ballot.

Russia, Ukraine show interest in limited grain, energy ceasefire: US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:50:25 UTC
01:50:25 KST

Russia and Ukraine have both expressed interest in a limited ceasefire covering grain and energy-related targets, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York.
“I think both sides have expressed an interest in some limited ceasefire that involve grain and energy,” Rubio told reporters on Wednesday, adding that reaching such an agreement “won't be easy”.
Ukraine has pressed for ceasefires covering energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping, amid concerns that Russia could target power and heating facilities with missiles and drones this winter.
Russia has not publicly indicated that it is ready to agree to a maritime or energy truce, and it was not immediately clear whether Rubio’s comments reflected any movement from Moscow following his talks with Lavrov.
Rubio said energy strikes were particularly difficult to address because they remain central to both sides’ tactical priorities in the war, which is now in its fifth year.
Kiev calls for maritime truce
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that he and US President Donald Trump had discussed a ceasefire covering energy-related targets. Zelenskyy was due to address the UN General Assembly later on Wednesday.
Earlier, Zelenskyy told world leaders that Kiev was ready for a maritime truce in the Black Sea based on proposals from countries including Türkiye, Egypt and India saying it was now up to Russia to respond.
“Kiev is ready to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too,” Zelenskyy said at Ukraine’s Crimean Platform summit. “We have to start somewhere.”
Top wheat importers in Asia, the Middle East and Africa that rely on supplies from the Black Sea region have faced difficulties securing shipments, while global wheat prices have risen.
Moscow remains open to talks
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told the UN Security Council that France supported moratoriums on attacks against energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea as an initial step towards de-escalation.
Ahead of the Rubio-Lavrov meeting, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said there were no conditions for broader peace talks with Ukraine, while maintaining that Moscow remained open to negotiations.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that he was ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in a trilateral meeting with Trump.

Israeli blast in Lebanon's Khiam damages school miles away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:48:42 UTC
01:48:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Massive Israeli blast in Lebanon's Khiam damages school miles away, cuts power
A massive Israeli explosion in the southern Lebanese town of Khiam late on Tuesday damaged a school, homes and other buildings in surrounding towns, forcing at least one school to close and cutting power to nearby areas.
The blast occurred at around midnight, when Israeli forces reportedly demolished several chalets in the hilltop town.
The force of the explosion was reportedly felt miles away, shattering windows and damaging doors in neighbouring Marjaayoun and Qlayaa.
Images shared online showed the scale of the explosion, which lit up the night sky over the area.
Among the buildings damaged was Marjaayoun National College, where several classroom windows were shattered, forcing the school to temporarily suspend classes while repairs were carried out.
💥تفجير إسرائيلي عنيف في مدينة الخيام في القطاع الشرقي جنوب لبنان#لبنان #اسرائیل pic.twitter.com/Xn4mN6QgX4
— ديوان (@DiwanDaily) September 22, 2026
Most students across Lebanon have begun returning to school, but thousands remain unable to do so because their families are still displaced from the south or because some schools elsewhere in the country continue to shelter displaced people.
Electricity infrastructure was also damaged by the explosion, cutting power to the Nabeh al-Hamam area and parts of the Arqoub subregion.
The blast comes as Israeli property destruction in southern Lebanon continues at a high rate following the June ceasefire, with Khiam the most affected village, according to exclusive figures shared with The New Arab.
Nasser Khdour, Middle East Assistant Research Manager at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), said more than 320 property destruction events were recorded in August, the highest monthly figure so far, followed by another 210 between 1 and 21 September.
"The number of property destruction events has been rising since June’s ceasefire, reaching more than 320 in August, the highest monthly figure so far. There were another 210 events from 1 to 21 September. Al Khiam has been the most affected village," Khdour told The New Arab.
"Israel’s destruction of villages puts pressure on displaced residents, including Shia communities in southern Lebanon. Many of these villages were also centres of Hezbollah activity and held symbolic importance for the group," he added.
Khiam has been largely devastated by Israeli attacks, with extensive destruction reported in the town.
The strategically located hilltop town is among a number of areas in southern Lebanon where Israeli forces have maintained a presence following Israel's invasion, which began in October 2024.
Later on Wednesday, videos shared online appeared to show Israeli troops raising the Israeli flag at the northern entrance to Khiam.
Khdour said September had also seen an increase in Israeli air and drone strikes across a wider stretch of southern Lebanon.
"In September, we have also seen more Israeli air and drone strikes around Nabatiyeh al-Fawqa, Kfar Tebnit, Zawtar al-Sharqiya and Qantara, down to Wadi Slouki. Some of these places are already within the Yellow Line," he said.
"This seems to be part of Israel’s efforts to clear the area after the fall of Ali al-Taher Ridge. Strikes on Nabatiyeh al-Fawqa have also become more frequent since then."
Further Israeli attacks were reported elsewhere in southern Lebanon on Wednesday, with airstrikes, shelling and home demolitions continuing despite the US-sponsored framework agreement signed between Lebanon and Israel in June.
Tensions have fuelled fears of renewed large-scale fighting between Israel and Hezbollah.
Israel has said it will not fully withdraw from southern Lebanon until Hezbollah is disarmed, while the group has rejected demands to surrender its weapons as long as Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanese territory.

Russia weighs charging heavy 5G users for international data as part of its VPN crackdown. For now, the country’s 5G is Android-only.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:46:54 UTC
01:46:54 KST

Russia weighs charging heavy 5G users for international data as part of its VPN crackdown. For now, the country’s 5G is Android-only.
The Russian government is once again considering a fee for international data traffic exceeding 50 GB on 5G networks, sources told the BBC Russian Service.
One source in the telecommunications industry said authorities want to use the fee to target VPN services outside the Kremlin’s control.
The fee could take effect on October 1, the BBC Russian Service said. However, a source at one of Russia’s “Big Four” mobile operators — MTS, Beeline, MegaFon, and T2 — said neither the effective date nor the amount has been set.
Reports in late March 2026 revealed that Russia’s Digital Development Ministry had proposed charging for VPN use and imposing fees on international mobile data traffic exceeding 15 GB a month. The BBC later said the average charge would be 150 rubles for each gigabyte over the limit. The deadline for introducing the surcharge was later pushed back until at least the fall, sources said.
On September 11, 2026, the Digital Development Ministry announced the launch of commercial fifth-generation (5G) networks in Russia. So far, 5G is available in only 16 cities, giving an estimated 10 million people access to 5G mobile internet, according to the ministry. Operators can use only the LTE (4G) frequencies already allocated to them; the spectrum commonly used for 5G elsewhere has long been reserved in Russia for the Federal Security Service and the Defense Ministry.
In addition, 5G is available in Russia only on Android devices. The Digital Development Ministry has said that iPhone owners’ access to 5G depends on a decision by Apple.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed an agreement Wednesday to expand defense and security cooperation, including in drone technology, Finland’s Defense Ministry said.
The agreement, signed in New York, provides for technology and knowledge transfers, joint research and development, and industrial production projects between the two countries, according to a ministry statement.

Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:44:57 UTC
01:44:57 KST

Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.
In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.
But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.
The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.
He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.
Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme but that it did not want to build nuclear weapons.
He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.
Insisting Iran was the victim of true terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”
He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa.
Ultimately Washington granted the permit, but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.
He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

The Fixer: Amjad M. Tadros on a life in Middle East journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:42:07 UTC
01:42:07 KST

Breadcrumb
The Fixer: Amjad M. Tadros' extraordinary 30-year journalism journey through the Middle East
For more than three decades, Amjad M. Tadros was one of the people behind some of American television’s most important coverage of the Middle East.
A Jordanian journalist and the son of Palestinian refugees, Tadros joined CBS News in 1990 almost by accident after a job in Saudi Arabia fell through in the aftermath of Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait.
He went on to spend more than 30 years as CBS News’ Middle East producer, working across Iraq, Yemen, Syria and the wider region and helping correspondents from CBS News and 60 Minutes report from some of the world’s most difficult and dangerous environments.
His career placed him at the centre of stories that shaped American understanding of the region. He was in Baghdad when a US cruise missile struck his hotel in 1993, leaving him injured and unexpectedly face-to-face with Saddam Hussein in an Iraqi hospital.
In Yemen, he pursued stories about al-Qaeda and Osama bin Laden’s network. He worked on reporting about the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib, the Arab Spring and Syria’s war, among many other major stories.
Yet Tadros never saw himself simply as a producer. For much of his career, he was known as a "fixer" — the person who could open doors, find sources, arrange access, navigate bureaucracy and help foreign correspondents understand the places they were reporting from.
That experience is at the heart of his new memoir, The Fixer: A Journalist’s Accidental Journey Through the Middle East. He spoke to The New Arab about his memoir, the extraordinary experiences that shaped his career and what has happened to American coverage of the Middle East.
The New Arab: Your memoir is called The Fixer: A Journalist’s Accidental Journey through the Middle East. Why did you choose that title, and what does being a “fixer” mean to you?
Amjad M. Tadros: I decided to call the book The Fixer because although I had many titles during my career, I had no problem with being called a fixer. We don’t really have this term in Arabic; the Americans called us “fixers,” and we do everything from getting the coffee to arranging interviews.
Some of my colleagues did not like the term, and eventually I got called a producer. But I was proud to be called a fixer. I was the best at it, and I fixed for all the major US networks. Plus, it was a nice title.
The book was actually going to be called The Accidental Journalist for a long time because I really did become a journalist by accident. But The Fixer felt more honest.
Being a fixer was not just a job title for me. It was about adapting, surviving and connecting — about being the bridge between two worlds.
One of your assignments was to go to Iraq, and it ended with you being caught up in a US missile attack on Baghdad while you were in a hotel. You ended up in hospital, where you met the then Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. Most people would have quit after that, but you kept going back to Iraq. What happened, and why did you keep going back?
It was in January 1993, and back then the Iraqis didn’t trust us Jordanians because we could speak the language. So when American reporters would go out on assignment, I stayed behind in the Baghdad hotel.
We didn’t think this would happen, as the hotel was meant to be a safe place. But we were hit by an American cruise missile, and I was injured.
I was taken to the hospital screaming. I was worried that people would go to my hotel room to see blood, see I was not there and assume I was dead. My parents would then see the news and think I was dead too.
Nobody knew where I was. After being stitched up, the hospital refused to let me go because they got word that Saddam Hussein was going to visit the injured. He wanted to show people he was still alive, which is why he was coming. I had only a few minutes to decide what to say to him, and I chose to avoid politics and just thank him for the humanitarian gesture.
When he came into the hospital, I pulled myself up and leaned forward to greet him with a kiss on the cheek. Iraqi television took a photograph of us, and that image was widely circulated. It became a defining moment in my career because Iraqi officials began to assume that I had a connection to Saddam. After that, I was able to work in Iraq largely uninterrupted for years and gained access that allowed me to pursue stories other journalists could not.
Up until a few years after the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, American media was always interested in Iraqi stories, but you also tried to get more interest going in Yemen too. What was it like trying to get the US media to cover Yemen?
Yemen was a hard sell. I have three chapters in the book about Yemen and the stories I covered there.
The first story that brought me to Yemen was about a Yemeni guy in Guantanamo Bay; while there, I discovered a guy who was Osama Bin Laden’s bodyguard.
I got CBS to greenlight the story, and after that one, I kept going back to cover more stuff. It was always hard to get American editors to approve these stories, though, but I managed it; I got CBS Evening News, 60 Minutes, and the website to do stories on Yemen.
I love the country; the Yemeni people are the nicest, and it's so scenic and fascinating. Dangerous at the same time, but very beautiful. There are over 40 million people who live there; they are part of an important global access point, and you can’t just ignore them.
Do you think your journalism made a difference in how the US saw the Arab World, and how would you assess where we are today with American coverage of the region?
I hope I made a difference. Journalists often like to take the moral high ground and believe they are making an impact, so I hope I made a difference.
I believe we covered stories that no one else did, and especially with something like 60 Minutes, where we could cover a story with great depth, I like to think this made a difference.
Unfortunately, in recent coverage, I think certain technological changes have challenged how things are covered. Things like social media and AI have created a demand for more news to be produced in less time.
But this approach doesn’t work for understanding developments in the Middle East; these are old societies with long histories, and you cannot convey this with these incentives.
I also believe news coverage has become shallower and more opinionated; this is not how I was taught journalism.
One of the reasons I wrote the book was to push back on claims that we are legacy media, fake news and so on. We did important stories like the US abuse of prisoners in Abu Ghraib, which had an impact in America; we were certainly not joking around.
While some outlets still do good work, unfortunately they are being pushed in the wrong direction.
Usman Butt is a multimedia television researcher, filmmaker and writer based in London who read International Relations and Arabic Language at the University of Westminster and completed a Master of Arts in Palestine Studies at the University of Exeter

Notes from Central Taiwan: Who gets to decide Taiwan’s future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:23 UTC
01:41:23 KST

The tussle between the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and its pro-People’s Republic of China (PRC) allies and fellow travelers, and the pro-Taiwan side in politics is in part a struggle over defining the nation’s agency in international spaces. What kind of agency does Taiwan have?
The United Daily News (UDN) recently reported that former National Security Council secretary-general and longtime KMT stalwart Su Chi (蘇起), popularizer of the fake “1992 consensus,” contended that the US was both unable and unwilling to protect Taiwan. He also asserted that the threat from the PRC was rising and that the future depended on the actions of PRC dictator Xi Jinping (習近平). According to a Taipei Times report, Su said that Taiwan should consider political action to address cross-strait tensions, and not rely solely on outside powers.
Observe how Su positions Taiwan in this series of statements. The country has no say in its own fate, and is the helpless subject of the actions or inactions of others. Taiwan relies “solely” on outside powers, Su claimed, a quaint exaggeration that omits the reality of its military and diplomacy. The political measures Su is apparently referring to, that follow inexorably from those assertions of inagency, are that Taiwan should accommodate itself to PRC interests and acquiesce in its own subjugation, accepting the faux “1992 consensus,” conduct exchanges on PRC terms and “make a deal before it is too late” (read: surrender).” For such individuals, Taiwan is a region of the PRC and should not have any agency of its own.
Photo: Reuters
Thus, an important thrust of the KMT anti-Taiwan propaganda campaign is denigrating Taiwan’s agency. The long history of US venality and unreliability helps give this campaign a veneer of rationality. So does Taiwan’s apparent smallness. What can little Taiwan do?
By contrast, the pro-Taiwan side affirms the country’s independent agency. Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said last week, partly in response to Su Chi, that the US remains committed to defending the First Island Chain. He took particular pains to show how Washington and Taipei are cooperating to “jointly managing risks” posed by Beijing. Taiwan is thus a partner, not a pawn. It follows from that logic that US-Taiwan cooperation, such as the 921 earthquake disaster cooperation that the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) lauded last week, helps affirm Taiwan agency from the American side.
ARMS SALES
Into this tussle fall US arms sales. The PRC demanded earlier this month that the US delay arms sales until after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ summit in China’s Shenzhen and that the US not announce any sales before the meeting between the two nation’s leaders on the 24th of this month. Xi is also expected to visit Florida in December for a G20 Summit, held at a property of US President Donald Trump, of course.
Voters are being treated to another example of the canonical pattern in US-PRC relations in which the US trades something permanent (time, in relation to weapons sales) for something transient (meetings). The correct US position should have been, upon hearing the threat from the PRC, to announce that it was considering giving the weapons to Taipei for free. Instead, PRC “anger” once again determined US policy.
(The New York Times even shamefully quoted a “scholar” at a “Center for Taiwan Studies” at a PRC university saying that “demanding a continued delay in any arms sales may be the most critical issue,” as if such individuals were actual scholars and not state propagandists whose sole purpose is to parasitize the authority and credibility of critical scholarship in the name of PRC expansionism. There is no earthly reason to give PRC “scholars” space in major US papers of record. Just quote Xinhua.)
This swirl of weapons sales news and meetings between various governments will take place as voters consider their choices at the polls in November. Normally I would argue that local elections are not strongly influenced by international events. But in this case the KMT has worked hard, intentionally or not, to create that linkage by degrading domestic governance and focusing the media spotlight on its defense budget machinations for the last year.
POST-SUMMIT SPIN
After the summit this week, both the pro-PRC and pro-Taiwan sides will be attempting to sterilize the results. The pro-PRC side will shake its head and claim that the summit shows Taiwan has no agency of its own, and because of that it should “make a deal” with the PRC. The pro-Taiwan side will contend that nothing has really changed and Washington and Taipei are continuing to cooperate. No doubt underlings in the US government will attempt to walk back what the US president says, that too being a canonical experience of US Taiwan policy. That will help the pro-Taiwan side.
Two conclusions. First, voters will be watching, because the debate in the aftermath of the summit will spill into the lead up to the local elections, and candidates may be asked about it, especially candidates suspected of harboring presidential ambitions. It might be useful to the pro-Taiwan side to ask such candidates whether Taiwan should embrace the “1992 consensus.”
Moreover, this debate over Taiwan’s agency will be sustained throughout the election because the APEC summit is in November. That will help maintain the local-national linkage.
PRC ELECTION INTERFERENCE
Another factor linking the local elections to the national level will be increasing PRC interference in this election. While some PRC disinformation is slick, many of its activities are crude and obvious to voters. Government and private agencies will also be out front, identifying the PRC disinformation. Voters will get constant reminders that this local election is about China too.
Taken together, these issues imply that voter choices may indicate something about where they want Taiwan to go in the future, if one party or the other does surprisingly well. Such signaling may be unclear even where one party shines, since much depends on how local candidates perform.
Second, the US can play a constructive role simply by changing none of its traditional verbiage and by loudly and clearly clarifying that it has not changed anything. The AIT can support Taiwan simply by doing what it does, emphasizing Taiwan-US cooperation and weapons sales. Turning up the volume, though, would help.
Further, much PRC disinformation involves providing false information about the US. This basically hands AIT a license to forcefully denounce such shenanigans, benefiting the pro-Taiwan side.
It’s shaping up to be the most international local election ever. All of us who love Taiwan should not waste this opportunity to pin the negatives on the pro-PRC side.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

North Korean weightlifter sets three world records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:21 UTC
01:41:21 KST

North Korean weightlifter Ri Song-gum yesterday gave her country their first gold of the Asian Games in style, setting three world records in the women’s 49kg class in Nagoya, Japan, and shedding tears of joy. The pocket powerhouse, who stands a mere 140cm tall, joined an elite club of just four weightlifters who have won three Asian Games golds.
The 28-year-old Ri was emotional as her country’s anthem was played at the medal ceremony.
Alongside her was the silver medalist from India, Mirabai Chanu, and bronze medalist from Indonesia, Diana Tri Wijayana. Ri’s exceptional achievement was cheered to the rafters in a lively atmosphere at the Nagoya Trade and Industry Center hall, made all the more raucous by a large number of Japanese-North Korean fans waving flags.
Photo: EPA
The reigning two-time world champion added to her Asian Games golds in Jakarta in 2018 in the 48kg class and Hangzhou, China, in 2023 at 49kg.
Ri hauled 94kg above her head in the opening snatch discipline, 1kg more than the previous world standard of 93kg.
She then smashed the clean and jerk world mark of 115kg twice by hoisting 116kg and then 121kg. Her total of 215kg also obliterated the world mark by 7kg.
“The reason I got this gold is for the feelings of my home country. The people had huge expectations for me,” Ri told reporters. “I wanted to lift my country up on these two small shoulders.”
From Aug. 1, governing body the International Weightlifting Federation introduced new weight classes leading up to the next Olympics and reset all its world records.
If an athlete beats the newly introduced world standard mark, they are deemed to have set a new world record.
Ri has never competed in the Olympics. North Korea were absent from Tokyo in 2021 because of COVID-19, and the country did not qualify in weightlifting for Paris in 2024.
There will be no 49kg class at the next Olympics in Los Angeles, because the competition has been slimmed down to six men’s and six women’s divisions.
However, when Ri was asked if she would consider moving up to 53kg, the lowest women’s category to chase Olympic gold, she replied: “Yes.”
India’s Chanu, the silver medalist at the Tokyo Olympics, finally won an Asian Games medal at the third time of asking.
She had a total of 198kg after a snatch of 87kg, and clean and jerk of 111kg, while Indonesia’s Wijayana took bronze on 191kg, with 88kg and 103kg respectively. A veteran now, the 2017 world champion Chanu is enjoying one of her best years. The 32-year-old in July won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, but said she had fulfilled “a dream” by standing on an Asian Games podium for the first time.
“I feel very good, very happy,” Chanu said. “This is my dream to win an Asian Games medal.
“I had the belief in me that I would be able to win. There were expectations, people who believed in me — my coaches, my support staff and I made sure to win a medal for my country,” she said.
Ri became only the fourth lifter, and first woman, to win three Asian Games weightlifting golds.
She joined Iran’s Mohammad Nassiri (1966-1974), South Korea’s Kim Tae-hyun (1990-1998) and Iran’s Behdad Salimi (2010-2018) who all won three golds. No one has ever won four.

Philippine Senate lowers threshold for VP conviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:21 UTC
01:41:21 KST

The Philippine Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, yesterday lowered the number of votes needed to convict Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte, reducing the threshold prosecutors must clear to secure a guilty verdict.
The court ruled that only senator-judges that are able to participate in the trial should be counted when determining the threshold for conviction. Four of the 24 senator-judges have been unable to participate in the proceedings and cannot vote.
The constitution requires a two-thirds vote to convict an impeached official, so the decision means prosecutors need 14 votes instead of 16 to gain a conviction. The decision could have broader implications if more senator-judges become unable to participate in the proceedings.
Photo: Reuters
Thirteen lawmakers voted in favor of the ruling, while six, most of whom are seen as allies of Duterte, did not participate in the proceedings. One senator voted against lowering the vote threshold.
Four senators have been unable to take part in Duterte’s impeachment trial due to legal actions against some, which include a scandal in a multibillion-dollar public works program and the International Criminal Court’s investigation into a bloody “war on drugs” led by Duterte’s father, former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte.
“The vote may also offer a glimpse of how the final [impeachment] voting could go, although nothing is assured at this time. Senators still have to weigh the evidence, and, admittedly, weigh public opinion,” University of Makati public administration professor Ederson Tapia said. “But if I were Vice President Duterte, I would be concerned.”
The impeachment trial follows a high-profile fallout between Sara Duterte and her former ally and running mate Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr and the outcome could shape the 2028 presidential election, which Sara Duterte intends to contest.
Marcos is limited by the constitution to a single term in office and is expected to back a successor.
Sara Duterte, a frontrunner in early opinion polls, faces a ban from holding political office if convicted by the court and would be out of the presidential running.
She stands accused of misusing public funds, amassing unexplained wealth and threatening the lives of Marcos, the first lady and a former House speaker. Sara Duterte denies wrongdoing.

Committee to decide on wage increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:19 UTC
01:41:19 KST

The Minimum Wage Review Committee is to meet today to decide whether to increase the minimum wage next year, with Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) saying the monthly rate could top NT$30,000 (US$946) and the hourly rate NT$200.
The committee — comprising representatives of labor groups, businesses, the government and academia — is required by the Minimum Wage Act (最低工資法) to meet in the third quarter each year. Changes to the minimum wage that are approved take effect on Jan. 1 the following year unless the Executive Yuan sets a different date.
The minimum wage is NT$29,500 per month and NT$196 per hour. A rise today would mark the 11th consecutive annual hike.
Photo: Screen grab from Pop Radio
Business groups have called for an increase of about 3 percent.
Labor groups are seeking 7.77 percent, calculated by adding the central bank’s forecast of 2.03 percent inflation plus half of its GDP forecast of 11.48 percent.
They say that workers should be protected against rising prices and share in economic growth.
Labor and business groups typically put forward their preferred figures before the annual review, but their proposals should be backed by sound reasoning, Hung said.
“The review is not simply a matter of adding two figures and dividing by two,” he said in a radio interview with host Huang Wei-han (黃暐瀚).
The committee would consider concerns expressed by labor groups that the minimum wage should provide workers with a basic standard of living with dignity, while taking into account the wide differences between industries, he said.
Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics data showed that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.04 percent year-on-year in August, adding to the pressure on low-paid workers, Hung said.
After gathering views from across sectors over the past two months, business groups have also agreed that the minimum wage should be raised, he said.
The economy is forecast to grow 11.05 percent this year, the highest rate in 39 years, adding to expectations of an increase.
However, the committee said that the adjustment should use CPI growth as a baseline while taking industry differences into account.
Manufacturing and other industries benefiting from growth in electronics and information and communications technology products have performed much better than other sectors, it said.
The committee is scheduled to meet at 10am today at the ministry in Taipei.
The Taiwan Confederation of Trade Unions has scheduled a news conference outside the ministry at 9am.
The groups said that it had offered a compromise proposal, but business representatives had failed to reach a consensus, prompting it to keep its demand at a 7.77 percent increase.

Is AI coming for us?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:16 UTC
01:41:16 KST

For years, artificial intelligence researchers have warned of ways the technology could wipe out humanity: AI bots could design an unstoppable disease, unleash a nuclear war, or transform all of Earth into paper clip factories, as one thought experiment goes.
Debates inside the AI industry and beyond over the plausibility of these doomsday scenarios have heated up since several executives endorsed slowing the technology’s development for safety reasons.
Despite warnings of the potential for humans to lose their grip on the technology, some suspect the worst-case scenarios described by the AI companies themselves have more to do with validating the importance of their work than reality.
Photo: AP
“These arguments just don’t really hold water. I think they’re sci-fi and they’re enticing to a certain childish style of thinking and it’s very tempting for the frontier labs because it helps them recruit certain types of folks,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne and a member of OpenAI’s Frontier Risk Council.
Still, more people are beginning to worry about the risks of the technology that has dazzled the world with its astounding capabilities.
Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic researcher who resigned from the company over concerns that it and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development, said on X recently that he needs to “work on” communicating to people more effectively exactly how AI would end humanity. “Unfortunately it is very difficult to convey specific scenarios,” he wrote earlier this month.
Here are some of the more widely discussed doomsday scenarios.
NUCLEAR WINTER
Researchers have long speculated that AI systems could trigger a nuclear war by getting countries to fire warhead-tipped missiles at each other. The nuclear blasts, and ensuing lingering radioactive atmospheric fallout resulting in a “nuclear winter,” could devastate life on Earth.
In a report last year, RAND Corp. researchers concluded that “at present” it wouldn’t be possible for AI to cause the use of nuclear weapons “because of strict safeguards built into the command and control systems.” However, the report said this could change if AI models are integrated into the nuclear weapon “decision chain” or gain unauthorized access to these systems.
For many AI researchers, that’s where the danger lies — not in AI agents suddenly deciding to end humanity, but people, nations or groups using it to wipe out their adversaries.
BIOWEAPONS
One of AI’s greatest promises is that it could help humans develop treatments and cures for diseases.
The flip side of curing diseases is creating or advancing them to harm humanity. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI for a host of malicious activities such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.
In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for assistance from its Claude tool for a research proposal seeking to enhance mutations to make the mosquito-borne chikungunya virus progressively more harmful. While such research could be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
Along the same lines, the RAND report noted recent progress in AI development “has the potential to transform the design of synthetic pathogens.”
Outlining a bioweapon doomsday scenario, the report said novel pathogens could be created in a lab, delivered to target locations, and spread to infect large populations of people in multiple places. But it still envisioned humans — and not autonomous AI — as overseeing and carrying out such an attack.
AI INTERNET TAKEOVER
Given the rate of AI’s development, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned this month that within months a swarm of AI agents could be capable of “taking over” the internet with a botnet (a network of bots linked together with malware), potentially causing billions of dollars in damage. This could mean hacks into electrical grids, water or transportation systems and financial institutions — attacks that might not spell the end of humanity but could cause chaos and lives lost.
Disruptions from software glitches in the past have highlighted the fragility of a digitized world dependent on just a few providers for key computing services, and more powerful AI models have raised concerns about vulnerabilities to cyber attacks. But some experts say the notion of bots overtaking the entire extremely bifurcated internet is far-fetched.
