Taiwan’s sovereign AI paradox: What exactly do we mean by sovereign?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:14 UTC
01:41:14 KST

Taiwan wants AI to know more about Taiwan. On Sept. 15, the Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) invited publishers, writers and electronic-book platforms to contribute to Taiwan’s Sovereign AI Training Corpus. The database now contains about 5,000 datasets and well over a 2.2 billion tokens of text.
Digital Minister Lin Yi-jing (林宜敬) explained that an AI model’s understanding of ideas such as democracy and checks and balances is shaped by its training data.
To let AI better understand Taiwan, he said, Taiwan’s language, culture and values need to become part of what AI learns.
Photo: Reuters
Taiwan is not alone in its move toward “sovereign AI.” Many countries are reconsidering dependence on US and Chinese technology companies. Chinese models can carry political assumptions shaped by the Chinese Communist Party, while American companies control access, prices and development of the most capable frontier systems.
Here, sovereign AI has three dimensions: Knowledge sovereignty means AI understands Taiwan accurately; Data sovereignty means sensitive information remains under local control; and Technological sovereignty means Taiwan is not overly dependent on a foreign model provider. Switzerland’s open Apertus model similarly prioritizes transparency and local control rather than competing with frontier models.
WHEN CHINESE DID NOT MEAN TAIWANESE
Taiwan launched the government-backed Trustworthy AI Dialogue Engine, or TAIDE, in 2023 to better handle Traditional Chinese and Taiwanese knowledge.
The need was clear. At the time, TAIDE project leader Lee Yu-chieh (李育杰) noted that BLOOM, a 2022 multilingual model from the international BigScience project, had trained on 16 percent Simplified Chinese data but only 0.05 percent Traditional Chinese.
Shortly before National Day in 2023, an Academia Sinica Traditional Chinese model based partly on Simplified Chinese datasets also gave incorrect answers about Taiwan’s National Day and president.
With Oct. 10 approaching, the lesson remains relevant.
TAIDE addressed this by adapting existing open-weight models, whose trained parameters can be downloaded and modified. Early versions used Meta’s Llama, while the current Gemma-3-TAIDE-12B is based on Google’s Gemma 3 12B, released in March last year.
Even in 2023, iKala founder Sega Cheng (程世嘉) questioned the economics of building a national foundation model from scratch.
“Anyone with some sense of the costs would not rush headlong into training their own foundation model,” he said. TAIDE’s later development largely followed that logic: Sovereign AI 1.0 meant taking a capable foreign base model and teaching it more about Taiwan.
DOES LOCALIZATION HELP?
Quite a bit, but only up to a point. MODA’s sovereign corpus contains 2.2 billion tokens, the units of text processed by an AI. Google trained Gemma 3 12B on about 12 trillion tokens. The scales are different because the datasets serve different purposes: foundation models need vast, diverse data, while Taiwan’s corpus adds concentrated local knowledge through further training, fine-tuning or retrieval.
Tests show that this localization works. TMMLU+, a Taiwanese benchmark developed by researchers including Cheng, contains more than 20,000 multiple-choice questions across 66 subjects reflecting Taiwanese contexts. The February TAIDE model scored 58 percent overall, compared with 54 percent for the original Gemma model. On Taiwan’s geography, it scored 70 percent versus 61 percent.
That is a clear improvement, but 58 percent still means getting roughly four questions in 10 wrong. Meanwhile, on the current TMMLU+ v1.1 leaderboard, Claude Opus 5 scores 96 percent, Grok 4.3 scores 76 percent and Google’s open-weight Gemma 4 31B scores 70 percent. The benchmark has since been revised, so these scores are not directly comparable, but they still illustrate a wide capability gap.
Taiwan-focused training improves local knowledge but does not erase that gap. If Taiwan closes it by relying on proprietary foreign frontier models, it gains capability at the cost of technological sovereignty.
FROM SOVEREIGN MODEL TO SOVEREIGN SYSTEM
That compromise helps explain why Taiwan’s strategy has expanded beyond TAIDE. MODA’s corpus can also support retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of trying to put every fact inside a model during training, RAG searches a trusted database and passes relevant documents to the AI before it answers.
Still, while RAG can improve accuracy, it can’t guarantee it. An April benchmark study found that while standard RAG provided increasing gains on complex queries, combining retrieval with dedicated large reasoning models improved accuracy by an additional 10 percent in that benchmark.
“A stronger reasoning model grounded in the same trusted Taiwanese data,” says Yung-Chun (Peter) Chang (張詠淳), Deputy Director of Taipei Medical University’s Research Center for AI in Medicine, “could outperform a weaker locally adapted model,” especially for tasks requiring “complex interpretation or synthesis across documents.”

Taiwan would apply its expertise in AI, virtual simulations and information technology to bolster its capabilities in train design, electromechanics, system integration and safety verification, improving its capability to facilitate the growth of the rail industry in Taiwan, Chen said.

Alliance calls for better NCD patient care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:10 UTC
01:41:10 KST

About one in six people receiving care for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) experience preventable harm, the Taiwan Alliance of Patients’ Organizations said yesterday, calling for better patient safety governance through enhanced patient engagement.
As part of World Patient Safety Day, observed annually on Sept. 17, the alliance invited the Joint Commission of Taiwan, Taiwan Healthcare Reform Foundation and the Formosa Cancer Foundation to raise public awareness on safe care for people with NCDs.
NCDs are chronic conditions, such as cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes and chronic respiratory diseases, that affect people of all ages and mostly require continued care throughout life.
Photo: CNA
Alliance chairman Wu Hung-lai (吳鴻來) said a new WHO-commissioned analysis found that about one in six people living with NCDs experience preventable harm during their medical care.
The rate of preventable harm is about three times higher than that of the general population, and medication-related problems are the most common source of harm, he said.
The WHO proposed ways to improve care for people with NCDs, including partnering with people with lived experience of such diseases; improving prevention and risk assessment; and providing early detection, accurate diagnosis and integrated management, Wu said.
They also include securing access, and safe use of medicines and medical devices; and strengthening care coordination, continuity and transitions of care, he said.
“Patient participation is key to improving medical quality and patient safety, and that it should not only be limited to ‘encouraging patients to speak up,’ but also ‘engaging patients in patient safety governance,’” he added.
NCDs often require long-term, interdisciplinary and cross-setting care, he said, adding that people with NCDs are crucial partners who can identify risks throughout the care journey.
Institutionalized mechanisms should also be established to involve patients and advocacy groups in patient safety event reporting and improvement, and overall patient safety governance, he added.
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said people with NCDs often require long-term medication, and comorbidities might also increase medication use, making them at high risk for safety events.
The commission has since 2003 made “medication adverse event control” an annual goal, he said.
That is still an important goal this year, but the focus has shifted from “avoiding giving the wrong medication” to “proper medication use,” he added.
The Healthy Taiwan Deep Cultivation Program launched last year also subsidized hospitals that introduced smart medical equipment, such as automated “three checks and five rights” to prevent medication errors, he said.
Patient safety requires patient participation, as relying only on the efforts of the government and healthcare providers yield very limited results, Shih said.
When establishing annual patient safety goals, the ministry invites patient advocacy groups to to help improve clinical environments and patient safety, he added.

Taiwan no longer just a US-China problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

Beijing has for decades insisted that Taiwan is a matter to be settled between China and the US — or, preferably, by China alone. The strategic environment around Taiwan is making that increasingly difficult.
The clearest evidence this week came not from Washington or Beijing, but from Tokyo.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday met with US President Donald Trump before his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Taiwan is expected to feature prominently in US-China talks, particularly as Beijing presses Washington over arms sales to Taipei. However, focusing only on what Trump might or might not concede misses the larger structural change: Taiwan is increasingly becoming part of Japan’s security geography, and therefore part of the wider architecture of US alliances in Asia.
A Taiwan Strait contingency would affect Japan’s southwestern islands, US forces based in Japan, major sea lanes and the First Island Chain. Pressure against Taiwan also increasingly resembles the “gray zone” pressure Japan has experienced around the Diaoyutais (釣魚台), which it calls the Senkaku Islands, so Tokyo has a direct interest in how Taiwan is handled.
Tokyo cannot dictate the US’ Taiwan policy, nor does it oppose US-China dialogue. Communication between the two is necessary for regional stability, but Japan has reason to resist a framework in which Taiwan becomes simply one item in a bilateral bargain.
Dialogue should not come at the expense of deterrence.
Takaichi’s Cabinet reshuffle last week adds another dimension. She replaced more than half of her ministers. In a system characterized by consensus-building and nemawashi — informal coordination before formal decisions — her choices suggest an emphasis on faster implementation and clearer political control.
She changed much of the political machinery while preserving that of external strategy. This was not a strategic reset, it was closer to strategic acceleration.
Tokyo’s approach to Washington is changing as well. Japan has traditionally sought reassurance from the US regarding the Diaoyutais, extended deterrence and its commitment to the alliance. However, Japan increasingly wants consultation before major US decisions on China.
Taiwan sits near the center of that transition. The formula that “peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait are important” tells only part of the story. Taiwan is increasingly discussed alongside the East China Sea, Japan’s southwestern islands, semiconductors, critical minerals and economic coercion.
Takaichi’s emphasis on artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical minerals in her meeting with Trump is significant. Military deterrence and economic security are becoming increasingly difficult to separate.
The world cannot completely decouple from China to avoid its economic coercion, so the US, Japan and their partners need to move from economic resilience to economic deterrence — building an economy that Beijing cannot easily coerce.
Taiwan should view this shift with reassurance and caution. Its security is becoming harder to isolate from the interests of Japan and other US allies. However, that does not guarantee particular US decisions, especially under a transactional president.
Taiwan’s stronger protection lies in embedding itself in the regional architecture, so that changing the “status quo” would impose costs well beyond Taipei and Washington.
Taiwan is moving from diplomatic concern to the structure of allied security. Beijing might continue to call Taiwan a bilateral red line, but geography is making it a multilateral reality.
Bonnie Yushih Liao is Tamkang University Department of Diplomacy and International Relations associate professor.

It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Managing Taiwan’s extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:03 UTC
01:41:03 KST

Taiwan’s approach to managing extreme heat is evolving. On Sept. 3, the Ministry of Environment held its first extreme heat response drill, running a scenario where temperatures reached 40°C or higher and bringing together dozens of central and local government agencies to test their responses.
Extreme heat is shifting from a weather phenomenon to an immediate public safety issue. If typhoons, torrential rain and earthquakes each have their own disaster-response systems, Taiwan should seriously consider similar measures for extreme heat. What is needed is a clear, tiered response system that the public can understand and that government agencies know how to implement.
Most people’s understanding of heat warning is still based on the yellow, orange and red alerts issued by the Central Weather Administration. There is less certainty when it comes to what actually happens when a certain level of risk is reached. Should local governments move to open more public spaces as cooling centers? Should there be welfare checks for older people living alone? Should outdoor activities be adjusted in schools? Should large-scale events provide more drinking water, shade or medical support? Should hospital emergency departments and fire and ambulance services raise their heat-injury response levels? If each agency is left to make these decisions on an ad hoc basis, all the public receives is an alert on their phone, without any knowledge of the protective measures the government has implemented.
Taiwan should establish responses based on factors such as temperature, humidity, duration, overnight temperature lows and population vulnerability in different areas.
Under ordinary high-temperature conditions, the focus could be on information alerts and self-protective measures.
At higher risk levels, local governments could open dedicated cooling spots, extend outreach to homeless people and elderly people living alone, and adjust outdoor public activities.
At extreme levels, the central emergency response system could take over with coordination between agencies.
This way, heat alerts would become more than just a color: They would represent the actions the government and the public must take. Ensuring that everyone knows their role and responsibilities before danger strikes is the most important part of disaster governance.
The risks posed by extreme heat do not manifest as obviously as typhoons. Trees do not fall, roads do not flood and buildings do not collapse, yet harm still accumulates.
An elderly person living in a rooftop addition without air-conditioning and an office worker sitting in an air-conditioned workplace might live in the same city, but they face vastly different levels of heat risk.
Heat response efforts cannot be limited to a flat warning for an entire administrative district. Taiwan should gradually develop a map of population vulnerability: areas with high concentrations of elderly people living alone, communities with aging housing and places lacking sufficient green space or shade could all become factors in how local governments allocate resources.
Mature heat governance is not about asking everyone to fight 40°C or hotter temperatures in the same way; it is about first identifying those who are least able to withstand it.
Taiwan’s decision to conduct its first full-scale extreme heat drill is a good first step, but the question is whether it can lead to lasting institutional changes. As climate change renders temperatures once considered unusual increasingly common, the government must shift how it thinks about natural disasters.
A disaster might not come with fierce winds and torrential rain, but arrive on a clear day. A city might appear to be functioning normally, but the number of hospital patients with heat-related illnesses would continue to rise.
As Taiwan conducts exercises for 40°C or hotter temperatures, we can no longer treat extreme heat as a blip in the weather forecast. The next step is ensuring that every heat warning is backed by concrete actions. Disaster preparedness under climate change is not just about forecasting how hot it is going to get; it is about understanding in advance who needs protecting and how to do so.
Chen Jie-an is a legal specialist for a technology corporation.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

Taiwanese artist receives Primetime Emmy for animation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

Artist Howard Chen (陳人豪), who earlier this month won a Primetime Emmy Award, said the cartoons he grew up with in Taiwan planted the seeds for his career in the US.
Chen won for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Animation for his background design on the first episode of The Mighty Nein on Prime Video, titled “Mote of Possibility.”
Chen is one of few artists born and raised in Taiwan to win an Emmy. He moved to the US at the age of 13 with his mother and later studied at the ArtCenter College of Design in Los Angeles.
Photo: CNA
He struggled when he first arrived in the US, as he did not speak any English, Chen told the Central News Agency yesterday in an interview at his alma mater.
After graduating in 2011, he worked with the production company Motion Theory before beginning his career in animation with Titmouse animation studio.
He has worked in character and background design over the past 15 years, participating in different styles of animated productions.
Chen said his passion for animation began when he was a child watching cartoons on TV in Kaohsiung.
He said he would check the newspaper every day to see what cartoons were playing on the three TV stations he could watch.
“Back then, I just thought cartoons were interesting. I never thought I would work in animation,” Chen said.
He was a fan of Japanese manga and anime when he was young, including Doraemon, Dragonball and Yu Yu Hakusho, as he admired how manga told stories through drawings, without relying heavily on text and dialogue.
Animation is appealing, as “a team works together to create an imagined world,” Chen said.
Chen created the setting in which The Mighty Nein’s main characters appear.
Since background design is like world-building, Chen said he studies the script and where the characters appear, while also considering the world’s history, culture, geography and building materials.
He also considers how the characters move through the space and how each scene would be framed.
Backgrounds should enhance storytelling without grabbing attention, Chen said, adding that they should blend seamlessly into the story, and be culturally and historically accurate to the setting.
After years of working behind the scenes creating backgrounds for animated stories, Chen stepped into the spotlight to accept the Emmy, saying he felt surprised and grateful for the recognition.

Solar energy producers targeting open US market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

Solar cell and module supplier United Renewable Energy Co (URE, 聯合再生) yesterday said its US revenue would double next year, mainly benefiting from a market realignment fueled by US solar reshoring policies and crackdowns on Chinese green energy companies.
To capitalize on the new market opportunities, URE is racing to launch a new solar module line through a new joint venture with Sino-American Silicon Products Inc (SAS, 中美晶) in the third quarter of next year, URE said. The new production line is designed with an annual production capacity of 1 gigawatt (GW), it said.
“We have no choice but to expand into the US market — it is the only arena where we hold a competitive edge. Otherwise, we are left to contend with the challenges posed by China,” URE chairman Sam Hung (洪傳獻) said at a news conference yesterday.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
Hung’s remarks came as the US administration is tightening restrictions on Chinese clean energy technology by adding minimum import prices from Dec. 4 this year after imposing a 15 percent import tariff and restricting Chinese ownership in subsidized US plants to 25 percent.
In the EU and Japan, URE faces stiff competition from Chinese rivals exporting heavily subsidized solar products, Hung said.
Additionally, the US remains one of the world’s largest solar markets, boasting annual demand of 40GW to 50GW of solar power generation, Hung said.
URE is targeting the non-China market segment, which is estimated to have 30GW to 35GW of demand per year, he said.
“We anticipate the US market to contribute a large portion of the company’s revenue in the future,” Hung said. “The company’s operation is on track.”
This year, the US is expected to account for less than 20 percent of URE’s revenue, URE chief executive officer Richard Chang (張為策) said.
Chang expected revenue from the region to double next year, driven by rapidly-growing demand from the decoupling supply chain and ballooning electricity demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
To feed the insatiable power hunger of AI data centers, operators are aggressively blending solar energy with other alternative power sources to prevent grid overloads, Chang said.
“Overall, we believe next year will be a much better year for URE in terms of business, supported by strong solar energy demand overseas and at home,” Chang said.
URE is accelerating efforts to expand its product portfolio to include solar modules for low Earth orbit satellites. The company’s satellite solar products are in the research-and-development pipeline, it said.
The space-based solar market is a smaller market with annual demand of less than 10MW a year in the US, URE estimated.
URE swung back to a net profit of NT$1.52 billion (US$47.9 million) in the first half, from a loss of NT$599 million in the same period last year, company data showed. The company attributed the improvement partly to a disposal gain of NT$2.1 billion from selling a solar plant in January.

Military shows off Cheetah tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:00 UTC
01:41:00 KST

The Armaments Bureau yesterday showcased the Cheetah (獵豹), a 105mm wheeled armored fighting vehicle, which is to enter mass production next year.
The vehicle, jointly developed by the Armaments Bureau and the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology, first passed army tests in 2023. The military has ordered 178 of the vehicles, with production to run from next year through 2033 under a budget of NT$57.07 billion (US$1.8 billion) budget.
The first eight vehicles are expected to be delivered next year, 202nd Arsenal Director Major General Chen Chien-chung (陳健中) said.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
At the Army Southern Area Joint Training and Evaluation Center in Tainan, the vehicle demonstrated “rapid synchronized firing upon target acquisition” from a stationary vehicle at a moving target, “hunter-killer mode firing” while moving against a stationary target, “main-gun firing on a slope” from a stationary position against a stationary target, and “multiple-weapons firing” while moving against moving targets, Chen said.
A total of six high-explosive anti-tank tracer rounds were fired, he said.
Compared with the D2 prototype of the Clouded Leopard (雲豹) family of vehicles, the Cheetah’s profile is more than 30cm lower and is about 2.95m tall, Chen said.
While its exact height would depend on tire pressure, it would remain below 3m, he said.
The Cheetah meets the army’s requirements for operation across all types of terrain, including underpasses and rough roads, and would provide greater convenience and maneuverability in urban combat operations, he said.
Lin Yu-min (林育民), head of the artillery development division at the 202nd Arsenal, said the 105mm gun was developed in-house, with all components, from the barrel to the recoil mechanism, manufactured domestically.
The gun generates 20 tonnes of recoil force when fired, compared with the M60A3’s 70 tonnes, while at a range of 1.2km it can hit a target within a circle 90cm in diameter, he said.
Its armor-piercing capability allows it to penetrate 500mm of homogeneous steel armor at 2km, Lin said.
The turret, developed by the institute, uses a dual-axis stabilization system and has a “hunter-killer mode” similar to that of the M1A2T, he said.
While the gunner aims at a first target, the commander can search for a second and, when appropriate, activate “hunter-killer mode” to take control of the main gun and engage it, Lin said.
The Armaments Bureau showed video of the vehicle’s remote-controlled weapon station destroying a drone.
The station has automatic ballistic tracking and has undergone hard-kill drone interception tests, Chen said.
The vehicle is to be equipped with a quick-release modular anti-drone net that can be moved aside when firing, although its material has not been determined, he said.
Wang Chien-ching (王劍青), a translator with the army’s Training Command, said the net would be given top priority during the first phase of mass production next year.
The mount on the remote weapon station would also be modified to accommodate chain guns or automatic cannons of 25mm caliber or larger, enabling it to carry the M230LF chain gun used on Apache attack helicopters.
The bureau also displayed ammunition for the Cheetah, including the TC113 105mm fin-stabilized discarding-sabot armor-piercing tracer round and TC113 105mm anti-personnel round.
The military also displayed, but did not fire, some of its US-made weapons, such as a Lockheed Martin-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket System.
Additional reporting by Reuters

Xi likely to press for US Asia withdrawal: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:41:00 UTC
01:41:00 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) will try to pressure US President Donald Trump to postpone arms sales to Taiwan and roll back deployments of US forces in the Indo-Pacific region, a senior Taiwanese official said yesterday.
Xi was expected to arrive in the US after press time last night and meet with Trump in Washington during his three-day visit, then possibly again on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China on Nov. 18 or 19.
Xi’s highest priority is to slow Trump’s approval of arms packages to Taiwan at the meetings, a national security official with knowledge of the matter said on condition of anonymity.
Photo: Reuters
Xi is sure to demand that the US postpone Taiwan-bound arms sales until the APEC summit in November, when he would again press Trump to delay authorizing the weapon packages until Christmas, the official said.
Belated delivery of US weapon systems would disrupt Taiwan’s force-building efforts, which would boost the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s ability to threaten the First Island Chain, they said.
That would facilitate China’s aims to push the US out of the First Island Chain and force unilateral changes to the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait, the official said.
Part of China’s strategy involves promoting the narrative that US military presence in the region is to blame for heightened tensions and that Washington can make peace by withdrawing, they said.
Should the US lower its presence in the Indo-Pacific region, it would create a strategic vacuum beneficial to China’s ambitions, they said.
Beijing is likely to exploit the distraction caused by the US-Iran conflict, the Russia-Ukraine war and US midterm elections by using a combination of coercion and incentives on the Trump administration, they said.
China, Russia, Iran and North Korea have formed an authoritarian regime bloc that Beijing could coordinate to raise regional tensions and dump exports to exert pressure on the US, the official said.
Beijing’s strategy is to dangle empty promises of buying US soybeans, offering cheap supplies of liquefied natural gas, easing tensions in the Middle East, and halting support to Iran and Russia, they said.
In exchange, Xi would ask Trump to reduce US forces and security guarantees along the First Island Chain, remove restrictions on exports of technology to China, resume use of Chinese supply chains and ease international trade blocks on China, they said.
A US-based think tank on Sept. 10 published a document recommending that Washington declare a policy of non-interference regarding a potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan, recall US military advisers from the nation and relocate US forces to the Second Island Chain, the official said.
Da Wei (達巍), director of the Beijing-based Center for International Security and Strategy, in an essay in Foreign Affairs on Sept. 7 called for the US and China to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability,” the official said.
There is a Beijing-directed campaign designed to make a strategic retreat from Asia palatable in mainstream political circles in the US, they said.
However, Xi’s chances of realizing the goals are not high, owing to the strategic value of the First Island Chain to the US and Washington’s vocal objections to China’s trade dumping, they said.
US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent earlier this month spoke against the economic effects of overproduction by Chinese manufacturing at the G20 summit, the official said.
Similarly, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a joint statement with the foreign ministers of Japan and South Korea underscored the importance of maintaining peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and cooperation in supply chains, as well as countering economic coercion, they said.
Those signal that Washington is aware of Beijing’s strategy and considers its interests incompatible with China’s, the official said.

As Taiex hits new high, Taiwan stock market ranks global No. 4 in market cap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:55 UTC
01:40:55 KST

With the Taiex, the Taiwan Stock Exchange’s benchmark index, repeatedly hitting a fresh high, the local bourse ranked as the fourth-largest stock market in terms of market value in the world as of Wednesday afternoon, according to the up-to-the-minute data released by MarketCapWatch.
On Wednesday, the Taiex rose 357.12 points, or 0.75 percent, at a new high of 48,157.29, pushing up the market capitalization of the local main board to about US$5.3 trillion, MarketCapWatch’s data showed.
As of 5 p.m. Wednesday, Taiwan replaced India, whose market value stood at US$4.94 trillion, to become the fourth-largest stock market in the world, according to MarketCapWatch’s statistics.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan has benefited from a global boom in artificial intelligence development, with the Taiex soaring 19,193.69 points, or 66.27 percent so far this year after a surge of 5,928.50 points for 275.73 percent in 2025.
According to MarketCapWatch, Taiwan lagged behind only the United States (US$82.7 trillion in market cap), China (US$21.22 trillion) and Japan (US$8.59 trillion).
The United Kingdom took the sixth spot with US$4.86 trillion in market cap, ahead of South Korea (US$4.5 trillion), Canada (US$4.45 trillion), France (US$3.08 trillion) and Germany (US$3 trillion), according to MarketCapWatch.
MarketCapWatch is a platform for tracking real-time data on global capital markets, covering listed companies across different countries, regions, and industries, and primarily ranking them globally and regionally based on market capitalization.
The website provides data on stock price, market capitalization, revenue, net profit, earnings per share, and historical market capitalization changes.
The platform also compiles total market capitalization rankings for various countries and major stock markets, allowing users to observe the size of global capital markets and changes in corporate market capitalization.

====================================================================================================

Book review: A furious exercise in score-settling by Princess Diana’s brother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:50 UTC
01:40:50 KST

Charles Spencer’s Swan Song, a memoir of his relationship with his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is a fascinating document that tells us a little about Diana and a great deal about Charles Spencer — perhaps more than we needed to know. If that sounds snarky, after 400 pages of score settling, chest thumping, wild indiscretion and some truly touching passages about his late sister, the reader is left with a head-spinning story of the world that created Diana and a certain sourness at the manner in which it is told.
Let’s start with the headlines in last week’s Daily Mail, the newspaper to whom Spencer sold serialization of a book that includes a line describing tabloid journalists as “those who inhabit the murky swamps of malevolence, and who need to suck their victims dry of their souls.”
Perhaps he meant a different set of hacks. Anyway the top line in the Mail was that, shortly after Diana’s death, King Charles insulted her in a phone call to Spencer: “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’”
Your take on this quote will likely dictate how you receive the book, and here’s mine: I’m willing to believe the king behaved badly, but “hissed” is a red flag, one of those embellishments, like “snarled” or “flounced,” that writers tend to use to make those they’re writing about appear worse. Spencer, always the injured party, has so many axes grinding away in this book that at times it’s impossible to hear what he’s saying.
Before we get to that, the question on everyone’s lips is: why write this book now? Spencer maintains it’s because, as the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death drew near, he kept being asked to contribute to other people’s projects. Rather than allow the narrative to be guided by “some TV producer” from a network “I will never watch” he promptly got on with his own. Likely that’s not the sole reason; elsewhere in the book he writes about how, back in the day, his father was always at risk of running out of cash to run Althorp, the family’s Northamptonshire estate, and one wonders if the present earl is having similar difficulties.
Never mind. For fans of petty grievances, among whom I count myself, the book is an absolute corker of resentment, and in Spencer we have a hero who, decades after the fact, is still harping on about a great many things involving a large cast of characters who he has absolutely not forgiven for any of it. While telling the story of his and Diana’s relationship, there are drive-bys on Peter Carter-Ruck, Princess Michael of Kent, Princess Margaret, his three ex-wives, whom he describes in an amazing parenthetical take down as “all double divorcees,” and members of a police protection squad who, in 1986, let sniffer dogs jump all over his furniture.
If too many words are spent on, for example, the perfidiousness of Martin Bashir, I could read an entire book on the subject of Spencer’s horror at what his stepmother, Raine, did to the interiors at Althorp, including installing “exceptionally ugly double glazing,” “shiny velveteen” upholstery and “unsightly wall-to-wall carpeting.” (This is before we get to the scene in which Raine, standing at the top of the staircase in search of breakfast, bellows to staff below, “where’s my fucking egg?”)
Interspersed with these delights is a portrait of Diana that is affectionate, sad and lovely in places. Spencer suffers the pain of the less famous sibling who doesn’t want to give up his own version of their childhood and there’s a stiffness to some passages as Spencer insists it was all less unhappy than the record implies. His portrait of their mother, Frances, feels like a useful corrective to a figure who has been publicly maligned, and who comes across in the book as the parent most responsible for Diana’s gifts: spirited, mildly eccentric, a more interesting character than the plodding males in the Spencer line. (Charles, winningly, allows that this is the case, pointing out that the men in his family have always been outclassed by the women.)
And of course there is the devastating account of the coldness and aggression of the then Prince of Wales. Spencer tells us that Charles’s poor behavior towards his sister began from the very start of their courtship, during which he commented on her weight, ignored her at parties and told her he didn’t love her, to the extent that, Spencer writes, Diana tried to get out of the engagement. Their father told her it was too late. This all chimes with other accounts of the doomed marriage, albeit in gorier detail, and explains the fury of Spencer’s finest hour, the speech he gave at Diana’s funeral in which he lambasted not only the press but the royals, reclaiming the young princes William and Harry for their mother’s “blood family.”
At his best, in these passages, Spencer acts as a proxy for the rest of us by registering the absolute lunacy of those days after Diana’s death — by which I mean not the public outpouring, but the behavior of the royal family, who remained deaf to the nation’s needs until they were forced to change course.
“What was Prince Charles actually doing there?” writes Spencer, incredulously, in relation to his former brother-in-law’s prominent role at the funeral, pointing out to some comic effect that no one wants their “ex” at their funeral? Diana’s former husband was there because the young princes were there, walking for two miles behind their mother’s coffin while mourners wailed and shouted out at them, an outcome Spencer had vigorously argued against. Now, he writes flatly, “It all seemed mad to me — the more so as I began to appreciate the extent of the ordeal we had embarked on.”
To be honest, at times in this book, they all seem quite mad.
“That’s it ... it’s curtains ... Duch is dead,” Spencer reports his sister Jane as saying to him on the phone when news of Diana’s death was confirmed.
Before the funeral, per Spencer’s account, Prince Charles wanted to walk behind the coffin in the middle, center stage, until brought up short by his father, Prince Philip, who said words to the effect of don’t be so bloody silly, and put Charles Spencer in the center, with the boys either side and Diana’s ex-husband and ex-father in law on the outside. There was a split second, writes Spencer, when it seemed as if the pall-bearers might buckle under the weight of Diana’s reinforced, lead-lined coffin. All of this is fascinating and Spencer tells it well.
Still, the book suffers from problems of self pity and self regard (I won’t get into the passages about Spencer’s ADHD or the weasily justifications he gives for telling Diana, in her hour of need, that she couldn’t move into a property on the Althorp estate; the main house has 90 rooms). Every few chapters we return to the unfolding play-by-play of how he wrote his speech — the decision he made to substitute the word “power” for the word “strength”; how his oratory gathered, his greatness formed, and look, it was a fantastic speech, but at some point in the book you start to think, alright Alexander Hamilton, give it a rest. Before the funeral, Spencer visits Diana lying in her casket and reads out his speech to her, sensing that his dead sister is “applauding my words, with soft insistence.” Even here, Spencer manages to take center stage.
After the book’s litany of bitter grievances I came away wondering whether Spencer has been in the ear of his nephew Prince Harry these last few years. Mostly, however, I felt sadness for the insurmountable difficulties his sister faced marrying into that family. The king is peevish all the way through and Spencer is peevish right back at him. You come away feeling the pair thoroughly deserved each other. And in the middle Diana, 30 years dead, frozen in time and — as she ever was — at the mercy of other people’s interpretations.

El Nino heat could add 451,000 deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:48 UTC
01:40:48 KST

This year’s powerful El Nino and the record global heat it is driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, a research report released yesterday said.
The grim warning by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab said that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be attributed to El Nino, compared with heat deaths expected in a typical year.
The heaviest toll is expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, partly due to climate change and the fallout of the war in Iran, the group said.
Photo: Bloomberg
Michael Greenstone, a cofounder of the group and the study’s coauthor, said the heat danger would likely persist beyond February — even though El Nino is expected to end by then.
The fallout of the weather phenomenon could be felt well into next summer, he added.
The research shows that heat is most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor, he said.
“If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous,” he said.
Wealthier places generally have greater access to air-conditioning, reliable water supplies and functioning health systems, he added.
The study combined seasonal temperature forecasts with localized estimates of how high temperatures affect mortality across more than 24,000 regions worldwide.
Researchers estimated the additional heat-related deaths by comparing deaths expected under El Nino-driven high temperatures with deaths expected if temperatures remained similar to what they have been in the last three decades. The projected fatalities are for the entire El Nino period, from June 2026 until the end of February 2027.
The study also warns that developing countries would bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.
The researchers behind the report found that the Sahel region in Africa — countries along the semiarid southern fringe of the Sahara Desert — is expected to be the hardest-hit, with about 66,800 additional deaths caused by El Nino-driven heat.
Other major hot spots include South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America, the report said.
The researchers projected about 19,400 additional heat-related deaths across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, as well as 19,300 in Indonesia, 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil.
With such staggering numbers, there are recommended measures that governments can take, the report said.
They include heat-warning systems, cooling centers, hydration stations, protections for outdoor workers, expanded hospital capacity and targeted outreach to elderly people and other vulnerable groups.
The authors also call for what they describe as anticipatory financing, so governments can move resources before dangerous heat peaks.
Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report’s projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.
While it is one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans and raising needed funds remains a challenge, he said.
“The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths,” Tiwari added.

Taiwan needs medical resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:47 UTC
01:40:47 KST

When discussing Taiwan’s resilience in an increasingly uncertain security environment, policymakers often focus on missiles, energy security, food reserves and semiconductor supply chains. Far less attention is paid to a simpler, but equally important question: Can Taiwan keep hospitals functioning and treat people if supply chains are disrupted?
This question deserves greater attention, because a blockade or prolonged period of “gray zone” pressure would affect far more than trade and transportation. The objective would not simply be to interrupt commercial activity, but to transform economic disruption into social fatigue and political pressure. A society might possess advanced technology, strong military capabilities and substantial economic resources, but still become vulnerable if citizens lose confidence in essential services.
Medical resilience should therefore be viewed not merely as a healthcare issue, but a pillar of civilian resilience.
Disruptions to medical supply chains could affect far more than hospitals. Shortages of essential medicines, dialysis supplies, blood products, antibiotics or temperature-sensitive therapies would affect many Taiwanese. What begins as a logistics challenge could evolve into declining public confidence and growing concern about whether normal life can continue.
A blockade does not necessarily succeed because it defeats a military force. It succeeds when sustained disruption weakens society’s willingness and ability to endure. If people are unable to obtain necessary treatment and healthcare providers face mounting operational challenges, the impact could extend well beyond the healthcare sector. Medical continuity should therefore be considered an important component of national resilience and deterrence by denial: the capacity to deny coercion its intended political effect.
Taiwan has already recognized some of these risks. Recent government initiatives have emphasized essential medicine security, stronger monitoring mechanisms and efforts to expand domestic manufacturing capacity. These are important steps, but preparedness discussions continue to revolve around a familiar question: How many days can Taiwan survive?
While stockpiles are necessary, survival is not the same as resilience.
A reserve can buy time, but it cannot automatically identify shortages across institutions, redistribute supplies, qualify alternative suppliers, restore supply chains nor ensure that products with limited shelf lives or specialized storage requirements remain available.
Resilience depends on whether a system can adapt and recover once disruption begins. The more relevant questions are whether authorities know where critical inventories are located, and whether hospitals can coordinate scarce resources, and regulators and private sector partners could transition rapidly from normal operations to crisis management. Clear authority and allocation protocols would also be essential when normal market mechanisms no longer meet urgent clinical needs. Resilience must therefore be measured not only by what Taiwan can store, but also by how effectively it can adapt, replenish and recover.
This challenge is particularly important for medical products. Many medicines have limited shelf lives, specialized storage requirements or complex global supply networks. Some depend on unique ingredients, devices or manufacturing facilities that cannot be replaced quickly. Attempting to stockpile everything would be costly and inefficient. Resilience requires a more targeted strategy.
Taiwan should focus on three priorities:
First, it should establish greater visibility across national inventories of essential medicines and medical supplies. Policymakers need accurate information about where critical products are, how quickly stocks are being consumed and how they can be allocated during emergencies. Hospitals and other healthcare institutions should also have clear procedures for reporting shortages and requesting assistance.
Second, Taiwan should continue diversifying suppliers and developing distributed reserves for selected essential medicines and healthcare products. Reducing dependence on any single source or storage location would help mitigate supply disruptions and avoid creating new points of failure.
Third, Taiwan should establish prearranged cooperation mechanisms with trusted partners. Medical resilience is ultimately a question of access and storage. Unlike larger continental states, Taiwan cannot assume that domestic reserves alone would sustain a prolonged disruption of maritime and air transportation. Working in advance with like-minded partners on emergency logistics, procurement arrangements, regulatory flexibility and supply-sharing would bolster preparedness before a crisis occurs. Such arrangements should be tested during peacetime rather than improvised under pressure.
Ultimately, the argument for medical resilience is strategic rather than medical. A coercive campaign succeeds when disruption turns into exhaustion and exhaustion becomes political pressure. Medical resilience helps ensure that disruptions do not produce that outcome.
Taiwan’s security cannot be measured solely by its military capabilities or the strength of its technology sector. It also depends on whether society can continue functioning under sustained pressure. In today’s security environment, resilience is about more than missiles and microchips. It is also about ensuring that hospitals remain operational, people continue receiving care and essential medical supplies remain available when normal supply chains come under strain.
Hanson Wu is a Taiwan-based healthcare policy professional with experience in pharmaceutical policy, health security and public affairs. He is a graduate researcher for healthcare policy at National Taiwan University.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from

Disapproval of legislature high: survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:47 UTC
01:40:47 KST

Strong public dissatisfaction with the opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan is a stinging rebuke of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), the Taiwan Inspiration Association told a news conference in Taipei yesterday, citing the results of a poll.
The survey of Taiwanese aged 20 or older from Sept. 10 to Tuesday last week showed that 63.4 percent of respondents disapproved of the legislature, while 34.8 percent approved of the institution.
Asked to rate the legislature’s performance, 5.9 percent of respondents said they strongly approved of it, 28.9 percent said they somewhat approved, while 29.4 percent said they somewhat disapproved, 34 percent strongly disapproved and 1.8 percent had no opinion.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
The survey showed that 41.9 percent of those who disapproved of the legislative branch were dissatisfied with partisanship obstructing the government’s business and 40.5 percent were dissatisfied that parties put themselves above national interests.
Also among those who disapproved of the legislature, 36.1 percent said the budget review process had been slow and inefficient, 25.3 percent said legislators did not solve problems affecting the livelihood of ordinary Taiwanese and 22.5 percent said important laws were not passed.
The public overwhelmingly supported the Cabinet’s plan to increase the share of military spending to 3 percent of GDP, with 68 percent backing the proposal, the Taiwan Inspiration Association said, adding that 39.4 percent highly supported the measure and 29.4 percent somewhat supported it.
It said that 30.4 percent disapproved of boosting defense spending — with 17.4 somewhat disapproving, 13 percent strongly disapproving and 0.8 percent having no opinion.
In a breakdown by political affiliation, 94 percent of Democratic Progressive Party supporters, 58 percent of independents, 48 percent of KMT supporters and 39 percent of TPP supporters approved of raising the defense budget, the association said.
It said that 57.7 percent opposed the KMT-backed slashing of the Presidential Office’s discretionary spending, while 40.7 percent supported the move. Among those who opposed the move, 26.3 percent strongly disapproved and 31.4 percent somewhat disapproved.
The survey showed that 79.8 percent supported a planned NT$10,000 cash handout as part of next year’s annual budget, with 34.1 strongly approving of the measure and 45.7 percent somewhat approving of it, while 19.9 percent disapproved of the handout — comprising 14 percent who somewhat disapproved and 5.9 percent who strongly disapproved.
More than 75 percent of respondents in each political party affiliation group agreed with the proposed payouts, making it the most widely supported proposed policy measure in the survey.
The poll, which was conducted by InvosData, garnered 1,200 valid samples and had a 95 percent confidence level with a 2.83 percentage point margin of error.

Trump to ask XI to free US scientist, his wife says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

The wife of a US expert on North Korean nuclear tests who has been imprisoned in China since late 2024 on Tuesday said the White House had assured her that US President Donald Trump would ask Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) to free her husband when the pair meet this week.
Rong Yufang (榮玉芳) said she feared that Beijing planned to try her Chinese-born husband, Chen Youlin (陳有林), on fabricated espionage charges even though his US-funded research was openly published, used publicly available data and was done in collaboration with Chinese scientists.
Trump was yesterday to welcome Xi for their second meeting since May as the heads of the world’s leading powers seek stability amid tensions ranging from trade to Iran and Taiwan.
Photo: Reuters
Rong said she was assured during a Tuesday meeting at the White House with officials from the US Department of State and National Security Council that Trump would ask Xi to free her husband.
Chen, 54, is one of two Americans held by Beijing that the US has designated as “wrongfully detained,” making their release a top priority. The other is Min Zin, an academic arrested in June.
Rong said she was told that Trump also would press Xi to release Min Zin.
Trump raised Chen’s case with Xi during a visit to Beijing in May, but it produced no action, Rong said.
“Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the president,” a senior US official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) said that the “relevant US person” is suspected of engaging in activities that endanger China’s national security and violate Chinese law.
“China is a country with rule of law, and there is no such thing as wrongful detention,” he told reporters in Beijing, without elaborating.
Chen, whose detention was revealed in July, is a seismologist with a US government contractor. His work detecting shock waves from North Korean underground nuclear tests has been openly funded by the US Department of State and the US Air Force Research Laboratory.
He became a US citizen in 2011 and settled in the Boston area.
He was arrested by Chinese state security officers on Nov. 5, 2024, at Beijing International Airport as he prepared to fly home after visiting family and lecturing at two universities.
Rong said her husband had been interrogated more than 100 times.
“I can’t imagine how hard his life is there every day,” she said.
She believes China wants to use her husband’s expertise to improve its ability to conceal nuclear tests using decoupling, a technique in which a device is detonated inside a large underground chamber to reduce the size of the shock waves.
The US has accused China of using decoupling to try to mask a low-yield nuclear test blast on June 22, 2020. China, which like the US has signed but not ratified a 1996 international ban on nuclear tests, denies conducting the test.
US embassy officials had been allowed to visit Chen for about 30 minutes once a month, always in the presence of Chinese officials, Rong said.
They read out letters she had written to him and he dictated his replies.

Prosecutors and police received a report alleging that a 38-year-old woman, surnamed Chiang (江), who worked as a supervisor at the Taipei Department of Social Welfare’s Senior Citizen Welfare Division from May last year to June this year, used her position to embezzle the savings of five elderly people under guardianship in Taipei’s Wenshan District (文山).
After Chiang resigned and transferred to the New Taipei City Government, the department noticed funds and properties were missing when it was conducting a handover inventory check, so it reported the case to the police, and prosecutors launched investigation.
Photo: Liu Yung-yun, Taipei Times
Police searched Chiang’s residence on Tuesday and seized several handbags and goods from luxury brands including Chanel and Hermes. She was arrested and detained that evening.
Ministry Department of Social Assistance and Social Work Deputy Director-General Yang Ya-lan (楊雅嵐) said the case is still under judicial investigation, but Chiang faces a professional license revocation if found guilty.
The ministry has requested the Taipei City Government to promptly conduct an administrative investigation and take subsequent measures in accordance with investigation results and the law, she said.
According to the Social Worker Act (社會工作師法), if a social worker commits a crime related to their professional duties and receives a final guilty verdict, their certificate and practice license may be revoked, Yang said, adding that the social worker would not be eligible to retake the licensing examination.
The ministry has a dedicated section on its Web site that publicizes the names of social workers who have received disciplinary actions to prevent them from re-entering the social work profession, and to protect the rights and interests of service recipients, she added.
Social and Family Affairs Administration Director Chou Tao-chun (周道君) said that according to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法) and the Civil Code, the court appoints a guardian after it declares an elderly person under legal guardianship.
The guardian can be family or relatives of the elderly person, third parties with relevant professional expertise or the local government, he said.
In Japan, a high percentage of adult guardianships is handled by professional third parties, including lawyers who specialize in that type of work, but it is relatively uncommon in Taiwan, Chou said.
The agency is in discussions with civil society groups on whether that practice should be introduced, what supporting measures would be needed and how to raise public awareness about such practices, he said.
After the agency receives more information on Chiang’s case, it would review whether laws or their implementation could be further improved for better property management mechanism, Chou said.
Separately, the Taipei Department of Social Welfare yesterday said it would not tolerate anyone who misuse their position to infringe upon public interest, and that it would never cover up illegal acts.
The department will fully cooperate with the judicial investigation and hold the person accountable in accordance with the law without leniency, it said, adding that it has reinforced its staff’s integrity awareness and legal education training.

ADB raises GDP growth for Taiwan to 11% this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

Taiwan’s economy is heading for its strongest growth in decades as the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom drives a surge in technology exports and investment, moving the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to raise its forecast for the second time this year.
The bank yesterday raised its growth forecast for this year for Taiwan to 11 percent from 9.5 percent in July, putting the economy on track to grow at the fastest pace among the 50 Asia-Pacific economies covered by the bank. It lifted its forecast for next year to 5 percent from 4 percent.
The upgrade comes after growth accelerated to 14.1 percent in the first half, the strongest pace in five decades. Second-quarter GDP expanded 12.9 percent, fueled by booming demand for chips and technology products, as companies around the world race to build AI computing capacity.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan’s tech exports jumped 65 percent in US dollar terms during the first half, while real exports rose 28 percent. Imports increased 22 percent as companies stepped up investment in AI-related capacity ahead of expected demand, the bank said.
The surge is no longer confined to Taiwan’s export manufacturers. Private consumption grew almost 6 percent in the first half, compared with 1 percent last year, while fixed investment increased almost 10 percent. Rising equity prices, stable home values and higher wages outside the technology sector have helped improve consumer confidence, the bank said.
That momentum is likely to ease next year. Investment in data centers and computing capacity should slow as facilities approach planned capacity, while the exceptionally strong expansion this year would make gains harder to achieve, the bank said.
The outlook faces pressure from inflation. The bank kept its forecast for this year’s inflation at 2 percent, but cut its projection for next year from 1.8 percent to 1.7 percent. Inflation averaged 1.5 percent in the first five months before accelerating to 2.6 percent in June and 2.5 percent in July, as higher oil prices linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran and weather-related vegetable costs pushed up consumer prices.
Energy prices, food costs and firm domestic demand could keep inflation elevated, although state-controlled energy prices could limit the extent to which higher costs reach consumers.
The AI boom remains the biggest upside to the growth outlook, but Taiwan faces risks from prolonged fighting in the Middle East, higher energy and food prices, new US trade measures and tighter global financial conditions. A sudden slowdown in AI investment could hit exports and corporate spending.
For the 43 developing economies covered by the bank, growth is forecast at 5 percent this year and 5.1 percent next year, underscoring how much faster Taiwan is expanding as it benefits from the AI-led export cycle.
