Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous | Kenneth Roth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:30:52 UTC
00:30:52 KST

Donald Trump’s speech on Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UN charter’s emphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address.
For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influence negotiations where he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice.
He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime.
In July, he already vowed to destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself a threat to commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russian military commanders for doing precisely that in Ukraine.
Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal.
He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated a deal to constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trump ripped it up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran far closer to a nuclear weapon than ever before.
Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls now predict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that he belittles.
Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, although hundreds remain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting his might-makes-right beliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
He noted the new agreement on Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member.
He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there is no real war, only a rhetorical one.
Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguably crimes against humanity.
Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may be why Trump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”.
It has been reported that Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’s statute.
Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated.
He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise the death toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues to kill Palestinians and block needed supplies, while Hamas has not disarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”.
Indeed, the Trump administration has rejected a leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny this reality.
He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues to occupy large swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’s mineral riches to the western market.
He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but to hand over additional chunks of its territory as well.
Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormous risks posed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.”
This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”.
Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display.
- 
  Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

Ukrainian forces have completed a nearly two-month operation that destroyed a Russian troop grouping and disrupted Moscow’s attempt to encircle Druzhkivka and advance toward Dobropillya in the Donetsk region, Ukraine’s First National Guard Corps Azov said.
According to a video report published by the corps on Wednesday, Sept. 23, the Russian troops had been accumulating in the area throughout the summer in preparation for further offensive operations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine claimed that 193 Russian soldiers were killed, 44 wounded, and three taken prisoner during the operation.
Ukraine launches joint clearing operation
The operation began on Aug. 7 and involved the Azov Brigade’s First and Sixth battalions, the Ultima Ratio special reconnaissance unit, the Tuman special operations detachment, and the Shkval Battalion of the 425th Skelia Separate Assault Regiment.
The Lasar’s Group special-purpose unit of Ukraine’s National Guard provided additional support.
Ukrainian forces first attempted to isolate the area where Russian troops had concentrated, using firepower to prevent reinforcements from arriving and stop the existing units from moving farther forward.
“The first task was to isolate the area where the enemy grouping had accumulated using firepower, prevent its further advance and create favorable conditions for the movement of our assault groups,” said Azov Brigade commander Lev, call sign Khorus.
Taiwan Cement Backs Ukraine’s Recovery With IFCEM Investment
“I consider this task completed,” he added.
The Ukrainian assault groups subsequently moved into Russian-held positions and conducted clearing operations.
Serhii, call sign Zamok, commander of the Shkval Battalion, said drones were used whenever a direct infantry assault would have created an excessive risk of casualties.
“If it was difficult to clear the enemy out because of shelters or the risk of our personnel being killed or wounded, we struck them with both our own weapons and those of the 12th Brigade, using FPV drones and bombers,” he said.
Russian plan threatened Ukraine’s fortress cities
According to Khorus, units from Russia’s 90th Tank Division and Eighth Combined Arms Army had attempted to reach Ukrainian logistics routes.
Capturing or placing those roads under fire control could have created conditions for an operational encirclement of Druzhkivka, threatened the wider Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban area, and supported a renewed Russian push toward Dobropillya.
The cities form part of Ukraine’s heavily fortified defensive belt in the northern Donetsk region. Russia has made capturing the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in the region one of its principal objectives for 2026.
Russian forces have increasingly attempted to bypass fortified cities and disrupt the roads supplying them instead of launching direct frontal assaults.
Azov’s First Corps was originally deployed to the Dobropillya sector in August 2025 as an emergency response to a Russian penetration of Ukrainian lines. Ukrainian reserves later contained the breakthrough and launched counterattacks against the exposed Russian units.
Moscow’s Dobropillya claim disputed
Russia’s defense ministry on Tuesday claimed that troops from its Center grouping had encircled Dobropillya and were advancing northwest toward Oleksandrivka.
Moscow did not publish maps, geolocated footage, or other evidence supporting the assertion.

Russian forces have nevertheless continued transferring equipment to the Dobropillya sector and could be preparing for mechanized attacks during the fall, according to Ukrainian and Western assessments.
Azov Corps commander Denys Prokopenko previously said that around 1,200 drone crews from Russia’s elite Rubikon unit were operating in the sector, indicating that Moscow intended to provide extensive unmanned support for renewed assaults.

The empty chairs of Minab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:28:10 UTC
00:28:10 KST

The empty chairs of Minab
MASHHAD — The courtyard was full before the first bell rang. Thousands of children in freshly pressed uniforms stood under a sky that felt too ordinary for the day. They hadn't gathered to start a new school year.
They'd come to remember children who never got to.
Today, in the Islami Inqilab Courtyard of the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad, thousands of schoolchildren gathered to pay tribute to the children of Minab and to honor the martyrdom of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei. Beneath the golden dome, the children stood together in a ceremony that turned the first day of school into a moment of remembrance, mourning and defiance.
“Death to America. Death to Israel.” The chant rolled through the crowd, familiar and practiced. In another setting it might have sounded routine. Here it sounded like grief that had run out of gentler words.
They were remembering Minab. On February 28, American and Israeli forces launched their war against Iran. The Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab was struck as classes were underway. UNICEF reported that 168 schoolchildren and teachers were killed at the school; for the families left behind, the number is not a statistic. It is a list of names nobody wants to finish reading.
And now there is another finding that cannot simply be pushed aside. On Thursday, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind the February strikes, including the attack on the Minab school, and concluded that both constituted war crimes. The mission said the Minab strike was an indiscriminate attack on civilian infrastructure and found that US forces failed to take feasible steps to verify that the school was a military objective.
That finding changes the question. This is no longer only about what Iran says happened. A UN-mandated investigation has now placed responsibility and international humanitarian law at the center of the discussion. The issue is no longer simply whether the world noticed the children of Minab. It is whether the world will demand accountability for their deaths.
In most of Iran, the first day back to school looks the same every year — new shoes still stiff from the box, the smell of fresh notebooks, kids nervously finding their classrooms. In Minab this year, that ordinary morning didn't come. Beds stayed made. Breakfast went cold on the table. No one packed a lunch, because there was no one to pack it for. The school gates opened onto absence instead of noise.
That's the part of war nobody puts in a press briefing. Officials in Washington and Tel Aviv talk about targets and deterrence, calculations made somewhere the rest of us never see. The language is built to sound controlled, almost administrative. But a missile doesn't know any of that. It only knows what's in front of it — a wall, a rooftop, a room full of children doing their morning lesson. When one hit Shajareh Tayyebeh, it did not pause to ask whether the room below was teaching arithmetic or reciting a poem. It just went off.
The children who gathered under the golden dome of the Imam Reza shrine understood something their own government has said for years and that, for once, felt true instead of rehearsed: in Iran, war isn't theoretical. It is a subject with a body count that includes people you knew.
The dead were not abstractions. They were girls who helped their mothers cook on weekends, boys who played street football until the light gave out, children who split a pencil in half so a friend would not have to ask the teacher for one. Teachers stayed late for a child stuck on a problem. They had names, routines, small arguments with siblings, plans for the weekend — and then they didn't, all at once.
The first day of school is supposed to be a beginning. In Minab it became something else — a reminder of everything that was cut short. Somewhere else in the country, buses were pulling up outside schools and children were arguing over seats. In Minab, families were walking to a cemetery instead, carrying flowers because there was nothing else left to bring. 
 
 Under the dome, the chant came back around: “Death to America. Death to Israel.” 
It is easy to hear only the slogan. Underneath it is a generation that has grown up absorbing decisions made in rooms they will never enter. To these children, the war is not a map with arrows on it. It is a photograph taped to a wall at home. It is a family that still remembers the child who should have walked through the door.
This is where the official language runs out. A government can call a strike strategic. A general can call a target legitimate. None of that answers the question a parent actually has, which is simpler and harder: Why didn't my child come home from school?
The UN finding makes that question even harder to dismiss. The mission said the United States failed to take feasible steps to verify that the Minab school was a military objective and concluded that the attack amounted to a war crime. The US government has disputed such findings and has not publicly released the full results of its own investigation.
So accountability cannot stop at statements of regret or carefully chosen words. If international law means anything, civilian lives cannot become secondary simply because the bombs were dropped by a powerful state. A school does not become a military target because someone, somewhere, claimed otherwise. The burden is on those who order and conduct an attack to distinguish civilians from military objectives.
Behind all the legal language sits a question that is painfully human: Who will answer the parents of Minab? 
 
 Under the golden dome, the children did not let the memory disappear. They stood where their classmates could not. They remembered the dead on the very morning when their own school year was beginning. For one morning, grief became something closer to a demand — that the world look directly at what happened in Minab instead of finding another reason to look away. 
And today, those children carried another message beyond the shrine. They carried it home with them: resistance is in our blood. We may be ready to sacrifice, but we are not ready to surrender.
The chairs are still empty. But Minab has not gone quiet. The names are still spoken, the families have not stopped asking, and the questions have already traveled beyond Iran's borders.

Uproar in France over award-winning author accused of using AI
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:28:05 BST
00:28:05 KST

Uproar in France over award-winning author accused of using AI
- Published
The French book scene is in uproar after a Canadian-Haitian author billed as a sensation was accused of using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his first novel.
Thélyson Orélien, 38, has just been awarded the Prix du Roman Fnac – the first of the literary season's prizes – for C'était ça ou mourir (It was either that or die).
He is also a finalist for the most prestigious annual French language awards, the Goncourt and the Renaudot, set to be issued soon.
But on Tuesday a little-known group called Balance ton Claude (Denounce your Claude, in reference to Anthropic's AI assistant) claimed the book was "almost totally" written by AI - a charge the author denied.
"We tested several passages, from different bits of the manuscript, to come up with the identical result: 100 percent AI," the group said on X.
According to the group – whose membership is unclear – the detection was carried out by a programme called Pangram, which it said was "by far the most accurate", with an almost negligible chance of making a mistake.
Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Montreal in 2010, immediately denied the accusation.
"I have always loved creation and literature. I can't see why I would feel compelled to use a machine," he told Libération newspaper. He said he was "compiling a dossier" with his editor to prove that he authentically wrote the book.
"My traditions are Haitian and Caribbean. The images, the repetitions and the rhythms are the living word, they are my own," he said.
The publishing house Grasset also came to his defence, saying the allegations "are atrociously injurious to a writer with an exceptional life-story" whose "work of creation is original and powerful."
The novel tells the story of a teacher who flees gang violence in Haiti and his adventures before he finally makes it to Canada, where he re-discovers "the right to breathe without fear".
The row recalls the controversy over Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir's The Serpent in the Grove, whose Commonwealth Short Story prize was initially withdrawn in July over allegations that it was written with generative AI.
The prize was subsequently re-awarded, after the organisers said they were satisfied the writing was genuine.
Critics of Pangram and other AI-detectors say they are unreliable – with different programmes often giving different results after analysing the same texts.
These tools do not actually know who, or what, wrote a piece of text. Instead, they look for patterns commonly found in AI-generated writing, but those patterns can also appear in human work.
Research has found that AI-detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI-generated and miss text that was produced by artificial intelligence, particularly if it has been edited or paraphrased.
Some also say that the programmes are built around the use of standardised language - English or French - and so cannot accurately interpret texts that use dialect from places like the Caribbean.
But the writers behind Balance ton Claude said that Pangram had been shown to make a wrong call about an AI-generated text only one time in every 24,400.
The latest detectors no longer compare text with text, to see if there has been plagiarism. Instead they analyse probabilities and statistics, to see if certain linguistic patterns betray the use of AI.
With AI becoming increasingly normalised, the row over C'etait ça ou mourir will feed the debate over what mix of human and AI creativity is deemed acceptable – it being perfectly possible for writers to generate AI then adapt it, or conversely write an original text then ask AI to review it.
Orélien was born in 1988 in the northern Haitian city of Gonaives.
His first work – before leaving his homeland – consisted of mainly poetic texts, and later in Canada he worked as a journalist.
The novel, described by his Canadian publisher as its biggest seller in 60 years, is due to be translated into around 20 languages.
Orélien told Libération that the first draft of the book was written in 2019 – well before AI programmes to generate text became generally available.

Paraguay calls for Venezuela’s return to Mercosur trade bloc
Sept 23 - Paraguay's President Santiago Pena called for Venezuela's reintegration into the South American trade bloc Mercosur on Wednesday, speaking to world leaders at the UN General Assembly.
Venezuela has been indefinitely suspended as a member of Mercosur, which comprises some of South America's biggest economies, including Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Chile's President Jose Antonio Kast, whose country is an associate member of the bloc, is scheduled to meet with Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez on the sidelines of the General Assembly on Thursday.
In his speech, Pena also said he wants to see Venezuela undergo a genuine and lasting democratic transition.
"We want a transition with strong institutions, security, a thriving economy, and a nation once again integrated into the international community, and specifically, integrated into Mercosur."
Pena visited Caracas before arriving in New York for the General Assembly, reopening dialogue between the two countries, whose diplomatic relations had been severed.
Mercosur has no provision for expulsion. It had suspended Venezuela in 2017 for not complying with the bloc's regulations, and toughened its stance following the arrest of several opposition leaders under ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. REUTERS

Rubio says US will try to secure energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Rubio says US will try to secure energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington will try to secure an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, although he acknowledged that doing so would be difficult.
Source: Rubio's remarks at a press conference in New York, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Rubio said reaching an energy ceasefire will be difficult because both Russia and Ukraine have identified attacks on each other's energy sector as a strategic objective.
Quote: "The Ukrainians are inflicting pain on the Russians by hitting their energy sector, which is a revenue source. The Russian side is inflicting pain on the Ukrainian side by targeting their electric grid, especially as we head into winter. So, there is the challenge, it's that both sides have identified energy as a strategic objective of their war aims… So that's why it's not easy to overnight just say 'Let's reach an agreement'."
More details: Rubio said, however, that an energy ceasefire would benefit both Ukraine and Russia.
Quote: "I think if you asked President Zelenskyy, he would argue that the ability to protect his electric grid is at the core of their interests. And that's something that we can help achieve through a deal. And obviously, the Russian side is facing strikes it has not seen before, deep in Russian territory and against key industries."
More details: Rubio added that the United States regards a "deal on a limited base" between the sides as an important step and will continue its efforts.
Quote: "It's something that I think is worth investing in, trying to make that happen – because I think it will be beneficial to the world and beneficial to both countries… And I think we're prepared to play a positive role, if we can, in making that come about."
Background:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Trump had not asked Ukraine to unilaterally stop strikes on Russia.
- At the start of his meeting with Zelenskyy in New York on 22 September, US President Donald Trump said he will be discussing Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries with the Ukrainian president.
- On 13 September, Trump urged Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian diesel fuel infrastructure, claiming that the attacks are causing a global shortage.
- Zelenskyy in fact said that Ukraine had proposed that its partners "secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure".

Iran 'victim' of terrorism, Israel kills, but Tehran gets sanctioned: Pezeshkian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:21:17 UTC
00:21:17 KST

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has rejected US President Donald Trump’s characterisation of Iran as a sponsor of terrorism, saying Tehran is itself a victim of terrorism.
“Yesterday, Trump said we are terrorists. We are not terrorists; we are victims of terrorism,” Pezeshkian told the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, referring to Trump’s address a day earlier in which the US president described Iran as the “number one sponsor of terror.”
Pezeshkian said Iran’s leader had been killed “without any justification", referring to the US-Israeli attacks against Iran that began earlier this year.
He also accused Israel of targeting neighbourhoods across Iranian cities and provinces and carrying out assassinations, describing such actions as “true terrorist” behaviour.
“The people of Iran have been defending their country for the past seven months,” Pezeshkian said.
"We have been the victims of terrorism. I come from an Iran in which our esteemed supreme leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason. I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school," Pezeshkian said.
He said Iran had been attacked using the latest technology and weapons systems, but that the Iranian people had "stood steadfast" in the face of the assault.
Hormuz
Pezeshkian said Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz to be used for aggression against his country.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," he said.
The Iranian president said that Iran has never started a war.
"Iran has never been an aggressor, has never started a war and has always shown her commitment to the negotiating table. They imposed the war on us, but we proved that we're not afraid of fighting," he said.
Iran's president struck a defiant tone, telling the US that Tehran would not "bend at the knee".
"US President Donald Trump must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, and increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," Pezeshkian said.
Israeli genocide
The Iranian president accused Israel of conducting assassinations “like a terrorist group” and committing genocide in Gaza, while arguing that Israel does not abide by international law.
“Israel kills, Tehran gets sanctioned,” he said, arguing that the international response to Israeli military actions and sanctions imposed on Iran demonstrated a double standard.
He said the world cannot speak of peace while ignoring Palestine.
“Gaza remains an example of failure of international mechanisms to prevent civilian suffering,” he said, adding that as long as occupation, aggression and injustice persist in the world, resistance will continue.
Nuclear technology
Pezekshian said Tehran’s defensive systems have been built so that no one can think that the bombing of Iranian cities will go unanswered.
“We do not accept nuclear technology being at the exclusive disposal of a handful; we need nuclear technology, not nuclear weapons,” he said.

Auchan’s Russian business gets a CEO from the Kremlin two days after transfer to “temporary management”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:21:04 UTC
00:21:04 KST

Ilya Berdnikov, who previously worked at Russia’s Federal Agency for State Property Management (Rosimushchestvo), has become CEO of Auchan Retail Russia. Berdnikov took up the post on Sept. 19 — two days after Vladimir Putin placed the French retailer’s Russian business under the temporary care of JSC L.E.V. Management.
As The Insider previously found, a week before the decree JSC L.E.V. was headed by former Ministry of Internal Affairs general Andrei Krayushkin, while the JSC itself was still listed among the ready-made shell companies available for purchase for 450,000 rubles ($5,340) — with the option to replace the CEO and complete the deal “same-day.”
The business outlet Kommersant reported Berdnikov’s appointment, citing Auchan’s press service. The previous CEO, Asya Balabai, will remain with the company as executive director.
Berdnikov held the post of executive director at Rosimushchestvo starting from December 2024, the paper writes, citing information from his social media accounts. Previously, he worked at the X5 retail group, the Georgian winemaker Askaneli, and the Canadian construction company Bothwell Accurate Co., and also developed the startup SolidRobots in Canada.
A Kommersant source in the retail market claims that previous CEO Balabai will in fact continue to run day-to-day operations, while Berdnikov will oversee the company. L.E.V. Management head Andrei Krayushkin, meanwhile, will manage the overall process without a formal job title at Auchan.
On Sept. 17, Putin placed the Russian assets of Auchan and Nestlé (along with those of several other companies) under the temporary authority of L.E.V. Management. The Insider found that L.E.V. Management was registered only in October 2024, with charter capital of 15,000 rubles ($178). In 2025 it had no revenue, posted a net loss of 15,000 rubles ($178), and had an average headcount of one employee.
On Sept. 10, one week before Putin’s decree, Andrei Krayushkin — the former first deputy head of Russia’s Main Directorate for Migration Affairs and a police major general — became CEO of L.E.V. Management.
After the assets were transferred, L.E.V. Management said it intended to keep Auchan operating as a single retail chain and to ensure that stores continued running without interruption. No leadership changes have yet been reported at the other companies placed under L.E.V.’s management. At Lemana PRO (formerly Leroy Merlin), the temporary administrator promised to preserve the existing management system and current senior leadership. Nestlé’s Russian division also continues to operate under executive director Denis Voityuk.
The mechanism for placing foreign assets under temporary management has been in effect in Russia since April 2023. Formally, the foreign owner retains ownership rights, but the structure appointed by Russian authorities receives broad powers to manage the assets. This scheme was previously applied to the Russian businesses of Danone and Carlsberg, which subsequently lost control of their companies in Russia.

Independent exit poll finds signs of over 10,000 stuffed ballots in Russian State Duma voting in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:20:47 UTC
00:20:47 KST

Official turnout at Russian precinct election commission No. 8158 in Cyprus during the recent vote for the State Duma was about 10 times higher than the turnout recorded by the independent Vote Abroad exit poll, organizers told The Insider. According to their estimate, more than 10,000 ballots were stuffed in Cyprus. The additional votes appeared to benefit not only Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party, but also A Just Russia and the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR).
Precinct commission No. 8158 covered voting locations in the coastal cities of Paphos and Limassol, as well as the Russian Embassy in the country’s capital, Nicosia. According to official data from the Russian Central Election Commission, 15,843 people voted at the precinct, where the ruling United Russia party received 10,897 votes — 68.78% overall. The LDPR came second with 1,095 votes (6.91%), the Communist Party was third with 954 (6.02%), New People was fourth with 785 (5.95%), and A Just Russia was fifth with 695 (4.39%).
Those results differ sharply from the independent Vote Abroad exit poll, which showed New People receiving 46.3% of the vote at the Cyprus polling locations, with United Russia taking just 12.8%. The exit poll’s organizers told The Insider that the discrepancy could only be explained by fraud. One of the organizers, Margarita Kuchusheva, said:
“At the three locations, we surveyed most of the people who came to vote and counted 945 people. We were there for almost 80% of the voting period. From 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday in Paphos, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Saturday in Limassol [voting in those cities took place only on Sept. 18 and 19], and on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday at the embassy in Nicosia from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., except during a heavy thunderstorm Friday morning and for two hours Saturday. During the storm, I was sitting in a car outside the embassy and recorded zero turnout.
All the polling places had one entrance and one exit. We counted turnout. How could the official turnout be about 10 times higher? The only major period we did not cover was Friday in Limassol. But that was a workday — it is impossible that 90% of voters came specifically during those hours, specifically in Limassol, on a working Friday. These are fantastical results. Even if you include embassy employees and their families, the numbers still do not add up. That means at least 10,000 ballots were stuffed. And they were added not only for United Russia, but also for A Just Russia and the LDPR.”
Voting in Cyprus also took place at precinct commission No. 8439 in Nicosia at the Russian Center for Science and Culture. That polling station was not covered by the independent exit poll, but it still remains statistically all but impossible that the official election results published for the country correspond to reality.
The Insider previously analyzed Central Election Commission data from overseas polling stations at Russian embassies worldwide, finding that New People’s share of the vote abroad was over three times higher than its official result inside Russia, while United Russia’s was about 18 percentage points lower. Russian voters abroad also produced results that differed significantly from the nationwide totals in the 2024 presidential election.
Cyprus, particularly Nicosia, stood out as one of the biggest anomalies in Russia’s 2024 presidential election abroad. Official results showed more than 53,000 votes cast in Cyprus (compared to just 5,276 in 2018), including about 42,000 at one Nicosia polling station, while independent monitors estimated actual turnout may have been closer to 13,000 and that roughly 40,000 official votes could have been fictitious or otherwise manipulated. Russian Election Monitor called the presidential vote in 2024 the “largest overseas electoral fraud in Russia's modern history.”

Senate gives final approval to law paving way for return to nuclear energy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:20:09 CEST
00:20:09 KST

The Senate on Wednesday gave definitive approval to a law drafted by Environment and Energy Security Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin paving the way for Italy's return to nuclear power. 
    Italy abandoned nuclear power following a referendum in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster but Premier Giorgia Meloni's government wants to return to atomic energy with small latest-generation reactors to reduce reliance on imports and cut greenhouse gas emissions. 
    "Today, Parliament definitively approved the nuclear law," Meloni said on social media. 
    "After nearly 40 years, Italy once again has a regulatory framework to produce nuclear energy. A bold and sensible decision. 
    "Today we import electricity generated by nuclear power plants in neighbouring countries, but we cannot produce it ourselves. . 
    "This law is needed to change that. 
    "Now the government will draft the implementing regulations on safety, authorizations, waste management, and relations with local communities. 
    "It was a commitment we made to the Italian people. Another commitment we have kept". 
    The law gives the government the power to issue decrees regulating this issue and it also sets out the areas of intervention: the construction and operation of power plants, hydrogen production using nuclear energy, spent fuel management and safety, and the establishment of regulatory bodies. 
    Pichetto Fratin has said that he intends to issue the implementing decrees by the end of the year. 
    "A significant step is being taken to for the country's energy future with the final approval of the enabling bill on nuclear energy," said Stefania Craxi, the Senate whip of the centre-right Forza Italia (FI) party. 
    "Next-generation nuclear power offers a concrete solution to ensure Italy's energy independence, shielding it from price volatility. 
    "We must meet rising energy demand while achieving our decarbonization goals. 
    "To this end, we need to strengthen our system with next-generation nuclear power while continuing to drive the expansion of renewables. 
    "This challenge will enable us to create a balanced energy system capable of supporting the country's economic development". 
    There were also dissenting voices. 
    "The Right presents nuclear power as a sort of answer to the climate crisis, high energy costs, and the country's foreign (energy) dependency," said Green-Left Alliance (AVS) Senate whip Peppe De Cristofaro. 
    "It is a gigantic mass distraction—a smokescreen to avoid accountability for the government's failed energy policies. 
    "After four years of Meloni in power, the country still faces some of the highest energy prices in Europe. 
    "The question to ask is: what benefit could be gained from a return to nuclear power in the coming years? The answer is that nuclear power will yield no benefits. 
    "The (new-generation) power plants and technologies are not yet available; in the meantime, we will continue burning gas and relying on imports, while Italians keep paying exorbitant bills. 
    "All this propaganda regarding nuclear power is precisely the way to prolong our dependence on fossil fuels. 
    "The government wants to turn Italy into a gas hub without having gas, and into a nuclear power without having uranium. 
    "AVS says no to a return to nuclear power, and no to giving the government a blank cheque".

Fire from Wednesday’s Russian drone strike ravaged Kyiv’s well-known Soviet-era covered market, the Zaliznychnyi, which locals nicknamed the “Puck,” resembling a hockey puck.

Firefighters douse the Puck with water.

ICC refuses to withdraw arrest warrant against Netanyahu
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has taken no steps to withdraw arrest warrants or related applications concerning Israeli officials, despite mounting pressure and sanctions from the United States, Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan has said.
“The case is still proceeding,” Khan told CNN in a weekend interview.
“We have taken no steps to try and withdraw any of those arrest warrant applications or the arrest warrants themselves, and the team continues to investigate in that situation.”
The ICC issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his then war minister, Yoav Gallant, over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023.
Since then, the U.S. has imposed sanctions on most of the court's leadership, including the former chief prosecutor Karim Khan, the two deputy prosecutors, and nine judges including the court's president.
Israel has also taken steps to challenge the warrants at the ICC. Two appeals remain in progress, including one challenging the court's jurisdiction over Israeli nationals because Israel is not a member of the court.
Meanwhile, Middle East Eye has reported that the prosecutor’s office had pursued further cases against senior Israeli officials over the past two years.
In May, MEE reported that the prosecutor’s office had filed a confidential application seeking arrest for Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalal Smotrich over crimes committed against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
The charges included forced displacement as both a war crime and crime against humanity, transferring Israel’s civilian population into occupied territory as a war crime, and persecution and apartheid as crimes against humanity.
An evidence review had also been held to consider two further applications, including one targeting National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
Khan’s comments came amid an escalating campaign by the administration of President Donald Trump against the Hague-based court.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in July that Washington would use every tool at its disposal to “dismantle the ICC – brick by brick, if necessary”, while urging member states to withdraw their support for the institution.
In other press statements, Rubio also described the court as a “stupid organization” run by “lunatics and crazies”, and warned that it would face consequences for attempting to exercise jurisdiction over American nationals.

Breadcrumb
Pezeshkian tells Trump that Iran will never 'bend at the knee'
Iran's president struck a defiant tone at the UN on Wednesday where he spoke for the first time since Washington and Israel launched an all-out war on his country, vowing Tehran would never "bend at the knee."
Masoud Pezeshkian accused Washington of "terrorism" for assassinating former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war.
He held up a photograph of the dead leader, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump had told the UN he was weighing whether to "annihilate" Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington's negotiators.
Pezeshkian made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war in his steely speech.
"(Trump) must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he said.
Pezeshkian insisted that Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz, which it has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war causing global energy prices to spike, to be used for aggression against his country.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," he said.
Soaring fuel prices threaten to cost Trump's Republicans their control of Congress in November's midterms.
Pezeshkian's attendance at the UN's signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear if the United States would issue a visa.
Ultimately Washington granted the permit, but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian's entourage.

00:18:36 KST

A nurse who objected to sharing a changing room with a transgender doctor has said she felt “discriminated against” by her union after raising the complaint.
Sandie Peggie, who worked for NHS Fife for more than 30 years, won a partial victory against her employer after a tribunal in December 2025, when a judge upheld her harassment claim against the health board but dismissed claims of discrimination, indirect discrimination and victimisation.
Now Peggie has begun a new tribunal proceeding, this time against her trade union, the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), which she accuses of failing to adequately support her in her original employment dispute. The union denies all allegations.
Giving evidence on the first day of the tribunal, Peggie said she had originally spoken to her RCN representative, Stuart Fraser, in January 2024 after being placed on special leave by NHS Fife. She told the tribunal: “I felt like he thought I was being disciplined because I had done something wrong.”
Peggie said Fraser was “non-committal” in their first conversation, and did not seem to agree with her that Dr Beth Upton should not be allowed in female changing areas. She said she felt she was being discriminated against and that she was not being supported, but acknowledged she did not say this to Fraser at the time.
She told the tribunal that by February 2024 she had “lost faith” in the RCN, because Fraser had not mentioned legal support in their earlier conversation.
Of the circumstances surrounding her original tribunal claim, Peggie said there had been “general chit chat” among NHS Fife staff about the use of a women’s changing room in Kirkcaldy’s Victoria hospital by Upton.
When asked why no colleagues had given evidence to support her case she said: “I think possibly it was fear … They had seen the way I had been treated at the hospital by senior staff members.”
Peggie’s case further claims that the union refused a request for legal support in January 2025, and that it did not provide adequate support when she asked NHS Fife to commit to ensuring changing facilities should be single-sex.
She argues that the union discriminated against her because of her “gender-critical and sex realist” beliefs. Peggie said: “I felt unsupported. Mainly because I felt I had been discriminated against.”
The nurse has also appealed against the decision from her original tribunal proceedings. That case is expected to be heard in the first half of next year.
The tribunal, taking place in Dundee before judge Melanie Sangster, is expected to continue for seven days.

Azerbaijan Pardons French Citizen Martin Ryan After EU Lifts Sanctions on Russian Oligarch Usmanov
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned French national Martin Ryan, previously accused of espionage, Reuters reported on September 23.
This came just one day after the European Union lifted sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov following an intense pressure campaign from France and Luxembourg.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ryan, the Chief Executive Officer of Baku-based food-import firm Mercorama, had been serving a 10-year prison sentence following an espionage conviction in March, according to Reuters.
Baku accused him of operating as an agent for France’s Directorate-General for External Security (DGSE), gathering sensitive information on Azerbaijan’s military cooperation with Türkiye and Pakistan, and secretly recruiting French-speaking Azerbaijanis—allegations Paris has consistently rejected.
Three European diplomats told Reuters that Ryan’s release appears to be the direct result of a highly controversial geopolitical trade that has fractured European unity.
The diplomats stated that Paris privately admitted Baku was using Usmanov’s sanctions designation to pressure France over its imprisoned citizens, leading France to successfully lobby Brussels to remove the metals and mining magnate from the EU sanctions list on September 22.
The pardon decree signed by Aliyev released Ryan alongside 19 others, including citizens from Türkiye, Pakistan, and a dual Russian-Israeli national, Reuters reported.
However, the deal did not secure the release of a second French national, Anass Derraz, an employee of French water management company Saur who was sentenced in 2025 to 12 years in prison on corruption charges.
A senior Azerbaijani diplomat rejected the allegations of a pressure campaign as “categorically unfounded,” telling Reuters that Baku openly supported Usmanov’s removal from Western sanctions lists but denied attempting to influence Western decision-making.
The delisting of Usmanov, alongside fellow Russian billionaire Mikhail Fridman, marks the first time the EU has removed sanctions against members of Russia’s billionaire elite who have not publicly condemned the war in Ukraine, Reuters noted.
The decision exposed deep divisions among EU governments, while Ukraine vehemently condemned the move as “shameful and unjustifiable,” according to the agency.
Relations between Paris and Baku have long been strained over France’s close ties to Armenia, Azerbaijan’s neighbor and rival, Reuters added. France maintains a large Armenian diaspora and actively supplies arms to Yerevan, compounding the diplomatic standoff surrounding the arrests.
In response to the EU’s decision to drop sanctions against Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Latvia’s Cabinet of Ministers had recently ordered the drafting of national-level sanctions to prevent the billionaires' assets from circulating within its borders.
Riga had been the sole holdout against the EU delisting but ultimately chose to abstain to secure a 36-month extension for the broader European sanctions framework.

Russia’s Fast Geran-5 Drone “Exploded Like a Comet” After Ukrainian Intercept, Video

- Category

Russia’s Fast Geran-5 Drone “Exploded Like a Comet” After Ukrainian Intercept, Video
Ukrainian border guards shot down a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered strike drone on September 23, one of Moscow's newest and fastest attack UAVs.
Operators from the 105th Separate Border Detachment, named after Prince Volodymyr the Great, carried out the interception, ArmyInform added.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The State Border Guard Service of Ukraine released footage of the strike on its official Telegram channel the same day.
The drone "exploded like a comet," as described by ArmyInform. By what means the operators reached the Geran-5, the Border Guard Service did not specify, nor did it disclose the strike's location.
In the same Telegram post, the service listed a broader set of targets hit by the unit's operators on September 23:
- a jet-powered Geran-5 strike drone;
- 82mm automatic Vasylok mortars;
- fuel, lubricant, and ammunition depots;
- electronic warfare equipment and radar stations;
- military vehicles;
- fortified enemy shelters.
Jet-powered Gerans fly considerably faster than the propeller-driven Shaheds that Russia has used against Ukraine for years, a gap that demands different interception means, ArmyInform explained.
Russia first deployed the Geran-5 against Ukraine in early 2026, according to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (HUR).
The jet-powered UAV closely resembles Iran's Karrar drone and reflects Moscow's shift toward faster, harder-to-intercept strike platforms.
According to HUR, the Geran-5 measures roughly 6 meters long, has a wingspan of up to 5.5 meters, and carries a warhead of about 90 kilograms.
Later assessments put its takeoff weight near 850 kilograms. The drone cruises at 450 to 600 kilometers per hour, with a range of up to 950 kilometers and a ceiling of up to 6 kilometers.
The drone runs on a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, and its airframe includes components sourced from China, the US, and Germany, HUR found.
The Geran-5 is estimated to cost around $100,000 per unit, similar to the newer Banderol cruise missile. That is far cheaper than a US-made Tomahawk, which runs more than $2 million.
The interception adds to a string of recent Geran-5 losses. Russian production of the jet-powered drone and its Banderol counterpart has expanded rapidly in recent months, moving from battlefield testing to large-scale manufacturing.
Ukrainian air defenses downed another Geran-5 over Kyiv's Holosiivskyi district in early September, when wreckage from the drone fell in the neighborhood.

Ukraine Smashes Russia’s Two-Month Push to Encircle Druzhkivka, 237 Troops Killed
Ukrainian forces have disrupted a Russian attempt to reach key logistics routes and create conditions for the operational encirclement of Druzhkivka in the Donetsk region following a nearly two-month clearing operation involving several Ukrainian units.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 1st National Guard Corps “Azov” on September 23, Russian forces had been building up in the area throughout the summer with the aim of advancing toward Druzhkivka and launching further attacks in the direction of Dobropillia.
The Russian grouping included elements of the 90th Tank Division and the 8th Combined Arms Army, according to Lev, callsign “Khorus,” commander of Ukraine’s 12th Special Forces Brigade “Azov.”
Ukraine reinforced troops already operating in the sector and launched a coordinated operation involving the Ultima Ratio special reconnaissance unit, the 1st and 6th battalions of the 12th Azov Brigade, the Tuman special forces unit of the 1st Azov Corps, and the Shkval Battalion of the 425th Skelia Separate Assault Regiment. Lasar’s Group of the National Guard provided additional support.
The first Ukrainian assault groups began advancing on August 7 after Russian positions and concentrations were targeted to isolate the area and prevent additional Russian forces from moving forward. Artillery and strike drones were used to support infantry clearing operations.
According to Azov, Ukrainian units sought to destroy or suppress Russian positions with FPV drones, bomber drones, and artillery before sending assault troops forward when direct clearing operations posed an increased risk to personnel.
The operation was complicated by dense vegetation, Russian infantry moving in small groups, and extensive Russian drone activity, which also made the evacuation of wounded Ukrainian troops more difficult.
Azov said the operation resulted in 237 Russian troops killed, 44 wounded, and three captured. The figures have not been independently verified.
The Ukrainian units also reported strikes on Russian artillery during the operation. Lasar’s Group provided fire support to assault units, while earlier Ukrainian operations targeting Russian artillery and armored vehicles helped reduce Russia’s ability to support troops operating in the sector.
The operation prevented Russian troops from reaching logistics routes that Ukrainian commanders said could have been used to threaten Druzhkivka and support an advance toward Dobropillia. According to Azov, losing positions in the area forces Russian forces to search for alternative routes and commit additional time and resources before attempting further advances.
The operation comes as Ukrainian forces conduct broader counteroffensive actions in northern Donetsk region. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps recently reported that its Operation Vivaldi had returned 125 square kilometers of territory to Ukrainian control during several stages of fighting.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Thousands of displaced in south-west Somalia could be in famine by year end, IPC says
NAIROBI, Sept 23 - Thousands of displaced people in Somalia's south-west could experience famine between October and December if El Nino causes worse-than-expected flooding and humanitarian aid remains insufficient, a global hunger monitor said on Wednesday.
Baidoa, one of Somalia's biggest cities, is home to hundreds of thousands displaced by conflict and hunger.
A report by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), an initiative of UN agencies, regional bodies and aid groups, said that 5% of displaced people in Baidoa, or about 26,000, were likely to face starvation and a collapse in livelihoods in October to December.
More than 5 million Somalis, 26% of the analysed population, are already suffering crisis-level food insecurity or worse due to repeated droughts, conflict and aid shortfalls, the report said.
The number suffering food insecurity is forecast at 5.4 million people in October to December.
Food aid is expected to reach only 70,400 people per month in October to December, or 1.3% of those in need.
An estimated 1.92 million children aged 6 months to 5 years will require treatment for acute malnutrition by next June, including 433,000 severe cases.
Somalia last experienced famine in 2011, when around 250,000 people died, and came close in 2017 and 2022. REUTERS

Morocco votes for new parliament amid hopes and concerns over cost of living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:15:27 UTC
00:15:27 KST

Hopes and concerns over jobs, wages, public services and cost of living dominate Morocco’s parliamentary election as the country prepares for the 2030 World Cup.
Moroccans went to the polls on Wednesday to elect a new parliament in an election shaped by mounting issues but also hopes for better opportunities generated by the country’s thriving economy.
The next government will oversee preparations for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal, while facing pressure to address everyday worries about unemployment and low wages, as well as issues with housing, schools and hospitals.
Voting centres across the North African kingdom are due to close at 7 pm local time (9 pm CEST), allowing nearly 16 million registered voters to cast ballots for the 395-seat House of Representatives.
A total of 7,288 candidates are standing, backed by 28 parties and alliances or running on two independent lists.
The vote will determine the next prime minister and the makeup of the government, which will serve alongside a powerful monarchy that retains broad authority over strategic affairs.
Morocco’s constitution requires the king to choose the prime minister from the top-performing party in legislative elections.
Since no single party is expected to capture an absolute majority, the winner will need to build a coalition government. Portfolios are split among the political allies, but the palace traditionally keeps key posts such as defence and foreign affairs under royal control.
Еconomy strong, jobs scarce
Morocco’s economy is growing and attracting foreign investment, and new industries are developing. It has also become Africa’s most-visited destination.
The kingdom is a close US ally and maintains strong ties with Western capitals. It is among the few Arab countries that have diplomatic relations with Israel.
Beyond the palaces, seas and mountains that draw tourists from around the world, development remains uneven across the country, economic growth is not creating enough jobs, and 12.7% of Moroccans live in relative poverty.
Politicians have said they have heard these grievances and have proposed solutions in their election manifestos. Many young Moroccans in particular said they have heard such promises before.
Who are the main contenders?
The outgoing government is a coalition of the National Rally of Independents (RNI), the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) and the Istiqlal Party. All three are competing to finish first.
The liberal, pro-business RNI won the 2021 election and has led the government for the past five years. Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch stepped down as RNI leader in February and is not standing for a parliamentary seat. Mohamed Chouki now leads the party.
Both the RNI and PAM have promised to create around 1 million jobs over the next five-year term. The RNI has also proposed a guaranteed minimum monthly wage of 5,000 dirhams (€455).
PAM is the second-largest party in the outgoing parliament. Its main figures in this election include Fatima-Zahra Mansouri, the mayor of Marrakech and urban planning minister, and Fouzi Lekjaa, the budget minister and president of Morocco’s football federation.
The party has proposed exempting salaries below 15,000 dirhams (€1,370) from income tax and providing 100,000 housing options for young people. If PAM finishes first and Mansouri is chosen to lead the government, she would become the first woman to hold the post.
Istiqlal, Morocco’s oldest political party, is led by Water Minister Nizar Baraka. The nationalist, conservative-leaning party has made faster treatment in public hospitals one of its campaign pledges.
The Justice and Development Party (PJD), led by former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, is also trying to make a comeback. The moderate party led the government for a decade before falling from 125 seats to 13 in the 2021 election. It says it wants to reduce the economic gap between Casablanca and other parts of the country.
Other established contenders include the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Popular Movement and the left-wing Party of Progress and Socialism, which has campaigned on education and tighter anti-corruption rules.
How does the election work?
Voters receive two ballot papers and choose a party list rather than individual candidates.
Of the 395 seats, 305 are filled through local constituencies. The remaining 90 come from regional, all-female lists. Seats are allocated under a proportional system.
Under Morocco’s 2011 constitution, King Mohammed VI appoints the head of government from the party that wins the most seats.
No party is expected to secure the 198 seats needed for an outright majority, so the winner will probably have to negotiate a coalition. The proposed cabinet must then receive royal approval.
The elected government runs domestic policy and public services, but the king retains broad powers over the country’s overall direction, defence and foreign affairs.
The constitution recognises the right to vote for Moroccans living abroad, but there is no voting by mail or ballot boxes at Moroccan consulates.
Instead, they must travel to Morocco to vote or authorise a registered family member or acquaintance to vote on their behalf.
Counting begins after polls close on Wednesday evening. Preliminary national results are normally announced the following day.
Morocco does not have election opinion polls, so there is no reliable public forecast of which party will finish first. Once the result is known, the leading party will begin talks with potential coalition partners.

Watch a robot dog run a marathon faster than the average human
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:14:55 UTC
00:14:55 KST

Hot on the heels of humanoid robots besting Usain Bolt’s record in the 100-meter sprint is a marathon-running dog bot.
The quadrupedal machine, named RAIBO2, ran the full 26.2-mile marathon course in a single battery charge, finishing in four hours, 19 minutes and 52 seconds—slightly ahead of the human average.
The feat shows how far researchers have come in making these bots energy-efficient. “What matters is energy consumed per unit of distance,” explains the study’s lead author Choongin Lee, a roboticist at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) in South Korea. To make their robot able to complete a marathon without needing a recharge, Lee and his team identified all the areas where walking robots waste energy.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
About two thirds of a robot’s energy budget is lost as heat in the motors and their drive electronics, the researchers found. The rest goes into friction in the gears, feet that slip and the jolt of each footfall.
Lee’s team tackled each issue one by one: The researchers cut the weight of each leg, designed low-resistance motor boards and spent the freed-up mass budget on a bigger battery, combined with motors that produced the same torque for less current. RAIBO2’s walking style was trained through simulation with reinforcement learning, in which the control algorithm was rewarded for setting the robot’s feet down softly and for not allowing it to slip or overheat.
On top of that, RAIBO2 was designed to recuperate and recharge the battery on downhill stretches. The robot is described in a study that was published in Nature on Wednesday.
The result of all this tinkering is that the robot needs less energy to carry a kilogram over a distance of one meter than the average human runner. RAIBO2 travels roughly three times farther per charge than other quadrupedal robots, with a projected range of around 40 miles.
“I’m impressed with their ability to combine efficiency with speed and mobility in a quadruped,” says Sarah Bergbreiter, a mechanical engineer at Carnegie Mellon University, who was not involved in the study.
Katie Byl, an engineer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, who also was not involved in the work, points out that the humanoid robots that were recently seen racing in China needed several battery swaps from a support team jogging alongside. “It’s akin to a ‘mobile pit crew,’” she notes.
Still, Lee’s robot required human help during the marathon. “RAIBO2 is basically running blind,” Byl explains. The robot carried a camera but no software to interpret the road. A human operator had to steer it remotely.
Adding more autonomy will cost power, Lee says. To minimize the loss of energy-efficiency an added electronic brain would cause, Lee’s team is currently working on smaller onboard networks and sensors. “This way the robot can become more capable without a large increase in power consumption,” Lee says.

Netherlands to return to Eurovision 2027 after boycotting Israel’s participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:40 UTC
00:13:40 KST

The Netherlands will join the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest after boycotting the event this year over Israel's participation, Dutch public broadcaster NPO said on Wednesday.
NPO took over from the original public broadcaster AVROTROS, which formally announced in August that they would not participate in the contest, stating that the event could "no longer be considered neutral" while a participating country, referring to Israel, remains involved in a large-scale military conflict, NL Time reported Wednesday.
In August, AVROTROS director-general Taco Zimmerman stated that the contest was meant to unite people and countries involved in international conflicts, undermining the contest's "neutrality" character, saying, "The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together." It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character.”
The broadcaster noted that it had returned responsibility for Dutch participation in Eurovision to the NPO. This organization oversees the overall Dutch public broadcasting system.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) had initially set a September 15 deadline for countries to confirm their participation. NPO requested additional time to evaluate its options after taking over responsibility for the Netherlands’ Eurovision entry and was granted an extension until the end of September.
Countries weigh Eurovision return as Bulgaria prepares to host 2027 event
The Netherlands was among five countries, together with Ireland, Spain, Iceland, and Slovenia, that withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision contest in Vienna. Ireland’s broadcaster RTÉ has since said it will also skip and not broadcast the 2027 contest, while Spain and Iceland are still reviewing whether they will participate, according to Eurovoix.
The contest's final semi-final rounds ad grand final will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria May 11-15, 2027 hosted by Bulgarian National Television (BNT) alongside the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Reuters and Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

Poverty, child labor, and child marriage partially behind Iran’s unfilled classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:38 UTC
00:13:38 KST

Thousands of Iranian children of elementary-school age have been unable to receive an education due to financial hardship, Iran’s Education Ministry reported on Tuesday.
Rezvan Hakimzadeh, deputy minister of primary education, said 140,562 students had been identified as not attending school last year, with the majority located in Sistan and Baluchestan, Tehran, Razavi Khorasan, and Khuzestan provinces. Of those children, 54,445 were in the first grade, he said.
Nearly 42,000 of the students had left Iran with their families, while 18,000 were not required to enroll due to disabilities, Hakimzadeh said. Thousands of others were out of school due to family financial hardship, child labor, a lack of adequate guardianship, or enrollment in unlicensed education centers, he added.
There were 86 cases in which a child of elementary-school age was not attending school because they had married, the report said.
Primary school in Iran is for children ages six to 12, while Iranian law generally requires girls to be 13 and boys to be 15 to marry. In some cases, however, a judge’s approval can allow for marriage at an earlier age.
The start of the school year in Iran has drawn greater attention to the country’s rapid demographic change.
According to the Razavi Foundation’s Astan Quds Razavi media site Quds Online, 1.154 million six-year-old children began primary school in Iran this year, about 76,000 fewer than last year.
Iran's challenged demography
Iran’s declining birth rates, delays in marriage and childbearing, economic pressures, and lifestyle changes have all impacted the country’s shifting demography, Quds Online reported.
Alireza Sajedi, head of Iran’s Population Monitoring Center of the National Organization for Civil Registration, told Quds Online the number of births had fallen from about 1.116 million in 2021 to fewer than 980,000 in 2024.
The downward demographic shift could eventually lead schools to reduce both classroom sizes and the actual number of classes in cities, Quds Online reported. In rural areas, however, it may no longer be viable to keep schools open, the report said.

Israel Navy moves toward semi-autonomous fleet with robotic ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:26 UTC
00:13:26 KST

The Israeli navy is moving toward becoming a semi-autonomous force and may eventually become nearly fully autonomous, the IDF said.
It has been reported that the Israeli navy has operated autonomous sea vehicles in recent years, though it is unclear when swarms at sea will be ready to roll out.
Elbit Systems has already been among the Israeli companies developing such technologies, including its publicized 12-meter Seagull autonomous surface vessel, designed to patrol offshore infrastructure for up to four days. It also "incorporates mine countermeasures (MCM), anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime security (MS), electronic warfare (EW) and other advanced systems and technologies."
Other countries like France, Singapore, and the Netherlands are also shifting their navies toward more autonomous operations.
Despite those navies' progress, Israel's navy said it is even more advanced in using robots and autonomy.
The need for robots and autonomous operations is clear, given that ships can spend weeks or longer at sea.
Even the most resilient sailors have trouble with this amount of time at sea, and an overwhelming portion of the population is just incapable of doing it at all.
Israel faces growing naval threats from Turkey, Iran, Houthis
In addition, Israel faces growing naval threats from Turkey, and possibly from Iran, the Houthis in Yemen, and others.
The navy said this means it will need more ships in the future to secure Israel's maritime national security interests.
However, the navy does not believe the country or the military will grant it additional staffing power for more ships, so the only stable way to expand Israel's naval fleet sufficiently will involve fewer human soldiers per ship, and eventually zero or close to zero.
At one stage, Israeli soldiers can focus solely on maintenance and safety issues with robots and autonomous systems operating most other systems.
Robots are a double-edged sword
At a later stage, robots may be able to undertake all or much of the maintenance work.
But robots are a double-edged sword.
Enemy forces are also expected to use robots and autonomous systems against Israel.
This will create a number of challenges: land-to-sea and sea-to-sea.
In addition, the IDF is aware that China, Russia, and other countries have explored cutting underwater cables, which foreign reports have confirmed going back to at least 2023 in the Baltic Sea, near Britain, Norway, and at other locations.
Israel is working on and will need to expand its defense of these underwater cables going forward.

Firms Linked to Putin Classmate Win $1.5Bln in Moscow School Meal Contracts, Report Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:22 UTC
00:13:22 KST

Four companies linked to a former university classmate of President Vladimir Putin won all 39 contracts to supply meals to Moscow schools from 2026 to 2028, the exiled news outlet Vyorstka reported Wednesday.
The awards, worth a combined 126.7 billion rubles ($1.5 billion), show how a lucrative school catering business once held by companies owned by late Wagner mercenary group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin has passed to firms with ties to Ilgam Ragimov, who studied law alongside Putin.
The four winning companies were registered in March 2024, less than a year after Prigozhin’s mutiny and death in a plane crash. Vyorstka reported that their owners, Sergei Yefimchuk, Nikolai Kuznetsov, Dmitry Aliyev and Olga Rusishvili, had previously worked at Grandtitul, a company in which Ragimov is the largest shareholder.
Verona Kapital won 12 contracts worth 38.2 billion rubles ($450.8 million), KDP won seven worth 29.1 billion rubles ($343.4 million), RSK won nine worth 34.8 billion rubles ($410.6 million) and ShYuZ won 11 worth 24.6 billion rubles ($290.3 million), according to Vyorstka.
The four firms succeeded suppliers called Verona, Kombinat Doshkolnogo Pitaniya, Russotskapital and Shkolnik-Yuz, which had been owned by Prigozhin, the outlet reported.
Ragimov studied with Putin at Leningrad State University, now St. Petersburg State University. Forbes estimated his fortune at $500 million in 2014, citing business interests that included Moscow’s Sadovod market, the Ukraina hotel and the Evropeisky and Panorama shopping centers.
The late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation has said that Ragimov and two other Putin classmates helped finance a lavish property near the Black Sea town of Gelendzhik that the group links to the Russian president. It said their company, Investment Solutions, spent 7 billion rubles ($82.6 million) on the project.

Gaza journalists operating under Hamas media controls were given platforms in Westminster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:14 UTC
00:13:14 KST

Gaza-based journalists who worked amid what photojournalist Motaz Azaiza has described as a “Hamas-controlled media environment” were given prominent platforms in Westminster, researcher Emma Schubart of the Henry Jackson Society (HJS) revealed to The Jerusalem Post exclusively on Tuesday.
Schubart’s discovery follows comments made by Gazan photojournalist Motaz Azaiza in a September 3 podcast interview with journalist Ahmed Biqui.
During this conversation, Azaiza mentioned the existence of a Hamas-administered WhatsApp group called Smart, which, he said, included “every journalist working in Gaza.” The group’s icon displayed a Hamas flag and was administered by “the director of media for the Rafah Border Crossing,” who has been identified as Wael Abu Mohsen.
According to Azaiza, the group coordinated media messaging and organized campaigns against journalists whose reporting departed from the sanctioned line.
“It was never a spontaneous thing,” he added.
Gazan photographers 'accustomed to lowering cameras' to criticism of Hamas
Azaiza added that photographers in Gaza had “become accustomed to lowering their cameras” when civilians criticized Hamas.
HJS reported that several journalists who operated within this Hamas-controlled media environment were subsequently welcomed into Westminster and presented to British parliamentarians as authoritative witnesses to the war. Other journalists from this environment have been involved more indirectly with the British government.
For example, Al Jazeera’s Gaza bureau chief Wael al-Dahdouh was hosted in Parliament in September last year.
MPs host Hamas-linked journalists
Hansard [the official report of all Parliamentary debates] records Labour MP Yuan Yang saying on September 10, 2025, that she had “co-hosted an event in Parliament for Wael al-Dahdouh” the previous evening.
During that visit, Dahdouh also met with Labour MP Afzal Khan for Manchester Rusholem (formerly Manchester Gorton), who posted publicly that he had met Dahdouh, calling the meeting “an honor.”
While neither the Post nor HJS has independently verified the membership of the group, Azaiza said it included every journalist working in Gaza at the time.
Then there is Azaiza himself, who on May 15, 2024, addressed a Nakba Day gathering at Westminster Central Hall, yards from Parliament, sharing the event with Sir Alan Duncan, the former Conservative Foreign Office minister.
Additionally, Scottish National Party (SNP) MP Brendan O’Hara co-organized a cross-party panel in a House of Commons committee room in mid-July 2025 with Oxfam GB and the Council for Arab-British Understanding.
Gaza journalist Abubaker Abed spoke alongside Oxfam’s then-CEO. Abed addressed MPs and journalists who were in attendance on conditions in Gaza and called for an end to UK arms support for Israel.
Finally, Al Jazeera and the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) held a sold-out Westminster screening of the documentary Gaza in October 2024, followed by a panel. Al Jazeera Gaza correspondent Youmna El Sayed appeared as a panellist, with MPs and peers attending.
“One of Gaza’s most famous ‘journalists’ has described, in his own words, how Hamas controlled the media environment,” Schubart said.
Schubart noted that this is of great importance to every international outlet that has relied on Gaza-based journalists yet still claims that their reporting is editorially independent of Hamas.
“The question is straightforward: Why were British politicians giving a parliamentary platform to journalism produced under Hamas control?”
Schubart has personally written to the Speaker of the House on these findings. The letter was viewed by the Post.
