curved mirrored steel walls multiply one tree into forest at infinite grove pavilion in shanghai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:15:09 UTC
23:15:09 KST

Infinite Grove pavilion reflects a single tree into infinity
One tree becomes an endless forest in Infinite Grove, a traveling pavilion by Chang Hao Studio in Shanghai. Two curved mirrored–steel walls reflect a single tree back and forth, creating a forest with no visible edge. First presented in spring at the 2026 Shanghai International Flower Festival, the pavilion has since moved across the city, pairing the same structure with different trees for each season.
One tree, multiplied, shapes a forest within two walls
Infinite Grove is a pop-up pavilion built by Chang Hao Studio around a single tree. Two curved mirrored-steel walls multiply it through reflection, while a circular entrance reveals only part of the interior. Frosted panels diffuse daylight into a soft haze, making it difficult to distinguish the real tree from its reflections.
Inside, the tree appears above while its repeated reflections surround the visitor, incorporating their own figure into the mirrored landscape. The experience unfolds through three stages: a partial view through the circular opening, the first glimpse of the reflected forest, and the realization that the entire scene originates from a single tree.
Infinite Grove multiplies a single tree into a forest of reflections
The traveling pavilion forms A garden for the city
Infinite Grove was selected by Xiaohongshu (RED) Design Week for the 2026 Shanghai International Flower Festival, held from April 18th to May 10th, 2026. The expanded festival brought gardens beyond traditional exhibition grounds and into shopping districts, parks, and streets across two main venues and ten sub-venues throughout Shanghai.
The pavilion was installed at the Huangpu main venue in Xintiandi among more than forty themed gardens. The festival received approximately 29.5 million visits. Within the dense urban setting, Infinite Grove uses a compact footprint to create an interior that appears much larger than its physical dimensions.
two curved mirrored-steel walls create the pavilion’s endless landscape
A Chinese garden of framed views and borrowed scenery
The design draws on two principles of the classical Chinese garden: framed views (kuangjing) and borrowed scenery (jiejing). These are used as spatial strategies rather than historical references. Traditional gardens often use a small doorway or window to frame a landscape beyond its apparent scale. Infinite Grove applies the same approach through its circular entrance, withholding the full view until the visitor enters.
Here, the borrowed scenery is the tree itself. Reflections extend it beyond the limits of the site, turning a pavilion only a few steps across into a forest-like interior.
the real tree becomes difficult to distinguish from its reflections
Curved mirrored steel, frosted panels, and a living tree
The pavilion uses a compact material palette of curved mirrored steel, frosted panels, and a single living tree. The mirrored walls create the repeated landscape, while the frosted panels filter daylight and soften the interior.
The structure is prefabricated in a factory and requires no foundations. On site, it is simply positioned in place, limiting its impact on the ground. The completed pavilion can be transported on a single truck, allowing the entire structure to move between locations.
a circular opening frames a partial view of the interior
Chang Hao Studio composes A pavilion that travels
Infinite Grove is designed as a mobile installation, with its central tree changing according to the season and setting. At the flower festival in spring, a flowering azalea stood at the center, its blossoms multiplying across the mirrored walls to create a forest of color.
For its second site in summer, the azalea was replaced by an olive tree. Its silver-green foliage and twisting trunk gave the reflected landscape a lighter character. The structure remained unchanged, while the different tree produced a new spatial and visual environment.
The pavilion continues to travel through Shanghai as a mobile installation, with each new tree reshaping the forest created inside the two mirrored walls.

Netherlands pushes EU action to safeguard ICC from further US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:14:59 UTC
23:14:59 KST

The Netherlands has asked the European Commission to prepare a "blocking statute" to protect the International Criminal Court (ICC) from possible further US sanctions, the foreign minister said on Wednesday.
In an interview with Dutch daily De Volkskrant on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York, Tom Berendsen expressed his concern over continued pressure on the ICC and court officials.
He said new sanctions are possible. "We are preparing for anything."
"Within the European Union, we stand strong together, but outside of it, there are individual countries that feel the US is increasing the pressure, and they cannot simply ignore that," said Berendsen.
His remarks came after The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that US President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to implement expansive economic sanctions against the court.
Saying that the US has never supported the court, Berendsen added there is now a "massive" hardening of attitudes that could make the institution’s functioning impossible.
"We will do everything we can to protect the court," he noted.
Berendsen added: "The Netherlands has asked the European Commission to prepare the blocking statute so that we can deploy that drastic measure. We are prepared to use it."
What is blocking statute?
The blocking statute is a legal mechanism designed to protect EU companies and individuals from the extraterritorial application of specific third-country laws, primarily secondary sanctions imposed by the US.
"The blocking statute is the last resort we have. As long as we can protect the ICC in other ways, we will do so," he said.
Berendsen noted that drastic measures should not be used just to send a signal, as it could lead to the situation "escalating even further."
Last month, the US imposed sanctions targeting ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye. This move sparked backlash across European countries, including the UK, France and Germany, as well as from the presidents of the European Council and European Commission.
The measures are part of sanctions against the ICC imposed by US President Donald Trump in February 2025.
The ICC said nine of its 18 judges, both deputy prosecutors, its former prosecutor and one staff member are currently under US sanctions.

US-backed board unveils $2.45B Gaza reconstruction plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:14:00 UTC
23:14:00 KST

The U.S.-backed Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion, six-month plan Wednesday to begin rebuilding devastated Gaza and establish Palestinian governance, as political deadlock continues to stall implementation of President Donald Trump’s cease-fire framework.
At a meeting of the group’s board, the governors unveiled a 66-project blueprint to get things started while acknowledging enormous hurdles that must still be overcome. The projects include ambitious infrastructure, education and health initiatives that are designed to support Trump’s 20-point plan to end the Israel-Hamas war.
"The need is immense,” the board said, noting that full reconstruction from the physical damage across Gaza will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next 10 years.
The cease-fire, which took effect on Oct. 10, was meant to clear the way for a broader process to rebuild Gaza under the guidance of the Board of Peace. The plan included additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas, the arrival of an international peacekeeping force and a new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory’s day-to-day affairs. It also envisioned an ambitious program for rebuilding war-ravaged Gaza.
But the U.S.-backed plan has largely stalled. While the cease-fire halted the heaviest Israeli attacks and humanitarian conditions have improved, the Israeli military has expanded its control of Gaza and now occupies some 60% of the territory and continues to kill civilians. Hamas has not given up its weapons. The international military force and new government still have not entered Gaza, and reconstruction has not begun. The vast majority of Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes.
The board’s high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said progress hinges largely on Hamas disarming - a step the group has refused to take so far. But he also has pressed Israel to scale back its attacks.
A key question the board faces today will be not only laying out plans for reconstruction, but a timeline for the deployment of the international force and new government, plans to disarm and bringing badly needed building materials into the territory.

Al-Sharaa vows Golan Heights will remain Syrian in UN speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:11:01 UTC
23:11:01 KST

At an Atlantic Council panel the day before, the Syrian president said he openly told Trump he had no right to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the Golan, quipping that the US president should give New Jersey to Israel instead.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa vowed in front of the UN General Assembly Wednesday that the Golan Heights region will remain Syrian despite Israel's claims over the strategically important territory.
"Any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law, will be stopped. Golan will remain Syrian territories," al-Sharaa said at the UN meeting of world leaders in New York.
The US had been the only country to recognise Israel's annexation of the Golan Heights in 1981, which it captured from Syria in 1967, until Colombia's new hard-right government in August recognised Israel's claim.
The UN maintains that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation, previously declaring Israel's 1981 annexation of the territory "null and void".
In July UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that the Golan Heights were part of Syria, describing Israeli occupation as "totally unacceptable".
Al-Sharaa also used his second turn at the UN rostrum since ousting former dictator Bashar al-Assad in a blitz offensive in December 2024 to denounce repeated Israeli strikes on his country.
"Israel is launching attacks against Syria. There have been 500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions, and 300 detentions. This is at odds with the orientation we're seeing at global level," he said.
"It is reminiscent of a era that we thought was long gone."
Yet Al-Sharaa held out hope that "the opportunity for peace and security is available to those who wish to live in peace, a just peace that maintains the rights of all."
Golan Heights — or Jersey City Heights?
Speaking at an Atlantic Council panel in New York on Tuesday, moderated by former senior US national security official Brett McGurk, al-Sharaa recounted telling US President Donald Trump directly that he had no right to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights.
"Why don't you give New Jersey to the Israelis?" al-Sharaa said he told the US president.
"You don't own the Golan Heights to give it to them, but you own New Jersey, and I believe New Jersey is full of Democrats, and they are not voting for Trump," al-Sharaa quipped.
"So it will be good to give it to the Israelis. At least this is something that you own."
"The Golan has its people," al-Sharaa told McGurk, who served under four US presidents including Trump, adding that neither the Syrian nor the US president had the right to cede it.
Trump — who has openly shown his admiration for al-Sharaa — formally recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights in 2019 during his first term.
Al-Sharaa derived his nom de guerre Abu Mohammad al-Jolani from his family's origins in the Golan.
At the Atlantic Council panel, al-Sharaa said Syria and Israel had held several rounds of direct talks, some facilitated by the US, and had reached "almost 90% of agreements" before Israel pulled back or introduced new conditions.
"It's not appropriate that what happened on 7 October set Israeli policy for Syria," he said. "Israel needs to change its policy because it's creating problems around it in order to maintain its security."
He accused Israel of twice bombing Syria's presidential palace and targeting airports since he came to power in December 2024.
"Since the fall of the former regime, Israel is repeating its attacks and aggressions against Syria. It is occupying new territories, territories that have been occupied after 8 December 2024," al-Sharaa said.
"Will that bring security to Israeli citizens? I believe the problem is with Israel, not with Syria."

Defeat against North Korea is unacceptable to me: Abdi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:10:55 UTC
23:10:55 KST

Defeat against North Korea is unacceptable to me: Abdi
TEHRAN - Hossein Abdi, head coach of Iran’s U23 football team, described his side’s heavy and unexpected defeat to North Korea as unacceptable.
Iran had taken the lead against North Korea at the Asian Games, but eventually suffered a 4–1 defeat and were eliminated in the group stage after finishing below North Korea on goal difference, missing out on a place in the quarterfinals.
“First and foremost, I apologize to my dear people. This result is unacceptable to me. This is the first time we have faced such a result in an official match at this level. I believed we could achieve a different result,” Abdi said.
“We could have produced any other result—except this one! I apologize to everyone who expected and believed that we could advance to the next stage,” he added.
The Iran U23 coach criticized his players’ mentality, saying: “My feeling is that the players entered the game with the mindset that we had already secured qualification for the next round. But, to be fair, North Korea were one of the teams we expected to face a difficult game against from the outset. The Koreans played very good football, and they deserve congratulations.”
“It is disappointing because we could have maintained our advantage in what appeared to be one of the toughest groups of the tournament—a group in which it was unclear until the final day which teams would advance. Unfortunately, we were unable to produce the performance we expected today or earn the points we needed. In any case, this is my apology to my dear people.”
“I hope we can do better in the future and that this experience will help us take a better path. The players need to understand that nothing is decided before a match is over, and no result is certain until the final whistle,” Abdi concluded.

The Cabinet of Ministers has appointed Olena Kramarenko, who previously served as first deputy minister of environmental protection and natural resources of Ukraine, deputy minister of economy and environment.
According to a government resolution published on its website, the prime minister's order appointing her is dated September 9.
According to the Economy Ministry's website, Kramarenko has more than 20 years of experience in environmental protection and public administration. On Taiwan, US ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Is Not Dead Yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.
To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.” Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.”
Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.
Trump has repeatedly made four points about Taiwan, all of which call into question a robust U.S. response to military action by Beijing. The first is that Taiwan is vastly smaller and less important than China. Second, he says Taiwan is indefensible – too close to China and far from the United States. Third, Trump thinks Taiwan free-rides on U.S. defense. Finally, he complains about Taiwan allegedly stealing America’s semiconductor industry. Shortly before he took office for the second time, Trump said he would respond to a Chinese invasion of Taiwan with economic sanctions.
On top of this, Trump avoids antagonizing Beijing over the Taiwan issue, presumably to clear the way for a China-U.S. bilateral economic deal. During his keynote speech at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not mention Taiwan, a change from his speech the previous year. The unclassified version of the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy also does not mention Taiwan by name.
After his May 2026 meeting with Xi Jinping, Trump criticized the Taiwan government for allegedly flirting with independence due to the presumption of U.S. support. “[W]e’re not looking to have somebody say, ‘Let’s go independent because the United States is backing us,’” he told Fox News.
For good measure, Trump announced that he was delaying a large arms sale to Taiwan already approved by Congress, calling such sales a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with China. He also dismissed the Six Assurances, part of U.S. policy toward Taiwan since the Reagan era.
The idea that strategic ambiguity has lost its usefulness, however, is wrong. Despite particular statements by Trump that are adverse to Taiwan, U.S. policy remains broadly supportive of Taipei.
The Pentagon’s 2026 National Defense Strategy said the United States will “erect” and “sustain a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain.” Even a cursory look at a map indicates that aspiration is meaningless without a U.S. intent to prevent China from absorbing Taiwan.
The large arms sale is delayed, but not canceled. This latest package of armaments is all business, not symbolic. It includes weapons systems appropriate for the scenario of an attempted amphibious invasion by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA): HIMARS rockets, ATACMS missiles, ALTIUS loitering munition drones, Javelin and TOW anti-tank missiles, and mobile howitzers.
U.S. military transits through the Taiwan Strait continue, albeit about half as often as during Trump’s first term.
U.S. security cooperation with the Philippines and Japan, highly relevant to deterring China from moving aggressively against Taiwan, has deepened during the second Trump administration.
The United States got access to, and set aside funding to develop infrastructure in, additional base sites in the northern Philippines, close to the Taiwan Strait. The annual Balikatan military exercises were larger than ever before in 2025 and 2026 and brought in Japan and Australia. U.S. forces deployed NMESIS and Typhon missile systems to the Philippines. The stridency of China’s complaints about these deployments indicate they present problems for Chinese planners.
Washington’s plan to upgrade U.S. Forces Japan to a joint force combat headquarters has proceeded under Trump’s second administration. U.S. and Japanese armed forces increased their interoperability in 2025 and 2026 through more integrated command-and-control structures, more complex joint exercises, and more sharing of data. The United States started supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Japan. Washington and Tokyo are engaged in serious discussions about Japan producing warships or components for the U.S. Navy to help it close the gap with China’s production.
Strategic ambiguity still holds because what look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
The stances of the Joe Biden presidency and the second Trump administration are different. Biden said on four occasions that the United States would militarily intervene in a cross-strait war, placing him close to an unambiguous pre-commitment to intervention. Trump is closer to the other end, a pre-commitment to non-intervention.
Both, however, represent forms of strategic ambiguity. One president seemed committed and the other reluctant, but who knows what either of them would actually decide to do at crunch time. Beijing still cannot confidently assume a Trump-led United States would not intervene in a Taiwan scenario despite Trump seemingly indicating reticence to do so.
Chinese analysts consider Trump to be unpredictable. They cannot be sure he will act in a way consistent with his past statements. The Chinese remember how quickly Trump turned on them in 2020. In January, he said “our relationship with China now might be the best it’s been in a long, long time.” Later in the year, largely over the COVID-19 pandemic, Trump regularly berated China with statements such as “I’m very angry at China” and “The world is now suffering as a result of the malfeasance of the Chinese government.”
There are, nevertheless, reasons to doubt the American commitment to defend Taiwan, and these reasons go beyond the current U.S. presidential administration.
First, the demographic trend in the United States is increasingly anti-war. Gen Z Americans, born 1997-2012, are significantly less fearful of China attaining a stronger global position and less likely to see China as an adversary. The succession of unpopular wars against Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran further strengthens the aversion of Americans toward getting embroiled in foreign conflicts.
Second, the costs and risks of maintaining U.S. strategic pre-eminence on the western Pacific Rim against the determination of China to achieve regional supremacy are rising. The United States already dominates the Western Hemisphere. The rationale for dominating the Asia-Pacific, as well, is that doing so makes war less likely and opens the door for U.S. commerce. This rationale is less persuasive, however, if China supports international trade and if opposing China’s aspirations for “rejuvenation” makes war more rather than less likely.
Military analyst Jennifer Kavanaugh’s September 10 proposal for a “Second Island Chain strategy” attracted much attention. Kavanaugh, a member of the “restrainer” camp in U.S. foreign policy, argued that to reduce the risk of war with China while still protecting the most vital U.S. interests, Washington should end its alliances with Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines, pull most of its military forces out of the region, and announce that it will not intervene to protect Taiwan in a cross-strait war. Expect arguments such as this to grow in volume and frequency.
Finally, the U.S. defense industrial base is currently unable to compete with China’s productivity. This weakness is not easily fixed, even with an increased defense budget. As the modernization of its armed forces have made China a near-peer adversary of the United States, China’s advantage in manufacturing capacity becomes potentially decisive in a theoretical China-U.S. war.
Recent wargaming suggests both China and the U.S. would suffer huge losses in a conflict. Even where the U.S. “wins,” China is better placed to quickly rebuild and rearm its forces, giving Beijing hope that it would prevail in a second round. If American leaders conclude the math leaves them without a path to victory, they will reconsider whether an intervention is feasible.
But for now, Beijing would be reckless not to assume that both the United States and Japan would militarily oppose an attempt to conquer Taiwan. And Xi is not reckless.

EU Commission poised to formally back Albania's 2027 accession deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:06:01 UTC
23:06:01 KST

The Commission is set to formally back Albania's 2027 accession deadline in a new roadmap, which is also due to include a list of key deliverables Tirana will have to prioritise to complete the process by the end of next year.
The European Commission is working towards closing the books on Albania's accession process by December 2027 — a timeline Tirana has long touted, and that is now set to receive formal recognition in the EU's upcoming enlargement roadmaps, EU officials told Euronews.
The Commission is preparing a roadmap to confirm Albania's stated goal of closing all negotiating chapters by the end of next year, and to lay out priority deliverables to plug the remaining accession gaps.
Albania has set the end of 2027 as its target for completing accession negotiations, a timetable Prime Minister Edi Rama and other senior officials have repeatedly described as an agreed plan with the European Commission.
But while Commission officials have backed the ambition, the EU executive does not typically set deadlines for accession, since enlargement is meant to be a merits-based process.
"As you know, enlargement doesn't work with dates. But the more the country is coming towards the end of the technical part of the accession, the more we can say about it or the more we can use the years," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in July.
That is set to change soon. In her State of the Union address to the European Parliament last week, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a series of "roadmaps" for candidate countries.
"We will soon be proposing roadmaps for the candidates that have made most progress," von der Leyen said, mentioning Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans as countries whose future lies in the EU.
The roadmaps are expected to set out an indicative timeline to give candidate countries a clearer sense of direction, echoing the 2002 enlargement strategy that paved the way for the "Big Bang" accession of 10 new members.
The roadmaps will be folded into the Commission's enlargement package, its annual health check on the accession process, expected in late October, which also includes country-specific assessments and recommendations for next steps.
In this context, the Commission is drafting a closing benchmark assessment report that assesses whether a candidate country has met the benchmarks set for it to be considered to have met accession requirements, notably in justice and the rule of law, the so-called "fundamentals."
In Albania's case, the plan is to include a list of key deliverables spelling out the reforms and measures needed to close the remaining benchmark gaps.
That was already the case for Montenegro, where the Commission used the closing-benchmark process to pin down the concrete reforms and results it needed to deliver.
The deliverables list is meant to clearly signal to candidate countries where the priorities lie, pushing them to complete the missing steps.
"Essentially, the Commission saw that this approach worked well with Montenegro and they want to replicate it," an EU official told Euronews, asking to remain anonymous given the sensitivity of the discussion.

TAF Industries signed a joint-venture memorandum with Danish firm Upteko for production but says bureaucracy is slowing the process. Meanwhile, Resist.UA agreed to invest in BlueShadow, a Danish maritime-defense startup whose founder commanded a US nuclear submarine and whose engineering team works largely in Ukraine, Defender Media reported.
Ukraine's defense industry has outgrown much of its own 2022-era hardware in two years of rapid wartime iteration, but a government fee of 20-30% on export permits and over 200 stalled co-production bids have left the country's foreign arms sales far behind battlefield demand. Deals like the two in Denmark route Ukrainian technology into allied markets without waiting for Kyiv's export apparatus to catch up.
Ukrainian first-person-view drones, made on Danish soil
Drone maker TAF Industries plans to produce its first batch in Denmark by the end of 2026, through a joint venture with local firm Upteko. The two signed a memorandum in August 2026, but paperwork on both sides has slowed things down.
"We need to pass a fairly large number of bureaucratic procedures to make it possible," chief business development officer Mykhailo Diachenko told NordicDefenceWatch.
He called the year-end target reachable, "though maybe it will look more like a miracle."
TAF wants footholds in other countries that support Ukraine. It has started the process in Norway and is negotiating with Sweden's Recas. Diachenko said the goal is local production plus sharing Ukrainian combat experience and technology with European partners. TAF builds FPV drones, with capacity near 1 million units a year.
A Ukrainian fund bets on Odesa's sea defense
Ukrainian fund Resist.UA signed a letter of intent to invest an undisclosed sum in Danish maritime-defense startup BlueShadow's €2 million ($2.29 million) pre-seed round, the company announced. BlueShadow's software collects data from maritime sensors, commercial feeds, and open sources, merges them into a single operational picture, and uses AI to detect threats, Defender Media reported.
The company has also built an open software platform it says can help intercept Shahed-type drones. BlueSentry, designed to protect ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, is one product that the company plans to launch in the Baltic and North seas in October. BlueDragon, now in prototype testing with Defense Ministry certification targeted for late 2026 and deployment planned for spring 2027, is designed to defend Odesa with autonomous swarms of armed sea drones meant to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Founder Charles Maher is a former US Navy submarine commander who ran a nuclear-powered boat, Defender Media reported. Almost his entire engineering team works in Ukraine, drawing on more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers. Resist.UA this summer launched Resist 2.0, an Estonia-based fund aiming to raise €50 million for Ukrainian defense-tech companies.

‘Free zones ready to take on country’s major economic missions’
TEHRAN- CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization said that free zones are ready to take on country’s major economic missions.
Mohammad Kabiri, expressing appreciation for the efforts of the country’s officials to achieve an honorable peace and also for the resistance of the Iranian nation, stated: “We hope that with the measures taken, the shadow of war will be removed from the country, and we will be able to pursue the path of development and progress with greater calm.”
Kabiri also thanked Hossein Forouzan, Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade-Industrial and Special Economic Zones, for his presence and continuous follow-ups, and added: “In this opportunity, I want us to first take a look at the experience of free zones in the world and see what achievements these zones have brought for their countries, what characteristics they have, and if we want to use these experiences and global best practices, what challenges we face in Iran and what the executive solution is.”
Referring to the extent of free zones in the world, he stated: “More than 169 countries in the world have free zones and special zones, and there are more than 6,000 free and special economic zones in the world, whose total exports reach about $3.5 trillion. These figures show that free zones play a significant role in the global economy.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization continued: “Successful free zones in the world have numerous common characteristics, and about 65 features and indicators have been identified in these zones. We have also reviewed the world’s top 50 free zones and identified their characteristics, among which five very important issues are seen as driving factors for the development of free zones and as laying the groundwork for increasing their share in the national economies of countries.”
Kabiri said: “The first characteristic is tax exemptions, the second is customs facilities, the third is special bank credit lines and dedicated banks, the fourth is support for the innovation sector, and finally, the most important issue, is managerial independence and the authorities that exist in many successful free zones of the world.”
He added: “Incidentally, our legislator has also envisaged such authorities for free zones in Article 65, but this article is not fully implemented. In many free zones of the world, healthcare, education, and other public infrastructure were first created, and then the regulatory system and laws distinct from the mainland were implemented in these zones.”
Referring to the experience of China’s Shenzhen Free Zone, the CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization stated: “Shenzhen covers only about two-hundredths of one percent of China’s area and houses about one-thirtieth of the country’s population, but its export value reaches about $383 billion, which is about 10 percent of China’s exports.”
Kabiri noted: “An important feature of free zones in the world is that they act as governance sandboxes. In these zones, more than a thousand reform measures in the field of governance have been implemented, and among these measures, China’s central government transferred 164 successful ones that could be generalized to the mainland to the entire country. Free zones can be places for testing new policies in areas such as energy and governance.”
He then referred to the experience of the free zones of the United Arab Emirates and Dubai and said: “In southern Iran, several free zones are also active in Dubai, including JAFZA in Jebel Ali and the Dubai International Financial Center. JAFZA is one of the most important logistics free zones in West Asia, and the Dubai International Financial Center is one of the most important financial free zones in the Middle East, with more than $240 billion in assets under management and having issued more than $150 billion in securities over the past 10 years.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization continued: “The important feature of these zones is also three issues: independent management and regulation, the existence of an independent and specialized judicial system, and also specialized and supportive credit lines for entities operating in these zones.”
Kabiri, raising the question of whether the world’s experience can be used to reform the situation of Iran’s free zones, said: “The answer is definitely positive. Article 65 of the Free Zones Law was formed precisely on the basis of this global experience, but unfortunately, this article is not fully implemented.”
He stated: “More than half of the time of free zone managers is spent on conflict and interaction with other bodies, while this time should be spent on driving, developmental work, and carrying out national missions. If Article 65 is implemented clearly and completely in free zones, many existing challenges will be solvable.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization described taxation and social security as one of the main challenges of free zones and said: “Free zones do not have one rial of government budget, and their resources are supplied from their own revenues. However, since 1401, taxes are also collected from free zones.”
Kabiri added: “A business operating in a free zone must, on the one hand, pay taxes to the central government, and on the other hand, must also pay duties, while the philosophy of free zones is that part of the resources generated in the zone should be spent on the development of that same zone.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization considered the lack of a dedicated bank to be another fundamental problem of free zones and said: “We do not have a dedicated bank, and during the war I realized more what a great injustice has been done to free zones in not having such a capacity.”
Kabiri continued: “When credit resources reach the provinces, free zones practically receive no share of them, because it is said that free zones have their own resources. As a result, instead of becoming a development capacity, free zones have faced an anti-development process in the banking and credit sector.”
He proposed: “Given that 19 free zones have now been formed in the country, creating a dedicated bank for free zones can be one of the important solutions to solve the financing problem of these zones.”The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization, emphasizing the importance of implementing Article 65 in the customs and trade sector, stated: “One strange example of the existing restrictions is that from many parts of the world it is possible to send a postal parcel to Tehran, but from Kish there is a restriction on sending a parcel to the mainland.”
Kabiri said: “You can send a postal parcel from Washington and Tokyo to Tehran, but from Kish such a possibility faces restrictions. For about 6 months, we have been following up on this issue in the corridors of the government.”
He also described privatization and the revenue model of free zones as other important issues and said: “One of our revenue axes should be investment by investment companies and the profit from it, but free zones are accused of land selling.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization added: “The only thing that can change this paradigm and move free zones toward sustainable revenues is the use of micro duties and profits from investment. But in this part, we also face problems.”
Kabiri stated: “On the issue of vehicle duties, the State Tax Organization has intervened, and on the issue of investment profits, the Privatization Organization has intervened, while the government had no role in these investments. Even the resources generated from investment, instead of being reinvested in the zone itself for redevelopment, are supposed to go to the treasury.”
Emphasizing that solving these problems can change the position of free zones in the country’s economy, he said: “If the super-challenge of implementing Article 65 is solved and the five main challenges of free zones in various areas are removed, Iran’s free zones can take on national missions like the successful free zones of the world.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization continued: “We can carry out major missions for the country in the areas of financing, logistics, and the digital economy. The country needs about $300 billion in financing, and if this figure is to be provided with the best performance and by benchmarking examples such as DIFC and Shenzhen, it may take decades. Therefore, free zones can take on part of this burden.”
Kabiri, referring to the performance of this zone in wartime conditions, said: “In the two recent wars, we tried not to stop our activities. Rail investment increased sevenfold, the imbalance reached zero, 11 hectares of land were reclaimed, and the problem of more than 18 vessels and about 10,000 billion tomans of problems were solved in the same period.”
He added: “Kish Airport and Port have also ranked first among these achievements.”
-------------------Request for immediate support for Kish businesses
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization, referring to the pressures imposed on businesses in southern Iran and especially Kish, stated: “I kiss the hands of all businesses in southern Iran, especially Kish businesses. These businesses have been under pressure for 9 months, and their conditions have become extremely difficult.”
Kabiri continued: “At one point, we had no flights for 80 days, but the bazaar merchants did not turn off the lights of their shops even for one day, even though they knew that no airplane would land at Kish Airport.”
He added: “We held a festival, and from the day we started the festival until today, tourist growth has increased fivefold, but despite all efforts, we have just reached one-tenth of last year’s number of tourists.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization, stating that the resilience of businesses in southern free zones has reached worrying limits, said: “This 9-month resistance of businesses must be taken into account so that economic pressure does not turn into a security-threatening incident. Some islands have become almost empty, but the people and businesses still stand by Iran.”
Kabiri proposed: “If deemed appropriate, a special representative of the president for the southern islands should be appointed to specially follow up on the issues and problems of these areas.”
He also called for immediate decisions in the areas of taxation, social security, banking, and customs, and said: “Our specific proposal is that, for damaged businesses, taxes and social security should not be collected for three months; we do not mean forgiveness, but deferral of payment so that businesses can stand on their own feet again.”
The CEO of Kish Free Zone Organization added: “The Central Bank must also remove, for free zones, the banking restrictions that have been lifted in some provinces. Also, in the customs area, permission must be given for goods warehoused in Kish to leave the zone for a specified period.”
Kabiri continued: “Because last year the tourism record in Kish was broken, many businesses procured goods, but now these goods are warehoused in Kish. For about four months, this issue has been followed up in the government, and it has even now been raised in the Reconstruction Headquarters.”

Ryanair CEO O’Leary says no fuel surcharge despite rising jet fuel price uncertainty

Ryanair Group CEO Michael O’Leary said the airline “will not levy a fuel surcharge” on passengers despite higher jet fuel prices, though he predicted competitors could introduce additional charges and forecast further consolidation in the aviation sector as rising fuel costs pressure weaker airlines, he told reporters on Wednesday.
O’Leary said airfares may need to rise by 10%, 15%, or even 20% next summer if oil prices remain at their current elevated levels in the coming months.
“Most of the airlines were well hedged into the summer of 2026, and therefore we absorb the kind of shock of the much higher oil prices this summer,” O’Leary told reporters. However, he said those hedging agreements are now expiring, meaning airlines will face higher fuel costs going into next year, which will likely be passed on to customers through higher fares and fuel surcharges.
He said Ryanair would not impose a fuel surcharge on passengers next summer, while taking aim at competitors that may do so.
O’Leary also said he hoped jet fuel prices would rise further next year, as this would accelerate consolidation in the European aviation market by putting additional pressure on struggling airlines.
O’Leary predicts airline consolidation as Ryanair targets further growth
“I very much hope that jet [fuel] prices will rise faster into next year because that will accelerate the extent to which other airlines will fail,” O’Leary said.
“Airlines who are currently loss-making will fail. It will accelerate the consolidation of Europe into four large airlines: BA [British Airways], Lufthansa, Air France, and Ryanair,” he added.
Looking ahead, O’Leary said Ryanair expects continued growth, with the airline targeting 200 million passengers by fiscal year 2028. He also said the company expects to begin accepting deliveries of 15 Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft in the spring, following anticipated certification of the aircraft in the coming weeks.

Canada on Wednesday announced new sanctions against Iranian officials and entities over the government’s alleged repression of its population, targeting those accused of digital surveillance and other rights abuses.
In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said Foreign Minister Anita Anand “today announced that Canada is imposing additional sanctions against five individuals and five entities under the Special Economic Measures (Iran) Regulations for their role in the Iranian regime’s brutal repression of its population.”
The statement said the sanctioned individuals and entities, including senior Iranian security and government officials, were allegedly involved in “digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation” aimed at suppressing dissent.

Since October 2022, Canada has imposed 24 rounds of sanctions against 237 Iranian individuals and 265 entities under related measures.

Czech journalists lure Russian propaganda project Rybar’s film crew to Prague to expose influence operation across Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:02:41 UTC
23:02:41 KST

The Czech outlet Seznam Zprávy has exposed an operation by the Russian propaganda project Rybar to film a documentary series in Europe. The publication’s journalists lured a film crew working for Rybar from Berlin to a meeting in Prague and conducted secret recordings before identifying themselves and asking questions. The two Russians then ran off in different directions. The investigation identified them and determined that the Rybar project had conducted interviews in several European countries.
According to Seznam Zprávy, the operation began with an attempt by Rybar to interview Czech media literacy expert Bohumil Kartous, a representative of the Czech Elves volunteer group, which monitors and counters disinformation online. A person using a Russian phone number contacted Kartous on WhatsApp and introduced himself as a producer for the project.
“My name is Boris. I am a producer at the Rybar analytical center,” he wrote. Seznam Zprávy’s journalists decided to use the invitation and arranged a meeting together with Kartous.
Vitaliy and Igor arrive from Berlin
The interview was scheduled in Prague’s Letná district, near the site where a monument to Stalin once stood. The film crew was not there at the agreed time, but Kartous soon received a message from a German number saying the team had been delayed on the road from Berlin.
Two men soon appeared and introduced themselves as Vitaliy and Igor. One of them made a point of telling Kartous that he had held a German residence permit for more than 10 years.
Vitaliy did not want to say much more about himself or who had commissioned the filming. “I don’t know. I was hired to do an interview,” he repeated, not knowing that the conversation was already being recorded by a hidden camera. At one point, however, he directly named the client: “It’s the Rybar project. You might know it. It’s Rybar.”
Seznam Zprávy journalists then approached the crew. They identified themselves and asked the men to give their full names and to explain why they had come to Prague. The reaction was unexpected: neither answered, and both ran off in different directions.
One of the men who fled was a correspondent for Russian TV channels
Using photographs, the journalists later identified both men. The cameraman was Igor Dolmatov, and his colleague was Vitaliy Chashchukhin, a Russian living in Germany. Chashchukhin works with the pro-Kremlin Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV — Russian media outlets that are under EU sanctions.
In his reports from Germany, Chashchukhin has portrayed the country as being in economic decline, reporting on empty store shelves and presenting an end to Berlin’s military aid to Ukraine and its restoration of relations with Russia as solutions to the economic problems he purports to show. It was Chashchukhin who confirmed on hidden camera in Prague that the filming was being done on behalf of Rybar, a major Russian pro-war Telegram project with more than 1.5 million subscribers.
Rybar openly describes its work as participation in an information war:
“Our team is at the forefront of the information war today and defends the interests of the Russian Federation. We know how to wage an information war easily and effectively and to present Russia in the correct light.”
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk is under EU sanctions, and the European documents note that Vladimir Putin appointed Zvinchuk to a working group created in December 2022 to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts for the war against Ukraine. In 2024, the U.S. Rewards for Justice program offered up to $10 million for information about Rybar employees over their role in influence operations and interference in the U.S. presidential election. According to the U.S. authorities, the project was previously funded by entities linked to Wagner Group co-founder Yevgeny Prigozhin and later received funding from Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec.
Filming organizer had ties to a foundation headed by SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin
Seznam Zprávy identified the person who organized the interviews as “Boris.” The profile picture on his WhatsApp account showed a smiling young man, and using leaked Russian databases, the journalists determined that the account belonged to Boris Dvorkin, a Moscow-based documentary filmmaker who had not previously been publicly linked to Rybar.
Dvorkin presents himself primarily as a producer of historical projects, but Seznam Zprávy found that he had ties to the History of the Fatherland Foundation, which supported an exhibition he organized titled “The Proletarian Flies Over Europe.” The foundation was established by decree of Vladimir Putin and is chaired by Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, or SVR.
Dvorkin’s questions for Czech interviewees, however, were not about history. He planned to ask Kartous, for example, whether right-wing and Euroskeptic ideas were becoming more popular in the Czech Republic, whether relations with Russia could be normalized, and what the Czech Republic and “the Western world as a whole” would have to do to make that happen.
He was also particularly interested in disinformation. “Anything that does not fit into one’s personal information bubble or system of specific political values is declared to be disinformation,” he argued. Kartous said the questions appeared designed to portray disinformation as a universal phenomenon “on both sides of the border,” rather than something directly linked to Russian propaganda, and to cast doubt on the Czech Republic’s sovereignty within the EU.
The Russian film crews traveled across Europe
After the Prague meeting, the Czech journalists established that this was not a one-off shoot. Even before the operation was exposed, Dvorkin had written to Kartous: “Our film crew was delayed in Slovakia, so we won’t be returning to the Czech Republic until next week.” Seznam Zprávy obtained a list of seven other Czech interviewees whom the project planned to approach. Some confirmed that filming had taken place.
Among them was Andor Šándor, a former head of Czech military intelligence who now works as a security expert. He said a man and a woman came to interview him and introduced themselves as people from Berlin. They did not tell him about any connection to Rybar.
“They told me they were from Berlin. I was surprised that they were willing to come for a quick visit. A man and a woman. They arrived and I had the feeling that their English had a Russian accent. They wanted to talk about the EU and the Czech Republic’s stance, but suddenly they started firing off questions about the Ukraine-Russia war,” Šándor said. After the filming, he withdrew permission to use the interview because he feared his remarks could be edited in a biased manner.
Šándor remembered the woman in the film crew by name: Margarita Kostiv. Journalists determined that she works with Chashchukhin and has worked for sanctioned Russian media outlets. Two months earlier, for example, Kostiv had produced a report for REN TV from Paris about Ukrainian troops taking part in the Bastille Day parade.
Kostiv did not respond to questions from Seznam Zprávy.
Rybar’s list of interviewees included an MEP, a political scientist, and a former intelligence chief
Other prominent Czechs appeared on the list of potential or completed interview subjects. They included sociologist Petr Hampl, who said Rybar representatives had not contacted him and that he had “not spoken to journalists from Russia for years.”
Also on the list were SPD member of the European Parliament Ivan David and political scientist Petr Drulák. They declined to say whether they had given interviews to the film crew. “Write whatever you like. Goodbye,” David told the journalists.
Energy expert Vladimir Štěpán, who has repeatedly spoken out in opposition to European sanctions against Russia and in favor of importing Russian energy supplies, confirmed that filming had taken place. He said the interviewers introduced themselves as “international television,” though a text message sent before the meeting said they were from Rybar.
“They were filming in nine or 10 countries. They came from Vienna and travelled to Bratislava. It was an international team. A kind of boss and a couple of young guys,” Štěpán said.
Another potential interviewee was found in Slovakia, where journalist and translator Samo Marec was invited to take part but declined. “I didn’t respond to their email. I’m familiar with Rybar; I know what it writes. Sometimes it’s even interesting, but the overall tone is very pro-Russian, and that’s not something I’d want to be associated with,” he said.
Marec’s invitation was signed directly by sanctioned Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk. The interview was being organized by a producer who called herself Tanya Petrova. Journalists were unable to establish her true identity.
“Just helping out a colleague”
When Seznam Zprávy contacted Dvorkin after the Prague meeting, he sent a response that ran to around 30 paragraphs. In it, he claimed Chashchukhin was simply a colleague who had agreed to help with one interview in his spare time. Because the interview ultimately did not take place and Chashchukhin allegedly received no payment, Dvorkin argued that no sanctions violation had occurred.
He also denied sending other film crews around Europe. However, that statement contradicted both his own messages before the exposure and accounts from people who had already been interviewed.
Work for Rybar could violate sanctions
A separate question is whether the film crews’ activities were legal.
The Czech Financial Analytical Office, or FAÚ, which is responsible for sanctions enforcement, declined to comment on the specific case. However, Czech Finance Ministry spokesperson Gabriela Krušinová said that if a sanctioned individual controls an organization, then providing services to that organization can be considered an indirect provision of economic resources to the sanctioned person.
Violating sanctions in the Czech Republic can carry criminal liability and result in a fine of up to 50 million Czech koruna.
Sanctions expert Jiří Skuhrovec of DatLab said a court’s decision could not be predicted in advance but that “given the scale, it could constitute a criminal offense.” In the most serious scenario, participants in the operation could theoretically face up to eight years in prison, according to Seznam Zprávy.
The Russians identified by the journalists as taking part in the filming did not have to enter the EU specifically for the assignment. Chashchukhin said he had held a German residence permit for more than 10 years, while other participants were also based in Europe. That allowed the crews to travel freely within the Schengen Area and to gather material in several countries for a project whose founder is under EU sanctions.

====================================================================================================

There are no elections in Russia, only theatre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:02:20 UTC
23:02:20 KST

There are no elections in Russia, only theatre
A man in a brown bear costume greets local residents at a polling station during Russia's parliamentary and regional elections in Istra, Russia, on September 19, 2026. (Contributor/Getty Images)
Daniil Ukhorskiy
Ukraine program manager at Legal Action Worldwide
This year's most expensive theatre production took place last week. Millions of Russians (and some Ukrainians, at gunpoint) played voters.
A host of Putin's cronies embodied democratically elected politicians. The props team did excellent work: ballot papers, boxes, and TV debates (although some actors missed their cues).
Reading the headlines, one could get the false impression that Russia was experiencing a sudden democratic turn. The word "election" dominates, while most outlets eventually provide context and caveats: "tightly controlled," "devoid of opposition," "carefully engineered."
Putin staged this farce to buttress his regime.
Describing this political performance is vital, particularly as it brings with it a campaign of violence, but we must not grant Russia any veneer of legitimacy with charitable descriptions of "elections."
Language matters
In 1958, an American observer covered Soviet "elections" for the New York Times.
The piece fundamentally questioned the practice, starting with the headline: "Why the Russians Bother With Elections." The piece highlighted absurdities ("The ballot needs no "X," it can be put in the box as printed, without further effort.”) and emphasized that, despite appearance, the exercise was a complete sham.
This week's Times piece ran with the more neutral: "Why Russians Hold Elections." Unfortunately, and unwittingly, many news outlets have used language that gifts Putin the democratic facade that he is looking for.
"Forget the words “election,” “majority,” “parliamentary,” “opposition,” when discussing this week’s events in Russia."
Al Jazeera presents "authorities'" and "critics'" views side-by-side, as if there is no independent information about Russia's authoritarian system. An unsuspecting reader of its "explainer" could come away thinking that Russia has suddenly turned into a flawed, but ultimately representative democracy.
"United Russia, which is supported by President Putin, is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma," writes Steve Rosenberg, arguably the world's foremost Russia correspondent, for the BBC. Putin does not "support" United Russia, he dominates it. And does it make sense to speak of "retaining" a "constitutional majority" in a completely totalitarian state?
ABC News coverage reads like something we may expect in a few months from the U.S. midterms: neutral descriptions of turnout and information about when polls are set to close. The election is "devoid of opposition," but the main reason why (mass repression by Putin and the ruling party) is buried deep in the piece.
This is a small but representative sample of mainstream coverage.
The better pieces make it clear that Russian "elections" are a sham with caveats of varying degrees. Yet in many places they fall back on the standard register used to cover democracies: polls, ballots, constituencies — one that is entirely unsuitable to describe the performance that took place in Russia this week.
At gunpoint
In 1937, the New York Times covered an "election" organized by none other than Joseph Stalin, writing: "The totalitarian autocrats may not command the complete affections of their peoples, but they are strong enough to manipulate the dead weight of their countries; and that is a good deal."
It captured the events with moral clarity, leaving no doubt in readers' minds that Stalin instrumentalized democratic trappings for his pernicious aims.
Putin is not only seeking to project legitimacy, but is also seeking to project strength. Across occupied Ukraine, the same soldiers who terrorize civilian populations brought "ballot" boxes.
Results suggest that turnout was higher in occupied territories than in Russia, a worrying signal of intimidation campaigns and coerced "voting."
In 2023, Russia held "referenda" across occupied Ukraine, seeking to legitimize its illegal invasion and occupation. A hallmark of the process was violence against civilians, including threats, detention, and torture.
Russian coercion extends beyond occupied Ukraine. After years of killing, imprisonment, and exile of political opposition, Russian authorities still managed to find dissenters to harass in the lead-up to last week's "election."
Predictable results, mixed messages
Putin's party will keep control, and the managed "opposition" got their allotted seats. Russia's war against Ukraine will continue, and mobilization and escalated attacks against Europe may soon come. 49 Russian servicemen who fought in Ukraine are set to join the ranks of Russia’s “lawmakers.”
Independent observers noted Russia's sloppy electioneering in the fraudulent results. Russian Election Monitor, an independent organization with longstanding expertise in the area, detailed the banning of opposition parties, ballot stuffing, and aforementioned repression. Nothing about this process was a genuine election.
We should avoid rose-tinted comparisons with the past. Russia has increased domestic repression since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but rigged results are nothing new. Russia has not had a free election since at least 2008. In 2021, the most recent previous "election," the United Russia vote was fraudulently doubled.
This is a plea to any editors who will listen – forget the words "election," "majority," "parliamentary," "opposition," when discussing last week's events in Russia.
This is especially important in the age of shrinking attention spans. As editors will be well aware, most readers do not get to the end of the story (Reader, if you're here, well done).
Headlines and ledes are critical, and here, most fail to convey the total emptiness of Russia's "elections." News readers should be left with no doubts: what happened in Russia this week is a mix of political theatre and brutal oppression.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.

Most Danes want the government to temporarily cut taxes on gasoline and diesel as fuel prices reach unusually high levels, a Voxmeter poll for the Danish news agency Ritzau shows.
In September, diesel reached a record 19.19 DKK per liter at gas stations.
The poll found that 53.8 percent supported temporary tax cuts, while 33.3 percent opposed them. Another 12.9 percent did not know.
Torben Kudsk, policy chief at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ organization, said rising prices were creating serious problems for motorists.
“Fuel is historically expensive. As far as we can see, prices have not been higher in recent times,” Kudsk said.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats said the government was monitoring the situation.
“If energy prices continue to rise, and the situation develops further, we are of course ready to do more,” he wrote on Facebook. He did not describe possible measures.
The poll also asked what should guide decisions on fuel taxes. A total of 39.2 percent said reducing motorists’ costs should come first.
Another 27.2 percent said taxes should remain because of climate and environmental concerns, while 25.9 percent gave both issues equal weight. The remaining 7.7 percent did not know.
The price increases have been linked to wars and conflicts causing a global fuel shortage.

Denmark registered 502 suicides in 2025, the lowest annual number recorded from 2015 through 2025, according to the Centre for Suicide Research.
The total included 370 men and 132 women older than 15. It was 91 lower than in 2024.
Denmark’s suicide rate fell to 9.9 deaths per 100,000 people, an 18 percent decline from 2015. The rate dropped 30 percent among women and 12 percent among men.
Erik Christiansen, research head at the center, linked the decline partly to a national action plan introduced in 2024 and greater willingness to discuss suicide.
“At one time it was believed that it was dangerous to talk about suicide because it could inspire doing it. Today we know that this assumption is incorrect,” Christiansen said.
Doctors asking people directly about suicide risk can help them receive support earlier, he added.
Merete Nordentoft, a professor, chief physician and member of Denmark’s Council for Suicide Prevention, said help had become more accessible.
Suicide prevention clinics in Denmark’s five regions received additional funding to offer consultations to more people with suicidal thoughts or previous suicide attempts.
Livslinien, Denmark’s national suicide prevention helpline, received about 28,000 inquiries in 2025, up from fewer than 16,000 in 2019. Current funding allows it to answer about half of them.

Mexican chef Froilán Mújica won the World Paella Day Cup 2026, according to a live blog from organizer Visit València Foundation. Japanese chef Keisuke Mutsuura finished second.
Holm has worked at the Spanish restaurants El Bulli and El Celler de Can Roca. He also owned the tapas restaurant Los Socios in Aarhus.
He qualified for the final by winning the Nordic-Baltic semifinal in Denmark on June 11. That competition included chefs from Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
The Valencia final brought together chefs from Europe, Asia and North and South America. Seven judges assessed the dishes based on taste and presentation.
Each finalist prepared an individual version of paella and selected the type of rice to use. The competition was held in tents at Valencia’s harbor.
World Paella Day is held annually on September 20 to celebrate the dish and its origins in Valencia.
Paella is a traditional Spanish rice dish originating from Albufera, south of Valencia. Farmers originally cooked it over an open fire using local rice and available vegetables.
The dish takes its name from the large, flat pan used to prepare it. The pan allows the rice to form a thin, crisp layer.
