Feature: 15 years On, Chinese-built Kribi port powers Cameroon's growth, improves livelihoods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:57:00 CST
22:57:00 KST

by Arison Tamfu
YAOUNDE, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Fifteen years ago, Mboro was a remote fishing hamlet on the edge of Kribi in southern Cameroon, with a handful of homes connected by narrow, winding dirt tracks.
Today, the same stretch of coastline is home to one of Central Africa's most modern deep-water ports, with the surrounding area being reshaped by a growing industrial and logistics economy.
Since the 1970s, Cameroon has envisioned a deep-water port to complement the Port of Douala, the country's only major port, which sits in a shallow estuary unable to accommodate large vessels. That decades-old ambition has been realized with the completion of the first and second phases of the Kribi Deep Seaport.
CITY OF FUTURE
Gu Gaobai was among the first Chinese workers to arrive in 2011 with China Harbor Engineering Company (CHEC), the builder of the Kribi Deep Seaport.
"When we headed to the project site, we bumped along narrow dirt trails. At the selected location, all we saw was a small sandy beach and a few reefs. At the time, those reefs were the only reference points for the port's location," recalled Gu, now general manager of CHEC's Cameroon Project Clusters.
The transformation is visible along the roads leading to the port. A narrow track is now a dual carriageway with a pedestrian crossing in the middle. New buildings, businesses and public facilities have emerged as economic activity has expanded.
For 50-year-old lifelong resident Jean-Kalvin Assembe, the changes have reached into everyday life. "For one thing, I'm happy and fulfilled in this city," he said.
The influx of workers and businesses has created more opportunities for local residents and supported household incomes. "Even the little neighborhood shop gets customers. It's really bringing positive changes," Assembe said.
Multi-story buildings, hospitals, universities and shopping malls now dot Kribi. Streetlights illuminate roads that were once dark, while the port area remains brightly lit after nightfall.
Truck drivers are among those who have benefited from the port's development. Long queues of trucks now fill the port area daily.
"The port has given us the opportunity to discover the region," said 68-year-old veteran driver Aboubakar Yaya, who has driven across four Central African countries. "Kribi has made things easier. The service is fast, too."
"Many clients and experts who know China often say Kribi is Cameroon's Shenzhen, a 'City of the Future,'" Gu said.
HUB FOR INDUSTRIALIZATION, REGIONAL INTEGRATION
As the port has grown, so too has its industrial complex.
Patrick Mpila Ayissi, chief infrastructure officer of Kribi Port Industrial Zone, said investment in the zone has accelerated since operations began in 2018.
"Since 2018, industrial operators have invested nearly 400 billion CFA francs (about 700 million U.S. dollars), and 93 occupancy permits have been issued, with 18 companies already operating," Ayissi said. "The ambition has grown from an initial 455-hectare logistics zone to today's 4,000-hectare integrated industrial zone."
The zone is expected to attract close to 900 million dollars in investment and create 50,000 direct jobs, with up to 150,000 direct and indirect jobs combined, over the next 15 years, he said.
The seaport has also become a strategic hub for Central Africa, serving neighboring markets.
"Container traffic has quadrupled since 2018, surpassing 555,000 TEU in 2025, while overall cargo volumes exceeded 12.7 million tonnes in 2024. Trade already flows from Kribi to Gabon, the Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, and Equatorial Guinea," Ayissi said, adding that the port's regional connections have been reinforced by shipping lines such as MSC.
To support the growing logistics network, CHEC also built the Kribi-Lolabe highway.
"This highway connects the Kribi Deep Seaport with major cities nationwide, facilitating personnel travel and goods transportation, thus promoting Cameroon's industrialization," said Emmanuel Nganou Djoumessi, Cameroon's minister of public works.
LIFE-CHANGING SKILLS
The changes brought by the port are also reflected in the careers of local workers.
In 2013, Ngatugirius Ndenya left his welding job in Yaounde to join CHEC in Kribi. "When I arrived here in 2013, the beginning was very difficult for me," said the 53-year-old.
CHEC adopted the approach of pairing Cameroonian workers with experienced Chinese colleagues, which allowed them to gain hands-on experience before taking on tasks independently.
"Before coming here, I was just a platform welder. But now, I can do everything concerning welding," Ndenya said. "The young people that came here were not technicians, but today they are technicians."
For some workers, the port has also brought changes to their livelihoods.
"When I arrived here, I had absolutely nothing. I left a job where I was earning maybe 100,000 CFA francs a month," said Armand Guehoada, now a business specialist with CHEC. "After a while, I was able to buy a vehicle. Today, I'm on my third. I can easily take care of my family."
"Over the past 15 years, we have trained a large cohort of local professionals in port construction and mega-project engineering. Many of those who worked on the port now contribute to the adjacent industrial zone," Gu said.
This year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Cameroon, while the Kribi Deep Seaport marks 15 years since construction began.
"Kribi remains a visible symbol of Cameroon-China cooperation. Its development has been structured from the outset around concessional financing from Chinese institutions, reflecting a genuinely long-term partnership." Ayissi said.
For Patrice Melom, general manager of the Port Authority of Kribi, the port's development has opened up new possibilities for the city and the country.
"The future of the port of Kribi looks promising, bringing concrete results and extremely positive prospects," Melom said. "It is now up to us to mobilize all our energies and make this infrastructure a true driver of sustainable growth, serving national prosperity and sub-regional integration." ■

TOKYO, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Teenage swimmers Yu Zidi and Zhang Zhanshuo led China's charge at the 2026 Asian Games on Wednesday, with Yu completing a hat-trick of individual titles and Zhang claiming his fourth gold as China won six swimming events.
Yu, 13, completed a sweep of her three individual events by winning the women's 400-meter individual medley in 4 minutes, 28.56 seconds, setting an Asian Games record. She led from the opening leg and finished 3.95 seconds ahead of teammate Ke Wenxi.
Yu had already won the 200-meter butterfly and 200-meter individual medley, setting an Asian record of 2:06.10 in the latter. Despite her success, the teenager admitted that her demanding schedule had taken its toll.
"There wasn't really a feeling that it was easy. I'm quite tired," Yu said.
"I was just a little short of the Asian record today, but I also improved my time, so I think that's okay," she added.
Zhang, 19, claimed his fourth gold of the Games by winning the men's 200-meter freestyle in an Asian record of 1:43.49. South Korea's Hwang Sun-woo took silver in 1:44.62, while Japan's Tatsuya Murasa finished third in 1:44.81.
Zhang had previously won the 1,500-meter freestyle and helped China secure gold in the 4x200-meter free and 4x100-meter medley relays. He anchored the former in 1:42.92 as China set an Asian record of 7:00.17.
"It was quite unexpected. Before the race, I didn't think I could swim such a time," Zhang said. "Form is built up race by race, and it will keep getting better and better."
Elsewhere, China's Yu Yiting edged teammate and defending champion Zhang Yufei by just 0.03 seconds to win the women's 100-meter butterfly in 56.41 seconds.
Neither swimmer was entirely satisfied with her performance, with Yu acknowledging that the narrow victory highlighted the importance of finishing strongly.
"Sometimes it comes down to the final 15 meters. For both of us, it was valuable experience," she said.
China's Peng Xuwei won the women's 100-meter backstroke in 59.30s, ahead of Japan's Rio Shirai in 59.89 and South Korea's Kim Seungwon in 1:00.10.
Peng said she had struggled with her pacing despite securing gold and described the Games as an important test ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"The Asian Games is like a 'midterm exam' for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. It's an opportunity to test and show the results of my training," she said.
Tang Qianting added another gold for China in the women's 100-meter breaststroke, setting a Games record of 1:04.98.
In the men's 100-meter butterfly, China's Xu Fang took silver behind Japan's Shoon Mitsunaga, who set a Games record of 50.56 seconds.
China rounded off the evening by successfully defending its mixed 4x100-meter medley relay title, completing its six-gold haul.
For Zhang Yufei, the relay victory provided a positive end to a frustrating evening after her narrow defeat in the individual butterfly event.
Competing alongside longtime teammate Xu Jiayu in a reshuffled relay lineup, Zhang said his continued improvement had given her renewed confidence in her own prospects.
"Seeing him come back from the bottom makes me feel that I can do it too," she said.
"Even though I made some mistakes this time and didn't swim the result I wanted, I still believe in my training and look forward to finding what I can do in the next race." ■

These shortcomings were identified by the EU in 2022, leading to the freezing of 55 percent of budgetary commitments for three Hungarian cohesion policy programs. Restrictions were also imposed on EU funding for Hungarian Public Interest Trusts, affecting participation in Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who took office after defeating Orban in the April 2026 parliamentary election, has made restoring Hungary's access to the suspended EU funds a key government priority.
The Council of the EU now has one month to decide whether to approve the Commission's proposal.
Hungarian Minister of Transport and Investment David Vitezy has welcomed the announcement, saying the European Commission had officially initiated the closure of the rule-of-law procedures against Hungary. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China now has 270 million people with a higher education background, or nearly one in five of its population, as the country expands higher education while adjusting its university system to changing demographics and evolving demand for talent, according to the Ministry of Education.
China's gross enrollment rate in higher education reached 61.3 percent in 2025, with total enrollment standing at 48.73 million, said Guo Peng, head of the Ministry of Education's development planning department, at a press conference.
According to official data, the number of people in the age group for higher education is expected to peak in 2032, underscoring the need to expand the overall supply of higher education resources and increase the supply of high-quality educational resources.
Against that backdrop, universities under China's "Double First-Class" initiative will expand undergraduate enrollment by 76,000 places from 2027 to 2030, Guo said. The initiative supports a select group of universities and academic disciplines with the goal of achieving world-class status.
The expansion will involve more than simply increasing enrollment, Guo said. Universities will adjust academic programs and improve the structure and quality of higher education to better match the needs of national and regional socioeconomic development, as well as industry demand.
The country's outline plan for the development of the education sector during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for expanding quality undergraduate enrollment and graduate training, with a focus on science, engineering, agriculture and medicine, while increasing the proportion of graduate-level education.
Guo said the government will provide greater support to emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, integrated circuits, biomedicine and new energy.
The government will also use central government funding and ultra-long special treasury bonds to support "Double First-Class" universities in building new campuses and upgrading basic facilities, including dormitories, cafeterias, sports facilities and laboratories, Guo said.
Despite a decline in the working-age population, China's total effective human resources are expected to remain at a high level over the next 10 to 15 years, initially rising slightly before edging down, said He Dan, head of the China Population and Development Research Center.
She said the trend highlights the advantages in human-resource quality brought by improvements in education and health sectors. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's growing RV travel market opens new business opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:56:02 CST
22:56:02 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- In Fuyuan, a border city in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, a tourist surnamed Sun has spent a week with her family in a recreational vehicle (RV) parked beside the river.
The public campsite in a riverside park offers free parking, round-the-clock water access and nearby toilets. Since June, the number of vehicles using the site has risen about 20 percent from a year earlier, while visitor numbers have climbed nearly 30 percent, according to local officials.
For Sun's family, the riverside stay offers a chance to slow down and enjoy the outdoors without giving up many of the comforts of home. For cities like Fuyuan, meanwhile, the growing number of RV travelers points to a new source of tourism spending -- from fuel and charging to food, supplies, repairs and local services.
RV travel, however, is still relatively uncommon in China. China sold more than 20,000 self-propelled RVs in 2025, surpassing that threshold for the first time, according to a report released by the Motor Homes (Motor Caravans) Committee under the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Even so, RV sales remain a tiny niche compared with the 34.4 million automobiles sold in China that year.
Yet some numbers suggest that the market is beginning to move beyond its niche status.
Sales of camping vehicles designed for shorter trips rose 85.6 percent year on year, while sales of new-energy motorhomes for longer journeys surged 229 percent in 2025, according to industry data. The momentum has continued into this year: 12,153 self-propelled RVs were registered in the first half of 2026, up 32.6 percent year on year.
The vast scale of self-driving travel in China also points to a potential market for RV tourism. If even a small share of those road trips were to shift toward RV travel and camping, it could open up new business opportunities.
In 2024, China recorded 4.35 billion self-driving tourist trips, 750 million more than a year earlier, according to a report by the China Tourism Automobile and Cruise Association (CTACA). The sheer volume suggests a large pool of potential customers for RV travel, particularly as travelers seek new ways to combine road trips with outdoor recreation, leisure and local experiences.
Recognizing the sector's growth potential, China has introduced a range of policy measures, from broad strategic guidance to targeted support programs, to promote the development of RV camping.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for developing RV camping as a form of leisure consumption. A separate national plan to expand consumption during the five-year period also highlights automotive aftermarket services, including vehicle rentals and RV camping.
In June, nine government departments issued measures to support RV camping. Three months later, 10 departments followed with further measures targeting bottlenecks ranging from vehicle registration and driving tests to parking, campsite development, rentals and insurance.
Some of the measures target practical barriers to RV ownership and rental. Small and micro non-commercial self-propelled RVs will no longer be subject to a mandatory scrappage age. The permitted service life of small and micro-sized rental self-propelled RVs will be extended from 15 years to 25 years. Local authorities are also encouraged to add more testing sites for the C6 license for light tractor-trailer combinations.
The policy push is also being matched by efforts to build a more RV-friendly travel network. Measures cover road access, parking and campsite services, while allowing simple campsites without paved surfaces to retain their original land classification, making it easier to develop such sites.
The infrastructure is expanding alongside these efforts. China now has more than 3,100 RV campsites of various kinds, according to industry data. In Heilongjiang, a provincial transportation investment group has developed 19 campsite and hotel projects since 2021 as part of a province-wide self-driving travel network. The province has also developed 10 summer self-driving routes designed to bring RV travelers to local restaurants, accommodations and tourist attractions.
Jiangsu Province in east China is pursuing a similar approach. Jiangsu Communications Holding Co., Ltd. is planning 78 RV stops at expressway service areas near major tourist attractions. In Chenji Town, local authorities offered 5 million yuan in RV purchase subsidies in 2025, a program they said helped drive sales of about 500 RVs and generate more than 100 million yuan (14.93 million U.S. dollars) in related spending.
Wang Xiaoqing, vice dean of Hongshan College at Nanjing University of Finance and Economics, said the growth of RV travel is creating opportunities not only for vehicle sales, but also for rentals, membership services and tourism operations.
Despite the policy push and infrastructure building, RV travelers and campsite operators still face practical hurdles.
In some cities, RV users have difficulty accessing or parking their vehicles, while drivers of certain tractor-trailer combinations need a separate C6 license. For campsite developers, lengthy procedures for land use and planning approvals can add another layer of difficulty.
The business itself is also proving challenging. According to a CTACA report, the gross profit margin of RV campsites fell to 21 percent in 2024, down from a peak of 45 percent in 2021 and back to the level seen in 2019.
As a result, operators are looking beyond simply charging for parking and accommodation. Many are adding restaurants, study tours, themed events and equipment sales to diversify their income. Campsites near major cities, which can attract repeat weekend visitors, and those linked to established tourist destinations, which benefit from existing visitor flows, are among the models seen as more viable.
For the sector to develop further, some industry observers say the supporting infrastructure and regulatory framework will need to catch up with growing demand.
Wang Hong, director of Shaanxi Hong Zhen Law Firm, said many RV campsites are privately invested and have yet to be fully incorporated into local public infrastructure planning. Simplifying land-use and planning procedures, he said, could help lower the barriers to developing such facilities. ■

"That is why they must always be ready to carry out tasks that arise unexpectedly and to defend critical facilities," Volfovich noted.

Saaremaa residents oppose Elering's planned Estonia–Latvia overhead power line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Saaremaa residents oppose Elering's planned Estonia–Latvia overhead power line
Many Saaremaa residents — as well as the Saaremaa municipal government — do not support Elering's plan to build a 330 kV Estonia–Latvia overhead power line across Saaremaa. Locals prefer an underground cable or a subsea cable running directly to Latvia.
The blue line drawn by Elering on the map of Saaremaa has caused confusion among residents for several years. Initially, there were several possible routes, but one particular line has now been chosen as the route for the fourth Estonia–Latvia electricity connection.
"It crosses my property and would run 300–400 meters from my home. It's definitely disturbing. I've collected signatures on behalf of the village, but they haven't been taken much into account," said Eve, a resident of Tõnija village.
Over the years, 500 proposals have been submitted regarding the route selection, and the entire planning process has already cost €1.5 million. At the public discussion held in Kuressaare, many still questioned why such a large‑scale overhead line must be routed through Saaremaa's nature to reach Latvia. Elering counts the costs and tries to secure a necessary Estonia–Latvia connection with cheaper costs, while Saaremaa residents worry about their homes and the island's environment.
"Underground cables or a subsea cable — which could easily be built — are not being considered. That topic has been pushed aside. I don't understand why they don't want to think about a subsea cable, except for saying it's more expensive," noted Mikk, a resident of Laimjala.
"Economically, the most efficient solution is to build most of it as an overhead line. That's why the planning was initiated. Elering has not taken any offshore wind farms into account in the context of the fourth Estonia–Latvia connection," explained Priit Heinla, Elering's head of external connections development.
According to Heinla, going directly through the sea and building one or two support substations on Saaremaa would be more expensive.
The Saaremaa municipal government has previously stated that only an underground cable or a subsea cable running from the island's southern coast to Latvia would be acceptable. The municipality therefore plans to submit its position once more during the planning procedure this month.
"Alternatives are not being considered! This is steamroller politics, and people are upset," added Mikk.
--
Editor: Mari Peegel, Argo Ideon

Golan will remain Syrian, annexation decisions null under UN resolutions, says president Sharaa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:52:29 UTC
22:52:29 KST

Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said Wednesday that the Golan Heights, occupied by Israel, will remain Syrian territory and that all annexation measures are null and void under UN Security Council resolutions.  
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Sharaa said attempts to impose facts on the ground cannot undermine Syria’s sovereignty, the rule of law or the applicability of international law. 
“The Golan will remain Syrian land,” he said, adding that all annexation measures are invalid under UN Security Council Resolution 497. 
Sharaa also referred to a UN General Assembly vote in December 2025 in which 123 countries backed a resolution concerning the occupied Syrian Golan, thanking countries that supported it and urging those that abstained to reconsider Resolution 497. 
He accused Israel of carrying out nearly 500 air and artillery strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and around 300 arrests and detentions of Syrians, saying the actions threaten Syria’s stability, defy the global consensus, and revive painful memories of an era Syrians had barely managed to leave behind. 
Sharaa said Damascus remains committed to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and continues to call for Israeli forces to withdraw to the lines held before Dec. 8, 2024. 
He rejected Israel’s attempts to impose “new facts on the ground” and said Israeli actions across the region undermine security and stability. 
The address marked Sharaa’s second consecutive appearance before the UN General Assembly. He attended the 80th session in September 2025, becoming the first Syrian president to participate in the gathering since 1967.

Can flurry of New York diplomacy lead to US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:52:27 UTC
22:52:27 KST

Can flurry of New York diplomacy lead to US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough?
Analysts say expecting a deal this week is unlikely – multiple actors are testing possible off-ramps, however, core disagreements between Washington and Tehran remain unresolved.
At the colloquium established shortly after the second world war to prevent future wars, United States President Donald Trump did just the inverse: He platformed his unceasing threats against Iran, suggesting almost casually on Tuesday that he could “annihilate” the country he has waged war against since February 28.
But behind closed doors on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), a flurry of diplomatic activity concerning the ongoing US-Iran war has also been unfolding, as world leaders gather in New York.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrives in New York for UNGA
- list 2 of 4‘Annihilate’ vs ‘crushing’ attacks: Why Iran, US up rhetoric amid talks
- list 3 of 4As Xi meets Trump, who’s winning their trade war?
- list 4 of 4Qatar on mediation efforts: ‘We can’t let diplomacy fail’
The US and Iran held indirect talks for three hours on Tuesday. US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, with Trump calling it a “very good” and “very productive” meeting. Trump also met Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) leaders that day, with senior officials from the region mulling a Qatari proposal for a common security framework involving Iran and the Gulf states.
Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in New York early on Wednesday – the first time a leader whose country is at war with the US has set foot on US soil to address the gathering. And Chinese President Xi Jinping will skirt New York to instead meet Trump one-on-one in Washington, DC – his first state visit to the US in just less than a decade. Xi lands on Wednesday evening.
All these separate diplomatic initiatives, analysts tell Al Jazeera, are parts of a push to bring Iran and the US back to the negotiating table. According to Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Tohid Asadi, Araghchi’s meeting with Witkoff and Kushner was to convey Tehran’s latest set of conditions to end the war, following the collapse of the June 60-day memorandum of understanding (MoU) finalised in Islamabad, Pakistan.
But analysts say expecting an actual deal to emerge this week from the diplomatic meetings in the US would be unrealistic. Multiple actors and mediators in the conflict are testing possible off-ramps, but core disagreements between Washington and Tehran remain unresolved.
“I am sceptical that a breakthrough deal can emerge this week, but a series of understandings can build confidence for renewed diplomacy,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
Too early for a breakthrough
Vakil is hesitant to call the current moment ripe for a diplomatic breakthrough – it is far too early, and there is a history of negotiations failing, she said.
“Both sides have been negotiating for over two years and on two occasions, that ended with military conflict and these negotiations continue amid persistent military threats,” she said.
Iran has long pointed to its previous rounds of diplomatic talks with the US – in 2025 and again this year – as evidence that Washington can veer from negotiations to military action. It has cited the 12-day war last June, and the current conflict, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on Tehran at a time Washington and Tehran were engaged in Oman-mediated dialogue.
Adel Abdel Ghafar, a senior fellow focusing on the Middle East at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said that there appears to be “genuine” movement towards reigniting negotiations – but also “a fair amount of posturing”. He referenced Trump’s praise for Tuesday’s indirect Iran-US talks and his pugnacious UNGA speech the same day.
A breakthrough hinges on whether Iran’s diplomats in New York can actually deliver, he said.
“Araghchi and Pezeshkian can negotiate, but any deal will need the consent of the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] and the hardliners in charge of the war back home,” Abdel Ghafar told Al Jazeera.
There are specific indicators to watch for another round of US-Iran contact, the analysts said.
“The signs to watch for are another confirmed round of US-Iran talks, agreement on sequencing or reciprocal steps, and language from both sides becoming more specific about implementation rather than simply repeating maximalist demands,” said Vakil.
Abdel Ghafar added that, against the backdrop of UNGA, signs could include Araghchi or Pezeshkian meeting directly with US officials, in addition to supportive statements from more hardline elements of the Iranian administration back home.
The appearance of such indicators could lead to a stronger push for such talks when Trump meets Xi, as well as an easing of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, which has escalated in recent weeks, the analyst added.
The limits of Gulf and Chinese diplomacy
The analysts agreed that the Gulf states remain crucial in brokering a return to talks because they have channels to both warring sides, as well as a very strong interest in preventing further escalation, having absorbed the cost of the fighting since February. Qatar, Oman and other Gulf states have been involved in mediation efforts throughout the conflict.
“Qatar and Oman, in particular, can help translate broad political messages into workable arrangements on issues such as Hormuz and regional security,” said Vakil.
China, meanwhile, has less capacity or interest to mediate, she argued.
Beijing, however, could use its economic and political leverage with Tehran “to encourage compromise and give Iran greater confidence that any agreement will not leave it completely isolated”, said Vakil.
Abdel Ghafar pointed out that China remains Iran’s main customer for its oil, explaining why Beijing has pushed for a return to the June interim deal and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“Still, I think neither can impose a settlement – it ultimately comes down to Washington and Tehran,” he said.
Hostilities and Hormuz
The tit-for-tat rhetoric has resulted in continued deadlock in the conflict, with each side unwilling to relinquish to the other’s demands and appear to admit defeat.
On Tuesday, following Trump’s remarks on annihilating Iran, Iran’s military warned that it is ready to respond with “crushing” attacks more severe than earlier in the war.
“The main challenge is finding a formula that both governments can present domestically as a negotiated compromise rather than capitulation,” said Vakil.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a key obstacle.
“It’s Iran’s strongest card and the thing Washington most wants back, with oil prices high and midterms approaching,” said Abdel Ghafar.
“Tehran will be reluctant to give it up without firm guarantees in return.”
Still, he warned that even if Washington and Tehran de-escalate, that does not automatically extend to the Red Sea.
The wider landscape of regional instability and conflict has created new conditions for Yemen’s unresolved war to flare up once again. The Bab al-Mandeb, now under effective Houthi control, has gained greater significance amid Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global oil and gas supplies.
“Calm in Hormuz won’t necessarily mean calm in Bab al-Mandab,” said Abdel Ghafar.

‘Watermelons’: Zack Polanski and the rise of the ‘green outside, red inside’ eco-populists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:52:20 UTC
22:52:20 KST

Watermelons: the term used to describe the members of the Green party of England and Wales who are green on the outside and red on the inside. People in this faction are environmentalists but bleed socialist ideologies.
Of the roughly 160,000 people who have flocked to the party since Zack Polanski became leader last year, most are thought to be in this camp, drawn to a political space on the left that they see as vacated by the Labour party.
But the author of a new book – The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future – says this flavour of Green is nothing new. “What you’ve got to understand is that the party has been watermelon for at least 10 years,” says Russell Warfield, a former party staffer who has worked on election campaigns, including Polanski’s.
“There’s often this dichotomy presented that there’s this ‘real core’ Green party who are these ecologists who really just care about conservation of the environment, then there’s this new cohort of hard leftists,” Warfield says. “Actually, this has been both an organic process but also one which reaches much more deeply into the past of the party, where a lot of the fundamental positions of the party can be traced back to the early 1970s.”
His book unpacks the history of the party to explain how Polanski fits into it, arguing that the leader and his “eco-populist” package is not a departure from Green tradition but the culmination of a 50-year evolution that has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left.
Not everyone agrees. During the leadership contest between Polanski and co-runners Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns in 2025, a senior Green source described Polanski’s rise as a “hostile takeover”. Even Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ first MP and a former party leader, has said, when pressed, that she would love him to talk about the environment more.
“It’s just obvious nonsense,” Warfield says of the hostile takeover comment. “Look at the mandate, it was 85%,” Polanski’s landslide leadership win. “He won across every wing of the party.”
But how green are the Greens? Since Polanski took over, he has been splashed across newspapers and TV screens discussing subjects ranging from Gaza to wealth taxes – progressive politics, but not necessarily or overtly green.
Warfield responds with a statistic: 34% of voters trust the Greens more than any other party on the environment, according to YouGov polling – the highest level of trust recorded for any party on any issue. “There is not a voter in this country, leftwing, rightwing, old, young, rural, urban, whatever, that does not strongly associate the Green party with taking action on the environment.”
Because of that starting point, he argues, the sensible move forward was to evolve into a broader message – one previous leaders paved the way for. “The reason the party exists is in recognition of the fact that just having a bunch of environmental conservation movements isn’t addressing the root political and economic causes of environmental degradation.
“We tried 50 years of that. And it got us so far, but the manifest moments of material advancement have been tied to moments where we’ve been able to be more responsive to the actual political context of the day.”
Warfield points out that many of Polanski’s positions are not his alone. Green party members vote on policy and the leaders are constitutionally duty bound to advocate for it. “Take the wealth tax,” Warfield writes. “He did not arrive at this policy personally. A ‘wealth tax’ is called for as ‘a means of limiting large accumulations of wealth’ in a Green party manifesto published long before Polanski’s leadership.”
The book finds links between the party’s past and present, even in unlikely places. It’s unavoidable, Warfield writes, that there were “some distinctly rightwing people present at the formation of the Green party”. The first key figure was Teddy Goldsmith, an environmentalist part of a famous Tory family. His writings formed key texts for People, the political party from which the modern Greens descend.
But even Goldsmith – whose “deep ecology” philosophy leaned into Malthusian concerns about human population and misanthropic views that blamed humanity as a monolith for ecological degradation – shares threads with Polanski’s Greens, Warfield says. Both share the golden Green rule that infinite economic growth and endless extraction are impossible on a planet with finite resources. Both reject the idea that capitalism can simply carry on with business as usual, green or otherwise.
As the party has shifted towards social ecology over the years, Warfield says Polanski’s eco-socialism simply represents a modern evolution: arguing that capitalism and the 1% – not all of humanity – are the root cause of environmental destruction.
But Polanski’s tenure has also brought controversies. There was his criticism of the police response to the Golders Green attack, which the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley, called “inaccurate and misinformed”. There was the false claim he was a British Red Cross spokesperson and the sharing of a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, a reference to Nigel Farage. YouGov polling shows Polanski’s approval rating has slumped since he became leader, while Green voting intention has dropped from 21% of the electorate in March to 11% this month.
Should the party take Polanski’s social media away? “Golders Green was a misstep,” says Warfield. “But what you don’t want to do is to get to a situation where every post needs double-tick signoff from different members of staff and you can’t just let Zack engage with social media in the way that allows him to reap the political points of authenticity.”
Polanski was criticised for his refusal to apologise for sharing the Farage guillotine picture. “Reform were trying to goad him into apologising for incitement to murder,” Warfield says. “If you do that, you legitimise the claim that they’re making. I think there’s a lot of strength in not succumbing to the pressure of playing that game.”
On 8 October, Polanski will contest the Holborn and St Pancras byelection after Keir Starmer announced his decision to vacate the seat. Warfield thinks Polanski can win. “You could vote Labour again and you get another backbencher who is one among literally hundreds of Labour MPs and that doesn’t make much difference to anything,” he says. “Or you can put a really prominent, independently minded Green in there and continue to put pressure on the Burnham project from its left.”

El Nino could cause 451,000 extra heat deaths: Research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:52:00 UTC
22:52:00 KST

El Nino could cause 451,000 extra heat deaths: Research
PARIS – The powerful El Nino weather pattern that started in 2026 could lead to 451,000 additional heat-related deaths worldwide through February 2027 as it turbocharges global temperatures, according to projections published on Sept 23.
The warming phenomenon, which was declared in June and is due to peak later in 2026, is on course to be the strongest on record, amplifying the effects of human-induced climate change.
The estimates by the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago found that developing countries would be hit hardest by the heat-related toll in the June to February period.
The Sahel region in Africa could have an additional 66,800 heat deaths compared to a normal year, with nearly half of that number in Nigeria alone.
An additional 19,300 are projected in Indonesia and 19,400 in the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia.
The toll could reach 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil.
The researchers projected that global land temperatures will be 1.2 deg C above normal in the coming months due in large part to El Nino, leading to 44 per cent more extremely hot days than in a regular year.
For the projections, the Climate Impact Lab used research on the relationship between temperature and excess mortality in 24,378 regions, taking local climate and vulnerability into account.
They then combined those findings with long-range temperature forecasts to estimate excess deaths that could result from El Nino compared with the 1996-2025 average.
Their method will be published in an upcoming peer-reviewed journal.
The report comes a day after the United Nations warned that El Nino represents a significant threat to global health.
The Climate Impact Lab researchers said their projections can help governments and humanitarian organisations take preventive measures to protect people, including heat warnings, cooling centres and hydration stations.
“This report allows decision-makers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months,” said Climate Impact Lab co-founder Michael Greenstone. AFP

Silent Hill: Townfall and Control Resonant - the main game releases on September 24
Kyiv • UNN
On September 24, Silent Hill: Townfall will be released on PS5 and PC - the first main first-person game in the series. The events will unfold in foggy Saint Amelia in 1996.
September 24 will be a key date for fans of the gaming industry, as this is when the double release of the psychological horror game Silent Hill: Townfall and the large-scale action RPG Control Resonant will take place. Both projects offer players deep paranormal stories, atmospheric locations, and updated gameplay, UNN reports.
Silent Hill: Townfall — release date, plot, and game features
The game "Silent Hill: Townfall" will be released on September 24 for PS5 and PC. It is being developed by the small Scottish studio Screen Burn Interactive, formerly known as No Code, while Konami and Annapurna Interactive are serving as publishers. The team consists of approximately 30 people, making this project exceptionally compact for a franchise of such scale.
The game is the first main installment in the "Silent Hill" series to be presented entirely from a first-person perspective. It takes place in 1996 in the fictional coastal Scottish town of St. Amelia, created based on real photographs taken in St Monans in the county of Fife.
Simon Ordell returns to the island of St. Amelia to "set everything right." There, he finds a town frozen beneath a dense veil of fog: at first glance, no one appears to be there, but it can hardly be called peaceful.
As he delves deeper and seeks to understand his connection to this place and its inhabitants, Simon uncovers fragments of the past that are slowly rising to the surface.
The game’s events are presented from a first-person perspective: Simon must explore the island, evade threats, and survive with a limited selection of weapons and tools, including the CRTV — a handheld television used to tune in to unstable signals.
Hiding is tense here, the fights are frantic, and the story puzzles reveal a truth that wants to come to the surface.
SILENT HILL: Townfall is a full-fledged psychological horror game with its own story, set in cold, isolated Scotland in 1996.
At present, "Silent Hill: Townfall" has been confirmed only for PS5 and PC, with no Xbox release announced, suggesting a possible console exclusivity agreement similar to those involving other recent games released as part of the series’ revival.

Control Resonant (Control 2): what is known about the plot and gameplay

This time, the main character is Dylan Faden. After years of imprisonment in the Federal Bureau of Control (FBC), Dylan Faden’s former captors enlist him to handle a case amid a paranormal crisis.
Dylan must confront a mysterious cosmic entity that is changing the very foundations of our reality. Having mastered his newly acquired abilities, he must fight back against the numerous threats engulfing Manhattan.
Join Dylan in the sequel to the multiple award-winning game CONTROL as you explore vast areas of a city consumed by the destructive influence of the chaotic Noise, an aggressive microorganism known as the Mold, and other warped paranormal threats.
As he works toward fully unlocking his paranormal abilities, Dylan will also search for his sister, FBC Director Jesse Faden. He seeks to understand and contain the dangers that have escaped the Oldest House and threaten to destroy our world.
Explore the diverse districts of devastated Manhattan in a vast, unfamiliar, and captivating world.
Visit locations that turn perceptions of reality upside down and overcome gravitational anomalies that alter the very understanding of horizontal and vertical space, adding new dimensions to puzzle-solving and tactical decision-making in combat.
Encounter familiar and new faces on a risk-filled path brimming with possibilities as the cityscape changes and reality is reshaped by a godlike force.
The lead gameplay designer confirmed that completing the main story will take around 30 hours, while completing it with all tasks will take around 50, making this the longest game Remedy has ever created.

Trump’s Russia tariffs could threaten to deepen Europe’s LNG squeeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:51:24 UTC
22:51:24 KST

The European Commission has said it will work with Washington to make sure that as little disruption as possible will come from the latest tariffs against Russian energy announced by Donald Trump.
The European Union is facing the prospect of another squeeze on its liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies, as US President Donald Trump’s latest Russia sanctions could disrupt the LNG flows the EU still relies on.
Trump recently signed the Lindsey Graham Sanctions Act, allowing him to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries still buying Russian oil or natural gas, especially those accused of helping Moscow evade sanctions, China and India chief among them.
While the law does not automatically impose tariffs on the EU, its practical application remains uncertain and creates a new risk for European governments and companies still exposed to Russian gas.
Trump's new sanctions, though widely welcomed by the EU as a tool to weaken Moscow's war machine, come at a critical moment. The EU is struggling to refill storage levels to at least 80% by November, according to real-time intelligence platform Global Energy Flow, with winter gas storage at the lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011. Fierce competition from Asian bidders is also leaving Europe behind.
When asked about whether the Lindsey Graham bill could harm European partners, EU Foreign Affairs chief Kaja Kallas said she "didn't think" of that, adding that she hopes it isn't true. She made the remarks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on 22 September.
Meanwhile, a European Commission spokesperson said that the EU has "clear expectations" that the Graham law "should not impose new commercial barriers in the bilateral EU-US relationship".
"We will engage with the US with a view to ensuring this outcome," the Commission spokesperson told Euronews on Wednesday.
Since the US and Israel bombed Iran on 28 February, escalation in the Middle East led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to a vital Saudi pipeline, ultimately disrupting LNG transit.
At the same time, the EU is ditching Russian LNG, albeit gas imports from Moscow rose to 17% as landlocked countries were granted exemptions as well as those with long-term contracts that feared legal challenges from Russian energy giant Gazprom. A full ban on LNG imports from Moscow is due on 1 January 2027.
To compound the sense of energy insecurity engulfing the EU, Washington's move to punish major Russian energy buyers with tariffs of up to 100% could create friction with countries still exposed to Russian gas, such as France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain.
Ben McWilliams, affiliate fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, said that Trump's new tariffs "should not change too much" since no Russian LNG should come into the bloc after the 2027 ban.
"I think Russia will be able to reach alternative markets, and do not expect a huge market impact. There has been plenty of time for utilities and traders to prepare," McWilliams told Euronews.
Beyond LNG, maritime services at risk
But if Washington sanctions all tankers found carrying Russian LNG, the consequences could extend beyond the vessels themselves, according to Urgewald, the German non-profit environmental organisation.
"The new US law covers foreign vessels determined to knowingly transport Russian-origin LNG, although designations are not automatic and national-interest waivers are permitted," reads the Urgewald press statement.
The new US sanctions, which will be reviewed by Congress on 18 October, could also target the owner or operator of a foreign port that allows a US-sanctioned vessel supporting Russia to call or receive services — including those in Europe, such as the Danish port of Odense Havn.
Fayard, a major Danish ship repair shipyard, has faced intense scrutiny and political pushback for servicing Russia-linked Arctic LNG carriers.
Swedish MEP Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left group) criticised the maintenance of a Russian Arc7 LNG tanker currently being repaired in Fayard.
“These vessels are a critical component in Russia’s arctic LNG export, transporting billions of Euros worth of Russian LNG. This must stop. European companies must not be allowed to keep Russia’s fossil-fuel lifeline running. Every repair helps sustain Putin’s illegal war against Ukraine," said Sjöstedt.
Echoing his words, German MEP Hannah Neumann (The Greens/EFA group) urged Fayard to stop carrying on "business as usual".
“By putting commercial interests ahead of our collective responsibility to isolate Russia, Fayard is undermining the pressure we are trying to build,” she said.

Vivaldi erased Russia’s Lyman pincer. Now Moscow is pushing toward Sloviansk instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:51:19 UTC
22:51:19 KST

Ukraine's Vivaldi counteroffensive rolled back a Russian advance north of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast. However, Moscow shifted part of its forces south, Roman Pohorilyi, co-founder of the Ukrainian battlefield mapping project DeepState, told Radio NV. Russian troops are now infiltrating Mykolaivka, a key strongpoint on the approach to the fortress city of Sloviansk, Pohorilyi said.
The halted advance was one arm of Russia's plan to encircle Ukraine's Donetsk fortress belt—the fortified cities of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka. Pohorilyi warned that losing Mykolaivka would create serious problems for Sloviansk's defenders. Russia is still pressing toward Dobropillia on the belt's southwestern flank.
Pohorilyi said Russia formed a "claw" north of Lyman by exploiting Ukrainian brigades short of personnel and pushing small groups into their lines. Ukraine's Third Army Corps stabilized the area, built up forces, and counterattacked. The push "multiplied all [Russia's] previous efforts by zero," he said.
Russian forces had repeatedly tried to capture or bypass Lyman, Pohorilyi said. Russian groups still infiltrate the approaches to the city, although Ukrainian forces have stabilized the situation there.
The corps says Vivaldi's first two phases regained control of 125 square kilometers, including 50 that had been under Russian occupation. It reported liberating Shandryholove and Derylove, securing Drobysheve, and inflicting more than 3,000 Russian personnel losses. Those battlefield figures have not been independently verified.
Vivaldi’s secret weapon was the targeting, not the robots: Third Corps reconnaissance mapped Russian command nodes, then hit them to cause panic
Pohorilyi noted that the area around Mykolaivka had, until recently, been under the responsibility of Ukraine's 11th Army Corps and is now under the Third Army Corps.
Ukrainian troops must now find and stop infiltrating Russian groups before they establish control, he said. Personnel shortages on the Lyman axis persist, although he said reinforcements are being distributed more evenly.
Operation Vivaldi and the wider fight for Donetsk's fortress belt
The Third Army Corps first disclosed Operation Vivaldi on 15 September after conducting the counteroffensive north of Lyman under information silence. Commander Andrii Biletskyi said the announced gains were only the first phase; the corps said its attacks had disrupted Russian supply routes.
A 60th Mechanized Brigade captain said Ukrainian units quietly assembled near Derylove and Drobysheve, then struck Russian drone launch sites at planned times so infantry could advance. The corps disclosed a second phase on 20 September.
Farther southwest, Dobropillia faces even heavier pressure, Pohorilyi said. Russia has concentrated large forces there and is pushing with relentless infantry across a wide front, backed by thousands of drones each month—reconnaissance, strike, FPV, and Lancets—with numbers still rising. Russian troops are moving on settlements south of Dobropillia to establish a strongpoint and push deeper into Donetsk Oblast.
The pressure is not new: Biletskyi said Ukrainian troops halted a Russian incursion there last year. After Moscow claimed on 22 September to have encircled the town, the Institute for the Study of War found no evidence to support the claim.

Türkiye eyes first small nuclear reactor by mid-2030s: Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:50:13 UTC
22:50:13 KST

Türkiye aims to bring its first small modular nuclear reactor into operation in the first half of the 2030s, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said.
Speaking after an energy roundtable at the 19th Türkiye Investment Conference in New York, Bayraktar said the government was preparing regulations that could offer incentives and exemptions to investors in small modular reactors (SMRs).
“There is a global race in this field,” he said, adding that Türkiye wanted to participate in developing the technology and draw on its existing nuclear industry capabilities.
Bayraktar said Türkiye Nuclear Energy Inc. (TÜNAŞ) had signed an agreement with the U.S. Trade and Development Agency on SMRs. The grant agreement covers assessments of the technical, economic and regulatory feasibility of new nuclear technologies.
He said the cooperation would also extend to Central Asia and Turkic republics.
Türkiye is exploring nuclear cooperation with Canada and plans to sign an agreement with French energy company EDF, Bayraktar said. Such partnerships would cover operational and safety experience as well as investment.
Describing nuclear power as essential to electrification, he said Türkiye wanted to bring projects into service as soon as possible. He projected energy demand from data centers in Türkiye at between 5 and 10 terawatt-hours around 2035.
Bayraktar also said electrifying transport was essential to reducing dependence on imported energy as the growing number of vehicles increased fuel demand.
Türkiye would need 13 million electric vehicles by 2035 to manage rising oil demand, supported by at least 1.3 million charging stations, he said.
He put electricity grid investment needs through 2035 at $50 billion for distribution and $30 billion for transmission.

At UNGA, Kyrgyz President Japarov Once Again Complains About Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:49:00 UTC
22:49:00 KST

Amid his 20-minute remarks before the United Nations General Assembly this week, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov took time to complain about sanctions and thank U.S. President Donald Trump for ceasing support to NGOs.
“…[T]oday sanctions are, in some cases, used by individual countries as an instrument of interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states,” Japarov said. “The negative consequences of unjustified unilateral sanctions also affect small countries such as ours, which are at the stage of formation and development, and this raises concern among other small states as well.”
Japarov went on to claim that “some major states, in pursuit of their own interests, put pressure on smaller countries such as Kyrgyzstan, attempting to force them to bargain over certain matters and issuing ultimatums.”
At no point did Japarov lay out specifically what countries he believes are pressuring Kyrgyzstan, and to what end.
Then, in the middle of his commentary about sanctions, Japarov pivoted to lauding the U.S. president – although the Trump administration has maintained the prior administration’s sanctions on various Kyrgyz entities.
“In this context, I would like to take this opportunity to note the decision made by the President of the United States His Excellency Mr. Donald Trump after taking office to halt funding of non-governmental organizations around the world,” Japarov said. “As a result, interference by NGOs in the internal affairs and policies of developing states has practically ceased.”
For Japarov, the two issues are inextricably linked. Last year at UNGA, he stated that “sanctions imposed on Kyrgyzstan are based on false information spread by certain non-governmental organizations and malicious citizens.”
Japarov has not specified which NGOs or “malicious citizens” have provided this “false information” that supposedly landed Kyrgyz business and banks on sanctions lists.
In April, Kyrgyzstan’s Bakai Bank won a case in a Belgian commercial court against the Open Dialogue Foundation (ODF) for its publication of reports alleging that the bank was involved in the circumvention of sanctions against Russia. Note that the bank had not been sanctioned. The court classified the NGO as a “commercial enterprise,” opening it to liability as if it were a market competitor.
As the World Liberty Congress, a global alliance of pro-democracy leaders, said in a statement: “The court required published information to meet a commercial verification standard designed for disputes between market operators, a test that is structurally impossible for any organization working in an authoritarian jurisdiction where access to primary banking records is unavailable.”
Meanwhile, also in April 2026, the EU aimed its “anti-circumvention tool” at Kyrgyzstan, the first country so targeted. In the subsequent months, Kyrgyz authorities pantomimed taking action. In June 2026, two state-owned banks claimed to have ended partnerships with more than 130 clients due to sanctions risks. In August, another round of cut connections was announced.
However, Kyrgyz authorities have never specified which companies were affected, making it all but impossible to confirm whether companies that present actual sanctions risks have been cut loose.
According to RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk, as of June 2026, 31 companies from Kyrgyzstan were under Western sanctions, including five banks. While three Tajik banks were removed from the EU sanctions list in May, the Kyrgyz banks – such as Keremet Bank, Kapital Bank, Eurasian Savings Bank, and EcoIslamicBank – remain designated by the EU, the U.K., and/or the U.S.
After thanking Trump “for ending the funding of NGOs,” Japarov continued discussing sanctions, arguing that the decision to impose sanctions should “be taken in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and exclusively within the mandate of the Security Council.”
Kyrgyzstan this year won a non-permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council.
Japarov went on to speak of the U.N. in terms that seem divorced from the body’s current hamstrung reality. “Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay. If a state fails to implement such decision and other countries cease cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase,” he argued.
The permanent members of the UNSC – China, Russia, France, the U.K., and the U.S. – stand on diametrically opposed ends of the global order and this has effectively neutered its possible decisiveness – whether on sanctions or anything else. For example, in September 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution condemning Moscow’s attempted annexation of parts of Ukraine. The U.S. has repeatedly blocked resolutions targeting Israel. China joined Russia earlier this month to veto an effort to extend the mandate of independent experts monitoring sanctions on Iran.
Suggesting that the UNSC become the central clearinghouse for all sanctions is effectively a call for there to be no sanctions, ever.

Dutch to return to Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 after boycott
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands will return to Eurovision in 2027, after pulling out this year over the participation of Israel.
Dutch public broadcaster NPO has taken over the reins after broadcaster AVROTROS announced earlier this year the country would not send a participant.
“The Song Contest was originally founded to bring people in Europe together. to bring together after the Second World War. We are seeking that connection again now,” Jet de Ranitz, of NPO’s executive board, said in a statement.
The Netherlands was one of five countries that refused to enter last year’s competition in response to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, although the contest in Austria was still shown on Dutch TV by public broadcaster NPO. Ireland has said it will stay away again in 2027, with Spain likely to follow suit.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has since changed its rules to ban winning countries from hosting the following year’s event if they are involved in a “sensitive geopolitical situation” that affects the “security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region”.

US reliance on outdated, obsolete technology for air traffic control systems could lead to disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:48:52 UTC
22:48:52 KST

America's aging air traffic control system - reliant on outdated telecom systems, decades-old Compaq computers and replacement parts bought on eBay - keeps failing.
In the latest example, thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast were delayed or canceled on Monday due to the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and the accidental cut of a fiber-optic cable near New Brunswick, New Jersey, by a construction crew.
"The architecture of our telecom is still a 40-year-old architecture, which means you could have a switch go down and a line be cut yesterday and the Northeast goes down," US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday.
The disruption underscores how fragile the nation's air traffic control network has become after decades of delayed modernization efforts, underfunding and piecemeal fixes.
Despite billions already spent or approved, the Federal Aviation Administration still relies on aging, often incompatible systems that can turn a single equipment failure or severed cable into flight chaos - a risk officials warn will persist without a far larger overhaul.
All US flights grounded in first since September 11 due to air traffic control issues
In January 2023, all flights departing the US were grounded for the first time since the September 11, 2001, attacks after a contractor accidentally deleted computer files, affecting a key pilot messaging database. The outage disrupted 11,000 flights before the issue was solved.
In September 2025, more than 2,000 flights were delayed and hundreds were canceled at two Dallas-area airports due to a telecom outage after a contractor cut fiber lines, impacting communication systems at the Dallas airports. It disrupted flights for 100,000 American Airlines passengers alone.
There have been repeated serious technology issues, which last year convinced Congress to approve $12.5 billion to modernize air traffic control systems. Duffy said on Tuesday he wants another $30 billion to complete upgrades and fix facilities.
"These incidents will continue to happen unless we get the resources and actually build the architecture fit for the 21st century," Duffy said.
Across the Atlantic, Britain has also suffered major air traffic control outages this month that have led airlines to question the resilience of its systems.
FAA unable to get spare parts for some air traffic control systems
The FAA has been forced to use 3D printing or to go to eBay for replacement parts for some of its aging systems. In other cases, the FAA can no longer get spare parts.
The Government Accountability Office in 2024 said the FAA needed to take "urgent action" to address aging air traffic control systems, noting that one-third are unsustainable.
The FAA's more than 300 air traffic facilities cannot talk to one another and operate on individual analog computers. "Every facility is a silo," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters in a recent interview. "We're behind 20 years."
He said effectively the FAA's towers are run on individual Compaq computers. The brand, which was acquired by HP, stopped producing computers in 2013.
The FAA still has aging telephone systems and three telecom systems that are not interoperable and have a "clunky connection" that often forces delays, Bedford said.
At the same time, the US has the world's most complex airspace and faces a shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers.
One big step is expected in late 2027 when air traffic control will move from analog to digital communications. The FAA will later shift all of the facilities from running on individual computers to the cloud.
FAA trying to modernize air traffic control systems for decades
The FAA has tried for decades to modernize the system, but those efforts have repeatedly fallen short.
In 1982, the FAA first released a comprehensive plan for improving air traffic control services, estimating it would cost about $10 billion by the late 1990s.
The Government Accountability Office in 1995 said the cost had ballooned to at least $36 billion on the effort to consolidate facilities and standardize computer hardware and software.
Another FAA reform effort dubbed "NextGen" launched in 2004 was pegged at $15 billion, but a report last year said it has faced numerous delays and cost overruns and is less ambitious than what was envisioned more than 20 years ago.
"FAA has delivered a delayed, over budget, and less transformational NextGen than originally planned," said the Transportation Department Office of Inspector General.
The FAA has also been working for years to end a long-ridiculed, decades-old practice of air traffic controllers using paper flight strips to keep track of aircraft. But adopting the change, which started in 2022, at 49 major airports will take the FAA until at least 2028. The FAA said 18 major airports have already gotten rid of the paper strips.

Central Elections Committee bars Arab Ra'am, Joint List parties from running in October elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:48:50 UTC
22:48:50 KST

The Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar Ra’am and the Joint List from competing in the October 27 election.
The Attorney-General’s Office said the evidence against both lists did not meet the stringent legal threshold for disqualification.
The committee barred each list by a vote of 18-5, with one abstention.
The decisions do not automatically go to the Supreme Court for approval, because they concern entire candidate lists rather than individual candidates. Ra’am and the Joint List may appeal, and the court is expected to hear election-disqualification proceedings next week.
MK Mansour Abbas is the chairman of Ra’am (United Arab List). The Joint List comprises three constituent parties: Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad.
The committee considered three requests against Ra’am that were filed by the Likud, Otzma Yehudit, and the Choosing Life forum of bereaved families and victims of terrorism.
Taken together, the applications invoked all three grounds for disqualification under Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset: rejecting Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state; inciting racism; and supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or terrorist organization.
The applicants cited alleged connections among Ra’am, the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement, and charitable organizations that they said had transferred assistance to bodies linked to Hamas.
They also cited statements by Abbas that showed his party presented different positions to Hebrew- and Arabic-speaking audiences.
Ra'am denies allegations of supporting terrorism
Ra’am refuted the allegations and said the petitions had failed to present clear and convincing evidence connecting the party to support for terrorism or any other prohibited objective.
Adalah – The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel attorney Suhad Bishara, representing Ra’am, told the committee the petitioners had not established the unequivocal factual record required for disqualification. She cited Abbas’s condemnation of the October 7 massacre and his calls for the release of hostages held in Gaza.
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Aisman opposed barring Ra’am. They said they had found no sufficient evidence connecting the list to support for armed struggle or allowing the conduct of the charitable organizations cited by the applicants to be attributed to the party.
The Joint List was barred following a separate request filed by the Likud, which said it had rejected Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state and supported armed struggle against it.
The request relied largely on Balad’s platform, statements attributed to it, and material concerning MK Ofer Cassif.
A representative of the Attorney-General’s Office told the committee the request should be rejected, previous rulings had found that Balad’s platform did not provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for disqualification, and agreed with the Joint List’s argument that the platform was old and did not reflect its current political agenda.
The Supreme Court has interpreted Section 7A narrowly, requiring clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that a prohibited objective is a dominant feature of a list’s activity rather than a marginal position or an isolated statement.
In 2019, the committee voted to disqualify a joint Ra’am-Balad slate, but the High Court of Justice overturned the decision and allowed it to compete.
Ra'am Chairman Mansour Abbas responds to disqualification decision
Wednesday’s decision was “political, improper, and anti-democratic,” Abbas said, adding that it contradicted the attorney-general’s position and rested on false allegations.
He accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies of seeking to prevent the formation of what he called “the next change government” by removing Ra’am from the race. The decision was an attack on Arab-Jewish coexistence and democratic participation, he said.
The Joint List said its disqualification was “a political, racist, and anti-democratic decision,” adding that it expected the High Court to overturn it.
Joint List calls ban 'attempt by Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, to steal election, disenfranchise over a million Arab Israelis'
The vote was an attempt to exclude the political representation of more than one million voters and was a continuation of a campaign by Netanyahu and the Right to delegitimize Arab citizens and suppress their turnout, the Joint List said.
Adalah, which represented all Arab parties and individuals before the committee, said: “The hearings, like the motions themselves, showed once again that this is an arbitrary, inciting, and racist process devoid of any legal process. The committee conducted an illegitimate political process aimed at persecuting ideas the majority does not accept, and it ended with the disqualification of all Palestinian representation in the Israeli Knesset.”
Earlier Wednesday, the committee voted to disqualify Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh. Because those decisions concern individual candidates, they require the High Court’s approval before taking effect.

Hope for progress after US, Iran hold first shuttle talks in months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:48:43 UTC
22:48:43 KST

The first shuttle talks between the United States and Iran in months raised hopes on Wednesday that the adversaries could make some progress towards ending the Middle East war, although neither side spelled out any change in their positions.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
"Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators. Let's see what happens with that," US President Donald Trump said. "They've been mediated for a while, but I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."
Earlier, Trump had told the UN General Assembly in a speech that he had to decide whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian was due to address the gathering on Wednesday.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with the United States through a Qatari mediator in New York and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to US "acts of aggression."
Some Iranian state media had earlier reported that Araghchi and Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified to Reuters that this was not face-to-face. Araghchi met the prime minister of Qatar, Sheik Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has been one of the main mediators at previous talks.
Oil prices hold at two-week low after Houthi attacks
The diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows, with Brent crude now holding just below the $100-a-barrel threshold it had shot through this month, after Houthi terrorists in Yemen launched a major offensive and fired into Saudi Arabia.
Trump repeated previous assertions that the war could end around the time of November's US midterm elections, though he has not explained why.
Since diplomacy broke off in July, the sides have repeatedly exchanged fire, although Trump has held back from a full-blown resumption of strikes after receiving advice from his military commanders that munitions were running low.
An interim agreement reached in June and signed by Trump and Pezeshkian would have given Iran its main demands: lifting financial sanctions and unfreezing assets in return for talks on limiting its nuclear program.
But that deal unraveled within weeks over shipping rules in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. Iran wants to exert greater control of the strait and collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects.
Shipping through Strait of Hormuz gradually increasing
Despite near-daily attacks on tankers, traffic through the strait has gradually increased in recent weeks. Oil producers have paid shipping companies fees worth as much as a quarter of a cargo's value to switch off transponders, navigate the route and transfer crude to other vessels beyond the strait.
Exports from the United Arab Emirates have already recovered to pre-war levels, and Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of Gulf oil for both this month and next, to be delivered beyond the strait off the coast of Oman, a big increase from August.
Even so, disruption continues to squeeze global energy markets. About a third of Gulf oil is estimated to be missing from global supplies. Shortages have particularly hit refined products such as diesel, causing inflation, pushing up interest rates and hurting Trump's Republicans ahead of the elections.
The risk of further disruption has increased since the Iran-backed Houthis advanced in Yemen this month, threatening traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, an alternative export route used by Saudi Arabia.
Washington, for its part, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, deepening Iran's economic crisis. Iranian officials say they are willing to endure the blockade to achieve their goals and will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until it is lifted.

Standoff with Trump administration sidelines UN refugee agency deputy, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:48:33 UTC
22:48:33 KST

The Trump administration is refusing to work with the newly appointed deputy head of the United Nations refugee agency, exposing tensions between the agency and one of its top donors at a time of acute funding pressures, diplomats said.
Tressa Rae Finerty, an American who took up the role of Deputy High Commissioner at UNHCR earlier this month, has taken leave as she seeks a waiver from the US government that would allow her to carry out aspects of her duties, according to seven diplomatic sources.
Her treatment by Washington, which previously considered cutting ties with the agency, is seen by several of the diplomats as a retaliatory response after UNHCR opted against Washington's preferred candidate, Simon Hankinson.
A State Department spokesperson said it could not comment on pending legal issues.
"We work with and through UNHCR when doing so advances US foreign policy interests," the spokesperson said.
Finerty did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The standoff comes as UNHCR grapples with one of its worst-ever funding crises following aid cuts by the Trump administration and others, at a time of record global displacement.
Finerty is currently unable to interact directly with US officials
Finerty, a career US diplomat who previously served as charge d'affaires at the US Mission to the UN in Geneva, is currently unable to interact directly with US officials because of post-employment restrictions that apply to former US government personnel, the sources said.
Violations of the restrictions, designed to prevent conflicts of interest, could in theory result in a prison sentence.
UNHCR told Reuters that Finerty requested a partial waiver from the US government late last month.
"This relates, in particular, to her participation in multilateral meetings that US Department of State officials attend," UNHCR said in a statement.
"We are hoping for a speedy and favorable resolution to this matter," it said, adding that the agency's operations and reform agenda continued "at full pace."
Key role for donors
The failure to obtain a waiver is seen as highly unusual because they are granted routinely for other former US staff entering the global body, diplomats and UN staff said.
The deputy high commissioner is traditionally one of the agency's most important interlocutors with major donors, including the US, diplomats and former officials said, adding Finerty’s situation may make it challenging for UNHCR to fundraise with the US.
The US, which has withdrawn from dozens of other UN entities under US President Donald Trump, had long been the agency's largest donor.
According to UNHCR data, Washington contributed more than $800 million in 2025, accounting for nearly a quarter of the agency's $3.6 billion in contributions. That dropped to around $110 million this year – of which $89 million was direct government funding, and the rest was from US companies and individuals.
The agency told Reuters that it estimated that its available funds in 2026 may reach just over $3 billion, 15% lower than last year and 43% lower than 2024.
