Partner content
Freelancing in the Netherlands? First get your tax sorted!
Setting up your own business or going it alone as a freelancer takes a lot of time and energy, and it is easy to forget some of the things you need to do. For example, if you are considering becoming a ZZP’er, how can you make sure you keep on the right side of the taxman?
Dealing with BTW
One of the first bits of paperwork you will be confronted with if you go into business in the Netherlands is dealing with BTW — omzetbelasting, or value added tax. “What people often forget is that they do have to submit their VAT return every three months even if they have only just started in business,” says Andra Radu, from Taxmo, an online bookkeeping and tax platform for freelancers, which largely focuses on helping internationals.
“Your first VAT deadline can arrive sooner than you expect. Starting a business doesn’t necessarily mean you have three months before you need to think about VAT. Depending on when you register, the VAT quarter may already be underway. And even if you haven’t made much money yet, you may still have a return to submit.”
Using a smart bookkeeping software, like that developed by Taxmo, means you can produce and send your invoices, keep a record of suppliers and upload the invoices they have sent you, calculate your personal expenses, and deal with your VAT and your income tax on one all-encompassing platform. You don’t even have to fill in the tax office’s own forms because Taxmo does it for you.
Understanding tax terminology
For many internationals, the difficult part isn’t running the business itself, it’s understanding the language and administration around it. You must file a VAT return if you are registered as an entrepreneur with the tax office (and have been assigned a VAT number starting with NL), if you are a ZZP’er — or freelancer — or if you are running a VOF, BV, or eenmanszaak (partnership, limited company, or sole proprietorship).
The jargon can seem incomprehensible and Dutch tax terms, unfamiliar deadlines and different rules for different types of clients can make a relatively simple freelance business feel much more complicated than it actually is.
Tax rules for freelancers
One rule freelancers may not be aware of, for example, is the KOR — yes, more jargon — the small business ruling, which, simply put, means that if you book annual turnover of less than €20,000 a year, you may be able to avoid dealing with VAT altogether.
Qualifying for the KOR doesn’t automatically mean it’s the best choice for your business. If you have significant business expenses, being unable to reclaim VAT on them can make a difference. It’s also worth thinking about how quickly you expect your business to grow rather than looking only at your turnover today.
“Business expenses are another area where new freelancers can easily get confused,” says Andra. “Keeping track of invoices, receipts and expenses from the beginning makes life much easier when it’s time to file, particularly when you’re still learning which costs actually count.”
Cross-border VAT
As an international freelancer, you may well have clients in other countries, and that’s something you’ll need to sort out too when keeping on top of your taxes. “This is particularly relevant for internationals, who often continue working with clients outside the Netherlands after setting up here,” Andra points out.
“You might have a Dutch client, an EU client and a US or UK client in your first few months of freelancing. How you handle VAT can depend on where the client is based, whether they’re a business or consumer and what you’re selling, so it isn’t always as simple as adding 21% to an invoice.”
File your tax returns yourself
Of course, smart software cannot solve all problems. There will always be situations where professional advice is useful, particularly as a business becomes more complex. But freelancers with relatively straightforward businesses don’t necessarily need to outsource every VAT return or routine piece of administration.
“Becoming a ZZP’er does not mean you need to understand every part of the Dutch tax system yourself or hire an expensive accountant for every filing,” says Andra. “Our platform has been designed specifically for the Dutch situation, to make sure you can do as much as you can yourself. We are all Dutch taxpayers even if we don’t speak the local language, or at any rate not much. Paying tax is not something you can avoid, but you can make it as easy as possible.”
Find out here how Taxmo helps freelancers handle bookkeeping, VAT and income tax in the Netherlands, without having to become Dutch tax experts themselves.

Two plants make 70% of Ukraine’s steel. Russia hit both. Then ports closed, rail costs rose 30%, and the EU’s carbon tax kicked in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:26:37 UTC
22:26:37 KST

Russian missile strikes shut down or damaged four of Ukraine's largest steel plants in August and September, halving steel output and prompting the operator of the country's largest plant to call on the government to pass a dedicated rescue plan, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Russia's full-scale war has already cost Ukraine the Azovstal plant in Mariupol, one of its largest steel mills, and more than two years of disrupted production across the sector. The latest strikes hit plants that produce the bulk of remaining capacity, concentrated in a single month, in what the industry describes as a deep crisis for a sector that supplies 6% of the country's GDP.
Steel output halved as missiles hit plants producing 70% of Ukraine's steel
The 11 August strike on Zaporizhstal killed seven workers and injured 21 as they headed for a shelter, Metinvest said; a second ballistic strike on the plant followed on 27 August. Two died and 13 were injured at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, and five were killed at Kametstal. Russia also hit the Dnipro Metallurgical Plant. On 12 September, Russia struck both Zaporizhstal and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih again with ballistic missiles.
Zaporizhstal and Kametstal, both part of the Metinvest group, stopped entirely. ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih—Ukraine's largest steel plant—partially shut down. Zaporizhstal and ArcelorMittal alone produce more than 70% of Ukraine's steel.
August steel production fell to 277,000 tons, down 57.3% year on year and 39.4% from July, according to Ukrmetalurhprom data cited by GMK Center. Rolled-metal output dropped to 270,000 tons.
Strikes, a port blockade, and rising costs hit at once
The strikes came on top of a Black Sea port blockade that has shut down maritime exports of iron ore and steel since late July. A 30% increase in rail tariffs took effect on 1 August. Alternative routes—rail through western border crossings, Danube ports, and roads—can carry at most 50% of what the Black Sea ports handled, GMK Center analyst Andrii Hlushchenko said. Steelmakers also have to compete with farmers for that limited rail capacity.
Rail exports of iron ore and metals dropped 2.5 times in the first 15 days of September compared with the same period last year, Ukrzaliznytsia said. Shipping iron-ore pellets through European ports costs $50–60 per ton, making many deliveries unprofitable.
The steel sector generated 6% of Ukraine's GDP last year, brought in 13% of all foreign-currency earnings, and paid UAH 27 billion (about $606 million) into budgets between January and July. Deputy chair of the parliamentary economic committee Dmytro Kysylevskyi called the situation "a perfect storm."
Meanwhile, Türkiye re-rolls Russian slabs and sells the resulting steel on Ukraine's domestic market. China uses cheap Russian energy to undercut Ukrainian prices.
"We are effectively importing Russian metal in the form of finished products," Ukrmetalurhprom President Oleksandr Kalenkov said.
ArcelorMittal calls for a Cabinet rescue resolution
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the government should pass a dedicated Cabinet resolution assigning specific tasks and deadlines to multiple agencies at once.
"No single agency can solve the full set of problems. Without a single document with assigned responsibilities and deadlines, each issue is dealt with in isolation and stalls," ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih representatives said.
The resolution should cover EU negotiations on deferring the carbon border tax (CBAM) until at least the end of martial law plus one year, restoring steel quotas to last year's level, stabilizing rail tariffs, securing long-term electricity contracts for industry, and launching anti-dumping investigations against Turkish and Chinese imports, Longobardo said.
Ukraine's Economy and Environment Ministry said it is in talks with the European Commission on easing CBAM and expanding quotas. A Cabinet source told the outlet that Black Sea trade negotiations with Russia are possible in October, after the Duma elections that ended on 20 September.

Outer rainbands of major hurricane Polo reach Mexico’s coast
Sept 23 - Hurricane Polo's rainbands reached Mexico's Pacific coast on Wednesday, posing life-threatening flooding risks, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Polo is expected to remain offshore, but its core will stay near the coast of southwestern Mexico during the next day or two, bringing heavy rain.
Conditions are expected to worsen, and the states of Guerrero and Michoacan could face between 3 and 8 inches (8 and 20 cm) of rain through Thursday, the NHC added in an advisory.
The heavy rainfall is expected to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in those states, and also affect nearby coastlines in Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco.
With maximum sustained winds near 155 mph (250km/h), and higher gusts, Polo is a Category 4 hurricane, after reaching Category 5 earlier.
"Fluctuations in intensity are expected, but Polo is expected to remain a very powerful major hurricane during the next few days," the agency added.
Mexico's government said it was coordinating efforts to strengthen preparedness and prevention measures along the Pacific coast.
Command posts are active in the states of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco, and Guerrero, the Security Ministry said in a statement.
"They are coordinating risk assessment inspections, condition evaluations, preparation of temporary shelters, and, if conditions require it, preventive evacuations," the ministry added. REUTERS

Military police are investigating the death of a 23-year-old Dutch woman after an all-terrain vehicle overturned on the Caribbean island of Aruba.

“We are investigating whether there is any question of liability, whether this is a case of reckless driving and whether anyone has made false statements,” he said.
“We already have a lot of information from social media, but we are still looking for witnesses.”
The family has asked anyone with information to contact them through the Facebook post or via Whatsapp on +31 6 40580456.

After Trump and Zelensky meet in New York, Ukrainian president says he hopes war will end ‘before winter’
Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky met on September 22 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, holding talks that lasted about 40 minutes. The two leaders discussed, among other things, prospects for negotiations with Russia, military aid to Ukraine, and a possible energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow.
Even before the meeting, Trump said from the U.N. podium that he expects the war to end soon: “We are working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will see this through to the end. It will happen, I think, sooner than people realize.”
After the talks, Zelensky also spoke about when the war might end:
I hope we will end this war, I hope that President Trump will help us end it. I think we need to do this as soon as possible — before winter, preferably before winter.
Zelensky’s hopes are shared elsewhere in Europe. “People are looking for a partial ceasefire come winter,” Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in an interview with Bloomberg.
Just two weeks earlier, speaking to Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Kyiv, Zelensky had said he expected the war to continue into winter.
In an interview with The Wall Street Journal after the meeting, Zelensky suggested that Trump would now try to reach an agreement with Moscow on an energy truce. Putin, he said, is unlikely to go along without additional pressure from Washington, such as increased sanctions. He added that Ukraine is willing to accept any format of truce and that he is ready for a three-way meeting with Putin and Trump.
The talks also covered a “winter package” of military aid. Zelensky asked Trump to give Ukraine Patriot missiles from American stockpiles, offering in exchange to later hand over to the United States part of the missiles Kyiv expects from a future delivery under an agreement with Germany. Trump did not agree, but Zelensky called the fact that he did not immediately reject the idea a “good step.”
The Kremlin said there are currently no preconditions for peace talks, though Putin is ready to meet with Trump. Presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called a meeting with Zelensky without prior expert-level preparation a waste of time and reiterated that it could only take place in Moscow.
Putin said that Zelensky, if he wants, can come to Moscow. All necessary security guarantees will be provided to him. He knows very well what decisions need to be made.
Discussions about the energy truce are expected to continue on September 23, when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to meet with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York, where he arrived for the U.N. General Assembly session. The U.S. State Department announced the meeting after the Trump–Zelensky talks.

How the British Crown profited directly from human trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:23:50 UTC
22:23:50 KST

How the British Crown profited directly from human trafficking
The question of slavery and reparations has recently returned to the center of international debate, particularly in Africa and the Caribbean. The conference held in Ghana on reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and slavery, as well as the petition filed by a Jamaican delegation to the British king, engaged in the struggle for historical recognition. The debate has also been brought into sharper focus by an investigation published by The Guardian, which examined the involvement of the British monarchy in the system of slavery and the historical links between the Crown and the trafficking of Africans.
Taken together, the developments raise a fundamental question: How can the British monarchy and the British state genuinely address a past in which the Crown was directly connected to the economic and political structures of slavery?
There are symbols that, on their own, encapsulate centuries of history. A crown branded with a red-hot iron onto the skin of an enslaved human being is one of them. It was a real, documented practice carried out by the South Sea Company, directly supported by the British monarchy during the reign of Queen Anne.
In 1713, this partnership secured for Britain the exclusive right to deliver nearly 4,800 enslaved Africans every year to the Spanish colonies in the Americas. This chilling figure was only the beginning of a broader system in which the British monarchy was a central actor.
The monarchy as a shareholder
History often portrays the transatlantic slave trade as an impersonal economic phenomenon, driven by commercial companies, far removed from political power. The reality is very different though. The Royal African Company, one of the most important slave-trading companies in British history, was directly led by James, Duke of York, who would later become King James II. Under his leadership, the company forcibly transported at least 150,000 Africans across the Atlantic.
Around 13,000 investors in the British slave trade have been identified, more than 10,500 of whom now have detailed biographical information. They include members of parliament, merchants, more than a thousand women from the aristocracy and bourgeoisie, as well as members of the royal family itself.
In total, the British slave trade forcibly removed more than 3 million Africans from their homeland and sent them to plantations in the Americas and the Caribbean, a figure that conveys the true human cost of the prosperity created by British colonialism.
Words, but no action
In the face of these facts, the official response of the contemporary monarchy remains, at best, cautious. King Charles III has described slavery as an “atrocious tragedy” and expressed support for historical research into the links between the monarchy and the slave trade. This is a symbolic gesture, and it marks a departure from decades of near-total silence on the subject.
However, a cold fact remains: To date, no official apology has been issued by the British government, and no serious discussion of possible reparations has been initiated at the state level.
The calculated caution is not unique to the United Kingdom, but it takes on particular significance there because it is precisely the monarchy, an institution supposedly embodying the continuity and unity of the nation, that is directly implicated by the historical evidence. Acknowledging “links” with slavery, as current royal communications do, is one thing. Acknowledging direct responsibility, with all the political, moral, and financial consequences that this entails, is another. Between the two lies the space in which the struggle over Britain’s colonial memory has been unfolding for years.
From the Koh-i-Noor to the Benin Bronzes
This unease can also be seen in the objects that the monarchy continues to possess. The Koh-i-Noor, the colossal diamond taken from the Indian subcontinent during the colonial era, is the most emblematic example. At her coronation in 2023, Queen Camilla chose not to wear the Queen Mother’s crown in which the stone is set, a choice apparently dictated by diplomatic caution rather than by any fundamental reconsideration, since the diamond remains preserved, as if nothing had happened, among the royal jewels.
The same pattern can be seen with the Benin Bronzes, looted during the 1897 British military expedition and still largely displayed at the British Museum, far from the African soil from which they were taken.
In both cases, the British position remains the same: Discuss, study, postpone – but do not return. These objects are material evidence of an organized system of looting, which official diplomacy continues to treat as a secondary issue.
This British debate is part of a much broader movement, driven for years by countries and peoples that directly experienced the slave trade and colonialism. Jamaica’s recent demand for reparations from the British government is one example among many, as are similar claims advanced by several African and Caribbean nations through international institutions and Pan-African forums.
These demands raise a very concrete question of the moral and material debt created by centuries of exploitation, a debt that the direct heirs of this system continue largely to evade.
The origins of the current wealth
One obvious fact, too often minimized, must be recalled here: The wealth accumulated by the British monarchy and by a large part of its aristocracy was not created in a vacuum. To a significant extent, it rests on forced labor, deportation, and the suffering of millions of human beings torn from the African continent. To celebrate royal heritage – its crowns, diamonds, and palaces – without clearly naming this origin is to erase an essential part of history.
Acknowledging “links” with slavery without drawing any concrete consequences turns a crime against humanity into a page of history accessible in archives. Words of compassion, however sincere, do not replace official apologies, reparations, or the restitution of looted cultural property.
For African peoples and their descendants in the diaspora, this question concerns the full recognition of a historical crime, the restitution of what was stolen – wealth, objects, and dignity – and the construction of an honest relationship at last between the former colonial power and the nations it plundered. As long as this recognition remains cautious and without concrete consequences, the debate will continue to impose itself with increasing force in British and international public life.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Drones are approaching gas stations: Kyiv is preparing a targeted alert system for filling stations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:22:05 EEST
22:22:05 KST

Drones are approaching gas stations: Kyiv is preparing a targeted alert system for filling stations
Kyiv • UNN
Gas stations in the capital will be able to operate during some alerts and suspend service only when a drone approaches. The protection is funded by network owners.
The capital's gas stations are planning to connect to an additional alert system for approaching enemy drones, which will allow gas stations to operate during part of an air raid alert and stop serving visitors only if an aerial target is directly approaching. This was stated by Kateryna Pop, a spokesperson for the Kyiv City Military Administration, on the air of Den.LIVE, reports UNN.
Details
According to Pop, gas stations in the capital are already subject to security protocols established by decisions of the Kyiv Defense Council. However, a separate alert system for the movement of enemy aerial targets is also being developed for them.
"Gas stations are subject to the protocols developed through the Defense Council's decisions on security levels, and an additional alert system for the approach of enemy targets to gas stations will be developed so that they can operate until an enemy target begins moving in their direction, and during that period finish accepting visitors and shut down the gas station," the KCSA spokesperson said.
The spokesperson clarified that this concerns a more targeted response system under which gas stations would not necessarily have to cease operations for the entire period of a prolonged drone threat. If an aerial target is detected moving directly toward a specific facility, staff will be able to finish serving customers in advance and switch to a safe operating mode.
However, funding for the engineering protection of the gas station complexes themselves will be the responsibility of the private owners of the networks. This includes, in particular, installing protective structures and shelters intended to reduce risks to employees and visitors in the event of a strike.
What preceded this
The new system is part of broader measures to protect fuel infrastructure following a series of Russian attacks on gas stations in Kyiv.
At the beginning of September, the capital introduced a differentiated alert system for aerial threats. It provides for different modes depending on the type of danger. The yellow level is used, in particular, during a drone threat, while the red level applies in the event of a missile, combined, or larger-scale attack. Such protocols are intended to allow businesses to continue operating during a less critical level of danger, provided they comply with the established safety requirements and have access to shelters.
Separately, on September 12, the government held an urgent meeting with fuel market operators following an increase in the number of Russian strikes on gas station complexes in the capital and along international highways. At the time, officials reported that they were testing a software solution intended to show the direction of enemy drones' movement and automatically warn gas stations of their approach. After testing at gas station complexes, a similar mechanism may also be applied to other types of businesses.
In addition, strengthening the physical protection of gas stations was discussed, including the installation of additional protective structures for above-ground infrastructure and the construction of shelters.
Similar measures began to be implemented earlier in the Kyiv region. On September 15, the Kyiv Regional Defense Council decided to provide gas station complexes with access to a special digital aerial-awareness system. It allows responsible gas station employees to receive real-time information about the movement of aerial targets and make decisions regarding the temporary suspension of operations.
Series of attacks on gas stations
The strengthening of security measures is taking place against the backdrop of a series of Russian attacks on the capital's gas station infrastructure.
On September 10, a Russian drone struck a gas station in Kyiv's Holosiivskyi district. People were injured in the attack. The Ukrnafta company reported at the time that the station was not operating when it was struck, and that staff and visitors had left the premises after the alert was announced.
On September 11, strikes on gas stations were recorded in the capital's Dniprovskyi and Obolonskyi districts, and on September 15, drones again attacked gas stations in the Darnytskyi and Holosiivskyi districts.
On September 23, strikes on two gas stations were recorded again in Kyiv. One of the UAVs hit a gas station in the Holosiivskyi district, while a fire broke out on the roof of another gas station in the Darnytskyi district.
Ukrnafta said that the strike on September 23 was already the sixth attack on the company's infrastructure in Kyiv over the past few weeks. According to the company, the personnel were in a shelter during the attack, so no one was injured at the affected facility.
Against the backdrop of regular attacks, fuel market operators have also begun installing mobile concrete shelters and gabions at gas stations. Previously, this practice was more common in frontline regions, but now protective structures are increasingly appearing in the capital as well.
According to Kateryna Pop, around 300 gas stations operate in Kyiv, with another approximately 600 in the Kyiv region. The Kyiv City Military Administration emphasizes that Russia has already used the tactic of striking fuel and transport infrastructure in frontline regions.
At the same time, the exact timeline for the full launch of an additional alert system for the capital's gas stations, the list of networks that will be connected to it, and the technical mechanism for transmitting warnings have not yet been publicly specified.

Why California Just Declared a State of Emergency Due to El Niño
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:21:35 UTC
22:21:35 KST

California’s governor Gavin Newsom has declared a state of emergency ahead of a potentially historic El Niño. In a statement released Sept. 22, Newsom said the declaration is meant to ensure communities have the resources they need to handle the impacts expected this winter.
“California is strongest when we look out for one another. That is what this action is about,” Newsom said. “Giving communities the support they need, giving first responders the tools to do their jobs, and giving families the confidence that their state is ready.”
Read more: How Should You Prepare For A Super El Niño?
The state of emergency allows the government to mobilize state resources: readying flood-fighting supplies such as sandbags and pumps, preparing the National Guard to assist with flood response and search and rescue efforts, and fortifying roads and infrastructure. State environmental and natural resources agencies will also fast-track permitting and engage in other efforts to better prepare for flooding and landslides.
How will El Niño impact California?
El Niño typically brings wetter, more intense winters to California—which could leave the state more vulnerable to severe winter storms, heavy rainfall, landslides, and flooding. An El Niño year does not guarantee that these conditions will occur, but it does increase the likelihood.
Climate change is also supercharging weather events, and El Niño is no exception. One study published in August found that El Niño events are now nearly 40% stronger than before the Industrial era. This year’s El Niño is predicted to be the strongest in recorded history.
What impacts has California already felt from this year's El Niño?
The governor’s office noted that the state has already experienced coastal flooding attributable to El Niño. The state can expect to see Kelvin waves, slow moving pulses of water that can stretch thousands of miles and raise sea levels along the coastline—increasing the risk for coastal flooding and erosion, and offshore Pacific hurricanes. Climate scientists also warn that the Pacific can expect to see a temporary 6-inch to 2-ft. rise in sea levels this winter.
A number of southern California towns, including Malibu, Laguna Beach, and Long Beach, have already seen significant coastal erosion due to El Niño and Pacific hurricanes this year.
How can Californians prepare for El Niño?
The state has urged residents to take action to prepare for El Niño by signing up for emergency alerts and learning their flood risk, and having an evacuation plan and emergency kit at the ready.
It’s all part of an effort to ensure that the state is not caught off guard by El Niño. “We are not waiting for this season’s storms to be on our doorstep,” Cal OES director Caroline Thomas Jacobs said in a statement. “By planning early and coordinating resources ahead of El Niño, we are working to ensure communities and first responders have the personnel, equipment, and support they need to prepare for severe weather, respond quickly when conditions change, and protect lives and property across California.”

Norwegian broadcaster voices concerns over Israel's participation in Eurovision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:18:54 UTC
22:18:54 KST

Norway's public broadcaster NRK has sent a letter to the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) following this year's Eurovision Song Contest, citing concerns about Israel's participation and how the competition rules were applied.
NRK's entertainment editor Jostein Olseng confirmed the letter on Wednesday, which was first reported by Norwegian newspaper VG.
“We send letters after each final to provide feedback on how the competition can be improved,” Olseng said, according to NRK, adding that the editorial team had raised “clear concerns” related to Israel's participation.
Olseng said NRK was particularly concerned about whether the contest's voting system reflects musical preferences or could instead be influenced by national or geopolitical considerations.
"We have come to suspect that the voting does not reflect which songs are the best, but rather which nation we support," he said.
Olseng stressed that NRK's position is that the rules should be applied equally to all participating countries.
"For us, it is important that the rules the EBU has are followed. If not, we are worried that the competition will be something other than what is intended," he said.
Asked whether NRK believes Israel should be allowed to participate, Olseng said countries that comply with the rules and are EBU members should be eligible to take part.
The Eurovision Song Contest has faced increased scrutiny over Israel's participation amid the genocidal war in Gaza and wider political tensions surrounding the contest.
Several countries, including Spain, the Netherlands and Ireland, boycotted this year's Eurovision Song Contest in protest over Israel's participation.

Swiss move house five times on average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

22:18:44 KST

Swiss move house five times on average
Swiss residents move home five times on average during their lives, and despite a housing shortage, only about half spend more than three months searching for a new place.
These are the two main findings of a survey conducted by the property portal Newhome, which interviewed 1,273 Swiss residents aged between 18 and 79.
On average, people moved house 4.9 times in their lifetime. One-third moved a maximum of twice, 41% between three and five times, and 32% over five times. Unsurprisingly, the proportion of those who have never moved house or have done so only once is particularly high amongst those under 29.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
Buying a property was the main reason for moving for one in three people. Twenty-four per cent cited a change in their relationship status and 27% a change in family circumstances as the reason for their most recent move. It is less common to look for new accommodation due to a new job or education (19%).
The survey also reveals some regional differences. For example, it is easier to find a home in canton Ticino in southern Switzerland than elsewhere – 35% took less than a month. Nationally, however, one in ten had to search for over a year, a figure that rises to 18% among 45–59-year-olds.

Confirmed Russian War Dead Top a Quarter Million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:17:24 UTC
22:17:24 KST

More than 250,000 Russian soldiers are confirmed to have died in Ukraine, and the actual figure is probably twice that, a report published jointly by the BBC and Russian outlet Mediazona on Tuesday says.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine started in 2022, a total of 258,980 individuals serving in the Russian military, identified by name, died either in combat or as a result of it, the report says.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The figure came from years of research into publicly available, verifiable sources such as social media posts by relatives, death notices and obituaries, reports in local media and statements from regional authorities.
The updated report marked the fourth anniversary of the Kremlin’s emergency mobilization of reservists following the September 2022 collapse of Russian defenses on the northwestern Kharkiv front to a Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The last time the Kremlin made public numbers of war dead and wounded was on Sept. 21, 2022, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said that 5,937 Russian service members had been killed in combat.
Practically all sources, including pro-Moscow milbloggers at the time, said the figure was minuscule and not credible.
According to current estimates published by Kyiv’s top headquarters, the General Staff, Russian military personnel losses in the war through Sept. 22, 2026, sit at 1,520,880 men killed or seriously wounded. The General Staff said its figures are backed by hard evidence, predominantly overhead drone video of the Russian soldier or soldiers hit.
Russian Mi-8 Helicopter Briefly Violates Polish Airspace, Poland Scrambles Fighters
International observer estimates are generally on par with Ukrainian estimates on Russian losses: The head of Britain’s armed forces, Air Chief Marshal Sir Rich Knighton, said British intelligence assessed about 1.5 million Russian military casualties since February 2022, including wounded, of whom about 500,000 had been killed, in his Sept. 11 comments to the media.
Per the Mediazona research, geographically, the death toll for Russian soldiers in Ukraine has been highest in peripheral territories with weak economies, particularly the interior Kuban region between the Black and Caspian Seas, and in the depressed regions in and around Chelyabinsk and Yekaterinburg.
The report says territories with majority non-ethnic Russian populations have been particularly hard-hit relative to their populations, including the predominantly Muslim Tatarstan and Bashkortostan along the upper Volga, and Buryatia and Zabaikalsky Krai near Mongolia.
Death rates in major cities with relatively well-off and educated populations, like the capital Moscow, along with the Russian heartland cities such as St. Petersburg, Tver, Yaroslavl, Vladimir and Smolensk, have been three or four times lower than in less-developed territories, data and graphics published in the report show.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and other Kremlin officials have, since the invasion, insisted Russia will eventually defeat Ukraine because Russia’s manpower reserves can support a continuous offensive that relentlessly gains ground and conquers parts of Ukraine the Kremlin wants to become part of the Russian Federation.
But increasing and sometimes rocketing soldier losses, especially since Ukrainian drone dominance made Russian armored operations obsolete and Russian troops shifted tactics to launching attacks on unarmored motorcycles or all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), have forced Kremlin recruiters to offer potential new recruits massive signing bonuses and to drum up volunteers in state prisons.
According to a report on current Russian recruiting practices published by the Conflict Intelligence Group (CIG) on Tuesday, the Russian state is working to replenish its ranks with a variety of tactics, but has not made the politically dangerous decision to conscript men into the army for combat operations.
Under current Russian law, a man drafted into army service may serve only on Russian Federation territory, though pressure on conscripts to “volunteer” for service in Ukraine is widely reported.
According to most reports, only a small percentage of potential recruits, despite those efforts, choose to go to war over Russian civilian life.
“In [the remote northeastern Siberian city of] Bratsk, the 2025 recruitment plan was increased from 548 to 645, but by Nov. 1, only 369 had been recruited,” the CIG report states.
“To fulfill the plan, city authorities visited over 14,000 addresses, conducted nearly 3,000 interviews, and targeted, among others, debtors, conscripts, foreigners, people with criminal records, and orphans. Of the 261 orphans and orphanage graduates ‘treated,’ only one signed a contract,” it adds.
Recruitment tactics used to fill the gap include offering the equivalent of a year’s factory worker’s salary as a signing bonus in the depressed central Russian region of the Republic of Mordovia, sending funding to and setting recruitment quotas for local governments and convincing them to sign up as soldiers in Yarsolavl, and even imposing fines and, in some cases, criminal liability on local officials failing to meet quotas, as seen in Stavropol, the CIG article says.
Cases of Russian unit commanders denying invalid soldiers, among them cripples and epilepsy sufferers, medical separation from the service, so that there might be more men available for the next attack are “multiplying,” as are incidents of men arrested on minor violations being forced by police to sign an army contract, a Tuesday Mediazona report says.
The article cited husbands of confirmed cases in the cities of Kirov, Penza, Petrozavodsk and greater St. Petersburg who were picked up by police for “questioning” and released only after signing an army contract.
Ukrainian news platforms and combat unit information feeds, citing Russian prisoners of war, have long reported limited training for new Russian recruits, usually 10 days to two weeks. Captured Chinese soldiers offered a broadly similar account of their training in their April 2025 press conference.
In a video published by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps from the eastern Lyman sector, Ukrainian troops encountered and took prisoner frontline Russian soldiers claiming not to have received food for days.
The images showed a poorly equipped Russian soldier, at one point unarmed except for a stick, surrendering to a 3rd Army Corps assault team. Four other Russian soldiers died in that single small battle, the same unconfirmed Ukrainian army report says.

Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:16:46 UTC
22:16:46 KST

Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
After a long pause, Russia’s authorities have renewed their campaign of nationalizing assets held by foreign companies — and they’ve gone big. On Thursday, Vladimir Putin issued a decree putting assets worth €6 billion under external management — specifically, the Russian divisions of retail chains Auchan and Leroy Merlin, food manufacturer Nestle and FM Logistics. Putin appointed an obscure company to manage them, with a former police general as its figurehead.
- Officially, the measure is not nationalization. Putin has imposed external management on the companies, not legally transferred their assets. This scheme was devised in 2023 and formed the basis by which Russia’s authorities seized hundreds of assets from Western owners — from energy firms to brewers and dairy companies. Foreign shareholders retain technical ownership but are stripped of all management rights (the right to repatriate profits was removed in 2022).
- Once a Russian asset is placed under external management, Western shareholders are often forced to sell to a Kremlin-backed owner, as in the case of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg. To complete the deals, Putin then suspends his own decree. But this is not always the case. Dozens of subsidiaries of Western companies have remained under external management for years.
- By default, Rosimushchestvo (the Federal Agency for State Property Management) takes charge of any assets that are put under local management by a presidential decree. But that route can be overruled. Often, assets are immediately acquired by a third party with the Kremlin's blessing. That is what is happening here. The Russian operations of Auchan, Nestle and FM Logistics went to a special purpose vehicle called LEV Management, a ready-made legal entity purchased by unknown individuals just before Putin issued his decree. The CEO is an obvious figurehead: Police Major General Andrei Krayushkin, who worked as deputy head of the Interior Ministry’s migration department in the late 2010s. Nobody has yet uncovered who is behind him.
- The Kremlin often justifies asset seizure on political grounds. For example, in 2023 many linked the decision to place Denmark’s Carlsberg under external management to Copenhagen’s willingness to supply F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine. Moscow views EU countries — and those in the “coalition of the willing” in particular — as its main opponents. With the exception of Switzerland’s Nestle, most of the affected companies are French. But why France has been singled out is unclear. Right now the Kremlin is in a bigger conflict with Germany, yet Metro Group, a German rival to Auchan, works without problem in Russia.
- Beyond politics, there are economic issues at play. First, amid fresh reports of a budget shortfall in Ukraine, plans to confiscate €200 billion of Russian reserves frozen in Europe since 2022 are back under discussion. This is a highly sensitive issue in Moscow, and all Russia has to threaten in return is the confiscation of foreign assets and funds already frozen in Russia. In this context, placing French companies with assets worth at least 600 million rubles (€6 billion) under external management looks like an attempt to gain a bargaining chip in the event of a future war of asset freezes.
- The Russian government’s own dire need for funds should not be overlooked. Over the first eight months of 2026, the budget deficit has already reached 2.5% of GDP. Placing a company under external management is not the same as nationalization. Russia does not have the right to sell Auchan and FM Logistics, nor plunder funds from their accounts to finance, for example, military expenses. But if Western countries move to confiscate Russian assets, this is the most likely next step.
Why the world should care
For whatever reason, the Russian government is reopening its battle with Western companies, in the biggest cases of de facto nationalization since 2024.

British plan to release prisoners sparks concern among Europeans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:16:28 UTC
22:16:28 KST

The UK is preparing to release thousands of prisoners early to alleviate prison overcrowding, a plan that has raised concerns among neighboring countries, reports Politico.
Five European Union diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Politico that the British plan worries their countries; some expressed fear that their nationals could be returned without prior warning or communication. One diplomat noted that returning criminals without advance notice carries significant risk.
The new policy threatens British efforts to rebuild relations with the EU at a time when both sides are preparing for a major summit on trade issues.
The UK plans to release more than 2,500 prisoners by the end of the year, with 700 set to be freed as early as the 1st of October. Starting the 1st of January, 2027, the British government will lift the requirement that foreign offenders must serve a minimum portion of their sentence in the UK before being deported. A British government spokesperson stated that discussions with European partners on this matter are ongoing and that those who have committed serious offenses will not be released. Likewise, individuals for whom there is evidence suggesting they might continue to commit offenses will remain in custody.
Meanwhile, EU diplomats have pointed out that communication is limited.
The British government maintains that it cannot provide further details; however, there ought to be a degree of cooperation between police forces, including notification when a criminal is released. A diplomat added that embassies are also concerned about the lack of inter-departmental communication, noting that one ministry keeps referring inquiries back and forth to another.
A third diplomat described the situation as complex, noting concerns among European capitals that newly released criminals could simply board a plane to their country of origin and move about freely. These countries would like more information on the individuals being deported, yet the British side acts as if there is nothing to coordinate, effectively making it a unilateral deportation.
Prison reform advocates point out that many of these offenders would be deported after serving their sentences regardless; the changes will simply accelerate the process. Mark Day, Deputy Director of the Prison Reform Trust, stated that whether an individual needs to remain in prison depends on the receiving country. Some of the deported foreign nationals would no longer need to serve out their sentences, while others might be subject to a less restrictive form of detention. It was added that deportations remain subject to legal and practical constraints, including the need to ensure compliance with human rights laws and protections for asylum seekers.
The latest data from the British Ministry of Justice indicate that
foreign nationals account for approximately 12% of the total prison population in the UK.
The majority come from various EU countries—such as Poland and Romania—as well as from Albania, an EU candidate country. Current regulations include reporting mechanisms regarding the convictions of citizens from European nations. The government is currently examining whether additional public safety measures are required.
The issue of prisoners poses yet another test for the Labour government’s pledge to move beyond Brexit and rebuild relations with European allies. A summit is scheduled for later this year to discuss agreements aimed at smoothing bilateral trade, facilitating travel, and fostering closer cooperation on climate issues. A date for the summit has not yet been set. The prisoner release issue will not make work in other areas any easier. One of the diplomats stated that if any of the released criminals were to return home and commit a heinous act, a serious diplomatic conflict could ensue. He added that it was a matter of simple trust; the British are seeking the status of a trusted partner, yet the British government’s evasiveness acts like a ticking time bomb.
Read also: Estonia rejects idea of housing British prisoners

The ambassador then noted that Italy is known and appreciated worldwide for the quality of its sports industry and its great athletes. This recognition has led to the organization of prestigious international sporting events, including the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympic Games and the Mediterranean Games in Taranto, which took place this year.

====================================================================================================

When Kremlin energy talking points come with an Oxford address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:15:20 UTC
22:15:20 KST

We have come to know the Kremlin's energy playbook well: "Europe will freeze without Russian gas," "sanctions hurt Europe more than Russia," "a managed, indefinite return to Russian supply is simply pragmatic." The respected European project EUvsDisinfo has repeatedly exposed these false narratives, carried by Russian state media, proxy outlets, and paid commentators. But Kremlin-friendly energy narratives do not travel only through obvious propaganda channels. They also enter policy debate through expert commentary, think tanks, media quotes, and institutional platforms, where they are far harder to see.
None of the apocalyptic forecasts came true. Europe cut Russian gas imports from 45% in 2021 to 13% by 2025 without blackouts or economic collapse. Yet the narratives predicting ruin kept circulating, sometimes from unexpected addresses. One of them, in my view, is worth a closer look: the work of Katja Yafimava, of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.
Across nearly two decades, her analysis has landed with remarkable consistency exactly where Gazprom would want it, the same firm whose money once helped fund her program. The record is public, and it is worth reading in full.
The narrative you don't notice
The most effective version of Kremlin-friendly energy messaging does not shout. It hedges, reframes, and omits. It raises "legitimate concerns" about sanctions costs, stresses the "legal complexities" of an LNG ban, and warns of "supply disruption risks" from moving too fast, without weighing Ukrainian lives or the cheaper, homegrown clean-energy alternative. Real concerns about European energy security did exist. What is worth noting is how reliably certain voices amplified concerns and how rarely they weighed counter-evidence.
This is not abstract. Surging oil and gas prices since the Iran war have handed Russia windfall revenues averaging, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, €604 million a day, money that funds the missiles falling on Ukrainian cities. Every argument for delay has a price, and Ukrainians pay part of it.
The Oxford label, and the money behind it
Katja Yafimava is a Senior Research Fellow at the OIES, which she joined in 2006. The institute is not part of the University of Oxford, though it carries the Oxford name, and its researchers appear regularly as authoritative, independent voices in UK and European media.
That independence has been questioned. Democracy for Sale, an investigative outlet, has documented the proximity between Russian oil and gas industry money and OIES, which previously received funding from Gazprom and its subsidiaries. The OIES Gas Program, where Yafimava works, was sponsored before the 2022 sanctions by Gazprom Marketing & Trading and by Nord Stream consortium partners, including Shell, OMV, Wintershall Dea, Uniper, and Engie. Gazprom Marketing & Trading and other firms with Russian business, such as Fluxys and TotalEnergies, appear as former benefactors in OIES annual reports up to the 2024 edition.
None of that, on its own, tells you what any individual researcher believes. What makes it worth raising is the alignment between that funding context and a published record that, across nearly two decades, has been remarkably convenient for Gazprom's positions.
Remarkable consistency
Consider the pattern. In 2017, Yafimava characterized EU and Polish legal objections to Gazprom's full access to the OPAL pipeline as an illogical obstruction driven by politics, language that would sit comfortably in Gazprom's own filings. In 2019, she framed the EU's Gas Directive amendment as an instrument "aimed primarily at Nord Stream 2." Russian state media have quoted her approvingly in pieces casting Brussels or Washington as acting in bad faith.
In 2021, she told Bloomberg the United States could not stop Nord Stream 2, a message Kremlin-controlled media amplified as proof of inevitability. In late 2021, as evidence mounted that Gazprom was deliberately withholding supply to squeeze Europe before the invasion, she described the company's conduct as "sensible, pragmatic behavior," at the very moment the IEA and EU lawmakers were pointing to deliberate "artificial tightness."
Each judgment is defensible in isolation. It is the direction of the whole series that is striking: over years and across cases, the analysis lands where Gazprom would want it to land.
The pattern holds as the war grinds on
Through 2022 and 2023, Yafimava warned that cutting Russian gas too fast risked "unavoidable" blackouts in Central and Eastern Europe. The blackouts never came. In 2025, she argued that REPowerEU created dangerous legal traps for importers and advised against a Russian gas phase-out, while a competing Forum Energii report concluded that full EU independence from Russian fuel by 2027 is feasible, and that Russia needs EU markets more than the EU needs Russian supply. In early 2026, she wrote that no complete phase-out "will happen either by 2027 or by 2028."
A forecast is not a crime. But the forecasts, like the analyses, keep pointing one way.
She has also stepped beyond technical commentary. In January 2025, she posted that peace in Ukraine "could only be achieved via a common European security architecture that would have to include Russia," a framing that mirrors a longstanding Kremlin strategic goal. And since March 2025, she has served as Vice-Chair of the UNECE Group of Experts on Gas, an agenda-setting role in a UN body that includes Russia. EUvsDisinfo has documented how the Kremlin uses UN platforms to lend its narratives multilateral legitimacy. A quieter UN gas group is a less visible version of the same channel, and quiet is what makes it effective.
The real question is why independent analysis, over nearly twenty years, has aligned so reliably with the interests of the company that once helped fund her program. That is a matter of record, and it deserves an answer.
Here is what the arguments for delay leave out: the alternative to Russian energy is not economic ruin. It is cheaper renewable power. The International Renewable Energy Agency found that in 2024, 91% of new renewable projects were cheaper than any fossil-fuel alternative; solar came in 41% below fossil power, and onshore wind 53% below. Renewables saved $467 billion in fossil-fuel costs in 2024 alone, and battery storage has fallen more than 93% in price since 2010.
This is the point that "supply disruption" warnings tend to bury, and it is why the warnings matter. Every year of delay, justified by the risks of moving too fast, is a year of continued payments to Moscow when a cheaper, domestic, un-weaponizable alternative already exists. Renewables reached 47% of the EU electricity mix in 2025; EU gas demand fell more than 17% between 2022 and early 2025; and the gas import ban agreed in December 2025 phases out Russian pipeline gas and LNG by the end of 2027, precisely the direction the delay arguments have worked against. The transition is not the risk. The delay is.
What should change
Editors, producers, and conference organizers could apply to energy analysts the conflict-of-interest standards already routine for pharmaceutical research: prior employment or program funding from Gazprom, Sberbank, or Russia-linked entities disclosed clearly every time such an analyst is presented as independent. UNECE could ask whether agenda-setting roles over European energy policy are well placed with analysts whose published record aligns so consistently with Kremlin positions. And Europe could close the transparency gaps that let think tanks with Russian-adjacent funding operate without disclosure requirements.
Every euro Russia earns from energy funds the war against Ukraine. The least we can do is know who is arguing for the payments to continue, and on whose past dime they built their expertise.

Iran’s president Pezeshkian to address UN general assembly before Zelenskyy takes the stage - live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:15:06 UTC
22:15:06 KST

Iran’s president said his country’s people had been the “victims of terrorism” by the United States. In Britain, the largest asset management company is planning major staff cuts
Kyiv • UNN
Britain’s Legal & General plans to cut about 10% of its workforce to simplify its structure and optimize costs. The sale of the company is not being considered.
British company Legal & General (LGEN.L) plans to cut its workforce by approximately 10% (or around 1,000 jobs) by mid-2027. CEO Antonio Simoes informed employees of this on Wednesday, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The publication notes that Britain’s largest asset management company is seeking to optimize costs and improve the efficiency of its operations.
The planned cuts are part of Simoes’ strategy aimed at simplifying the structure of the large financial group, which has a 190-year history. The company previously sold its homebuilder Cala and merged its investment divisions, promising shareholders higher returns.
L&G shares were down 0.8% at the latest close, while the FTSE 100 index fell 0.2%.
Although the share price has risen 13% since the beginning of 2026, the company’s performance in recent years has lagged behind that of competitors such as Aviva (AV.L) and the broader market. This has prompted speculation that the company could become a takeover target. Simoes said the company was not considering a sale.
"To successfully implement our strategy, we must ensure that our ways of working are aligned with the business we are becoming. Across L&G, we need to change our approach to work and, as a result, become a leaner organization. By the middle of next year, we plan to reduce our workforce by approximately 1,000 positions," Simoes said.
He added that L&G’s structure had become overly complex over the past decade. The company is launching a voluntary workforce reduction program but does not rule out compulsory redundancies.
An L&G representative said the changes would help the company focus investment on areas with the greatest growth potential, and also noted that trade unions would be consulted regarding the cuts.
Jaguar Land Rover confirms job cuts to save $2.3 billion05.09.26, 20:29 • 6277 views
The asset management division—one of L&G’s key business areas, alongside life insurance and pension products—will not be affected by the cuts, as it underwent restructuring last year.
Simoes, who took over as head of L&G at the beginning of 2024, is working to improve operational efficiency and increase the value of the group’s shares. In August, L&G reported an increase in operating profit for the first half of the year and raised a number of its performance targets, although it noted a decline in the number of deals in the pension risk transfer segment, despite forecasts of a significant volume of future contracts.

Preventing President Mahmoud Abbas from attending the UN General Assembly in New York “proved to be a failure", as the Palestinian issue featured prominently in speeches by Arab and international delegations, a Palestinian official said.
In a statement cited by Palestinian news agency WAFA on Wednesday, Palestinian presidency spokesperson Nabil Abu Rudeineh said attempts to prevent the Palestinian delegation from participating in the UN General Assembly and delivering its speech had failed to sideline the Palestinian cause.
For the second consecutive year, the US refused to grant Abbas and Palestinian officials visas to attend the UN General Assembly meetings, he said.
That forced Abbas to address the session via pre-recorded video on Thursday.
On the first day of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, several leaders slammed Israeli actions in Palestine.
Condemnation of Israeli violence in the occupied West Bank and Gaza featured prominently in speeches of UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Jordan’s King Abdullah II.
Under the UN Headquarters Agreement signed between the organisation and Washington in 1947, the US, as the host country, is committed to facilitating access by representatives of states and entities participating in UN meetings to its New York headquarters.
On September 17, the UN General Assembly approved allowing Abbas to participate via a recorded speech after Washington refused to grant him an entry visa.
“The voice of the Palestinian people has become strongly present on all continents of the world,” Abu Rudeineh said, adding that it is enshrined in UN resolutions and the positions of the majority of its member states.
He affirmed that Palestine will continue to participate in the UN General Assembly and all international forums despite restrictions imposed on its participation, according to the statement.
Palestine has held nonmember observer state status at the UN since 2012.
Of the 193 UN member states, a majority recognise the State of Palestine, while its efforts to obtain full membership continue to face a lack of UN Security Council approval.

The China-Russia Factor in the Iran War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:14:00 UTC
22:14:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Stephen J. Blank – non-resident senior fellow in the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s Eurasia Program and author of numerous publications on Soviet/Russian, U.S., Asian, and European military and foreign policies – is the 527th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
How is China-Russia cooperation supporting Iran’s resistance against U.S. military actions?
Sino-Russian cooperation supports Iran in many ways. Russia is transmitting satellite intelligence about the location and movement of American troops, ships, and aircraft. Iran used this intelligence to strike U.S. bases in Jordan and Saudi Arabia and may also have obtained Russian intelligence to strike at secret CIA installations.
Second, Moscow is making good Iranian drone losses, having helped Iran restock about 60 percent of its losses, often with improved versions of drones Iran sent to Russia. Russia also gives Iran tactical guidance on drone use, e.g. how many drones Iran should use and should use and from what altitudes it should shoot. Thus, Iran benefits from Russian lessons in Ukraine.
Third, Russia’s “Caspian Express” has become a major logistical lifeline for Iran. Lastly Russia provides diplomatic support for Iran.
China and possibly Russia are selling Iran shoulder-fired air missile defenses MANPADS. Chinese engines power the Russian drones sent to Iran, which reportedly also incorporate Chinese radio modems and cameras. China also has recently closed a deal to sell Iran supersonic anti-ship missiles with a range up to 290 km to deter or strike U.S. vessels.
Likewise, Chinese entities provide chemical precursors and dual-use items for Iran’s ballistic missile program. Chinese entities are also reportedly loading Iranian vessels with the solid rocket-fuel precursor, sodium perchlorate, and may be preparing to supply spare parts and missile components. Iran also has military-grade access to China’s Beidou satellite navigation system and China has given Iran geospatial intelligence through state-affiliated commercial satellite companies.
What is the strategic calculus for Beijing and Moscow in bolstering Tehran’s position?
Both Russia and China share a common motivation to weaken the U.S. either leading to its defeat or to a protracted war that bleeds U.S. strength, ties it down in the Gulf, and prevents greater military support for Ukraine, Taiwan, and Washington’s Asian and European allies. They also aim to weaken American alliances, damage America’s global standing and economy, and increase its domestic polarization. Moreover, this war validates their ideology about the decline of an American-led world order and the alleged rise of a new multipolar order, thereby lending credence to that ideology.
How is China benefitting from protracted conflict in both the Ukraine and Iran wars?
These wars benefit China in many ways. Since it previously built up its energy reserves the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz does not threaten it. China already gets Turkmen and Russian energy at a discount. Iran’s dependence has grown while Washington’s military-political-economic capabilities and strategy have failed. Meanwhile Russia’s economy gains a reprieve, and a distracted Washington is increasingly unable to support Taiwan or other Asian allies as needed. Trump has proven himself to be strategically incompetent, giving China more freedom to threaten Taiwan, the Philippines, Japan, etc. In Ukraine, the lack of aid to Kyiv and energy windfalls for Russia thanks to Iran divert Western attention from Asia while Russian dependence on China grows. Lastly the war has enabled China to project air and naval power into the Middle East at an unprecedented scale.
Examine the impact of the Strait of Hormuz imbroglio on China-U.S. competition in the Middle East.
The stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz benefits China by showing what can only be described as Trump’s egregious strategic malpractice. When his ravings and utter lack of strategic capability are juxtaposed – or more precisely contraposed – to China’s steadiness, refusal to commit its military but substantial support for Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine, Beijing looks better and better. Moreover, it diverts Washington, which has done little or nothing to push back on Chinese encroachments against Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, or against Russia since the May summit in Beijing.
Assess the effectiveness of U.S. leadership vis-à-vis China-Russia cooperation in advancing U.S. interests in the Iran war.
As I noted above, egregious strategic malpractice and incompetence have characterized Trump’s wartime policies, and arguably almost all of his foreign and defense policies. This war had no strategic planning, its goals change daily, and enormously damaged U.S. interests. Indeed, as of today Iran has arguably won, which benefits Russia and China.
While the Moscow-Beijing axis is tightening in economics, politics, and military affairs; every U.S. alliance system – NATO, our alliances in Asia and in the Middle East – is under pressure or in growing disarray. Although there are some structural causes for this trend, the common denominator is Trump and his team, many of whom are equally strategically incompetent, for their attacks on allies, reckless ignorance of strategic realities, and failure to plan for this war.
Consequently, there is diminished pressure on Russia; indeed there are secret talks with it rather than support for Ukraine, China advances on our Asian allies while the administration is either silent or spouts platitudes as Assistant Secretary Colby’s tour of Southeast Asia and speech there show. There is apparently no effort to strengthen our alliances against this Moscow-Beijing axis or the larger axis including Iran and North Korea, i.e. the CRINK. Instead, leading members of this administration regularly depreciate, devalue, or even threaten our allies, giving them reasons for distrusting America’s commitment.
So, while our alliances are all faltering Russo-Chinese ties, along with ties among the CRINK, e.g. Iran-North Korean ties, are expanding. The contrast with the Trump administration policy is both telling and ominous.

New powerful synthetic opioids behind sharp rise in Scottish drugs deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:12:54 UTC
22:12:54 KST

New forms of a powerful synthetic opioid have contributed to a sharp rise in Scottish drug deaths, with the latest data showing an 11% increase in fatalities last year
Annual figures released by National Records of Scotland (NRS) on Wednesday recorded 1,133 drug-related deaths in 2025, 116 more than the previous year. The 2025 figures are the sixth highest on record.
Opiates and opioids, which include drugs such as heroin, remain the most deadly drug types, implicated in 78% of all deaths. But the presence of nitazenes – a highly potent type of synthetic opioid – rose by more than 200%, from 76 deaths in 2024 to 247 in 2025.
Maree Todd, the minister for mental wellbeing, public health, sport, alcohol and drugs, said an “increasingly toxic and unpredictable drugs supply” required “more coordinated action across the country”.
Last year’s data showed Scotland’s lowest drug deaths since 2017, but the charity Scottish Drugs Forum (SDF) warned at the time that this was most likely a blip, masking a recent surge in synthetic opioids in Scotland’s illicit drug market.
Unlike plant-derived drugs such as heroin, nitazenes are created in illegal laboratories and can be hundreds of times stronger than traditional opiates and opioids. They are also often mixed with other drugs, increasing the risks to users who do not always know what is present in the supply.
SDF’s chief executive, Kirsten Horsburgh, said the increase in drug deaths reflected a range of factors “including an increasingly unpredictable drugs supply”. The increased presence of nitazenes was “a stark indication of [the] changing risks”, she added
Horsburgh said: “It is too simplistic to say that 1,133 people died because of the contaminated drug supply, or indeed because of drug use itself. The truth is that these deaths are shaped by a much wider set of factors, including poverty, trauma, deprivation, housing insecurity and mental health inequality.”
The figures showed drug-related deaths were 15 times higher in Scotland’s most deprived areas than in the least deprived. There was a 19% rise in deaths among men, withthe average age of death 46.
Todd said the government had funded more than 1,100 residential rehabilitation placements last year and widened access to treatment. But, she added, “despite these policy interventions, and the actions of our valued frontline workers, it is clear we need to do much more to reduce this tragic loss of life”.
The new figures mean Scotland remains Europe’s “drug deaths capital”, with the worst fatality rate in the continent.
Before the figures were published, the Scottish government announced that a new drug-checking service, which will allow users to submit drugs for rapid testing and provide harm reduction advice, would open early next month in Glasgow’s safer drug consumption facility. Similar drug-checking services have been approved in Aberdeen and Dundee, with a fourth expected in Edinburgh.

Earlier incidents
The incident is the latest in a series of Russian military aircraft and drone incursions into Polish airspace since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
On Feb. 11, 2025, a Russian Su-24MR military aircraft entered Polish airspace over the Gulf of Gdańsk, penetrating about 6.5 kilometers (4 miles) and remaining there for roughly 72 seconds. Russia later acknowledged the incident and attributed it to a navigation-system malfunction.
On April 25, 2025, a Russian military helicopter also entered Polish airspace over the Baltic Sea’s territorial waters. Poland said the incident appeared to be an attempt to test its air-defense readiness.
NATO Keeps Article 5 Trigger ‘Deliberately Ambiguous’
The most serious incident came on Sept. 9-10, 2025, when 19 Russian drones violated Polish airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland scrambled fighter jets and subsequently requested NATO consultations under Article 4.
Most recently, Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine and increased military activity near its borders, although not every such incident has involved a violation of Polish airspace.
