‘It’s inescapable’: will new revelations about enslavement force Britain to finally confront its past?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:49 UTC
22:00:49 KST

Over the past 10 days, a series of registers, documents and reports have been published, all revealing the scale of Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade. The overall picture is one of a nation powered by enslavement and investment in it. This week, I spoke to Chris Osuh, a community affairs correspondent at the Guardian, about these new revelations and Britain’s persistent difficulty in confronting its own history.
Last week, a Register of British Slave Traders, compiled by historians, was published. Its length and detail exposed that the British financial system was much more involved in enslavement than previously thought. Scrolling through the names is chilling in its prosaicness. There are owners and co-owners of slaving voyages from London to various locations in the Caribbean. There are investors in the Royal African Company, an English trading company that trafficked more Africans to the Americas than any other. There are ordinary people – soap boilers and cheesemongers, surgeons and diplomats – all with various interests, shares, ownerships and investments in the trading of Africans. The register is 636 pages long.
The commodities they traded and profited from were also named a few days later. Earlier this week, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers was published, making almost 4 million records of enslaved people across 20 former British colonies searchable to the general public.
People will have different responses when perusing these accounts. But I was most struck by seeing the names of those who were sold into hundreds of years of enslavement and suffering, expressed through the banality of trade and profit details. The relics of the entire system: the ledgers, the neatly written names of the enslaved and their children, reduced to units. Grappling with these records vertiginously brings you face to face with a history that does not feel distant or unrelatable, but something intimate and familiar. This was a business.
Chris draws another parallel between these accounts and the present: there is still a persistent impulse to minimise what happened. “The common thread, to put it bluntly,” he says, is “the same tendency to minimise African pain, suffering and labour. That is something that cuts across centuries. It just expresses itself in different ways.”
“Once upon a time it expressed itself with justifications of slavery,” Chris tells me. “Now it expresses itself with ‘we don’t have to apologise, we don’t owe you anything’.”
Why disavow this part of British history?
Britain is a nation with a vast cultural appetite for its history – from period dramas, to Henry VIII, to the world wars of the 20th century. So I am always astonished by the absence of enslavement from mainstream historical accounts. If you are a nation interested in documenting your past, forget about the morality of it, you would surely be interested in including a system that played a significant role in Britain’s politics, economy and industrialisation for almost 250 years. Perhaps there has been an offshoring of enslavement in the British collective consciousness, in the same way slavery was geographically offshored to British colonies.
Chris says that these blind spots partly result from the ways that history has been leveraged for national fantasies. There is a perpetual culture war surrounding British history, Chris says, “where one side uses history to engage in a kind of national myth making that makes everybody feel good about their identity. This approach values a heroic narrative in which you are always the good guy.” I am reminded here of the scholar and first prime minister of Trinidad and Tobago Eric Williams, who remarked that “British historians wrote almost as if Britain had introduced Negro slavery solely for the satisfaction of abolishing it.”
In the competing historical practice, history is about learning from the past and preventing future mistakes. In 2023, the Guardian published the Cotton Capital series on its founders’ links to enslavement in Manchester, England. In response to these revelations, it launched the 10-year Legacies of Enslavement programme, which included the creation of the Long Wave and Chris’s role.
“There is a huge blind spot about the reality of empire in the UK,” Chris tells me. “It’s a strange blind spot. It’s almost a taboo. You’re not really supposed to connect the dots. You’re not supposed to ask: ‘Where was Manchester getting its cotton from? Where were the ships from Liverpool going? The insurance industry and stockbrokers in London – what were they selling shares in? Why is there a place called West India Docks’?”
The interesting thing, Chris has gleaned from his reporting, is that “there was much more transparency at the time. Church of England clergy were basically saying ‘we need to colonise for gain’s sake, because England is overcrowded’. That ‘Africans are the fittest hands for plantation work’. Churchmen saying ‘we use African bodies for our support and happiness’. They were not pretending.”
That clarity has become obscured over the years by an enveloping myth about Britain. One that has resulted in, Chris says: “a lot of amnesia about inconvenient histories.” This notion that Britain has built itself alone is challenged by honest accounts of its past, which show that the building of modern Britain was made possible by the unpaid labour and resources of millions of people. Chris tells me: “They interfere with this idea of an island nation that punches above its weight.”
It’s time to face the facts
The old myths are colliding with these new accounts. “The scholarship is thriving on different continents,” Chris says, and he describes much of it as an evidence-based account of “who did what, where, and the impact”. Black scholars are at the forefront, but they are joined by white scholars in Europe and America. “This takes it from a place where critics can argue that this is driven by Black self-interest,” Chris says. “Critics would love to frame this in terms of identity, or minimise what happened and make it ideological. But beyond the desire for justice, there is a desire for knowledge.”
By resisting this knowledge, we are denying ourselves a full understanding of Britain’s past, and its present. “This was a commodification of human life on a scale that has never been seen before or since, and an industrialisation of the process sustained by prolonged violence and cruelty,” Chris tells me. He emphasises that these histories show us how that dehumanisation was made possible, with people treated as objects, property, products, as units to generate capital. “It’s inescapable.”
But people and institutions still do want to escape it, not just to avoid shame, but to avoid material loss. As Caribbean nations increasingly mount reparations claims, these records bring us closer to establishing a legal picture of liability.
Even those who refuse to engage with a moral argument must face the fact that there is a case here. “The backlash is being kept alive because it goes to the heart of two things so dear to western societies,” Chris says. “Their identity as heroic, and their money.”

Social anxiety drives people to conform specifically to negative feedback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:40 UTC
22:00:40 KST

People with high social anxiety are highly prone to adjusting their own emotions to match negative feedback from their peers, a tendency backed by sustained brain activity. A small study published in Biological Psychology reveals that this biased conformity may help maintain anxiety symptoms by causing individuals to overthink critical social information.
Social anxiety involves an intense fear of being evaluated poorly by others, combined with a strong motivation to be accepted. This psychological tension often leads people to conform to group norms as a defensive strategy against social rejection. Past research on social influence has mostly focused on how people change their outward opinions, such as rating the attractiveness of a face or answering a factual question.
Lixia Cui, Xiaofei Dong, and a team of researchers from Capital Normal University and Zhejiang Normal University wanted to understand a deeper phenomenon known as emotional conformity. Emotional conformity happens when individuals actually adjust their internal anticipated feelings to match the emotions of the people around them. For someone with social anxiety, shifting their internal emotional state to match a group could slowly erode their authentic self-expression and reinforce negative thoughts.
The researchers designed a study to map the exact brain mechanisms that drive this process. They focused on two distinct stages of information processing in the human brain, which can be measured using sensors placed on the scalp.
The first stage is an early, automatic reaction to social conflict, often called a conflict detection signal. When a person realizes they disagree with a group, the brain typically produces a specific electrical dip about 400 milliseconds later.
The second stage involves deliberate, prolonged mental effort. If the brain decides that a piece of information is highly relevant to a person’s goals or fears, it sustains an electrical charge over a longer period. This late signal acts as a marker of deep engagement, showing that a person is spending mental energy trying to integrate conflicting information.
To test how these brain signals operate during emotional conformity, the research team recruited 44 young adults. Half of the participants scored high on a questionnaire measuring social anxiety traits, while the other half scored very low.
During the experiment, participants sat in front of a computer monitor wearing a cap fitted with electrodes. They viewed a series of 300 images depicting different social scenes. Half of the images showed neutral situations, and the other half showed socially threatening or negative situations.
For each image, participants were instructed to imagine themselves as the person in the scene. They then rated how pleasant or unpleasant they would feel in that situation on a nine-point scale.
Immediately after locking in their answer, the participants saw a feedback screen. This screen displayed what was supposedly the average rating given by 200 college students who had previously viewed the same image. In reality, the researchers pre-programmed this feedback. For one third of the trials, the peer rating matched the participant’s rating. For another third, the peers appeared slightly more positive. For the final third, the peers appeared slightly more negative.
The participants then took a 30-minute break. After the break, they were asked to rate all the same images a second time, but this time without seeing any peer feedback. By comparing the first and second ratings, the researchers could measure exactly how much each person changed their anticipated feelings based on the social pressure.
The behavioral results showed a sharp contrast between the two groups from the very beginning. During the initial rating phase, participants with high social anxiety rated the neutral social scenes much more negatively than participants with low anxiety. This suggests that people with elevated social anxiety carry a generalized negativity bias, causing them to anticipate unpleasant feelings even in harmless situations.
When the researchers looked at how the ratings changed after the break, they found a lopsided pattern of conformity. Individuals with high social anxiety were highly sensitive to peer feedback that was more negative than their own initial rating. When told that peers found a scene more unpleasant than they did, the anxious participants drastically lowered their second ratings.
They did not show the same level of conformity when the peer feedback was more positive than their own. If the peers rated a situation as relatively pleasant, the anxious participants mostly ignored it. This means they selectively absorbed social information that confirmed their fears while disregarding information that contradicted those fears.
The brain wave recordings provided a biological explanation for this behavior. When the participants with high anxiety saw that peers gave a more negative rating to a negative scene, their brains produced a large spike in the late electrical signal associated with mental effort.
This amplified late signal showed that the anxious participants were dedicating intense, sustained cognitive resources to process the negative feedback. They were not just automatically mimicking the group. Instead, they were actively overthinking the social disagreement and working hard to integrate the critical information into their own emotional expectations.
The researchers also examined the early electrical signals that track automatic conflict detection. This early brain wave did not reveal any robust or interpretable differences between conditions; although an overall three-way interaction was detected, no specific comparisons reached significance. This suggests that the biased conformity seen in social anxiety is not an immediate, uncontrollable reflex, but is driven by the later stages of deep, motivated thinking.
A few limitations to the study should be kept in mind. The research utilized static images and pre-programmed numbers on a computer screen to simulate peer pressure. Real-world social influence usually involves dynamic cues, such as shifting facial expressions, tone of voice, and interactive dialogue.
The participant pool was largely female. Because men and women can sometimes experience social pressure differently, the unequal gender ratio limits how broadly the findings can be applied. The group with high social anxiety was also identified through a self-report survey rather than a clinical evaluation. Studies involving patients formally diagnosed with social anxiety disorder will be needed to confirm these exact brain patterns in clinical settings.
Despite these limitations, the research offers a detailed look at how anxiety hijacks social learning. Because people with social anxiety spend extra mental energy processing negative opinions, they constantly validate their own insecurities. Future psychological therapies might help by training individuals to recognize this mental trap, teaching them how to disengage from critical feedback and break the cycle of emotional conformity.
The study, “Aberrant emotional conformity among individuals with social anxiety,” was authored by Lixia Cui, Chuanji Gao, Xiaoqing Yan, and Xiaofei Dong.

Beluga whale rescued from closed Canadian marine park dies in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

An Illinois aquarium has said that a third beluga whale it rescued from a closed marine park in Canada this summer has died after it struggled to acclimate to its new environment.
Osiris, a 26-year-old female, was one of 30 belugas removed from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland amusement park, and among 10 rehomed at the Shedd aquarium in Chicago, which said the whale died there on Monday.
Over the last month two other rescued belugas, named Peekachu and Rain, have died at the Shedd; and a 19-year-old male, Jelly Bean, one of two relocated to Oceanogràfic de València in Spain, died “suddenly and unexpectedly” last week.
“When Shedd was asked to help with this rescue, we understood that these animals arrived with significant vulnerabilities and that the outcome for every individual could not be guaranteed,” the aquarium said in a statement.
Beluga whales are particularly vulnerable to changes in their environment, such as climate change, pollution and other sources of stress, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).
Native to Alaska’s Cook Inlet, belugas are classified as an endangered species, and their numbers have declined by almost 80% from 1979 to 2018.
The 30 whales, and a number of bottlenose dolphins, became the subject of what marine activists said was akin to a hostage situation following the 2024 closure to the public of Marineland, a troubled theme park on the southern shores of the Niagara river.
More than 20 whales and dolphins had died there since 2019, and a calamitous drop in visitor numbers and income forced the owners to abandon the venture. The Canadian government blocked the sale of the surviving animals to China, leaving them facing the threat of euthanasia.
A complex international operation moved 30 whales to aquariums in the US and Spain over the summer, but many did not take well to their new surroundings. The deaths were sudden and unexpected as their health wavered amid the challenges of adjusting to a new home, according to statements from the aquariums.
The rescued belugas were moved in custom-made slings and temperature-controlled containers, Shedd staff told the Associated Press. Aquarium personnel traveled to Marineland to examine their health records in preparation for the move. They have monitored their health minute by minute since they arrived, staff said.
Peekachu and Rain died at the Shedd in late August and early September after arriving from Canada. Another beluga, at the aquarium for decades, died around the same time.
Osiris was a “whale of clinical concern” since she arrived, according to the aquarium. The whale did not eat as consistently as her fellow animals, which complicated the efforts to keep her well-fed and hydrated, according to the statement.
“Osiris experienced periods of meaningful progress, both nutritionally and socially, but her overall condition remained closely monitored,” the aquarium stated.
Osiris’ caretakers noticed sudden changes in her behavior and breathing patterns the morning of her death, according to the aquarium. She was moved to the medical habitat, but “her condition declined rapidly,” and she “passed away despite lifesaving efforts”.
José Rafael Serra Díez, spokesperson for Oceanogràfic de València, said Jelly Bean’s death was also unexpected. The whale “experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring”, despite periods of improvement, the spokesperson said in an email to the AP.
The Georgia aquarium and SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio have also accepted whales from the Canadian park.
The two rescued whales at the Georgia aquarium showed decreased appetites and were examined, but no issues were found, the aquarium said in a social media post on Friday. The whales at SeaWorld are in “stable health”, according to AnneMarie Iturrizaga, a spokesperson for the company that owns the parks.
The Shedd aquarium notified Noaa of Osiris’s death Monday, according to John Chu, a spokesperson for Noaa Fisheries. Within 30 days of the whales’ deaths, the aquarium must formally submit their names and causes of death, and on request, provide copies of necropsy reports, Chu said.
The Shedd aquarium said it will conduct necropsies and share the confirmed results.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

From Tian Shan peaks to Silk Road history: A journey through Turkistan

13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

Ranked among Kazakhstan’s top five domestic tourist destinations, the Turkistan region blends nature, history and spirituality, revealing the rich heritage of the country’s southern region.
Modern Nomads has already explored the city of Turkistan and the magnificent Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, the renowned Turkic Sufi poet and mystic. This time, the journey continues across the Turkistan region in southern Kazakhstan, beginning in Sairam-Ugam National Park at the foot of the Western Tian Shan mountains.
A mountain escape in southern Kazakhstan
The landscape changes dramatically as the road climbs into the mountains. Cool air replaces the heat of southern Kazakhstan, while alpine meadows, crystal-clear rivers and forested slopes create striking scenery.
Local rangers say the water in some of the park’s streams is clean enough to drink. Climbers, hikers and campers come from Kazakhstan and abroad to explore its mountain trails and spend nights surrounded by alpine scenery.
For German traveller Fenja Schreiber and American tourist Kaleb Shumway, camping in the park became one of the highlights of their journey through Kazakhstan.
"We didn't make it up to the second lake, but we camped by the first lake for two nights. It was amazing," says Shumway. "We saw a group of about 30 goats in the morning," adds Schreiber.
The park's rich biodiversity also requires visitors to tread carefully. Rangers ask people to keep noise to a minimum, as Sairam-Ugam is home to some of Kazakhstan's rarest wildlife.
"The park is home to a rich variety of wildlife, including snow leopards, Tian Shan brown bears and Siberian ibex," says park ranger Daniyar Otegenov. "Near the lakes, visitors can often spot marals grazing. Many people come here hoping to see these animals, and it's not unusual for wildlife to come quite close to visitors."
Interest in the park continues to grow. More than 71,000 people have visited Sairam-Ugam so far this year, according to park officials, with the busiest part of the season still ahead. Tourism infrastructure is expanding alongside visitor numbers, with accommodation ranging from capsule cabins to hotels. A new visitor centre, scheduled to open in 2027, is expected to make the park more accessible to visitors.
Walking through a Silk Road metropolis
Leaving the mountains behind, our journey continues to Otrar, once one of the most important cities along the Silk Road. Today, little remains beyond wind, sand and the outlines of ancient streets. Yet walking through the 200-hectare archaeological site, visitors can trace the outlines of the city that once stood here.
The heart of Otrar was its citadel, the city's heavily fortified centre and home to its wealthiest residents. Reconstructed houses offer a glimpse into everyday life centuries ago, revealing that many features associated with modern living were already in use.
"During the winter, the underfloor heating served several purposes," explains tour guide Ismail Omaraliyev. "People baked bread and cooked food here, and in the evenings, they would rest and sleep on the warm floors."
Just beyond the homes stood the public bathhouse, where residents relaxed in communal bathing pools. Nearby were the mosque, the central square and the palace of Berdibek Khan. As one of the busiest trading hubs on the Silk Road, Otrar welcomed hundreds of merchants and travellers every day.
"At least two caravans arrived every day, each with around a hundred camels. On average, between 400 and 500 people spent the night in the city every day," says Omaraliyev.
Although Otrar flourished as a centre of trade for centuries, much of its story still lies beneath the ground. A research project supported by a grant from the International University of Tourism and Hospitality is helping archaeologists uncover new chapters of the city's past. Led by Mukhtar Kozha, a professor and doctor of historical sciences at Akhmet Yassawi University, the team continues to excavate new areas of the settlement, revealing how Otrar evolved over the centuries.
One of the latest discoveries is the oldest mosque found in Otrar so far, dating to the late 13th and early 14th centuries. After it fell out of use, the site later became a burial ground before eventually being transformed into a pottery workshop. Layer by layer, each excavation reveals another chapter of the city's history.
"What makes this discovery remarkable is that we've found evidence of massive stone blocks being brought into the centre of Otrar," says archaeologist Mukhtar Kozha. "The city is far from the mountains, so transporting them here must have required enormous resources and careful planning. It reflects the high level of urban culture and engineering that existed here."
With history stretching back more than 2000 years, Otrar reached the height of its prosperity before being destroyed during the Mongol invasion in the 13th century. It was later rebuilt and remained inhabited until the 19th century. Today, visitors can continue the journey through the nearby Otrar Museum, where many of the artefacts uncovered during excavations are preserved.
A place of pilgrimage
Just 15 minutes from Otrar stands the Mausoleum of Arystan Bab, one of Kazakhstan's most important pilgrimage sites. Believed to have been the teacher and spiritual mentor of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, Arystan Bab remains a symbol of the region's deep spiritual heritage.
The structure standing today is the fourth version of the original mausoleum. Inside, two original 14th-century columns have survived centuries of wars, earthquakes and rebuilding, offering a rare connection to the monument's earliest history.
As interest in cultural tourism continues to grow, the Turkistan Region is attracting more visitors eager to discover its combination of mountain landscapes, Silk Road history and sacred traditions.
In 2025, the Turkistan Region accounted for 10% of domestic trips, placing it among Kazakhstan's top five most visited destinations, according to the country's Bureau of National Statistics.

First series of adult T. rex footprints hints at its walking speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

First series of adult T. rex footprints hints at its walking speed
An estimated speed of 1.6 meters per second roughly matches a person’s brisk walking pace
Four ancient footprints are helping scientists step into a T. rex’s shoes.
The prints form the first set of tracks probably left behind by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, researchers report September 8 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Measurements of the 7-meter-long trackway suggest the ancient predator was ambling along at about 1.6 meters per second, roughly equivalent to a person’s quick walking pace.
A few single adult T. rex footprints exist in the fossil record, as do trackways possibly from T. rex juveniles or other dinosaur species, says Peter Falkingham, a paleontologist at Liverpool John Moores University in England. “But an individual track doesn’t tell you a lot. A trackway tells you more about foot placement as the animal’s moving along.” And younger and older dinosaurs probably walked differently, just as human toddlers and adults do.
“Finding an adult trackway is cool,” Falkingham says. “It’s unique. It brings something new.”
High school teacher and paleontologist Kent Hups stumbled on the footprints in 2025, while fossil hunting along a steep incline in the Hell Creek Formation in North Dakota. The tracks stick up out of the ground because sediment filled in the originally muddy footprints, which then eroded away more slowly than the surrounding rock.
When Hups saw the first track, he noted that it was three-toed and enormous, measuring 80 centimeters across. “I’m going, ‘this has to be a T. rex,’” says Hups, of Northglenn High School in Colo. and the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
Slender toe impressions and fossils unearthed in the area signal a T. rex left behind the footprints roughly 66.5 million years ago. “There’s always the possibility that we haven’t found the skeletons of some species that we don’t know about,” Falkingham says. “But as far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track maker that could have made these.”
The team used stride length and body size to calculate the dinosaur’s speed. Unfortunately, the footprints aren’t well-preserved and estimating speed from tracks is tricky, so the T. rex may have been walking slightly faster or slower than calculated. Better tracks could have revealed whether the foot landed flat or toe-to-heel, or how foot pads supported the predator’s weight.
More tracks are sure to follow. In fact, a fifth step may be concealed in the hill. But the team is waiting for Mother Nature to wear away the surrounding rock, Hups says. “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”

America loves free speech, except when it comes to Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Ed Sheeran thought he was taking the safe route. Prioritizing personal gain over principle, he thought he had more to fear from the corrupt, pro-genocide billionaire Robert Kraft than he did from the general public.
It turned out he was wrong.
Sheeran’s decision to bow to the billionaire and kick Macklemore off his tour was met with a resounding howl of condemnation. And that response has been so strong that it is swiftly turning into a major, and very important victory for the struggle for Palestinian rights.
While the importance of the response must not be understated, the decision by Kraft to shut down speech about the genocide in Palestine does not stand alone.
Palestine is both a major issue for right wing forces and the vanguard issue for their assault on free speech and dissent more broadly. Robert Kraft’s ability to control speech in the public sphere is a problem we must address more broadly.
A billionaire can call a few of his friends and slam the door on an artist who wants to use his stage to express solidarity with people suffering genocide and apartheid. In other areas, politicians try to use state power to silence critics of Israel’s actions and the United States’ support for it.
They do all of this because Palestine is an exception to the principles of free speech and the right to dissent. But if it is not successfully challenged, the assault on free speech will not end with Palestine, it will only begin there.
What Macklemore said
It all began in New Jersey, where Macklemore was opening for Sheeran at MetLife Stadium. Introducing his song, “Hind’s Hall,” the rapper explained to the crowd what the song was communicating. It’s worth examining what he said in full.
I’ve been trying to figure out a way to say this all day. One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine.
I said, Free Palestine.
I want those words to be loud and clear, so the people from Gaza, all the way to the occupied West Bank, know that we have not forgotten them.
And this next song was inspired by the bravery of Columbia University students who led an encampment movement that mobilized the entire world; open up hearts, myself included, so thank you to those students that risked their diplomas, that risked their tuition, that risked their scholarships, that stood up and said, no. CUAD students, Students for Justice in Palestine, and Jewish Voices for Peace. Thank you, guys.
To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.
So I say Free Palestine, I say Free Lebanon, I say Free Cuba, I say Free Congo, Free Sudan, I say Free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”
It was a genuine call for freedom, for equality, for justice and respect for the rights of all at the expense of, and with the exception of no one.
Somehow, Bob Kraft twisted that into what he called “hate speech.”
Kraft himself is a leading sponsor of propaganda trips to Israel, and for anti-Palestinian advocacy in the United States. He has been a leader in conflating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, while supporting initiatives that strengthen the apartheid economy, sometimes under the guise of creating “opportunity for Palestinians”.
He is, unsurprisingly, a major donor to AIPAC, an actual hate group with the power to act on their agenda, unlike Macklemore.
When Columbia University students protested their university’s involvement in Israel’s genocide, Kraft withdrew support from Columbia because it was too slow, in his view, in stifling the dissent from students. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu once said that “Israel has no greater friend than Robert Kraft.”
What is perhaps most distressing is that we have a system where someone like Kraft can own the public sphere, and thus can dictate what is permitted in that sphere.
Control of the public sphere
While Massachusetts case law says that Kraft cannot cancel an existing contract over constitutionally protected speech, federal law does not. But this is also one reason that Kraft went out of his way to claim that Macklemore was engaging in “hate speech.”
Macklemore might have grounds to sue Kraft in Massachusetts, and we can hope that he would. The idea that “Free Palestine” is hate speech must be challenged in court, and this would be the perfect opportunity to do so.
Yet as egregious as Kraft’s action is, it is far from an isolated incident.
In Texas, the University of Texas, Austin is facing controversy over hosting pro-Palestine Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.
That appearance, scheduled for the end of this month, was condemned by Texas officials and members of Congress from both parties, including Governor Greg Abbott, Senator Ted Cruz, Senate candidate Ken Paxton (all Republicans) and Democratic Congressman Henry Cuellar.
Their condemnation came with calls for the university to cancel Piker’s appearance.
While the university has not, thus far, agreed to force the cancellation of the event, the students who organized it report that the school has refused to give them a space for it that can accommodate the much larger than anticipated number of people that signed up to attend Piker’s September 30 talk. This could put the event at risk based on safety concerns.
While Piker’s public persona has generated a lot of attention and overhyped controversy, it cannot go without notice that the University of Texas is a public institution. It is not owned by a billionaire like Robert Kraft, but rather by the state. As such, First Amendment protections are unequivocal.
Despite this, a bipartisan group of legislators have called for the university to cancel the Piker event. While I can’t claim to be a constitutional lawyer, I can certainly state that this violates the spirit of the First Amendment, if not the letter.
This is hardly new. Free speech is treasured in the United States like nowhere else in the world, one of the few truly positive claims the U.S. can still cling to. But, like any expression of popular will, it is inconvenient for those with power.
That’s where the Palestine Exception serves such a useful purpose.
Palestine stands above and beyond other controversial issues in its ability to stifle free speech because it can so readily be manipulated to be presented as antisemitism. Where the focus of pro-Israel advocacy has long been to equate criticism of Israel with antisemitism, now any expression that affirms Palestinian rights has been twisted into an attack on Jews.
Across the country, in local, state, and federal courts and legislatures, the battle is being waged. Even the online world has become a battlefield.
But in the face of the supremely cynical effort to portray “Free Palestine” as antisemitic, it’s impossible not to recall the chant, made into a song in the 1980s to “Free Nelson Mandela.” An Afrikaner of the day might have argued that this was hate speech because it called for the freeing of a convicted terrorist, thus making them feel “unsafe.”
The idea seems absurd. But if so, is not calling “Free Palestine” hate speech even more insane? That is an explicit call for restoring the human, civil, and national rights of an entire people, the overwhelming majority of whom cannot, even in the harshest, most prejudiced view, be accused of being guilty of anything except the “crime” of being Palestinian.
By labeling Palestine solidarity as hate speech, pro-Israel forces open a door to quash political speech they disagree with. The same could have been done with South African apartheid if Afrikaners were perceived as a group targeted for hate. That was impossible; so much so that when, more than three decades after apartheid, Afrikaners still weren’t treated like minorities in western (and other) states so often are, white supremacists like Donald Trump and Elon Musk had to make up stories of their persecution.
Jews, of course, have a horrific history of persecution, and there is real and growing antipathy and bigotry against us today. That circumstance is cynically used to quash not just the rightful accusations of genocide and other crimes against humanity that Israel commits as a matter of course—and has done since long before October 7, 2023—it is used to silence even the claim that Palestinians deserve the same rights as every other human being on Earth. Indeed, it is meant to send the message that Palestinians are less than human.
The idea that “Free Palestine” is threatening to supporters of Israel is probably true, and not limited only to Jewish supporters. But why is it threatening?
For the same reason that “Free Nelson Mandela” was threatening—oppressors fear that if the oppressed escape from under their boot, they will seek retribution. Not just accountability, but vengeance.
It is the same racist fear that always reinforces supremacist thinking.
But the response to Ed Sheeran dropping Macklemore from his tour shows that the force needed to stand against that weaponized fear is here. Even when that weapon is used by powerful billionaires or politicians, more and more people are resisting.
There has been a realization among people everywhere that Palestinians are suffering unspeakable cruelty and that this must be confronted. First they will try to eliminate the Palestinian people, but it will not stop there. As more people realize that fact, the numbers in support of Palestinian rights will grow even more quickly.
Whether it’s Macklemore, Hasan Piker, Palestinian-American human rights lawyer Prof. Noura Erakat (who was just arrested for insisting on public debate about Florida’s intention to invest in Israel bonds), or your neighborhood activist, this is a fight to make sure billionaires and politicians cannot stop free speech and will have to hear the calls to “Free Palestine” whether they like it or not.

PM’s new anti-disinformation unit gets cross-party backing, as Farage declares it an attack on free speech – UK politics live

PM's new anti-disinformation unit gets cross-party backing - as Farage says it's Orwellian attack on free speech
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has claimed the Andy Burnham’s new National Centre for Information Defence (see 8.50am) will be used to launch an Orwellian attack on free speech.
In a post on social media, Farage referred to the new unit and said Burnham was setting it up “using the excuse that Russia wants to interfere with elections”. Farage went on:
Be in no doubt, there are bots online, they come from Russia, they come from India and elsewhere, that do try to influence our thinking, and that’s not a good piece of news.
But you know what will happen with this government.
Already, he’s said it’s to stop far-right tropes etc.
This will be like George Orwell’s Ministry of Information. This will be used to clamp down on free speech.
And the one lesson I’m learning, as time goes on, whether it’s funding of parties, whether it’s cancelling elections, is never, ever trust this authoritarian government.
Farage has no evidence to back up his claim and, given that the government has already said that it will not be using the new unit for “policing domestic political dissent”, it seems little more than a scare.
The PM’s initiative has been warmly welcomed by the cross-party Commons foreign affairs committee. Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair, gave a statement quoted at 10.57am.
Other committee members have backed her up. John Whittingdale, a Tory former culture secretary, said:
During our inquiry, the committee received extensive evidence of the scale of Russian disinformation targeting both the UK and our allies, particularly in order to influence the outcome of democratic elections.”
Having seen how countries like France and Sweden have established national centres to counter this threat, the committee strongly recommended that the UK needs to follow suit as a matter of urgency. At the time, the government only partially agreed, saying it would consider it alongside the findings of the Rycroft review.
It is very welcome that the prime minister has now shared our assessment that Russia is conducting information warfare against the West and is taking action.
And Richard Foord, a Lib Dem member of the committee, said:
As recommended in our report, this should be a public-facing body, placed on a statutory footing, and accountable to parliament.
We look forward to helping ensure that this new centre is a success. We hope it demonstrates a new and robust response from the UK to hostile state information warfare.

Anti-Reform UK tactical voting up significantly over past year, poll suggests
There are two YouGov polls out today with bad news for Reform UK.
The first is the regular weekly poll for the Times. It shows the Tories level with Reform UK for the first time in 18 months. Kemi Badenoch’s party had been behind Nigel Farage’s party since spring last year.
The second is a longer polling exercise focusing on tactical voting. It is based on responses to questions about how people would vote in a constituency where only two parties had a realistic chance of winning, and it shows that, in Labour/Reform or Tory/Reform contests, Reform would do a lot worse than they would have done a year ago. They would also do worse against the Lib Dems. Only against the Green party are Reform doing better than they were in February this year (the Greens weren’t included in the earlier surveys) – but not by much, and the Greens would still win.
As Pippa Crerar reported yesterday, Andy Burnham has not ruled out fighting the next election on a commitment to rejoin the EU.
The briefing Pippa attended did not leave journalists super-confident that Burnham will adopt this step. But he is being urged to by Ben Judah, who was a special adviser to David Lammy when Lammy was foreign secretary. In a post for Arguably, a platform for policy debate on Substack, Judah argues that there are three reasons why Burnham should fight the next election on rejoining the EU. He says:
The first is that this cause is now more popular than at any time since the 2016 referendum. Average support for rejoining the EU now stands at 61%, according to Prof John Curtice, reflecting both ‘Bregret’ on the part of Leave supporters and a new generation who did not vote in 2016 entering the political marketplace …
The second is that, regardless of when Burnham chooses to call an election, he will not be able to run on Labour’s record. Staking everything on a cost-of-living agenda is a fool’s errand when global economic forces, not the government, determine prices … The economic headwinds from the Iran war and the China shock mean that Labour’s best hope is to run against the Brexit settlement that deepened our economic plight – turning Nigel Farage into the representative of a failed status quo …
Thirdly, this left-right dividing line won’t last for ever and there are ominous political trends. Relatively early in the life of this Labour government, the public are tiring of high taxation (at a postwar peak of 37% of GDP and rising). YouGov polling shows that only 23% now believe that the government taxes too little and spends too little on services, compared to 41% who believe that it taxes and spends too much … Brexit is a time-limited card that, played soon, could help Labour fire up progressives and retain high-earners desperate for growth.
Judah suggests the government should commit to rejoining the EU, either at the budget or in the 10-year plan being published soon, subject to three tests: “which relationship with Europe makes us richest, most secure and best able to manage migration?”
And he ends suggesting that the bravest option would be to announce an election on this at the Labour conference next week.
The bravest thing Burnham could do, of course, would be to stand up on stage at Labour conference and call an election to put Britain back at the heart of Europe, with the three tests in the party’s manifesto. It would probably be the smartest too – the right is more divided than ever but Burnham’s personal popularity has likely peaked and Labour faces a tough winter. Running an election on Europe is the best tactic available to the party, not only to squeeze the left but to motivate our base and explain to an exhausted and demoralised public why we are having an election at all. The alternative – just waiting as things get worse – is ultimately the far riskier move to make.
'Malign networks' will use free speech arguments to attack new anti-disinformation unit, RUSI thinktank warns
RUSI, the foreign policy thinktank, has welcomed the creation of the National Centre for Information Defence. In a statement released at around the same time as Nigel Farage put out his video saying the new unit was an Orwellian attack on free speech (see 1.58pm), RUSI also warned about “malign networks” using free speech arguments to undermine its credibility.
Sophie Williams-Dunning, a RUSI research analyst, said:
The new National Centre for Information Defence is a welcome, if overdue, step towards the UK mounting a more strategic response to foreign information warfare in the age of social media and AI.
Despite having a legal basis for countering foreign malign interference under the National Security Act 2023, the UK’s response has been lacking to date, especially when compared to those of countries like France, Sweden, Ukraine and Taiwan, which already have dedicated agencies or centres for information defence. A centre with the job of detecting, attributing and disrupting foreign information operations, and pulling together intelligence, law enforcement and government departments that haven’t always coordinated well, is a sensible response.
Challenges will no doubt emerge. This announcement will stoke debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention – and genuine free-speech concerns will also be instrumentalised and amplified by the same inauthentic or malign networks that the new agency seeks to combat.

Burnham says his Labour conference speech will set out how Britain needs to be honest with itself about need for change
Andy Burnham has said that he will use his speech to the Labour conference next week to say Britain needs to be honest with itself about the need for change.
The speech will define what he wants to achieve as prime minister, Burnham told the New Statesman, in an interview with its editor, Tom McTague.

[The speech] is a moment to weave all of these threads together and to lay out the path, I think, and say, ‘Look, Britain’s here, we can be there’ – a much better place – ‘but we’re going to have to be honest with ourselves about what it takes to get from where we are right now to where we should be.’
This has to be a point where the country says, ‘Right, we can’t carry on like this, we need to set a new, clear direction, a new clear path.’
Burnham told McTague that he thought he would be “seriously letting down the country” if he failed to spell out this message.
At another point in the interview, Burnham said he would be building on ideas he has promoted in the past, not toning them down.
Referring to the so-called Manchesterism agenda he set out before he became PM, he said:
People might say you get into government and you dial down. I don’t feel like that. I won’t be dialling it down, put it that way.

Beneath Burnham’s bashful, almost apologetic exterior lies a will to power as strong as I have seen in Tony Blair or Gordon Brown. He is gripped by a certainty of what he – and he alone – can do with the job.

Alan Milburn writes to 100 ‘business leaders’ asking them to provide work for Neets
The former Labour minister leading the government’s review into youth unemployment has written to 100 firms to ask them to provide work placements and jobs for young people, the Press Association reports. PA says:
Alan Milburn, who was commissioned by former prime minister Keir Starmer to lead the government’s review into worklessness, has approached “business leaders” in sectors including rail, transport and utilities to ask them to provide more chances for young people.
The Milburn review said Royal Mail, Octopus Energy, Greene King and Lloyds bank are among the companies who are already offering opportunities to school and university leavers. They are taking part in the review’s First Chance scheme, which has come from the review.
In the last 10 years the number of mid-skilled and lower-skilled jobs in the economy has fallen by about 1.6 million, the department said.
Its statistics showed six in 10 young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neet) have never worked.
Andy Burnham has previously said he wants to replicate a system from Manchester which guaranteed some young people six-week work placements.
Milburn, chair of the young people and work review, said: “Since starting this review I’ve been struck by how many employers have come forward wanting to help address our country’s Neets crisis.
“More and more businesses are stepping up to the plate and looking to take action to stop the risk of a lost generation of young people.
“More than eight in 10 young people who are Neet want to be in work or training. They just lack the workplace opportunities to get them a foot in the door.
“The First Chance movement is about closing that gap – bringing together employers ready to respond to young people desperate for a chance to show what they can do.”
Thinktank linked to Reform UK calls for abolition of state pension
A thinktank linked to Reform UK has called for the abolition of the state pension and £75bn worth of sweeping tax cuts in a “radical” report likely to influence the party’s platform for the next election, Kalyeena Makortoff reports.

Streeting confirms annual £120m payments to Mauritius on hold while Chagos Islands deal being reviewed
The Conservatives have urged Andy Burnham to fully drop the proposed Chagos Islands deal – giving sovereignty of the islands to Mauritius in return for guaranteed control for the Diego Garcia military base for at least another 99 years – in the light of Donald Trump calling the deal “terrible” yesterday.
James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, said in a statement:
It shouldn’t have taken another intervention from the president for Andy Burnham to ‘review’ Labour’s Chagos Surrender deal.
If Burnham was really serious about our defence he would know that this deal should be binned entirely. It is absurd to hand over British sovereign territory, not to mention billions of pounds of hard-pressed taxpayers’ money, to an ally of China.
Trump was originally sceptical about the deal, but supported it earlier this year after Keir Starmer’s government explained why it thought it was sensible. (Starmer argued it would secure the future of Diego Garcia for at least a century, and that without a deal, the UK would continue to lose sovereignty cases in international courts, which would ultimately make protecting the base more difficult.) But, as Trump’s relationship with Starmer soured, the president reverted to attacking the deal as foolish.
In interviews today Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said that while Trump’s comments last night were not new, they did show that this was now “his settled view on the treaty”.
Streeting said this meant that the deal that has been negotiated would now be subject to a rethink. He explained:
This deal, as it is currently constituted, can’t go ahead without American support. We have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support, as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.
Earlier this year Mauritius and the UK were all set to ratify the treaty. But the legislation going through the UK parliament to make this happen was shelved after Trump started objecting.
Under the deal, the UK would have paid around £120m a year to Mauritius for ongoing control of the Diego Garcia military base, which is mainly used by the US for surveillance in the Pacific and as a base for long-range bombing missions. Washington regards it as a vital military asset.
Streeting said annual payments are not going ahead now while the deal is on hold.
But, asked on Sky News if the UK was still minded to cede sovereignty, Streeting replied: “That’s not really been in doubt since we decolonised.”
Hannah Perry, director of digital policy at Demos, said:
Right now, Britain’s information supply is being written in Moscow and spread by algorithms nobody voted for. The prime minister is right to call for a national effort. This is a national security threat, and it ends in real-world harm.
Our research has found Russian propaganda poisoning the chatbots people use every day, disinformation campaigns targeting London, and social media stoking division during crisis moments from the Southport riots to recent asylum housing rows. The door is wide open to these attacks.
We have been calling for a national response and a new centre to coordinate is extremely welcome, but it can’t just mop up the mess. It has to shut the door.
Government has other levers it can pull: protect elections from AI manipulation, bring in tougher protocols for crisis flashpoints, and back trusted news by securing the BBC’s future, protecting local news and making sure public interest journalism shows up on social media. The current green paper proposing regulating algorithms to give trustworthy news prominence needs to be implemented.
Some will say this is a threat to free speech. But there’s nothing free about speech written by a hostile state and amplified by a machine. Britain should decide how information reaches its people, not the Kremlin or Silicon Valley.
Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the Commons foreign affairs committee, has warmly welcomed the PM’s announcement about setting up a National Centre for Information Defence. (See 8.50am.) It is an idea her committee proposed in a report earlier this year.
In a statement, she said:
For too long, the approach of successive governments to disinformation has been disjointed and without organisation, allowing states like Russia to amplify lies about this country, to sow division and stoke tensions. This new National Centre for Information Security is an opportunity to finally take on this very serious threat.
The foreign affairs committee recommended exactly this in March. We were extremely worried about what seemed to be a complacency of the British establishment at the disinformation being promoted from abroad, particularly from Russia. We thought the response from Whitehall had essentially been ‘talk to the hand because the face ain’t listening,’ but it seems we were wrong. I’m absolutely delighted.

What Burnham said in his speech to UN - summary and analysis
You can read the whole of Andy Burnham’s speech to the United Nations general assembly here.And here are the key points.
Burnham said there is “no national security without a strong, cohesive society”. This is interesting because Burnham was strongly criticised by the Tories and Reform UK, and rightwing papers, after saying at PMQs earlier this month: “We do everything to support our national security, but it can’t come at the expense of social security.” Critics claimed this meant Burnham thought avoiding benefit cuts was more important than deterring Russia. But Burnham did not resile from the argument, and in his speech overnight he restated the same idea in slightly different language. He said:
True resilience depends on this military strength.
But the last 10 years also tells us that it is about something deeper as well.
It’s about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together.
There is no national security without a strong, cohesive society.
That’s the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve.
He said the UK was facing “an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors” promoting disinformation. (See 8.50am.)
He said youth unemployment and the cost of living crisis made Britons more vulnerable to disinformation.
And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience – because faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home.
If you’re struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving – or if you’re a young person not in employment, education or training – then you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence.
So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need.
He said new National Centre for Information Defence would tackle misinformation not just in the UK, but also directed against allies.
Today I am tasking our security chiefs to begin work on a new National Centre for Information Defence – to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks. To support and defend our democracy.
And I know this is a shared challenge.
So we are going to use our experience in the UK – and the fact that we have already been through this shock – to help other countries.
We have already supported Moldova to protect its elections from Russian interference.
As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues – some for the first time.
Burnham said the climate crisis was a national security threat. He said:
The climate crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world – as this summer of extreme heat, wildfires and floods has proved beyond doubt.
Britain will continue to lead with others to fight this threat.
He said he wanted the UK to be an “honest broker” in international affairs, mediating between the US and Europe. Although some in British politics, notably the Liberal Democrats, argue that having Donald Trump in the White House means Britain should seek a closer relationship with Europe, Burnham’s words imply he agrees with Keir Starmer, who repeatedly said he did not accept the need to choose between Europe and the US. Burnham said:
I believe the UK has a unique position as an honest broker to help drive this forward.
We are America’s closest ally.
We have deep ties with our friends in the European Union and will deepen them further.
We work with China and emerging powers like India and Brazil.
We sit on the security council. In the Commonwealth. In the CPTPP.
In a divided world, we have the ability to bring people together – and we will.
We are going to step into that role.
This has been the establishment view of Britain’s foreign policy role at least since the 1960s. Most previous postwar PMs would have said the same thing. But there are those who argue that Trump has made this stance less tenable.
Burnham said that he was going to put AI at the centre of the UK’s presidency of the G20 next year. He said:
The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world.
And when it comes to guarding against the risks, we have our world-leading AI Security Institute – working hand in glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety.
But we need to go further.
Building on the meeting convened by His Majesty King Charles last week, I can announce today that I am going to put AI at the heart of the UK’s G20 Presidency next year.
I look back at how we responded to the financial crisis back in 2008.
We moved quickly in the G20 and smaller groups to deliver an urgent, practical response.
We came together to agree principles – which everyone implemented at home in a way that was right for them. And it worked.
That is the kind of approach we need now.
He said he wanted the world towards “agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness – and to ensure that AI development is safe”. This is different from Trump’s view; he told the UN yesterday he was opposed to international regulation of AI.
He praised Manchester mill workers for boycotting cotton made by slaves during the US civil war and cited this as a good example of bottom-up people power. He said:
Outside [No 10 North in Manchester] office stands a statue of Abraham Lincoln.
It marks the personal connection he made with Manchester, and the bond between our two nations. A bond which he described in a letter to working people of the city as “perpetual.”
This was not due to some military or material support.
There was no quid pro quo.
It was because Manchester’s humble mill workers took a principled stand.
During the American civil war, despite the hardships it brought them, they refused to touch raw cotton that had been picked by slaves.
In 1862, people with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world.
The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people.
And whatever distorted view social media offers today, the world is still full of good and decent people who are ready stand up for what is right.
While this story might relate to a “bond” between the US and the UK, it won’t help relations with Trump. The Trump administration has hounded museums that remind Americans of the negative impact of slavery, and the president gives every indication that, if he had been around at the time of the civil war, he would have sided with the Confederates.
Burnham said the UK should “always stand for the underdog against the bully”.
Nothing brings the British people together across age, race and class more than their hatred of injustice – the misuse of power against the powerless.
We will always stand for the underdog against the bully.
That’s why we are so united behind Ukraine.
And let me say, we salute the Ukrainian people.
They are showing depths of resilience and courage that is an inspiration to the whole world.
This is another rewrite of a line that he used at his most recent PMQs. Some rightwingers complained that always standing with the underdog would mean siding with Hamas against Israel, or Iran against the US.
Streeting says government needs to help people 'to separate fact from fiction'
In an interview with the Today programme about the government’s plans for a National Centre for Information Defence, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said it was needed to help people “to separate fact from fiction”.
He said:
What we need to do is not just better co-ordination at the centre of government, but the better mobilisation of the whole of society. And that’s supporting the public to separate fact from fiction, and to be able to discern the legitimate, real BBC, or indeed legitimate, real British universities, from the fake and the manufactured. That is extremely challenging in the new world of AI.
Come the next general election, it will be hard to discern the real versions of politicians and BBC presenters from the artificial versions.
UK to launch military squadron to protect satellites in space
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, was giving interviews this morning to promote a government announcement about the RAF launching what the MoD is calling its “first ever space squadron”. Ben Quinn has the story here.
PM’s new anti-disinformation unit won’t target ‘domestic political dissent’, defence secretary Wes Streeting says
Good morning. Andy Burnham delivered his speech to the United Nations in what felt like the middle of the night in UK time and he announced that he is setting up what he is calling a National Centre for Information Defence.
Burnham said this was necessary because “over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality”.
Over at GB News they seem a bit worried this morning about the prospect of a crackdown on corrosive narratives about Britain which bear no resemblance to reality, and they are running a story with a headline referencing “free speech fears”. It includes a quote from a rightwing commentator claiming the Burnham speech was all “talk of control and censorship – exactly the kind of messaging that the Trump administration absolutely hates”.
But close reading of the speech makes it clear that Burnham is not aiming his fire at any parts of the UK media. Burnham said he was concerned about hostile state actors waging disinformation warfare, especially Russia. He told the UN:
In recent years we have seen an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies.
Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears.
They’ve used bots and fake websites.
Falsified newspaper articles.
Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC.
They’ve amplified far-right narratives.
And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.
(Burnham did not address the fact that there are some within the Trump administration who have also been amplifying far-right narratives with claims about the UK which certainly count as misinformation, and arguably meet the disinformation threshold too.)
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has been giving interviews this morning and, speaking to GB News, he was asked about claims that Burnham’s new unit could be used against Britons who” simply disagree” with the government. That would not happen, he said.
He told the programme:
One of the great things about Britain, and one of the things that I have a responsibility to defend, is the freedom and democracy that we all enjoy.
And that includes the freedom to disagree, the freedom for people to challenge their government, to challenge government policy, to criticise robustly what we are doing and then to have the opportunity to choose a different government.
That is a stark contrast to the position that our friends the Russian people endure under the political system that they suffer under.
Russia is just one of a number of malign state and non-state actors that seek to threaten and disrupt our democracy, including through misinformation and disinformation.
Streeting added:
We’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent.
You can read Burnham’s UN speech in full here. I will be posting more from it soon.
The Commons is still in recess, and most people in government are getting ready for the Labour conference next week, and so there is almost nothing in the Westminster diary. But there was enough news at the UN yesterday to pad out the week, and so I’m sure there will be enough to cover.

ICC convicts former Central African Republic militia leader

ICC convicts former Central African Republic militia leader
Mahamat Said Abdel Kani oversaw brutal detention tactics, including torture, at Bangui facility, ICC judges rule.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has convicted a Central African Republic militia commander of crimes against humanity, including torture.
Judges in The Hague on Wednesday found Mahamat Said Abdel Kani guilty over his role of running a Seleka detention facility in Bangui, where supporters of then-President Francois Bozize were rounded up and tortured during the country’s 2013 civil war.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Dutch court hands life sentence to Rwandan man for genocide role
- list 2 of 4Mladic died a happy man
- list 3 of 4Convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic gets hero’s burial in Serbia
- list 4 of 4Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
Said, 56, was acquitted of three war crimes charges as the judges ruled that the armed conflict had already ended when some of the alleged crimes happened.
A separate hearing will determine his sentence.
Judge Miatta Maria Samba said Said oversaw the torture at the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry, where detainees were whipped, waterboarded and bound using a method called “Arbatacher”, in which detainees’ hands, elbows and feet are tied together behind their backs.
Some prisoners were held in underground cells with no bathrooms or showers.
“The floor was covered in waste, and it smelled of faeces and urine,” Samba said.
She said a victim described how his life had been destroyed by the mistreatment.
Said, who denied the charges, appeared in court in jeans and a blue sweatshirt, looking unbothered as he shook his head when the verdict was read.
He was a senior figure in the Seleka coalition, which ousted Bozize in 2013, plunging the country into a conflict that killed thousands of people.
Bozize’s response, arming the “anti-Balaka” militia, fuelled more bloodshed before French troops helped secure the country in 2014 under a United Nations mandate.
The ICC has investigated violence in the Central African Republic since 2014 and has already convicted two anti-Balaka leaders, including former Sports Minister Patrice-Edouard Ngaissona, who was sentenced to 12 years, and former MP Alfred Yekatom who was sentenced to 15 years.
Said is the first Seleka member to be convicted.
The country has experienced relative stability since a 2019 peace agreement.

Economic growth in developing Asia projected at 5% in 2026 — report

TOKYO, September 23. /TASS/. Economic growth in developing Asia and the Pacific is expected at 5% this year compared to 2025, the Manila-headquartered Asian Development Bank (ADB) said in its September Asian Development Outlook (ADO). The 2026 forecast is 0.1 percentage points higher than the previous outlook in July.
India is still the leader in the region in terms of growth rate, ADB experts said. They expect the country’s GDP growth to reach 7%, which is 0.4 percentage points higher than projected in the previous report.
The forecast for China’s GDP growth remained intact at 4.6%. GDP in Southeast Asian countries is expected to grow by an average of 4.7%. The report does not cover Japan, the Republic of Korea, Australia, and New Zealand.

South Africa sends black rhinos to Botswana

Unknown Publisher

South Africa sends black rhinos to Botswana
The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) South Africa’s Black Rhino Range Expansion Program (BRREP) has successfully translocated 20 black rhinos from KwaZulu-Natal to Botswana.
The rhinos were moved in early September in a cross-border conservation operation involving two 36-hour road trips to a remote and secure location where the animals can breed and establish a new population.
The translocation effectively doubles Botswana’s black rhino population. The International Rhino Foundation estimates that about 25 black rhinos remained in the country following years of poaching pressure, particularly in the Okavango Delta region.
The 20 rhinos were captured in KwaZulu-Natal in early June and held in a boma during a quarantine period before being transported to their new home. According to BRREP leader Jeff Cooke, all 20 animals have arrived safely and are settling in well.
The Botswana operation is only the second cross-border translocation undertaken by BRREP. The first took place in 2019, when rhinos were moved to Liwonde National Park in Malawi. Since 2003, the programme has moved groups of up to 20 rhinos to suitable areas to help re-establish populations. It targets areas of about 20 000 hectares or more to provide sufficient space for populations to grow.
Cooke said finding areas large enough with suitable habitat for black rhinos is becoming increasingly difficult, prompting the programme to expand its operations across national borders.
”These newly translocated populations serve as incubators for the broader continental species recovery programme,” he said, adding that they could support further local range expansion in other black rhino range states.
WWF South Africa CEO Dr Morné du Plessis thanked the South African and Botswanan governments, Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife, funding and donor partners, and the recipient site owners for their role in the operation.
The organisation said the initiative demonstrates the value of collaboration and coordinated conservation efforts in supporting black rhino population recovery.

Syria's Sharaa, Iran's Pezeshkian to address UN General Assembly, likely denouncing Israel
