Feature: China draws on painful lessons to reclaim Asian Games volleyball crown
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:20:31 CST
21:20:31 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Trailing 19-13 in the third set of Tuesday's Asian Games women's volleyball final, China faced an unexpected challenge. Despite holding a 2-0 lead, the team was suddenly under pressure as host Japan threatened to extend the match.
For China's young squad, the situation presented another test of resilience it had developed since a painful defeat to Thailand in last month's Asian Championship final.
Just 23 days after that setback, China overcame Japan to claim its 10th Asian Games women's volleyball title, completing a remarkable turnaround for a team still finding its feet on the international stage.
Assembled in April 2025, the squad had endured its biggest disappointment when it surrendered a 2-1 lead against Thailand in the Asian Championship final, missing out on both the continental title and a direct berth at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"The defeat to Thailand at the Asian Championship hit us really hard," outside hitter Zhuang Yushan acknowledged.
Since resuming training in April this year, the players had focused on winning the Asian Championship and securing the continent's direct Olympic qualification berth. Falling short left the squad struggling to recover emotionally.
But with the Asian Games approaching, there was little time to dwell on the defeat.
"We returned to Beijing after the Asian Championship with only around two weeks to get ready for the Asian Games," captain Gong Xiangyu recalled.
"The team was in a low mood for a while. With such a short gap between competitions, we needed to address our issues quickly and rise above the hardships."
The opportunity to demonstrate their progress came in the Asian Games semifinals, where China faced a full-strength Thailand side less than a month after their previous encounter.
Once again, China took a 2-1 lead before Thailand forced a deciding set. This time, however, the Chinese players held their nerve, dominating the fifth set 15-6 to advance to the final.
The victory reflected both tactical adjustments and improved mental resilience.
"We had to rely on training to turn things around," said 18-year-old middle blocker Wang Aoqian.
During the Asian Championship final, China had struggled to contain Thailand's attacking combinations, with its blockers frequently caught out by the Thai setter.
Wang acknowledged that hesitation had undermined her performance.
"I was hesitant and overthinking my blocks at the Asian Championship. After reviewing the game, my coach urged me to trust my reads," she said.
The improvement was evident in the rematch, where China outscored Thailand 11-4 in blocking points and recorded a 17 percent blocking success rate, compared with Thailand's 8 percent.
China's serving also disrupted Thailand's reception, creating opportunities for its blockers, particularly in the deciding set.
The team made adjustments in attack, reducing its reliance on individual hitters and using drop shots and varied attacking angles to unsettle Thailand's defense.
Thailand's defensive performance had been a major factor in its Asian Championship victory, but China finished the semifinal ahead in both total digs and digging percentage.
Beyond the tactical improvements, the tournament demonstrated the team's growing ability to handle pressure.
Tuesday's final against Japan provided another example.
Holding a 2-0 lead, China appeared to be closing in on gold before Japan fought back in the third set. The hosts established a 19-13 advantage, threatening to extend the contest.
With Japan gaining momentum, 20-year-old outside hitter Dong Yuhan came off the bench and helped China regain its attacking rhythm.
"I simply went out to play aggressively without overcomplicating things," Dong said.
Supported by Gong's effective serving, Dong converted four of her eight attacking attempts into points, helping China close the gap.
"We shook off the mental burden and played fearlessly. We came in looking to challenge them, with no extra distractions," she said.
Wu Mengjie, who delivered important attacking contributions in both the semifinal and final, said the team had learned to approach difficult situations with greater composure.
"We braced ourselves for hardships. When these moments arrived, we remained composed and level-headed," she said.
Japan fielded a less-than-full-strength squad in the final, and China's victory did not necessarily represent a fundamental transformation in its technical ability. Nevertheless, the tournament provided evidence of improved preparation and growing maturity.
With an average age below 22, many of China's players have only recently begun competing at the highest international level. Over the past year, they have experienced their first Asian Championship, World Championship and Asian Games, learning to cope with both the disappointment of defeat and the pressure of competing for major titles.
For Zhuang, the ability to recover from setbacks was as important as the gold medal itself.
"China's women's volleyball spirit is about never surrendering, just as we showed in the third set versus Japan today. If you don't give up, you stand a chance," the 23-year-old said.
That determination has long been associated with China's women's volleyball team.
The country's five consecutive major international titles in the 1980s established the foundations of its success, while its Olympic triumphs in Athens in 2004 and Rio de Janeiro in 2016 reinforced that legacy.
In Athens, China recovered from two sets down to defeat Russia in the final, ending a 20-year wait for Olympic gold. 12 years later, it overcame host Brazil, the Netherlands and Serbia in the knockout rounds to reclaim the title in Rio.
For Gong, one of the experienced players guiding the current generation, Tuesday's victory carried particular significance.
Now in her 10th year with the national team, the captain collected her third Asian Games gold medal.
"I cherish my decade-long career with the national team deeply. Not everyone gets the chance to train here every single day. This is my third Asian Games, and also my third Asian Games gold medal personally. I am truly grateful for this opportunity to keep winning glory for our country."
Standing alongside Gong on the podium was 30-year-old veteran Wang Mengjie, with a new generation of Chinese players celebrating behind them.
For Zhuang, their responsibility extends beyond winning individual tournaments.
"We didn't let the loss at the Asian Championship break us. We cannot let the legacy of China's women's volleyball team be tarnished on our watch. It is our duty to uphold it," she said. ■

Across China: Sheep eat up harvest work in Xinjiang's win-win circular farming approach
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:20:31 CST
21:20:31 KST

URUMQI, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- While drones and tractors hum across China's autumn harvest, fields in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region are filled with a very different sound: "Baa."
As a 200-hectare seed zucchini plantation enters its harvest period in Karamay in northern Xinjiang, 10,000 sheep have been sent into the fields in batches to graze on weeds and vines. A clip featuring the white sheep wandering and feeding in the yellow-green fields has become a hit on social media.
Similar scenes are playing out across Xinjiang's main seed zucchini-growing areas. In Shuanghe City, farmer Chen Weiwei has also welcomed the four-legged animals into his fields. "They walk around, eat weeds and make harvesting easier," Chen said.
They are not intruders but helpers.
Seed zucchinis are pumpkin-like plants grown specifically for their white seeds. The skin and flesh are not eaten. The seeds are a popular snack in China and can also be pressed for oil.
The plants grow thick with vines and leaves, hiding the yellow zucchinis beneath. The sheep trample the vines and graze on leaves, exposing the zucchinis to sunlight directly. After several days, the zucchinis grow stronger and the vines wither away.
The field then becomes open after weeds and vines are cleared by the flocks, putting plump zucchinis in plain sight.
Chen said the sheep's "contribution" also includes their manure, a natural fertilizer that helps improve the soil.
More importantly, the sheep do not eat the zucchini. Its skin is hard and thick, so that people have to smash it on the ground to break it.
As pastures in the mountains begin to dry up in early autumn, local herders move their flocks to the zucchini fields. Farmers set up yurts and fences, turning the fields into temporary pastures for a few days.
It is a win-win business, and no money changes hands. The herders save on feed, the farmers save on weeding, and the sheep get a free meal.
Chen has grown seed zucchinis for six years. For him, the old methods were slower and costly. Stopping irrigation to dry out the vines would take more than 20 days, and mechanical harvesting alone would cost over 30,000 yuan (about 4,447 U.S. dollars).
Maidbaye, a herder in Karamay, raises more than 200 sheep. He said the arrangement would save him nearly 10,000 yuan on feed costs.
The "sheep helpers" are part of a broader push toward green, circular farming. Local officials said other methods include turning corn straw into animal feed and returning manure to the soil. The goal is to reduce reliance on chemicals.
China's newly revised Agriculture Law includes a chapter on green agricultural development, calling for a nationwide green transition. It gives priority to ecological circular agriculture, promotes the recovery, harmless treatment and comprehensive utilization of agricultural waste. It also encourages the circular agriculture integrating crop production with livestock breeding.
With policy guidance, this farming wisdom is expected to be taken up more broadly, with animal helpers being seen working alongside machines more often, and other fields across China echoing with the sound "Baa." ■

ALEXANDRIA, Egypt, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- "We hope Chinese companies will establish a manufacturing base here and take advantage of local investment opportunities," Alexandria Governor Ayman Attia said recently.
In an interview with Xinhua on Tuesday, Attia expressed hope to deepen cooperation with China in industry, trade, logistics, and education, while welcoming more Chinese companies to invest in the governorate.
As a major Egyptian port city, Alexandria has distinctive advantages in economic and trade cooperation with China. Attia said the historic Mediterranean city has extensive economic ties and is well-positioned to handle trade flows from China to Egypt, Africa, and the wider region.
Chinese investors are already operating in Alexandria's industrial sector, the Egyptian official said. "Our relations have deep historical roots and broad prospects for cooperation."
Attia said Egypt has made significant infrastructure progress under President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, noting that improvements in Alexandria's roads, energy, and transportation have created favorable conditions for investment.
In addition to its infrastructure, Alexandria has a well-trained workforce capable of meeting the technological needs of various industries, an important advantage in attracting investment, he added. "We welcome Chinese investors from all sectors with open arms."
Turning to people-to-people exchanges, Attia said that cooperation in language and education can bring the two sides closer together. He noted that Alexandria has long served as a crossroads of civilizations, with Mediterranean and other communities shaping its open and inclusive character.
"The people of Alexandria are open to different cultures," the governor said, adding that young people in the city have strong language-learning abilities, and the governorate hopes to use this strength to better serve economic development.
Attia said Alexandria has a range of universities, including public, private, and technological institutions. Alexandria University already offers Chinese-language courses and is ready to expand, he said, expressing hope for more jobs where local youth can use Chinese and for greater Chinese investment to further motivate students at universities across the city to learn the language.
Chinese-language education should not be confined to universities, Attia said. Some schools have already introduced Chinese to children at an early age, and he hopes to expand such programs to give more young people the chance to learn the language.
"Chinese is a very important language with a long history and a promising future," Attia said, adding that it is vital for Egyptians to learn it, and that Alexandria offers ideal conditions for learning and using the language. ■

Such a system could have prevented the current Iran war and without it, he warned, vital facilities could be attacked and important waterways closed.
Any lasting agreement with Tehran should protect the whole region, including Iran, Sheikh Tamim said.
“The opportunity for a peaceful diplomatic solution, which we believe is both possible and realistic, must not be missed," he added.
Underlining that Qatar is "a trusted mediator," Sheikh Tamim called for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened and warned that Gulf countries were being drawn into a war that was not theirs.
“We remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war,” the Qatari emir said.
Qatar was doing “everything in our power to address the conflict in the region through diplomatic means," he added.
On Gaza, Sheikh Tamim stated that what had happened there was “genocide in every sense of the word."
“There can be no talk of a just international order as long as Palestine remains in its plight," he said, adding that the scale of the destruction had not been matched by the international response.
He called on Israel to fully implement the ceasefire by ending military operations, withdrawing from Gaza, lifting the blockade and allowing humanitarian aid to enter without conditions.
The emir also criticised Israeli actions in Syria and Lebanon, adding that the international response would show whether international law was being applied equally.

He added that letting the war spread to neighbouring countries would help no one.
On Gaza, Erdoğan described the territory as the “most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time” and urged UN members to increase pressure on Israel.
He also called on countries that have not recognised Palestine to reconsider their position.

The Turkish president also criticised Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas's absence from the General Assembly. Abbas could not attend after the US denied him a visa for the second consecutive year.
Erdoğan renewed his demand for UN Security Council reform, arguing that decisions affecting more than 190 countries should not depend on its five permanent members.
He repeated his long-standing slogan that the “world is bigger than five” and said international law should not be applied differently to strong and weak countries.
Jordan says international inaction is a choice
Jordan's King Abdullah contrasted the international response to Israel with the sanctions, asset freezes, embargoes and diplomatic isolation used in other conflicts.
When it came to Israel, he said, resolutions had repeatedly remained on paper.
He called the failure to act a political “choice” and said the problem was not a lack of available tools.
The Hashemite kingdom's monarch accused Israel of seizing land, expanding settlements and allowing settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, and said that forced displacement constitutes a war crime.
He described Gaza and the occupied West Bank as two parts of an effort to make a viable Palestinian state impossible.
King Abdullah said decades of managing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict instead of tackling its causes had allowed temporary measures to become permanent policy.
He also warned that Israeli actions in southern Syria, including territorial expansion around water resources, posed a direct threat to Jordan’s northern border and water security.
On Iran, King Abdullah said the war was hurting trade and investment and raising energy and food bills worldwide.

China tightens control over orphine-related substances
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:19:59 CST
21:19:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese authorities announced on Wednesday that the entire class of orphine-related substances will be placed under control as non-medicinal narcotic and psychotropic substances.
The measure will take effect on Oct. 1, 2026, according to the Ministry of Public Security, the National Health Commission, and the National Medical Products Administration.
China has previously placed the entire categories of fentanyl-related substances, synthetic cannabinoids and nitazene-related substances under control.
The production, trading, transportation, use, storage, import and export of such substances are prohibited for all entities and individuals, according to management rules for non-medicinal narcotic and psychotropic substances.
China has expanded its controls over such substances. From July 1, 16 additional non-medicinal narcotic and psychotropic substances have been brought under control.
Meanwhile, the country has also strengthened its controls over precursors of fentanyl-related substances.
In November 2025, China added 13 types of precursors for fentanyl-related substances to its export control list and applied country-specific measures to the United States, Mexico and Canada. In May 2026, three additional types of fentanyl-related precursors were added to the list applicable to those three countries.
Also on Wednesday, Chinese judicial and law enforcement authorities issued guidelines on handling criminal cases involving fentanyl-related substances, emphasizing severe punishment for such crimes in accordance with the law.
Law enforcement efforts have been intensified against the illegal trafficking of precursor chemicals and other sensitive substances.
The Ministry of Public Security said in May that, since 2025, Chinese police had solved 29 criminal cases involving such materials, arrested 157 suspects, and seized 720 kg of drugs, 1.3 tonnes of new psychoactive substances, 0.9 kg of stimulants and 27.7 tonnes of non-scheduled precursor chemicals. ■

Drugs were planted on an ex-soldier of the "Magura" unit: the fourth member of the scheme, who broke into Shyrshyn’s car, was detained
Kyiv • UNN
The man is suspected of breaking into the car of an ex-soldier of the 47th Brigade to plant drugs. There are already four suspects in the case.
In the case involving an attempt to discredit Oleksandr Shirshyn, the former commander of the 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade "Magura" battalion, another participant in the scheme has been identified; he has already been detained and notified of suspicion, UNN reports citing the Prosecutor General’s Office.
Law enforcement officers detained a man who, according to the investigation, provided his accomplices with access to the serviceman’s car so they could plant drugs. Under the procedural guidance of prosecutors from the Prosecutor General’s Office, he was notified of suspicion
Details
According to the prosecutor’s office, on August 28, 2026, acting on the instructions of other participants, the man used mechanical tools to open the former battalion commander’s car, which was parked in Kharkiv. After that, previously purchased narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances were planted inside the vehicle.
He is charged with aiding and abetting the unlawful entry into another person’s property, committed by a group of persons acting in prior collusion (Part 5 of Article 27, Part 2 of Article 28, Part 1 of Article 162 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
This is already the fourth participant in the scheme to be exposed. Earlier in the criminal proceedings, three former law enforcement officers, who are now serving in the military, were notified of suspicion.

In this way, they attempted to create artificial grounds for bringing the serviceman to criminal liability.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing. Other persons involved in organizing and carrying out the scheme are being identified.

Tigrayan leaders say new war with Ethiopian government has begun, as fighting erupts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Tigrayan leaders say new war with Ethiopian government has begun, as fighting erupts
Sept 23 - Forces from the northern Ethiopian region of Tigray launched a major offensive against the federal government on Wednesday, a senior Ethiopian official said, shattering a four-year-old peace deal and threatening a wider regional conflict.
Tigray's leaders said in a statement they had entered a "defensive" war to counter aggression by the federal government.
A civil war that began in 2020 between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and federal forces resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths before the Pretoria Agreement was signed in November 2022.
The new hostilities follow months of growing animosity between the two sides, capped by Sunday's announcement that the TPLF had formed an alliance with six other armed groups from across Ethiopia aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
The TPLF-led regional administration said there had been an "intensification of the invasion conducted through various methods" by Abiy's government against the people of Tigray.
"The Tigray Forces have been instructed to counter the attack and have entered a defensive war," it said in a statement.
Getachew Reda, an adviser to Abiy and a former TPLF official, wrote on X that the TPLF had seized control of federally controlled airports in Tigray and launched an "all-out offensive" against government positions in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.
"The TPLF politico-military leadership has obviously taken irresponsibility to new heights," he said.
Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to the region.
FEARS OF A WIDER WAR
Spokespeople for Abiy, the federal government and the TPLF did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday.
Regional diplomats and analysts have warned for months that a resumption of the conflict in Tigray could quickly escalate into a wider war, overlapping with fighting in neighbouring Sudan and further roiling the volatile Red Sea region.
A civil war that broke out in 2023 in Sudan has drawn in powerful states from outside the Horn of Africa and created what the UN describes as the world's largest humanitarian crisis.
In the 2020-2022 Tigray war, Ethiopia's neighbour and historical adversary Eritrea backed the government militarily against the TPLF.
But relations between the two countries have soured since then. Abiy's spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters on Monday that members of the newly announced alliance had been collaborating for a while with Eritrea's financial backing.
Eritrea has repeatedly denied accusations it supports Ethiopian armed groups. Its information minister declined to comment on Wednesday about the latest developments.
ARMED GROUPS SIDE WITH TPLF
In Afar, Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside a local armed group, and in Amhara, they were fighting alongside the Fano militia, according to a senior Ethiopian government official, a diplomatic source, a humanitarian source and another source with links to the TPLF and Fano.
Fano sided with the federal government during the 2020-2022 war, but rose up against it in 2023 in an ongoing insurgency that has resulted in thousands of deaths. It is a member of the new alliance with the TPLF.
In a statement on Wednesday, the regional government in Afar accused the TPLF of launching an invasion and said Afari forces would defend themselves in coordination with their allies.
In Amhara, federal forces were firing heavy weapons from a camp in the town of Lalibela, which is famed for its rock-hewn churches dating back to the 12th and 13th centuries, two residents told Reuters.
The firing targeted Fano forces some 50 km (30 miles) outside the town who were advancing as part of the new offensive, the residents said.
The wider scale and intensity of the fighting were not clear. Jawar Mohammed, a political analyst and formerly a close ally of Abiy, said the federal government was limiting its engagement to try to prove to the international community that the TPLF was the instigator.
The federal government is in a tactically stronger position than in 2020 due to its large stocks of drones and divisions within the TPLF, said Edward Bach, Senior Africa Analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
DRONE STRIKES
The TPLF dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy's appointment as prime minister in 2018.
Tigray is yet to recover from the devastating humanitarian toll of the 2020-2022 war, which pushed hundreds of thousands into famine conditions. Around 750,000 Tigrayans were still internally displaced as of February, according to the UN refugee agency, and the region is currently facing drought linked to El Nino.
The Ethiopian military has carried out several drone strikes against Tigrayan forces in recent months, according to data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project.
On Tuesday, the US government said it condemned a recent drone strike on a Catholic Relief Services humanitarian assistance convoy in Tigray and called for an investigation, without saying who was responsible for the attack.
According to a statement by the Catholic Eparchy of Adigrat in northern Tigray, the drone strike on Sunday destroyed a truck carrying food aid destined for internally displaced people.
The federal government has not commented on any of the reported strikes in Tigray. REUTERS

Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa (AP Photo)
Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa has said his government is working to give legal status to Turkish military bases in the country’s northwest, subject to approval by the country’s People’s Assembly.

“We are now entering the stage of giving legal status to the Turkish bases in northwestern Syria,” he said, adding that the proposed arrangement would require approval from the People’s Assembly.

Türkiye has maintained a military presence in northwestern Syria, primarily citing border security and efforts against terror groups.
Sharaa also met Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on the sidelines of the General Assembly, with the two leaders discussing efforts to strengthen coordination and cooperation between Syria and Iraq.

“Five countries, one ecosystem, one future”: COP7 calls for stronger Caspian Sea cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:15:41 UTC
21:15:41 KST

“Five countries, one ecosystem, one future”: COP7 calls for stronger Caspian Sea cooperation
TEHRAN – “Five countries, one ecosystem, one future” was the message highlighted by Shina Ansari, head of Iran’s Department of Environment, at the seventh meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP7) to the Tehran Convention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea in Tehran on Wednesday, underscoring the vital importance of preserving the Caspian Sea and its unique ecosystem for the present and future generations of the region.
Ansari said protecting the Caspian Sea is a shared and transboundary responsibility, stressing that the five littoral states must move from legal commitments to practical action, from fragmented information to shared data, and from national monitoring to coordinated regional monitoring. She called for greater use of science and technology to protect the shared ecosystem and build a more sustainable future.
Addressing the opening ceremony of COP7, Ansari welcomed officials and representatives from the Tehran Convention’s member states, the United Nations and international organizations, ambassadors, government officials, academics, experts, civil society representatives and members of the media. She described Tehran’s hosting of the meeting as an opportunity to renew the countries’ shared commitment to protecting the Caspian Sea and strengthening regional cooperation.
Referring to the significance of the Caspian Sea, Ansari said the body of water is “not merely a stretch of water,” but a shared heritage, an interconnected ecosystem and a vital asset for present and future generations.
The unique sea, with its rich biodiversity, is home to species such as the Caspian seal and constitutes one of the world’s most important breeding grounds for sturgeon. Millions of people living around the Caspian also depend on the health and sustainability of the sea for their livelihoods and future.
Ansari stressed that protecting the Caspian has become more than ever a shared and transboundary responsibility, noting that pollution from land-based sources, habitat degradation, pressure on biological resources, climate change and fluctuations in water levels are challenges that no single country can address alone.
She also referred to Iran’s experience over the past year, saying the Islamic Republic had faced aggression by the United States and Israel, during which, in addition to the loss of the lives of Iran’s leader and civilians, including women, men and children, infrastructure, scientific and medical centers, and historical heritage were damaged. She added that the environment, protected areas and some international environmental obligations and rules were also affected.
The head of the Department of Environment said explosions at fuel storage facilities in Tehran, which caused widespread pollution, as well as attacks on oil facilities in the Assaluyeh region, were examples of what she described as “ecocide” or environmental crimes.
“The environment is the silent victim of wars,” Ansari said, warning that water and soil pollution, damage to habitats and environmental infrastructure, and increased pressure on natural resources can leave the impacts of wars for years or even generations.
She stressed that environmental protection and strengthening ecosystem resilience should therefore be an integral part of countries’ efforts to promote peace, security and sustainable development.
 
 Turning to the history of the Tehran Convention, Ansari said that in 2003, the five Caspian littoral states – Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan – established a common regional legal framework for protecting the Caspian Sea by signing the convention.
The agreement, she said, went beyond the signing of an international document and reflected the five countries’ shared determination to cooperate in protecting a common ecosystem.
Over more than two decades, cooperation among the littoral states has expanded into areas including oil pollution response, biodiversity conservation and transboundary environmental impact assessment, Ansari said, adding that the time had come to take another step forward.
She described “Five countries, one ecosystem, one future” as one of the central messages of the meeting, saying the phrase is more than a symbolic slogan.
“Five countries” represents a shared responsibility; “one ecosystem” reflects the scientific reality of the Caspian Sea’s interconnected nature; and “one future” serves as a reminder of the responsibility the countries have toward future generations, she explained.
Ansari emphasized that the fate of the Caspian cannot be divided along political borders, as water currents, biological species, pollution and climate change do not follow such boundaries.
 
 “The future of the Caspian cannot be five separate futures; it is a shared future for all the littoral states,” she said.
According to Ansari, advanced technologies, including remote sensing, satellite monitoring, smart environmental systems, ecological modeling, shared databases and modern analytical and forecasting tools, offer valuable opportunities to better understand changes in the Caspian and respond more rapidly to emerging threats.
She said another message of the meeting could therefore be to move “together, with the support of science and technology, to protect the Caspian Sea ecosystem and build a more sustainable tomorrow,” stressing that the message must be translated into practical action.
Ansari called for stronger scientific data-sharing mechanisms, joint monitoring systems, regular assessments of the ecosystem’s condition, joint preparedness for pollution incidents, biodiversity conservation and measures to reduce the discharge of pollutants into the sea.
Emphasizing the littoral states’ responsibility toward future generations, she said their duty extends beyond the present generation.
“We are custodians of a sea that must be handed down to future generations healthier, more sustainable and more resilient,” Ansari said.
She added that Iran is ready to deepen cooperation with the Caspian littoral states, the Tehran Convention Secretariat, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), scientific and research institutions, and other regional and international partners.
Ansari expressed hope that the decisions adopted at COP7 would not only reflect the shared political will of the littoral states, but also provide a clear roadmap for practical and measurable action to protect the Caspian Sea.
She concluded by expressing her appreciation to the littoral states, the Tehran Convention Secretariat, UNEP, experts, researchers, civil society organizations, local communities, the media and all institutions that have worked for more than two decades to protect the shared heritage.
“We hope the Caspian Sea will remain healthy, vibrant, sustainable and resilient – for today, tomorrow and generations to come,” she said.

Breadcrumb
Is Washington using the Yemen war to push Saudi-Israel normalisation?
As the war between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia rages on, with the Yemeni rebel group launching missiles at targets deep inside the kingdom and expanding the territory it controls in Yemen, the US is still refusing to get involved militarily, amid reports of long-brewing tensions between Washington and Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia has appealed to the US to launch strikes against the Houthis, but President Donald Trump’s administration has resisted.
The US at one point appeared likely to intervene, with bombs even loaded onto planes to strike Houthi targets, but Trump reversed the decision at the last minute.
“There is a history of disappointment between the two parties. The Americans don’t feel that the Saudis have helped them in the war on Iran and before, when the US attacked the Houthis, the Saudis refused to intervene,” Maysaa Shujaa Al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana’a Centre think tank, told The New Arab.
“The Saudis also felt that the Americans abandoned them in the Yemeni war at some point beginning in 2018," she said.
She added that the US’s continued conflict with Iran and upcoming congressional midterm elections meant that a potential intervention in Yemen was very inconvenient for Washington.
Saudi Arabia has in recent years tried to diversify its global relationships in an apparent effort to reduce its dependence on the US for defence. It signed a China-brokered agreement with Iran in 2023, which helped reinforce a 2022 ceasefire in the Yemen war.
With much fanfare, it also signed the Mecca Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Turkey last August, but this does not seem to have benefited it in its war with the Houthis so far.
It has also so far resisted normalising ties with Israel, despite heavy speculation before the Gaza war began in October 2023 that it was on the verge of a deal with Tel Aviv.
'Blackmailing' Saudi Arabia
Amid Saudi Arabia’s setbacks in the war in Yemen, there has been increasing speculation that the US and Israel are using the conflict to put pressure on Saudi Arabia to agree to normalisation.
“The Americans may be trying to blackmail the Saudis as much as they can to force them to join the Abraham Accords,” Shujaa Al-Deen told The New Arab.
“They may delay their support until they get more concessions, especially the ones regarding the Abraham Accords and normalisation with Israel. The Israelis definitely will benefit from that," she said.
She said Israel was using Iran’s attacks on Gulf countries to its advantage.
“The irony is that Iran has weakened many Arab states and because it has done this, it is pushing them more towards the Israelis. It’s a zero-sum game. Iran feels that its [Arab] neighbours are an easier target than Israel and this strengthens the Israeli position in the region," she said.
“Some countries see Israel as a real regional ally against Iran because they share the same enemies. It’s not the same thing with the US because they can withdraw at any time.”
Israel has previously bombed the Houthis in Yemen after the group attacked Israel-linked ships in the Red Sea and launched rockets at Israeli cities, saying the attacks were carried out in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
Last week, Israel signalled that it was ready to offer assistance to Gulf countries as part of a wider campaign against the Houthis.
Israel, however, appears to be linking assistance to Saudi Arabia to normalisation.
Israeli sources and officials believe Saudi Arabia could change its calculations regarding normalisation due to its setbacks against the Houthis, the Israeli newspaper Maariv reported.
“An escalation like this could actually help the Abraham Accords,” it quoted Israeli sources as saying.
The sources said Saudi Arabia was finding that its new relationships and alliances were unable to handle the threat from the Houthis, potentially forcing Riyadh to turn to Israel.
In the US, pro-Israel commentators have blamed Saudi Arabia’s current predicament on its failure to normalise ties with Israel.
According to The American Conservative, Commentary magazine editor John Podhoretz recently said on a podcast that the US was not providing support to Saudi Arabia “to teach MBS a lesson”.
“Oh, the Houthis are blowing up your pipelines? Maybe sign those Abraham Accords!” Podhoretz said.

Üllar Lanno: So that treatment queues don't turn into death sentences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

Üllar Lanno: So that treatment queues don't turn into death sentences
If the state tries to save money in healthcare by stretching waiting lists and cutting services, someone will eventually pay with their life. The next government will have little choice but to sharply expand medical training and close the funding gap, because the state is obligated to provide timely care, writes Üllar Lanno.
More and more often we must remind ourselves that Estonia still has a solidarity‑based healthcare system, and every social tax payer must have access to a specialist within a reasonable time. Unfortunately, more and more people from rural counties are traveling to hospitals or private clinics in Tallinn or Tartu.
In private clinics, a quick paid appointment is often obtained with a phone call. No e‑consultation filter — you get everything you need if you pay, even though you have already paid social tax. In this way, the state reaches deeper into our pockets to cover the Health Insurance Fund's deficit. The poorest are left without help, and the system becomes expensive and unequal.
The Health Insurance Fund calls next year's cuts "modernization." Behind that word is a €3 million reduction in specialist outpatient funding and nearly €10 million in cuts to radiology. This year, laboratory funding was also reduced by one‑sixth. In total, specialist care faces more than €24 million in negative changes.
On paper, a small miracle happens: specialist care still ends up €1.81 million in the black. The rabbit is pulled out of the hat using a €15 million "modernization and demand assessment reserve."
A reserve for modernization
It is unknown which services will receive this money, how it will be allocated, or how much of the reserve will actually be used. The Health Insurance Fund wants to reduce its deficit from nearly €90 million this year to €44 million next year. Meanwhile, healthcare costs continue to rise. Doctors and nurses want wage increases above average salary growth, while the Ministry of Finance forecasts average wage growth at around five percent.
Salaries make up two‑thirds of a hospital's budget. Giving hospitals less money while saying salaries must rise is like ordering someone to remove five kilos from a backpack and then pack ten kilos more into it. Something must disappear — most likely appointment slots and treatment capacity.
This year, specialist contact appointments in the first half of the year were down six percent compared to last year, and 15 percent compared to 2023. Meanwhile, e‑consultations increased by 27 percent. E‑consultations are not the enemy when a family doctor quickly receives specialist advice. But a slow, drawn‑out e‑consultation becomes a barrier behind which the patient waits while their illness progresses. And e‑consultations are answered by the same doctors — the bottleneck remains until more of them exist.
Unlimited waiting time
Take a family doctor who asks a cardiologist for advice. The cardiologist replies: first do an ECG, an echo, blood tests, and a few more examinations. Then the results are sent again. The clock ticks, and the patient still has not seen a cardiologist. The system saves money until the disease decides it will not wait any longer.
During the 2009 economic crisis, the maximum waiting time for outpatient specialist care was extended from four weeks to six. The crisis ended, but six weeks remained. Last year, nearly a quarter of planned first specialist visits exceeded that limit. In regional hospitals, more than a third exceeded 42 days.
After an e‑consultation, 23 percent of patients who needed an appointment were scheduled more than 42 days later. Current rules say a person may be placed on a waiting list only if waiting does not worsen their health, disease progression, or prognosis — and this is not a recommendation.
If the system cannot fulfill its duties, the solution cannot be lowering the bar. If a house's foundation sinks, there is no point in sawing the doorframe crooked so the door closes again.
We need more doctors
First, the University of Tartu must increase medical school admissions by at least 30 percent and maintain that level for at least ten years. The number of lecturers and clinical supervisors must grow alongside student numbers. If we decide we need more doctors, we will get a specialist with some experience in ten or eleven years.
A warning sign: in the past five years, one‑third of residents dropped out of specialist training. Last year, 115 specialists left the workforce due to age. Each year, 140–160 registered doctors turn 65, and those aged 65 and older already make up 23 percent of working doctors.
Society invests hundreds of thousands of euros in training each specialist. Training doctors is expensive — but their absence is even more expensive. Shortages lead to massive overtime, burnout risk, and declining quality. Patients wait longer, illnesses worsen, and cheap treatment becomes expensive treatment.
Second, the state must stop burning millions on fragmented, outdated IT systems. Around twenty hospitals and nearly a thousand family doctors use different software, and next year yet another new system will be added. A unified standard system would save money and time, make data exchange more secure, and create better opportunities to use AI.
Third, the state must create long‑term workforce plans for each hospital. Based on population forecasts, we can calculate how many cardiologists, surgeons, radiologists, psychiatrists, anesthesiologists, nurses, and other specialists each region needs now and in ten years. A staffing system cannot rely on doctors doing overtime for life — overtime is a backup generator, not the electrical grid.
Fourth, video consultations must become a normal nationwide specialist service. A doctor should not have to drive hours across Estonia just to talk to a patient and review test results. A patient should not have to travel hundreds of kilometers when the same consultation can be done on screen. In Ukraine, people can speak with a family doctor from a shelter via phone. Estonia already has the technology. We lack decisions, not cables or megabytes.
Fifth, clearer limits must be set on e‑consultations to protect family doctors. E‑consultations must bring the patient closer to a specialist, not become a tool to keep them waiting. If a specialist determines that a patient needs an appointment, they must receive it within a medically justified time. We need teamwork and less bureaucracy.
Record number of new specialist trainees
A two‑speed healthcare system is emerging. In the Health Insurance Fund system, you go through a gauntlet of e‑consultations and tests, but in a private clinic you often get an appointment within days if you are willing to pay over €100. Those with money buy time; those without lose time to illness.
Sixth, the state must stop pretending that the healthcare costs of an aging society can be shaved down a little each year. The ratio of taxpayers to dependents is changing, the population is aging, and the number of working‑age people is shrinking. Healthcare funding needs will grow as older people's treatment needs grow. If the Health Insurance Fund is short €100 million, the state budget must cover it.
At the same time, we must examine how much the Health Insurance Fund invests in prevention. That amount must grow, and the activities funded must produce measurable results.
It is easy to add clichés like "medical care must be accessible to everyone" to election programs, but in reality we are moving further away from that goal. Inequality is already high, and access to medical care cannot become its newest expression.
For decades, Estonia has had internationally recognized, cost‑effective, high‑quality medical care. The most foolish thing would be to make this success story more expensive through underfunding — and let people wait until cheap treatment becomes expensive treatment, and a treatable disease becomes untreatable.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Rampant malpractice was committed on a massive scale in the by-elections,” he said.
The EC has rejected the suggestion that its decisions were taken without the participation of all three commissioners. It said decisions, including those related to SIR, were taken unanimously with the approval of the CEC and the two other election commissioners.The poll panel said written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks were standard practices within a multi-member constitutional body. It said differing views were part of institutional deliberations before final decisions were taken and that all official orders had legal sanction and followed established procedures.

Minister: Teachers, rescuers, police to get pay rises in 2027 budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:14:00 UTC
21:14:00 KST

Minister: Teachers, rescuers, police to get pay rises in 2027 budget
Teachers, cultural workers, rescuers and police will receive modest pay rises next year, Education Minister Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) said as union talks resumed Wednesday.
Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi (Reform) said the broad framework for next year's state budget is in place, with the four sectors receiving equal additional funding for wages.
A one-hour warning strike by education workers protesting at pay ran Tuesday from 8–9 a.m. at preschools and 9–10 a.m. at general and vocational schools.
Kallas confirmed to ERR that the four groups can expect a "small" pay rise next year, but did not specify the exact percentage ahead of negotiations with the Education Personnel Union (EHL) continuing Wednesday afternoon. She said the additional funding for the wage bill would be the same for all four sectors.
"The budget situation is so difficult that, in order to be able to raise these salaries at all, even by a little, we have to make cuts somewhere," Kallas said.
She added additional revenue from economic growth will be consumed by increases in pensions. Assuming 2.4 percent growth next year, the most optimistic estimate is €350 million in additional tax revenue.
"Of that €350 million, €200 million will essentially go immediately and automatically toward covering indexed expenditure, meaning pensions and a few other expenses, such as parental benefits," Kallas said. "Very little of the money generated by economic growth will remain available."
According to Kallas, cuts will have to be found in infrastructure and real estate investments. She said the government should decide not to launch any new real estate investments at all. "Finish those that are currently in progress and do not launch any new real estate investments for now. Then look at the infrastructure situation as a whole to see whether any savings can be made there."
The government will discuss the state budget again at a Cabinet meeting Thursday, and hopes to finalise it Monday before submitting it to the Riigikogu.
The EHL is seeking to raise the minimum teacher salary to €2,312, the projected Estonian average for 2027, up from the current €1,970. Union chair Reemo Voltri said the government has been backing away from its pledge to raise salaries to 120 percent of the national average. The EHL said 69 percent of Estonian teachers have considered leaving the profession in the past year, citing workload and low pay.
Teachers had also been joined by rescue workers in picketing the Riigikogu earlier this month (pictured). The average national wage reported for the second quarter of this year is €2,243 per month gross.

Hainan steps up efforts to develop international consumption hub

2026-09-23
12:13:16 UTC
21:13:16 KST

HAIKOU /China/, September 23. /TASS/. The authorities of Hainan Province will step up efforts over the next five years to develop the island into a leading international tourism and consumption hub, China News Service online news portal reported.
It was noted that the offshore customs supervision regime, which took effect in December 2025, is expected to provide a major boost to Hainan’s retail sector. According to Li Yong, an official with the provincial Department of Tourism, Culture, Radio, Television, and Sports cited by the portal, local authorities plan to establish a world-class tourism and consumption cluster on the island by 2035.
Hainan’s economic and institutional openness is expected to increase steadily in the coming years. In line with the objectives for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), recently outlined by China’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the provincial capital Haikou and the resort city of Sanya on the island’s southern coast will play key roles in developing the international consumption sector of China’s southernmost province. The main focus will be on projects related to maritime, island, and cruise tourism.
According to the five-year plan for the development of the consumption hub, released by the Hainan provincial administration in June, this sector of the economy will become an important link in ensuring the effective integration of domestic and international economic cycles in the region. This is expected to enhance the province’s competitiveness and provide additional incentives for the long-term development of the free trade port.
In line with these objectives, the authorities and businesses will work to expand the range of high-quality tourism products in five key areas: shopping, medical and wellness tourism, maritime, cultural, and sports tourism. Eight additional areas have been identified for intensified efforts, including hosting exhibitions, making use of the island’s ring-shaped tourist highway, theme parks and attractions, and developing routes through tropical rainforests. Plans also call for expanding the cruise and yacht tourism segments and promoting projects involving visits to and sightseeing in cities and rural areas.
Under the official plan, the island is expected to welcome 154 mln Chinese and international tourists in 2026-2030, who will spend 363 bln yuan (approximately $54 bln at the current exchange rate of the People’s Bank of China) in the province. To maintain and increase tourist arrivals, the authorities plan to establish more than 120 international passenger air routes, providing air connections with over 60 foreign cities. As a result, Hainan is expected to rank among the world’s top three most competitive island tourism destinations that are not archipelagos.

Russia pounds Kyiv with drones, killing two and wounding 23 hours before Zelenskyy's UN address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:12:58 UTC
21:12:58 KST

Zelenskyy is in New York for the annual UN gathering as part of his diplomatic effort to shore up and recruit further international support for his country’s gruelling fight against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Russia hammered Ukraine's capital Kyiv with drones in daylight attacks on Wednesday, hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was due to address world leaders at the UN General Assembly.
Two people were killed and 23 were wounded in Kyiv, and palls of black smoke floated above the city following the latest in what have been daily Russian attacks that torment Ukrainian civilians.
The drones set off fires and damaged buildings in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine overnight, authorities said.
Ukrainian Railways chief Oleksandr Pertsovsky said Kyiv's rail network was "under fire" and urged "maximum" vigilance from passengers using the city's central station.
In Zaporizhzhia, in southeastern Ukraine, two men aged 37 and 39 were wounded by a strike that started a large fire at a shopping mall.
Emergency services said the fire spread across about 6,000 square meters before coming under control.
In Ukraine's southern Black Sea port of Odesa, the captain of a cargo ship was killed in a Russian attack, part of a wave of strikes from both sides on commercial vessels designed to hit export revenues.
The head of the Odesa region, Oleg Kiper, said the Ukrainian captain was in charge of the vessel, which was sailing on the Black Sea under the flag of Antigua and Barbuda.
At least 226 civilian and commercial vessels have been hit on the Black Sea since the start of the conflict, Turkey's IMEAK chamber of shipping said.
Around 70% of those attacks took place in the first eight months of this year.
Turkey, whose vessels are increasingly in the firing line, has sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end strikes on civilian ships but the two foes have failed to act on it.
"The recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea are unacceptable, regardless of who is responsible," Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.
International support
Zelenskyy is in New York for the annual UN gathering as part of his diplomatic effort to shore up and recruit further international support for his country’s gruelling fight against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump on Tuesday, who has shown impatience with the lack of progress in talks aimed at ending the war and the escalating aerial attacks by both sides this year.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, who is accused by NATO officials and European governments of sabotage, espionage and other hybrid attacks, is not scheduled to attend the General Assembly this year.
Ukraine has hit back at Russia by damaging oil refineries that are a vital pillar of the country's economy.
Zelenskyy said at the start of his US visit that he had proposals to make about possible de-escalation in the war.
Urgent issues for Kyiv are halting devastating Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and ensuring Ukrainian grain can be shipped to world markets through the Black Sea despite the war.
Ukraine also needs more US-made Patriot air defence systems as a shield against Russian ballistic missiles, but Patriots are in short supply after the war in Iran began.
The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces struck Ukraine’s military-industrial and energy sector facilities, logistics centres and sea vessels overnight.
The ministry said its air defences intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

'Taiwan's TCC Group plans to acquire Ivano-Frankivskcement, awaits regulatory approvals'
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:12:10 EEST
21:12:10 KST

Taiwan Cement Corporation (TCC Group) intends to acquire 100% of the shares in Ukrainian cement producer PJSC Ivano-Frankivskcement (IFCEM), the company's press service reported.
"The partnership will combine IFCEM's leading position in the Ukrainian market, its modern production facilities, long-standing industrial traditions and strong team with TCC's global experience, technologies and investment capabilities. It creates a foundation for the group's further development and active participation in the large-scale reconstruction of Ukraine and deeper economic integration with Europe," Ivano-Frankivskcement said on its website.
The deal will be concluded between IFCEM's majority shareholder CemInWest S.A. (Switzerland), together with the owners of related companies Ivano-Frankivskdakh LLC, Krugips LLC and Krumix LLC, and TCC Group EMEA Holdings B.V. (Netherlands), a subsidiary of TCC Group Holdings Co., Ltd.
The completion of the deal is subject to obtaining the necessary antitrust approvals and other regulatory clearances in the relevant jurisdictions, as well as fulfillment of customary closing conditions.
As reported by Chairman of the Board and member of the Supervisory Board of Ivano-Frankivskcement Mykola Kruts, he will remain a member of the company's board of directors for the next several years.
"Today, the company is entering a new stage of its development. Partnership with a global strategic investor from Taiwan opens up new opportunities for IFCEM in investment, technological development and further strengthening of its position. In the coming years, I will remain a member of the board of directors to contribute to continuity, stability and the company's further development," Kruts said, according to the company's statement.
The preliminary value of the deal is about EUR 750 million, Forbes Ukraine reported, citing Focus Taiwan.
PJSC Ivano-Frankivskcement produces cement, roofing materials, concrete and reinforced-concrete products, and dry construction mixes. Its production capacity is 4.3 million tonnes of cement per year. About 2,500 people work at the group's enterprises.
Before the full-scale war, NEQSOL Holding was close to acquiring Ivano-Frankivskcement, but later withdrew from the deal.
According to YouControl, in 2025 Ivano-Frankivskcement increased net profit 1.4 times year-on-year to UAH 4.2 billion, while net revenue rose 20.3% to UAH 16.2 billion. In the first half of 2026, net profit fell by a quarter year-on-year to UAH 1.4 billion, while net revenue decreased 4.2% to UAH 7.1 billion. The company's assets were valued at UAH 14.9 billion.
TCC Group Holdings Co., Ltd. is a global industrial group from Taiwan and one of the world's largest cement producers. The group has more than 40 production sites, with combined cement production capacity exceeding 112 million tonnes per year, and employs 13,800 people. TCC also develops renewable energy, energy storage systems and advanced materials. TCC has a significant presence in Europe and Africa, including Portugal, Türkiye, Spain, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and Italy.

Senior Polish presidential official detained amid probe into misspending of funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:08:04 UTC
21:08:04 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Agents from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) have detained a senior official from opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s chancellery as part of a probe into alleged misspending of funds under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
An employee of a major right-wing broadcaster, Republika, was also taken into custody as part of the same investigation, which relates to the activities of the Polish National Foundation (PFN), a body created under the PiS government to promote Poland abroad but which was also used to further the party’s political interests.
Dzisiaj rano w Warszawie na polecenie Prokuratury Regionalnej w Rzeszowie agenci @CBAgovPL zatrzymali Piotra M. i Annę P.
▶️ Zatrzymane osoby przewożone są do @Prok_Regio_RZE, która prowadzi śledztwo dotyczące nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej.

— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) September 23, 2026
On Tuesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, announced that two individuals, named only as Piotr M. and Anna P. under Polish privacy law, had been detained by the CBA at the request of prosecutors investigating irregularities in the PFN.
Both suspects previously worked in the chancellery of Prime Minister Beata Szydło, who was head of the PiS government from 2015 to 2017. Piotr M. was head of the Government Information Centre (CIR) and Anna P. led the media services department.
Anna P. now works for Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. She is director of the Presidential Events Office, which organises the president’s schedule. Piotr M. currently works as a commentator for Republika, a station generally supportive of Nawrocki and PiS.
Agenci CBA zatrzymali w Warszawie Piotra M. i Annę P. Sprawa dotyczy nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej! pic.twitter.com/e3jw3ekdOA
— Iwona Hartwich (@iwonahartwich) September 23, 2026
In 2017, while still working in Szydło’s chancellery, Piotr M. and Anna P. founded a PR company called Solvere. Later that same year, the company was hired to run a prominent and controversial campaign for the PFN called “Fair Courts”, receiving a reported 1.2 million zloty (€275,000) for the project.
The PFN had been set up the previous year under Szydło’s government with funding from 17 state-owned companies. Its publicly declared and statutory mission was to promote Poland abroad.
However, the “Fair Courts” campaign, which cost around 8.4 million zloty, was run in Poland itself, with material in Polish, and aimed to show the alleged failings of the justice system in Poland in order to justify why controversial reforms being implemented by PiS were necessary.
Echoing PiS rhetoric, the campaign suggested that judges saw themselves as a “special caste” and highlighted cases of alleged wrongdoing by individual judges, including one who had been caught stealing a sausage. (The judge in question had not ruled on a case since that incident in 2006 and had died in 2015.)
In 2018, a Warsaw court ruled that the “Fair Courts” campaign was inconsistent with the PFN’s statutory goals, saying that not only did the adverts fail to enhance Poland’s image abroad, “on the contrary, they significantly weakened it, creating a negative image of the judiciary based on individual cases”.
In February 2025, just over a year after PiS lost power, a newly appointed PFN board accused its predecessors of criminal negligence that caused damages of over 30 million zloty to the foundation’s finances. They notified prosecutors of potential crimes.
In July this year, two men who had served as PFN board members at the time of the campaign were detained as part of an investigation into the misspending of the foundation’s funds. At that time, the CBA also announced that it had searched the homes of Anna P. and Piotr M.
A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds.
The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026
Today’s detentions of Anna P. and Piotr M. were welcomed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. He told Polsat News that the “Fair Courts” campaign was a “double scandal” because it was “not only an abuse of public funds, but also for the very clearly malicious purpose” of “attacking the independent judiciary”.
Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, told the media that the authorities intended to find out “who stood behind” the actions of Anna P. and Piotr M., because “it’s hard to believe this was their initiative”.
However, Jarosław Olechowski, a senior executive at Republika, condemned the detentions, calling them an act of “political revenge by the Donald Tusk regime for an information campaign exposing pathologies in Polish courts”.
At the time of writing, the presidential chancellery had not commented on the detention of Anna P., the head of its events office. Earlier this year, Nawrocki’s deputy chief of staff was charged with ordering the falsification of documents, an accusation he denies.

The “Fair Courts” campaign was just one of a number of controversial initiatives launched by the PFN under the PiS government. The foundation was regularly accused of spending money to support PiS’s political goals or on seemingly wasteful projects.
One of its most famous initiatives involved the purchase of a yacht for almost €1 million, which was renamed “I Love Poland” and sent on an around-the-world cruise to mark the centenary of Poland’s independence in 2018 (though it suffered damage and spent weeks stuck in a port, accruing further costs).
In 2021, the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) accused the PFN of violating the law by refusing to provide documents required for an audit.

‘Lifting Restrictions Must Not Become a Precedent,’ Kyiv Says After Russian Billionaires Delisted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:06:29 UTC
21:06:29 KST

Ukraine has criticized the EU’s decision to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list, with an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that the move could set a precedent for weakening the bloc’s pressure on Moscow.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelensky’s adviser on sanctions policy, told Kyiv Post that Ukraine found the EU decision “very strange,” arguing that there was no change in circumstances.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia continues the war, and their ties with the Kremlin,which were among the grounds for the sanctions, have not disappeared,” he added.
Ukraine warns against weakening sanctions unity
Vlasiuk said Russia could seek to exploit divisions within the EU over sanctions and warned that removing restrictions from individual Russian businessmen should not become a broader precedent.
“Russia is attempting to fracture EU unity, and it is crucial not to let this crack widen and lead to a weakening of the common sanctions policy,” he said.
“Lifting restrictions on individual Russian businessmen must not become a new precedent,” Vlasiuk added.
He said Kyiv would respond by proposing additional sanctions, particularly against Russian oligarchs linked to the country’s military-industrial complex who have not yet been targeted.
“Right now, it is vital to focus on increasing sanctions pressure on Russia.”
Despite its criticism of the delistings, Kyiv welcomed the EU’s decision to extend the broader sanctions regime for three years.
Germany Probes Drone and Suspected Explosives Near Air Base
“At the same time, we appreciate the EU’s decision to extend – for another 36 months – sanctions against individuals and entities responsible for undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence,” Vlasiuk said.
“This is an important decision that provides the sanctions regime with necessary long-term stability.”
The measures currently cover more than 3,000 individuals and entities and include asset freezes, travel restrictions, and a ban on making funds or economic resources available to those listed.
As part of the decision, however, the EU removed Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list, along with another individual and a company. The names of Usmanov and Fridman are explicitly listed in the EU’s implementing regulation.
The decision followed weeks of disagreement among EU member states over whether the two Russian businessmen should remain sanctioned. Reuters reported that France and Luxembourg pushed for their removal, while Latvia initially had opposed the move.
Riga accepts EU compromise but vows to keep pressure on Russian billionaires
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs announced the decision on X late on Monday, saying Europe’s pressure on Russia should become “stronger, not more convenient for the Kremlin.”
He said Latvia supported extending the broader sanctions regime but could not accept dropping Usmanov and Fridman as the price.
EU sanctions decisions require the unanimous support of all 27 member states. Without an agreement, the current listings would have expired Tuesday at midnight.
Given that, Latvia ultimately agreed to the compromise and adopted a stance of “constructive abstention” during a new vote on Tuesday.
“It was a choice not between a good and a bad decision, but between a bad one and a significantly worse one – a choice between altering the status of two individuals and the future of the entire sanctions regime, which affects nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russian aggression,” Kulbergs said.
“By opting to maintain sanctions against these individuals, we achieved an outcome that is more beneficial for Latvia, Ukraine, and Europe in the long run,” he added.
At the same time, the Latvian government imposed financial and entry restrictions on Fridman and Usmanov at the national level, according to documents attached to the Cabinet of Ministers’ meeting agenda.
The government pledged that Latvia would continue to use all available legal instruments to prevent the unfreezing of the individuals’ funds and economic resources in Latvia.

French President Emmanuel Macron has sharply criticized US President Donald Trump’s efforts to establish peace in Gaza during his address to the UN General Assembly, noting that not a single humanitarian aid corridor has been opened, writes Reuters.

In response to Macron’s criticism, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly stated that President Trump had ended the war between Israel and the terrorist group Hamas, freed all surviving hostages, repatriated the bodies of the deceased, and is now leading the implementation of a 20-point peace plan. While others merely talk, Trump has set about solving the problem, and no one else has achieved as much for peace in the region.
In France, Macron has faced criticism for taking no action following the recognition of Palestinian statehood.
Despite the sting of such criticism, Paris has toughened its stance against Israeli settlers, whose settlement expansion is linked to violence against Palestinians. Several national-level sanctions have been imposed, and a process has been initiated to ban the import of products originating from settlements in the occupied West Bank. Macron also addressed this issue in his remarks, urging people to look at the West Bank, where violations occur daily—despite the fact that Hamas has never operated in that territory.
France’s relations with Israel have become more strained over the past year. Macron stated that those who believe Israel’s security can be ensured by undermining the sovereignty of its neighbors are mistaken; such actions, he argued, weaken Israel’s security both now and in the future. Macron has always been a staunch supporter of the multilateral system and warned against a return to the “law of the jungle” in international politics. Nations must choose between a world governed by force and subjugation and a civilized international community. It is everyone’s duty—now more than ever—to stand up for the UN, and the new order of impunity that some seek to impose must not be accepted.

Ancient wall found beneath Paris could confirm site of first settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:06:21 UTC
21:06:21 KST

An ancient wall discovered beneath Paris has been described as a “major breakthrough” by France’s culture ministry, with the archaeological find possibly confirming the location of the city’s original settlement.
A roughly 20-metre (65ft) stretch of wall dating from the Gallo-Roman period was discovered in Paris this summer beneath a building on the Île de la Cité, near Notre Dame Cathedral in the heart of the French capital.
The stone-and-wood structure is thought to be a fragment of the ramparts of Lutetia – the ancient name for Paris – built by the Gallic Parisii tribe who lived along the River Seine in the iron age.
The Île de la Cité has traditionally been regarded as the centre of Lutetia, but a rival theory, backed by some archaeological research, contends that it was in Nanterre, a suburb to the west.
“We may be looking at one of the most important remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia,” the culture minister, Catherine Pégard, said in a statement on Wednesday. “Scientific caution still requires that we verify its function and its chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable at this stage.”
Lutetia was first mentioned in book seven of Julius Caesar’s Gallic Wars series, where it was said to be on an island in the River Seine – a vague description that has given rise to many theories about its location.
The wall, uncovered in the course of excavations beneath the Hôtel-Dieu hospital, bears traces of fire, which may correspond to Caesar’s account that the Gauls set fire to their town before the Battle of Lutetia against the Romans.
Carbon dating of the charred evidence dated the find to between 200BC and 10BC, the ministry said in its statement – a timeframe that covers the Battle of Lutetia, in 52BC.
The Île de la Cité is the largest island in the Seine in the Paris region and became the centre of the Roman settlement of Lutetia.

Ethiopia: Fighting resumes in Tigray

Wednesday's clashes are the latest of several in recent months and have sparked fears of renewed intense fighting in the war-ravaged region.

On Wednesday, state-owned Ethiopian Airlines announced that it had canceled service at Mekelle, Tigray's capital, as well as Axum and Shire regional airports "due to the current situation."

Abiy and his Prosperity Party won reelection in June, though the vote was boycotted by Ethiopia's main opposition groups.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 until 2018, when it was replaced by Abiy, whose election sparked the country's civil war.
The Pretoria Peace Agreement brought an end to the conflict, but peace has remained elusive, with government troops resuming drone strikes in 2025 as TPLF rebels began amassing troops at regional borders.
Ethiopia has accused the TPLF of allying with neighboring Eritrea and other armed groups.
An advisor to Prime Minister Abiy called Wednesday's development "heartbreaking," saying rebels had launched offensives against government forces in Afar and Amhara as well as taking control of airports in Tigray.
However, the Tigray army "has been instructed to counter the attack and genocidal invasion launched against us, and has entered into a defensive battle," the Tigray government said in a statement on Facebook.

Fire fighters investigating a gas leak turn out to be the cause
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
When the residents of the Brabant town of Oisterwijk smelled the pungent odor of gas on Wednesday, they called their local fire department, who turned out to be the culprits.
Fire fighters spent the morning searching for a gas leak to no avail. Together with gas provider Enexis, they tested levels throughout the town but could not find a source, only the smell.
Meanwhile, back at the fire station, staff discovered a canister of THT was missing. The chemical is added to gas, which is naturally odorless, to so that people can smell any leak immediately.
The cannister had been accidently thrown out and had spent the morning in the back of a garbage truck, which was making its rounds.
“We were able to have a laugh about it for a moment,” firefighter Ronald Blokpoel told Omroep Brabant.
Residents may continue to smell gas for a time while the chemical dissipates. The fire depart warns there is no danger to public health.

Strike copters lead Ukraine’s 650 new military drone approvals—jam-proof and interceptor models close behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:03:34 UTC
21:03:34 KST

Ukraine's Defense Ministry has approved 650 unmanned aerial systems for military use since the start of 2026, most of them Ukrainian-made, the ministry said on 22 September. The approved types range from strike copters and jam-proof fiber-optic drones to interceptors and deep-strike systems, expanding the arsenal Ukraine fields against Russian aerial attacks.
The approvals are expanding the range of systems available to Ukraine's military in the fifth year of Russia's full-scale war, including drones designed to operate despite electronic warfare and others intended to intercept enemy drones. For Ukraine, the growing range gives its forces more options to counter Russian drones and the electronic warfare used against them. In July, the ministry said the number of UAV systems approved at that point in 2026 was more than 30% higher than during the equivalent period in 2025 and more than 73% above the same point in 2024.
What was approved
The approved systems include 238 strike copter-type UAVs, 231 fiber-optic-controlled systems, 42 interceptor UAVs, 32 middle-strike UAVs, and nine deep-strike drones. The five named categories account for 552 of the 650 systems.
Fiber-optic-controlled drones use a physical cable rather than radio signals to communicate with their operator, making them resistant to jamming from electronic warfare. Interceptor drones are designed to destroy other unmanned aircraft in flight, providing another way to counter drone attacks alongside conventional air defense.
The 650 figure counts types of systems that have cleared the ministry's codification process—the step that allows equipment to be procured for the armed forces—not individual drones produced or deployed.
The interceptor race
By mid-year, the ministry had cleared 413 drone types—more than two a day—with copter-type strikers and fiber-optic systems dominating the list. The interceptor category has filled especially fast: the ministry ordered 8,000 Octopus interceptors, and by September at least 20 firms were racing to field interceptors against Russia's jet-powered Shaheds, with two having completed combat tests.
Domestic share rising
In the first eight months of 2026, the ministry codified 1,526 new weapons and military equipment models for the armed forces, with nearly 91% produced domestically, the ministry said—of those, 565 were Ukrainian-made unmanned aerial systems. In the same period last year, the ministry had approved 983 models, with 86% made domestically.
