Russian Drones Over Kyiv – War of Speed and New Deep Strike Tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:33:00 UTC
20:33:00 KST

Russia’s “Shahed / Geran” drones are attacking Ukraine’s civilian cities almost continuously. Their targets of choice include shopping malls, gas stations, energy infrastructure, food warehouses, office centers and other civilian facilities. They increasingly deploy jet-powered Geran 4 and 5 variants of the drones that have replaced the so-called “mopeds” – powered by piston engines.
Ukraine recorded around 180 uses of jet-powered drones in the whole of 2025. In August this year alone, they launched around 2,800 – Russia used 15 times the annual total of jet-powered drones in a single month. Russia’s once experimental weapon, that it occasionally launched to test Ukraine’s air-defense capabilities is now one of mass deployment.
nd this creates new challenges for Ukraine. Having learned relatively quickly to effectively intercept conventional Shaheds – open-source data shows interception rates reached 90-95%. These jet-powered targets present a more complicated challenge for Ukraine with currently only around 60% interception rates.
The success Russia is currently achieving with jet-powered drones clearly demonstrates one of the fundamental principles of modern warfare – the race to implement new technologies faster than the enemy. Each side constantly probes the other’s vulnerabilities and can rapidly scale up a technology or tactic that works.
Russian Drone Attack on Kyiv Kills 2, Injures 22 as Explosions Rock Central Kyiv
Changes in Russian tactics
Russia has not simply increased the number of attacks; it has constantly changed how those attacks are conducted. These changes likely have several objectives: to overwhelm Ukraine’s air-defense system, forcing it to use expensive missiles against relatively cheap targets, create prolonged panic, and ultimately identify areas where Ukrainian defenses are weaker.
Where Ukraine’s defenses are thinnest, Russia tries to scale up its attacks. Constant attacks on civilian as well as military infrastructure in major cities serve to disrupt the functioning of the country. When air-raid alerts last for hours, logistics are disrupted, people move to shelters and businesses suspend operations. Even if a drone does not hit its target, the threat itself creates an economic impact and reduces the country’s financial capacity.
This effect is especially visible in Kyiv. When air-raid alerts are repeatedly declared, the capital simply cannot operate in a normal way which, in my view, is one of Moscow’s objectives: not simply to destroy something, but to gradually paralyze normal life. Russia is also trying to destroy residents’ morale by striking warehouses in an attempt to cause shortages and disruption to food and other essential supplies.
There is another aspect to these air attacks. They do not necessarily have to end with a strike against a specific target. The use of aircraft for reconnaissance can provide data about Ukraine’s response: where and how air defenses operate, which routes are being blocked, how quickly Ukraine responds to a target, and which systems are used to intercept it.
Even though not every drone launched by Russia is designed to explode, the objective ultimately remains the same: to destroy Ukraine.
Energy infrastructure, military and government facilities, communications towers, telecommunications infrastructure, media offices, gas stations, shopping malls – the list of potential targets is endless. Drones can be manually controlled and switch between targets in real time.
Every single attack can serve several purposes simultaneously: inflicting physical damage, overwhelming air defenses, collecting intelligence or simply keeping up constant psychological pressure. Nighttime attacks disrupt sleep and reduce productivity of Ukrainians throughout the following working day.
Why jet-powered drones are difficult to Intercept?
Conventional Shaheds fly relatively slowly allowing Ukraine’s air-defense forces time to detect them and assign the appropriate weapon system to destroy them. A jet-powered that flies twice as fast or more aircraft significantly reduces that window.
Speed is not the only factor; flight altitude, trajectory, terrain, buildings and the number of simultaneous targets present air defense with an entirely different and more complex problem.
Jet-powered drones operate at altitudes above 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles), meaning that some of the conventional tools – mobile fire teams, machine guns, Gepard anti-aircraft systems and MANPADS – become ineffective. This leaves three main tools: fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missile systems and interceptor drones.
Russia does not rely on a single design with various types of jet-powered drones emerging, with some already approaching the capabilities of cruise missiles.
The Geran-5, for example, reportedly has a range of around 950 kilometers (590 miles) and a warhead of up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds). The Bandrol develops a speed of approximately 500-560 km/h (310-350 mph) and can go even faster during an attacking dive. The Dan-T drone-missile has a payload of up to 135 kilograms (298 pounds).
“Mother Drones” – another new Russian tactic
Recent attacks on Kyiv involved the use of so-called “mother drones.” These are Shaheds acting as carriers for smaller, faster and more maneuverable first-person view (FPV) drones which are released closer to and can be directed on to a potential target deep behind the front lines – distances that would otherwise be beyond the FPV drone.
The limited use of the tactic so far suggests it is yet another Russian testbed prior to mass deployment
What new threats could emerge?
Ukrainian defense engineers today must identify trends, understand the direction of technological evolution, and anticipate the direction Russian technology might take and develop countermeasures before they become a “game changer.”
When assessing the threat, it is not just technical or tactical capability that is important – scale. We have already seen that Russia was able to rapidly increase the production of relatively inexpensive guided munitions. It is not solely important to be able to effectively intercept a particular target but also in sufficient numbers.
Even the world’s best interceptor will not suffice if production is limited while the enemy can manufacture thousands of cheaper targets.
We need asymmetry.
The countermeasure should preferably cost significantly less than the target it faces or Ukraine could literally be exhausted by the financial cost of war. Ideally Ukraine should make mass attacks economically unattractive to Russia.
The future will be largely defined by a war of quantity – more missiles, more UAVs, more types of munitions opposed by more countermeasures – with lower cost being essential for both offensive and defensive systems.
Just as essential as quantity and price alone the decisive advantage will see a struggle for quality and autonomy with artificial intelligence (AI) inevitably becoming part of that process.
As the number and type of munitions increase, they will by necessity become “smarter,” requiring fewer external commands for guidance. They will be able to analyze their surroundings, adjust their routes, and independently select the moment or direction from which to approach a target.
With hundreds or thousands of different targets flying simultaneously, it will be impossible to train and field the same numbers of pilots. Both sides will rely on decisions being delegated to algorithms.
AI will be used to both strike targets and launch countermeasures. Systems will be able to analyze the airspace more quickly, predict flight paths, filter out decoys, allocate weapons to genuine targets, and operate without constant human intervention.
Future warfare will increasingly see humans defining the rules, while machines perform most of the work. This is already happening in civilian life. Vehicles can now operate without drivers, and AI systems are capable of independently analyzing enormous volumes of information. The next logical step is greater autonomy in military systems.
What Ukraine needs to do to protect its skies
The technological race is already underway – at full speed. If Ukraine is not to lose, it needs to prepare for this race now.
In 2023, when the first Shaheds appeared Ukraine could only counter them effectively by using expensive missiles, which were already in short supply. Kyiv went through a rapid and productive evolution – from detecting drones with searchlights to effectively destroying them over Ukraine. When conventional “mopeds” stopped delivering the results Russia needed, jet-powered unmanned aircraft began to appear.
Ukraine cannot afford to simply catch up with Russia every time it introduces a new technology. It needs to develop its own solutions in advance – both offensive systems and countermeasures. In no time at all fast, high-flying drones will be able to independently decide where to fly, what to attack and how to circumvent its defenses.
Several Ukrainian companies are already developing and combat testing jet-powered interceptor drones. The next steps will be scaling up production which should significantly improve Ukraine’s ability to intercept jet-powered UAVs.
Ukraine needs to think more broadly. It needs domestic production of jet engines and to avoid becoming dependent on third countries, including China. Similarly it should also increase the number of radars, protection for aircraft and strike drone bases and production facilities to manufacture its own jet-powered drones combined with strong intelligence capabilities and sufficient strike assets.
At the same time, Ukraine will have to adapt to the new reality of round-the-clock air threats and attacks. It is impossible to live for months in a situation where every air-raid siren automatically means a complete halt to normal life. It needs a much more precise system for understanding where the danger actually exists and how immediate it is. Where life can safely continue, the country should keep working. Where there is an immediate threat, people should receive a clear warning and be able to move to shelters.
Kyiv has already introduced different levels of air-raid alert. The same principle applies not only to protection, but to active defense as well. This calls for the introduction of a range of countermeasures as new types of target appear. Air-defense effectiveness is not only about the number of targets destroyed but also the cost of interception.
If an attacking munition costs $10,000 while the defensive system used to destroy it costs $100,000, the engagement may be won but the overall economic race will be lost.
Electronic warfare is another critical element of this development. For example, BlueBird Tech is constantly improving its Hrets systems in close cooperation with the military to respond quickly, because tactics and technologies are changing every day. As long as electronic communications exist, there will be ways to detect, intercept, jam or protect against them. Even if some systems become autonomous, warfare will not become fully automated overnight.
In addition electronic warfare itself will gradually move toward greater automation. Systems will be able to analyze the electromagnetic spectrum independently, identify signals, determine their source and select an appropriate response. AI will be an integral part of the electronic warfare system itself.
However, it is important to understand that Russia will not stop with jet-powered drones. By the time we learn how to intercept them effectively, Moscow may already have the next iteration: cheaper weapons, greater numbers, new tactics or increased autonomy.
Ukraine’s task, therefore, is not simply to catch up with every new threat as it emerges. It is to build a system capable of adapting faster than the adversary – and staying one step ahead.

'Iron fist'

Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they are "one alliance and one body".
"Iran is a friendly, allied, and brotherly country to us, but it does not direct us. We are independent in our decisions and in our sovereignty," he said.

‘She’ll give birth before 18’: mother says northern community pushed daughter into underage marriage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:31:33 UTC
20:31:33 KST

“That’s my daughter,” Deborah, a 42-year-old mother from Bnei Brak, said as she pointed to a photograph taken during a police raid on an underage wedding in the northern Israeli town of Yavne’el.
Her daughter was 17 at the time. Deborah told the Knesset Committee on the Status of Women and Gender Equality on Wednesday that the marriage took place despite her repeated attempts to stop it and persuade her daughter to wait until she turned 18. The committee held a follow-up session on underage marriages in Yavne’el, an issue it has examined repeatedly in recent months.
Deborah said she traveled to Yavne’el with her younger daughter on the night of the wedding. Shortly after the bride sat down and began reciting the traditional bride’s prayer, police entered the house and took Deborah and her daughter for questioning. By the time they returned, Deborah said, she was being blamed for bringing the police to the wedding.
Her daughter and other relatives stopped speaking to her, she said, and the chuppah ceremony was eventually held after she left. “I never got to accompany my daughter to the chuppah,” Deborah told the committee. “To this day, she barely speaks to me.”
About two months after the wedding, her daughter became pregnant. “She never told me,” Deborah said. “Do you know how I found out? About three months into the pregnancy, I received an alert from the health fund because she was still a minor. She’ll give birth before she turns 18. To this day, she hasn’t told me she’s pregnant.”
Deborah told lawmakers that her former husband remarried shortly after their divorce and later moved to Yavne’el.
When their daughter was 16, she went to live with him. Within three months, Deborah said, the teenager was engaged to a man three years older than her. “I heard about the engagement from relatives,” she said. “She didn’t tell me.”
The engagement was initially broken off, but Deborah later found a letter her daughter had written to a rabbi describing how difficult it was for her to see the young man around town.
“She wrote that she didn’t like him,” Deborah said. “She signed the letter: ‘I wanted to hear the righteous man’s advice and accept upon myself whatever the righteous man tells me to do.’”
Not long afterward, Deborah said, her daughter became engaged to the same man again. “She didn’t tell me.”
Before the wedding date was set, Deborah said, her daughter spent a Shabbat with her. “I asked her to stay engaged, but continue living with me and wait until she was 18 and one day old,” she recalled. “But they refused. The wedding was set for her 17th birthday.”
Her daughter knew how strongly she opposed the marriage, Deborah said, but she also tried to make clear that her opposition would not change their relationship. “I kept telling her that she was my daughter, that I loved her and that I would be there for her no matter what.”
On the wedding night, Deborah and her younger daughter arrived in Yavne’el. “After my daughter sat in the bride’s chair, she began saying the bride’s prayer, and then police entered the house,” Deborah said.
“We were taken for questioning that lasted for hours at the Tiberias police station. I was the one who opposed the wedding, but I was accused of calling the police.”
When she returned to Yavne’el, she said, the atmosphere had changed completely. “From the moment we came back, I was totally ignored. My daughter and the family members acted as though I didn’t exist. I was trying to be there for her while also taking all the blame.”
After Deborah left, she said, the wedding ceremony went ahead. “They held the chuppah without me. I never got to walk my daughter to it.”
Deborah also sharply criticized the authorities’ response, arguing that responsibility did not rest with police alone. “There is also the welfare system, and its conduct in these cases is beyond criticism,” she said. “It makes no sense for social workers to send a girl home when she lies to them and says she isn’t getting married.”
She called for stronger intervention and for those involved in arranging underage marriages to face prosecution. “If the police do an excellent job, but when the evidence reaches prosecutors there are no indictments, then we haven’t done anything,” she said.
Police have carried out several operations in Yavne’el over suspected underage marriages. Earlier this month, officers detained 16 adults and minors suspected of having recently married or of preparing for illegal wedding ceremonies.
Committee chair MK Meirav Cohen said the cases exposed so far may represent only a fraction of the phenomenon. “We are seeing only the very tip of the iceberg,” Cohen said.
She said she had spoken with a woman who previously worked in Yavne’el’s education system and claimed that by around ninth grade, as many as 80% of girls in the community were already married.
“The message is that if you haven’t married, you’re strange, that something is wrong with you,” Cohen said, citing the woman’s account. The same allegation was raised publicly at Wednesday’s committee hearing.
Cohen also said she had heard allegations of sexual abuse involving young girls and described what she believed to be a wider system that enabled the marriages to continue.
“For something like this to happen, you need an entire mechanism of silence,” she said, listing nonprofits, educators, welfare officials, bridal instructors and wedding organizers.
Cohen criticized the head of the Yavne’el local council for refusing to attend the Knesset hearing with municipal employees, and accused local figures of enabling the practice.
“The boycott only tells us that we are moving in the right direction,” she said.
“The way to solve this is to dismantle this cult and stop ignoring a phenomenon that leaves these boys and girls with no way out. We will be there for those children.”

38 Global Civil Society Organizations file joint brief in US lawsuit challenging legality of Trump’s ICC sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:31:23 UTC
20:31:23 KST

The Trump administration’s escalating campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC) is reaching far beyond the judges, prosecutors, and human rights groups it has sanctioned, chilling civil society engagement with the Court and undermining victims’ access to justice, Amnesty International, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), and 36 other Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) said today.
We will not sit back and let President Trump destroy the Rome Statute
Agnès Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International
On 23 September 2026, 38 civil society groups jointly filed an amicus curiae (‘friend of the court’) brief with the US District Court for the Southern District of New York in support of a lawsuit filed by the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute, which challenges the legality of sanctions imposed under Executive Order (EO) 14203. The sanctions have targeted ICC prosecutors and judges, a UN human rights expert, and three Palestinian human rights groups.
“Behind every civil society organization being silenced or pushed away from the ICC are victims and survivors waiting for justice. These sanctions are disrupting the networks of people and organizations that stand with victims who bring their stories and evidence before the Court, and spreading fear far beyond those directly targeted,” said Alexis Deswaef, President of FIDH.
“For victims who have already been failed by justice at home, closing these pathways can mean losing one of their last chances for accountability.”
“As the Trump administration steps up its attacks on the ICC and the civil society organizations essential to its work, it is crucial to demonstrate to the US Federal Court how sanctions are harming global civil society, victims and survivors of crimes under international law, and the very idea of international justice,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“We will not sit back and let President Trump destroy the Rome Statute. The sheer number of civil society organizations submitting this brief demonstrates the resilience and determination of civil society to oppose the US sanctions and protect the ICC.”
The CSOs’ brief makes two fundamental arguments. First, the sanctions are fracturing civil society networks that are essential to the functioning of the ICC. CSOs and human rights defenders, including lawyers, victim representatives, and survivor-advocates, carry out a wide range of activities which the ICC depends on: connecting victims and witnesses to the Court; documenting atrocity crimes; supporting victim participation and reparations; contributing critical legal, contextual, and cultural expertise; and advancing state cooperation and domestic investigations and prosecutions, particularly in situation countries where the Court has limited access.
It is crucial to demonstrate to the US Federal Court how sanctions are harming the very idea of international justice
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
Second, by imposing and threatening draconian financial and legal penalties on CSOs and individual actors, EO 14203 violates their rights to freedom of expression and association and has severely damaged the collaboration and infrastructure upon which the international system of justice depends. EO 14203 has already caused the Designated Entities to lose funding, staff, banking access, and partnerships; deterred CSOs from engaging with the ICC; and fractured relationships between and among many CSOs. The result is measurable and irreparable harm not only to civil society, but to the ICC, to the administration of international criminal justice, and, ultimately, to the victims and survivors the system exists to serve.
Background
The 38 CSOs filing the brief are (alphabetical order):
1. Action for the Reform of Justice and Promotion of Human Rights (ARJPDH)
2. Amnesty International

"Not like any role before": Tom Cruise opens up about his new film from the Oscar-winning director
Kyiv • UNN
Tom Cruise said that his character in "Digger" is unlike any previous role. The film will be released worldwide on September 30.
Hollywood actor Tom Cruise called his character in the film "Digger" "absolutely incredible" and unlike any role he had encountered before. The movie star made the statement at the film’s world premiere in London on Tuesday, September 22, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
"He’s the kind of character who says things that some people think about, and some people can’t even imagine," the Hollywood star told Reuters.
"I have never read about a character like this. I have never read about a film like this," Cruise added.
The release of "Digger" was marked by a royal premiere attended by Britain’s Prince William and Princess Kate, following what actress Sandra Hüller described as nearly 10 years of work by Oscar-winning director Alejandro G. Iñárritu.
The film generated considerable anticipation after the trailer showed Cruise transforming into eccentric oil magnate Digger Rockwell, with gray hair, facial prosthetics and a soft jumpsuit.
Cruise said that this transformation was far from the most demanding aspect of the role, pointing instead to a 10-minute monologue filmed in a single take.
Hüller, the star of "Anatomy of a Fall," said it was "wonderful" to watch Cruise perform. "It feels as though everything he has learned during 46 years of acting has come together in this character," she added.
In the film, Rockwell inadvertently triggers an environmental catastrophe that pushes the world to the brink of nuclear war before he sets out to save the planet. But the filmmakers have revealed little about the story, fueling speculation about the plot and rumors that it could be a musical, which Cruise denied.
"If you watch the film without knowing anything about it, it’s much better than if you (knew) beforehand," Hüller said, adding that the secrecy was not intended to create intrigue for its own sake.
Although Cruise described the story as an exploration of "power and greed... responsibility and irresponsibility," Australian actress Sophie Wilde said it also contains a message that art is a "vessel for catharsis."
Iñárritu, whose previous works include "Birdman" and "The Revenant," compared the process of making "Digger" to painting, saying that every shot was carefully created to immerse viewers in the film’s world.
For Emma D’Arcy, this attention to detail made working with the Mexican director feel like being part of an orchestra led by a conductor. "In "Digger," musicality was really, really important... it’s a comedy, so rhythm is kind of key," they noted.
Michael Stuhlbarg, the star of "Call Me by Your Name," recalled scenes that kept evolving during filming, with new dialogue, alternative versions and unexpected additions emerging day by day.
The actor joked that so much unusual material had been filmed that he hoped a DVD with additional production footage would be released one day.
"It was a lot of fun," he said.
"Digger" will begin its worldwide theatrical release on September 30 and will be released in cinemas in the United States and the United Kingdom on October 2.

Netanyahu calls Macron's remarks on West Bank in UN speech 'grotesque'
- Published
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank during his address to the UN General Assembly.
"Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," Macron said in French, according to the UN's interpreter.
Netanyahu called the remarks a "grotesque absurdity" and said members of the Palestinian armed group there "carry out attacks against Jews almost every day".
There was no response from Macron's office, but one French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation".
The source told the Jerusalem Post, external that the meaning of the French sentence spoken by the president, "Le Hamas n'a jamais sévi en Cisjordanie," was, "Hamas has never governed the West Bank."
Macron also rejected US President Donald Trump's assertion that he had ended the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Violence there has continued despite last October's ceasefire, including almost daily Israeli strikes, while humanitarian conditions remain dire
"Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second," he said. "Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?"
After the address, the Israeli prime minister's office said in a statement: "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering."
"On Sunday, the eve of [the Jewish holy day of] Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun - a French citizen and father of six - was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria," it added, using a biblical term for the West Bank.
"Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria."
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, also denounced Macron's remarks as "out of touch with reality".
Shukrun, 36, was shot dead when a Palestinian opened fire on a group of Israelis at a spring near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, according to Israeli police. The suspect was arrested later at a hospital in the city of Ramallah, they said.
Hamas praised the attack but did not say it was behind it.
The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, France and other countries - is a rival of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank that are not under Israeli control.
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
The settlements are illegal under international law.

UK to revisit Chagos Islands deal after Trump rejects terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:30:56 UTC
20:30:56 KST

Aysu Bicer
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
 Britain is set to take another look at its agreement to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, after US President Donald Trump made clear that he does not support the deal in its current form.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC on Wednesday that Washington’s position became clear following Trump’s description of the agreement as a “terrible deal” during talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York.
Under the agreement negotiated by former Premier Keir Starmer’s government, Mauritius would take sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago, while Britain would pay about £101 million ($136 million) a year on average to retain access to the joint UK-US military facility on Diego Garcia.
The arrangement was put on hold indefinitely in April after Trump withdrew his backing. Streeting said the government would now work with the US to alter the agreement sufficiently to secure its support.
“We have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it,” he said.
The future of Diego Garcia is at the center of the dispute. Britain has maintained that uncertainty over the island’s sovereignty could threaten the long-term security of the base.
Mauritius disputes the existing territorial settlement, arguing that it was compelled to surrender the islands in 1965 as part of the process leading to independence.
Starmer said he had “inherited the situation” and that a resolution was needed, stressing the importance of protecting the base.
The government is not expected to launch a formal review with a fixed timetable. According to the BBC, officials have indicated that the fundamental position remains unchanged: any final agreement would need the backing of the United States.

As of September 23, Ukrainian farmers had sown 741,400 hectares with winter grain crops, or 14.2% of the projected area, and 958,800 hectares with winter rapeseed, or 86.7% of the projected area, the press service of the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food said.

Earlier strike on Russian drone site

SANAA – A Houthi military adviser told AFP that the group would attack US interests in the Middle East if Washington intervenes in Yemen’s conflict in support of Saudi Arabia or tries to unblock the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Iran-backed Houthis seized control of the narrow shipping lane, gateway to the Red Sea, in September, while Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested American and international military assistance against them.
“If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab el-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else... we will fight over it,” military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr told AFP in an exclusive interview.
The Houthi blockade has shaken Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, which was already hit by Tehran’s stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz as part of its war with the US.
The pro-Iran Houthis dislodged Saudi-backed government forces from Yemen’s Red Sea coast in fighting that left hundreds dead.
Houthi drones and missiles have also targeted Saudi sites, including the capital Riyadh, for the first time in years.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested help from US President Donald Trump in fighting the Houthis, according to US reports.
Yemen’s government also made the request, a well-placed source told AFP.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since fighting resumed in July, effectively ending a four-year truce.
“If America gambles on supporting Saudi Arabia with air strikes or air support... We will consider any American interests around us to be targets and we will not exclude anything,” Thawr told AFP, adding that they will “close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships”.
While the Yemen civil war predates the US-Iran war by years, renewed fighting in Yemen pits allies of Washington and Tehran against each other while the two foes are in a stalemate in the Gulf.
Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they are “one alliance and one body”.
“Iran is a friendly, allied and brotherly country to us, but it does not direct us. We are independent in our decisions and in our sovereignty,” he said.
The UN on Sept 22 said the number of people displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.
“As long as Saudi Arabia insists on and continues killing our country and striking our people, we will strike with an iron fist,” Thawr said.
“We possess sufficient capability to discipline Saudi Arabia, punish it and force it out of the game in the fields of oil and the economy.” AFP

China’s storage makers aim to climb value chain with advanced packaging bets
Biwin Storage Technology invests US$672 million in latest example of a storage firm looking to upgrade its business model
Chinese storage makers, long known for packaging chips into modules, have been moving up the value chain into wafer-level operations, with the latest firm to make the jump investing 4.5 billion yuan (US$672 million) in an advanced packaging project.
The sum, which Shanghai-listed Biwin Storage Technology will pour into the third phase of its advanced packaging and testing project in Dongguan, in southern China’s Guangdong province, will exceed the 3.09 billion yuan it put into the first two phases combined.
The project, including the first two phases, had yet to generate mass production revenue, as it was still undergoing customer sampling, process verification and small-batch production, according to Biwin’s stock filing on Tuesday. The company estimated that the facility’s monthly capacity would more than triple to 10,000 wafers by the end of 2027, according to the filing and earlier investor meetings.
The gamble marks a move into more sophisticated wafer-level technologies, as Biwin already operates a traditional memory and system-in-package, or SiP, packaging base in Huizhou, also in Guangdong, where it sources chips from external suppliers.

Roundup: Chinese mainland welcomes more discussion from Taiwan on reunification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:28:47 CST
20:28:47 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland welcomes more discussion in Taiwan on national reunification and is willing to conduct broad and in-depth democratic consultations with people from various sectors on the island on relations across the Taiwan Strait and the future of the Chinese nation, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a regular press conference when commenting on a recent article by a Taiwan scholar suggesting that the mainland should explore ways to end hostility and build mutual trust across the Taiwan Strait before reunification.
The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China (PRC) was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Zhu said that peaceful reunification and "one country, two systems" remain the basic policy for resolving the Taiwan question and the best way to achieve national reunification.
She said the Taiwan plan under a proposed "one country, two systems" framework would fully take into account Taiwan's realities, absorb opinions and suggestions from people on both sides of the Strait, and consider the interests and feelings of Taiwan compatriots.
"On the common political basis of adhering to the 1992 Consensus and opposing 'Taiwan independence,' we are willing to carry out broad and in-depth democratic consultations with political parties, groups and people from all sectors in Taiwan on cross-Strait relations and the future of the Chinese nation," Zhu said.
She added that the mainland welcomes suggestions from Taiwan compatriots on advancing national reunification, saying that earlier and broader discussions on reunification could create more opportunities for Taiwan's economic and social development and bring more tangible benefits to Taiwan compatriots.
Her remarks came as a recent annual survey on cross-Strait relations in Taiwan showed that more than 60 percent of respondents supported continuing cross-Strait exchange platforms, expanding tourist exchanges and increasing exchanges in areas such as film, arts and sports.
Zhu said the findings demonstrated that peace, development, exchanges and cooperation remain the mainstream public opinion in Taiwan and a broad consensus among different sectors in Taiwan.
She said the mainland will continue to uphold the principle that people on both sides of the Strait are one family, roll out more policies and measures benefiting Taiwan compatriots, strengthen institutional support for cross-Strait integrated development, and promote personnel exchanges and cooperation in various fields.
Separately, Zhu said the mainland would continue to promote cross-Strait economic exchanges and cooperation so that people on both sides of the Strait can share the benefits of peaceful and integrated development of cross-Strait relations.
She noted that relevant parties on both sides have been working to implement 10 policy measures announced by the mainland in April to promote cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation, helping more Taiwan farmers and fishermen expand into the mainland market.
According to Zhu, multiple Taiwan packaging plants, orchards and food enterprises have been registered on the mainland, while customs clearance efficiency has improved and logistics have become more convenient.
On transportation links, Zhu said direct cross-Strait passenger air services have yet to fully return to normal due to obstruction and interference by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities.
From January to August this year, 4.22 million passenger trips were made on direct cross-Strait flights, up 12.9 percent year on year, reflecting strong market demand and a strong desire for exchanges among people on both sides of the Strait, Zhu said.
She called on the Taiwan side to remove unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transportation and allow airlines on both sides to arrange flights based on market demand.
Commenting on the annual Shanghai-Taipei City Forum, Zhu described it as an important platform for city-to-city exchanges across the Strait and said both cities had remained in communication over arrangements for this year's event.
The forum, which has been held for 16 consecutive years, has developed well-established practices and is expected to proceed as scheduled this year, she said.
In response to recent remarks by Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te on increasing Taiwan's "defense spending" to "safeguard peace through strength," Zhu reiterated the mainland's position that there is only one China in the world and Taiwan is part of China.
She said the DPP authorities' stubborn pursuit of "Taiwan independence," deliberate escalation of confrontation across the Taiwan Strait, and attempts to seek "Taiwan independence" through military means and external support make them the chief culprit in undermining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
No matter how much is spent on military budgets or weapons purchases, Zhu said, it cannot change the historical trend toward national reunification. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Al-Attiyah adds Asian Games shooting gold to sixth Dakar Rally title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:28:44 CST
20:28:44 KST

by sportswriters Lin Deren and Liang Chen
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Six-time Dakar Rally champion Nasser Al-Attiyah added another title to his remarkable sporting career on Wednesday, helping Qatar win the men's skeet team gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
The 55-year-old, who claimed his sixth Dakar Rally title in January, secured his third Asian Games gold medal and sixth shooting medal overall, 32 years after making his debut at the 1994 Hiroshima Games.
"To start from the Hiroshima Asian Games and to come back here again, and today for our team to win two gold medals, is really amazing," Al-Attiyah said.
Despite having just two months to prepare for the Games because of his rallying commitments, Al-Attiyah hit 120 of 125 targets in qualification, posting one of the day's three highest scores. He qualified third for the individual final but finished fifth.
"My performance was really very good and strong," he said. "I made a very high score, one of the highest scores in the field."
"Motorsport is very important to me, but when it comes to the Asian Games or the Olympic Games, I put everything into it and try to achieve the best result."
Al-Attiyah made his Asian Games debut in Hiroshima in 1994, finishing 17th in men's skeet. He subsequently won team gold medals at Busan 2002 and Guangzhou 2010 before claiming team silver and individual bronze at Hangzhou 2023.
His international shooting career stretches back even further. Having taken up the sport in 1993, he qualified for his first Olympics at Atlanta 1996 and went on to compete at six consecutive Games.
He finished sixth at Sydney 2000 and fourth at Athens 2004 before finally reaching the Olympic podium at London 2012, where he won bronze in men's skeet at the age of 41.
Alongside his shooting career, Al-Attiyah has established himself as one of rallying's leading competitors.
He made his Dakar Rally debut in 2004 and narrowly missed out on the title in 2010 before securing his first victory in the car category the following year.
In January, he claimed his sixth Dakar crown after holding the overall lead throughout the final four days of the 13-day event.
While shooting and rallying demand different skills, Al-Attiyah believes his involvement in both sports has helped him maintain his competitive edge.
"They work together," he told Xinhua.
"Shooting helps me a lot in rallying, and rallying also helps me a lot in shooting, especially in making me mentally stronger, so I love both sports."
Despite competing against athletes considerably younger than himself, Al-Attiyah believes experience remains one of his greatest assets.
"I'm still strong," he said. "My advantage is experience."
Having last competed at the Olympics in Rio de Janeiro in 2016, Al-Attiyah is now targeting a seventh appearance at Los Angeles 2028.
"The World Championship will be in Qatar, and there will also be quota places for the next Olympic Games," he said.
Should he qualify, his Olympic career would span 32 years, from Atlanta 1996 to Los Angeles 2028, another milestone in a sporting career that has taken him from Olympic shooting ranges to the deserts of the Dakar Rally. ■

Morocco goes to polls in legislative elections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:28:44 CST
20:28:44 KST

RABAT, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Polling stations opened on Wednesday morning across Morocco for legislative elections to renew the 395 members of the House of Representatives, parliament's lower house.
Voting is scheduled to run until 7:00 p.m. local time (1900 GMT), and approximately 15.8 million voters are expected to cast ballots.
Of the 395-seat House of Representatives, 305 are contested through local electoral constituencies, while the remaining 90 are allocated exclusively to women through regional lists.
According to the Interior Ministry, a total of 7,288 candidates registered nationwide, representing 28 political groups in the election.
Women account for 2,658 of the candidates registered for the election, representing 36.47 percent of the total, it added.
Morocco has a bicameral parliament consisting of the House of Representatives and the House of Councilors. The 2026 election will determine the members of Morocco's House of Representatives across the country's 12 regions. The election of the House of Councilors is scheduled for 2027.
The major parties in the election are the National Rally of Independents, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, and the Istiqlal Party, which formed the outgoing government.
They will compete alongside the Justice and Development Party, which led coalition governments following the 2011 and 2016 general elections, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Popular Movement, and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
Under the constitution, Morocco's king appoints the prime minister from the party that wins the most seats, which then forms a government. ■

PARIS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Global economic growth is projected to be 2.9 percent in 2026 and 3.0 percent in 2027, according to the Economic Outlook Interim Report released by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.
Growth in the advanced G20 economies, as well as in the G20 emerging-market economies, is projected to remain broadly stable, the report said.
G20 headline inflation is expected to rise from 3.4 percent in 2025 to 4.1 percent in 2026, before easing to 3.6 percent in 2027, according to the report.
In the advanced G20 economies, headline inflation is projected to rise from 2.5 percent in 2025 to 3.2 percent in 2026, before falling to 2.6 percent in 2027, while in emerging-market G20 economies it is expected to increase from 4.1 percent to 4.8 percent before easing to 4.3 percent.
The OECD noted that the projections are based on a technical assumption that Brent crude prices and TTF gas prices will peak in the fourth quarter of 2026 and then decline steadily through the end of 2027.
The assumed Brent crude price path is broadly consistent with the "short disruption" scenario in the OECD's June 2026 Economic Outlook, while the assumed gas price path is about 60 percent higher.
Persistent uncertainty over the evolution of the conflict in the Middle East remains a key risk to the baseline projections, the OECD warned, adding that constraints on exports through the Strait of Hormuz, additional disruptions to alternative export routes such as the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, or further significant damage to energy production facilities in the region could prompt a further sustained rise in energy prices and potentially lead to shortages of key commodities, particularly in net importing countries.
Low European gas reserves and uncertain scope for sustained further reductions in oil inventories in some countries could exacerbate supply disruption risks.
"Further monetary policy rate adjustments may be needed," the OECD said, noting that faced with renewed energy price shocks, stronger-than-expected demand pressures, and above-target inflation in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained.
The OECD also called for further structural policy reforms to help economies cope with future supply shocks, including diversifying energy supply, improving energy efficiency, enhancing product and labor market adjustment, and ensuring workers have adaptable skills. ■

Roundup: Türkiye moves to contain fallout from investment fund turmoil
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:28:27 CST
20:28:27 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye is taking a series of measures to contain the fallout from a major investment fund crisis that has triggered a sharp stock market sell-off, fund liquidations and a widening investigation.
The developments have raised concerns among nearly half a million investors and prompted high-profile arrests.
The full scale of the investor base affected by the liquidation became clearer on Wednesday. The country's Capital Markets Board (SPK) said 455,758 unique investors were registered in the 131 funds involved in the crisis.
The funds, managed by seven portfolio management companies, were ordered to be liquidated on Sept. 17.
The SPK urged investors to rely solely on official statements amid conflicting reports, stressing its commitment to protecting investor rights and maintaining confidence in the capital markets.
The crisis stems from alleged stock market manipulation that created the appearance of rapid and substantial gains, attracting retail investors.
Resat Yilmaz, a gold trader and financial expert at Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, highlighted the devastating consequences for retail investors.
"The number of victims is truly very high. We witnessed shares intrinsically worth 5 liras (about 0.1 U.S. dollars) suddenly pumped to 500 liras through aggressive manipulation," Yilmaz told Xinhua.
Investors were trapped when the scheme eventually collapsed, he said. "The financial cost to these small retail investors has been devastating."
Yilmaz warned of broader macroeconomic consequences, particularly the flight of foreign investment.
"Developing countries like ours rely heavily on foreign capital. The panic and manipulation we witnessed create significant hurdles for foreign investors. This is a very painful period for our national market," he said.
However, Yilmaz expressed confidence that the Turkish authorities would implement strict regulatory measures to restore market trust.
Regulators extended the liquidation period for the affected funds from three to six months, citing the funds' portfolio structures and market conditions and allowing their assets to be sold under more favorable conditions.
Clarifying this process, capital markets lawyer Yalcin Ozge Okat explained that fund liquidation differs from a standard corporate bankruptcy.
Speaking to a local broadcaster, Okat noted that the process involves selling off the funds' assets, calculating debts and receivables, and distributing the remaining balance to investors.
He said investors' legal rights remain intact, though exact payment timelines depend on forthcoming SPK regulations.
The liquidation process comes as a criminal investigation widens following a sharp sell-off on Borsa Istanbul last week. The benchmark BIST 100 index plunged more than 7.5 percent at one point, sparking concerns over market stability.
In recent days, Turkish authorities have detained or arrested dozens of suspects, including high-ranking fund management executives.
Authorities have also frozen assets, imposed travel restrictions and blocked social media accounts as part of the investigation into suspected illicit gains. ■

Economic Watch: Pinglu Canal boosts China-ASEAN connectivity, win-win cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:27:59 CST
20:27:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Using the newly opened Pinglu Canal, a cargo ship carrying potassium fertilizer from Laos arrived at a plant in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region five to seven days sooner than using traditional routes.
Using the same canal, 3.1 tonnes of Guangxi specialty tea arrived in Vietnam in a much shorter time, cutting hundreds of kilometers off the journey and eliminating multiple transfer, waiting and loading procedures.
The 134.2-kilometer canal, stretching from Hengzhou in Guangxi to the Beibu Gulf, opened on Sept. 16. It is the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
"Steel and machinery equipment from southwest China including Yunnan, Guizhou, Sichuan and Chongqing can now reach ASEAN markets more easily through the Pinglu Canal, while ASEAN products can also flow more efficiently into China's vast domestic market," said Du Jianjun, chairman of China Railway Eryuan Engineering Group.
For instance, the new waterway will significantly cut logistics costs for Thai goods entering China -- including computers, fruits and rubber products -- allowing them to reach consumers in southwestern China faster than ever before. Philippine exporters of fresh fruit and seafood with short shelf lives stand to benefit too, as the canal cuts transit times and improves delivery efficiency.
The Pinglu Canal will help further boost trade growth between ASEAN and China, said Ngeow Chow Bing, director of the Institute of China Studies at University of Malaya.
China and ASEAN have been each other's largest trading partner for years. Bilateral trade surpassed 1 trillion U.S. dollars for the first time in 2025, reaching 1.05 trillion U.S. dollars. In the first eight months of this year, bilateral trade totaled 862.75 billion U.S. dollars, up 25.6 percent year on year.
On the very day the canal opened, a cargo ship carrying knock-down (KD) vehicle kits from Dongfeng Liuzhou Motor passed through the waterway bound for an assembly line in Cambodia.
Describing the canal as a golden corridor, Liu Xiaoping, an executive of Dongfeng Liuzhou, said the company will incorporate the canal into its regular export logistics system.
Official data showed intermediate goods now account for two thirds of bilateral trade between China and ASEAN. The two sides are moving beyond simple "buying and selling" to building shared industrial ecosystems.
As intermediate goods and processed products move more efficiently, China's relationship with ASEAN is shifting toward a production partnership, said Zhou Yamin, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, noting that the change will significantly promote regional economic integration.
Experts said the canal's long-term significance lies not just in what it transports, but in what it will attract in the future. As logistics costs fall, new investment is expected to flow into industries related to the canal, including warehousing, processing, cold chain and industrial parks. Capital, technology, talent and labor from southwestern China and ASEAN will converge to spur growth and generate new employment.
The canal's opening comes at a moment of steady development of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (FTA).
The Version 1.0 of the FTA was fully established in 2010, with zero tariffs on more than 90 percent of goods. A subsequent Version 2.0 protocol took full effect in 2019, expanding services and investment access. In October 2025, a 3.0 Upgrade Protocol was signed, extending cooperation into digital trade, green economy, standards and supply chains.
Against that backdrop, the Pinglu Canal is more than a feat of engineering. Experts said it is the physical expression of decades of deepening economic ties and the artery through which the next chapter of China-ASEAN win-win cooperation will flow. ■

Industry: Defense contractor funding could be more transparent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:27:00 UTC
20:27:00 KST

Industry: Defense contractor funding could be more transparent
Estonia is spending €100 million a year on defense products for Ukraine, but the companies receiving the funding and the basis for selecting them remain unclear.
The Defense Week defense industry trade fair is being held in Tallinn for the second year. A third of the participants are Estonian companies, many of whose products have been used in Ukraine for years. The companies will not say whether the state has funded their products; that information is classified.
Each year, the state provides €100 million in funding for products proposed by Estonian companies, deemed necessary by Ukraine and approved by the Ministry of Defense and the Estonian Center for Defense Investments. The question is: On what basis were they approved?
"Overall, we can be satisfied with the criteria. As for how the decision-making process works, I can't say. It would certainly be good to know how decisions are made so that companies can prepare for future projects," said Kalev Koidumäe, executive director of the Estonian Defense and Aerospace Industry Association.
"The Ministry of Defense knows precisely what was bought from whom and where it went. There are no questions in that regard. In light of recent days, it should also be fairly clear why the identities of those companies are being withheld. Do I plan to do anything about that or change it? Not at this point," Defense Minister Martin Herem said.
Urmas Reinsalu, chairman of Isamaa, said the secrecy is unjustified, particularly after the decisions have been made.
"The [Riigikogu] State Budget Control Select Committee has repeatedly requested the documents showing how the funds were actually distributed among companies. But we have not received them," Reinsalu said.
Peeter Tali (Eesti 200), chairman of the Riigikogu National Defense Committee, also does not know how the money was distributed. He said the committee would examine whether it went to companies that manufacture their own products and test them in Ukraine.
"That allows them to improve and develop their products under wartime conditions. We have that expertise here. If we need to, we can produce for our own use. That was the political intent. Now we probably need to look into whether that intent has become reality or whether this is simply business," Tali said.
The National Audit Office did not examine the transactions in detail in its completed audit and cannot say what grounds there are for classifying the information.
"I want to emphasize that information cannot always be classified in its entirety. Some aspects may be classified and must be redacted and withheld from the public. But that does not prevent officials from discussing the overall framework of the project and the selection criteria publicly," said Ines Metsalu-Nurminen, a principal auditor at the National Audit Office.
Estonia's defense industry had revenue of €750 million last year. Two-thirds came from exports.

====================================================================================================

33 years since Oslo: Shimon Peres has no heir, and Israel is paying the price - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:26:50 UTC
20:26:50 KST

This month brings together two dates that call for Israeli soul-searching: the 33rd anniversary of the signing of the Oslo Accords, and the 10th anniversary of the death of the man who brought them about, Shimon Peres. More than three decades on, it has become easy - even fashionable - to deride the accord, but hard to admit that no real alternative to the logic of Oslo has yet been found.
The collapse of Oslo resulted from a destructive combination: Hamas terrorism, the impotence of the Palestinian leadership, the settlement enterprise that tripled the number of Jews living in the West Bank, and right-wing governments that preferred to strengthen Hamas rather than the Palestinian Authority. Yet the failure of the process does not disprove the logic at its core.
Oslo’s logic was Zionist and realistic. It was neither an act of moral atonement toward the Palestinians nor naïve wishful thinking. Peres sought to address an existential challenge: if Israel wishes to remain both Jewish and democratic, it cannot permanently rule over millions of Palestinians. The division of the land therefore serves Israel's interests in terms of demography, identity, security, and geopolitical standing. Tellingly, Peres did not initially regard an independent Palestinian state as the preferred solution. For years, he advocated either a Jordanian option or a confederative arrangement. It is no coincidence that the term "Palestinian state" does not appear in the original Oslo Accords.
The October 7 massacre deeply - and justifiably - shook the public's trust in a Palestinian partner. Yet the enormity of the disaster does not exempt us from deciding our own future. To that end, we must separate two questions: what should Israel's permanent borders be, and what should be the character of the entity beyond them? The first requires urgent resolution, the second can wait.
Israel's borders and what lies beyond
Israel cannot remain indefinitely without a recognized eastern border. The absence of a border prevents the formulation of a coherent national strategy, hinders the normalization of Israeli life, and damages the country’s regional and international standing. In this context, a distinction must be made between the sovereignty border and the security border: the former should ensure a Jewish majority and democracy, while the latter should allow security control up to the Jordan River for as long as circumstances require it.
As for the route of a permanent border, there is no room for illusions. The 1967 lines will remain the baseline of any internationally accepted agreement, with land swaps. But Israel cannot assume that the terms available to it today will remain available indefinitely. Under less favorable circumstances, it could face growing pressure to accept a border far closer to the 1967 lines, with less accommodation for the major settlement blocs and Israel's security needs.
That is what makes the present moment so consequential. Trends in the United States offer no guarantee that the exceptional level of support Israel has enjoyed will continue indefinitely. Donald Trump's presidency therefore presents a historic opportunity that may not return: to secure American, Arab, and broader international acceptance of a permanent eastern border on the most favorable terms Israel can realistically expect. Such a border would keep the major settlement blocs under Israeli sovereignty and give substantial weight to Israel's security requirements.
Trump has demonstrated an ability to break diplomatic conventions and enlist Arab states. With American backing and by leveraging the Arab Peace Initiative, it may be possible to pursue an international resolution that enshrines Israel’s permanent borders without, at this stage, determining the political character of the entity beyond them. Such a move could pave the way for expansion of the Abraham Accords, peace with Saudi Arabia, new economic opportunities, and the weakening of Iran.
Setting a sovereignty border would not constitute a security withdrawal, nor would it determine whether the territory beyond it would become a confederation with Jordan, a demilitarized Palestinian state, or another political framework. The status of Jerusalem's Holy Basin could likewise be deferred to future negotiations.
Once a sovereignty border is established, the incentive to "create facts on the ground" would diminish, because the territory's fate would already be sealed. There would be little reason to invest in infrastructure or expand settlements in areas that will not fall under Israeli sovereignty.
Over time, this reality will lead a growing number of settlers to move voluntarily back into sovereign Israel. The proposed course - which is first and foremost the realization of an Israeli interest - will at the same time strengthen those Palestinians who seek compromise, because they will see a credible horizon capable of replacing despair with hope.
Ten years after the death of Shimon Peres, Israel does not need to return to the Oslo of 1993, but rather to the logic that underpinned Peres’s initiative: securing Israel’s future as a Jewish and democratic state requires the division of the land. This objective should be pursued from a position of military strength and clear-eyed realism regarding the other side.
The relevant question today is not, "A Palestinian state: yes or no?" but rather, "Permanent borders for Israel: yes or no?" Perhaps President Trump, for reasons of his own, will ultimately answer this question for us and lead the country toward permanent borders. Or perhaps he will lose interest in the vision of regional peace he once championed.
Either way, the likelihood that such a move will emerge from within Israel itself appears slim, because it would require a leader who does not currently exist: one willing to fight for a political alternative to occupation without shame and without apology. Indeed, a look at those competing to lead Israel makes one conclusion difficult to avoid: Shimon Peres has no heir.
The writer is a former director-general of the Foreign Ministry. His latest book, The Leviathan Option: A Deep State Story, is available on Amazon.

ADL launches research, resource hub for online pathways to youth violence, extremism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:26:41 UTC
20:26:41 KST

The Anti-Defamation League Center on Extremism launched a new research and resource hub on Wednesday. It is intended to monitor online communities that influence young people to engage in targeted and mass violence.
The initiative focuses on digital spaces that glorify mass shooters and killers, which the ADL says contribute to the normalization and desensitization of violent content.
These spaces include gore forums, sextortion networks, and self-harm groups such as the transnational network known as “The Com” and its prominent sub-group 764, the ADL said.
It said The Com operates across four primary spheres: Extortion Com, which focuses on sexual exploitation and child sexual-abuse material; Anti-Extortion Com; Offline Com, which focuses on physical attacks such as stabbings and arson; and Cyber Com, which specializes in hacking and swatting.
These networks operate as pipelines that turn vulnerable youth into victims, perpetrators, or both through a subculture called the True Crime Community (TCC), which is built around a fascination with violent criminals, the ADL said.
“These online communities are hateful, violent, and dangerous pipelines that reward cruelty with status and turn vulnerable children and young adults into either victims or perpetrators, and sometimes both,” said Jonathan Greenblatt, the ADL chief executive officer and national director.
ADL hub provides TCC attack map, online slang guide
The ADL said it had been tracking and analyzing online propaganda, digital footprints, visual aesthetics, and real-world incidents connected to these networks since 2024.
The hub features interactive tools such as a global TCC attacks map, a memetic violence field guide that decodes online slang and symbols, and behavioral threat assessment and management (BTAM) guidance for parents, educators, and law enforcement, it said.
BTAM is presented as an early intervention framework designed to help schools, workplaces, and professionals distinguish between individuals who merely make angry statements and those who genuinely pose a threat by exhibiting recognizable warning signs such as grievance, ideation, planning, and preparation.
Through its monitoring efforts, the ADL Center on Extremism reported contributing to at least 16 arrests globally since 2024 by flagging potential threats to law enforcement.
Antisemitism is deeply embedded in the culture of The Com and 764, the ADL reported. Anti-Jewish hate manifests through online propaganda, screen names, swatting campaigns against Jewish institutions, and physical violence, which are all utilized by members seeking status and notoriety within the network, the ADL said.
As examples, it cited a 764 member who live-streamed the fatal stabbing of an elderly woman he suspected of having Jewish or Roma ancestry, groups claiming credit for swatting hoaxes at synagogues in Florida, and abusers coercing victims into carving swastikas into their skin or writing antisemitic messages in blood.
The ADL’s research detailed how these digital networks operate across popular platforms such as Discord, TikTok, Roblox, and Telegram, utilizing a social hierarchy in which actors compete for notoriety through increasingly extreme acts.
Within these spaces, abusers employ tactics such as compiling “lorebooks” containing compromising personal data to blackmail victims, alongside forcing targets to create “cut signs” by carving names into their skin or “blood walls” to demonstrate submission, the ADL reported.
Online ecosystems lead to footage of mass shootings, terror propaganda
Furthermore, the report connected these ecosystems to gore forums such as WatchPeopleDie (WPD), a site with more than 5.5 million registered users that is part of the Marsey Network and serves as a hosting ground for mass-shooting footage, terrorist propaganda, and gamified features such as the “Marseypass.”
“The online spaces that promote hate and glorify violence do not stay online; they fuel and animate acts of violence, posing one of the greatest threats we face to children, targeted communities, and our society as a whole,” said Oren Segal, the ADL’s senior vice president for counter-extremism and intelligence.
To address these threats, the ADL outlined several recommendations. It called on federal and state lawmakers to expand investments in community-based violence prevention programs, increase funding for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, and pass legislation that holds technology platforms accountable for the spread of extremist content through improved transparency and cross-platform reporting safeguards.
The ADL said it plans to share its findings with state attorneys general and district attorneys to encourage the enforcement of relevant laws.

Greenland's government and residents expressed relief that a military pact with the US and Denmark may end anxiety over US President Donald Trump's threats to seize their Arctic island, but many remain distrustful of Washington.

But it stopped short of Trump's unsettling previous demand that the US annex Greenland to head off the growing Arctic presence of Russia and China.
"There has previously been a significant American presence in Greenland, so this is nothing new," added Nathanielsen. "However, in light of the unrest over the past few years, there is likely greater skepticism in Greenland, and consequently, work needs to be done to reassure the local population."
US to potentially reopen military bases in Greenland
The US first built military bases in Greenland during World War Two. During the Cold War, it maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel to monitor Soviet forces. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 US military personnel.
Pitanguaq Mikissen, 69, a retired ship assistant, said the potential reopening of some old US bases gave greater security to the territory's 57,000 people.
But not all residents were happy.
"I think that Trump is really good at creating a lot of worry and a lot of fear," said Jensia Dam-Davidsen, 40, a voice and choir teacher.
"It (the deal) seems wrong in every way – especially now that Denmark has expanded their military presence here."
Denmark has significantly increased its own military footprint in Greenland since Trump's threats peaked in January, deploying additional troops, boosting Arctic defense spending and hosting allies under military exercises.
US must respect Greenlandic way of life in new agreement
Malene Vahl Rasmussen, mayor of Kujalleq municipality in southern Greenland, where the US is looking to reopen the Narsasuaq military base, said that under the agreement US military expansion must respect the Greenlandic way of life to protect hunting and fishing.
"You can't simply say, 'Okay, we’ve signed this, so now we trust you again'. Trust really needs to be rebuilt within that partnership," she told Reuters.
Some Greenlanders worry that expanded military activity - including increased aircraft and vessel movement - could disrupt hunting and fishing grounds that communities rely on for a living, though the agreement states such activity must respect Greenlandic society and traditional ways of life.

Eisenkot’s silence is no longer enough to win over Israeli voters - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

20:25:57 KST

The Israeli campaign conversation has shifted abruptly – and will probably keep shifting. As the anti-Bibi forces sag, fears of deadlock grow. Strategists in Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar should be more nimble. Weary of Bibi and his vipers, but wary of voting for a Will-o’-the-Wisp, Israelis want a strong, effective unifying leader.
The empty posturing around the movie NAZA, using 24 anonymous malcontents – from over 300,000 soldiers – to libel a nation 10 million strong – revealed why both major parties barely attract 20% of Israel’s dangerously balkanized electorate. Netanyahu and his Rottweilers enjoyed snarling, posturing, and sacrificing Israeli democracy while pretending to defend it.
Responding to an insignificant, sloppy, one-sided film by canceling the filmmakers’ citizenship is fighting a cold with chemotherapy. This counterproductive defense threatens the body politic.
The hysteria publicizes the film unnecessarily. Overreacting encourages the liars claiming Israel has turned authoritarian. And the empty threat violates a core democratic value, treating free speech as a one-way street, not a robust, noisy, occasionally hazardous superhighway. If our haters worldwide mimicked that “freedom for me but not for thee” principle, people like me would be silenced when celebrating Israel, Zionism, Jewish pride, and Western values. (Admittedly, these useful idiot critics are also self-sabotaging, emboldening Netanyahu and his followers while claiming to oppose them, but blind hatred usually backfires).
Polling estimates the Likud at 18 to 24 seats – a stunning fall from its 32 seats in November 2022. That repudiation speaks well for the Israeli people. They’re not friers – pushovers. Trash-talking two turncoat filmmakers and the Stalinist fools who applauded them for 25 virtue signaling minutes – no matter how well-deserved – doesn’t compensate for this polarizing, incompetent, endlessly appalling government.
True, I have repeatedly acknowledged this government’s (and the army’s) effectiveness in smiting so many enemies after October 7 and performing the improbable feat of accounting for every hostage and bringing 168 home alive. But it’s as juvenile to say the government could do no right as to say the government – or Netanyahu – can do no wrong.
Nevertheless, for four-of-five Israelis, those achievements cannot obscure the October 7 debacle, the refusal to learn from that catastrophe with a proper commission, the mishandled judicial reform’s divisiveness, the haredim (ultra-Orthodox) making reservists feel exploited, the cost of living spiking, the Arab murder rate tripling, vigilantism by an easily controlled minority going unchecked in the territories, and the relentless assaults on internal rivals, democratic norms, and Israel’s reputation worldwide.
Naturally, in their take-no-prisoners approach to rivals, Bibi’s lapdogs and their right-wing echo chambers claimed Gad Eisenkot didn’t condemn the NAZA film. Not true!
@gadi_eisenkot tweeted a defense of Israel’s fighters and officers against these “one-sided, amoral” lies. Describing the war as “just and hard,” while condemning Israel’s “cruel enemies,” Eisenkot noted the “yawning gap between legitimate criticism in a democratic society and maligning our soldiers to harvest accolades at festivals abroad.”
Oops.
If Eisenkot and his supporters simply mock Israel’s right-wing attack machine for using the anti-Zionist propaganda mill to score cheap electoral points, they deserve to lose. They must learn from the traction this devastating lie gained so easily – and Eisenkot’s slowing momentum.
Too many bought the falsehood about Eisenkot’s silence because it resonated with two broader truths. For months, Eisenkot’s silence reinforced his image as the anti-Bibi: honest, reasonable, quiet, preferring effective action and good values to bombast and barbs. But, ultimately, a Sphinx strategy is an hourglass maneuver, hoping that voter patience doesn’t run out before Election Day and the political cachet your candidate’s ambiguity generates outlasts the opposition’s campaign to muddy this blank slate.
Sphinxes are for Egyptians, not Israelis – or most responsible democratic citizens. Israel faces serious military, economic, social, and political challenges. At a certain point in a campaign, simply not being the guy in charge, while not being bold enough to rock the boat, leads candidates to start sinking in public esteem. Perhaps in a more placid 1950s America, Dwight Eisenhower could be elected twice based on his military record and his reserve; that’s a much tougher sell in Israel 2026.
Eisenkot must figure out how to rouse votes, inspire them to vote, to believe in him, to feel optimistic, without undermining his reassuring image. It’s easy to demand in this column – hard to pull off. And it’s especially hard when the Eisenkot-was-silent lie also resonated with many because Netanyahu keeps running against Yair Golan and other Eisenkot allies.
Ben-Gvir's impact on Israel, Netanyahu abroad
It’s paradoxical. Indulging flame-throwers like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has stained Netanyahu’s status abroad and Israel’s standing worldwide too. But it hasn’t hurt Bibi much in Israel. Bibi-bashers didn’t need Ben-Gvir to hate Bibi.
By contrast, the many foreign reporters profiling Eisenkot adoringly and the many American Jews jonesing for him to win overlook Eisenkot’s problematic allies – while their extreme attacks on Israel’s army and the war have hurt Eisenkot with Israeli voters.
Eisenkot’s vote-sharing agreement with Yair Golan has been a gift to the Right, making it even easier to define Eisenkot by the far Left’s harshest rants. Even more devastating, the arrangement is stirring just a few too many doubts among Israel’s muscular moderates about whether Eisenkot will be too beholden to the loony Left.
Silence, we’re told, is golden, and certainly helped propel Eisenkot past other rivals. But Eisenkot must remember the eternal Jewish charge to leaders: be strong and of good courage, especially because, in modern politics, strong silent types often end up delivering concession speeches.

Details
