Ukraine’s army seeks to give frontline commanders more authority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:21:33 UTC
20:21:33 KST

Ukraine’s army seeks to give frontline commanders more authority
- Ukraine’s army is training frontline commanders through an intensive course to empower them with decision-making authority and promote battlefield initiative.
- The military aims to shift from Soviet-style top-down control to a more flexible, NATO-style command culture prioritising soldiers' welfare.
- New commander-in-chief General Drapatyi is addressing command reforms, including expanding non-commissioned officers’ powers, improving pay, and enhancing battlefield effectiveness.
AI generated
KYIV - Ukrainian staff sergeant Vitalii Tomchyshak believes he knows how to beat Russia on the battlefield: empower frontline leaders such as himself to make critical decisions.
Too often, Tomchyshak says, combat commanders are overruled by senior officers who do not understand the specifics of a battlefield situation.
“It doesn’t matter who you are – a sergeant, an officer, anyone – you need to be listened to,” the 27-year-old former software developer said.
Tomchyshak was among 103 battle-hardened squad commanders pulled from the front line by Ukraine’s military and put through an intensive three-month course this summer aimed at increasing their effectiveness as leaders.
As Russia wages its war in Ukraine, the Ukrainian army is trying to transform itself – not just in terms of technological innovation, but also in its culture and leadership.
That means dismantling a Soviet-era culture of rigid, top-down command and encouraging more initiative from battle-tested troops.
Despite innovating its way through more than four years of war to hold back a bigger, better-armed enemy, Ukraine’s military has faced criticism for heavy losses in some units and poor treatment of some troops – factors blamed by some for discouraging men from joining the military.
Expectations are high that the new commander-in-chief, 43-year-old General Mykhailo Drapatyi, will deliver on his pledge to promote better command practices and prioritise soldiers’ lives.
Many of the men and women on the course are in their twenties and early thirties.
It aims to train a younger generation of leaders – already expert in infantry tactics, drone warfare, artillery and logistics – to make autonomous decisions on the battlefield.
Crowded around a map covered in tokens denoting military units, a dozen commanders are war-gaming how to repel a Russian assault on a village.
A roll of a dice decides whether operations succeed or fail, forcing them to improvise and communicate with colleagues.
Run by the Military Institute of Kyiv National University and partly financed by charity Come Back Alive, the Captain’s Course has trained more than 1,200 officers since it was launched during the first year of the war.
With Ukraine struggling to draft frontline troops, the emphasis is on preserving manpower, said Artem Chukharev, a 23-year-old sergeant in the Territorial Defence Forces.
This is in stark contrast to Russian infantry assaults that have come at a high human cost.
“We simply cannot afford to treat them the way our age-old enemy does,” Chukharev said, praising the course for encouraging commanders to take informed decisions.
“I finally realised what an officer is, and what he should be like.”
The programme is not easy.
Although 88 commanders graduated on July 18, 15 students did not – two for health reasons and the remainder for academic shortcomings.
Old habits
Battlefield flexibility is not a traditional feature of Ukraine’s military.
Despite efforts to modernise after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, Soviet-style attitudes have persisted among some senior officers trained at traditional top-brass institutes, said battalion commander “Houston”, asking to be identified only by his military call sign.
“Officers there are immediately instilled with a certain hatred toward sergeants and soldiers,” said Houston, a career soldier who signed up long before the war, unlike much of Ukraine’s 800,000-strong military.
Drapatyi took over as commander-in-chief in July from 61-year-old Oleksandr Syrskyi, whose critics said he tolerated heavy losses and imposed a heavy-handed style, micromanaging the 1,200km front line.
In September, Drapatyi held a high-level meeting with senior sergeants to discuss ways to empower the NCO corps.
“A sergeant was a soldier himself yesterday. Today, he is the commander who is closest to the soldier,” he said. “They are the ones who care about the interests and needs of the ordinary soldier first and foremost.”
Ukraine’s armed forces, in response to questions for this article, said Drapatyi had published a list of problems to be addressed after the meeting – including an expansion of powers for non-commissioned officers, a clearer command structure and better pay.
Work on solving the problems was underway, it said.
Drapatyi has promoted several senior commanders known for embracing NATO-style command culture – including Andriy Biletsky, who commands the Third Army Corps - to oversee critical parts of Ukraine’s eastern defences.
‘Never stand still’
With new technology rapidly changing the nature of warfare, the course pushes commanders “to constantly seek out and find new solutions, adapt old solutions, modify them, modernise them,” Chukharev said. “But never stand still.”
Tomchyshak, who did not comment on the reforms at the highest level of the military, said that showing initiative was still often punished, particularly among sergeants.
Letting local commanders take more of the initiative would hand Ukraine an advantage on the battlefield, he said, especially over an enemy known for treating its troops poorly.
“We would begin to see radical change,” he said. REUTERS

Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. 'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.

During remarks to reporters, Rubio said that the US was working to “create the groundwork and rebuild the institutions necessary to have free and fair elections in Venezuela.”
But he caveated that free and fair elections would have to wait until Venezuela was in the shape to support an “enduring Republic,” and that its first elected leader could not inherit “a complete catastrophe, economic and social.”
The conditions for such a democratic transition, per Rubio, include rebuilding Venezuela’s independent media, creating the infrastructure for a trustworthy electoral process, and bringing back opposition political parties exiled abroad. Here Rubio name dropped María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who had maintained close tied with Trump before the administration ultimately backed Rodriguez.
Speaking to reporters at the UN, Rubio alludes to regime change in Cuba
Addressing reporters at the United Nations, Marco Rubio reiterated, in so many words, that the Trump administration is seeking to replace the current Cuban leadership, and did not rule out the use of force to achieve that goal.
“The Cuban Revolution has failed. It has failed for sixty-something years, it’s a failure now,” Rubio said. “The question is what replaces it.”
He continued: “We’re open to measures moving forward that begin that process of change.”
Pressed on whether the Trump administration would try to repeat its tactics in Venezuela – where it raided the country in the dead of night, arrested former autocrat Nicolas Maduro, and ushered in a more US-friendly leader to replace him – Rubio equivocated, but did not rule out the possibility.
“If there is a threat to the national security of the United States, the president has both the power and the obligation to address it,” Rubio said. “That said, our preference always is to deal with these things – I don’t want to call it diplomatic – but in a negotiating way.”
He also said he believed that American business could play “a positive role in a future Cuba,” and that any new government would have to be friendlier to business interests. That comes in light of reporting by the Guardian that shows businesses close to the administration have been buying up assets in Cuba in light of chaos wrought by the US’s latest efforts to cripple the island’s economy.
Iranian President to United Nations: "We will never bow our head"
Jakub Krupa
In a speech to the United Nations following on the heels of President Trump’s threats to “annihilate” his country, Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, struck a defiant tone.
“He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying,” Pezeshkian said, referring to Trump. “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”
He continued: “It must be understood by Mr Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations - without accepting the language of force.”
Trump, in his speech the day earlier, said Iran faced a choice between “greatness” and annihilation, warning Iran that he would its people “into hell” if they didn’t make a deal. It was latest of several apocalyptic-sounding threats from Trump toward Iran since the beginning of the conflict.
Earler in his address, during which the US delegation walked out of the room, Masoud also decried the US and Israel’s campaign against his country as “terrorism.”
“The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism,” he said.
He said that while Iran has avoided attacking civilian populations, the US “bombed a school” and “children perished under bombs with weapons used by the US and Israel.”
“They impose the war on us but we have proven that we’re not afraid of fighting, of war, that is defensive in nature, and we will stand in defence of our beloved Iran, our homeland, until our last breath.”
Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him - analysis
Robert Tait
Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.
Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.
But this seemed more shocking.
The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.
Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.
Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.
Trump administration set to defend its White House press ban in court
Trump administration lawyers will face the three new outlets banned from the White House by the president – Politico, CNN, and MS Now – in court today, as the organizations ask a federal judge to restore their access.

The three banned outlets swiftly sued, and other news organizations have halted some coverage of the president in solidarity, including the other rotating members of the president’s standard TV pool (which take turns filming the president’s press-open events and distributing the footage to others).
The three barred news organizations have accused the president of violating their First Amendment rights by retaliating against them over coverage he disliked. The Trump administration, in a new filing, countered by saying that White House access is a “privilege,” not a right, and that the three outlets’ reporting of information the administration deems sensitive constitutes a national security threat.
Trump himself has said he’ll “probably lose” the lawsuit, which has landed in the courtroom of a judge he appointed.

Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.

Her treatment by Washington, which previously considered cutting ties with the agency, is seen by several of the diplomats as a retaliatory response after UNHCR opted against Washington’s preferred candidate, Simon Hankinson.
A State Department spokesperson said it could not comment on pending legal issues. “We work with and through UNHCR when doing so advances US foreign policy interests,” the spokesperson said.

NEW DELHI: Kashmiri socio-political activist Tasleema Akhtar has raised concerns over the treatment of people in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK), alleging that Pakistan has failed to protect their basic rights and provide adequate infrastructure and essential services.
Addressing the 54th session of the UN human rights council in Geneva, Akhtar contrasted the situation in PoK with developments in the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir (JKUT). She alleged that people in PoK were living at the mercy of the Pakistan government amid poor infrastructure, limited investment and disregard for their basic rights.Her remarks come against the backdrop of concerns raised at the UNHRC over the human rights situation in PoK and Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan.At the 63rd session of the council, United Kashmir People’s National Party chairman Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri had alleged intensified repression in PoK since June 5 citing reports of arrests, violence, deaths, injuries, alleged disappearances and restrictions on internet and mobile communications.Kashmiri had called for an independent investigation into the reported violations and urged Pakistan to stop using force against peaceful protesters.
'Strategic developmental differences'
Akhtar told the UNHRC that there were significant differences in development between JKUT and PoJK.“Mr Vice President, being a native to J&K through UNHR Council, I would like to bring forth the strategic developmental differences of Union Territory of J&K, i.e. JKUT and Pak Occupied J&K.”
She said the Indian government was investing in infrastructure and development projects in Jammu and Kashmir, while alleging that PoJK faced inadequate investment and misuse of its resources.“While JKUT is bringing transformational changes for the betterment of the region, people of POJK are living at the mercy of Pakistan Government having uttered disregard for the people over there and their basic human rights and amenities.”Akhtar also alleged that Pakistan was struggling with its financial obligations while shielding terrorist outfits involved in what she described as a proxy war against India.“While the Government of India is investing in infrastructure and developmental projects in J&K besides bringing peace and prosperity to the region, Pakistan is struggling to meet its basic financial obligations and is shielding terrorist outfitters to wage a proxy war against India.”
Education concerns
Akhtar highlighted education as one of the key areas where she said JKUT had an advantage over PoK.“PoK lacks even basic infrastructure and amenities, with negligible investment and built-in misappropriation of its resources by Pakistan. In terms of education and literacy rate, JKUT is far ahead of PoK. Government of India spends nine times more on education in JKUT compared to its counterpart.”She alleged that schools in PoK lacked basic facilities such as buildings, roofs, clean water and toilets. These shortcomings, she said, were creating hardships for students and contributing to a high dropout rate.“PoK is facing a major crisis in its education sector, lacking basic infrastructure including building and roofs, clean water, toilets, etc., causing acute hardships to students, resulting in severe drop-out ratio.”
Healthcare access
Akhtar also pointed to differences in access to healthcare. She said people in JKUT were able to access health benefits under national schemes even in remote areas, while similar access remained a distant prospect for people in PoJK.“Change is also possible in health sector. PoK of health, UT are availing health benefits in even their remote areas with national health schemes, which is a distant dream for the people of PoK.”She further highlighted the government's health insurance coverage in Jammu and Kashmir.“Government of India facilitates people of the Juman Kashmir with universal health insurance coverage of far-reaching... Thank you.”
Broader concerns over PoK
Akhtar’s remarks followed wider concerns raised at the UNHRC over alleged restrictions and human rights violations in the Pakistan-occupied parts of Jammu and Kashmir.
Kashmiri, while addressing the council’s 63rd session under Agenda Item 4, had called for independent monitoring of PoK and PoGB, an investigation into reported violations and the release of people he described as arbitrarily detained.“Peaceful dissent is not terrorism, and demanding rights is not a crime,” Kashmiri said.He also called for the whereabouts of missing people to be established and for unrestricted internet and mobile communications to be restored across PoK.“The Council must act now to safeguard the lives and fundamental rights of millions of Kashmiris,” he said.

A Latvian business trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) has begun in the United States. Running alongside Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs’s working visit until 27 September, the mission covers New York, Los Angeles and San Diego. Its four sector programmes bring together representatives of start-ups, the film industry, defence and dual-use technology companies, and biomedical and pharmaceutical businesses.
“The United States is Latvia’s strategic partner and trusted ally, and this September marks 35 years since the restoration of diplomatic relations. Successful cooperation with US partners, including those in California, demonstrates the international competitiveness of Latvian companies. The delegation includes representatives of the defence and dual-use sectors, biomedicine, start-ups and the film industry. I hope this visit will help Latvian businesses establish valuable contacts in the United States and, in turn, support Latvia’s economic growth,” said President Edgars Rinkēvičs.
The first business meetings are taking place in New York and Los Angeles on Wednesday, 23 September. Over the following days, Latvian entrepreneurs will meet major US companies, investors, universities and technology transfer centres to pursue export deals, joint technology projects and investment partnerships.
“Trade between Latvia and the United States reached €1.63 billion in 2025, up 13% year on year. This is more than a strong statistical result: it is a foundation for much greater ambition. We need Latvian companies to enter US supply chains, become partners in joint product development, and attract US capital to new projects in Latvia. The United States is a strategically important economic and security partner for Latvia, and the President’s visit lends additional weight to these economic discussions. The goal is clear: new projects, orders and investment,” said Raivis Bremšmits, State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Economics.
Three cities and four sector programmes
In New York, representatives of Latvia’s start-up ecosystem will meet US investors and representatives of ServiceNow, a global developer of enterprise AI and digital workflow platforms. Latvian start-ups will present their solutions at the “Pitch to a President” event, receiving feedback from US investors on their prospects in the market.
In Los Angeles, the film industry programme will begin with a meeting at Paramount. Separate programmes for Latvian defence and dual-use technology, biomedical and pharmaceutical companies are also scheduled in the city over the following days.
“Three cities, four sector programmes and dozens of carefully prepared meetings within just a few days make this one of LIAA’s largest and most complex trade missions. Its pace and scale match the ambitions of Latvian companies in the United States. Last year, Latvia’s services exports to the US rose by 10% to €510 million, with information and communications technology services accounting for more than 40% of the total. Latvian companies have the expertise and technology to sit at the same table as global leaders as equal partners. We will judge the mission’s results by the deals, joint technology projects and investments that follow these discussions,” said LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
Latvian delegation includes 44 companies and organisations
The trade mission includes 44 Latvian companies and organisations.
The defence and dual-use technology programme includes Aumeux, SAF North America, Origin Robotics, Raw-tech, SIA Ardlat, Perkons Energy, LMT, LMT Defence, VIC TEC and LAT Security, as well as the Latgale Special Economic Zone, the Latvian Exporters’ Association “The Red Jackets”, the Federation of Security and Defence Industries of Latvia, the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the University of Latvia and Riga Technical University.

War continues; wheat buyers brace for higher prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:17:34 UTC
20:17:34 KST

As Russian aggression in Ukraine persists, buyers worldwide seeking to replenish dwindling wheat stocks face painfully high prices, reports Reuters.
Major wheat importers in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa—who relied on supplies from the Black Sea region—are struggling to restock, as attacks on ships and port infrastructure have virtually halted the movement of cargo since July. These disruptions have driven up wheat prices. Benchmark prices on the Chicago exchange have surged 40% from their June lows to a three-and-a-half-year high, raising the risk that some of the world’s most vulnerable consumers will once again face a new wave of food price inflation.
For the past few months, most international importers have held off on seeking alternative suppliers, hoping for an agreement between Russia and Ukraine that would allow grain shipments. Meanwhile, local stockpiles have dwindled to critical levels, particularly in Asia, a region heavily dependent on imports. Competition for supplies is expected to intensify—and prices to keep rising—until the Southern Hemisphere harvest enters the market at the end of the year. Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, stated that the Black Sea region is crucial for grain transport; if buyers cannot source grain there, they will look elsewhere, driving prices up further. While some buyers in the Middle East and Africa are already seeking alternatives, others have indicated that their current stocks are sufficient to last until November or the end of the year before they need to source larger volumes of grain.
Russian wheat exports are projected to drop to one million tonnes in September (compared to five million tonnes in September of last year), while Ukraine could export one million tonnes this month—half the volume exported in September last year.
In the near term, the reduction in exports will hit Asia the hardest.
Ishan Hanu, an agricultural analyst at Kpler, noted that very few ships are being loaded, and even the small volumes leaving Russia or Ukraine will go to the Middle East and Africa rather than Asia. He reported that Indonesia, the world’s second-largest grain importer, received only 60,000 tonnes of grain from the Black Sea region in September—significantly less than the half-million tonnes received in September of the previous year.
Indonesian grain processors have begun seeking alternatives from other suppliers, including Argentina, and Australian grain is commanding a price 20–25% higher than grain from the Black Sea region.
Egypt, the largest grain importer, will receive significantly less grain from Russia and Ukraine compared to last year, though it does hold some reserves. A European trader noted that while Egyptian importers cannot wait indefinitely, they do have some time, as harvests from the Middle East and North Africa have recently come in. On the 20th of September, Egypt’s Minister of Supply, Sherif Farouk, stated that Egypt had turned to France and other European suppliers, thereby shifting away from the Russian and Ukrainian markets.

Canada seeks deforestation law carveouts as EU ties deepen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:14:41 UTC
20:14:41 KST

Ottawa does not expect Brussels to create a unique exemption from the deforestation rules specifically for Canada. | Marion Thibaut/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Canada's man in Brussels wants to rework how the European Union's landmark anti-deforestation law applies to Canadian businesses as the two sides explore ways to deepen their relationship.
Following Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member,” Ottawa wants to “clean up some of the long-standing irritants that have existed” between Canada and the EU, Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's ambassador to the EU, told POLITICO at a Brussels Playbook Live event on Tuesday.
Chief among those grievances is the EU's new Deforestation Regulation, which kicks in on Dec. 30 and requires companies importing goods like palm oil, coffee and wood into the EU to prove those products were not produced on deforested land.
Advertisement
The law has faced fierce backlash from several EU countries and the bloc's trading partners. Critics argue it will generate hefty compliance costs for businesses and doesn't provide enough exemptions for countries classified as having a low risk of deforestation.
The application of the new rules “could be done in a manner that was easier for third parties,” said Wilkinson. While Canada has “no argument” with the EU's aim to halt deforestation, the law doesn't include any “carveout that said you don't have to put in place all of these burdensome requirements” for low-risk countries, he added.
Wilkinson said Ottawa does not expect Brussels to create a unique exemption from the deforestation rules specifically for Canada, but is “hoping to actually have a dialogue about how could you actually fix this.”
Canada has been pursuing stronger links with Europe to reduce its dependence on the U.S. amid a trade dispute between the two countries. The EU is also eager to deepen ties with Ottawa as the bloc looks to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and as its own relationship with the U.S. grows increasingly tense.
Canada's exports to the EU were valued at $34.5 billion in 2025, trade data shows, including $242 million in wood and wood products and $174 million in paper and pulp.

UK says will revisit Chagos deal after latest Trump criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:12:36 UTC
20:12:36 KST

Breadcrumb
UK mulls retreat from Chagos deal after latest Trump criticism
Britain will rework its deal to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, a minister confirmed Wednesday, after US President Donald Trump branded the agreement "terrible" during his first meeting with UK leader Andy Burnham.
London's decision to hand back the Indian Ocean archipelago to its former colony and pay to lease a strategic US-UK military base on Diego Garcia has been a bone of contention with Trump's administration for months.
The UK confirmed in April that it was pausing the plans agreed last year between the Mauritian government and Britain's then-prime minister Keir Starmer.
It faced vocal opposition from Trump, who had initially supported the pact, but then later branded it "an act of great stupidity".
The unpredictable American leader railed against the deal again Tuesday in his first face-to-face Tuesday with Burnham, who replaced Starmer in July.
Meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Trump said he believed Burnham would be reconsidering the "terrible deal", as the UK leader sat beside him, nodded and said "yep".
Burnham later told broadcasters Britain would "work hard" to find a resolution on the thorny issue and that he was "confident we can find it working with our US partners".
Hours later, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Trump's opposition was "not news to us" but that his latest comments "provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing".
"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where we can support it," he told the BBC on Wednesday.
Streeting confirmed that annual payments worth at least £120 million ($159 million) to lease back the military base from Mauritius would not be made "at this stage".
Starmer struck the deal after insisting that international legal rulings have put Britain's ownership of the Chagos in doubt and only a deal with Mauritius would guarantee continued US and UK use of the base.
'Millstone?'
Britain kept control of the Chagos Islands after Mauritius gained independence in the 1960s, evicting thousands of Chagos islanders who have since mounted a series of legal claims for compensation in British courts.
In 2019, the International Court of Justice recommended that Britain hand the archipelago to Mauritius.
The deal would have given Britain a 99-year lease of the base, with the option to extend.
James Cartlidge, defence spokesman for the main opposition Conservative party, said the agreement "should be binned entirely".
But Streeting told Times Radio: "The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it (will) go away ... is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world."
Jack Pannell, a senior researcher at the British Foreign Policy Group think-tank, said Burnham's priorities with Trump would be on "the big international issues" like AI regulation, Ukraine and the Middle East.
"Success for Burnham means avoiding this issue becoming a millstone around his neck while he pursues his other foreign policy priorities and focuses on his domestic agenda," Pannell told AFP. "The chances of a breakthrough on this issue are slim, and that may suit the prime minister just fine."
On Tuesday, Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark that will allow the US to build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland.

"Thus, a church server of one of the UOC (MP) temples who called for the seizure of the capital of Ukraine has been exposed in Kyiv. According to the investigation, the sexton distributed enemy propaganda in his own Telegram channel," the agency informs.

"In addition to him, a blogger was detained in the city who called on Facebook for the physical liquidation of representatives of one of the national minorities and the arson of their houses of worship," the report says.
Also, as the SBU clarifies, on this internet resource, the suspect threatened servicemen of the Defense Forces and their families.

Comprehensive measures were carried out by employees of the Main Department of the SBU in Kyiv and Kyiv Region, and the SBU Office in Zaporizhia Region, jointly with the National Police under the procedural guidance of Desnyansky District Prosecutor's Office of Kyiv, as well as the Zaporizhia and Kyiv Regional Prosecutor's Offices.

On Wednesday, the Kremlin said the grounds for future peace talks with Ukraine were still not in place and there were no plans for any high-level meetings.

Energy worker Mykola Nechypurenko, one of a team repairing damage to the power network, was skeptical about the prospects for any energy cease-fire with Russia.
"I don't think they'll agree on anything. As long as the war goes on, energy infrastructure remains under threat," said Nechypurenko, 55. "I don't believe it will work. Not until the war ends."

Hungary could receive €4.2 billion from the EU: what has changed since the funds were frozen
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:08:29 EEST
20:08:29 KST

Hungary could receive €4.2 billion from the EU: what has changed since the funds were frozen
Kyiv • UNN
The European Commission has proposed unfreezing €4.2 billion for Hungary following reforms. The decision must be approved by the Council of the EU.
The European Commission has proposed lifting restrictions on €4.2 billion in cohesion policy funds for Hungary after the country's new government carried out a series of reforms in the areas of the rule of law and the fight against corruption. Brussels also wants to restore access for some Hungarian universities to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes. The final decision must be made by the Council of the EU. UNN reports this, citing Reuters and European Commission data.
Details
On September 23, the European Commission proposed that the Council of the EU lift the protective measures imposed against Hungary in 2022 under the conditionality mechanism, which allows funding for member states to be restricted in the event of violations of the rule-of-law principle that create risks to the EU budget. The European Commission said that Budapest had taken sufficient measures to address some of the problems that had led to the funding being frozen.
These include, in particular, changes in public procurement, anti-corruption safeguards, the prevention of conflicts of interest, and the operation of law enforcement and prosecutorial bodies. The assessment was carried out after Hungary officially informed Brussels on September 9 that it had implemented the relevant reforms.
Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union's financial interests. Today, we are proposing to unblock €4.2 billion and reopen the doors of Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe to Hungarian students and researchers
The European Commission clarified that this concerns the restoration of approximately €4.2 billion in previously suspended budget commitments under cohesion policy. The European Commission's decision itself does not mean that this amount will automatically be transferred to Hungary – the proposal must be approved by the Council of the EU. In addition, if the proposal is approved, restrictions on Hungarian universities managed by so-called public-interest trusts will be lifted. Because of the sanctions previously imposed, students and researchers at these institutions had limited access to the European Erasmus+ student-exchange programme and the Horizon Europe research programme.
Why the EU froze Hungary's money
At the end of 2022, the Council of the EU suspended approximately €6.3 billion in funding for Hungary under the conditionality mechanism. Brussels cited shortcomings in the country's anti-corruption system, risks of conflicts of interest, and systemic violations in public procurement.
The restrictions included freezing 55% of budget commitments under three cohesion policy programmes concerning the environment and energy efficiency, transport infrastructure, and territorial development. Separately, the EU prohibited the conclusion of new financial commitments with a number of Hungarian public-interest trusts and the institutions they maintain.
Of the initial €6.3 billion, the amount of funds that can now be restored has fallen to approximately €4.2 billion.
The new government and the agreement with Brussels
After the government of Prime Minister Péter Magyar came to power, Hungary stepped up negotiations with the European Commission on unblocking European funding. In May, Magyar and von der Leyen agreed on the possibility of gradually opening access to a total of €16.4 billion in frozen funds, provided that Budapest implemented the necessary reforms. Of this amount, approximately €10 billion consists of funds from the NextGenerationEU Recovery Fund, another €4.2 billion is cohesion policy funding, and approximately €2.2 billion is linked to the fulfilment of other EU requirements, including those concerning academic freedom.
At the same time, unblocking the current €4.2 billion will not mean the automatic release of all funding for Budapest. The European Commission is separately considering the issue of approximately €10 billion from the Recovery Fund, while more than €2 billion in cohesion policy funding remains blocked because of Brussels' concerns, related in particular to the asylum system, child-protection legislation, and academic freedom.
It will be recalled
The Council of the EU must now consider the European Commission’s proposal to lift the measures introduced in 2022. Under the conditionality mechanism procedure, after the Commission submits its proposal, the member states must adopt the relevant decision.

Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:08:01 UTC
20:08:01 KST

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

'UP ke ladke' in for political 'brawl'? SP, Congress spar over who can beat BJP in 2027

'UP ke ladke' vs each other? SP-Congress spar over who can beat BJP in 2027
NEW DELHI: The "UP ke ladke" bonhomie is beginning to look less like a united front and more like a contest for the upper hand, with Congress and Samajwadi Party leaders trading jabs over who can take on the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. With the 2027 assembly election approaching, are cracks emerging in the INDIA bloc's battle plan against Yogi Adityanath's BJP?
Iqra Hasan’s remarks trigger Congress pushback
SP MP Iqra Hasan set off the latest bout of sparring by saying Congress "can't achieve much on its own" and projecting party boss and former CM Akhilesh Yadav as the only leader capable of defeating the BJP in Uttar Pradesh.Her remarks drew a quick response from the Congress, with party leaders pushing back against the suggestion that the SP could take on the BJP by itself.Congress MP Imran Masood said, "She (Iqra Hasan) also cannot do it alone. What is the problem with that? Iqra is our child. She is like our niece.""People from the Trinamool Congress were also saying a lot. Look at what happened in Bengal. Let us move together, and we will remain in peace," he added with a reference to Mamata-led TMC's big defeat in Bengal after contesting solo.Congress leader Udit Raj pointed to the SP's performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha election while questioning Iqra's claim."That may be her (Iqra Hasan's) own statement, but we can understand this through an example: when the alliance was formed in 2024, the Samajwadi Party won 36 seats. What was its performance before that? The Samajwadi Party had only six MPs in 2019. So, in politics, one plus one does not always make two; one plus one can make eleven.
Therefore, I think she should correct her understanding," Udit Raj told IANS.
BJP joins SP-Congress war of words
The saffron party, meanwhile, was quick to weigh in on the disagreement. Uttar Pradesh BJP vice-president Neeraj Singh said, "Congress will not be able to achieve anything on its own across the country. And even if it forms an alliance with the Samajwadi Party or any other party in Uttar Pradesh, the people of Uttar Pradesh have already formed an alliance in their hearts with the BJP government..."Iqra, who made the remarks on Monday, had said, "It is an absolutely foolish statement. I think that if there is anyone in Uttar Pradesh who can defeat the BJP, it is only Akhilesh Yadav. Congress will not be able to do anything on its own. If the alliance remains, it will be very good; if it does not, it is a loss for them (Congress), not for us."
SP-Cong face a new test: Who gets how many seats?
The "UP ke ladke" chemistry that helped Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav pull off a striking upset in the 2024 Lok Sabha election has yet to turn into a clear seat-sharing formula for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls.The two leaders have continued to share the stage on occasions, including protest for students, maintaining a public show of camaraderie. But behind that familiar chemistry, the alliance arithmetic is still taking shape.There has been no concrete discussion on how the 403 assembly seats could be divided between Congress and the Samajwadi Party.
How 2024 ‘UP ke ladke’ formula worked
Their partnership took shape months before the 2024 Lok Sabha election, and the results that followed gave the alliance a strong political imprint.The SP contested 62 of the state's 80 Lok Sabha seats and won 37, including Faizabad, the constituency covering Ayodhya. Congress fought 17 seats and won six. Together, the two parties crossed the halfway mark of UP's Lok Sabha tally, handing the BJP a major setback in a state that sends the most MPs to Parliament.For the SP, it was very much the bigger share of the alliance pie. Akhilesh's party emerged as the largest opposition force in the state, and second largest in country, while Congress revived its presence with six seats.
Ayodhya loss added to BJP’s UP setback
The result also had a powerful political backdrop. Uttar Pradesh is the home turf of chief minister Yogi Adityanath and the parliamentary constituency of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The BJP had also invested enormous political capital in Ayodhya, where the Ram temple consecration took place in January 2024 in the presence of PM Modi and RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat.Yet, months later, the BJP lost the Faizabad seat to the SP.The result turned Rahul and Akhilesh into the "UP ke ladke" of the 2024 campaign, a political pairing that seemed to have found the right formula for the state's electorate. But as the next election approaches, the partnership is facing a different kind of test: Seat-sharing.Akhilesh has repeatedly said that the SP will contest the 2027 election with the INDIA bloc partners with whom it fought the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, effectively keeping the door open for Congress. But Congress has not made a similar formal commitment. Neither Rahul Gandhi nor party president Mallikarjun Kharge has publicly announced a seat-sharing arrangement with the SP.
SP gets its 403-seat election machinery moving
Meanwhile, the SP is already getting its electoral machinery moving.Sources told TOI that the party's top leadership has finalised candidates for more than 100 of the 403 assembly seats, while the process is under way for the remaining constituencies. The party has not yet released a formal candidate list.SP strategists say the early exercise is deliberate, giving prospective candidates time to prepare their constituencies, build networks and hit the ground running once the campaign begins.The strategy is not entirely new. Political observers point out that the SP followed a similar approach before the 2022 assembly and 2024 Lok Sabha elections, beginning the candidate-selection process well ahead of polling but releasing the actual lists only a few months before the election.
Congress prepares for all 403 seats too
Congress, meanwhile, has indicated that it is preparing to contest all 403 seats. That ambition could make the eventual negotiatins with the SP considerably more interesting.
Owaisi offer adds another variable
And there is another piece on the chessboard. AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi has made an open offer to Akhilesh, potentially bringing another party into the opposition's seat-sharing calculations.
AIMIM's performance in Maharashtra, UP and Bihar
If the SP chooses to engage with Owaisi, the equation could become even more complicated for an alliance that has so far largely revolved around SP and Congress.
What happened in 2022 assembly polls
The Lok Sabha 2024 friendship was a renewed one. Just two years earlier, the grand old party and Akhilesh Yadav’s Samajwadi Party had contested the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections separately, as they sought to take on Yogi Adityanath, who was then seeking a second term as chief minister.Yogi comfortably retained his Lucknow throne, while the Samajwadi Party increased its numbers. The Congress, however, suffered a major setback, winning just 2 of the 403 assembly seats.
Big heart or bigger share?
Rahul, personally, also appeared hesitant when it came to announcing the Mahagathbandhan’s chief ministerial face in Bihar last year.He also appeared to have reservations about Tejashwi Yadav’s eagerness to project himself as the alliance’s face, as well as over seat-sharing, with a large chunk of seats going to Lalu Yadav’s Rashtriya Janata Dal.A similar story could now unfold in Uttar Pradesh, where the Congress may look to expand its footprint with an eye on the next Lok Sabha elections. Uttar Pradesh remains at the heart of national politics, making a strong presence in the state crucial for any party with larger ambitions.Akhilesh Yadav, meanwhile, would be looking to return to power in Lucknow and reclaim the chief minister’s chair.Congress’ delayed decisions and its cautious approach towards trusting allies have also been visible more recently in Tamil Nadu. Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav have previously urged the Congress to show a “big heart” and back “regional players” in their home turfs.
What next for UP ke ladke?
So, while the Rahul-Akhilesh bond now may still look intact in public, the real test could come away from the cameras: How many seats each party wants, how many it is willing to give up, and whether the "UP ke ladke" formula can survive the hard arithmetic of 2027.
The BJP under Yogi Adityanath, meanwhile, is preparing to defend its position in Uttar Pradesh and seek another term in the state's 403-member assembly, ensuring that the opposition's alliance arithmetic will remain under close watch.With a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, Yogi would match former CM Mulayam Singh Yadav's record of three consecutive terms in the state, while he already holds the record for the longest uninterrupted tenure as UP chief minister, having been in office for nearly a decade.

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. The creation of the US AI Force follows the logic behind the creation of the country’s Space Force, which was largely formed in the interests of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and key giants of the military-industrial complex, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"This move, again, is comparable to the earlier creation of the Space Force, when entities de facto affiliated with [US President Donald] Trump’s inner circle became key contractors. The Space Force was created largely in the interests of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and key giants of the military-industrial complex, including Boeing, Northrop Grumman, and other companies that are implementing the US military-space program," the expert said.
Stepanov emphasized that the creation of the new agency legitimizes the participation of the largest US high-tech giants in government policy and will grant them access to massive US budgets. Among the key beneficiaries, he singled out Palantir, a major player in the field of security and intelligence analytics.
Stepanov also noted that the new organization will be headed by a person whom Trump himself has called the "AI Czar" – the nation’s digital leader. "It will be interesting to see who is appointed to lead this agency," he added.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump announced the creation of the AI Force, modeled after the US Space Force, which was established in 2019. "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Tigray rebels seize airport and clash with federal forces as fighting in Ethiopia reignites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:03:33 UTC
20:03:33 KST

TPLF forces took control of Mekelle airport and fought federal troops at two locations in the Afar region, while Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to three Tigray airports in an apparent collapse of the Pretoria Agreement that ended the 2020-2022 war in the country.
Tigrayan rebels in northern Ethiopia seized control of a key airport and clashed with federal troops in the neighbouring region of Afar on Wednesday, as long-standing tensions spilt into open battle.
Fighting escalated "since last night in Abala and Erebti (in Afar) between TPLF and federal forces," an NGO source in the region said, requesting anonymity.
"We are expecting it to expand. We just sent a truck with food to help the people displaced," they added.
Abala lies in the mountain ranges that mark the border with Tigray. Erebti lies around 100 kilometres further into Afar.
Another humanitarian source confirmed clashes in the two locations, as did a foreign security source in Ethiopia.
A former TPLF senior official said the rebels were in control of Berhale, Erebti, Abala, Megale, Dalul and Konoba in Afar.
The federal forces are "fast-retreating", he added.
Meanwhile, local and security sources said Tigrayan forces were in control of the airport in the regional capital Mekelle.
Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to three airports in Tigray — Mekelle, Axum and Shire — "due to the current situation".
"While we were on our way to the airport for work, our supervisor called the driver and told him that the airport had been taken over by Tigray forces. Since there were no flights, he told us to return home," an employee at Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle said.
A foreign security source based in Ethiopia confirmed the information.
A small number of federal police guard the airport and their situation was unknown.
Between 2020 and 2022, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fought a devastating war with the federal government that resulted in the deaths of some 600,000 people, according to African Union estimates.
Sporadic clashes in recent months have raised fears of a return to war.
Abiy under fire
Ethiopia faces multiple insurgencies, including in its most populous regions, Oromia and Amhara.
On Sunday, the TPLF announced it had joined a seven-group military alliance dubbed Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival aiming to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and install a transitional administration.
The alliance also includes Amhara nationalist Fano militias — who fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the last war — and the Oromo Liberation Army, an active insurgency in Ethiopia's most populous region, along with four groups from three other regions, making up half of the country's 12 regional states.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, which eventually triggered the war in 2020.
The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the war and maintained an uneasy calm until late 2025, when clashes resumed.
The federal government has since launched drone strikes in Tigray and massed troops at the regional border.
Rights groups have accused the TPLF of a campaign of forced recruitment this year as it prepares for renewed fighting.
The region has not recovered from the last war, with around 1 million people still displaced and many parts of the peace deal unfulfilled.
Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 partly for brokering a peace agreement with neighbouring Eritrea.
Good friends and neighbours
The federal government has a significant military advantage, having ramped up production of military drones since the last war.
Yet the TPLF's Tigray Defence Forces retain a significant inherited arsenal from their years at the helm of Ethiopia's military before 2018, including tanks, artillery, long-range guided rockets and ballistic missiles documented by open-source military analysts during the 2020-2022 war.
Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos said in June that TPLF hardliners had been "actively accumulating and acquiring new arms" in violation of the Pretoria Agreement.
Neighbouring countries have also been implicated in backing the rebels.
ACLED conflict monitoring group assessed earlier this year that Eritrean forces had moved troops toward western Tigray in coordination with the TDF and that Eritrea was providing weapons and hosting Tigrayan fighters.
Ethiopia's government formally accused Sudan's armed forces in May of providing "arms and financial support" to TPLF-linked forces and described Sudan as "a hub of anti-Ethiopian forces". Sudan denied the allegation.
Locked in a long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, Egypt is assessed by analysts at the Soufan Center as providing diplomatic cover and logistical support to Ethiopian opposition factions, although no direct weapons transfers to the TPLF have been documented.

Thus, the SBGSU notes, information regarding the mobilization of a foreign citizen directly at the checkpoint does not correspond to the actual circumstances of the incident.

According to available data, 49-year-old Yonatan Karlinsky-Mashak was born in Ukraine and emigrated to Israel about 14 years ago. He is an Israeli citizen and a father of six.
Mashak's wife confirmed his mobilization. She was told at the embassy that everything took place in accordance with the law, but that they would try to help.

AI and ski to cruises and Gen Z: dnata’s CEO on the trends driving travel in the UAE and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:02:25 UTC
20:02:25 KST

From AI-powered travel offers to growing demand for ski holidays, cruises and food experiences, dnata’s new Group CEO Nabil Sultan Al Murr says consumer habits are evolving rapidly.
Travel in the Middle East is evolving rapidly, with shifts in technology and consumer behaviour transforming both the industry and how people explore the region and beyond.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is already changing how holidays are planned and sold, while ski trips, cruises and experiences are gaining popularity among Middle Eastern travellers, according to the new Group Chief Executive Officer of global aviation and travel services company dnata.
Nabil Sultan Al Murr, who took over the role in June 2026, told Euronews Travel that these changing preferences are pushing companies to adapt more quickly, while technology is influencing everything from inspiration and booking to the airport experience.
Part of the Emirates Group, Dubai-based dnata operates across several divisions in aviation and tourism, including ground handling, cargo, travel services, catering and retail.
Overseeing its businesses across 162 cities in 37 countries, Sultan says the company has been assessing opportunities in emerging markets, including the Middle East, Africa, the Indian subcontinent and Eastern Europe. But it is technology and changing traveller behaviour that could have some of the biggest impacts on how people plan and experience their holidays.
How could AI change the travel experience?
AI has quickly become one of the biggest talking points in tourism, with travellers increasingly using tools to research destinations and plan their next trip. Sultan believes new technologies also have the potential to improve the passenger experience by allowing travel companies to process information and get relevant offers in front of customers much more quickly.
“I honestly think that AI and technology will bring in huge advantages in terms of improving the whole passenger experience and being able to put out the best offers and products,” he told Euronews at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai.
One example is the thousands of hotel contracts handled by dnata. Sultan says information from these contracts was previously processed manually, meaning getting deals into the system could take months.
“Now with AI we've adapted the whole thing and of course everything happens in almost real time,” he said. “That just shows the importance of how AI actually brings in that agility and speed and improvement in the whole work process.”
Ski holidays and winter travel grow in popularity
Technology isn't the only thing changing. Where – and how – people want to holiday is evolving too. One of the most noticeable shifts dnata is seeing in the UAE is growing demand for winter travel. “People going out for skiing, which was never the trend almost four to five years ago, is becoming such a huge trend,” Sultan says.
Responding to that interest, dnata has launched a winter programme featuring around 10 ski destinations. The company is also looking beyond conventional ski holidays towards other winter experiences. Sultan gives the example of Finland and seeing the Northern Lights as the types of trips attracting interest.
“These are all new kinds of features and experiences that we're trying to bring to the traveller and actually meet their emerging demand that we continue to see,” he said.
How cruises, Gen Z and food will drive the next era
Sultan expects traveller preferences to continue changing quickly over the next five years. Cruising is one area already gaining momentum in the Middle East and Gulf, he says, despite historically being a less established form of holiday in the region.
“I think the tourism and travel industry has been so dynamic and has been changing so rapidly and we've been seeing that,” Sultan said. “I think the key thing, of course, is to keep up with all of these changes and continue to introduce new elements in the whole entire experience.
“We see cruising now is becoming a huge trend. And you know that was never the case in this part of the world.”
The next major shift could come from younger travellers and how the industry adapts to their preferences. “Five years from now there's probably going to be a whole new trend, especially with the Generation Z, who probably look at different sorts of priorities in their travel experience,” he said.
Sultan points to food tourism as one example of how those priorities could change. “Food and healthy food is becoming a real trend,” he said. “So how do we bring that element into travel? It is a revolution and we're staying very close to the customer to really understand how we position our product offering.”

German state election losses risk snarling Merz’s reform agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

German state election losses risk snarling Merz’s reform agenda
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz faces a political challenge after his conservatives suffered historic losses in eastern German state elections, risking delays or dilution of his tax, pension, and health reform agenda.
- Coalition partner SPD, also weakened in elections, demands a new policy approach to address voter concerns over inflation, living standards, and early retirement rules, especially affecting eastern states.
- Economic experts warn that reworking reforms risks undermining policy confidence amid Germany's modest growth, while far-right gains highlight political fragmentation complicating Merz's efforts to revive the economy.
AI generated
BERLIN - Chancellor Friedrich Merz may have survived the triumph of the far right in September’s state elections in eastern Germany and Berlin but the shock to his coalition could force him to water down his promised reform agenda.
Merz took the unusual step of announcing immediately after exit polls showed his conservatives were on course for their worst-ever defeat that he would stay in office to get a raft of reforms to the tax, pensions and health systems through Parliament.
His partners in the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), who also lost heavily in elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin while holding on in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, also pledged to continue their alliance with his Christian Democrats (CDU).
But there has been increasing pressure from within the coalition for the government to do something to reflect the votes.
“There can’t be a simple carrying on as normal after the state elections,” an SPD strategy document circulated this week said, calling for a “German ‘New Deal’ that doesn’t leave people alone in a period of transition”.
It said a special party meeting would be called in December where the leadership would issue new policy proposals.
Despite stronger-than-expected growth in the first half of the year, surveys showed Sept 20’s election results were heavily influenced by squeezed living standards and voter worries over economic issues, notably rising inflation.
Aware of the mood of the electorate, two days before Sept 20’s votes in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz announced a €2.5 billion (S$3.65 billion) tax cut and plans for a price cap to help motorists deal with fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war.
There has also been pressure from his partners to change sections of the reform package that have drained support for the ruling parties in the eastern German states which voted in Septemberh, including plans to change the rules on retiring early.
The SPD letter said there were “open questions” about the proposed scrapping of the option for people to retire on a full pension at the age of 63 as long as they had paid contributions for at least 45 years.
The measure was recommended by a government-appointed pension commission as part of a package of measures that included adding a capital markets element to public pensions to keep the system affordable as the population ages.
But many in the east, where people typically have lower savings than in the west and lots went through long spells of unemployment in the wake of German reunification in 1990, feel such a change would hit them disproportionately hard.
Eastern state premiers from both the CDU and SPD have already called for the proposed change to be scrapped and the SPD letter said the proposals had caused “enormous uncertainty” among both workers and employers.
Surveys after the elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania showed many voters feared for their personal economic security and mistrusted Merz, whose ratings have hit historic lows.
Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, who has argued strongly against changing the early retirement rules, said this week Merz needed to regain the trust of voters. “I don’t know if he will succeed,” she said.
Reform pledges
In the wake of the defeats, Merz himself recognised that the government needed to acknowledge that many voters did not feel it was being “fair” in its reform plans.
But already there have been warnings that picking apart reform plans agreed over the summer would undermine confidence in German policy planning just as Europe’s largest economy looks like achieving modest growth after years of recession.
“If we start this whole process again now, it just delays these reforms and we need them,” said Martin Jacob, a professor at Spain’s IESE Business School and a member of the German finance ministry’s scientific advisory board.
“And this matters, because international investors, German investors, companies in Germany need to know what policy environment they’re in,” he said.
However, opinion polls this week showing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with almost 3 per cent% support across the country underline the political realities facing the government.
Merz, an instinctive pro-business fiscal conservative, came to power in 2025, pledging broad reforms to revive a German economy which has seen its industrial base steadily eroded by relentless competition from China and by the abrupt loss of cheap oil and gas from Russia due to the Ukraine war.
Turning his back on years of German fiscal orthodoxy, he unleashed a €500 billion spending package to rebuild Germany’s creaking infrastructure and its shrunken armed forces and, after months of wrangling, approved the reform package in July.
But the political crisis laid bare by September’s elections could now put those reforms at risk, said Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING.
“Years of economic stagnation helped produce that fragmentation. Now the fragmentation will make the stagnation harder to escape,” he said. REUTERS

MOL has completed construction work at the AV3 unit of the Danube refinery which was damaged by a fire in October last year, the company said.
"Once the construction equipment has been removed, the gradual restart of production can begin. Following the commissioning and testing of the AV3 unit, MOL's Szazhalombatta refinery will once again be able to operate at full capacity, further strengthening the security of fuel supply for Hungary and the entire region. The repair budget totaled HUF 18 billion [around EUR 50 million]," MOL said in a statement.
In the near future, specialists will carry out the flushing of systems, pressure testing and functional testing of process control and safety equipment, and will connect auxiliary power sources and also ensure coordination of the operation of the AV3 unit with other facilities of the Danube refinery. It is expected that the production of petroleum products will resume in stages in October.
MOL carried out a comprehensive restoration over the past year - it dismantled and reassembled the damaged reinforced concrete structure and restored the damaged equipment, control and power supply systems. A total of 27 new pumps were installed, 8 km of pipelines were replaced and 100 km of electrical cables were laid.
The refinery in Szazhalombatta is one of MOL's main facilities. It is the largest refinery in Hungary and one of the largest in Central and Eastern Europe. Its capacity is 165,000 barrels per day (8.1 million tonnes per year). The plant processed Russian oil supplied via the Druzhba pipeline.
