Texas turning blue may hinge on Democrats harnessing data center opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

TEXAS — Mason McCallister said it was an act of God that sent him down a gravel road near his home in Bells, Texas, one Sunday last December.
It wasn't the normal route he and his family take back from church, but he decided to detour so his daughters could shout hello to their grandmother as they drove by her home.
What he saw that day catapulted him into a debate playing out around the country — and especially in Texas — over data centers. It's one that may now affect the outcome of key elections in the Lone Star State.
As they rolled past, flashes of red caught McCallister's eye among the lush green of the area's gentle hills.
"Driving down that road, I just see survey markers everywhere," McCallister, a real estate agent, told CNBC. "And I knew at that time what was happening. I could feel it" — a data center is coming, he said.
McCallister's home is less than a mile from the survey markers, in a rural stretch between Dallas and the Oklahoma border. He and his wife, Heather, built the house on 26 acres, where they keep three horses and a donkey and host frequent family gatherings at a long farmhouse table on their spacious back patio.
The outcry over data centers — warehouses that contain the hardware for powering artificial intelligence and other technology — was only a faint murmur when McCallister first saw the survey markers. In the months since, it's become a dull roar, as increasingly more projects are proposed and built, and general anxiety over AI and its potentially humanity-ending powers grows.
Across Texas and the country, people have flooded local meetings to protest proposed projects, citing concerns about the use of water and other resources, noise and light pollution, rising utility costs and falling property values. Some towns and cities have moved to block their development, as anti-data center advocacy groups and social media pages proliferate.
Polling shows the economy and cost of living are top of mind for voters in the runup to the 2026 midterm elections. But some political strategists say data centers are a potent enough issue that they could shift the balance of power in Texas, potentially paving the way for Democrats to win statewide for the first time since 1994. Democrats have their sights set on the governor's mansion, as well as an open U.S. Senate seat, and the outcome of the Senate race could determine control of Congress.
Populists on both the left and the right — including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo. — were quick to try to rein in data centers and protect consumers against associated utility cost increases. But Democrats have broadly staked out a clear position against data centers, as President Donald Trump cheers development of new facilities.
That dynamic has left Republicans — including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who is running for reelection, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate — playing defense as public opinion turns against the facilities.
"I don't think Republicans have a clear, standard message on data centers and AI at this moment," said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI Action, who has called data centers a "sleeper issue" of this election cycle.
The survey markers set McCallister on a hunt for answers that included knocking on neighbors' doors, approaching surveyors in fields near his house, chasing down local officials and eventually cornering Rhett Bennett, the CEO of Black Mountain, a Fort Worth-based energy and natural resources development company he discerned had designs on the land.
Black Mountain did not respond to multiple requests for comment from CNBC about the potential project. But McCallister said Bennett — whom he confronted at a public meeting, with a Texas Tribune reporter in tow — confirmed the company was exploring a data center near his house. McCallister fears that if it is completed, it could effectively envelop his property.
McCallister said he and his wife never planned to sell their house, so any potential hit to their property value isn't particularly worrying. He says his primary concerns are water and power usage. Other data center opponents CNBC spoke with in Texas said they were concerned about noise and light pollution as well as the long-term economic and job displacement impacts of AI, which some of the facilities power.
More than anything, the ordeal has made McCallister — who said he's a lifelong Republican and voted for Trump three times — question his political leanings. The GOP, he said, has been too slow to react.
"I'm definitely frustrated with the Republican Party. I have gone literally out of my way to warn them, to tell them what's happening," he said. "Y'all should have picked up on this much earlier than y'all did."
'Let Data Reign'
Trump's outright dismissal of data center concerns and his reluctance to regulate rapidly evolving AI have complicated the issue for Republican leaders such as Abbott and Paxton, who are fighting for their political lives in one of the most closely watched states in the 2026 election.
"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump posted on Truth Social on Aug. 31.
With Trump's unyielding stance on the issue, Abbott and Paxton face a dilemma: Either they defy Trump, the de facto head of the Republican Party, and their donors with tech and data center-industry connections. Or they anger a sizable bloc of data center opponents that has emerged within their base.
Fifty-seven percent of Texas voters polled by the Texas Politics Project said they opposed a data center being built in their community, including 43% of Republicans, 54% of independents and 60% of rural voters.
The cross-partisan grassroots movement could threaten Republicans' hopes of keeping Texas red in what is already expected to be a difficult year for the GOP, amid high consumer prices and Trump's falling approval ratings.
"This issue is politically toxic, and if Republicans have a message that says let Big Tech run wild and let them do these hyperscale data centers all over the country, Republicans are going to pay a price at the ballot box," Steinhauser said, though he said he sees the GOP starting to coalesce around a stronger, pro-regulation platform.
Amid that political environment, both Texas GOP leaders have dipped their toes into data center opposition in recent months.
Abbott — who is polling slightly ahead of Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter labels "likely R" — in 2015 signed legislation creating new sales tax exemptions for large data centers and as recently as November called Texas the "epicenter of AI development."
But Abbott in recent months has shifted his posture toward data centers. In August, he unveiled a new plan that instructs state regulators to audit all proposed data centers seeking to connect to Texas' power grid before allowing projects to proceed. Abbott went a step further this week, ordering the state's environmental regulator to halt all data center-related permits, including those that aren't seeking to connect to the state's power grid, while an audit of the existing waitlist is completed. He's also suggested the state legislature, which will not meet again until 2027, repeal the data center tax break.
Paxton — who has faced scandals including a 2023 impeachment over corruption allegations, in which the state Senate acquitted him, and felony securities fraud charges, which were dropped in 2024 — voted in 2013 as a freshman member of the state Senate in favor of a sales tax exemption for data centers. He also has refrained from issuing an opinion — first sought by local officials in February — on whether Hood County had the legal authority to halt data center development in the area.
But in late August, he introduced a "Texas first" data center plan, which called for the passage of legislation to bar Chinese technology from powering U.S. data centers and hold AI companies criminally liable if their chatbots harm children. Paxton also said he'd support legislation introduced by Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., that would ease federal regulation to allow data centers to build customized electricity systems, sparing the existing power grid and preventing utility cost hikes, according to Paxton.
Paxton's announcement of the plan, posted to X, was flagged by the social media platform as being "made with AI."
Both Abbott and Paxton, through their spokespeople, declined multiple requests for interviews.
"Governor Abbott is taking decisive action to ensure data centers pay their own way, protect Texas water and power, and meet strict standards before connecting to the grid," Eduardo Leal, Abbott's campaign press secretary, said in a statement.
Abbott has received millions of dollars in contributions from AI and data center interests, including $500,000 donations from xAI founder Elon Musk and from Bennett, the Black Mountain CEO. Paxton's campaign and affiliated groups have received more than $400,000 from individuals and companies with data center ties, The Washington Sun reported.
In response to CNBC's questions, Paxton's campaign, through spokesperson Madison Cercy, shrugged off those contributions and instead attacked his opponent, state Rep. James Talarico, calling him a "hypocrite and a liar."
A pro-Talarico super PAC, Lone Star Rising, which has spent more than $3 million in support of the Democratic Senate candidate, has received more than $11 million from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, a key AI and data center investor.
Campaigns are legally forbidden from coordinating with super PACs, and Talarico has called for the political fundraising groups to be banned.
'Epicenter' of a crisis
Anxiety over AI and data centers has only grown following a call to action by former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who resigned from the company, then posted to X: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." That prompted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to urge other tech leaders to slow AI development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Musk endorsing Amodei's call.
"I think data centers brings together a lot of the issues that people are concerned about: cost of living, corruption in our government, artificial intelligence, and the fact that our government seems to be MIA when it comes to creating guardrails for this new technology," Talarico, who is leading Paxton in most Senate race polls, told CNBC on the sidelines of a food drive in Dallas in early September.
"All of those issues are kind of combined in this problem of data centers, and it's why it's so emotional for Texans. We're the epicenter of this data center crisis," Talarico said.
The Cook Political Report lists the Senate race as a "toss up," though Republican groups are flooding Paxton with campaign cash in the closing months of the campaign. The new super PAC tied to Trump, the No Going Back PAC, has spent about $935,000 on Paxton.
But as much of Washington scrambles to get its arms around emerging AI risks, elsewhere in the country, opposition to data centers does not necessarily indicate animosity toward AI.
"I never used it," McCallister said, when asked his thoughts on AI. "I could go the rest of my life without using it, but I know a lot of people can't. So I'm not pro- or I'm not anti-AI." When it comes to data centers, he said, "I'm just focused on regulations. Put these in places that make sense for the communities, not places that make sense for the data centers."
A boon or a burden?
Data center developments have flooded into Texas, with its pro-business ethos and vast swaths of open land, in recent years. The state could overtake Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to projections from the real estate services company JLL.
That interest from developers could have benefits, industry advocates argue.
Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, said projects often come with massive capital investments and added tax revenues that can be reinvested into schools and local infrastructure. Diorio said data centers are also job creators, particularly for construction workers during build-out, and don't sap natural resources to the extent many opponents believe.
"We see throughout the country data centers using as much, if not less, water than a large commercial office building," Diorio said.
While Talarico and Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor, have been outspoken in their desire to rein in data center development, both are taking a nuanced position.
Hinojosa has called for a moratorium until laws can be passed to protect people from potential impacts on the environment, local economies or the power grid. Talarico has rolled out a plan that he said would require data center companies to pay for their own energy, recycle water and provide jobs as a condition of being built.
"It's not a black-and-white issue," Talarico said. "Because if a community feels like these data centers can be a benefit, then I trust those communities to make those decisions for themselves."
'An existential threat'
On a Thursday night at the University of Texas at Austin, Hinojosa sat in an upstairs common room of a fraternity house.
Downstairs an hour earlier, more than 100 college students had skipped the local bars — or at least delayed their arrival — to hear Hinojosa speak about her campaign. They crammed into the musky parlor of the Tejas Club, where the only beverages that night were of the non-alcoholic variety.
It was the latest in a series of unusual rooms in which Hinojosa has found herself on the campaign trail.
Recently, that included a trip to a home in Red Oak, a suburb of Dallas, where she sat in the host's living room with a group of data center opponents that she described as "all MAGA."
"It was people who typically don't give someone like me a chance. And they were very curious about my campaign. They were very curious about me," Hinojosa told CNBC in the upstairs living room after the event. To her right, a concert poster for the band Geese hung on a door. Behind her, a shotski — a prop for communal shot-taking popular on college campuses — leaned against a wall in the corner.
There was not universal agreement on all issues in that room in Red Oak, Hinojosa recalled. But the first question the group asked her, she said, was about data centers, one of which is proposed nearby.
"It is a threat to their families, to their homes, to their communities, to their way of life, to their water that they drink," she said. "So it is, for many Texans, a kind of existential threat. And I have met single-issue voters on it."
Appealing to those voters will be key for Hinojosa and Talarico in a state where Republicans have dominated for decades. And Talarico, in particular, may have a plausible path to victory. Not since Beto O'Rourke came within a few points of defeating Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018 has a Texas Democrat generated the national attention Talarico has.
But it remains unclear just how many Republicans in deep-red Texas will be willing to defect and how big of an issue data centers are for the average Texas voter.
"Concern about the economy and cost of living remain far and away the most important issue to Texas voters right now," said Joshua Blank, research director at the nonpartisan Texas Politics Project. Data centers have become a "persistent area of focus," he said.
But Blank said the question of whether they play a role in determining election outcomes will depend on "broader questions about economic stewardship and whether or not data centers or data center developers are getting preferential treatment when people feel like ... their own cost of living is going up."
Red to blue?
Chris Tronzano is a landscape architect and a "hobbyist" rancher who moved with his wife in 2021 from Dallas County to Fannin County, where they hoped to retire. Shortly after, a battery energy storage system —which can be used to help power data centers — went up next door. Then, they learned a data center could also be coming to the area.
Tronzano, a Trump supporter who said he has always voted straight down party lines for Republicans, said the news scuttled their plans. They sold their property and moved again, this time to nearby Grayson County. The experience soured him on Trump and other Republicans who have advocated for data centers. And it tested his political loyalties.
"Why is he on this huge push for data centers?" Tronzano asked, of Trump. "If they're so important and so needed for national security, or there's this fight between us and China — what exactly is it? I don't think the normal citizen understands it."
Citing his data center frustration, Tronzano said he likely won't vote for Abbott this year and is undecided on Paxton. But it's more likely he'll skip those races than vote for Democrats, who as a party he feels espouse a progressivism that doesn't sync with his values, he said.
Meanwhile, McCallister said he's never voted for a Democrat but he's considering it for the first time. He still hasn't settled on his choice for governor and Senate, but he said data centers will be the top issue as he makes his decision.
He is soft-spoken and mild-mannered, with a bushy beard that covers the lower quadrant of his face, and he has an aversion to social media. He didn't set out to get into the weeds of Texas data center politics, but he's become an unlikely and outspoken grassroots leader on the issue.
Overcoming his social media skepticism, McCallister recently created a Facebook page and launched a nonprofit calling for stricter data center regulations. There, he's connected with a network of Texans opposed to data centers. He says many are just as disillusioned with the Republican Party as he is.
"No longer do we just vote red all the way down," McCallister said. "If your elected official is not listening to you ... you should replace that person."
— Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

She’s 28, Loves God and Her Family, and Might Be the Reason You Can’t Have Kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

By 5 am every morning, Emma Waters is on the sofa with a blanket, plotting America’s baby-making future. For two hours, she stays off her phone, inspired by Deep Work, the self-help bestseller. At 7:30, she does emails. Waters, 28 years old, is a monk of productivity who makes motherhood look like all-natural Adderall.
At 8 am, it’s time for breakfast and the Bible. Waters tries to live her life according to the mantra “Love God, get married, have babies.” She asks that I not use the real names of her two daughters for their safety, even though they’ve been printed elsewhere. I’ll call them Gertie and Ophelia, which are close enough.
All morning, they play. Ophelia, the baby, runs around in white tights, shirtless, clutching a pink purse; Gertie’s doll won’t stop crying. Jack, Waters’ husband, flits in and out. There isn’t much to say about Jack, other than that he’s hot, is studying to be a preacher, and has a big desk at home, much bigger than Waters’, featuring a bust of Nietzsche. In the same room, Waters has a pull-out secretary where she takes meetings, not far from a portrait of a glowering President Trump.
The only thing Waters doesn’t really do is exercise; she hasn’t found the time.
Not many people outside of DC have heard of Waters, who mostly works from home in a dreary Pennsylvania suburb named after a long-offshored manufacturer. Yet Waters is a factory for policy papers and op-eds extolling the harms of unregulated reproductive technology, probing the moral issues that liberals don’t want to touch with a 10-foot turkey baster. At least once a month, reporting on fertility, I ask for an academic source and am instead directed to Waters, author of a biblical women’s leadership book that basically says the best thing about the Barbie movie was the patriarchy.
The craziest thing is that, in certain ways, she’s a voice of reason. America’s $10 billion fertility industry is suffering a massive PR crisis that makes the embryo mix-ups and baby-selling schemes of yore seem quaint. A few recent headlines: “The Chinese Billionaires Having Dozens of US-Born Babies Via Surrogate,” “The Family Law Loophole That Lets Sex Offenders Parent Kids,” “California Couple Busted for Running Suspected Baby Mill,” “Surrogate Mother Who Refused to Abort Baby Gives Birth Amid Ongoing Legal Dispute.” Polygenic testing companies promise today’s parents that they can pick the tallest, smartest, least-bald offspring, mainstreaming debates about the “Black-white IQ gap.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—a father via surrogacy—and Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong are invested in an embryo-editing startup. If you believe what they told The Wall Street Journal, their first gene-hacked baby has probably already been born.
Many right-wing techies are jazzed about these developments, which might bump up birth rates or create “better” spawn. Many liberals don’t know how to talk about the ethical pitfalls. Emma Waters fills in the gaps. As a kind of backroom wheeler-dealer and political strategist, she is the mastermind behind Florida’s recent ban on international surrogacy, the Texas GOP’s souring on IVF, and the squashing of Trump’s “fertilization president” initiatives. This God-loving, JD Vance–stanning Gen Z-er might be standing between you and your ability to have a family, or she might be, somehow, the force that makes it possible. Waters has so much to teach us about optics and politics and why, in so many arenas, Democrats are losing so dramatically. Waters wants to dismantle fertility as we know it. And she wants to do it politely, during nap time, with her husband’s permission.
Waters wasn’t always political. She and her three younger siblings were homeschooled by their mother in a poor, rural part of southern Georgia, while their father worked 60-hour weeks as a facilities manager and HVAC repairman. (Waters describes her local high school as the kind of place where one-third of students got chlamydia.) Growing up, Waters never felt aligned with either party: Republicans praised free trade and cheap widgets; Democrats pushed equal pay and shoved kids into day care.
Then, in her junior year at a Christian college in Tennessee, Waters heard a podcast interview with JD Vance. “Everything he says, I relate to,” she remembers thinking. When she graduated a year later, in 2021—as valedictorian—she applied for an internship at American Moment, a training ground of sorts for rising conservatives. They gave her a full-time job.
Around this time, she met Jackson Waters at a mock-government event. Emma recounts their “whirlwind romance” in her book, Lead Like Jael. After “a summer of tense conversations,” she broke up with him “on a whim.” She wanted a career in politics; the thought of being a wife and mother felt like “a major letdown.” With the help of a pastor, she realized she only had these notions because of girlboss feminism. She begged Jack to take her back and got married at 24. She was an anomaly even among Republicans. Waters had heard older colleagues refer to women who got married at that age as “child brides.”
Waters loved life in DC: walking 24,000 steps a day, getting coffee with everyone and their mom, hosting dinners in her basement. When she got pregnant with Gertie, she and Jack wanted to prove that life didn’t end with a baby. But she needed a job with more flexibility that would eventually allow Jack to attend in-person seminary. In 2022, Waters approached the Heritage Foundation, the most influential conservative think tank. Heritage had recently shed its intellectual bona fides to become a MAGA mouthpiece; the next year, it would release Project 2025, the playbook for Trump 2.0.
Waters pitched Heritage that she would cover emerging fertility tech as an analyst: crafting policy briefs, penning op-eds, whispering into politicians’ ears. Waters found traditional pro-life policy banal—everything was about abortion. Debates around IVF started and ended with “Are embryos people?” She wanted to apply her dual major in political science and biblical studies to cutting-edge science. At the time, it seemed like “the least popular policy issue,” she says, but she promised the bosses it would soon be a big deal. They were sold.
Waters found her conservative colleagues ignorant about the state of assisted baby-making. One Hill staffer emailed Waters about a test that counts embryos’ chromosomes, asking, “Will this be around in 10 years?” It had been around for decades. At that point, a Chinese scientist had already embryo-Crispr’d babies, gone to jail for it, and gotten out. Sex selection had become a standard part of American IVF; the first sex-selected people were in their thirties. It was easier to open a surrogacy agency than an ice cream cart or a tanning salon.
Then there was China. In 2023, more than two years before mainstream media outlets reported on Sino-US infant import-exports, Waters was on Fox News, accompanied by an article headlined “Chinese ‘Rent-a-Womb’ Industry Using American Surrogates Is a National Security Threat.” She called it “the new face of birth tourism.” Intended parents didn’t even have to leave the country. Our nation’s lax laws meant that you could ship sperm over and get an American citizen shipped back.
Waters hates it when people harp on what she’s anti. Instead, she wants people to focus on what she’s pro: pro-“human flourishing”; pro-“the human person,” including embryos; pro-man-woman marriage; pro-life (duh); pro-Natural Procreative Technology, by which infertile heteros of breeding age clean up their diets, reduce their plastics, and ultimately get knocked up according to God’s will. Pronatalist? She prefers “pro-family,” which implies more straight marriages where straight penises and vaginas produce tons of babies. (Critics would add that the goal is really white Christian babies.)
Waters never says she’s against IVF per se. She doesn’t talk about “murdering” embryos; she makes it sound more like negligent manslaughter. She mostly argues that IVF doesn’t work. It encourages young women to postpone their true calling by falsely reassuring them that there’s still time.
To Waters, IVF is the conduit for many horrors. Ranking and selecting embryos tricks parents into thinking they can choose and control what kind of children they have, cheapening God’s handmade gift into an off-brand dustmop plucked off an Amazon wish list. It allows you to outsource reproduction to surrogates, objectifying women and commoditizing babies. Decoupling sex, marriage, and procreation distorts the natural order. Infertility explodes. Civilizations collapse. In her work, Waters fastidiously avoids mentioning gays, singles, or women over 40. When I ask her about this omission, she gets defensive: “It’s not about the desires of adults. It’s about the rights and well-being of children.”
Waters is a Republican, but that doesn’t mean all Republicans agree with her. The vast majority of Republicans support IVF as is. The pronatalist movement has two factions, the tech right and the trads. The tech right sees artificial wombs, surrogacy, and genetic optimization as tools to boost birth rates. Trads, like Waters, think these things will make the problem worse.
Besides China, nothing rankles Waters like embryo screening tools that promise to let parents “have your best baby.” Nobody really expects these so-called polygenic tests to move into the mainstream or ever become very accurate, but they set the tone for a future where parents can edit their children’s genes. On X, Noor Siddiqui, CEO of the startup Orchid and one of Waters’ least favorite founders, wastes no time in shaming breeders who fail to optimize. Getting knocked up the old-fashioned way is irresponsible: “What if your baby never walks?” Siddiqui has posted. “What if they’re never able to live independently? What if you could have stopped it … but chose not to?” (Stopping it, in this case, means making sure your disabled child isn’t born.) “Just be honest: You’re OK with your kid potentially suffering for life so you can feel morally superior, or because you can’t be inconvenienced.” In a decade, Siddiqui warns, all babies will be born using IVF and her test—Waters’ definition of dystopia.
Like many at Heritage, Waters was disappointed when Trump included free IVF in his 2024 platform, later declaring himself the “father of IVF” and “the fertilization president.” But Waters still found fertile ground (sorry) filled with low-hanging fruit. There were zero federal regulations governing surrogacy—she would shepherd the first one. “We have model legislation to SHUT DOWN foreign nations who rent the wombs of American women,” she wrote on X. She would rail against the creepy, unpopular polygenic tests that are opposed by every professional society. With the nation’s most influential conservative organization backing her, she’d push to mainstream so-called restorative reproductive medicine that co-opted the language of social justice while addressing the root causes of women’s broken, barren bodies.
Last November, waters sat onstage at the Heritage Foundation wearing a faux leather dress, slouchy boots, and a periwinkle double-breasted blazer while dozens of protesters in red Handmaid’s Tale cloaks screamed on the sidewalk outside.
I’d come to DC to meet Waters in person. It was a tough week for the organization. Its president had taken heat, and nearly had to resign, for defending Tucker Carlson’s choice to platform Nick Fuentes, a white supremacist. (Fuentes: “Hitler was awesome. Hitler was right. And the Holocaust didn’t happen.”) I wondered if there were always a dozen cops outside of the building. Sometimes the roar and the sirens were so deafening it was hard to hear Waters, but the disturbance seemed to make her smile.
First, Waters warmed up the room by having a “chat” with a mom who gets told by libs that she should’ve aborted her disabled son. Then Waters turned to the main event. “Welcome, gentlemen,” she said. She had assembled four white experts for “Editing Destiny,” a panel on the subject of polygenic tests and gene editing. Two seemed like MAGA partisans. Two were legitimate academics.
Waters had the energy of a high school newspaper reporter with a blowout and makeup that perfectly concealed her prominent chin. Everyone agreed that somatic gene editing on “born people” was good. Waters pointed out how it served the MAHA goal to eliminate disease at the source. But germline gene editing, the panel also agreed, was risky and unnecessary. No one said “fetus” or “God”; instead they evoked “the human person” and “flourishing.” Ben Hurlbut, one of the academics, made a moving, secular argument against polygenic selection. This was the “first relational act” you make with your future children, he told me, and it invites a serious rift.
Around the room, young female staffers in tight dresses held microphones for Q&A. The panel took a few questions. One attendee noted the harms of Tylenol.
After the event, Waters introduced me to Austin Rogers, then general counsel to Florida senator Rick Scott. Rogers wore a green Rolex with his hair gelled up in the front—he wouldn’t have looked out of place at a nightclub. Rogers told me they were using Waters’ model legislation to try to ban surrogacy from “foreign adversaries.” He was looking for a Democratic partner. He mentioned the latest story, covered by every major outlet, of a Chinese couple in California who had commissioned at least 25 surrogates to carry their children—a perfectly legal scheme—only to allegedly abuse most of those children in a mansion. He said, “I read it and my hair was on fire.”
That night, I walked Hurlbut, the academic, back to the train station and asked him why he agreed to speak at the Heritage Foundation. It wasn’t about party politics, he said. These issues couldn’t be split cleanly into left and right. “Anyone taking this seriously is creating a service to the public discourse,” he said. I asked who the big players were on the liberal side. “Big players? There are no big players. Just a few voices crying in the wilderness.”
Two months later, I visit Waters at home, in the type of town where hotels keep their lobby doors locked at all times. “I’ll have lunch to share with you,” Waters emails. When I arrive, she is wearing heeled boots and trendy jeans, making a butternut squash soup with bacon and brie. Ophelia watches from her high chair, wearing white tights underneath a fancy outfit. Over the next 27 hours, Waters will serve her husband and me a parade of elaborate orange foods: frittata with broken spaghetti, clementines, clam chowder (yes, also orange). (The girls will also eat Cheez-Its, Goldfish, and chicken nuggets.)
I recognize her hospitality tactics from Lead Like Jael, specifically the chapter titled “Motherhood as Warfare.” Waters advises women to embrace distinctly feminine means of influence. “No woman in the Bible picked up a sword to fight,” she tells me. Waters named her book after a biblical matriarch who offered an enemy commander a place to stay and then pierced his head with a tent peg, thus winning the battle.
I fear I am the enemy commander in this story.
In the book, Waters urges: “Take up your ladle like a sword. Stand behind your stove like a sentinel.”
Her house is modest yet beautiful, full of damask furniture. Christmas cards ring the kitchen doorway. In one photo, Simone and Malcolm Collins, the prominent pronatalist couple who embrace the term “hipster eugenicists,” smile from behind thick black glasses. On the credenza next to the dining room table, there’s a gilded Bible, a Venetian clock, and a ring light that never turns off.
Jack, home for lunch, says grace. Even 13-month-old Ophelia clasps her hands, closes her eyes, and bows her head.
Waters gets things done by being very, very nice. Simone Collins tells me, “I don’t know a single person in the pronatalist movement who doesn’t like Emma. She’s golden.” Even though the Collinses promote polygenic testing, IVF, and surrogacy, Waters considers them friends and makes a point not to publicly criticize them. In any given hour, Waters laser-focuses on a single issue. Another conservative tells me, “She could do an event with someone on Tuesday and be on the opposite side of a protest on Friday.” When she gets into a flame war with someone on X, she invites them to collaborate.
That’s how she secured the special guest for today’s Zoom working group: the founder of a polygenic testing company. One Tuesday a month, during nap time, Waters hosts private discussions with a group of bioethicists, activists, and policy wonks. Many potential collaborators do not want to be associated with Heritage, so Waters does much of her work in secret. She paraphrases a sign that Ronald Reagan kept on his desk in the Oval Office: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”
In the glow of the ring light, Waters and I huddle around her dining room table. I’m allowed to join if I don’t name names: I recognize a few prominent pro-lifers, and one or two liberals. “There is no dispute about how the technology works,” the polygenic testing founder says. He hammers home that two papers a day are being written about the associations between genes. His vibe oscillates between nerd and evil professor. He repeats at least a dozen times that his technology works. “There are ideologues masquerading as experts. You can easily fool a WIRED reporter into writing into her story that it doesn’t work.”
Waters asks a question about “children who have been born already.” Then someone asks about a recent paper showing that the sibling with the tallest-seeming genes is actually only the tallest about 25 percent of the time. This implies that, three out of four times, “picking the tallest baby,” well, wouldn’t work. The founder is irritated. One person might be predicted to be taller by 1 centimeter, but the error bars are 2 centimeters. “Falling within the error bars of the model means it’s successful,” the founder says.
Waters chimes in: “If the solution from a polygenic risk score for breast cancer was euthanasia, people would have a problem with it.” Then, she adds with a smirk, “That’s probably already happening in Canada.” To Waters, embryos are “human people”—but she won’t belabor the point or argue about metaphysical priors. The founder reminds us, “If you want to call it eugenics, you can, but don’t say it doesn’t work.”
Many of Waters’ critics dismiss her as a fool because of her retrograde gender views, which underpin all her other ideas.
I read Lead Like Jael in one sitting; my eyes got dry from popping so far out of my head. “There’s a hierarchy in marriage,” Waters writes. She advises her readers to become “good at being a woman” by “cultivating distinctly feminine strengths,” such as good posture. In an analysis of Greta Gerwig’s Barbie movie, patriarchy was “the first real innovation,” she writes. “Strong and godly men propel society forward.” Waters analyzes how, in the official portraits of First Lady Melania Trump, even her nails and eyebrows focus on the greater mission. She urges readers to redefine success as a joint pursuit, beginning with a husband’s career. Parents should start talking about marriage and motherhood at the same age as they ask kids what they want to be when they grow up. Women’s work should be flexible and easy to pause: “To neglect the home to pursue work is to invert God’s design.” Women are there to “support and strengthen” but not replace men. “Rightful authority” begins with husbands in the home. Women can lead, but only about 8 percent of the time.
Sitting in a trendy café, radiant in a puffy-sleeved red sweater and an Oura ring, Waters explains to me that the difference between men and women goes back to Genesis. Adam’s names mean “ground” and “man.” Eve’s names mean “fire,” “woman,” “mother.” So men are supposed to dig holes while women launch rockets? No: “A man is pulled toward the ground,” Waters says. “The wife is pulled to her husband and her children.”
She goes on: “We don’t want to go back to the 1950s. God put us in our time for a reason.” Still, there’s a lot to learn from the halcyon days when all 50 states allowed marital rape. Waters explains that the problem with the 1950s was that technology, like the dishwasher, stripped women of meaningful labor. “What would have been amazing is if women had radically rethought what they could do with the time they’d been given”—instead of just turning to wage labor. Despite providing most of the childcare, working full-time, and supporting her husband through school, Waters claims that balancing work and motherhood hasn’t been that hard. (Waters isn’t even so hot on federal paid family leave, since it encourages moms to go back to work.)
Here’s where I admit that Waters and I have more in common than I could have imagined. I got married at 25. I love being married and raising my child. We both go to church every Sunday (though mine has a gay pastor). I find it sad how young people see pregnancy as a funeral dirge for their hopes and dreams. I, too, expect low birth rates to cause big problems, and I suspect many “childfree” people will experience regret in 20 years. I’m inspired by Waters, how she cranked out more than 150 policy papers, interviews, and op-eds while I wrote this measly profile. I’m jealous of the time she spends with her daughters and how well behaved they are and how she managed to travel alone with a 4-month-old to Hungary to speak at a conference. But when Waters tells me that once you become a wife you have to subjugate yourself to your husband, it’s hard to keep a straight face.
If she wants to boost marriage rates, I ask, wouldn’t egalitarian partnership be an easier sell? She doesn’t have an answer. “It never crossed my mind.”
There’s a glaring gap between what Waters professes—that a woman’s highest calling is the home—and what she does, which is support her family financially while being way more influential and successful than her husband. She reconciles this by, literally, doing it all, while swearing she will slow down her career at a moment’s notice. By that same token, it’s also hard to distinguish between what Waters really thinks, what she is supposed to say, what’s rage-bait, and if there’s any meaningful difference between those categories. Her X background used to be a photo of “What’s Wrong With ‘Equal Rights’ for Women?” by Phyllis Schlafly, an activist who started speeches by thanking her husband for allowing her to be there. When I ask her about it, Waters says, “If your enemies think you’re oppressed, play up the trope.”
On the right, optics are everything. “How you project yourself is a political message,” Waters says. Before coming to DC, she had eight piercings, including belly button and eyebrow rings, but she didn’t want to be perceived like that. “Your appearance shows what you value,” she says. “I really value dressing well and pleasing my husband.”
If Waters had her way, there might be some IVF, but it wouldn’t involve ranking, destroying, or indefinitely freezing embryos. The only lawful surrogacy would be altruistic for heterosexual married couples with a documented history of infertility. (The gays, singles, and AOCs of the world would, in other words, put children’s well-being first and just not have them.)
In an international context, some of Waters’ views are perfectly normal. Almost every wealthy country besides the US bans elective sex selection. Every other wealthy country bans commercial surrogacy, which the UN called a form of violence against women and “the sale of children.” UN committees see anonymous gamete donation as incompatible with children’s rights. Most Western countries require tests to undergo some kind of approval process before going to market, so polygenic tests are out. In Germany, parents need government approval to genetically test embryos. Through a global lens, American Big Fertility is bizarro.
But for Democrats, it’s often seen as too politically toxic to criticize the largely unregulated industry. Challenging almost anything about it—even just that private-equity-backed clinics conduct most IVF cycles—opens the door for critics like Waters. Businesses have framed picking the sex of your baby, or even picking your Aryan-est baby, as a matter of “reproductive autonomy” on par with abortion. Lefties who disagree mostly keep their mouths shut. It’s almost too easy for Waters. Google will send anyone disturbed by the status quo straight to her op-eds.
While Waters invites journalists to her home and cooks them elaborate meals, some fertility professionals blame the reporters who dissect the scandals. After I wrote about a surrogacy gone wrong last year, Ron Poole-Dayan, the executive director of Men Having Babies, told me, “You are the problem. Journalists like you are a big part of the reason gay men can’t have families.”
People working in assisted reproduction see so many happy stories of family formation, they don’t even seem to understand what the problem is. At a recent conference for a surrogacy and egg donation ethics group, one attendee remarked, “An airplane takes off and lands a thousand times, and no one writes a story. A plane crashes once—everyone writes about it.” Someone else chimed in, “And flying is safer than driving!”
At the conference, surrounded by attorneys and professionals who seemed earnestly invested in doing the right thing, I thought of the left’s purity test problem: wanting so badly to be 100 percent correct that you forget how you look; ceding the hard topics to your opponents, who can wrap a kernel of truth in a bundle of nonsense; getting defensive when you could’ve invited the enemy in for a bowl of orange soup.
The biggest criticism lobbed at Waters is, obviously, that she wants to turn America into The Handmaid’s Tale. The second biggest criticism is that she’s a hypocrite. Waters’ kids aren’t in day care, but that doesn’t mean she doesn’t have help. At Waters’ house, I was surprised to meet a relative who consoled sobbing dolls and occupied the children while Waters entertained me and Jack studied the Bible or whatever. Waters’ mom is also a “full-time grandma” to Gertie and Ophelia.
The third biggest criticism is, let’s say, her credentials. “She’s not an academic. She’s not someone who actually has experience in these things,” says Lauren Hall, a political science professor at Rochester Institute of Technology. The feminist writer Jessica Valenti has essentially called Waters a failed influencer.
It’s not easy being an influential conservative mom who tells other moms of young kids to stay home. Criticisms of the Heritage Foundation, meanwhile, come from both the left and right. It’s “the worst-case scenario for a woman,” says Hall. She says Heritage puts “token” women forward, who have to hew to “a very particular party line.” In early 2025, an anonymous staff member sent letters to Heritage trustees alleging discrimination against childless women.
Waters disagrees, of course—she’s a fierce defender of Heritage. “America first,” she tells me. “MASS DEPORTATIONS NOW!” she tweets. She admits that Nick Fuentes says some “disgusting” things and describes him as “a young white man” who was “disenfranchised by the Republican Party because he dared to question our relationship with Israel.” When I ask her about the GOP’s unofficial strategy of “no enemies to the right,” a big-tent welcome for neo-Nazis and white nationalists, she snaps back, “Don’t you think the left is the same? Normalizing pedophilia. Abortion until birth. Rampant antisemitism … Why do you think Josh Shapiro wasn’t the vice presidential nominee?”
Waters’ master plan to undermine the fertility industry seems to be working. In November 2025, Senator Rick Scott proposed the SAFE KIDS Act, banning citizens of “hostile foreign regimes” from participating in surrogacy. In Florida, a similar law passed at the state level in May. At the start of 2026, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier stepped in to try to get two French dads un-recognized as their son’s legal parents, calling surrogacy “unconstitutional” and “modern-day slavery.” In July, Uthmeier intervened in another case, arguing that Florida should ignore an intended parent’s California parentage order, seemingly in opposition to the Full Faith and Credit clause of the Constitution. A proposed bill in Kentucky would ban all commercial surrogacy.
When Trump called himself “the father of IVF” in 2024, it looked like Waters had lost the battle against petri dish kids. But in June, Texas’ GOP denounced the procedure, and Trump has thus far reneged on his promises to make it free. In a recent grant application, the Department of Health and Human Services called frozen embryos “children.”
Many observers tell me they think Waters’ work is “the driving force” in pushing fertility regulation out of the fringes and into the mainstream. They also tell me the new laws are insincere and bad, fraught with unintended consequences. For example, the Florida attorney general’s anti-surrogacy argument would seem to prohibit Evangelicals’ sacred cow, adoption. Courts may challenge some of these laws in the coming months and years, but there’s no denying that American baby-making is going trad. On August 6, Trump issued executive orders banning birth tourism and denying passports to surrogate babies with foreign parents—measures proposed by Waters.
Her star continues to rise. Waters got a second book deal earlier this year (working title: Rethinking Fertility) and is contributing to a documentary about cryopreservation called Frozen Orphans. She recently presented at a Harvard summit on embryo law and ethics; four of the 20 other speakers have referenced Waters in their work. She is not opposed to running for office, although of course it will have to wait until her kids are older. In early September, she gave birth to her third child: another girl.

- U.S. prosecutors accuse Sebastian Marset of being one of South America’s biggest kingpins, charging him with money laundering, smuggling cocaine on the high seas and narco-terrorism.
- Marset, a native of Uruguay, is fighting his case, arguing there is no jurisdiction to prosecute him in a Virginia federal court because his alleged crimes had no connection to the U.S.
- In his first interview since being captured earlier this year, Marset spoke to The Times from jail and questioned the charges against him: “I still don’t know what I’m doing here,” he said.
Prior to his capture this year, Sebastian Marset was reputed to be one of the world’s most prolific drug traffickers, allegedly sending mountains of cocaine — 10 tons or more per shipment — from South America to Europe.
A native of Uruguay, where authorities say he proclaimed himself “King of the South” and led a criminal network dubbed “Primer Cartel Uruguayo,” or the first Uruguayan cartel, Marset, 35, has been described in some media reports as his country’s version of Pablo Escobar.
But unlike the infamous Colombian kingpin, who flooded American cities with cocaine in the 1970s and ‘80s, there is little evidence to show Marset ever moved any product to the United States.
And yet for six months, Marset has been jailed in Alexandria, Va., facing a list of federal charges that has grown longer since his arrival. Initially indicted only for alleged money laundering, he has since been accused by federal prosecutors of conspiring to smuggle cocaine on the high seas and narco-terrorism.
The case, Marset’s lawyers and some legal experts say, reflects the degree to which the Trump administration has stretched the purview of the Department of Justice when fighting its war on drugs.
Beyond blowing up dozens of boats suspected of carrying cocaine — a campaign critics denounce as both cruel and ineffective at staunching the flow of drugs — the White House has taken to labeling cartels as terrorist organizations and pushed countries to hand over suspected traffickers without going through the standard extradition process.
Marset’s prosecution offers a new twist, with the U.S. attorney’s office in the Eastern District of Virginia pursuing charges against him despite few indications his alleged criminal activities had any impact on Americans.
Marset’s lawyers have pointed out in court filings that he is not “alleged to have ever sent even a gram of cocaine to the United States,” arguing there is no jurisdiction to prosecute him in Virginia.
Even the charge that he laundered money through the U.S. financial system, his lawyers say, is flimsy, hanging on a single transaction — out of more than 200 identified by prosecutors — that the feds say was routed through a bank server in Richmond, Va.
In a phone call with The Times from jail, his first interview since his arrest, Marset fumed about the case.
“I don’t owe the United States anything,” he said in Spanish. “I still don’t know what I’m doing here.”
It was around 3 a.m. on March 13 when Bolivian intelligence agents came for Marset.
He claims they stormed his residence with guns blazing, firing indiscriminately into the room where he lay sleeping with his partner and their children.
“They dragged me out naked because I was in bed,” he said. “They rushed me into a vehicle and took me straight to the airport.”
For years, Marset had slipped through the fingers of law enforcement in multiple countries. He was jailed for a time in Dubai, but managed to secure his release and vanish just as authorities resumed their manhunt for him.
To build his trafficking network, U.S. prosecutors charge that Marset partnered with the Primeiro Comando da Capital, Brazil’s largest criminal organization, and the Clan del Golfo, a paramilitary group that controls cocaine production and smuggling routes in Colombia. Both were recently designated by the Trump administration as foreign terrorist organizations.
He amassed a fortune, much of it held in cryptocurrency, U.S. court records show, and lived a life of luxury while on the run, sometimes hiding in plain sight. Lanky, with sleeves of tattoos that extend to his neck and wrists, he cuts a striking figure. He allegedly used his illicit wealth to fulfill his dreams of playing professional soccer, buying himself a spot in the starting lineup for teams he bankrolled.
He’s also been accused of ruthless violence, including allegations — which Marset denies — that he ordered the detonation of a grenade at the headquarters of Uruguay’s federal anti-narcotics police, killed members of his organization he suspected of betrayal, and directed the assassination of a Paraguayan prosecutor who was gunned down while on his honeymoon at a private beach resort in Colombia.
His pursuers managed to track Marset to Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia’s economic hub, by planting a GPS tracker in his girlfriend’s luggage as she traveled through Brazil, according to U.S. court filings.
The Bolivians promptly handed Marset over to agents from the U.S Drug Enforcement Administration, who flew him to Peru and then Washington.
The justification for prosecuting Marset in Virginia is that one wire transfer for $31,800, sent from a bank in Portugal to a bank in China on Feb. 18, 2021, allegedly passed through a Bank of America computer server.
Marset, his attorneys maintain in court filings, “did not personally take any action to conduct the wire transfer,” adding that there’s evidence it actually occurred in Pennsylvania, not Virginia. The transaction’s link to the United States, they say, was both “ephemeral and unforeseeable.”
Even if Marset was smuggling drugs as prosecutors allege, his attorneys argue that his “conduct had no connection to this country whatsoever.”
After Marset’s lawyers pointed out that the charging documents allege he only smuggled drugs to Europe, prosecutors filed a response that said if the case went to trial, they would introduce evidence that he did, in fact, send cocaine shipments to the United States. They have offered no explanation as to why Marset is not already charged with that crime. The U.S. attorney’s office in the Eastern District of Virginia did not respond to questions about the case.
The government’s resources, Marset’s legal team asserts, would have been better spent pursuing other targets.
In his phone call from jail, Marset echoed that sentiment. “I never even talked about the United States,” he said. “I didn’t even want to know where on the map it was. I wasn’t interested in the United States at all.”
Marset hails from a neighborhood on the outskirts of Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo.
His father worked for a factory that manufactured plastics — “trays, bags, and all that kind of stuff,” he said — and as a truck driver. His parents split up when Marset was 8, leaving him to be raised by his mother.
“It’s been a hard life,” he said. “I grew up very humbly.” His first serious run-in with the law came in 2012, when he was reportedly caught receiving a large shipment of marijuana. Marset was imprisoned from 2013 to 2018 in Uruguay, but maintains there was never any hard proof of his involvement in the drug trade.
“To this day, all they’ve done is call me a suspected drug trafficker,” Marset said. “Because no country has been able to prove the drug trafficking everyone’s talking about.”
Despite his efforts to avoid incurring the wrath of Uncle Sam, Marset eventually came into the crosshairs of the DEA.
On March 27, 2025, according to court filings, DEA agent Michael Greisen tried a direct approach: He messaged Marset on WhatsApp, warning that he was under indictment and should turn himself in.
“We wanted to inform you and explain how you could resolve your issues with the United States discreetly and professionally,” Greisen wrote, according to a translation provided by prosecutors. “You have the chance to set things right. Otherwise, you are simply waiting for the day of your imminent capture.”
Marset did not take kindly to the admonition.
“Justice doesn’t exist,” he responded in one message, according to U.S. prosecutors.
“I am smarter than the entire DEA put together,” he allegedly said in another.
Marset’s lawyers claim the exchange so enraged the DEA that it set out to capture and prosecute him by any means necessary. They assert that the DEA orchestrated the raid on Marset’s home in Bolivia, arranging for him to be turned over immediately to avoid the usual extradition process.
Federal prosecutors said in court filings that, although DEA agents were “briefed on the operation before and after it occurred,” they were “not involved” in planning or executing the raid. They dispute that the Bolivian agents shot up Marset’s home, stating he was “arrested without incident.”
The DEA’s handling of Marset after he arrived in the U.S. has also been a point of contention.
While being transported from the airport to jail, Marset’s lawyers say, the DEA agents asked him to “donate” $4 million in cryptocurrency that was held in various accounts.
Marset, his attorneys say, “believed that the request for a ‘donation’ was the equivalent of an extortion attempt.”
“In every country, it’s become clear to me that all they want is my money,” Marset told The Times. “I thought it wouldn’t be like that in the United States.”
Prosecutors said the agents never asked for a “donation” from Marset and allege that he has sought to “intentionally mischaracterize as unscrupulous what are in fact standard law enforcement practices.”
Some former federal prosecutors said the government may have overplayed its hand with the case. They questioned why the narco-terrorism charges against Marset were added only after he began fighting his case.
“This is a reach, so far as I can tell,” said Bonnie Klapper, a former federal narcotics prosecutor in the Eastern District of New York. “They’re really trying to bootstrap one statute on top of another.”
David Weinstein, a defense attorney not involved in Marset’s case, who previously worked as a narcotics prosecutor in Miami, echoed that assessment. He suggested the narco-terrorism charges were probably brought to ramp up the pressure on Marset to make a plea deal.
“It gives a more salacious nature to what was originally just a money laundering conspiracy case,” he said.
The judge presiding over the case ordered a hearing on Wednesday, where both sides will argue why the charges should stand or be dismissed.
Meanwhile, Marset has been biding his time in jail. He said he passes the days by watching soccer on TV, though he has been unable to play since suffering a knee injury prior to his capture.
He called the narco-terrorism charge against him “absolutely ridiculous” and claimed that his efforts to combat the charges had made things personal with the U.S. attorney’s office.
“The justice system today, worldwide, is rotten to the core,” he said. “The prosecutor doesn’t want to do justice. The prosecutor wants to beat me.”

UK police arrest six at protest against migrant boat that spent 36 hours at sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:59:59 UTC
18:59:59 KST

The Home Office said in early September that the number of crossings in August had fallen to their lowest level since records began in 2018, with migrant arrivals also at their lowest number since 2020.
UK police said they arrested six protesters after an anti-immigration demonstration in southern England "became hostile towards officers" as a boat carrying migrants spent 36 hours crossing the Channel from France.
Facing a crackdown from French and British authorities, migrants desperate to cross to the UK have been adopting new strategies in recent months, including relying on larger dinghies and utilising new routes.
That has sparked renewed anger in England, with anti-immigrant protesters gathering in southern coastal towns with plans to foil the arrival of asylum seekers.
Around 200 protesters, some in black clothing and wearing face coverings, gathered in Gosport in the south to protest the anticipated arrival of a migrant boat, UK media reported.
The flimsy vessel had spent 36 hours at sea according to the UK's volunteer coastguard. The dinghy carrying 51 migrants landed in Dover in the southeast instead.
French authorities said migrants on board the "ill-suited" boat had refused assistance because they were "determined to take all risks to reach the United Kingdom."
The occupants had spent "more than 33 hours at sea in precarious conditions," said a statement issued by the French government's Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea.
Earlier this month, hundreds of demonstrators gathered in an attempt to block asylum seekers who had arrived by small boat in Portsmouth, in the southern county of Hampshire.
Authorities fear Hampshire, where the arrival of small boats has been rare, is becoming a new destination for crossings.
The vessels usually arrive further east in Kent, where the distance across the Channel between the French and British coasts is shorter.
French officials also say they are facing "increased" pressure as migrants attempt to depart from further west, where the border patrol is more sparse.
Britain has been grappling with how to curb the perilous journeys, which have spurred support for the hard-right Reform UK party.
The Home Office said in early September that the number of crossings in August had fallen to their lowest level since records began in 2018, with migrant arrivals also at their lowest number since 2020.
But in recent months authorities have reported an increase in the number of passengers travelling per boat.
According to Home Office data as of Sunday, 17,480 migrants have crossed the Channel in small boats since the beginning of the year.
This is a tiny fraction of the overall number of people seeking to move to Britain every year. The vast majority arrive via legal routes, government data shows.

3 killed, over 40 injured as Russia, Ukraine trade accusations about overnight airstrikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:59:46 UTC
18:59:46 KST

Burc Eruygur
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
- Ukraine claims it shot down 122 drones launched by Moscow overnight
 
At least three people were killed and over 40 others were injured in Russia and Ukraine as both countries continued to trade accusations concerning overnight airstrikes on Wednesday.
 
In Ukraine, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said on Telegram that a warehouse, a fuel station, and an office building in the Holosiivskyi district and another fuel station in the Darnytskyi district were damaged in an overnight attack on the country’s capital, during which drone debris also fell at a location in the Solomianskyi district.
 
“As of 10 am (0700GMT), one person has died and seven others have been injured following a hostile attack on the capital,” it said.
 
*The KMVA later said that the number of those killed in the Ukrainian capital had risen to two, while 23 others were injured.
 
Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said that one person was killed after Russian strikes targeted port and civilian infrastructure in the southern region, including an Antigua and Barbuda-flagged commercial cargo vessel and an unspecified number of warehouses.
 
“Due to numerous Russian attacks, rescuers from the Mykolaiv region have joined in the efforts to extinguish the fires,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said, commenting on strikes in the Odesa region.
 
The DSNS also reported that 12 others were injured due to strikes in the country’s Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr regions.
 
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses shot down 122 Russian drones overnight.
 
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed hitting a storage facility and an industrial enterprise in Kyiv and its surrounding region that are allegedly involved in the production of drones and drone components.
 
It also claimed striking three logistics centers in Odesa used to supply Ukraine’s military, a drone warehouse in the Odesa region, and a vessel “while it was delivering military cargo to the port of Odesa.”
 
Earlier, the ministry further claimed that it shot down 514 drones launched by Ukraine overnight over 18 regions, as well as the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
 
Alexander Shuvaev, acting governor of Russia’s border region of Belgorod, said in a statement that eight people were wounded in five districts due to Ukrainian strikes over the past day, with two of them in serious condition.
 
In the border region of Bryansk, acting governor Yegor Kovalchuk said two people were injured due to Ukrainian drone strikes in the villages of Kryukov and Churovichi.
 
Ukrainian authorities have not yet commented on strikes in Russia.
 
Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
 
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

A young man was stabbed with a knife at Brøndbyøster Station on Wednesday.
A young man was stabbed with a knife at Brøndbyøster Station on Wednesday, Copenhagen West Police said on Politi Update.
The man was taken to Rigshospitalet for treatment. Police said they could not immediately provide information about his condition.
Police have arrested a suspect in connection with the stabbing.
Copenhagen West Police’s press unit told Ritzau shortly before 4 p.m. that it would not provide further information about the case at that time.
Police were still working at the scene Wednesday afternoon. S-trains were running but were not stopping at Brøndbyøster Station, according to DSB’s website.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.
Stena Line has ordered two new hybrid ferries for the route between Frederikshavn and Gothenburg, with the vessels expected to enter service in 2030.
The company announced the order in a press release Wednesday.
The ferries will be built at a shipyard in China. They will be E-Flexer vessels with room for 1,500 passengers.
The hybrid ferries will run on both electricity and conventional fuel. They are expected to continue doing so until charging options allow them to operate fully on electricity.
“It is a historic investment for Stena Line, which gives us the opportunity to take another step in the sustainable modernization of our fleet,” Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line, said.
“They support our goal of reducing CO₂ emissions and preparing the fleet for future environmental requirements,” he said.
Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.
Educational institutions nominate candidates for the prize each year. Relevant groups of rectors then assess the nominations and decide which candidates are put forward to the Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization.
Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
