Russian Regions Slowly Reimpose Fuel Purchase Limits Amid Ongoing Refinery Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:23:34 UTC
18:23:34 KST

A growing number of Russian regions have recently seen the reintroduction of fuel rationing measures to combat shortages of gasoline and diesel caused by Ukrainian drone strikes against major oil refineries throughout the country.
In the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, Governor Vladislav Shapsha announced the return of an odd-even system based on vehicle license plate numbers and a ban on sales into portable canisters starting Wednesday.
“The lines [at gas stations] are back. This causes reasonable frustration,” Shapsha wrote on Telegram.
In Siberia’s Zabaikalsky region, authorities announced a cap of 15 liters (4 gallons) per vehicle on AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline grades across 48 gas stations. Fuel reserves in the region stood at 17,000 metric tons, which are expected to run out in 20 days.
Zabaikalsky’s regional government stressed that 106 out of its 249 functioning gas stations were selling fuel without any restrictions.
Both announcements follow Ukrainian drone attacks on three key Russian oil refineries in Moscow, Samara and Ufa over the last three days. The Ukrainian military claimed this week that it has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity.
Last week, authorities in the Leningrad region surrounding St. Petersburg capped gasoline sales at 30 liters (8 gallons) per vehicle until at least Oct. 1. They described the region as the epicenter of a second wave of Russia’s summer fuel crisis after Ukrainian attacks on the Kirishinefteorgsintez (KINEF) refinery knocked it offline in August.
Nearly one in five independent and small gas stations had suspended work because they have been unable to buy wholesale fuel on the St. Petersburg exchange, Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko said.
Drozdenko said oil companies expect fuel supplies to stabilize in October.
The average price of gasoline in Russia has climbed 21% since the start of the year, with a single-week increase pushing the national average to 78.51 rubles per liter ($3.39 per gallon) as of Sept. 14.
Russia has banned gasoline exports through Jan. 31, 2027, along with diesel until the end of October, to stabilize the domestic fuel market.

Türkiye’s Hakan Fidan hosted Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan al-Saud, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty at the Turkish House for the sixth meeting of the R4 on Sept. 21.
A joint written statement about the meeting was released on Sept. 22. The meeting comes at a moment when Saudi Arabia is under constant attacks from Houthis in Yemen who are also threatening the maritime security through the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The ministers said the meeting provided an opportunity to exchange views on recent regional and international developments and affirmed the importance of continued consultation and coordination among the four countries to support peace, security, stability and prosperity in the Middle East and the broader region.
“Expressing deep concern over continued tension and hostilities in the region, the ministers underscored that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only path to a sustainable resolution and, in this context, underscored the need to uphold the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding for lasting peace and stability,” read the statement.
The ministers also strongly “condemned all attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including the recent Houthi attacks, and reaffirmed their unwavering support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and security of the Kingdom.”
They also “affirmed the Kingdom’s inherent right to defend itself, its territory and its people, in accordance with international law and the Charter of the United Nations.” They also stressed the importance of safeguarding the safety and freedom of maritime navigation.
According to the statement, the ministers also discussed recent developments in the Middle East, especially the Palestinian issue.
“The ministers reiterated their support for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including their inalienable right to self-determination and to establish an independent, sovereign, viable and contiguous State of Palestine on the basis of the June 4, 1967, lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions,” read the statement.
Türkiye, Syria, Saudi Arabia trilateral meeting
In the meantime, the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Syria have met for a trilateral meeting, according to Turkish officials.
Fidan and al-Saud meet with Syria Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shibani again at the Turkish House on Sept. 22. There was no statement after the meeting.
As part of his bilateral meetings, Fidan met British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband as well. Later, he attended a multilateral meeting under the leadership of France, Canada and the United Kingdom on the first anniversary of the New York Declaration and the 20-Article Comprehensive Peace Agreement that paved the way for the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas.

Black Sea drone strikes endanger Turkish sailors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:20:12 UTC
18:20:12 KST

The damaged Turkish flagged Lider Bordo Mavi container ship is parked at the Trabzon port after being attacked near the Russian port of Tuapse, in the province of Trabzon on September 15, 2026. (AFP Photo)
They’d just had breakfast when a huge blast brought the crew of the Turkish fishing boat racing out onto main deck, where they were standing when the second strike hit.
“There was fire and smoke, the blast lifted us up and threw us left and right, it was very powerful,” said Ahmet Özlü, 40, one of five fishermen on board the Turkish-flagged Duru 67 that was hit by a drone off Crimea on June 5.
Such attacks on commercial vessels have multiplied in recent months as the Russia-Ukraine war has spilled into the Black Sea, with Turkish ships increasingly in the firing line.
A fire broke out and the boat began taking on water, so the fishermen rushed to the bridge where they found their captain and childhood friend Cüneyt Varlık, 45, lying in a pool of his own blood, his carotid artery severed by shrapnel.
The attack was never claimed but the Turkish coastguard told them it was a Ukrainian drone which hit them “by mistake,” he said.
“We never thought Ukraine would hit us because our flag was raised. We are civilians, our boat doesn’t carry weapons,” said his older brother, Mehmet Özlü, who suffered extensive internal and external injuries.
Both deeply traumatized, neither brother has been back out to sea due to their injuries, Mehmet explained while helping mend nets in the northeastern port of Trabzon.
“I still ask myself why Ukraine hit people like us, Turkish civilians. As a state, they owe us an answer and compensation because this has ruined my and my children’s future,” he said.
Despite its ties with both Russia and Ukraine, Türkiye has been infuriated by the violence, accusing the warring sides of “attacking all commercial shipping without distinction.”
“The recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea are unacceptable, regardless of who is responsible for them,” President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22.
Since the start of the war, 226 civilian and commercial vessels have been attacked in the Black Sea, the vast majority this year, Türkiye’s Chamber of Maritime Commerce (IMEAK) says.
“The fact that 163, more than 70 percent, were targeted in the first eight months of 2026 clearly shows the gravity of the situation,” IMEAK chairman Tamer Kiran said on Aug. 27.
Of that number, 22 Turkish-owned vessels were attacked in the preceding two months, he said. Four more have been hit since then, industry sources say.
Earlier this month, a Turkish defense source said “almost 90 ships” were hit in August, with a Turkish diplomat telling AFP last week Ankara had reached out with a fresh proposal.
Confirming the approach, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the sides had come back with “demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile.”
The Turkish Maritime Workers’ Platform has accused Russia and Ukraine of blatant disregard for civilian lives.
“Both states are disregarding the lives of seafarers solely to undermine each other’s economic interests,” spokesman Ahmet Baran Can told AFP.
Torun said many sailors were refusing Black Sea jobs.
“If the ship gets hit, the shipowner gets insurance money, and if it doesn’t, he earns 10 times what he’d get in Europe. But we’re the ones on board who get hit.”

Scientific progress must always
defend human dignity, Pope Leo XIV said at his weekly general
audience in the Vatican on Wednesday.

whole person and for all people—technical and scientific

The latest in a long spate of workplace tragedies in Italy occurred overnight at the Colosseum. 
    Around midnight, a 22-year-old rope-access worker—engaged in installing a new lighting system for the monument at height—fell approximately 10 meters. 
    Despite resuscitation attempts by Ares 118 emergency medical personnel, he died. 
    Carabinieri from the Rome Central Company and the Investigative Unit arrived at the scene, along with the medical examiner, the duty public prosecutor, and staff from the Labor Inspectorate and the local health authority's workplace safety unit (ASL SPRESAL). 
    The worker who died overnight inside the Flavian Amphitheatre was named as Andrea Moretti; he specialized in high-altitude rope work. 
    The Colosseum Archaeological Park and the Ministry of Culture (MiC) announced the news of the incident. 
    As a mark of mourning, the Park initially decided to close the second-tier section where the accident occurred to the public for the day; however, the area has not been seized by judicial authorities, who are currently working to determine the circumstances of the incident. 
    But after trade unions protested that the whole of the Colosseum should have been closed in a mark of respect and mourning, authorities subsequently ordered it to be shut for the day. It will be closed on Thursday too,
    Workplace deaths are a major problem in Italy and Premier Giorgia Meloni's government has said boosting health and safety is a major priority. 
    In November the cabinet launched a digital badge for contractors and sub-contractors on construction sites, aimed at improving safety. 
    Trade unions say an average of three workers a day die in workplace accidents in Italy. 
    On Tuesday workplace accident insurance agency INAIL said in its annual report that Italy registered 1,189 work-related deaths in 2025. 
    Although this was 37 fewer than in 2024, a drop of 3.02%, it still means that Italy is averaging over three work-related deaths every day. 
    The workplace-accidents-and-occupational-illness agency said nine students died in situations related to their educational activities in 2025, four fewer than in the previous year It said it received 600,000 reports of injuries in 2025, an increase of 1.2% on 2024, including 519,000 regarding workers and 81,000 regarding students.

Capturing the extremes: Meet the photographer that calls the top of Mount Fuji home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:17:56 UTC
18:17:56 KST

For most people, Mount Fuji is a destination. For Megumi Ueda, it has been a workplace and home for much of the past 17 years.
Japanese photographer Megumi Ueda spends the climbing season living and working at a Shinto shrine near the summit of Japan's highest mountain.
From 3,776 metres above sea level, she photographs sunrises, sunsets and the changing weather while warning climbers about the conditions they may encounter.
Ueda first climbed Mount Fuji in her early 30s after a friend recommended the ascent. She later applied for a job at a mountain shrine, allowing her to spend more time at the summit and take photographs.
A life at the summit
The first season was difficult. She says she had no access to a bath and little freedom, while large numbers of climbers passed through the summit. But the views convinced her to return.
“When I finally came down and turned around and looked at Mt Fuji, all those views came rushing back to me, and I just started crying,” she says.
Ueda has since returned for most climbing seasons. She now works at the shrine, helping prepare meals for staff, while also photographing the mountain.
Every morning, she wakes at around 04:00 to capture the sunrise. “You can’t create that scenery,” she says.
Ueda is particularly drawn to the shared experience of watching the sunrise with climbers from around the world.
“There probably aren’t many places where everyone, people from all different countries, looks in the same direction and shares that sense of awe together,” she says.
Showing the mountain's risks
Ueda's photography is not only about Mount Fuji's spectacular views. She also documents its harsh and unpredictable weather.
Human-caused climate change is having a severe impact on the mountain's weather patterns. The peaks of Mount Fuji typically get a sprinkling of snow by early October, but rising temperatures meant the Sumit was without snowfall until the beginning of November back in 2024.
This marked the longest period without snow since records began some 130 years ago.
Each day, Ueda measures the temperature and wind speed at the summit and posts the information online, together with videos showing the conditions.
She says the visual evidence can help people understand the risks better than figures alone. “At the summit, the temperature is like midwinter in February,” she says.
Strong winds can make it impossible to walk, while poor visibility can make conditions particularly difficult. “I think a lot of people simply don’t expect the weather to be that severe,” she says.
Helping climbers stay safe
More than 200,000 people ascend Mount Fuji during its official climbing season.
Ueda has been trained in wilderness first aid and says she has repeatedly helped with rescues near the summit. She has encountered people suffering from hypothermia after arriving inadequately dressed, as well as climbers who have fallen and been unable to continue.
The photographer says she wants her real-time updates to give people a clearer picture of conditions at the top.
“There aren’t any webcams or anything like that at the summit, so I want to be the one to communicate those conditions instead,” she says. “I’m doing this because I hope that seeing the actual conditions will help raise awareness about safety.”
Japanese media reported that at least six people died on the slopes of Mount Fuji during this year's climbing season.
Beauty and danger
For Ueda, documenting Mount Fuji means showing both sides of the mountain. She continues to photograph the sunrises that first drew her back to the summit, while using her social media posts to highlight the dangers that climbers may face.
“I want to keep thinking about how we can make sure everyone can enjoy climbing the mountain safely and return safely,” she says.
The climbing season has now ended. Ueda plans to return next summer, continuing to document life at the summit and the changing conditions on Japan's iconic mountain.

Daily extra cost of high diesel prices in EU exceeds $220M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:17:06 UTC
18:17:06 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Rising diesel prices driven by geopolitical developments cost the EU economy an additional €200 million (around $228 million) daily.
 
The Brussels-based environmental organization Transport & Environment published a report on Wednesday on the economic impacts of rising diesel prices in Europe.
 
The report noted that conflicts in the Middle East and production cuts at Russian refineries reduced the supply of refined petroleum products.
The organization highlighted the widening gap between crude oil and diesel prices. It said rising fuel costs in road transport added a daily burden of €270 million to the European economy, with €203 million stemming from diesel consumption.
 
The document revealed that the total extra cost faced by the EU economy due to road diesel reached €40 billion since the US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
The report said road transport accounted for 77% of diesel and gas oil consumption in the EU. It added that diesel vehicles made up 38% of passenger cars on EU roads, making the bloc the world’s most vulnerable region to high diesel prices.
The report said EU diesel car users faced an average extra cost of €19 per tank, while truck operators incurred an additional €236 per week. It noted that 30% of diesel vehicles in Europe were older than 15 years.
The organization suggested that lowering highway speed limits by 10 kilometers per hour, promoting eco-driving techniques and expanding carpooling could reduce diesel demand by 15% in the short term.
 
It also recommended implementing scrappage incentives for old diesel vehicles, accelerating the transition to electric vehicles, taxing oil companies’ windfall profits and increasing investment in electrification.

Türkiye follows Ukraine, adapts anti-tank missile against drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:15:36 UTC
18:15:36 KST

- Roketsan's KARAOK anti-tank missile struck an aerial target for the first time, following a pattern seen in Ukraine of anti-tank missiles adapted against drones.
- The Turkish Army has used KARAOK against ground targets since 2022, and Roketsan has not disclosed further details on the aerial test.
Roketsan, the Türkiye-based missile manufacturer, said its KARAOK anti-tank missile struck an aerial target for the first time, firing the shoulder-launched weapon from a turret mounted on a light tactical vehicle. The company announced the milestone in a Sept. 23 post on X, along with footage showing the missile launching from a turreted mount on a pickup truck and intercepting a target drone built to mimic a Shahed-type one-way attack drone.
KARAOK is a man-portable, fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile designed to be operated by a single soldier from a shoulder-fired tube. It weighs less than 16 kg (35 pounds) including its launch tube, measures 125 mm in diameter, and uses an imaging infrared seeker to track targets in day or night conditions, with an effective range beyond 2,500 meters. Mounting the missile on a vehicle-based turret lets it be aimed and fired without a soldier holding the launcher, a configuration more common among dedicated air-defense systems than infantry anti-tank weapons. Türkiye’s army has used KARAOK against ground targets since it entered service in 2022.
The test follows a pattern that has become common in Ukraine’s war with Russia, where anti-tank guided missiles built for armor have repeatedly been adapted to hit aerial targets, including the Shahed-type drones Russia has used extensively against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment demonstrated its Stugna-P anti-tank system shooting down a Russian drone on Sept. 13, and Ukrainian forces have separately built an improvised air-defense system called STASH that pairs U.S.-made AGM-114 Hellfire anti-tank missiles with a RADA radar to intercept jet-powered Shahed-type drones traveling too fast for interceptor drones to catch.
That overlap exists because many anti-tank guided missiles already carry the sensors needed to track a moving target and the terminal guidance to steer into it, qualities that work against a drone or slow cruise missile almost as well as against a tank. The U.S. Javelin was designed with some capability against slow, low-flying aircraft from the outset, and Hellfire missiles fired from Apache helicopters have long been used against aerial drones in addition to their primary anti-armor role.
KARAOK has also drawn interest beyond Türkiye. Malaysia signed a contract to become the system’s first foreign buyer, with Roketsan planning to deliver an initial batch of launchers and missiles to the Malaysian Armed Forces in early 2026 to replace the Russian-made Metis-M anti-tank system already in service there. Roketsan has not said whether the turreted, anti-drone configuration shown in this test will become a standard offering or remains experimental.

"We remove places where young people can gather in small groups, then panic when they gather in large ones"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:15:06 UTC
18:15:06 KST

"We remove places where young people can gather in small groups, then panic when they gather in large ones"
Paranoia over so-called "teen takeovers" ignores the fundamental problem: that our cities have left young people with nowhere to go, writes Christopher Martin.
America this summer acquired the phrase "teen takeover". Large gatherings of young people, organised online, appearing in downtowns, malls and parks.
Some involved violence and yes, plainly these incidents require a response. But the phrase itself is revealing.
Perhaps before asking what is wrong with these gatherings, we should ask a more uncomfortable question
Takeover. As though young people appearing en masse in the centre of their own city constitutes a territorial incursion.
London had its own version this spring, and across Europe, anxiety about youth alienation, political disengagement and unrest is growing.
A recent academic paper calls the way cities respond to young people the "patronising city", highlighting that young people are tolerated in public space principally when supervised, consuming or behaving according to adult expectations.
So perhaps before asking what is wrong with these gatherings, we should ask a more uncomfortable question: where did we expect young people to go?
Disappearing youth clubs, the library that no longer opens late, the cheap cafe that is now a chain, the recreation ground, the shopping arcade, the public bench, and the ordinary bit of city in which nobody particularly minded if you spent an afternoon doing nothing. All gone.
These "third spaces" – neither home, nor school or work, but the informal spaces between them – are where relationships form and social life happens. For young people, they are particularly important because home and school are not really theirs. They generally do not own property, are too young for bars and often lack the money required to participate in an increasingly commercial urban culture.
The contemporary city has become remarkably intolerant of people without obvious economic purpose
Axios reported this summer that the disappearance of malls and affordable hangouts, combined with public spaces that frequently feel hostile to teenagers, is leaving American teenagers with fewer places to gather.
The resulting mass meet-ups are then treated as evidence of the problem rather than, perhaps, evidence of the demand. We remove the places where young people can gather in small groups, then panic when they gather in large ones. There is a wonderful circularity to this.
The contemporary city has become remarkably intolerant of people without obvious economic purpose. Pavements must move pedestrians. Kerbs must load or charge something. Squares need events. Walls carry advertising. Parks acquire cafes. Railway concourses funnel passengers past retail with more enthusiasm than they guide them onto trains.
Connected to this is the issue we have, as adult society, with loitering. There are few words in the municipal vocabulary more suspicious than loitering. Nobody describes an elderly couple sitting outside a cafe in Rome as loitering. They are participating.
Loitering is what other people do. More precisely, it is what people without obvious economic purpose do.
Artist Nils Norman began documenting the architecture of this anxiety in the 1990s. His Contemporary Picturesque recorded the studs, barriers and small devices appearing in increasingly managed and privatised city centres. While the original picturesque gave us ruins, grottoes and serpentine lakes, the contemporary version gives us stainless-steel knobs attached to a granite ledge so that a 15-year-old cannot grind a skateboard along it. One civilisation built follies. Ours builds anti-follies.
We worry about screen time while removing the reasons to leave the screen
And the skateboard stud is more interesting than it looks. Its entire purpose is to prevent somebody finding an unintended pleasure in an object.
Skateboarders read architecture incorrectly. A staircase becomes an event. A handrail becomes recreational equipment. A ledge becomes a playground. They refuse the instruction manual set out by future generations, precisely as young people should.
This built environment, hostile to young people, is exactly what is being questioned by groups like Bristol-based campaigners Playing Out, saying Yes to Ball Games.
We worry about screen time while removing the reasons to leave the screen. We fret about social skills while closing third spaces. We complain that teenagers organise their lives through Snapchat and TikTok, then treat their physical arrival in the city as a public-order incident.
Apparently, we would like young people to spend less time online, provided they don't turn up anywhere. This is where the public realm stops being a discussion about paving materials and becomes something considerably more important.
The Council of Europe's new charter on youth participation says young people require the "means, space and structures" to participate in society. Space is not metaphorical. Democracy does not begin when somebody turns 18 and receives a polling card.
If we want young people to participate in society, society needs to find somewhere for them to participate
It is rehearsed through years of occupying shared places, encountering strangers, negotiating behaviour and discovering that other people are both fascinating and tremendously irritating. The public realm is where we learn to live with people we didn't choose.
This makes London's transformation of Oxford Street timely. One of the world's most commercial streets is now beginning its most significant reinvention in generations. Through this, Oxford Street can demonstrate that commercial success and civic generosity are not opposites; that one of Europe's great shopping streets can also provide something increasingly scarce in prosperous cities: space with no entry price and no instruction manual.
It matters far beyond London. Cities everywhere are worried about young people's alienation, their relationship with democracy, their social skills, their mental health and the amount of their lives disappearing into screens. Perhaps we should stop treating these as entirely separate problems.
If we want young people to participate in society, society needs to find somewhere for them to participate. A city that makes room for its young is not surrendering control. It is investing in its future.
Christopher Martin is co-founder and managing director of Urban Movement.
The photo was released by Tampa Police Department.

These are the most affordable Michelin Key hotels in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:15:01 UTC
18:15:01 KST

From a wine estate in the UK to an eco hotel in Spain’s Costa Brava, here are some of the world’s best hotels priced between €130 and €220 a night.
Now in its second edition, the Michelin Guide has just unveiled its latest selection of One-, Two- and Three-Key hotels across the globe.
As you might expect, those at the higher end of the scale have the price tag to match, with some properties coming in at upwards of €5,000 per night.
But that doesn’t mean you have to take out a second mortgage to experience the best hotels around the globe as there are some far more affordable One- and Two-Key options, particularly if you visit in off-season.
From the 2026 selection, Michelin Guide has rounded up the best-value gems across the globe that will set you back between €130 and €220 a night.
The most affordable Michelin Key hotels in Europe
Italy has the most hotels in Europe that have been awarded a Michelin Key, with 224 properties making the cut in 2026.
For an option that won’t cost you an arm and a leg, take a look at La Barchessa di Villa Pisani in Vicenza.
The 15-room Renaissance-style property is part of the City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto UNESCO World Heritage Site, yet a stay here is just €155 a night.
France boasts 220 keys, but for an affordable option around €160 per night, book a stay at Le Clair de la Plume.
The property in Grignan is just moments away from a medieval castle and fields of lavender, and it’s also home to the Michelin-starred Le Clair de la Plume.
The UK also has a healthy showing on the list, with 131 hotels with Michelin Keys.
For a stay that will cost around €218 per night, try Tillingham Winery in Rye. This wine estate has just 11 rooms, plus two glamping tents, and the Michelin-selected Tillingham restaurant on-site.
Spain has 122 Michelin Key hotels, and Can Mascort Eco Hotel in Costa Brava is among the most affordable.
Priced between €95 and €157 a night, the restored 17th-century property focuses on wellness with its Roman bath-inspired spa area.
Over in Greece, the best priced of its 74 Key hotels is Montanema Handmade Village in Thessaly.
At this sustainability-focused spot, shoulder season rates are around €220 a night, and for that price you can relax by the pool or in the spa with a cave sauna.
Last but not least, Neuwirt. Hotel & Wirtshaus in Bad Vigaun is among the least expensive of the 72 awarded hotels in Austria at €130 per night.
The family-run hotel has just 24 rooms, and has been welcoming guests to experience its hospitality and local gastronomy for more than 100 years.

El Nino-driven heat ‘could cause nearly 500,000 more deaths’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:11:50 UTC
18:11:50 KST

A firefighter sprays water in an attempt to extinguish a wildfire burning through a peatland forest in Pulang Pisau, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, Sept. 5, 2026. (AP File Photo)
This year’s powerful El Nino and the record global heat it’s driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a research report released on Sept. 23.
The grim warning by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab says that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be attributed to El Nino, compared with heat deaths expected in a typical year.
The heaviest toll, the group says, is expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, partly due to climate change and the fallout of the war in Iran.
Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the group and the study’s co-author, said the heat danger will likely persist beyond February, even though this El Nino is expected to end by then. The fallout of the weather phenomenon could be felt well into next summer, he added.
The research, he said, shows that heat is most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor.
“If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous,” he said. Wealthier places, he added, generally have greater access to air conditioning, reliable water supplies and functioning health systems.
The study by Greenstone and his colleagues also warns that the Global South, a term that isn’t geographical but a reference to developing countries in general, will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.

Skills for a new generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:10:28 UTC
18:10:28 KST

Skills for a new generation
Hong Kong has sent its largest construction squad to WorldSkills, where nine young competitors are putting their trades to an international standard while offering a glimpse of how careers in the industry are changing
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Some former CIC competitors have returned to construction sites, stayed at HKIC as skills ambassadors or started businesses of their own, including former welding competitors. Among this year's nine competitors, very different paths have led to Shanghai.
A different path into construction
Huang Tsz-ho was studying social science at university when he put his degree on hold for a year and turned to joinery.
With no family tradition in the trade, Huang had encountered woodworking before, became interested and searched online for courses. When the opportunity to compete came up, he decided to see how far he could take the craft.
Practice could run for more than 10 hours a day. Among the hardest demands is interpreting technical drawings at speed. Shortly before competition begins, competitors can be given dozens of pages of dimensions, structures and assembly details, with about an hour to absorb the information before work starts.
The hours have changed how he approaches work. “I used to find it hard to stay on one job,” Huang said. “Now I can keep at it.”
Tse Yu-lok, Hong Kong's welding competitor, took another path. Already working and with welding experience, he entered the local selection competition and earned his place in the squad.
Pipe welding is among the more demanding parts, he said. “If the method is right, you don't need force. Pipes are harder.”
Competition welds are subjected to X-ray inspection, making quality beneath the surface particularly important to the score.
Preparation has included mock competitions, physical conditioning and sessions with a psychologist. Two days before the squad left for Shanghai, previous welding representatives also medallion, returned to share their competition experience and talk Tse through what to expect.
Training against the world
Preparation began roughly two years before Shanghai.
What impressed Cheng was sometimes less about the workbench than what happened around it. At some camps, competitors were up at 7am and training until 10pm. Young people once reserved or uncertain about their prospects gained confidence as their work improved, he said, making the experience more valuable than winning a medal.
Parents seeing the team off for Shanghai suggested attitudes were changing too. Cheng believes more families are coming to regard skilled construction work as a career with opportunities for advancement.
The jobs awaiting them are changing as well. Some construction operations can already be controlled remotely, while off-site production has changed where and how certain tasks are performed. Manual skills may therefore be the starting point for a career that increasingly embraces technology.
Teaching the machines
That connection between established skills and new technology was also apparent at the WorldSkills Expo, where the CIC presented an AI assistant for construction safety, MiC tracking and sensing systems, a remote-controlled tower crane, a welding robot and S960 ultra-high-strength steel.
Cheng sees craftsmanship and automation as complementary. Robots can handle repetitive tasks, but someone who understands the trade still has to teach a robotic arm how to work or an automated spraying system how material should be applied.
Over the next five years, he wants HKIC to train what he calls construction's “special forces”: tradespeople who can work with their hands, operate robots, read BIM models and provide the knowledge needed to train AI systems.
A career with somewhere to go
CIC has participated in WorldSkills since 1997 and received seven Medallions for Excellence, including two at Lyon in 2024 in joinery and welding.
Shanghai also provides a chance to compare training with international standards. Cheng has arranged discussions with specialists from countries including Korea and Canada on vocational education and career progression, bringing lessons back to Hong Kong on how young tradespeople can advance.

Muslim bloc holds Kashmir meeting on sidelines of UN General Assembly in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:10:12 UTC
18:10:12 KST

Aamir Latif and Saadet Gokce
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
- New Delhi says ‘entire Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are integral and inalienable part of India’
The Organization of Islamic Cooperation's (OIC) Contact Group on Jammu and Kashmir, met Tuesday on the sidelines of the ongoing UN General Assembly session in New York, reaffirming its support for the Kashmiri people's right to self-determination
The foreign ministers and senior officials of the contact group's member states – Azerbaijan, Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Niger – attended the meeting, the OIC said in a statement.
OIC Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed reaffirmed the organization's commitment to supporting the Kashmiri people's "inalienable" right to self-determination, as a foundation for a "just and lasting" peace in South Asia, in accordance with UN Security Council resolutions and the principles of international law.
In a joint statement, the group expressed "serious" concerns over the "continued detention and denial of bail" of prominent Kashmiri leaders, Yasin Malik, Asiya Andrabi, and Shabbir Shah, who has been diagnosed with cancer, according to Pakistan's Foreign Ministry.
The group expressed solidarity with the government and people of Pakistan and indicated deep concern over military escalation in the South Asian region in May 2025, including the "unlawful and unwarranted" strikes carried out on multiple locations in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. They also stressed the need to exercise maximum restraint and avoid actions that would destabilize the region.
However, India Wednesday rejected what it called "unwarranted and factually incorrect references" to Jammu and Kashmir.
"The OIC has no locus standi to pronounce on matters that are strictly internal to India. The entire Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are integral and inalienable part of India, and no amount of repetition of politically motivated propaganda can change this reality. Repeated endorsement of such motivated narratives only raises serious questions on the credibility of OIC," India's Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.
The group welcomed the ceasefire between Pakistan and India following military escalation and expressed their appreciation for “the constructive efforts made by all countries to mediate and bring the two parties together to reach this agreement.”
Pakistan's top diplomat Ishaq Dar highlighted the "continuing" restrictions on political and civic space in the disputed valley and “attempts to alter its demographic, political, and cultural character.”
He said that Jammu and Kashmir remains an internationally recognized dispute on the agenda of the UN Security Council and stressed that no domestic legislation, judicial verdict, electoral exercise, or demographic manipulation could substitute for the Kashmiri people's inalienable right to self-determination.
The disputed region has been a key bone of contention between Pakistan and India since 1947. The two nuclear rivals have fought three full-scale wars -- two of them over Kashmir in 1948 and 1965 -- in addition to the Kargil skirmish in 1999.
India divided and downgraded the state of Jammu and Kashmir into federally ruled union territories -- Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh -- in 2019, a move rejected by Islamabad.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen held a tense meeting at UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday, according to the source.
The Ukrainian side expressed concern about a possible escalation by Russia in winter, particularly due to limited air defense capabilities to protect cities. Kyiv also voiced dissatisfaction with the EU’s decision to lift sanctions on two Russian oligarchs as part of an agreement to extend the sanctions.
“More defence support is coming. And as reforms in the Rada progress, more budget support too. We have €37 billion still available in this calendar year,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X after the meeting.
Ukraine has also asked its allies to help cover an unforeseen budget shortfall of about €26 billion ($30 billion) and called on the EU to speed up the disbursement of a €90 billion loan. The funds are intended to help Ukraine secure financing through the end of next year.
The EU, for its part, raised objections to some of Ukraine’s calculations and proposed involving other partners, including Canada, Norway, and Japan, in the additional financing. Zelensky told reporters that the sides’ teams would meet again in 7–10 days for further negotiations and expressed hope that an agreement would be reached.
Zelensky, following a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, said Ukraine was ready for an energy truce with Russia as a first step toward ending the war, provided Moscow stops attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. He said he had asked Trump to convey this position to the Russian side and involve Chinese leader Xi Jinping in the discussions, as he believes Xi has influence over Moscow. Trump is hosting Xi in Washington this week.

As previously reported by Ukrinform, the European Parliament and the Council of the EU, in February 2026, adopted a regulation establishing a loan of up to €90 billion to support Ukraine. The assistance consists of two complementary components: strengthening Ukraine’s defense capabilities and defense-industrial capacity, and support for the functioning of state institutions, provision of public services, and economic resilience.

Azerbaijan's President Aliyev pardoned French citizen Martin Ryan, jailed for espionage, as part of a deal in which France secured Usmanov's removal from the EU's Russia sanctions list. Ryan is expected to fly to Paris on Wednesday.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a decree on Wednesday pardoning several convicted individuals, including French citizen Martin Ryan, whose release was part of a wider agreement with Paris tied to the delisting of Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the EU's sanctions list.
Ryan has been released from prison and will arrive in Paris today, Euronews understands.
On Tuesday, Brussels renewed its sanctions list of more than 2,600 individuals and entities considered close to the Kremlin or supportive of Russia's war effort in Ukraine. France, however, secured the removal of Usmanov as part of the prisoner release deal.
Ryan was freed the following day under the presidential pardon, along with 19 other prisoners, four of them foreign nationals, though none an EU citizen.
According to a statement from Azerbaijan's presidential office, the pardon was "based on the principles of humanism" and "taking into account the personality, health, family status of the convicted persons, the nature of the crimes they committed and the degree of public danger, the period of their sentence and their behaviour during that period."
A French businessman, Ryan was arrested in December 2023 and later sentenced to 10 years in prison on espionage charges, accused of gathering information on the Azerbaijani armed forces for France's foreign intelligence service, the DGSE.
France publicly challenged the Azerbaijani proceedings, considering them arbitrary and based on an unfair trial.
Last week, Euronews reported that Paris was pushing to remove Usmanov from the sanctions list to secure the release of two French nationals detained in Azerbaijan, as part of a prisoner swap.
Euronews also reported on Monday that Azerbaijan would issue a presidential pardon.
Earlier this year, Azerbaijan was named alongside Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan in a letter sent by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, requesting Usmanov's delisting.
The other prisoner believed to be part of the agreement is French water-management executive Anass Derraz, who was sentenced to 12 years in prison for allegedly accepting a bribe in 2018 from an Azerbaijani-Russian businessman in connection with efforts to free an impounded yacht. Derraz currently remains in detention.
Usmanov denies any ties to Vladimir Putin's regime.

Study: Switzerland remains among top countries for pensioners

Study: Switzerland remains among top countries for pensioners
Switzerland remains one of the world's best countries for pensioners, ranking fourth in an international study after slipping one place from last year. In 2024, it topped the ranking.
Norway currently offers the best conditions for retirees, according to the “Global Retirement Index 2026” published on Wednesday by the French firm Natixis Investment Management. It is followed by Ireland and the Netherlands.
The ranking covers a total of 44 countries. Experts from the French financial institution analyse four criteria: retirement finances, material well-being, health and quality of life. In Switzerland, 400 private investors and 150 financial advisers were surveyed.
High life expectancy
Switzerland comes second in the health category – outperforming all other countries in terms of life expectancy. The country ranks a respectable third in the area of retirement finances, with low interest rates on savings being the main downside.
More
Retiring in Switzerland
By contrast, Switzerland still manages eighth position in terms of quality of life. The experts note a significant decline concerning “material well-being”, where it now ranks 15th. The study points in particular to the deteriorating situation in the labour market as a result of US tariffs, the strong Swiss franc and the UBS-Credit Suisse merger.
Pressure on systems
Overall, financial security in retirement is under increasing pressure worldwide, warn the study authors. They highlight the rapidly ageing population, record-high public debt and persistent inflation in many countries.
More
Pensions
Policy plays a crucial role in facilitating access to pension solutions and promoting long-term saving, they state, adding that each individual must also take personal responsibility for preparing for retirement.

Official: Russia’s satellite constellation nears 400 spacecraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:07:04 UTC
18:07:04 KST

- Roscosmos chief Dmitry Bakanov said Russia's satellite constellation has reached nearly 400 spacecraft, with about 60 launched in 2026.
- Roscosmos also touted the first Soyuz-5 rocket launch, a hydrometeorological satellite, and plans to improve GLONASS navigation accuracy to 2.8 meters by 2027.
Russia’s satellite constellation has grown to nearly 400 spacecraft, Roscosmos chief Dmitry Bakanov told Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin during a meeting this week, with roughly 60 satellites launched in 2026 alone.
The Russian government’s press service disclosed the figures as part of a broader update on the state space corporation’s activities.
Bakanov said two privately built optical-electronic Earth observation satellites are scheduled to launch from the Vostochny Cosmodrome in October, adding to a constellation Roscosmos says can already photograph the planet’s surface at any time of day. The Russian government did not name the companies building those satellites or disclose their specifications.
Mishustin, in the same meeting, described space research as a priority area that feeds new ideas into fields including economics, engineering, and science more broadly.
Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov and Bakanov also discussed Russia’s national space program and the industry’s broader development plans, according to the government’s readout.
Roscosmos separately listed several milestones from the third quarter of 2026. The agency launched a hydrometeorological satellite that transmits data on cloud cover and atmospheric conditions. It is also working on a next-generation configuration for the GLONASS satellite navigation system, Russia’s answer to GPS, which Roscosmos says will improve navigation accuracy from 8 meters to 2.8 meters by 2027.
The quarter also included the first launch of the Soyuz-5 rocket, a medium-class launcher Roscosmos says carries the world’s most powerful liquid-fueled rocket engine, the RD-171MV. That engine, built by NPO Energomash, produces roughly 740 tonnes of thrust at sea level and can lift up to 18.5 tonnes into low Earth orbit. The rocket lifted off from Baikonur Cosmodrome on April 30 as part of a joint Russian-Kazakh program called Baiterek, marking the first flight in a series of test launches for the new rocket generation.
Roscosmos also said it compiled what it describes as the most detailed X-ray map of the universe to date during the quarter, though the agency did not disclose further details on the instrument or survey behind that claim.
Russia’s satellite growth this year has run alongside a separate, long-delayed effort to build a domestic broadband constellation called Rassvet, intended to compete with SpaceX’s Starlink. That project remains far smaller in scale, with roughly 32 serial satellites launched by September 2026 against a longer-term goal of more than 900 by 2035. Roscosmos has not said whether Wednesday’s 400-satellite figure includes Rassvet spacecraft or Russia’s military satellites, which the agency does not itemize separately in public statements.

Greenland welcomes US military pact but trust still shaky

Greenland welcomes US military pact but trust still shaky
- Greenland welcomes the US-Denmark military pact, ending fears of US annexation but many remain distrustful of Washington.
- The agreement allows reopening of Cold War-era US bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, promising jobs but demands respect for local lifestyle.
- Residents are divided; some feel safer, others worry about increased military presence disrupting traditional hunting and fishing.
AI generated
NUUK/COPENHAGEN – Greenland’s government and residents expressed relief that a military pact with the US and Denmark may end anxiety over US President Donald Trump’s threats to seize their Arctic island, but many remain distrustful of Washington.
“I am incredibly relieved and think the outcome is very sensible. We can be satisfied,” Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic MP in the Danish Parliament, told Reuters.
Parliament Speaker Kim Kielsen urged households to raise the Greenlandic flag on Sept 23. Activist and influencer Orla Joelsen encouraged residents in the capital Nuuk to show up at the airport to welcome the prime minister and foreign minister back from New York where they struck the deal.
New US bases
The agreement allows the US to expand its military presence on Greenland, reopening Cold War-era bases in the settlements of Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, with a prospect of renewed spending and employment potential.
But it stopped short of Trump’s unsettling previous demand that the US annex Greenland to head off the growing Arctic presence of Russia and China.
“There has previously been a significant American presence in Greenland, so this is nothing new,” added Nathanielsen.
“However, in light of the unrest over the past few years, there is likely greater scepticism in Greenland, and consequently, work needs to be done to reassure the local population.”
The US first built military bases in Greenland during World War II. During the Cold War, it maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel to monitor Soviet forces. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 US military personnel.
Residents divided
Pitanguaq Mikissen, 69, a retired ship assistant, said the potential reopening of some old US bases gave greater security to the territory’s 57,000 people.
But not all residents were happy.
“I think that Trump is really good at creating a lot of worry and a lot of fear,” said Jensia Dam-Davidsen, 40, a voice and choir teacher.
“It (the deal) seems wrong in every way – especially now that Denmark has expanded their military presence here.”
Denmark has significantly increased its own military footprint in Greenland since Trump’s threats peaked in January, deploying additional troops, boosting Arctic defence spending and hosting allies under military exercises.
Malene Vahl Rasmussen, mayor of Kujalleq municipality in southern Greenland, where the US is looking to reopen the Narsasuaq military base, said that under the agreement US military expansion must respect the Greenlandic way of life to protect hunting and fishing.
“You can’t simply say, ‘Okay, we’ve signed this, so now we trust you again’. Trust really needs to be rebuilt within that partnership,” she told Reuters.
Some Greenlanders worry that expanded military activity – including increased aircraft and vessel movement – could disrupt hunting and fishing grounds that communities rely on for a living, though the agreement states such activity must respect Greenlandic society and traditional ways of life. In first, French presidential candidate gives birth during campaign
PARIS – French Greens leader and candidate in the 2027 presidential election Marine Tondelier said on Sept 23 that she had given birth to a son, emphasising that she would press on campaigning while prioritising the health of her child.
Tondelier, 40, was the first candidate in French politics to campaign while pregnant and, while acknowledging the challenges, she had expressed hope it would push issues including infertility and motherhood up the agenda.
Her boy Leon was born in Lens in northern France on Sept 18, Tondelier told AFP, saying the family had kept the news private for a few days.
He was born hours after Tondelier as Greens chief had attended a rare meeting at the Elysee Palace where President Emmanuel Macron had warned France’s political leaders over the risk of Russian hybrid attacks.
She told AFP that the birth had gone “very well”, adding that she would be “working differently” for a while and “trying to figure out how to balance a presidential campaign with a newborn, whose health and well-being come first”.
Already the mother of a seven-year-old boy, Tondelier was confirmed as the candidate for the Greens on Sept 21. In December, the party will decide whether to maintain her candidacy or withdraw and throw the party’s weight behind another left-wing figure.
Polls currently show Tondelier, who has the slogan “another Marine is possible!” in reference to far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen, lagging well under five per cent in the first round of voting.
She is planning on Sept 23 to take part in a video conference with her party and may even join a climate march at the weekend if her health and that of her baby allow.
The unplanned pregnancy followed a miscarriage and several unsuccessful attempts at assisted reproduction and in vitro fertilisation (IVF), which had put her plans for another child on hold.
She had carried on campaigning throughout her pregnancy while openly admitting to difficulties including vomiting in the toilets on a high-speed train.
“In the weeks ahead, we’ll have to get creative to balance a presidential campaign, daily life with a newborn, and both of our health, which will come first,” Tondelier wrote on social media platform X after the birth of her child.
“This campaign will also be an opportunity to talk about building the country which our children deserve,” she said.
She added it would also be a chance to discuss issues including reproductive health, infertility and the difficulties experienced by some women in the postnatal period. AFP

Gokhan Ergocun
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD) reported that global economic growth faces downward pressure from energy market shocks and the Middle East conflict, while investment in artificial intelligence (AI) supports trade.
 
Global economic growth moderated to 2.6% in the first half of 2026, down from 3.6% in the latter half of 2025 as output fell sharply in countries directly affected by the conflict in the Middle East.
 
A sharp reduction in energy supply from Gulf economies pushed up consumer prices globally while China helped balance energy markets by reducing its energy imports and oil consumption.
Global merchandise trade recovered gradually despite rising transportation costs; shipments of goods related to artificial intelligence significantly boosted trade growth in Asian economies.
EU natural gas stocks dropped to their lowest levels for this time of year in more than 15 years.
The US government introduced new bilateral tariff rates for multiple countries in July.
Headline inflation remained stable in June and July but increased in August across many G20 economies.
Long-term sovereign bond yields reached their highest levels in 15 years in most major advanced economies.
The organization projected global GDP growth of 2.9% in 2026 and 3% in 2027.
 
The US economy expanded rapidly amid strong investment in artificial intelligence, leading the OECD to forecast growth of 2.2% in 2026.
The OECD projected growth of 1% for the euro area in both 2026 and 2027.
 
China’s growth moderated to 4.5% in 2026 due to the government’s anti-involution policies.
India demonstrated strong momentum and received a 7.1% growth projection for the current fiscal year.
Türkiye had a 2.7% growth forecast for 2026 despite facing strong inflationary pressures.
Severe weather events such as El Nino raised concerns about global food commodity prices.
Many central banks raised their policy interest rates to ensure underlying inflation pressures remained contained.
Governments across the globe faced increasingly pressing fiscal challenges due to rising debt and defense spending.

Shifting to physical AI, Cognex to acquire Intel spinoff RealSense in $500 million deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:03:04 UTC
18:03:04 KST

RealSense, an Israeli company that develops AI vision technology for robots, has signed an agreement with Cognex Corporation, a US machine vision company.
The $500 million transaction marks one of the most significant strategic moves in Cognex’s recent history and will be financed entirely from Cognex’s existing cash reserves and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, pending regulatory approval. Cognex will also grant a $50m.stock option and incentive plan.
RealSense was originally founded by Intel in 2014 as its internal innovation division and was spun out as an independent company in 2025 when Intel was looking at major cuts. In August 2025, it signed a deal with Nvidia to integrate its advanced perception technology with Nvidia’s Jetson Thor robotic platform and has since become a key supplier of perception systems for autonomous mobile robots, industrial robotic arms, quadrupeds and emerging humanoid platforms.
The company employs 180 people in Israel, with 135 based in its development center in Haifa and the rest in Cupertino, California. Approximately 80 of those Israeli employees are expected to receive at least NIS 1m.each.
"RealSense was built on a simple idea: robots and autonomous systems can’t act intelligently in the physical world if they can’t first perceive it accurately. We’ve called that mission the Visual Cortex of Physical AI. Joining Cognex puts that mission on an entirely new scale, giving us access to a global industrial customer base and go-to-market reach that would have taken us years to build on our own. This is a combination that makes both businesses stronger," said Nadav Orbach, Chief Executive Officer of RealSense.
Prior to the completion of the deal, RealSense will spin out its Facial Authentication product line into an independent company, and will continue to focus on growth in the biometrics market.
With the acquisition, the company is expected to generate between $80m.and $90 m. in revenue in 2026, representing more than 50% growth over the previous year. The broader robotic perception market, currently valued at roughly $600m., is projected to grow more than 25% annually and reach approximately $1.6 billion by 2030.
Cognex, headquartered near Boston and operating in more than 30 countries serving over 30,000 customers worldwide, develops machine-vision systems that help manufacturers and distribution companies automate tasks such as inspection, measurement, identification, and robotic guidance.
The acquisition of RealSense is the company’s first purchase in Israel and expands the company into robotic perception and the emerging Physical AI market.
Physical AI refers to artificial intelligence systems that operate in the real world rather than in purely digital environments. These systems must perceive depth, motion, obstacles, and human behavior in real time, and then act on that information safely and intelligently. That requires a sophisticated blend of sensors, cameras, spatial understanding, and real-time processing- that’s the foundation for robots that can navigate crowded warehouses, drones to avoid obstacles, and humanoid robots that interact with people.
RealSense’s depth‑sensing cameras and perception software form the foundation of this capability, giving machines the ability to see and understand their environment with accuracy and reliability.
Cognex President and CEO Matt Moschner described the acquisition as a natural evolution for a company that has spent more than four decades building machine‑vision systems for factories, warehouses and distribution centers around the world.
“RealSense represents a compelling strategic expansion for Cognex into robotic perception, one of the most attractive adjacent markets in machine vision,” he said. “RealSense brings a leading 3D perception platform with proprietary technology, a strong developer community, and a compelling value proposition for customers. Combined with Cognex’s machine vision expertise and global reach, RealSense positions us to offer a full-stack visual intelligence platform, spanning industrial ID, 2D and 3D machine vision measurement to 3D depth perception and robotic navigation, built to serve the full spectrum of Physical AI.”
The rise of Physical AI is reshaping global industries from logistics and manufacturing to defense, healthcare, and consumer robotics. Robots are increasingly expected to operate in dynamic, unpredictable environments rather than fixed, pre‑programmed settings.

Estonian police detain 46 migrants in one week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:01:13 UTC
18:01:13 KST

In less than a week Estonian police detained 46 foreign nationals who had entered the country illegally from Belarus via Latvia; meanwhile, a court has remanded a 54-year-old Romanian citizen in custody on suspicion of organizing illegal migration, reports ERR News.
Over the past week, police detained foreign nationals lacking the legal right to be in the country in several Tallinn neighborhoods and near the Latvian border. Police learned of the unauthorized individuals through reports from local residents and information gathered by officers.
Five of the 46 migrants were detained in Pärnu County. On the 19th of September, around 11:00 AM, officers from the Pärnu precinct, together with Finnish border guards, conducted checks at the former Ikla border crossing point, where they stopped a car with Latvian license plates driven by a 54-year-old Romanian citizen. While an officer was speaking with the driver, a colleague noticed a human hand amidst the bags. Upon further inspection, police discovered five individuals attempting to hide behind the luggage. It was discovered that five individuals of South Asian origin were in the car with the Romanian national; they were attempting to travel illegally from Belarus, through Latvia, to Estonia.
The migrants are currently being held at a detention center in Tallinn, while the court has ordered the Romanian national to be remanded in custody. A criminal case has been initiated regarding the illegal transport of foreign nationals into Estonian territory. Prosecutor Keili Tiirik stated that the criminal investigation would determine the route the foreign nationals took to reach Estonia, though
preliminary information suggests they arrived in Latvia from a camp in Belarus.
Gathered evidence indicates that the Romanian citizen picked up the individuals within Latvian territory, concealed them, and instructed them to keep their heads down. This implies the suspect was aware he was illegally transporting people into Estonia and knew he would be punished if the transport were discovered.
So far this year, nearly 50 criminal cases have been opened in connection with the illegal transport of people into Estonia. Five individuals are currently in custody for the offense.
Since July, Estonian police have detained 187 individuals who entered the country illegally. Seventy-two individuals—who had no legal grounds to stay in Estonia and had arrived via Latvia from Belarus—have been returned to Latvia.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday observed that Gautam Buddha Nagar district magistrate Medha Roopam could not be isolated from the larger decision-making process that led to the detention of student protester Akriti Chaudhary under the National Security Act (NSA).While hearing Roopam's plea challenging Allahabad high court judgment, a bench of justices SC Sharma and NK Singh observed that if the decision-making chain ran "from top to bottom", the district magistrate could not be singled out.
"We can't isolate her... as fine of Rs 5 lakh," the apex court observed.Senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, appearing for the Uttar Pradesh government, submitted that the DM had acted on reports that passed through the SHO, DCP and commissioner before reaching her. He also pointed out that the NSA Advisory Board had examined the detention.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for Roopam, said there were five stages before the DM issued the detention order and that her role was to form an opinion after the statutory safeguards had been followed.
The hearing comes days after the Allahabad high court quashed the NSA detention of Akriti Chaudhary, a 25-year-old student who was taken into custody in connection with a workers' protest in Noida in April.
The high court found that the detention was based on a story "concocted" by the state and directed Chaudhary's immediate release if she was not required in any other case.It also directed that Rs 5 lakh in compensation be deducted from Roopam's salary and ordered that the court's displeasure against the DM and police officers involved in preparing the dossier be recorded in their service records.The Allahabad high court had also warned Roopam that continued "despotic" conduct by an "errant" bureaucracy could reduce Uttar Pradesh to an Orwellian dystopia.

====================================================================================================

peter zumthor’s expanded fondation beyeler begins its gradual opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:00:16 UTC
18:00:16 KST

The swiss museum’s new ensemble begins gradual opening
Peter Zumthor’s expansion of the Fondation Beyeler in Riehen near Basel begins its opening to the public, with the new ensemble gradually revealed from September 26th, 2026, ahead of its full opening in January 2027 (find designboom’s previous coverage here). Three new buildings, an expanded park, and restored historic structures extend the museum beyond Renzo Piano’s existing structure, creating a larger setting for art, architecture, nature, and public life. ‘This understanding of the place was important to me. I wanted my buildings to blend in so naturally, that it felt completely self-evident. It makes me happy when people now tell me they look as if theyʼve always been here. Thatʼs a wonderful compliment for my work,’ the architect says of the new architecture.
Zumthor has distributed the functions of the expansion across the Wyss Museum, Ammann Pavilion, and Erlen Torhaus, each responding differently to the existing landscape. The project also opens a formerly private section of the heritage-listed park to visitors, adding almost 10,000 square meters of gardens, meadows, trees, and water features to the museum grounds.
the expanded ensemble of the Fondation Beyeler, Wyss Museum by Atelier Peter Zumthor | Louise Bourgeois, Maman, 1999, Bronze with silver nitrate patina, stainless steel and marble, 927,1 x 891,5 x 1023,6 cm; Collection The Easton Foundation, New York© The Easton Foundation / 2026, ProLitteris, Zurich | image by Iwan Baan
three buildings instead of one large extension
Following a study involving 11 architecture practices, Zumthor’s proposal was unanimously selected by the international jury. The acclaimed Swiss architect divided the new functions between three buildings with distinct forms and materials, reducing the overall volume of the extension. ‘If we’d crammed all the functions onto a single plot, we’d have ended up with one big building with everything squeezed into a single box,’ Zumthor explains. ‘I like art museums that really only serve art, so I split up the different functions.’
The approach to the project also reflects his understanding of the site as a place shaped by an older pattern of villas, gardens, paths, and water. Zumthor says he wanted the new architecture to feel as though it belonged to the location rather than announcing itself as a separate intervention. ‘I wanted my buildings to blend in so naturally, that it felt completely self-evident,’ he adds.
the Wyss Museum adds around 1,500 square meters of exhibition space | image by Mark Niedermann
Peter Zumthor’s Wyss Museum centers on stone and side light
The Wyss Museum adds around 1,500 square meters of exhibition space across three floors. Its irregular Y-shaped plan was developed around an existing ginkgo, a redwood, and a group of plane trees, turning the constraints of the site into the organizing principle of the building. The large windows of the museum frame views of verdant surroundings, including the Jura and Black Forest on clear days. An upper-level terrace connects back to the park by an external staircase, extending the sequence of movement beyond the galleries.
The museum is constructed largely around Jura limestone, a material Zumthor uses across the building. The stone appears in benches and staircases, terrazzo floors, ceiling aggregate, and mineral plaster, while the rammed-concrete facade takes on a warm yellow tone from the local limestone. For the architect, the material was connected to the character of the site and to the idea of a new villa within the historic park. ‘It was clear to me that this park needed a new villa. And now it has one. Of course, a villa is not made of wood. It’s made of stone. And if it’s made of stone, it has to be my favorite stone: Jura limestone,’ he shares. The rammed-concrete facade was built by hand over almost a year by a single team, leaving subtle variations and traces of the construction process visible on the surface. Zumthor deliberately accepted these irregularities because they reveal how the building was made rather than presenting the facade as a perfectly uniform skin.‘You have to see how it came about,’ the architect highlights. ‘I want people to realize that this isn’t just a facade. It’s moulded, layered, made by hand.’
The interior is also organized around movement and changing views rather than a conventional gallery corridor. Zumthor describes the Wyss Museum as ‘one big spiral’, with visitors moving upward from the street and through a continuous sequence of spaces before returning toward the garden. This circulation allows the landscape to remain part of the museum experience. ‘Art doesn’t compete with the landscape; the two work together,’ Peter Zumthor notes, describing a building in which side light and framed views replace the more enclosed character of a conventional gallery. While Renzo Piano’s museum draws on industrial construction and top lighting, Zumthor chose a language based on stone, rammed concrete, and light entering from the side.
the museum is constructed largely around Jura limestone | image by Mark Niedermann
a pavilion for art, music, and public life at Fondation Beyeler
Between the two museum buildings and the historic structures, the Ammann Pavilion acts as a social center for the expanded ensemble. The single-story building combines glass and oak, opening broadly onto the park, while cherry and pear wood give the interior a warmer character. The pavilion is free to enter and can operate independently of museum hours. During the day, it functions as a public lounge where visitors and passers-by can sit, read, meet, or spend time in the park. In the evening, it becomes a venue for concerts, performances, talks, film screenings, and other cultural events for up to 250 people.
Its acoustic design was an important part of the architecture. The room had to accommodate both music and social gatherings, which require different acoustic conditions. Zumthor describes the challenge as creating enough horizontal reflection for music while also allowing the space to absorb the higher noise levels generated by receptions and dinners.
Set into the slope at the level of the upper garden, its interior steps gently toward the stage, taking advantage of a height difference that was already part of the historic landscape. ‘For me, the landscape, the urban cityscape, the urban landscape and nature, is the greatest thing we have,’ Peter Zumthor says. ‘If we carefully construct in response to the landscape, if we genuinely see it as it is, then the building we design naturally recedes in importance.’
the acclaimed Swiss architect divided the new functions between three buildings | image by Mark Niedermann
reopening the park as part of the museum
The architectural expansion is accompanied by an equally significant change to the landscape. Almost 10,000 square meters of formerly private parkland are being opened to the public, extending the existing 19th-century English landscape gardens designed by Jean-François Caillat. The new section has a more enclosed and informal character than the existing park, with species-rich meadows, native orchids, wooded areas, and water features. The park is also connected directly to the Landschaftspark Wiese nature reserve, creating a larger ecological setting around the museum.
A delicate bridge designed by Zumthor crosses the pond, offering visitors a slow passage through the landscape with views of artworks placed among the trees, meadows, and water. Works by Alexander Calder, Jenny Holzer, Ellsworth Kelly, Philippe Parreno, Thomas Schütte, and Fischli/Weiss are joined by new works by Louise Bourgeois, Pierre Huyghe, Rachel Whiteread, and Fujiko Nakaya. For Zumthor, the landscape shapes both the architecture and the way visitors move through the site. The new structures frame views, establish paths, and create a public square between the Torhaus, museum, and pavilion. The square follows the line of a former village brook, which Zumthor sees as one of the less visible historical traces connecting the site. ‘You don’t need to analyse it intellectually, you can simply feel it,’ he proposes.
the Erlen Torhaus marks the transition from the village to the nature reserve | image by Katalin Deér
historic buildings become spaces for new uses
Several existing structures have also been restored and given new functions. The heritage-listed Orangerie, redesigned by India Mahdavi, combines a small greenhouse with a shop for plant lovers. Its planting scheme focuses on species already capable of thriving in Switzerland and considers how plants may respond to changing climatic conditions, with botanical gardens and research institutions contributing to the project.
The Ammann Atelier accommodates up to 50 people for art education programs. During the opening year, its free Open Studio will also give visitors a place to work on their own at weekends. Nearby, the Salon is set up as a listening room with more than 2,000 vinyl records, ranging from Baroque and jazz to electronic music. The smallest of the new spaces is the Folly, a compact exhibition room whose column-like form recalls a small classical temple.
The Erlen Torhaus marks the transition from the village to the nature reserve. Its lower level handles artwork deliveries before they move down to the exhibition preparation areas, while the upper floors contain workspaces. The simple timber-frame facade is finished in stained oak and takes its cue from Zumthor’s studio in Haldenstein, Switzerland.
the lower level of Erlen Torhaus handles artwork deliveries | image by Iwan Baan
an ensemble rather than an extension
The expanded Fondation Beyeler will first open through a limited preview phase before welcoming visitors every day from January 15th, 2027. The inaugural program will bring exhibitions, concerts, performances, workshops, film screenings, music sessions, and botanical events to the new and restored spaces.
The first major exhibition, Constellations, brings more than 200 works from the Fondation Beyeler collection and private collections across the two museum buildings, the park, and the historic structures. The exhibition will change with the seasons, allowing different works and spaces to come into focus as visitors move through the ensemble.
 With the expansion, the Fondation Beyeler becomes a larger place to experience art, but also somewhere to spend time outside the galleries. Visitors can move between exhibitions, gardens, cultural events, and the restored buildings, with the architecture and landscape forming part of the experience. Asked what he wants people to associate with the new buildings, Peter Zumthor is clear about his intention: ‘I try to build buildings that are loved.’   
the expanded Fondation Beyeler will first open through a limited preview phase | image by Iwan Baan

Iraq suspends Iranian flights to Baghdad after US sanctions threat
Iraq ordered its civil aviation authority to suspend Iranian flights to Baghdad airport starting Wednesday, two sources told Reuters, after the United States threatened to sanction any airport that services Iranian carriers.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that all Iranian airlines would be shut down on 23 September by the threat of secondary sanctions on air services providers, seven months into the war between the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The Iraqi government is discussing diverting Iranian Airways flights from Baghdad to Najaf airport, two sources familiar with the matter said to the agency. They spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.
The suspension of flights will begin Wednesday midnight.
Iranian news agency Tasnim said earlier, citing the Iranian Civil Aviation Organisation, that flights from Tehran to Baghdad and Muscat have been canceled starting Wednesday and that all the remaining international flights including Istanbul will operate according to schedule.
"Iranian travelers are not currently being admitted at the airport in Oman, and consultations regarding this matter are ongoing," a spokesperson for Iran's Civil Aviation Organisation told Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency.
Bessent told CNBC that when Iranian airlines land at an airport, "you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system."
