George Lucas planned three more "Star Wars" films but "decided to step away" from directing
Kyiv • UNN
Lucas wanted to make three more "Star Wars" films, but after "Revenge of the Sith," he left directing to focus on his museum. The museum opened in Los Angeles.
George Lucas, creator of the legendary "Star Wars" franchise, said that he intended to make three more films, but instead decided to step away from directing after the release of "Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith" (Episode III: Revenge of the Sith) in 2005. UNN reports this with reference to The Hollywood Reporter.
Details
In a recent interview with CBS Sunday Morning, Lucas and his wife and business partner Mellody Hobson spoke about the creation of the new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles.
After Hobson noted that the "level of detail" Lucas put into the museum "nearly killed him," the director added: "Well, I'm 82 years old, so there's a limit to everything…"
"When I was doing it," Lucas continued, referring to the creation of the museum, "I decided to leave the movie business, which was a big deal, because I needed to make three more Star Wars movies. But I realized that I was running out of time, and I really wanted to create this museum, and I had spent a lot of time developing digital technologies for the film industry. You know, all art depends on technology."
How many Star Wars films Lucas directed
Lucas directed four Star Wars films during his career, beginning with the first installment in the franchise, "Star Wars: A New Hope" (Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope), in 1977. Although he handed directing duties to Irvin Kershner and Richard Marquand for the next two films in the original trilogy, respectively, he still wrote the screenplay and served as executive producer on those films before returning to the director's chair for the prequel trilogy.
In 2012, Lucas sold Lucasfilm and the "Star Wars" franchise to Disney for $4 billion. In addition to the sequel trilogy, Disney continues to expand the universe through television series. The franchise's next film, "Star Wars: Starfighter" (Star Wars: Starfighter), starring Ryan Gosling, will be released next year.
The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opened to the public on Tuesday.

Oil falls below $100 after Trump reports talks with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:38:13 UTC
14:38:13 KST

Brent crude fell on Wednesday morning after Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had held what he called “very productive” talks. Reports that Saudi Arabia is restarting a key oil pipeline also weighed on prices.
Oil prices fell on Wednesday after US President Donald Trump said American and Iranian representatives had held talks at the United Nations.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at $98.41 a barrel in the morning in Europe. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate cost $89.21 a barrel for next month delivery.
Brent has repeatedly risen above $100 since the Middle East war began in February.
The three-hour meeting was “very good” and “very productive”, Trump told reporters during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He said another meeting was planned soon.
His comments came hours after he told the UN he faced a “big decision” on whether to reach a deal with Iran or “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.
The US and Iran remain at an impasse. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, while the US has maintained a blockade of Iranian ports. Fighting involving Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has also disrupted energy exports through the Red Sea.
“The three-hour US-Iran meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant,” said Stephen Innes of Quintex Intel.
Prices also fell following a report that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations along its East–West Pipeline. The route allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia said this month that drones launched from Iraq had forced it to close the pipeline.
The kingdom hopes to resume exports later this week, Bloomberg reported, citing a source. Saudi Aramco has reportedly told Asian refiners that they may soon be able to collect crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. European refiners, however, have reportedly been told they will receive no Saudi crude under their October supply agreements.
Global stocks edge higher ahead of Trump–Xi meeting
European stock markets had mixed reactions at the open.
The Euro Stoxx 50 was about 0.1% lower in early trading while the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 traded over 0.3% higher.
The UK's FTSE 100, France's CAC 40, Italy’s FTSE MIB and Switzerland's CH20 all traded around 0.1% higher.
However, Germany's DAX 30, Spain's IBEX 35 and the Netherlands' AEX all traded between 0.3% and 0.4% lower than their Tuesday close.
Asian shares mostly rose. South Korea’s Kospi gained 1.2%, with Samsung and SK Hynix both up more than 2%. Taiwan’s Taiex rose 0.9%, according to the Reuters report you supplied. The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.5%, its sixth consecutive daily rise. Japan’s stock market was closed for a holiday, although Nikkei futures traded higher.
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq rose 0.5% to a record close on Tuesday. The S&P 500 was little changed, while the Dow fell 0.4%.
In currency markets, the euro traded at $1.1429, near a two-month low, as investors considered the possibility of another US interest rate rise. The dollar also edged up against the yen to 157.60 yen.
Gold traded at $4,379 an ounce. US Treasury futures rose slightly as oil prices eased, keeping the yield on the 10-year government bond below 5%.
Investors were also looking ahead to a meeting on Thursday between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trade and competition over AI are expected to be on the agenda.
Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said the war in the Middle East could prove more consequential for markets, including whether the US could persuade China to use its influence with Iran.

Trump rallies Latin American allies against drug cartels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:34:40 UTC
14:34:40 KST

Trump rallies Latin American allies against drug cartels
US-led Shield of the Americas coalition backs sanctions against crime groups after Trump urges stronger action.
United States President Donald Trump has pledged to use “unmatched military might” against drug cartels in the Western Hemisphere during a meeting of the Washington-led Shield of the Americas coalition in New York City.
In a meeting with leaders and foreign ministers from the anti-cartel alliance, Trump on Tuesday urged member countries to join the US in targeting 24 criminal organisations, which he earlier described as the “ISIS of the Western Hemisphere”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US removes Venezuela from drug list, Trump says
- list 2 of 3Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
- list 3 of 3Venezuelans protest interim leader Delcy Rodriguez at UN headquarters
He said he was asking “all nations in the Shield of the Americas to formally designate narco-terrorists as common threats to stability and apply crushing sanctions” against all of the groups. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City.
The coalition’s 15 governments later issued a joint statement saying they intended to impose asset freezes and visa restrictions on members and supporters of the groups and to pursue criminal charges against them.
At the top of the list are two groups that have been declared “terrorist” organisations by Washington: Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) – one of Central America’s most powerful criminal gangs – and Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan gang that is also active in Colombia, Peru and Chile.
The list also includes major Mexican cartels, Colombian armed groups such as the National Liberation Army, Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho groups, and Peru’s Shining Path.
Al Jazeera’s Alessandro Rampietti, reporting from Bogota, Colombia, said the statement was largely symbolic for now, because each country must follow its own legal procedures.
“For example, here in Colombia, it will require a law to pass in Congress. We understand that the government here has asked Congress to move forward in drafting such a law. So while the consequences may not be immediate, this is clearly an important step towards building what the US has been trying to do in Latin America [through] this alliance,” he added.
The coalition is made up of governments closely aligned with Trump, including Argentina, Ecuador and El Salvador, whose leaders he has praised or endorsed. Colombia and Peru joined after Trump-aligned presidents took office in recent months.
Brazil and Mexico have not joined.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also attended, praised “the emergence of strong leaders who are committed to the challenge of taking on transnational terrorism”.
The gathering was the administration’s latest effort to rally the region behind a more aggressive approach to drug trafficking. Since returning to office last year, Trump has designated cartels as foreign terrorist organisations and ordered dozens of strikes on boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific that US officials say were carrying narcotics bound for the US.
The strikes have killed more than 223 people, and UN experts say they violate international law and could amount to crimes against humanity.
The Trump administration’s National Security Strategy, released late last year, laid out plans for a revamped Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century policy asserting US primacy in the hemisphere that critics associate with decades of US intervention.
Trump has also spoken of retaking the Panama Canal and annexing Greenland and Canada. On Tuesday, he signed an agreement on Greenland that stopped short of his demand that the island become US territory.
The focus on the hemisphere has raised concerns across the region.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, in his UN speech, bristled at the approach, warning countries in Latin America and the Caribbean of “renewed hegemonic temptations”.
“Brazil is nobody’s back yard,” Lula said.

2026-09-23
05:30:25 UTC
14:30:25 KST

Falling demand from November and increased shipments from Asia are expected to leave Europe with enough jet fuel in the coming months, although analysts warn that smaller airports could still run dry.
Nearly 900,000 tonnes of jet fuel from Asia are scheduled to arrive in Europe in the coming months, according to trade intelligence company Kpler. The shipments should reduce the risk of shortages, but prices are likely to remain high, said George Shaw, Kpler’s senior insight analyst for distillate markets.
“Jet fuel will likely be subject to higher prices, especially as it is deeply linked to the diesel market, which is becoming even tighter and experiencing record prices recently,” Shaw told Euronews.
Last week, the average European jet fuel price rose to $207.56 (€176) a barrel, the highest of any region and 27.8% above the previous month’s European average, according to the International Air Transport Association’s fuel price monitor.
The figure is a regional refinery-price assessment and does not necessarily represent the price paid by individual airlines.
Jet fuel has become more expensive because of higher crude oil prices and widening refinery margins—the difference between the cost of crude and the price of the finished fuel.
Europe is particularly vulnerable because it relied heavily on jet fuel imports from the Middle East before the disruption to production and shipping routes. It has since turned increasingly to South Korea, Nigeria and the United States.
These additional imports have so far prevented a widespread physical shortage and should help Europe through the final quarter of the year, according to Shaw.
“Q4 should see less tightness than earlier in the year,” he said, adding that European aviation demand normally begins to fall significantly in November.
The seasonal decline reduces the likelihood of airlines or airports being unable to secure enough fuel, but it does not remove the pressure on prices.
IATA declined to comment on how the latest increase could affect European airlines and passengers.
South Korea becomes a major supplier
Kpler’s latest monthly data put European jet fuel imports at an average rate of approximately 672,000 barrels per day in September, including movements between European markets. South Korea, Nigeria and the United States together accounted for around 60% of the total.
As September was not yet over, the figures covered shipments that had arrived when the data were supplied, rather than a final full-month total.
Kpler’s figures also show that approximately 1.31 million tonnes of jet fuel moved from the Asia-Pacific region to Europe between July and September. South Korea accounted for around 1.14 million tonnes, or almost 87% of the total.
A further 900,000 tonnes from South Korea and elsewhere in Asia are scheduled to reach Europe over the coming months, Shaw said.
Although imports from the US have recently declined, American inventories remain comparatively high. According to Kpler, this should allow suppliers to respond if a shortage emerges as Europe’s peak aviation season ends.
European refiners have also increased production. Combined with additional supplies from the US and Nigeria, this “staved off a shortage”, Shaw said.
The International Energy Agency reached a similar conclusion earlier this year, saying that refining capacity in Europe, Nigeria and the US had helped ease pressure on the aviation-fuel market.
Smaller airports remain vulnerable
Kpler identified the UK and France as the European markets most vulnerable to renewed disruption because both are major consumers and importers of aviation fuel.
Its September data put UK imports at an average rate of approximately 177,000 barrels per day, making it the largest destination covered. France received around 73,000 barrels per day.
The Netherlands received approximately 118,000 barrels per day, although some of that fuel may have been distributed elsewhere through the country’s storage and trading hub.
But securing enough fuel for a country does not guarantee that it will reach every airport. Aviation data and analytics company Cirium says smaller airports would be the first to face shortages if deliveries were disrupted again.
That happened at Italy’s Brindisi airport on 6 April, when commercial aircraft could no longer refuel normally. The local supplier fell short of the fuel deliveries it had agreed to make. Fuel was reserved for state aircraft, air ambulances and search-and-rescue flights.
Six other Italian airports were rationing fuel during the same week, according to Cirium. Most aircraft were limited to 2,000 litres, less than an hour’s fuel for a Boeing 737.
Italy was not short of jet fuel overall: the country consumed 14.5% more between March and May than during the same period last year.
“Major hubs have avoided fuel shortages this year. Smaller airports have not,” Mike Malik, chief industry officer at Cirium, said in a report.
Smaller airports tend to have fewer suppliers, less storage and fewer alternative delivery routes, leaving regional and short-haul operators with less room to adapt.
How Europe replaced the missing fuel
Cirium estimates that European jet fuel imports from outside the region were 22% lower between March and May than during the same three months of 2025, and Kpler’s figures broadly support this finding.
Yet consumption across the UK, Germany, France, Spain and Italy fell by just 0.2% over the same period.
Europe filled the gap in three ways. Refineries increased the proportion of crude oil turned into jet fuel, traders secured additional cargoes from the US and Nigeria, and suppliers drew fuel from storage.
“Europe closed the gap by running refineries differently and emptying its tanks. Neither of those works a second time,” Malik said.
He warned that these safeguards have weakened. Refineries cannot keep increasing jet fuel production indefinitely, while drawing down stocks leaves less fuel available to deal with another disruption.
What needs to happen for pressure to ease?
The IEA’s September Oil Market Report said continuing disruption in the Gulf and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait was preventing oil flows from returning to normal. It expects a full recovery in supplies from Middle Eastern producers to be delayed until 2027.
According to Shaw, more refinery capacity needs to return, and greater volumes of aviation fuel must once again pass through the Strait of Hormuz before pressure on jet fuel and diesel markets can ease substantially.
For European airlines, the more immediate risk is therefore higher operating costs rather than widespread fuel shortages or grounded aircraft.
Whether passengers ultimately pay more will depend partly on how long prices remain elevated and how much fuel individual airlines bought in advance at previously agreed prices.
Airlines for Europe, which represents major European airline groups, had not responded to Euronews’ request for comment at the time of publication.

AI risks, Iran war dominate agenda at UN
France convenes a UN Security Council meeting Wednesday on artificial intelligence (AI) and international security, which includes briefings by leading industry figures, including the heads of OpenAI and Anthropic. The meeting comes as world leaders jostle over how to address the risks of the new technology. On the second day of the UN General Assembly, the Iran war is also set to dominate the agenda.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The future of Artificial intelligence and the stalled US war against Iran, with its ripple effect on the global economy, are expected to dominate the UN gathering of world leaders Wednesday.
Following weeks of worldwide headlines about risks of uncontrollable AI – and calls for a slowdown – industry leaders are set to brief a UN Security Council emergency meeting convened by France.
Sam Altman of OpenAI, Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face will brief the 15-strong Council, the United Nation's top body.
Hugging Face, a repository of AI models, was the target of a recent cyberattack by autonomous OpenAI software, the first in a series of incidents that have raised alarm bells over the rapidly evolving technology.
Meanwhile, the annual parade of UN General Assembly speeches is set to continue, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arriving late Tuesday, according to Iranian state media, to address the world body for the first time since the United States and Israel launched attacks on his country.
Read moreLive: Pezeshkian set to address UN for the first time since US, Israel launched Iran war
The strikes in late February sparked a war that engulfed the Middle East, and the Trump administration has so far yet to reach a deal with Tehran to end the conflict.
Tehran retaliated by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for energy transit, sparking a surge in global oil prices.
The recent Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast has also heightened fears over global trade and shipping through the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Pezeshkian's speech will come a day after Trump raised the possibility that he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" and "drive them into hell". During his remarks, all but one member of the Iranian delegation walked out.
Ukraine, AI showdown
Trump made the comments in a fire and brimstone speech Tuesday, but he also revealed that there were talks between the two sides for the first time in months.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Trump's roving envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner on the sidelines of the UN's signature diplomatic gathering.
Araghchi said that Tehran's demands included "the immediate lifting of the (US) naval blockade, the prompt payment of all Iranian assets that have been frozen, and an end to the war on all resistance fronts," state news agency IRIB reported.
Outside the UN on Tuesday, there was a vigil with protesters demonstrating against Tehran's use of the death penalty.
Besides conflict in the Middle East, Russia's war against Ukraine will again be raised among global diplomatic circles on Wednesday.
A Security Council meeting on Ukraine is scheduled for 11am (15:00 GMT), while President Volodymyr Zelensky is due to address the UN General Assembly as well.
Zelensky, after meeting with Trump on Tuesday, said that Washington and Kyiv want the war with Russia to end "before winter".
He added that he is ready to halt strikes on Russian energy sites if Moscow agreed to do the same.
In his speech Tuesday, Trump rejected international regulation of AI, calling such proposals a "globalist scheme".
"The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming ... are now saying that AI is going to kill us all," Trump said.
But just hours after Trump spoke, Macron took to the rostrum and defiantly called for the creation of an open-source AI model not dependent on the United States or China.
"I don't want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers," he said. "Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Election panel weighs bid to bar Arab party leader who called Oct. 7 an 'important historic event'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:28:25 UTC
14:28:25 KST

Israel’s Central Elections Committee begins two days of hearings Wednesday on a series of requests to bar parties and individual candidates from competing in the October 27 Knesset election, with a closely watched case against Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh at the center of the proceedings.
Ten disqualification requests have been filed against parties and candidates across the political spectrum, including Ra’am, the Joint List, Otzma Yehudit, the Democrats and the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut slate, as well as individual candidates including Abu Shehadeh and Joint List lawmaker Ofer Cassif.
Wednesday’s hearings are due to include the petition against Cassif, followed by the request to disqualify Abu Shehadeh and challenges involving Ra’am, the Joint List and Balad. Petitions targeting Otzma Yehudit, the Democrats and the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut slate are scheduled to be heard Thursday.
The most prominent case is Otzma Yehudit’s request to disqualify Abu Shehadeh personally from running for the 26th Knesset.
The petition focuses in part on an article Abu Shehadeh published on October 8, 2023, one day after the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. In the article, he described the events as an “important historical event from a military, political and strategic perspective” and referred to what he called the attack’s political consequences.
Otzma Yehudit argues that the statements constitute support for an armed struggle against Israel by a terrorist organization, one of the grounds for disqualification under Israeli law. Abu Shehadeh has rejected that interpretation, arguing in his response that he has consistently opposed harming civilians and that he did not yet know the full scale of what had happened when the article was published.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Eisman told the Elections Committee that the evidence, particularly the October 8 article, could indicate support for an armed struggle by a terrorist organization against Israel and that Abu Shehadeh’s explanation did not eliminate those concerns.
They nevertheless stopped short of formally recommending his disqualification, noting the stringent legal standard established in previous cases and saying the committee should give the petition serious consideration.
Yashar!, the party led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot, has announced that it supports the petition against Abu Shehadeh.
What the law requires
Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset allows a party list or candidate to be barred from an election on three grounds: negating Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting an armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel.
The Supreme Court has historically interpreted those grounds narrowly, requiring clear and persuasive evidence before denying a party or candidate the right to contest an election. A Central Elections Committee decision to disqualify an individual candidate must also be approved by the Supreme Court.
Baharav-Miara and Eisman found no sufficient legal basis to disqualify the other parties and candidates covered by the petitions before the committee, including Ra’am, the Joint List, Otzma Yehudit, the Democrats, the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut list and Cassif.
Ra’am faces three challenges
Three separate petitions seek to bar Ra’am, the Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas.
The requests were filed by Otzma Yehudit, Likud and the Choosing Life Forum, which represents families affected by terrorism. The petitions allege, among other claims, that Ra’am fails to accept Israel as a Jewish and democratic state or has links amounting to support for armed struggle. Ra’am rejects those allegations.
Likud has also sought to disqualify the Joint List, while other petitions seek to bar Otzma Yehudit and the Democrats.
The Democrats argue that Otzma Yehudit should be excluded on grounds including incitement to racism and undermining Israel’s democratic character. Otzma Yehudit has filed its own petition against the Democrats, accusing the party of conduct that it argues falls under the same section of the Basic Law. Both parties reject the allegations against them.
The hearings are also likely to become part of the broader political battle surrounding the election.
Coalition parties backing Ra’am’s disqualification could use opposition votes against the petition to argue that their rivals are preserving Abbas as a potential future political partner. Opposition parties supporting a ban, meanwhile, could face criticism from Ra’am and its voters.
Yisrael Beiteinu has said it intends to support disqualifying the Joint List, Ra’am, Cassif and Abu Shehadeh.
Abu Shehadeh to appear remotely
Abu Shehadeh had sought to postpone Wednesday’s hearing after being injured and hospitalized at Rambam Medical Center in Haifa.
Central Elections Committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg rejected the request to delay the proceeding but ruled that Abu Shehadeh could participate by video link.
Otzma Yehudit leader and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and fellow party lawmaker Tally Gotliv, both lawyers, are expected to appear before the committee in connection with the petition.
The committee has repeatedly been the first arena for battles over candidate and party disqualification in previous Israeli elections, but its decisions have frequently reached the Supreme Court, which has applied a demanding evidentiary standard in deciding whether a party or individual can be excluded from the race.
That legal threshold will be particularly important in Abu Shehadeh’s case: whether his October 8 article and the broader evidence submitted against him are sufficient to establish the sustained support for armed struggle required to prevent a candidate from standing for election.

Araghchi, who arrived in New York at the head of a diplomatic delegation on Monday afternoon, held separate meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session.
In his meeting with Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, the two sides held talks and exchanged views on bilateral relations and regional and international developments. No further details were immediately released.
In his meeting with Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, the two sides discussed bilateral relations between Iran and Switzerland as well as regional and international developments.
Araghchi set out Iran's positions on regional developments following U.S.-Israeli aggression against Iran and the continuation of interventionist measures, the naval blockade and economic war against the Iranian people. He stressed the responsibility of all countries to protect the UN Charter and international law, especially the principle of the prohibition of the use of force.
Referring to U.S.-Israeli war crimes committed against Iran during the military aggressions of the past year and a half, he underlined the Islamic Republic of Iran's determination to defend its security and national sovereignty decisively.
Araghchi noted America's repeated violations, including its breach of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and its escalation of aggressive actions against Iran, and reminded the international community of its responsibility to hold the United States accountable for the consequences of its wrongful acts.
The foreign minister also cited flagrant violations of humanitarian law by the United States and the Zionist regime and the commission of numerous war crimes, including the Minab and Lamard disasters. He stressed the duty of all states party to the 1949 Geneva Conventions to punish war criminals in accordance with the fundamental rule of "respecting and ensuring respect for international humanitarian law."
He warned that indifference to genocide and war crimes, and continued impunity for the criminals, would have very broad consequences for the entire world and all countries.
The two sides also discussed Iran-Switzerland cooperation to help strengthen peace and stability in the region.

Cyclone from the Black Sea will bring heavy rain and storm-force winds - weather forecast for September 23
Kyiv • UNN
On September 23, significant rainfall, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of up to 20 m/s are expected on the left bank. Temperatures will be seasonal.
The weather in Ukraine on September 23 will be influenced by a cyclone from the Black Sea; rain and stormy winds are expected in parts of the country, with temperatures ranging from 4 degrees above zero at night to 18 degrees Celsius during the day. UNN reports this, citing data from the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center.
On September 23, a cyclone moving from the Black Sea will bring heavy rain, thunderstorms, and stormy winds with gusts of up to 15–20 m/s to the left-bank part of the country. The rest of the country will also see some rain, but it will be less intense. Cold air will continue to flow in from northwestern Europe, so temperatures will be typical for this period
Details
According to the forecast, today will be cloudy with sunny intervals.
At night, there will be heavy rain and thunderstorms in the east and southeast; during the day, in the left-bank part of the country. Elsewhere, there will be occasional showers.
Winds will be northwesterly in the right-bank part of the country, at 5–10 m/s, and southeasterly in the left-bank part, at 7–12 m/s, with gusts of 15–20 m/s.
Temperatures will be 4–9°C above zero at night, 10–15°C in the east and southeast of the country, and 13–18°C during the day; in the Carpathians, 0–5°C above zero at night and 7–12°C during the day.

Battlefield sees 247 Russian attacks, heaviest fighting on two fronts – Ukraine's General Staff

Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 23 September

The Russians launched three airstrikes using six guided aerial bombs and conducted 149 attacks on Ukrainian troop positions and settlements, eight of which involved MLRS.

On the Kupiansk front, Russian troops made one attempt to improve their positions by conducting an assault towards the village of Borova.
On the Lyman front, Ukrainian forces repelled Russian attempts to break through their defences. The Russians conducted three attacks near Novoselivka and Stavky.
On the Sloviansk front, Russian soldiers conducted two assaults near Kalenyky and Kryva Luka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians conducted one attack towards the village of Fedorivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 25 Russian attacks were recorded, according to updated information. The Russians conducted assaults near Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Rozkishne, Novopavlivka, Kucheriv Yar and Vilne.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 23 attacks, seeking to advance near Novyi Donbas, Bilytske, Novohryshyne, Vodianske, Molodetske, Muravka, Myrne, Serhiivka, Novopidhorodnie and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, Russian forces conducted two assaults near Berezove and Solodke.
On the Huliaipole front, Russian troops attacked the positions of Ukrainian defenders four times, attempting to advance near Huliaipole, Charivne and Vozdvyzhivka.
On the Orikhiv front, the Russians made two attempts to improve their positions near Mali Shcherbaky and Mala Tokmachka.

Taiwan labor minister returns from China APEC meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:24:20 UTC
14:24:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Labor Minister Hung Shen-han (洪申翰) returned to Taiwan on Tuesday after attending an APEC ministerial meeting in Nanjing, becoming the first minister-level official to visit China since former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) took office in 2016.
Hung said in an interview with POP Radio Wednesday that Taiwan received the same rights and treatment as other APEC member economies. He entered China through a dedicated channel using an APEC invitation and did not apply for or use a Taiwan Compatriot Permit, per UDN.
Hung said the APEC Secretariat assisted his delegation during the trip, allowing it to participate fully in the meeting and receive the same treatment as other member economies. He said the experience demonstrated the importance of the group's established rules and principle of equal participation.
Taiwan has participated in APEC under the name Chinese Taipei since joining the 21-member organization in 1991. Hung said the designation has remained unchanged under different administrations.
The Nanjing meeting focused on human resources development amid changes in labor markets caused by artificial intelligence, technological advances, and demographic shifts. Ministers discussed employment, vocational training, and social security systems.
The meeting concluded with a joint statement calling for greater cooperation on high-quality employment, investment in people and vocational training, and stronger, more adaptable social security systems.
Hung said his attendance should not be interpreted as a sign of improving cross-strait relations. APEC holds ministerial meetings throughout the year covering areas including tourism, trade, and human resources development, and his attendance was related to his responsibilities as labor minister, per UDN.
“As long as my schedule permits, and the topic is related to labor affairs under my jurisdiction, I should attend important international conferences,” Hung said. He questioned whether Taiwan should skip an important international meeting simply because it was held in Nanjing.
He said participating in international forums gives Taiwan opportunities to increase its visibility and share its experience on issues including AI's impact on employment and workers' rights.
Hung also addressed questions about the safety of Taiwanese citizens traveling to China. He said the risks faced by ordinary travelers should not be assessed based on his APEC trip, which was conducted under the organization's established arrangements.
He said the Mainland Affairs Council and Straits Exchange Foundation were better positioned to assess the risks of traveling to China because they have monitored cross-strait developments for years.

Philippines formally receives Taiwan-donated patrol vessel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:23:59 UTC
14:23:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) has formally taken custody of a 61-meter patrol vessel donated by Taiwan through the Manila-based We Protect Our Seas Foundation (WPS Foundation) for use as a training ship.
The handover ceremony took place Monday at the PCG national headquarters, where WPS Foundation President and CEO Jeffrey Ordaniel and PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan signed the donation agreement, per UDN. The foundation is a nongovernmental, nonprofit, and nonpartisan organization that facilitated the vessel's transfer from Taiwan.
The Philippine military-focused Facebook page Modern Arms Philippines reported the handover Monday. Images indicate that the vessel is the Lienchiang, a retired 500-tonne Kinmen-class patrol ship formerly operated by Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration. UDN said the foundation's involvement could provide a channel and model for future Taiwanese vessel donations to the Philippines.
According to the foundation, the donated vessel will support humanitarian assistance, search and rescue, disaster response, and marine environmental protection operations. The ship is expected to provide an additional platform for training and maritime capacity building as the PCG expands its personnel and fleet, per Modern Arms Philippines.
The WPS Foundation said the vessel will be deployed in Mindanao in the southern Philippines. It emphasized that the initiative is civilian, humanitarian, and nonconfrontational and is not directed against any country.
The defense outlet MaxDefense Philippines said the transfer through a nongovernmental organization may have been intended to avoid legal and diplomatic complications arising from a direct donation by Taiwan, particularly given the Philippines’ relations with China. It also suggested the donation could indicate Taiwan’s willingness to set aside its overlapping South China Sea claims to strengthen ties with the Philippines.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to invoke the 1982 US-China joint communique in an effort to persuade US President Donald Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan when they meet Thursday.
Three sources familiar with bilateral talks told Reuters that China is likely to cite its interpretation of the communique. In the document, the US said it intended to gradually reduce arms sales to Taiwan and did not seek to pursue “a long-term policy of arms sales to Taiwan.”
However, then-US President Ronald Reagan said in an accompanying memo that this position was “conditioned absolutely upon the continued commitment of China to the peaceful solution” of its differences with Taiwan.
The sources said China has also asked the US to halt deliveries of weapons already ordered by Taiwan, per Reuters. Xi could “emphasize to Trump that Taiwan is the provocateur and the sole source of instability in US-China relations, and that Taiwan is the one changing the status quo,” one source said.
In a People’s Daily article, Chinese Ambassador to the US Xie Feng said that “China’s sovereignty, security, and development interests cannot be violated, and four red lines — the Taiwan question, democracy and human rights, development paths and systems, and development rights — cannot be challenged,” Reuters reported.
“China is committed to pursuing peaceful development and hopes the US will move toward this as well,” Xie said.
Several US lawmakers have urged Trump to reject Beijing’s demands regarding arms sales to Taiwan. US Representative John Moolenaar, chair of the House Select Committee on China, wrote in a letter Friday that China’s efforts to interfere with US arms exports and security cooperation with allies should be “rejected out of hand.”
He argued that China’s military buildup and increasing hostility toward its neighbors, rather than US arms sales or its allies’ defense efforts, were the main cause of regional instability.
A group of Democratic senators issued a joint statement Tuesday warning that China poses an unprecedented threat to US security and prosperity.
“The Chinese military continues its pressure campaign against our vital democratic partner Taiwan as President Trump has retreated from longstanding security commitments,” they said.
“We can’t let President Xi leave stronger than when he arrived. That is not diplomacy, it’s weakness,” they added.
The signatories included Senate Foreign Relations Committee Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen and Senators Chris Coons, Patty Murray, Jack Reed, Mark Warner, Elizabeth Warren, and Andy Kim.
Taiwan is still awaiting a delayed NT$444.91 billion (US$14 billion) arms package that includes Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems. In May, acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the pause was related to US military operations against Iran.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s minimum wage will likely rise next year, with monthly pay potentially exceeding NT$30,000 (US$997) and the hourly rate surpassing NT$200, Labor Minister Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) said Wednesday.
The labor ministry will convene its annual Minimum Wage Review Committee on Thursday to discuss the 2027 adjustment, with representatives from labor, business, government, and academia participating, per CTS News. The current minimum monthly wage is NT$29,500, while the hourly rate is NT$196.
Business groups have proposed a roughly 3% increase. Labor representatives argue that the adjustment should fully reflect consumer price inflation, with their calculations putting the increase at 7.77% based on half of the Central Bank’s projected economic growth rate.
Speaking on a radio program hosted by Huang Wei-han (黃暐瀚) on Pop Radio, Hung said labor and business groups typically present their preferred adjustment rates ahead of the annual review. He said the committee must examine the reasoning behind each proposal and build consensus through discussion, rather than simply averaging the two figures.
Hung said the likelihood of a minimum wage increase next year was “very high,” citing the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics’ forecast that consumer prices will rise by more than 2%, CTS News reported. He said inflation puts greater pressure on low-wage workers because living expenses make up a larger share of their disposable income, while the committee will determine the final adjustment.

“There is a doctrine about the nature and place of the mind… which hails chiefly from Descartes: Every human being has both a body and a mind… His body and his mind are ordinarily harnessed together, but after the death of the body his mind may continue to exist and function… People can see, hear and jolt one another’s bodies, but they are irremediably blind and deaf to the workings of one another’s minds and inoperative upon them… Such in outline is the official theory. I shall often speak of it, with deliberate abusiveness, as “the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine”… It is not merely an assemblage of particular mistakes. It is one big mistake and a mistake of a special kind. It is, namely, a category mistake. It represents the facts of mental life as if they belonged to one logical type or category (or range of types or categories), when they actually belong to another. The dogma is therefore a philosopher’s myth.”
— Gilbert Ryle, The Concept of Mind

Many countries are optimistic about AI, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:15:00 UTC
14:15:00 KST

Many countries are optimistic about AI, poll finds
Damien Cave
NEW YORK – It may come as a surprise for world leaders discussing artificial intelligence at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, but a large majority of people surveyed across the globe for a new Gallup poll said they felt mostly positive about AI.
Gallup, an opinion research organisation, interviewed at least 1,000 people in each of 37 countries and found that in 34, positive emotions towards AI outweighed negative feelings.
An average of 72 per cent of respondents said they felt curious, happy or excited about AI, compared with 41 per cent who felt worried, sad or angry.
It was among the most comprehensive portraits of varied emotional responses to the new technology yet, and the margins between hope and fear were wide.
In China and Vietnam, more than 90 per cent of people polled said they believed that AI would mostly make daily life better.
In Nigeria, Israel and Singapore, more than two-thirds of the respondents agreed.
But in the United States, only 36 per cent saw AI as mostly helpful rather than harmful.
The seven Western high-income countries that Gallup surveyed (US, Britain, Ireland, Canada, New Zealand, Malta and the Netherlands) dominated its ranking of the most concerned, with the US at the top.
Gallup plans to eventually include AI surveys in 140 countries, but this early snapshot – conducted with Microsoft, featuring a margin of error of 2.2 per cent and 4.9 percentage points – appeared to show a clear divide.
“The most consistent finding that is emerging is that this cluster of attitudes that we see in Western countries is pretty unique,” said Pablo Diego-Rosell, a senior scientist at Gallup.
The “worried West”, he added, tends to feature high adoption, high concern and a belief that while AI might be good for the individual, it was less likely to be positive for their country.
Across 37 nations surveyed, the median percentage who have never tried AI is still relatively high – 57 per cent.
In the US, it is 32 per cent. But intense use is no predictor of dismay.
Some countries where survey respondents said they felt positively towards AI were also rapid adopters.
Singapore, China and Israel all have a higher proportion of daily users than the US.
Others have lower rates of use: In Vietnam, only 12 per cent of those surveyed use AI daily compared with 23 per cent in the US.
Husan Chahal, an AI risk researcher for the National Bureau of Asian Research, said that many governments, especially in Asia, frequently framed the technology first and foremost as a tool for economic development, and were eager to drive AI uptake.
“That doesn’t necessarily mean they’re unconcerned about catastrophic risks,” she said. “But those risks may not be as prominent in their policy priorities.”
In almost every country polled by Gallup, the heaviest AI users said they were the least anxious about it.
For example, 68 per cent of daily AI users in the US were worried about the technology compared with 80 per cent of less frequent users, and 74 per cent of those who had never used AI.
Edward Lim, Vietnam country director for NUS Enterprise and Block71, a start-up accelerator connected to the National University of Singapore, said that views of AI were evolving rapidly and in different directions.
He suggested that concerns were increasing in Singapore as the news of AI agents going rogue continued to spread, but in Vietnam, where human talent remains cost-competitive with AI agents, there is mostly excitement.
“What strikes me is how open people in Vietnam are to trying new things,” he said, adding: “The poll reflects what I see on the ground.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

S. Korea's consumer sentiment rebounds in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:11:11 CST
14:11:11 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's consumer sentiment rebounded in September, driven by reduced volatility in the domestic stock market and growing optimism over improved income, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The composite consumer sentiment index (CCSI), which gauges the sentiment of consumers over the economic situation, rose 2.1 points from a month earlier to 106.6 in September after falling 2.3 points in August, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
A reading above the benchmark 100 indicates that optimists outnumbered pessimists. It was based on a survey of 2,226 households nationwide conducted between Sept. 9 and 16.
The sub-index for future household income gained 2 points to 102, supported by expectations for improving wage conditions amid expanding economic growth.
The sub-index for current economic situation advanced 4 points to 83 on the back of robust economic performance, particularly in exports and consumption, combined with a stabilizing stock market.
The index for housing price outlook was unchanged at 125 as soaring apartment prices in the Seoul metropolitan area were countered by the government's real estate stabilization measures and the central bank's interest rate hikes.
The BOK delivered back-to-back rate hikes in July and August, raising its benchmark interest rate to 3 percent.
Inflation expectations, which measure the outlook among consumers over headline inflation for the next 12 months, stood unchanged at 2.7 percent in September compared to the previous month. ■

China strengthens crackdown on fentanyl-related crimes with detailed rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:10:59 CST
14:10:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's judicial and law enforcement authorities have issued a set of guidelines on handling criminal cases involving fentanyl-related substances, stressing severe punishment for such crimes in accordance with the law.
The guidelines, jointly issued by China's Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate and the Ministry of Public Security, aim to ensure the accurate enforcement of the law, protect public health and maintain social stability.
The 18-article document sets out clear thresholds and standards for the conviction and sentencing in fentanyl-related cases, with different standards applying to cases involving pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical fentanyl-related substances.
It defines the scope of fentanyl-related substances covered by relevant laws and rules, and specifies requirements for evidence collection and the recovery of illicit proceeds in related cases.
The guidelines further clarify the respective responsibilities of judicial and law enforcement authorities in handling such offenses.
The top procuratorial and police authorities also jointly issued a set of rules on investigation and prosecution standards for related criminal cases.
The three authorities said in a statement that they would continue to strengthen law-based punishment and comprehensive prevention of crimes involving fentanyl-related substances, while advancing efforts to combat all drug-related crimes. ■

Argentina hails Malvinas Islands bill as "milestone" in sovereignty rights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:10:56 CST
14:10:56 KST

BUENOS AIRES, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Argentine government on Tuesday hailed a proposed bill concerning the disputed Malvinas Islands as a "milestone" in the process of recovering the archipelago and an "unprecedented" step forward on the legal front.
Presidential spokesperson Adrian Ravier made the remarks at a press conference at Casa Rosada, the presidential palace in Buenos Aires, urging lawmakers to consider the bill as soon as possible.
The bill submitted to Congress repeals Law 26.659 and replaces it with a framework that increases criminal penalties for companies or individuals involved in unauthorized hydrocarbon exploration and exploitation on the Argentine continental shelf.
It also redefines national defense as a permanent function of the state to guarantee independence, territorial integrity and the capacity for self-determination in the face of threats.
The bill seeks to provide Argentina with "a comprehensive, permanent, and coordinated regulatory framework" to strengthen its efforts to assert sovereignty over the resource-rich islands, known in Britain as the Falkland Islands, Ravier said.
He added that such a comprehensive legal framework would enable the government to "defend its sovereignty and protect vital and strategic interests," as well as "strengthen its institutional capabilities in the face of threats."
The bill marks a "milestone" in Argentina's efforts to recover not only the Malvinas Islands but also South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime and insular areas, Ravier said.
According to Ravier, the proposed legal framework would "punish" those who illegally exploit the area's natural resources and provide Argentina with the "indispensable tools to protect itself against foreign threats."
Argentina claims sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago, while the United Kingdom has exercised control over the islands since 1833.
The Argentine government recently announced sanctions against companies and individuals involved in oil and gas exploration and extraction on the Argentine continental shelf without official authorization. It has also announced plans to build a naval base in the country's south.
Argentina and the United Kingdom fought a war over the Malvinas Islands in 1982. The conflict lasted from April 2 to June 14 and resulted in the deaths of 649 Argentine service members, 255 British military personnel and three islanders. ■

Most European men would try new contraception methods if available, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:10:11 UTC
14:10:11 KST

Most men would embrace contraception designed for them, such as on-demand pills taken before sex, a daily hormonal gel or a thermal silicone ring, but funding gaps are keeping these products years away from pharmacy shelves.
Most men in Europe would use contraception designed for them if available, a new survey spanning Germany, France, Italy, Poland, Sweden, Türkiye, and the United Kingdom has found.
Out of surveyed 14,000 men, more than half in all countries said they would start using a novel male contraceptive within 12 months of approval, and only 9% said they would never use one. That ranged from 55% in Sweden and Denmark to 69% in the United Kingdom.
Currently, the only contraceptive methods for men include condoms and vasectomy. The majority of contraceptive methods available in the market are designed for women, from hormonal IUD implants to oral contraceptive pills.
However, there are eight novel products under development at different stages of clinical trials, such as on-demand pills taken before sex, a daily pill, a daily hormonal gel, a long acting vas-occlusive hydrogel, and a thermal silicone ring.
While a third of men willing to use male contraception would do so within three months of the product being available on the market, they might need to be patient. According to researchers, the main barrier stopping these products from reaching the market is funding.
“The contraceptive field has just been funded almost exclusively by the philanthropic and public sector for 30 years now. So, there's just not a pathway that pharma has been involved,” said Heather Vahdat, executive director of Male Contraception Initiative, a non-profit organisation working on non-hormonal, reversible male contraception.
Men who wanted to use these products earlier cited more autonomy, protection from unwanted pregnancies, dissatisfaction with condom use and a desire to relieve women of the burden of protection, said Steve Kretschmer, executive director of DesireLine, who conducted the survey, during the presentation of the results on Tuesday.
Another barrier to unlocking male contraception potential is the perception and acceptance of the broader population, including women.
“I think one of the key issues has been this belief that, well, men may not feel the interest and that women may not trust them,” Kretschmer added.
Which method would men prefer?
A non-hormonal pill taken 30 minutes before sex is the single most preferred product in every country by men, followed by a daily pill.
The vas-occlusive hydrogel — a non-hormonal and non-permanent gel that blocks sperm transport — reached 12% acceptance in Germany and France, while the silicone ring — which warms the testicles to reduce sperm production — was more accepted in Türkiye.
Of all respondents, 10% of men in the United Kingdom said they would not use any of the products — the lowest share — while Italy and France recorded the highest, at 17%.
The survey noted that although interest was broad among all men, those who were more sexually active or visited the doctor more frequently showed greater interest.
Currently, condoms are the most common contraception method among men, but only half of users use them every time, the survey found.
If men who are currently unprotected were to use contraception as stated in the survey, the overall coverage would increase across Europe, ranging from a 31% rise in France to a 73% rise in the UK.
The survey was presented on the same day as the World Health Organization (WHO) said that the main goal is to expand the choices of male contraception and reduce the disproportionate contraceptive burden on women in its new Target Product Profiles (TPPs) guide for male contraceptives.
There are three main targets for development: methods that inhibit sperm production, methods that interfere with sperm mobility and methods that block the passage of sperm through the sperm ducts, WHO said in its guide.

====================================================================================================

El Niño transforms Chile's Atacama Desert as thousands of hectares bloom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:03:38 UTC
14:03:38 KST

Exceptionally heavy El Niño rains have awakened millions of seeds lying dormant underground, carpeting vast swathes of one of the planet's driest places with flowers.
The Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, has changed appearance after heavy rains in northern Chile. Vast stretches of land that are normally parched have been carpeted with violet and white blossoms in a natural phenomenon known as the "flowering desert".
Under the Atacama's soil, seeds and bulbs from around 200 different species lie dormant for long periods, waiting for the right conditions to germinate. Rainfall linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon has allowed many of them to bloom. The result has transformed parts of the desert landscape and drawn large numbers of visitors, who stop to photograph the unusual flowering.
Rainfall has been particularly heavy this season. In some areas it has exceeded 180 millimetres of rain, an amount that "had never been recorded before", said César Pizarro, Atacama biodiversity manager at Chile's National Forestry Corporation (Conaf), speaking to AFP.
The water has soaked into the sand deeper than usual, encouraging vegetation to appear in the nature reserve about 800 kilometres north of Santiago. According to Conaf's forecasts, the spectacle will reach its peak in October. The agency estimates that around 15,000 hectares could be blanketed in flowers.
El Niño behind the exceptional rains
The blooming follows a period of intense rainfall linked to El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterised by the warming of surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
This warming can disrupt wind and rainfall patterns in different regions of the world and trigger extreme weather events. The current El Niño episode could be the most intense since comparable records began four decades ago.
The rains that hit Chile in July also had serious consequences. At least 13 people were killed and around 4,000 homes were destroyed or suffered major damage.

AI trade outlook brightens on falling oil and Meta’s Muse agent ahead of Xi-Trump meeting

Inside Türkiye’s masterplan to electrify the world at COP31 – and why experts aren’t convinced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:02:37 UTC
14:02:37 KST

Türkiye says electrifying daily life can protect families and businesses from “volatile energy markets”. But could their plan keep us stuck in the fossil fuel era?
COP31 host Türkiye will put “climate-responsible AI” in the spotlight when it stages the UN summit this November, amid growing fears of its carbon footprint.
On Monday (21 September) COP31 President-Designate and Minister of Environment Murat Kurum said that pushing tech companies to power data centres with clean energy would be one of the talks’ main priorities.
It follows Türkiye’s centrepiece electrification target, which aims to raise the global share of energy demand by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035.
The 35-by-35 pledge was announced back in June as a way to help shift the world to a low-carbon future. It comes after what has been described as the “worst energy crisis in our history” due to worsening climate change and the fossil fuel shock from the war on Iran.
“By electrifying daily life, from transport to buildings and industry, we can protect families and businesses from volatile energy markets,” Kurum said.
“This 35 per cent by 2035 target will be one of the defining priorities of our COP31 presidency.”
Inside Türkiye’s electrification pledge
Electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels, such as switching a diesel-powered car or bus with an EV. However, this doesn’t necessarily eradicate the use of polluting fossil fuels.
The World Resources Institute (WRI) describes electrification as an “enabler, not an end goal in itself”, adding: “An electric car powered by a coal-heavy grid could be worse for the climate than a car that runs on [petrol]. Its benefits, in other words, depend on how the electricity is generated.”
Experts are now concerned that the 35-by35 pledge could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targets – a move they say will “seriously undermine climate goals”.
“Let’s not let electrification become the Trojan horse of our times, used to hide new fossil fuel consumption rather than promote renewable energy,” says Claire Smith of campaign coalition Beyond Fossil Fuels.
Smith argues that the Presidency’s pledge as it currently stands “leaves the backdoor open” for governments to conceal or justify expanded fossil fuel use under the “guise of electrification”.
“We’re already seeing data centres divert electricity and renewable energy away from the sectors that genuinely need to decarbonise, driving higher fossil gas dependence and pushing up electricity costs for consumers,” she adds.
“Clear guardrails are essential to ensure that electrification advances both climate justice and equitable access to renewable energy, and not the fossil industry’s agenda.”
Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner at Beyond Fossil Fuels, similarly warns that electrification is not “inherently synonymous” with decarbonisation.
“Globally, we must ensure that the electrification agenda does not come at the expense of the urgent transition away from fossil fuels,” she adds.
Where does Türkiye’s electricity come from?
According to energy think tank Ember, 43 per cent of Türkiye’s electricity was generated from low-carbon sources last year.
Despite drought conditions, hydropower remained the country’s largest source of clean electricity (16 per cent). The country’s wind share in generation (11.1 per cent) is ahead of many G7 nations, including Italy (8.1 per cent) and nuclear-mad France (8.2 per cent).
Solar power generation (10.5 per cent) has doubled in Türkiye over the last couple of years, but still lags far behind southern European countries with similar potential like Italy (17 per cent) and Spain (22 per cent).
Coal remains Türkiye’s largest power source, covering 34.3 per cent of its electricity generation in 2025. This is 1.2 per cent above the world average and 25.07 above the EU average.
Almost two-thirds of Türkiye’s coal generation relies on imports, which analysts warn has implications for energy security. Türkiye is also heavily reliant on gas, which made 22.1 per cent of its electricity share last year. Again, this is above both the world and EU average.
The country’s power sector emissions almost doubled over the last two decades due to an increase in fossil fuel generation to meet rising demand, although the growth of wind and solar over the last decade has helped curb that trend.
Türkiye’s emissions per capita were level with the global average in 2025. The country now aims for 47 per cent of its electricity to come from renewables by 2030, slightly more ambitious than the EU’s binding target of at least 42.5 per cent.
“The global fossil fuel crisis experienced for the second time in the past four years has further highlighted the importance of the transition to clean energy,” says Ember’s Ufuk Alparslan.
“In this context, Türkiye has the opportunity to take on a leading role in the regional energy transition.”

Tsikhanouskaya: Ukraine has shattered the myth of ‘all-powerful’ Russia
She said this in a comment to Ukrinform on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
According to the Belarusian opposition leader, Ukrainians have changed their attitude toward Belarus and understand the difference between Alexander Lukashenko’s regime and the Belarusian people.
“I remember what attitudes Ukrainians used to have – that Lukashenko was the batka, the ‘father,’ that the streets were clean. That is no longer the case. And I am very grateful to Ukrainians for reconsidering their attitude toward Belarus and understanding the difference between Lukashenko’s regime and Belarusians,” Tsikhanouskaya said.
Belarusian volunteer fighters are fighting alongside Ukrainians, while civilian volunteers are helping Ukraine, she added.
“I am very glad that our relations with official Kyiv have improved, and we are working on joint projects,” the opposition leader said. “Ukraine, which naturally now occupies a leading political position in Europe, understands the value of a free, independent and democratic Belarus.”
She stressed that independent Belarus is important for the security of Ukraine and Europe.
“And the very strong rhetoric from President Volodymyr Zelensky and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha regarding cooperation with Belarusian democratic forces is very inspiring for Belarusians,” Tsikhanouskaya said.
She also expressed her conviction that Ukraine’s victory “will open up great opportunities for changes in Belarus, as well as in other countries – Moldova, Georgia and Armenia.”
“We all look at Ukraine, at the strong Ukrainians, at the military who are defending Ukraine, with admiration,” she stressed.
“Overall, Ukraine has shown the whole world how this image of an ‘all-powerful’ Russia can be destroyed. After all, you are not only defending yourselves, you are attacking! It was absolutely impossible even to imagine this before. For us, Ukrainians are, of course, heroes,” the Belarusian opposition leader said.
She expressed gratitude to Ukraine’s leadership and people “for understanding that Lukashenko cannot be forgiven or what he has done to Ukraine be forgotten.”
As reported, on September 21, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, a ministerial event was held on the role of Belarus in Russia’s war against Ukraine and its impact on regional and international security.

From Cyprus to the Canaries: Where to go for a warm autumn holiday in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

A new ranking reveals the top 10 European destinations offering plenty of sunshine during the autumn months.
As the summer sun has now set, Google searches for “October holiday” have skyrocketed, reaching 80,000 in the past month and marking a 28% month-on-month increase. But where might these searches lead travellers to?
Villa holiday company Solmar Villas analysed 105 destinations to find where delivers best on great weather – including the likelihood of rain, alongside affordable flight fares across October and November.
In its study of the best destinations for autumn sun in Europe, Cyprus dominates the top of the list. The Mediterranean island takes the top four spots, thanks to its sunny weather, which usually sits between 24C and 29C.
“Whilst we can’t predict the weather, this data is as close as we can get to determining the best spots for the perfect autumn-sun holiday,” Sharon Bradbury, Managing Director at Solmar Villas, said.
“Cyprus seems to be a clear winner, other locations on the list are also fantastic choices based on your personal preferences.”
Cyprus as the go-to choice
Ayia Napa takes first place in the ranking. With an array of beach offerings, it was highlighted that during the autumn season visitors can enjoy its "more relaxed side" with no more than an average of just 2.3 wet days each month from September to November.
The other Cypriot destinations featured include Limassol, which ranks second. Famed for its nature trails, beaches and being a prime yacht destination, Solmar says Limassol is “perfect for those who love a combination of city and coast”.
Third on the ranking, Larnaca is described as a “peaceful port city”. Here, the Finikoudes promenade is lined with palm trees and surrounded by the sands of the Finikoudes Beach.
Meanwhile in fourth place, Paphos is ideal for history buffs. The Archaeological Park is a UNESCO World Heritage site, containing monuments and remains from the Roman era and the Middle Ages. Visitors can also marvel at the floor mosaics, which are considered to be among the finest across the eastern Mediterranean.
Try the Canaries
For holidaymakers keen to escape wet weather and "if you want as close as you can to a guarantee of no rain”, the Canary Islands “are it".
The study also highlighted that in Lanzarote and Fuerteventura, which ranked sixth and seventh on the list, the average highs sit around 26C. The former features more than 150km of sandy beaches and turquoise waters, while the latter, a volcanic island, is known for its landscapes of lava fields, rolling mountains and rock formations.
Greece and Malta
The remaining destinations on the list are Greek and Maltese, with the Athens Riviera, Rhodes and Kos ranking fifth, eighth and ninth respectively. Rounding out the list is Malta.
The Athens Riviera is a 70km coastal stretch of long beaches and coves alongside an array of waterfront dining concepts. Rhodes' Old Town, with its picturesque alleyways and historic stone-paved Street of the Knights, is considered one of the world's best preserved medieval towns. In Kos, the mountainous settlements offer panoramic views of the island.
Malta, the archipelago’s largest island, is also a draw for set-jetters, destinations that once served as filming locations for Games of Thrones scenes. The cobblestoned streets of the old capital of Mdina were the backdrop of the series. Meanwhile, the city’s bastions offer sweeping views across the island.
Top 10 best destinations for autumn sun in Europe
- 1. Ayia Napa, Cyprus
- 2. Limassol, Cyprus
- 3. Larnaca, Cyprus
- 4. Paphos, Cyprus
- 5. Athens Riviera, Greece
- 6. Lanzarote, Spain
- 7. Fuerteventura, Spain
- 8. Rhodes, Greece
- 9. Kos, Greece
- 10. Malta, Malta
