Xinhua Headlines: Xi builds friendship across the Pacific
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:28:25 CST
12:28:25 KST

* Over the years, Xi has personally stayed in close touch with people from all walks of life in the United States through meetings, visits, letters and speeches.
* In November 2023, Xi announced in San Francisco that 50,000 young Americans would be invited to China on exchange and study programs in the next five years. The target was reached in just two and a half years, as young Americans traveled across China, met their Chinese peers and experienced the country's history, culture and development firsthand.
BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- "The foundation of China-U.S. relations lies among the people, the hope is in the people, the future lies in the youth, and the vitality lies in sub-national areas," Chinese President Xi Jinping once said.
For many years, Xi has consistently championed people-to-people friendship between China and the United States, seeking to bring the Chinese and Americans ever closer and rally stronger public support for the two countries to get along.
BRINGING HEARTS CLOSER
China-U.S. relations are widely regarded as the world's most important bilateral relationship. On how the two major countries can deepen cooperation and navigate differences and challenges, Xi has highlighted the vital role of people-to-people friendship and cultural exchanges.
Speaking to the American public, Xi has often stressed, "state-to-state relations ultimately rely on the support of the people and serve the people."
He once used his fingers to form the Chinese character "ren," meaning "person" to illustrate how the Chinese and American people should support each other in Seattle during his state visit to the United States in 2015.
Over the years, Xi has personally stayed in close touch with people from all walks of life in the United States through meetings, visits, letters and speeches.
During his visit to San Francisco in 2023, Xi set aside time to meet with representatives of Americans who had long supported friendship with China. Smiling, he warmly shook hands and exchanged greetings with each of them.
On Monday, just two days ahead of his state visit to the United States, Xi replied to students from 10 U.S. universities who wrote to him after attending youth exchanges in China.
He encouraged the students to join the vast number of young people in both countries in striving to carry forward, uphold, and advance China-U.S. friendly cooperation, and work together to foster mutual understanding and affinity between the two peoples.
"The peoples of China and the United States are both great peoples. Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand. We can help each other succeed and advance the well-being of the whole world," Xi once said.
FRIENDSHIP SPANNING DECADES
Over the decades, Xi's encounters with people from across American society have become cherished chapters in the story of friendship between the Chinese and Americans.
Recalling his visit to the Midwestern U.S. state of Iowa 41 years ago, Xi said he was warmly received, and those wonderful memories remain fresh in his mind to this day.
In the spring of 1985, Xi, then a young official, led a delegation to Iowa. During the visit, he spent three days in Muscatine, a city in rural eastern Iowa, where he stayed with local hosts. Through long hours of friendly exchanges, they gained a genuine understanding of the people living across the Pacific.
"You were the first group of Americans I came into contact with," Xi told his Iowa friends in 2012 when visiting Iowa once again as China's vice president. "To me, you are America."
Today, 2911 Bonnie Drive, the place where he stayed, has been turned into a museum and renamed the Sino-U.S. Friendship House, while Muscatine has become a "city of friendship."
For friendship to endure, youth exchanges and educational cooperation matter.
"Young people, full of vitality and dreams, represent the future and hope of China-U.S. relations and of the world," Xi said, describing education as "a bridge linking the people of China and the United States."
In 1993, Xi, then secretary of the Fuzhou Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, visited Lincoln High School during a trip to Tacoma, the state of Washington, as Fuzhou and Tacoma explored establishing sister-city ties.
Twenty-two years later in 2015, he returned to the school during his state visit to the United States, presenting books on China and table tennis equipment and encouraging students to visit his country for "a more comprehensive and profound understanding of China."
The following year, more than 100 Lincoln students and teachers traveled to China.
In November 2023, Xi announced in San Francisco that 50,000 young Americans would be invited to China on exchange and study programs in the next five years.
The target was reached in just two and a half years, as young Americans traveled across China, met their Chinese peers and experienced the country's history, culture and development firsthand.
BUILDING BRIDGES
"We should build more bridges and pave more roads for people-to-people interactions. We must not erect barriers or create a chilling effect," Xi once said.
Over the years, Xi has worked to expand channels of contact between the two countries, including through exchanges in the business sector.
During his 2015 U.S. visit, he toured companies like Microsoft and Boeing. He has on many occasions met with U.S. business leaders and attended China-U.S. business roundtables and dialogues.
Most recently, in May, Xi met U.S. entrepreneurs accompanying Trump to China. He expressed confidence that U.S. companies would enjoy even broader prospects in China. China's door "will only open wider," he added.
Xi has also emphasized exchanges between the two countries at local levels. He has attended events such as the China-U.S. Governors' Forum and met with U.S. governors on many occasions.
Today, the two countries have 50 pairs of sister provinces and states, and 238 pairs of sister cities. On June 5, such a network brought hundreds of representatives together in San Francisco for the 8th China-U.S. Sister Cities Conference.
The long history of friendship is a shared legacy of the two peoples. At various events, Xi has recounted stories of the Flying Tigers, the Hump route, the Doolittle Raid rescue and Ping-Pong Diplomacy.
He called on the two peoples to carry forward the friendship that "withstood the test of blood and fire," and urged younger generations, in particular, to "draw wisdom and strength from history."
Noting that China-U.S. relations concern the well-being of the over 1.7 billion people of both countries and affect the interests of the over 8 billion people of the world, Xi said both sides should rise up to this historic responsibility.
That view is echoed by Jeffrey Greene, chairman of the Sino-American Aviation Heritage Foundation.
The United States and China "have a duty to humanity to cooperate," he said.■

====================================================================================================

Column: A better path for China, the United States and the Global South
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:28:24 CST
12:28:24 KST

by Maya Majueran
The Asia-Pacific is increasingly at the center of the global economy, home to some of the world's most dynamic markets, manufacturing networks and technological ecosystems. How Beijing and Washington manage their differences and competition will therefore shape far more than their bilateral relationship. It will affect the prosperity, security and development of the broader region.
The economic reality is straightforward: China and the United States are the world's two largest economies, deeply embedded in an interconnected global system. Neither can sustainably prosper in complete isolation, and neither should assume that holding back the other's growth automatically guarantees its own.
Competition is inevitable. But competition does not have to become confrontation. The more productive approach is to strengthen domestic competitiveness while preserving space for trade, investment, dialogue and cooperation where interests align.
China and the United States experienced extraordinary economic expansion during decades in which their economies became increasingly interconnected. That history was not without disagreements or costs. But it also demonstrated that economic competition and mutual benefit can coexist.
The stakes are especially high in the Asia-Pacific, where economies are deeply connected. Growth in one major market can generate demand, investment and supply-chain opportunities elsewhere. Conversely, disruption between the world's two largest economies can transmit costs throughout the region.
Cooperation should therefore remain a foundation of the relationship. Competition needs boundaries, and disagreements must be managed before they become confrontation.
Countries across Southeast Asia and the Pacific want to trade with China, cooperate with the United States, and pursue relationships with both according to their own interests. Their future should not be reduced to a choice between Washington and Beijing.
But there is an even larger question: Where will the next generation of global growth come from?
For much of modern economic history, a disproportionate share of global wealth, capital, technology and consumption was concentrated in a relatively small group of advanced economies. That geography of prosperity is changing.
Across Asia, Africa, Latin America and other emerging regions, billions of people aspire to higher incomes, better infrastructure, greater industrial capacity and improved living standards. Their development will create new consumers, producers, investors and sources of innovation, expanding the global economic pie.
For China, the United States and other economies, this represents not simply a challenge but a major opportunity. A growing Global South will generate demand for technology, healthcare, energy, infrastructure, transport, financial services and advanced manufacturing.
Today, developing economies increasingly possess sophisticated technology, skilled workers, advanced manufacturing capacity and expanding consumer markets of their own. Affordability and technological capability are no longer necessarily opposites, while high-quality products and services are no longer confined to a small group of advanced economies.
This shift should encourage all major economies to improve their own competitiveness.
For the United States, for example, competitiveness cannot be built simply by restricting competitors. Tariffs and technological restrictions may serve particular policy objectives, but they cannot substitute for better infrastructure, stronger research institutions, more affordable housing, lower energy costs, higher productivity or greater innovation.
The same broader principle applies to every economy: Sustainable competitiveness comes from building, investing and innovating.
The objective should not be a race toward higher barriers, but higher productivity, greater innovation, lower structural costs and stronger living standards. This is why the Asia-Pacific and the wider Global South have a strong interest in a stable and open international economic environment.
The future of the global economy will not be determined by whether China and the United States compete. It will depend on how that competition is managed and whether there remains sufficient room for cooperation, economic exchange and development.
Neither country needs the other to fail in order to succeed. A more constructive path is for both to focus on strengthening their own economies while preserving the space for cooperation and growth that benefits the wider world.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

U.S. youth receive Xi's reply letter ahead of his state visit
China

WASHINGTON, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- "When we sent the letter, it honestly felt like a shot in the dark," said Kiana Haywood, a senior student at Central Michigan University. "I didn't know if President Xi would actually read it, let alone take the time to respond to us."
Haywood was among nearly 100 students from 10 U.S. universities who recently wrote to Chinese President Xi Jinping after participating in the Future Makers 2026 China-U.S. Youth Tour for a Shared Asia-Pacific Future and other exchange events in China.
And a reply did arrive on the eve of Xi's state visit to the United States.
In his letter, Xi welcomed the students' appreciation for Chinese civilization, their hope for friendly cooperation between China and the United States, and their willingness to act as envoys of friendship bridging the Pacific Ocean.
Noting that young people from both countries share the same planet Earth and jointly shoulder the mission of the times, Xi urged them to advance China-U.S. friendly cooperation, foster mutual understanding and affinity between the two peoples, and contribute the vitality of youth to building a better world.
Xi has long maintained correspondence with American friends -- from Iowa acquaintances he first met in 1985 to veterans of the historic Flying Tigers who fought alongside China in World War II.
The exchange of letters also extends to a younger generation, as Xi replied in February, 2024 to students from Muscatine High School who had previously visited China and sent them Chinese New Year cards.
This growing connection is rooted in Xi's consistent championing of youth exchanges as a vital bridge between the two nations.
During his 2023 trip to San Francisco for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting, Xi announced an initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China for exchange and study programs over the next five years. By May this year, that goal had been reached two and a half years ahead of schedule.
"There are obviously much bigger conversations happening between our two countries," Haywood said, but the exchanges gave the students "the opportunity to meet each other, ask questions and actually experience one another's cultures instead of only hearing about them from far away."
Xi's reply letter reminded her that "relationships between countries are also built through relationships between people," she said.
Reflecting on her trip, she noted that while China's long history, rich culture and advanced technology have impressed her greatly, "the people left the biggest impression."
"We could ask each other questions, laugh together and realize how much we have in common," she said.
"I want to keep the friendships I made in China, share my experience with other students at Central Michigan University," she said, expressing hope that more U.S. students will have opportunities to visit China so that the personal connections will give them a "completely different perspective."
Similarly, Marlon Forrester, an associate in Harvard's Faculty of Arts and Sciences, also participated in the 2026 China-U.S. Youth Tour. He noted that true affinity requires proximity.
"Mutual understanding and affinity between two people can only happen when we share space together," Forrester said, adding that participating students will become "ambassadors for this work through the direct partnerships with institutional and privately funded sources that can benefit their exploratory research in policy, science, humanities and the arts with our peers across the Pacific Ocean."
"As young people from different countries sharing the same planet, they have a responsibility to respect cultural differences, promote understanding, and work together to address global challenges," he said.
"Their mission is to use creativity, innovation, and collaboration to create a more just, sustainable and peaceful world. By learning from one another, caring for the environment, and contributing positively to their communities, they can help build a future that benefits people across borders and generations," Forrester said.
For Haywood, living out that grand mission can start with something small.
"To me, being an 'envoy of friendship' can start with something as simple as listening to each other and being willing to learn," she said. ■

What's next?
Police continues to make enquiries regarding fan behaviour at the preliminary final. Meyer will umpire in this weekend's AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane.
A 34-year-old Seaford man is expected to be charged for allegedly throwing a plate of food at a woman and child during last week's AFL preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane.
He is expected to be charged on summons with aggravated unlawful assault and discharge a missile.
Police have interviewed the man and another 56-year-old Tullamarine man, who was identified after allegedly throwing a bottle onto the MCG's field of play at the conclusion of the match.
The Tullamarine man has been fined $418 under the Major Events Act.
He is the second man to be fined after security detained a 40-year-old Croydon man for throwing a bottle onto the field of play, before he was spoken to by police.
Bottles and cans were thrown onto the field after the game, including some aimed at the umpires as they walked off the MCG after a holding-the-ball decision by field umpire Hayden Meyer against Jarman Impey that gave Brisbane a go-ahead goal with 18 seconds remaining.
Umpire says he felt 'threatened' by Hawks duo
Meyer, who will officiate in this weekend's AFL grand final, was confronted by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass in the aftermath of his decision.
He said he had received an apology from Barrass but was still waiting to hear from Sicily.
"The abuse that came my way, I felt threatened," Meyer told reporters on Wednesday.
"I expressed exactly that [to the AFL] — the language, and the way that those two players, James [Sicily] and Tom [Barrass], came at me, I felt threatened and intimidated in that situation.
"So I spoke to [umpires boss] Steve McBurney the day after and gave my view of the situation, and how I felt and what occurred, and he then transferred that to Swanny [AFL football boss Greg Swann] and the MRO to eventually come up with a decision around the fines.
"[Barrass] was very apologetic and very sincere in his apology. I accepted his apology and thanked him for taking the time out of his day to give me a call."
Meyer refused to make a call on whether the Hawks pair, who were fined over their actions, should be suspended instead.
"That's out of my control, that's not my decision … I suppose what I take from it is that it's not a great look for junior umpires and kids that are sitting on the couch that we want to recruit into umpiring," he said.
"They see that after the game on the weekend and, if I'm sitting on the couch, I'd be like, 'Do I really want to go to my local umpiring community group and sign up to be an umpire?'
"That was the big disappointing thing for me, that we struggle with umpiring recruitment in local communities, and that doesn't help."
Despite the protestations from Hawthorn fans, Impey admitted the umpires made the right call.
"It was the right decision," he told the Kick It Forward podcast at the Brownlow Medal on Monday night.
"Naturally, when you think there are 30-40 seconds to go, you try and hold it in go from there, but credit to Hayden.
"I hope there was no hate message towards him, so sending love to him."
Ahead of this weekend's grand final, Meyer pleaded for fans to not "cross the line" again.
"I've never experienced bottles being thrown at me post-game. It was pretty scary, to be honest, and I hope it never happens again in any game, any sport," he said.
"[To fans attending the grand final], I would say be passionate, cheer for your team, but respect others, respect the people you're sitting next to, respect the umpires — have fun, but don't cross the line."
Police are continuing to make enquiries regarding the fan behaviour during and after the match.

Coalition vows to 'take a chainsaw' to climate laws, offshore wind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

12:25:49 KST

Coalition vows to 'take a chainsaw' to climate laws and offshore wind
In short:
The Coalition would cancel offshore wind zones, scrap climate laws for heavy industry and car makers, and attempt to lift the ban on nuclear if it wins power.
Its energy plan formalises a commitment to slow down renewables and jettison several core emissions reductions policies.
What's next?
The Coalition has urged states to reconsider the ban on nuclear, which it says could be used to power massive expansion of AI data centres across the country.
The Coalition has vowed to abolish most of Australia's "offshore wind zones" if it wins government, massively limiting where wind farms can be built, as part of a commitment for a major slowdown of the nation's energy transition.
Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan said revoking the offshore wind zones along the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury coasts would be part of an eight-point plan to unpick Australia's key climate policies.
"We will take a chainsaw to Labor's ideologically driven, energy-restrictive approach to energy," Mr Tehan will say in an address to The Australian's energy summit.
As well as winding back the offshore wind rollout, the Coalition would also repeal laws committing Australia to reach net zero emissions by 2050, remove laws requiring the nation's biggest polluters to cut their emissions or face penalties and remove laws requiring car makers to provide more efficient vehicles to Australia, including electric vehicles.
The Coalition would also attempt to lift the prohibition on nuclear power — though that would require laws to be passed by the Senate, where there is no chance for the Coalition to win support without either Labor or the Greens changing positions on nuclear energy.
The power plan formalises the Coalition's abandonment of most of the major policies attempting to drive down carbon emissions and speed up the transition of Australia's electricity networks from coal towards renewable power.
"Within 30 days of getting into government we will introduce the scrap net zero bill … which will get rid of Labor's egregious taxes across energy in our country, taxes on vehicles, it will get rid of the vehicle emissions standards … it will get rid of the safeguard mechanism, which is sending industry offshore," Mr Taylor said.
While the Coalition is vowing to unpick most of the measures being used to cut emissions, the party says it remains committed to addressing climate change, but says the cost of energy to home owners and industry should be put first.
The CSIRO says solar and wind power remain cheaper power sources than coal, even after accounting for transmission costs.
However, the pace of transition has been slower than intended, and has required major investment support through the government's Capacity Investment Scheme.
The Coalition says that scheme should not be picking winners, and should also be allowed to underwrite coal, gas and nuclear power.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the Coalition's plan would "take a chainsaw" to the economy and household budgets.
"It will make Australia poorer, weaker and less secure from global shocks," Mr Bowen said.
"Their plan to stop renewables and household batteries, and sweat coal, would mean Aussie households are left to pick up the bill of global shocks."
Coalition would unpick nascent offshore wind industry
While the Coalition says Australia should have "energy abundance", it has vowed to cancel most of the declared offshore wind zones which have been opened for potential investment.
Repealing four of Australia's six offshore wind zones would leave Gippsland in Victoria and the Bass Strait in Tasmania as the only approved coasts for wind farms.
Mr Tehan was supportive of offshore wind when he joined Energy Minister Chris Bowen at the announcement of the Southern Ocean offshore wind zone in 2023, which is within his federal electorate of Wannon.
"The scale of these offshore wind farms is something to behold, and it's going to need all the community coming together to make sure that we benefit from it … we want to make sure that it continues and continues to provide jobs, and offshore wind can provide that," Mr Tehan said at the time.
Since then, the party has abandoned many of the climate commitments it signed up to under former prime minister Scott Morrison, as high industrial gas costs put pressure on Australian industry, and high power bills stress households — both of which the Coalition blames on limits put on coal and gas.
While offshore wind is an established industry overseas, particularly in Europe and China, the industry is still developing in Australia.
The Albanese government identified six regions as priority areas for offshore wind to help kick-start the industry, opening space for developers to conduct feasibility and environmental studies and begin community consultation.
There are no active wind farms or projects under construction, though about a dozen projects have been granted licences to begin planning.
Offshore wind can harness stronger and more consistent winds than onshore farms, while avoiding taking up valuable agricultural land.
But they are also much more expensive than onshore wind, disrupt marine life during construction as well as fishing activities, and have faced resistance in some communities neighbouring the offshore zones.
The Coalition's eight energy priorities
Read more
Repeal the Climate Change Act 2022, which commits Australia to net zero emissions by 2050.
Remove the safeguard mechanism, which requires heavy industry to cut emissions or face penalties.
Repeal the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard, which requires car makers to import more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles or face penalties.
Revoke four offshore wind energy zones across the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury regions.
Repeal all legislative prohibitions on nuclear energy.
Introduce a renewable energy code of conduct "to ensure developers earn their social licence from the community that they operate in".
Require that any energy funding provided to the states and territories is conditional on prioritising energy affordability and reliability.
Redirect the Australian Energy Regulator to have primary regard to affordability and reliability, which will put households and businesses at the centre of regulatory decision-making.
The Coalition argues the offshore wind push has failed, with no projects under construction four years after the first wind zone was declared, adding that the government was forced to commit about $50 million last year in financial relief for stalled proposals.
United States President Donald Trump's moves to cancel funding and permits for offshore wind projects also cooled global investment.
The energy minister conceded in his National Press Club address in August that offshore wind was reducing in cost more slowly than previously predicted.
"Offshore wind has faced structural constraints around the world which make starting the industry from scratch harder than it would otherwise be," Mr Bowen said.
The minister noted that offshore wind was never expected to contribute to the government's 2030 goal of 82 per cent of power coming from renewables, and the government remained focused on delivering that renewables power, "while keeping our eye over the horizon".
The only measure in the Coalition's priority list that would encourage renewable power is a renewed pitch to lift the ban on nuclear power, which is prohibited under state and federal laws.
The Coalition argues states may want to reconsider those bans as energy-hungry AI data centres roll out across the country, saying the stable renewables source would become a much more realistic option.
However it will not re-adopt the proposal by former opposition leader Peter Dutton for the federal government to fund and part-own those nuclear plants — instead suggesting the only taxpayer support they would receive would be the same that is made available to any other energy source, such as through a reworked Capacity Investment Scheme.
Independent MP Monique Ryan said the Coalition's proposal was "dumb, dangerous and desperate" and would make energy more expensive.
"Australians have embraced clean energy because it works. We've spent years investing in rooftop solar, electric vehicles, household batteries and home electrification because these technologies save money and reduce emissions," Ms Ryan said.
"The Liberals' retrograde attempt to appease the Nationals and woo One Nation voters would drag the country backwards."

As Japan swelters, farmers turn to new heat-resistant rice varieties to boost staple crop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
03:23:13 UTC
12:23:13 KST

When schoolchildren in Shiroishi were enlisted to plant rice seedlings in June, Shinto priests blessed the land and asked the deities for a bountiful crop. Judging by the fields behind farmer Haruki Kawasaki, their prayers have been answered.
The 63-year-old is preparing to harvest this year’s crop of hinatamaru, a variety of rice whose plump grains have thrived despite exposure to another hot and dry summer, conditions that typically punish rice yields.
Hinatamaru is one of growing number of heat-resistant rice varieties that are giving fresh hope to farmers across Japan that they can overcome a climate emergency that is threatening the country’s staple crop.
Kawasaki and his team once spent the entire day in the fields, but the heat has made that impossible. “Now we start early in the morning and work until around noon,” he says. “It’s way too hot in the afternoon … although the mornings are not what you would call cool.”
Kawasaki and other farmers in Saga are at the centre of the boom as Japan finds ways to cope with a warmer future. The long process of developing heat-tolerant strains involves cross-breeding existing varieties, cultivation in controlled environments and, finally, real-world trials.
Japan’s ageing farmers have toiled through record-breaking heat and below-average rainfall over the last three summers. After heat records were broken again this year, the meteorological agency added a new category – “cruelly hot days” – when the mercury exceeds 40C. El Niño is expected to bring even more extreme weather.
Those conditions create havoc with crops of Japan’s staple cereal, producing chalky, anaemic grains that are susceptible to cracking when polished for commercial sale.
When the temperature stays abnormally high for prolonged periods after rice plants have flowered, what should be translucent, starchy seeds end up as immature grains that can’t be sold as grade 1 polished rice on the open market.
In a report published this month, Greenpeace Japan warned that four of the country’s “iconic” autumn crops, including rice and sweet potatoes, were at risk because of exposure to long periods of high temperatures.
“Over 50 years of accelerating heatwaves have pushed Japan’s most iconic agricultural hubs past their thermal limits, placing both crop viability and supermarket prices on the line,” Ikumi Toyota, from Greenpeace Japan, said in a statement.
“While farmers are showing incredible ingenuity to adapt, single operations cannot outrun systemic climate disruption. When the people who feed us run out of options, national food security becomes everyone’s crisis.”
Embracing heat-loving crops
The climate crisis has made growing traditional rice varieties a calculated risk that fewer farmers are willing to take. In Saga prefecture, located on the coast of the Ariake Sea in Kyushu – a large island in Japan’s south-west – growing numbers are instead taking a chance on something new.
According to the agriculture ministry, Saga now leads the county in the adoption of new strains that can withstand the stifling, bone dry summers that have become the norm.
Heat-tolerant varieties account for almost 67% of Saga’s rice acreage. Neighbouring Nagasaki follows with just under 50% and Shimane, on the Japan Sea coast, with 47%. However, uptake in regions in the north-east, where farmers are traditionally more accustomed to battling cold weather, is still very low.
Heat records have tumbled in Japan in recent years. Record-breaking heat in 2023 was partly to blame for the “Reiwa rice crisis” the following year, when the government was forced to take the unprecedented step of releasing emergency stockpiles to ease severe shortages and price hikes.
Farmers in Saga raised the alarm a decade ago, when low yields of poor quality rice sent prices plummeting. “They were determined to grow delicious rice that could withstand the heat,” says Kazuhiro Matsumoto, a senior official in the crop department of the Saga Prefecture Agricultural Testing and Research Centre.
The solution came in the form of hinatamaru – the product of 12 years of research that is now spreading quickly after successful trials in 2024 – propelling Saga prefecture to the forefront of agriculture’s rearguard action against climate change.
Kawasaki’s crop of hinatamaru is this year is expected to total a modest 600kg but the outlook is promising. And other regions in Japan are following suit.
The use of heat-tolerant rice has expanded to all but three of Japan’s 47 prefectures as agriculture officials rush to combat declines in quality and yield. They covered 248,000 hectares last year – a record 18% of the overall rice crop – according to the agriculture ministry, a dramatic increase from the 42,000 hectares the previous year.
The climate emergency is also changing the way Japan’s farmers work. Fruit and vegetable farmers in some regions have taken to inspecting their crops at night, to avoid higher temperatures, while others are switching to heat-loving crops such as avocado, bitter melon and okra.
Kawasaki, who has been growing rice for more than three decades, says the day could come when farmers across Japan are all growing new heat-resistant varieties. “The priority is that it has to taste good.”
As he prepares to harvest this season’s crop – some of which will be included in an annual ritual at the imperial palace in Tokyo – Kawasaki also notes the spread of heat-tolerant grains as a race against time. Almost 70% of Japan’s agricultural workers are 65 or older.
“Lots of farmers around here are in their 70s, and I’m in my 60s,” he says. “So as a farmer, I’m just grateful that we have found something that works. And it tastes great.”

First introduced in 2020, the national strategy also aims to reduce the country's trade dependence on the West by bolstering domestic markets.

The Solar System chose fire over ice from the very beginning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
03:06:29 UTC
12:06:29 KST

The Solar System chose fire over ice from the very beginning
- Date:
- September 22, 2026
- Source:
- Yale University
- Summary:
- Ancient iron meteorites reveal that some of the Solar System’s first solid bodies were built mostly from tiny heat-forged rock beads called chondrules, while water-rich dust was largely excluded. The finding pushes this selective planet-building process back to within the Solar System’s first million years.
- Share:
The earliest stages of planet formation may have been far more selective than scientists once realized. As the young Solar System began assembling solid objects such as planets, moons, and protoplanets, two major types of material were available. One was chondrules, millimeter-sized pieces of rock formed at high temperatures. The other was matrix, a cold, fine-grained dust rich in water ice and organic material.
New research led by Yale University suggests that the Solar System strongly favored the heat-formed material almost immediately.
Researchers have found the first geochemical evidence showing that chondrules were already being preferentially incorporated into solid bodies during the Solar System's first million years. Until now, scientists had only been able to document this type of sorting in objects that formed 2 to 4 million years after the Solar System began.
The study was published Sept. 18 in Nature Astronomy.
The Solar System Was Selective From the Start
"Our work shows that this assembly process was remarkably selective from the very beginning," said Damanveer Grewal, an assistant professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and first author of the study. "The earliest bodies in the outer Solar System were built from 83% to 92% chondrules, with very little of the icy, volatile-rich dust that dominates later-forming objects."
Chondrules are small rocky spheres found inside chondrites, which are among the most primitive meteorites preserved in geological collections. These tiny structures offer scientists a direct physical connection to the earliest stages of the Solar System.
"You can hold them in your hand and know that they began as part of a process that started billions of years ago," Grewal said. "It's a timescale that's hard to wrap your head around."
Scientists have long known that carbonaceous chondrites (primitive, stony meteorites that contain organic compounds and water among their silicate minerals) from the outer Solar System show a pattern related to age. Older examples tend to contain a greater proportion of chondrules and less matrix, while younger ones contain more of the cold, volatile-rich material.
That pattern suggested that the regions where the first solid objects, known as planetesimals, were forming were already favoring heat-formed chondrules while excluding much of the icy dust.
Searching for Evidence From the First Million Years
Confirming what happened during the Solar System's first million years has been difficult because no preserved undifferentiated bodies from that period remain. Scientists therefore lacked a direct way to determine the original balance between chondrules and matrix in those earliest objects.
Grewal and his colleagues approached the problem by examining chemical clues preserved in iron meteorites from the outer Solar System.
The parent bodies represented by these meteorites contained so much radioactive aluminum-26 that they eventually melted completely. That process erased the physical structures that could have revealed what those bodies originally contained.
However, their chemistry still preserved useful information.
The researchers identified two independent chemical tracers associated with matrix. One was sulfur, which is highly concentrated in matrix. The other was the oxidation state of iron, which can indicate how much water ice and oxidized dust had been incorporated into the original body.
Meteorites Reveal a Chondrule-Rich Beginning
Using these two tracers, the team reconstructed the compositions of the ancient parent bodies. They calculated that matrix accounted for just 8% to 17% of their original material, a smaller proportion than has been measured in any known chondrites.
That means the remaining material was overwhelmingly dominated by chondrules.
"Both tracers independently tell the same story: these early planetesimals were remarkably matrix-poor," Grewal said. "That convergence is what makes the result robust."
The findings may also solve another puzzle involving the meteorite record. Very old chondrules are surprisingly uncommon today, even though they appear to have been abundant during the Solar System's earliest history.
According to Grewal, many of those ancient chondrules were probably incorporated into the first generation of planetesimals. Those bodies subsequently melted, destroying the physical evidence and making the oldest chondrules much harder to find in surviving meteorites.
Reconstructing the Birth of Planetary Bodies
The results indicate that the process of separating and selecting planetary ingredients began almost as soon as solid bodies started forming. Rather than mixing chondrules and icy dust evenly, the young Solar System strongly favored chondrules in some of its earliest planetesimals.
"These ubiquitous little beads of rock are the basic building blocks from which the planets themselves were eventually assembled," Grewal said. "And now we know they were already being sorted and incorporated into the first generation of solid bodies from the very start."
Co-authors of the study are Zhongtian Zhang of Princeton University and Joanna Drążkowska of the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research in Germany.
Funding for the research came from Yale University.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Yale University. Original written by Jim Shelton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Damanveer S. Grewal, Zhongtian Zhang, Joanna Drążkowska. Planetesimal compositions governed by aerodynamic sorting from the onset of Solar System formation. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02976-6

Gal Gadot's $3m. Genesis Prize initiative funds 24 Israeli mental health and trauma care NGOs

12:05:34 KST

A $3 million initiative built around Israeli actress Gal Gadot’s Genesis Prize will fund 24 Israeli nonprofit organizations providing mental health treatment and trauma care, the Genesis Prize Foundation announced on Wednesday.
The 2026 Genesis Prize laureate directed her $1 million award toward organizations helping Israelis recover from the psychological consequences of the October 7, 2023, attacks and the wars that followed. A matching campaign led by Jewish Funders Network generated another $2m. in private and corporate donations, according to the foundation.
Recipients include Make-A-Wish Israel, United Hatzalah, and CareGivers Israel. The grants will support treatment, trauma counseling, caregiver training, and social work services, including assistance for professionals who have spent the past three years caring for others.
“After three years of war, loss, and extraordinary hardship, I believe recovery starts from within,” Gadot said in a statement.
“I want to dedicate these funds to the people who care for others every day: the doctors, nurses, medics, mental health professionals, and caregivers doing the difficult work of helping people recover and rebuild.”
Initiative focuses on those delivering care, i.e., health professionals, social workers
The initiative’s focus includes the pressures facing those delivering care. Mental health professionals, social workers, educators, and caregivers have faced heavy demand while many have experienced trauma themselves, the foundation said.
The selected organizations operate in northern, southern, and central Israel. Their programs serve mental health professionals, frontline workers, educators, social workers, family caregivers, children and young people, survivors of war and combat trauma, and underrepresented communities.
The foundation and Jewish Funders Network received 150 applications from Israeli nonprofits over two months. Fifty-four organizations advanced through the review process, and 24 were selected.
Applicants were evaluated on their demonstrated impact, organizational capacity, and ability to strengthen Israel’s mental health and caregiver services. Each recipient had to secure a matching contribution from a new donor or an increased gift from an existing donor.
The foundation published a link to the full list of recipients alongside its funding announcement.
The announcement named three recipients but did not provide individual grant amounts or a timetable for distributing the money. It also did not specify how many people the funded programs were expected to reach.
Gadot said the organizations shared a commitment to helping people through periods of vulnerability, even when their work and the communities they served differed.
“Some of these organizations bring different communities together by their very nature. Others are simply there for people at their most vulnerable,” she said. “But they all share the same idea: Caring for one another is how we begin to move forward.”
Stan Polovets, co-founder and chairman of the Genesis Prize Foundation, said the initiative reflected the prize’s philanthropic purpose.
“Awarding the Genesis Prize is not an end in itself; it’s a means of making the world a better place,” he said.
Genesis Prize a 'Jewish Nobel' for supporting humanitarian causes
“Gal joins an extraordinary group of past honorees, including Michael Bloomberg, Barbra Streisand, Natan Sharansky, Steven Spielberg, and Robert Kraft, who have used the Genesis Prize to support humanitarian causes they believe in.”
The annual $1m. prize, described by Time magazine as the “Jewish Nobel,” recognizes professional accomplishments, contributions to humanity, and commitment to Jewish values or Israel.
According to the foundation, prize funds and matching donations have supported efforts to combat antisemitism, advance inclusion, and provide humanitarian relief. Other initiatives have supported the rehabilitation of former hostages and their families, as well as strengthening ties between Israel and Latin America.
Jewish Funders Network, which led the matching initiative, connects philanthropists across countries and fields of giving. Its work includes research, partnerships, and opportunities for funders to exchange experience.
“Gal chose to focus on trauma and mental health in Israel,” Polovets said. “Her $1 million Genesis Prize became the foundation for a $3 million initiative supporting organizations helping Israelis heal.”
Gadot connected her decision to direct the award toward care providers with her Jewish heritage and the responsibility to help people who are suffering.
“That value is deeply connected to my Jewish heritage and to our responsibility to care for those who are hurting and help repair what has been broken,” she said.
“By strengthening the people who care for others, we can begin to heal families and communities, restore a sense of connection, and create the possibility of a more peaceful future.”

====================================================================================================

Freedom of worship demands both physical safety and sanctuary autonomy - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
03:05:03 UTC
12:05:03 KST

Two Jewish communities, separated by thousands of kilometers, were forced to think about their safety as they gathered to observe Yom Kippur this week.
In Jerusalem, vandals entered the Reform congregation Kol HaNeshama sometime overnight, after worshipers left following Sunday evening’s service and before they returned for morning prayers, and they removed a Pride flag from the sanctuary.
In Belleville, Ontario, a man armed with a shotgun opened fire on a police officer stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue while about two dozen worshipers were inside.
These were fundamentally different events. The Jerusalem break-in formed part of a documented series of incidents targeting the congregation. In Canada, authorities had not established by press time whether the synagogue or Jewish community was the gunman’s intended target.
Their connection begins and ends with their timing and setting: Both disrupted Jewish prayer on Yom Kippur. That narrow connection raises a basic question: whether freedom of worship protects not only the right to gather but also a congregation’s safety and its authority to determine what happens inside its own sanctuary.
Jews across countries, denominations, time zones gather on Yom Kippur
The holiday gives that setting particular meaning. On Yom Kippur, Jewish communities do something at once local and collective: Each congregation follows its own customs, but Jews across countries, denominations, and time zones gather to recite the same confessions and account for the year that has passed.
That shared observance does not require Jews to agree about how Judaism should be practiced. A Reform congregation in Jerusalem and a Conservative congregation in Ontario need not share the same liturgy, politics, or understanding of Jewish life to be participating in the same religious act. That plurality is precisely what freedom of worship protects.
The Pride flag hanging inside Kol HaNeshama’s sanctuary reflected the values the congregation had chosen for its own community. Anyone is entitled to reject what the flag represents or to disagree with Reform Judaism, but that disagreement does not confer authority over another congregation’s place of worship.
By entering the synagogue and removing the flag, those responsible turned disapproval into action. Through trespass and intimidation, they sought to determine which symbols the congregation would be permitted to place in its own sanctuary.
The overnight break-in was not an isolated incident. Vandals had previously smashed a window, damaged artwork, and removed Pride flags from the building. During Rosh Hashanah, a group of youths threw eggs at worshipers arriving for services. It has not been established that the same people were responsible for each episode, but the repeated targeting requires a response proportionate to the pattern, rather than the treatment of each incident as minor mischief.
Belleville presents a separate responsibility. Police said the gunman fired first at the officer securing the synagogue, prompting him and a second officer to return fire. The gunman and the first officer were seriously wounded, while none of the worshipers inside was physically harmed. The congregation subsequently canceled its remaining Yom Kippur services.
Jewish worship under threat even in Israel
The duty to protect Jewish worship does not end when it takes place in a Jewish state. In Jerusalem, Jewish authorities must protect a Jewish congregation whose religious choices some other Jews reject.
The identities of those responsible for the Yom Kippur break-in remain unknown. During Rosh Hashanah, however, the youths who threw eggs were described as Jewish and wore kippot, and the pattern has centered on a Reform synagogue, its worshipers, and its Pride flags. Authorities must treat those incidents as repeated targeting and identify those responsible.
Belleville and Jerusalem require different investigations, but the public obligation is the same. Canadian authorities must determine why the gunman opened fire and ensure that the synagogue can reopen safely, while Israeli authorities must prevent hostility within Jewish society from restricting how another Jewish community worships.
In both countries, protection should not depend on officials sharing the congregation’s beliefs.
Jewish sovereignty cannot mean protecting Jews only from religious hostility outside of Israel - it must also preserve disagreement within the Jewish community in Israel and ensure that no group can enforce its definition of legitimate Judaism through trespass or intimidation.
Yom Kippur does not make Jewish communities identical; rather, it shows why their different ways of praying must all be protected.

Israel captured and has since occupied a “security zone” that includes the summit of Mt. Hermon following the ouster of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad.

How does Xi Jinping’s ‘special plane’ compare with Air Force One?
A look at the Chinese leader’s aircraft, which is bound to become part of the visual choreography of his state visit in Washington
The aircraft carrying China’s leader, often referred to in state media and official statements as a zhuan ji, or special plane, remains far less known to the world than Air Force One, despite both countries using Boeing 747s for presidential travel.
For a head of state, a presidential aircraft is more than a means of transport. Its range, on-board facilities and security systems reflect the practical demands of presidential travel and diplomatic missions, and the aircraft itself becomes part of the visual choreography of a state visit.
In one sense, it is one of the first symbols of a country to arrive in the host country, appearing in the sky before the president steps onto the tarmac.

Anthropic, OpenAI release cheaper AI even as safety fears grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Anthropic, OpenAI release cheaper AI even as safety fears grow
- Anthropic and OpenAI released new, cheaper AI models, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol/Luna, offering high performance amid rising safety concerns and competition.
- Both companies faced security breaches in July, leading to pauses in AI development and calls from leaders for slowing AI progress.
- Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 includes advanced safeguards and shows improved alignment, but its unpredictability in real-life use remains a challenge.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic and OpenAI on Sept 22 released new, cheaper artificial intelligence models within hours of each other, days after the heads of both companies called for a slowdown in AI development.
Anthropic said its Opus 5.5 comes close to the performance of its flagship model at a significantly lower price. It matches Fable, Anthropic’s cutting-edge model, on most tasks at a 20 per cent lower price, the company said.
OpenAI followed shortly after with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and claimed they handle tasks substantially better than Anthropic’s top models.
The new models are cheaper, faster versions of GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s most powerful model, launched earlier in September.
The duelling launches highlight the tension facing the two San Francisco companies as both warn of the dangers of the technology they are building.
The companies are, however, under pressure to generate returns on massive investments amid stiff competition from low-cost models, particularly Chinese ones.
Anthropic’s release comes a few weeks before its expected stock market debut. OpenAI has delayed its IPO plans until 2027.
Concerns about AI have grown since July, when OpenAI models undergoing a cybersecurity test got around controls meant to isolate them from the internet and broke into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI model repository.
Anthropic reported similar incidents, and the two companies briefly paused work on their new AI systems.
Earlier in September, Jacob Coxon, a British researcher, announced his resignation from Anthropic in a viral post on X, saying neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was acting responsibly in the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident.
In the wake of the Coxon’s warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing down AI improvement. He was joined by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, but mocked by Trump, who described such warnings as “hoaxes.”
Opus 5.5 is the first Anthropic model released since then.
Anthropic said the new model applies the same safeguards as its state-of-the-art model Fable in the areas of cybersecurity, biology and AI model design.
In practice, a request deemed risky by these safeguards is rerouted to an older, less powerful model.
Anthropic also said that, based on its own testing, Opus 5.5 is the best-performing model it has tested to date on alignment – that is, how closely it adheres to what its designers intend.
But the model also showed signs that it often suspects it is being evaluated, which the company acknowledged makes it harder to predict how it will behave in real-life use. AFP

Venezuelan opposition leader Machado fails to enter country, acting President Rodriguez meets Trump
CARACAS – Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado tried three times in the past 24 hours to return home but was unable to complete the journey.
Machado sought to travel from Panama to Venezuela by several routes, according to a source with direct knowledge of her plans. The attempts came as acting President Delcy Rodriguez visited New York for the United Nations General Assembly, where she met with US President Donald Trump.
The efforts included plans to travel by boat and to fly to the Caribbean islands of Aruba and Curacao before continuing by sea, the source said. Colombia’s NTN24 first reported the attempts earlier on Sept 22.
The failure to get home underscores the obstacles Machado continues to face as she seeks to carve out a role in the US-backed political transition following Nicolas Maduro’s capture in January. They also highlight the divergent paths of Machado and Rodriguez as Washington deepens its engagement with the acting president while shunning the opposition.
Rodriguez met with Trump on Sept 22 on the sidelines of the UN meeting, according to a White House official. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also attended.
Machado’s daughter, Ana Corina Sosa, said on Sept 22 that her mother was actively trying to return but acknowledged that the process was complicated.
“Right now she is trying to return, at this moment,” Sosa told NTN24 in New York, adding that there were “many forces” involved and that returning was not as simple as boarding a plane.
Sosa spoke after accepting the 2026 Concordia Leadership Award on her mother’s behalf in New York. Machado participated virtually in the ceremony.
Machado is expected to address the issue later.
The latest efforts follow several previous failed attempts by Machado to return to Venezuela, including one in late June when her plane was forced to divert.
Machado has publicly said she intends to return to take part in Venezuela’s political transition. In an interview with the Wall Street Journal, she said she was prepared to leave at a moment’s notice and could enter the country by land, sea or air, though she gave no specific date.
It wasn’t immediately clear whether the latest attempts were coordinated with Washington or whether Machado had received security guarantees. Trump has said he doesn’t oppose her returning to Venezuela.
Her efforts come as the Trump administration has increasingly worked with Rodriguez since Maduro’s removal, recognising her authority, easing sanctions and deepening economic ties with her government. The relationship has expanded further with a major oil agreement between the two countries and Rodriguez’s visit to New York in September.
Machado’s return would present a new challenge for Rodriguez, whose government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to come back, including some of Machado’s closest allies.
She remains Venezuela’s most popular political figure, with a 53 per cent positive image in the latest AtlasIntel survey conducted for Bloomberg News.
Machado went into hiding shortly after the disputed 2024 presidential election, saying she feared for her life as Maduro’s government targeted opposition leaders. She left Venezuela late in 2025 in a clandestine operation to collect her Nobel Peace Prize and subsequently met Trump and other senior US officials in Washington. After the failed attempts to return in June, she remained largely in Panama. BLOOMBERG

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

"Grain from Ukraine feeds people all over the world": EU urges Russia to stop attacks on Ukrainian food exports
Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, has urged Russia to stop attacks on Ukrainian grain in the Black Sea to restore grain exports and prevent a global food crisis.
Source: Kallas's speech at the opening of a UN General Assembly event on the Black Sea and global food security
Quote from Kallas on X (Twitter): "Grain from Ukraine feeds people all over the world. But Russia is blocking exports through the Black Sea and is deliberately causing global food insecurity.
The EU is calling for attacks to stop and grain to flow again. Food must never be used as a weapon of war."
Details: Kallas said that the consequences of Russia's military aggression do not just affect Ukraine, since it is one of the world's most important agricultural exporters.
Ukraine accounts for 15% of global maize exports, 10% of wheat exports, 15-20% of barley exports and around 50% of sunflower oil exports. Almost 90% of these products are transported through the Black Sea corridor.
To help address the problem, the EU is looking for new grain storage options in Ukraine, supporting farmers and small and medium-sized agricultural businesses and facilitating the cross-border movement of goods.
Background:
- Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also discussed global food security, including Russian attacks on Ukraine's maritime corridor, with Carl Skau, Acting Executive Director of the World Food Programme.
- Sybiha stressed that the consequences of Russian strikes will be felt far beyond the Black Sea region, as Ukraine supplies a significant share of grain and sunflower oil to global markets.
- He therefore described ensuring freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, protecting Ukrainian ports and holding Russia accountable as urgent global priorities.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s largest drone competition received 152 team entries ahead of preliminary rounds beginning in October, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said Tuesday in a press release.
Registration closed on Aug. 31. The preliminaries will be held from Oct. 24-25 at the Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center in Chiayi County, while the finals will take place Dec. 25 at the International Convention Center Tainan.
The competition received 69 entries for the obstacle challenge, 50 for the precision-drop challenge, and 33 for the building-block challenge. Of the 152 entries, 65 came from individuals, 65 from public agencies, and 22 from schools and companies. The ministry said public-sector participation was the highest in the competition’s history.
The competition aims to showcase technological developments, encourage interest in the drone industry, and raise awareness of non-China supply chains.
The ministry also held a warm-up event in Taipei to explain the rules and safety precautions. The building-block challenge evaluates flight stability and spatial awareness, the obstacle challenge tests route control, and the precision-drop challenge assesses positioning and accuracy.
Entries must be free of Chinese parts, including the drone platforms, modules, and key components. The ministry said that in addition to evaluating performance, the competition promotes supply-chain integrity, traceability, and reliability.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taichung mayoral candidate Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) is seeking to defeat her KMT rival, Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), by emphasizing policy and the local connections she has built through more than 20 years of public service.
Born into a political family, Ho said she initially had little appetite for a career in politics, per NOWNews. Her mother, Lin Shu-man (林淑滿), was a KMT Taichung County councilor, and Ho recalled that her mother was frequently absent during her childhood.
Ho said the corruption-ridden election culture she witnessed, along with the discrimination her mother faced on the county council, further strengthened her desire to keep her distance from politics. However, Taiwan’s democratization in the 1990s drew Ho, then a university student, into politics and the DPP, per KNews.
Lin initially scolded her daughter but eventually gave her greater autonomy. She also tried to persuade Ho to join the KMT if she ever decided to run for office.
Ho’s political career began after she was forced to end her postgraduate studies at the University of York when her mother fell ill and the family faced financial difficulties. Her first attempt to enter politics, as an independent candidate for county council, ended in defeat.
Ho later secured a position with the county government through a university professor, eventually becoming a councilor in 2002, per Wealth Magazine. Beyond her family background, Ho said her belief that structural reforms are needed to improve people's lives was another major reason she entered politics.
For her 2026 mayoral campaign, Ho is focusing on transportation, per UDN. Ho has criticized Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) for failing to expand the city's MRT network, arguing that inadequate transportation affects both Taichung's development and residents' daily lives. She also said poor planning for bus services and parking has created problems across the city.
Ho's education policies prioritize safety, per KNews. She has proposed allocating more funding for school security personnel and improving traffic conditions around school districts so students can travel safely from the moment they leave home until they return. Ho also supports greater food traceability to promote public health and consumer confidence.
On economic development, Ho said the Taichung International Exhibition Center should do more than provide a venue for investors from around the world to see local businesses, per KNews. She argued that the city should also attract visiting businesspeople to nearby shops and businesses.
Ho said insufficient surrounding infrastructure, including parking, restaurants, and hotels, limits the facility's potential to generate broader economic benefits.
Looking ahead, Ho has criticized Chiang for supporting the KMT's plan to fund development of the drone industry only through the regular budgeting process, per NOWNews. She argues that a special budget would provide the steady investment needed to develop the industry and strengthen national security.
Ho said the DPP has more cohesive plans for developing the drone sector and other advanced manufacturing industries that have become important to Taichung's economy.

11 hospitalized after Kaohsiung power plant accident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
02:55:44 UTC
11:55:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Eleven people were hospitalized Tuesday after a contract worker fell into a hydrochloric acid tank during maintenance work at Taipower’s Southern Power Plant in Kaohsiung, with one suffering serious chemical burns.
The accident occurred at about 9:30 a.m. near Unit 4 in Kaohsiung’s Cianjhen District. A contract worker surnamed Tseng was transferring hydrochloric acid when he stepped through the top of the tank and fell inside, per PTS.
Kaohsiung Fire Department First Brigade Deputy Captain Cai Zong-han (蔡宗翰) said Tseng’s colleagues had already pulled him from the tank when firefighters arrived. “He was not fully conscious and had extensive burns,” Cai said.
Ten other Taipower and contractor employees who assisted with the rescue subsequently reported discomfort after apparently inhaling hydrochloric acid fumes and were also taken to hospitals. Taipower said Tuesday evening that of the 11 injured, one remained in serious condition, three were hospitalized for observation, and seven had been discharged.
The company said the accident did not affect the plant’s generating equipment and its units remained in normal operation, with no impact on electricity supplies. Taipower immediately suspended the relevant work and launched an emergency response, per CNA.
Firefighters sprayed water at the site to reduce the concentration of hydrochloric acid fumes and maintained a safe distance while responding to the incident, local reports said.
Taipower Southern Power Plant Deputy Director Tsao Tsan-jui (曹燦瑞) said the worker had been wearing protective equipment and a safety harness when he climbed to the top of the tank. He said the exact cause of the fall and why the top of the tank gave way remain under investigation.
The accident involved a hydrochloric acid storage system associated with the plant’s seawater treatment process. Reports said the acid is used to prevent microbial growth.
The Kaohsiung Labor Bureau’s Labor Inspection Division ordered work at the site to stop and is investigating whether the employer violated the Occupational Safety and Health Act. Violations can result in a fine of up to NT$3 million (US$94,700), per Newtalk.
Established in 1955, the facility is Taipower’s only thermal power plant located in a metropolitan area.

11:51:53 KST

An Israeli man has been missing since Sunday while hiking on Mount Olympus in Greece, with his family saying they have been unable to contact him since he sent photos while making his way toward the summit.
Ami Yogev, 46, from the central city of Modi’in, last spoke with his mother, Shosh Debi, around noon Sunday. His phone has since become unavailable and his family does not know what happened to him.
“Contact with Ami was lost on Sunday. At noon was the last time he picked up,” Debi told ynet. “At 4 p.m., I sent him a message. He saw the message but didn’t respond, and since then there has only been one check mark. His phone is unavailable.”
A thermal-drone company located with the help of the Israeli Embassy in Greece has volunteered to assist in the search, including at night, ynet has learned. The company is expected to deploy drones over areas considered relevant to the search.
Debi said her son flew from Israel to Athens the previous Tuesday on a spur-of-the-moment trip and remained in regular contact with her after arriving.
“He spoke with me from the time he landed in Athens,” she said. “He got a phone plan and contacted me every day. On Sunday, he told me he intended to climb Mount Olympus. He spoke with me while he was climbing and sent me pictures. He also spoke with a friend and sent him pictures.”
“After he sent a picture saying he was on his way to the summit, he stopped answering and hasn’t contacted us since,” she said.
Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece and the legendary home of the gods in ancient Greek mythology, rises to 2,918 meters, or about 9,573 feet. Its upper reaches include steep and exposed terrain, and weather conditions can change rapidly.
Debi, 65, said she had barely slept since her son disappeared.
“I haven’t slept for two days,” she said. “I can’t stop crying. I’m afraid. I just want to know that he’s OK, that everything is OK. I don’t need anything. I just want them to tell me he’s alive and everything is fine.”
“If he doesn’t want to come back, I just want him to take care of himself,” she added. “I can’t travel there, as they suggested at the Foreign Ministry. I’m 65. I can’t go there to conduct searches.”
Yogev left Israel without travel insurance, and his mother said she cannot afford to privately finance a search for him.
“We notified the Foreign Ministry and the police,” she said. “Yesterday, someone at the Foreign Ministry told me to contact Magnus, and maybe they could help, but they can provide assistance for $8,500 for three days. I don’t have that kind of money.”
Magnus International Search and Rescue is an Israeli company specializing in locating and rescuing travelers overseas.
Debi said the Foreign Ministry told her it had provided the relevant information to Greek authorities and that Greek police were searching for her son.
“We also filed a missing-person report with the police,” she said. “They received all the information and said they were forwarding it to Interpol. We are all worried about him and hope to find him safe and sound.”
The Foreign Ministry said its consular officials were working with Greek authorities to help locate Yogev.
“From the moment the case became known, the Israeli consul in Athens and the Foreign Ministry’s department for Israelis in distress abroad have been in contact with the local authorities and are working to provide all possible assistance in locating the Israeli citizen with whom contact has been lost in Greece,” the ministry said.

Trump, whose war on Iran is nearing the seven-month mark, said US and Iranian officials would hold another round of talks in the “very near future”.
Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, said signs of diplomatic progress between the US and Iran had refocused investor attention on the potential of AI to generate profits after years of multibillion-dollar investments.
“We have been searching for a clear consumer use case to justify the AI spend, and many see Muse as just that product,” Goldberg told Al Jazeera.
“Personally, I think Muse is just a step in the right direction; there will be better products – probably soon – but Muse is one of those things that are so useful they get investors excited about AI prospects again,” Goldberg said.

Ageless "Chuso" vaults into her seventh Asian Games - and won't stop there
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:42:32 CST
11:42:32 KST

by sportswriters Cao Yibo, Ji Jiadong, Yue Chenxing
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- "Chuso" is old enough to be the mother of most of her rivals.
At Nagoya City General Gymnasium, where artistic gymnastics is underway at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, a familiar figure lined up at the end of the vault runway.
When the announcer called her name, several spectators in the stands did a double-take: the woman preparing to sprint down the runway and launch herself over the vaulting table was 51 years old.
Oksana Chusovitina, the Uzbek gymnastics legend, was competing at her seventh Asian Games, a run of continental competition stretching back 32 years to Hiroshima 1994. Along the way, she has collected eight Asian Games medals: two golds, four silvers and two bronzes.
On Tuesday, she added another chapter to that remarkable career, qualifying fourth for the vault final with a score of 13.266.
But medals tell only part of Chusovitina's story. Her longevity in gymnastics has been shaped by two enduring forces: devotion to her son and love for the sport itself.
A MOTHER'S BARGAIN
Chusovitina won Olympic team gold as a 17-year-old at Barcelona 1992, competing for the Unified Team. At the time, it appeared to be the high point of a promising career.
Then, in 2002, her three-year-old son Alisher was diagnosed with leukemia. Facing medical bills she could not otherwise cover, Chusovitina turned gymnastics into a lifeline, competing wherever prize money and support were available. In search of better treatment for her son, she switched allegiance to Germany.
At the Beijing 2008 Olympics, competing for her adopted country at the age of 33, she won silver on vault. Before she had even left Beijing, she received the news she had been hoping for over six years: her son was cancer-free.
For many athletes, that might have marked the natural end of the journey. Chusovitina kept going.
STILL RUNNING, STILL VAULTING
She competed at Tokyo 2020, her eighth Olympics, at the age of 46. A lower-leg injury forced her out of Paris 2024, and many assumed her career was finally over.
In February 2025, at 50, she announced she was not done. A month later, she underlined the point by winning vault gold at a World Cup stop in Baku with a score of 13.516.
On Sept. 18, she posted on social media: "My seventh Asian Games. I'm here."
In Nagoya on Tuesday, with her fingernails painted in the blue, white, and green of the Uzbek flag, Chuso walked into the mixed zone afterward, beaming.
Asked when she planned to retire - a question she inevitably gets - she shot back with a grin: "What, don't you want to see me anymore?"
What keeps her coming back, she says, is not the crowd or the competition - it's the fight with herself.
She said overcoming herself gives her a huge sense of satisfaction, adding, "If what I do can inspire others, that makes me happy too. Doing what I want to do matters a great deal to me."
NO FINISH LINE IN SIGHT
In 2017, Chusovitina was inducted into the International Gymnastics Hall of Fame and remains the only inductee still actively competing.
By the time Los Angeles hosts the Olympics in 2028, Chuso will be 53, and she is not ruling out a ninth appearance.
"I will try to qualify for 2028," she said at the ongoing Asian Games, repeating: "It's sport, it's gymnastics. If it's possible, I will try to compete at LA28."
Over 32 years, her rivals have changed generation after generation. She now shares the competition floor with gymnasts born in the 2000s and 2010s. But age, to her, is not the obstacle many assume it to be.
"I feel like I get smarter every year," she said. "I'm feeling great, and it's great to perform here when we have so many fans and so much support from the spectators, and I will perform as long as I can. I'm not competing against anyone else - I'm just enjoying the process." ■

New Zealand passes legislation for new resource management system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:41:54 CST
11:41:54 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's parliament has passed legislation to replace the Resource Management Act (RMA), marking the country's most significant overhaul of its planning system in more than three decades.
The Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill replace the 35-year-old RMA with a system that is intended to be simpler, faster and more consistent, RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said in a statement on Tuesday night.
More than 100 planning documents will be replaced by 17 regional combined plans, while nationally standardized zones and rules will reduce unnecessary variation across the country, Bishop said.
The government estimates about 45 percent of consent and permit applications currently required under the RMA could be removed, representing 15,000 to 22,000 applications based on 2023/24 volumes.
The new system will also set environmental limits for effects on ecosystems and human health, supported by national instruments and regional plans covering freshwater, coastal water, air, land, soil and indigenous biodiversity, Parliamentary Under-Secretary Simon Court said.
The government said independent analysis projects the new planning system will boost gross domestic product by an additional 0.56 percent annually by 2050, worth up to 3.1 billion NZ dollars (about 1.77 billion U.S. dollars) a year.
The new system is intended to be operational by 2030. ■

France rebukes world over Gaza as Canada, UK back Palestinian state at UNGA
France’s Macron says suffering in Gaza should ‘shame all of us’ as Canada’s Carney pledges $71m for two-state efforts.
UK Prime Minister vows not to ‘stand by’ as Palestinians suffer
France, Canada and the United Kingdom have called for Palestinian sovereignty at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) with French President Emmanuel Macron condemning the world’s failure to act against Israel’s restrictions on aid to Gaza as shameful.
Macron’s impassioned address on Tuesday came as Israeli forces killed at least three Palestinians in Gaza City despite a “ceasefire” brokered by the United States in October. More than 73,900 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023, including 1,399 since the “ceasefire” took effect.
