UN chief calls for steps to manage AI risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:26:42 CST
06:26:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday called for steps to manage artificial intelligence (AI) risks, including creating a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework.
"For centuries, power came from territory. Then industry. Then finance. Today, power increasingly comes from data, computing capacity and algorithms. This new power is highly concentrated. It is advancing at extraordinary speed, and racing ahead of our ability to understand its full consequences," Guterres said in an address to the opening of the General Debate of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly.
The danger is not technology -- the danger is technology without accountability, capability without oversight, and decision-making without transparency. And that danger cannot be minimized. The very developers building these systems are now pulling the alarm, said Guterres.
The first duty of government is to protect its people. Governments must assume their responsibilities. And governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation, he said.
At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks. They built mechanisms to reduce misunderstandings, manage escalation and prevent catastrophe. At that time, it was nuclear armaments. Today, AI demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency, said the UN chief.
"Those countries leading this technological revolution must share information on emerging safety risks, cooperate on testing and evaluation, and work towards common safeguards that protect us all," said Guterres. "But because this affects us all, global coordination is indispensable. And there is only one place where every country has a voice in shaping our common future: and that place is the United Nations."
Through the Global Digital Compact, UN member states agreed for the first time on universal principles for AI governance; through the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, a platform was created for governments, scientists, industry leaders and civil society to work together; through the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, the United Nations has brought together global expertise to ensure that policy is guided by evidence, he noted.
Building on these efforts, UN member states must take the next steps: first, to advance the conditions for the responsible pacing of AI and the additional safeguards needed to address risks; and second, to work toward a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework, supported by credible and independent oversight, said Guterres.
AI must be shaped by humanity, with humanity, and for all humanity. Children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems. Life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future, he added. ■

48th WorldSkills Competition kicks off in Shanghai
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
05:26:36 CST
06:26:36 KST

The 48th WorldSkills Competition opens in east China's Shanghai, Sept. 22, 2026. Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a congratulatory letter to the event, which was read out at the opening ceremony. Chinese Premier Li Qiang attended the opening ceremony and declared the competition open. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
SHANGHAI, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The 48th WorldSkills Competition opened in Shanghai on Tuesday evening, with 1,385 competitors from 68 countries and regions vying in 64 skill events.
Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a congratulatory letter to the event, which was read out at the opening ceremony. Chinese Premier Li Qiang attended the opening ceremony and declared the competition open.
China has sent 71 competitors, who will compete in all 64 events, covering six sectors -- transportation and logistics, construction and building technology, manufacturing and engineering technology, information and communication technology, creative arts and fashion, and social and personal services, according to organizers.
The competition brings together young skilled professionals from around the world to showcase their expertise and exchange experience.
The WorldSkills Conference 2026 and the WorldSkills Shanghai 2026 Expo will also be held alongside the competition. Competition events will conclude on Sept. 27.
The WorldSkills Competition, held every two years and operated by WorldSkills International, is widely regarded as the world's leading vocational skills competition.
Seven skills are making their debut at this year's competition, including rail vehicle technology, unmanned aerial systems, intelligent security technology and software testing, reflecting emerging industry trends and evolving demand for vocational skills.
The changing mix of WorldSkills events has followed shifts in industries and occupations. The first competition, held in Spain in 1950, focused largely on traditional trades such as construction and manufacturing, while automation, the expansion of the service sector and the rise of the internet later brought new skills onto the competition floor.
China joined WorldSkills International in 2010 and has since competed in seven editions of the competition. It has ranked first in both the gold-medal tally and overall group points at the past four editions.
Official data showed that China has more than 220 million skilled workers, including over 72 million highly skilled workers. Skilled workers account for about 30 percent of the country's employed population, providing an important talent base for economic development and industrial upgrading.
According to organizers, discussions at the WorldSkills Conference cover issues that include artificial intelligence, vocational education and future skills, bringing together policymakers, educators and industry representatives from around the world to exchange views on skills development and changing workforce needs.
Skills development has also become an expanding area of cooperation between China and countries in the Global South. A total of 17 Luban Workshops, vocational education programs jointly set up by Chinese and overseas partner institutions, have been established in 15 African countries, training more than 10,000 young African people. At the Shanghai event, 10 African countries are jointly presenting an African exhibition area. ■

ANTANANARIVO, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The death toll linked to measles and malaria in Ifanadiana District, southeastern Madagascar, has risen to 37, with children accounting for about 75 percent of the deaths, a health official said Tuesday.
Andrianina Desire Rakotoarimino, general director of preventive medicine at the Ministry of Public Health, said at a press conference that seven people are currently receiving treatment at health facilities, while the health situation in the affected localities has now been under control.
In response, health authorities have launched vaccination campaigns against measles and distributed protective materials and equipment to local residents, the general director added.
Cases showing symptoms of measles or malaria appeared about two months ago in some localities of Ifanadiana District. However, the remoteness of some areas has made it difficult for health workers to reach affected populations, complicating both their intervention efforts and the treatment of patients, according to a ministry statement issued last Sunday. ■

US President Donald Trump called Tuesday on countries participating in the Shield of the Americas initiative to formally designate narco-terrorists as a common threat to regional stability and impose sanctions on US-designated foreign terrorist organizations.
Speaking at a Shield of the Americas event on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Trump described the initiative as a major economic and national security alliance in the Western Hemisphere.
"I'm thrilled to be here at the second meeting of the Shield of the Americas. The Shield of the Americas is a big deal," he said.
He described the grouping as "the largest and most powerful alliance for economic and national security ever to convene in the Western Hemisphere."
"For years, cartels have waged war on the people of this hemisphere. Now we're waging war on them," Trump said.

The Shield of the Americas, also known as the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, was launched by the Trump administration as a regional security initiative focused on combating transnational criminal organizations and drug trafficking.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, addressing the event, said the emergence of regional leaders committed to combating transnational criminal organizations was among the notable developments in the hemisphere.
"One of the most exciting developments in our region over the last couple of years has been the emergence of strong leaders who are committed to the challenge of taking on transnational terrorism, which is an enormous threat to all of us," Rubio said.

Iran and US have held talks on sidelines of UN summit, says Donald Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:21:59 UTC
06:21:59 KST

Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump disclosed on Tuesday.
He said there would a further meeting in the very near future.
Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation to agree a memorandum of understanding in Switzerland in June.
Iranian officials confirmed the meeting with Witkoff involved its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and was mediated by diplomats from Qatar.
A senior Iranian official also indicated that the country was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week, as long as the US took reciprocal steps to ease the military and economic pressure it is applying on Iran.
Previously, Iran had set seven onerous preconditions for lifting its blockade on the strait, one of the world’s key oil shipping routes, including an end to the US war “on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to end all aggressive actions against Iran, including sanctions.
The new position, revealed amid frantic backstage negotiations at the UN general assembly in New York and set out by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo and then to Reuters, would involve relaxing some of those preconditions.
The official claimed the position had been approved by Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and the country’s supreme national security council, although some Iranian media close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) denied any new position had been adopted, reflecting disputes in Tehran.
Diplomats had been testing the ground for possible talks between the US and Iran, with Qatar’s diplomats in talks with Araghchi. A meeting between Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Trump had largely been ruled out as too combustible, however.
Pezeshkian is due on Wednesday to address the UN general assembly, where most of the Iranian delegation left the hall during Trump’s speech on Tuesday after he described Iran as the bully of the Middle East and the number one terror organisation on Earth.
But earlier, the IRGC issued a statement that said there was no contradiction between staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, in recent remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament.
The official said Iran was seeking signs from Washington that it was prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward ending its military blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. In that case, Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official.
Such preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other senior Iranian figures in the previous 48 hours.
Experience has shown that initially appealing Iranian offers can emerge to be more complex once the small print is revealed, and there is a barely disguised tussle being played out in Tehran between hardliners and figures like Pezeshkian over the value of any talks.
Resolving these disputes is not made easier by the low profile kept by the supreme leader, normally the arbiter in such internal ructions.
Trump, in his remarks to the general assembly, said he had a big decision to make: whether to annihilate Iran, or to help it become a great country.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, adding he expected Iran to make a deal immediately after the US midterm elections. “There are two options; one could be a very bad thing, and the other could lead to greatness and progress for this country. Therefore, I think they want to do this.”
Overall, his demeanour, and the mixed signals out of Tehran, suggest the two sides are still too far apart to reach a deal, which would have to start with agreement between Iran and Oman on a new route for commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz that largely goes through Iranian waters. The Gulf states have not endorsed such a deal.
Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted it had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways pass – Iran and Oman.
Tehran is also under growing pressure as the US blockade of its oil exports plays havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation. In his speech, Trump called on other countries to isolate Iran economically, including by demanding that all nations prevent any Iranian civilian planes from landing at their airports. US diplomats have warned Turkey and Iraq to comply or face sanctions.
Many of the Gulf states were also planning to urge Trump to do more to press Israel to meet its commitments under the six-month-old peace plan to withdraw from Gaza.
The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prompted a walkout by the Israeli delegation when he described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard and the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”.
He added: “Israel refuses to stop the occupation. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity, mercy or compassion, no one guided by justice and conscience, can possibly remain indifferent to this picture.”
Jordan’s King Abdullah, in his address, claimed: “With Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper. This result is a state without restraint. This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels. It no longer feels compelled to ask: ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”
He added that what was unfolding across the occupied West Bank was not a series of isolated acts but rather “elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime.”
A statement from eight Gulf foreign ministers also called on Israel to immediately fulfil its outstanding commitments under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and early recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.
The ministers reiterated their categorical rejection of any measures aimed at the expulsion or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from their homeland or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.

Zelenskyy ready to meet Putin in Trump-brokered trilateral talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:18:09 UTC
06:18:09 KST

United Nations, New York — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed his willingness to meet with the Russian President Vladimir Putin in a bid to end the Russia-Ukraine war, telling reporters at the UN headquarters that Moscow has yet to show it is prepared to move.
Speaking to reporters after talks with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the US remains central to bringing Moscow to the table.
“I’m underlining and I underlined it several times today, any kind of negotiation from Russians will give a signal that they are ready to move,” he said. “I’m not sure that they are ready to move. That’s why I think we need the US.”
He said Trump told him he would “do everything” to help end the war and that the most important step Washington could take would be to organise a leaders’ meeting where “all the sensitive things” could be raised directly.
Asked whether he would sit down with Putin in a three-way format, Zelenskyy was blunt: “I’m ready. I’m ready any time when they all decide. I think that we all need to move as quickly as possible.”
Zelenskyy dismissed the idea that historical grievances must be resolved before talks can start.
“If you say that this is ending the war through the dialogue, it means that you have to meet and have a dialogue,” he said. “If you want to end the war, sit, speak.”
When journalists asked whether his openness to a trilateral meeting with Putin meant he agreed with Trump that Putin wants to end the war, Zelenskyy declined to endorse that assessment.
He framed the meeting itself as the test.
“I think that I’m ready for a trilateral meeting. It means that I’m agreeing to end the war, and I want to end the war,” he said.
He compared the moment to earlier US pressure for an unconditional ceasefire at the start of Trump’s term. Ukraine had resisted that formula, he said, because of the scale of Russian killings and the need for accountability.
Accountability “will come,” Zelenskyy said, but refusing a ceasefire or talks was itself a choice to continue the war.
Looming winter
Winter, he argued, cannot wait for diplomacy.
Regardless of whether negotiations advance, Ukraine must prepare for another season of Russian strikes on the power grid.
He said he asked Washington for two things — the first is immediate help with energy and electricity supply.
The second request, he said, is longer-term.
He said it would be licenses and security arrangements that would let Ukraine begin producing Patriot interceptors at home.
He said his military adviser spoke on Tuesday morning with Raytheon and asked Trump to help accelerate the licenses.
“He’s (Trump) positive,” Zelenskyy said of the US president’s response. “God bless, we will start this project.”
Even if Ukraine later fields its own anti-ballistic missile system, he added, domestic Patriot production would still be needed.
Pressed on whether he received a firm US commitment to deliver Patriot interceptors for this winter, Zelenskyy said no one told him no, “and that’s good stuff in my job, but he did not get a concrete answer.
He said he had already signed a production contract with Germany, which has licences and is manufacturing, covering two packages totalling 600 interceptors, 300 plus 300.
He said he told Trump he needed US help now “to save our people now,” and offered to return the missiles in 2027 if Washington later needed them back.
Defence experts say the US has been experiencing a global shortage of Patriot interceptors because many have been expended in war against Iran.
A TRT World question about whether the US war on Iran has complicated Ukraine’s war efforts yielded no response from Zelenskyy.
Pause in energy strikes
On energy targeting, Zelenskyy said Ukraine is not the side that started strikes on energy infrastructure and would not unilaterally stop responding if Russia continues to hit Ukrainian power plants, oil and related facilities.
“I suggest not to play this game,” he said. “He (Putin) attacked us, we respond. If he couldn’t respond, he could already occupy us totally. This is our strong side — that we are not weak.”
Asked how Trump compares with a year earlier, when Zelenskyy called him a “game changer,” the Ukrainian president pointed again to the US leader’s ability to convene talks and push for an end to the fighting before winter.
The Ukrainian president said teams would stay in contact on both the winter energy package and the Patriot licenses.
He did not claim a final deal on either.

Copper takes a breather
Having enjoyed six winning sessions and a series of record highs, copper looks like it's having a bit of a breather today, weighed down by a stronger US dollar.
Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.7% at $14,651/tonne.
The most-traded copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange edged 0.2% lower to $US16,550.57/tonne.
Chinese demand had been boosted by buying ahead of smelter shutdowns for the country's public holidays. The country's upcoming holidays are on September 25 to 27 and from October 1 to 7.
Copper had been supported in recent months by strong imports to the US ahead of a potential tariff on refined metal, though the pull weakened after Reuters reported that US officials were concerned that tariffs may raise costs for manufacturers.
The stronger greenback is also putting pressure on other industrial metals as a more expensive dollar can weigh on dollar-denominated commodities such as copper by making them more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
On the LME, aluminium was down 0.6%, zinc lost 0.7%, and nickel was down 0.4%.

Will lower global prices flow through to Australian motorists?
We've seen global oil prices as measured by Brent and WTI crude futures trudge down this week as hostilities in the Middle East ease marginally and the Saudis wrap up repairs to their strategically important, missile-damaged East-West pipeline — but does that mean price relief at the local servo is at hand?
Probably not. Here's more from Tessa Fleming.
Business Daily podcast
Today's edition of the ABC's Business Daily podcast has just dropped for edification.
Host Carrington Clarke welcomes Millie Muroi, economics writer from the SMH/Age, into the studio to discuss RBA Governor Michelle Bullock's last round of jawboning ahead of Tuesday's rates meeting, as well as Donald Trump's backing of plans to turn off US diesel taps to the rest of the world.
Trump backs a ban on US diesel exports
US President Donald Trump has backed calls from within the Republican Party to ban diesel exports from the US to drive down fuel prices ahead of November’s mid-term elections.
Diesel prices have shot to record highs in the US and around the world as wars in Iran and Ukraine sharply cut exports from some of the biggest producers such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel ... I've called for it. I've called for it within my people," Mr Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
High fuel prices are a vulnerability for Mr Trump in the November 3 elections in which Republicans are trying to maintain majorities in both chambers of Congress.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, speaking at the same meeting, said the administration was examining whether such a ban was feasible and whether a full or partial ban would work.
Several Republican candidates in the most competitive congressional races nationwide, such as US Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, US Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa, and Mike Rogers in Michigan, have called for the Trump administration to implement the ban.
"American fuel should stay home with Americans," Senator Sullivan said in a statement on Tuesday.
"The cost of diesel is just too damn high. I'm calling for a temporary pause of American diesel exports so that we can rebuild our reserves ahead of winter and put American and Alaskan families first."
However, the move has far from universal support, even within the Trump administration.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week a ban would lead to a glut of diesel in the US Gulf Coast and prompt US refiners to cut production rates, which would quickly reduce gasoline production.
"If you start putting barriers on flows, pretty quickly you will reduce the production, and you'll have less supply. We need more supply, not less supply," Mr Wright said.
US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum noted that a ban would be unlikely to lower petroleum prices and could lead to retaliatory measures by energy exporting countries, which states like California rely on for some of their energy.
The powerful US oil and gas lobby is even less impressed.
"Restricting US diesel exports would wreak havoc on fuel markets at home and abroad, destabilize refinery operations and deepen a global refining crisis already putting upward pressure on US prices," the American Petroleum Institute said in a statement.
"Gulf Coast refineries produce more diesel than the region consumes, while geography and infrastructure constraints prevent that surplus from simply being redirected to every US market that needs it."

Key Event
Federal government nominates ACCC chair for reappointment
In what is effectively a formality, the chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) Gina Cass-Gottlieb is heading for a second five-year term starting in March next year.
The Albanese government is nominating Ms Cass-Gottlieb for reappointment and is seeking state and territory agreement to recommend the appointment to the governor-general.
Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers described Ms Cass-Gottlieb as "an outstanding leader of our competition and consumer watchdog".
"Over the past four and a half years as chair, Ms Cass-Gottlieb has led the implementation of the most substantial merger laws in more than 50 years, and reforms to protect Australians from unfair trading practices," he said.
"Under her leadership, the ACCC has won landmark law cases against supermarkets, airlines and digital platforms, and established the National Anti-Scam Centre."
Ms Cass-Gottlieb's career includes 25 years as a senior partner in competition and regulation at Gilbert + Tobin, serving as a non-executive member of the Reserve Bank of Australia's Payments System Board, and serving as a member of the Financial Regulator Assessment Authority from September 2021 to March 2022.
Call that a bubble? Sydney's bubble risk is easing
It might feel like a massive bubble, but in a global context our property market is a bit mid-table in the bubble stakes, according to UBS.
The giant global investment bank has scanned a swathe of the world's big cities — largely in developed economies — and found Sydney (the only Australian city in the survey, and arguably the most "bubbly") ranked only 10th out of the 23 surveyed for "bubble risk".
For what it's worth, Zurich and Tokyo are the only two cities facing high housing bubble risk, according to UBS
The report found that, overall, risk levels have remained broadly stable compared with 2025.
"Inflation-adjusted global house prices, rents, and incomes have been largely unchanged over the past year," UBS said.
"Driven by inflation concerns, average financing costs have increased slightly over the past four quarters, reducing affordability and weakening incentives to buy.
"Housing shortages in many urban markets, however, continue to support prices."
Sound familiar?
From a local perspective, Head of Investments at UBS Global Wealth Management Australia Andrew McAuley said this year's report shows that Sydney's bubble risk had eased when compared to 2025, remaining in the "moderate" category.
Mr McAuley said the risk of a major correction in prices is lower, due to a fall in prices in real terms, driven by a combination of high inflation and interest rate rises.
However, he said affordability was still the key point.
"With rate rises increasingly likely, and the federal government's new policies limiting negative gearing, buyers may benefit from lower house prices," Mr McAuley said.
"That said, higher interest rates can also reduce borrowing capacity, so not all buyers will experience improved affordability."

Betting app Palmerbet let self-excluded person bet over 300 times
The media regulator (ACMA) has found that sports betting app Palmerbet breached self-exclusion laws.
The company failed to close an individual's account after they registered with BetStop, the national self-exclusion register.
Palmerbet also accepted 312 bets from that person between December 2024 and February 2025.
Under self-exclusion rules, companies must close the accounts of anyone registered with BetStop as soon as practical and must not let them place any wagers.
ACMA has accepted an 18-month court-enforceable undertaking from Palmerbet, committing the company to an independent review of its compliance systems and make recommended improvements.
Palmerbet was also required to repay all deposits to the individual during this period.
The ABC has requested comment from Palmerbet.
Key Event
Australian output expands, but more slowly
The latest reading of the Australian economy via S&P Global's "flash" PMIs shows economic output is still expanding, but at a slower pace.
The composite PMI, which includes both manufacturing and services PMIs, slipped from 52.7 points in August to 50.8 points in September, with 50.0 being the break even level between expansion and contraction.
Within that, the services sector PMI came in at 51.4 points, down from 53.3, while manufacturing slipped into contraction at 49.3 points, down from 52.0.
A fall in export business weighed on growth in overall new orders, with a slower expansion in new business triggering the first round of job losses since May.
On the price front, the rate of input price inflation picked up to its highest in three months but remained weaker than seen through the second quarter.
"The Australian economy closed out the third quarter on a weaker footing, having signalled a continued loss of growth momentum in September," S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Eleanor Dennison said.
"Although only slight, the economy managed to sustain the trend of expansion over the quarter, an improvement on the second quarter's subdued performance.
"While still upbeat, businesses lost some confidence in their growth prospects in September.
"This coincided with cutbacks to payrolls, stronger cost pressures, signs of softer demand and renewed export weakness."

Pedro Sánchez reaffirms Spain's commitment to the WHO Pandemic Agreement during a meeting with the President of Namibia
President's News - 2026.9.22
United Nations Headquarters, New York (United States)
Pedro Sánchez holds a bilateral meeting with the President of Namibia (Pool Moncloa / Borja Puig de la Bellacasa)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has held a meeting with the President of Namibia, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, on the fringes of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. During the meeting, he reaffirmed Spain's commitment to the World Health Organisation (WHO) Pandemic Agreement, adopted by the World Health Assembly in May 2025.
Furthermore, the President of the Government of Spain expressed the Government's support, in coordination with the European Union, for the ongoing negotiations to finalise the Annex on Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS). The aim of this annex is to ensure that the exchange of pathogens with pandemic potential and of information on their genetic makeup is linked to fair and equitable access to the benefits arising from their use, including vaccines, diagnostics and treatments.
Pedro Sánchez also emphasised that Spain is prepared to redouble its efforts and play a more active role in driving these negotiations forward, with the aim of making progress in the process and strengthening a more effective, solidarity-based and equitable international health architecture in the face of future pandemics.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that Kyiv and Washington want to see the war in Ukraine end "before winter" following what he described as a "positive" meeting with his US counterpart Donald Trump.
Zelenskyy and Trump met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, where the Ukrainian leader said they had discussed potentially "de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy."
"I just had a positive and productive meeting with President Trump," he wrote in a post on social media. "Both the U.S. and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter".
He added that he and Trump had also spoken about a winter air defence package for Ukraine as well as "other bilateral and multilateral issues."
Russia has kept up an almost relentless bombardment of Ukrainian cities and regions since launching its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022, but it has particularly sought to target Ukraine's energy infrastructure over winter periods.
Ukraine has also targeted the Russian energy sector as part of its deep strike campaign, which aims to degrade a key driver of the Russian economy and impact the Kremlin's war machine.
Ukrainian forces have launched frequent strikes against oil facilities including refineries, terminals, and depots as part of this strategy. Earlier on Tuesday, Zelenskyy announced that one oil refinery had been hit in Bashkortostan and another in the Samara region over the past 24 hours.
Speaking to the press together with Zelenskyy in New York, Trump addressed Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, saying they had been a "very serious hit" on Russia but also "a serious hit on the price of diesel."
Trump said on Monday that Russia had "unfortunately lost control of its diesel oil industry due to its war with Ukraine" while calling for what he described as the "ridiculous and never ending" war to come to an end.
"A large number of their diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission," he wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "The whole world suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!"
Zelenskyy responded by insisting that Ukraine was willing to halt strikes on Russia's energy industry if Moscow agreed to do the same.
"Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible," he wrote on X.

Trump Administration to Cancel Obamacare Coverage for 760,000 Enrollees Over Alleged Fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:11:44 UTC
06:11:44 KST

Trump Administration officials on Tuesday announced that they would terminate the Obamacare coverage of 760,000 enrollees, alleging widespread fraud in enrollment.
Vice President JD Vance, who leads a White House task force aimed at eliminating fraud, said while speaking to reporters that $2.2 billion in taxpayer funds would be saved by removing the hundreds of thousands of Affordable Care Act (ACA) enrollees from the public insurance marketplaces.
“We expect that most of these people are fraudulently enrolled,” Vance said. He added that the Administration would also work to verify the eligibility of roughly 419,000 additional enrollees by ensuring that they are legal residents of the U.S. and meet the income threshold to receive Obamacare coverage.
The Administration will also place a six month moratorium on new health insurance brokers and agents, who help individuals sign up for health plans, Vance said.
Read More: Trump Pledges to Issue $500 Refunds to Nearly a Million Obamacare Enrollees. Are You Eligible?
The Administration’s move to eject fraudulent enrollees from the Obamacare insurance marketplaces is the latest in its broader efforts to crack down on fraud. An online “ledger” maintained by the White House asserts that the Vance-led anti-fraud task force has uncovered nearly $250 billion worth of fraud since Trump returned to office last January, including almost $100 billion at the Department of Health and Human Services.
That crackdown also saw the Administration pause $867.5 million in Medicaid payments to California and $199 million in Minnesota in July, an action for which Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cited “suspected fraud and noncompliance.” Both states have pushed back on the claims.
The Administration has additionally targeted alleged fraud in food stamps, childcare facilities, COVID-era relief funding, student loans, and homelessness funding, among other areas. Critics have accused it of disproportionally focusing on Democratic-led states in its crackdown.
An analysis from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released last August estimated that 2.3 million Obamacare enrollees improperly claimed premium tax credits by intentionally overstating their income in 2025. The Trump Administration has also claimed that agents and brokers have been responsible for illegally enrolling tens of thousands of people in ACA plans.
The 760,000 enrollees now being removed from the ACA rolls by the Trump Administration represent about 4% of the estimated 19.2 million people receiving coverage through the marketplaces in 2026.
That total has sharply declined from its peak of more than 24 million last year as ACA premiums have surged following the expiration of subsidies that helped reduce costs for millions of enrollees at the end of 2025.
A poll conducted by health policy research group KFF in June found that most voters believe there is at least some fraud in government health programs, and that more than 70% feel it is an extremely or very important issue for candidates to discuss ahead of the midterm elections. For Republican voters, fraud topped all health care issues asked about in the survey, including costs.
But health care costs, which have become increasingly expensive in the U.S. in recent years, weighed more significantly for voters overall, and the poll found that only a minority of those surveyed believed that reducing fraud in government programs would reduce such costs for them personally.
Amid the Trump Administration’s moves to withhold millions in Medicaid payments, 71% also voiced the belief that preserving access to coverage through the insurance program was more important than rooting out fraud. Meanwhile, 65% believed that the Administration’s Medicaid payment deferrals were mostly politically motivated.

Qualcomm releases Android chip built for AI as memory shortage weighs on smartphone market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:09:17 UTC
06:09:17 KST

Qualcomm unveiled its newest Android phone chipsets, which will be tuned for on-device artificial intelligence and will compete with Apple's A20 Pro in iPhones.
The new chips, under the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 brand name, will be built on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s 2-nanometer manufacturing process, and will be included in premium smartphones from companies including Motorola, Xiaomi and ZTE, Qualcomm said in a press release on Tuesday.
Qualcomm is introducing two versions of the chip, one with extra capabilities and "extreme" branding.
The launch comes as the broader smartphone industry is reeling from a worldwide contraction due to skyrocketing memory costs that have driven up the price of finished devices.
The overall smartphone market is expected to shrink 14% in terms of units shipped in 2026, and potentially another 1% in 2027, according to Counterpoint Research.
Smartphone companies have responded by focusing more on the premium tier of devices, which are targeted at consumers with more disposable income.
Qualcomm is positioning phones running on its high-end chips as an "AI hub" able to process AI models and produce tokens without relying on the cloud. At a launch event earlier this month, Apple framed its iPhones as "intelligent personal hubs" that can do on-device AI processing.
"We're going into this transition from what is a very phone-centric model to now an agentic-centric model for new experiences," Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said on Tuesday at a launch event.
In addition to the central processor (CPU), the new Qualcomm chipsets also include a graphics processing unit (GPU) as well as a neural processing unit (NPU) to handle AI workloads, which can handle agents running in the background. Qualcomm also added security features to control agentic access to sensitive data.
During Tuesday's launch, which was livestreamed, Amon brought up Google's Rick Osterloh, the head of platforms and devices at the search giant. He said Google's Gemini will be able to understand the user's context — if the person is in a car, for example — thanks to the chip's processing power and sensors. Qualcomm said the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset can run models with 30 billion parameters.
"AI will now require the device to do much more than just execute commands, and it's going to be less about navigating apps, and and it's going to be about completing tasks for you," Amon said.

Trump administration removes around 760,000 Obamacare enrollments, alleging fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:07:21 UTC
06:07:21 KST

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said on Tuesday it canceled roughly 315,000 Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollments covering about 760,000 people last month, alleging unauthorized enrollments, characterized by Vice President JD Vance as "rampant fraud."
The enforcement action also involves verifying roughly 419,000 people to ensure they are legal U.S. residents and meet the income threshold requirements to receive benefits from the public exchanges of the ACA, also known as Obamacare, according to a CMS release.
The vice president's White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud led the cancellations, and it estimates the action will save roughly $2.2 billion in taxpayer-funded subsidies. Speaking at a Tuesday briefing, Vance accused the Biden administration of maintaining a system that enabled fraud.
"You have a system where, on the one hand, brokers are paid money to feed patients into the system, while on the other hand, the government isn't even checking whether the people enrolled are actually eligible for the program. What do you have? Of course, rampant, rampant fraud," Vance said.
It is unclear how many of those 315,000 enrollments involved people who were not eligible to receive coverage, or whether the Biden administration hadn't actually verified they could enroll. The action comes as the Trump administration has made widespread accusations of fraud in U.S. health programs and restricted funding and eligibility for the federal-state Medicaid program.
During the briefing Tuesday, CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz claimed that around 35% of people currently in the Obamacare system "have never used the program." He said those people never used a prescription or saw a doctor.
The law has an individual mandate, or requirement that most people buy insurance, in part because having healthier people who use less care in the patient pool makes the system more affordable. However, the federal penalty for going without coverage has been $0 since 2019.
Obamacare plans, created by President Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act, offer subsidies based on household size and estimated yearly income. President Donald Trump failed to overturn the legislation during his first term, but has proposed modifications that would make those insurance plans less comprehensive.
Oz argued that bad actors were attracted to ACA marketplace subsidies during the Covid-19 pandemic, when federal spending surged dramatically. He pointed to enrollment growth from about 10 million people before the pandemic to roughly 22 million after, arguing that weakened safeguards and a lack of enforcement by the Biden administration contributed to improper enrollments.
Obamacare plans experienced "unprecedented enrollment growth from 2021 to 2024," according to a June report from the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, the principal advisor to the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services on policy development. The report said of this enrollment that "nearly half ... was suspected to be improper, phantom, or fraudulent." The report defined improper or fraudulent enrollment as individuals misstating their income to gain access to free plans.
The spike in enrollment came after the American Rescue Plan, a Covid response bill passed in 2021, enhanced available subsidies to make healthcare more affordable during the crisis. Those broader credits were extended but later expired at the end of 2025, raising premiums for many covered by ACA exchanges.
An estimated 19.2 million Americans are currently enrolled in Obamacare plans, according to the report.

'Remarkable' progress made on AUKUS, one of the architects of pact says
One of the original architects of AUKUS has given a very frank assessment of some US political dynamics around the landmark nuclear powered submarine project.
Kurt Campbell – who was a key advisor to then US President Joe Biden when the pact was born – has told a United States Studies Centre conference in Sydney that AUKUS has made "remarkable" progress in the five years since it was born.
He says there is now "pretty strong buy-in" from the Trump White House on AUKUS, although it wasn't easy to convince everyone in the president's inner circle that it was a good idea.
But he says there are "still some people in the (US) Department of Defence who would love a stumble" on AUKUS, and it will be "important to keep those folks on their back heels".
He also said when the Biden Administration conceived AUKUS it had to push aside a "bizarre bureaucratic alliance" in the US, which drew in both State Department officials worried about nuclear proliferation, and Defence officials who didn't want to share its most sophisticated military technology.
Campbell has also taken a bit of a swipe at the media over its coverage of AUKUS, saying there are only three to five journalists who regularly write about the project, and that they "tend to focus on the negatives" – which he says gives an overly pessimistic picture of how it's tracking.
Cost of raising a family has risen by 134 per cent: advocates call for parental support
The CEO of the Parenthood Georgie Dent has told the National Press Club outdated policies from another era are preventing parents from having the children necessary for Australia's future economic prosperity.
Dent said the cost of raising a family had risen by 134 per cent over the last generation while income had risen by just 102 per cent.
"Raising one child now costs an Australian family around $17,800 a year. Two or more, more than $36,500," said Dent.
"Whatever is left after the essentials to cover kids' clothes and shoes, haircuts, swimming lessons and birthdays isn't much."
The Parenthood is calling for parents to have a full year of paid parental leave, affordable childcare and workplace rules recognising parent's caring responsibilities.
Dent said without reform services and Australia's future economic health would suffer because birth rates are at record lows as parents struggle with outdated support.
Triple dividend: parenting groups call for major reforms to outdated family policies
A parental advocacy group has told the National Press Club women's advancement in the workforce is being held back by outdated policies on childcare and parenting.
The CEO of the Parenthood Georgie Dent said one-third of Australia's workforce with dependent children were being let down.
Dent argued for a full year of paid parental leave, affordable accessible childcare and workplaces that gave parents flexibility.
"Getting these things right delivers a triple dividend: healthier children and stronger parental wellbeing, greater workforce participation and productivity; and less inequity, giving more children the chance to thrive," said Dent.
Dent said these policies contributed to Australia's record low fertility rate, which dropped to just 1.48 children per woman in 2024.
She said if birth rates remained low, it would put pressure on services and public finances.

In the meeting Takaichi reassured Trump that key Japanese ministers who worked closely with the US, including in defence and foreign affairs, had been retained in a recent cabinet reshuffle, saying the "person-to-person counterpart relationship" would drive "policy coordination" and "deepen" the alliance between the countries.
Takaichi also pointed to "economic security" on areas like "AI, semiconductors, and critical minerals" which she said was "steadily advancing".
Trump praised Takaichi as "very highly respected" and said she was doing a "great job" and the country is "doing very well".
In the aftermath of the meeting the US Ambassador in Japan tweeted that the meeting between "two visionary and determined leaders" represented a "dynamic and unbreakable alliance" with focuses including "upgrading and strengthening our shared deterrence".
National emergency-style response needed to violence against women and children: Lib
As many of us gear up to celebrate the AFL grand final this weekend, women's shelters and crisis hotlines are readying themselves to try and help even more women and children than usual.
According to the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics, domestic, family and sexual violence surges around major sport events. Shadow Minister for Families Melissa McIntosh says the federal government should be treating this crisis in a similar way to a bushfire or flood.
"We know how to deal with oncoming crises, bushfires, floods," she says.
"We are prepared for a pandemic, why aren't we prepared for what is now declared as a national crisis when it comes to women and children's safety?"
Specifically, she'd like to see a "women and children's safety war room", similar to the kinds of control centres set up during a natural disaster.
While this exact approach isn't something experts and advocates have asked for, there have been sustained calls for this crisis to be treated with more urgency and coordination by federal, state and territory governments.
Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner Micaela Cronin has repeatedly said a national watchdog with teeth is needed to hold all levels of government to their commitments and ensure they enact the hundreds of recommendations already made by royal commissions, inquests and reviews.
At its last meeting, national cabinet agreed to prioritise action to stop violence against women and children by tasking their ministers to focus on areas like alcohol reform and holding perpetrators to account.
Queensland minister hits back at Butler over Thriving Kids
The Queensland government has defended its refusal to sign onto a NDIS alternative for some children with developmental delay or autism and accused the Commonwealth of trying to give the state a "substandard" deal.
In an interview with the ABC today, NDIS Minister Mark Butler denounced Queensland’s Liberal National government over being the only state not to formally sign up to deliver Thriving Kids, a week before the first phase of the program is set to begin.
"All other states and territories, Liberal and Labor alike, [are] just getting on with the business of developing their programs. So I'm frustrated with Queensland; it's a big state with a dispersed community … We're losing time, frankly, for Queensland parents and children," he said.
The Albanese government gave states and territories an extra $25 billion in hospital funding in exchange for taking on Thriving Kids, but Queensland has held out on signing up over concerns around cost shifting and a lack of information.
Queensland's Acting Disability Minister Ros Bates repeated those concerns to reporters a short time ago, and said her government was just doing "due diligence" for state taxpayers.
"Because of the federal government's mismanagement [of the NDIS], they are trying to make the Queensland government and other governments across the country pay for their ineptitude. We just want the details. We're not being belligerent," Bates said.
Additional reporting by Laura Lavelle
Nampijimpa Price accuses federal government of failing to take action in child protection space
Liberal senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price has renewed her calls for an inquiry into Indigenous child protection, slamming the government for brushing the issue off to state and territory governments.
Last week, Western Australia's Department of Child Protection was accused of failing to take action to address the neglect of a group of up to 15 children living unsupervised in a home in South Headland, despite reports from neighbours, police and Indigenous elders.
When Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was asked for comment earlier this week, he said "state governments have responsibility for child protection".
Nampijinpa Price says its "criminal neglect" for the prime minister to "disregard" the issue.
"If the government put as much effort into supporting the lives, saving the lives of Indigenous children in this country as they do into a racism inquiry, we might see something happen in this space," she said.
"We've got a prime minister who does not care at all, who's been given a global citizenship award in New York but brushes off this issue, it disgusts me".
Nampijinpa Price says the federal government should be putting more pressure on their state counterparts to lift standards in child protection.
"I have previously called for a royal commission into the sexual abuse of Indigenous children in this country. These are considerations that this government doesn't even have."
Digital duty of care bill not in national interest: Taylor
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has repeated his criticism the government's digital duty of care bill amounted to "political censorship".
The proposed bill would force platforms to take actions to mitigate and respond to harms caused by digital platforms.
Late yesterday, the Trump administration warned the legislation would be an "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech" and called on Australia to exclude US social media companies from plans to give users more choice about their algorithms.
Speaking to reporters on the Central Coast, Taylor said the bill wasn't in the national interest.
"We should always do what's in our national interest regardless of what anyone else says we should do," he says.
"It's not in our national interest to give a blank check to the minister on political censorship, which is what the bill does right now."
The Coalition has previously ruled out support amid concerns the laws would hand the minister too much power to determine what constitutes online harm.
Coalition releases eight-point energy plan
Angus Taylor has also been asked about the Coalition's energy policy.
The opposition today released an eight-point plan, officially jettisoning many of the key climate policies trying to push down emissions or speed up the renewable rollout.
It includes scrapping laws committing Australia to net zero, laws requiring heavy industry to cut emissions, and removing laws requiring car makers to import more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles. The plan also includes the push to end a ban on nuclear power.
So does this mean the Coalition is formally abandoning the renewable transition? Taylor says that choice should be left to Australians.
"We should have all the energy sources available. Our coal, our gas, our nuclear, our household solar — where we lead the world. I mean all of these should be available and we shouldn't restrict it in the way that [energy minister] Chris Bowen does," he says.
"What we'll continue to see is technologies emerging with lower emissions that Australians want to choose, and that's fine.
"I put faith in the Australian people on this because they get it, they understand it."

New political donation caps will leave too much money in Australian politics and disadvantage emerging political candidates.
The Grattan Institute policy brief released today says a $90 million political party spending cap, due to take effect in 2027, is "too high".
It proposes slashing the total cap to $40 million, a limit that would still exceed the $30 million cost of previous national campaigns.
"Capping electoral expenditure puts a ceiling on money in politics and, if well-designed, can reduce its influence," Grattan Institute democracy expert Kate Griffiths says.
It also recommends new independents and new parties should be allowed to spend up to $1.2 million on their campaigns, while keeping an $800,000 electorate limit for established candidates.

Amid a global oil crisis and with the world climate conference looming, Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has headed overseas to talk energy security.
Bowen will stop in India to meet with his counterparts and visit the Jamnagar oil refinery in Gujarat — which is the world's largest refinery — and convene a roundtable with clean energy industry representatives.
In Saudi Arabia, he will hold meetings with Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud about the evolving situation overseas, including the closure of the East-West pipeline, and its implications for global energy security.
The pipeline had become a critical alternate route for oil since Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, carrying about 4 per cent of the world's supply prior to the recent attacks that forced its closure.
Australia is exposed because many of the Asian refineries it relies on for imported fuel use Saudi crude.
Bowen is also planning to visit the world's largest solar farm while in Saudi as he seeks to highlight the importance of electrification in future energy security, which is a key priority for COP31.

Princess Diana joked about her own funeral two months before her death
Kyiv • UNN
On her 36th birthday, Diana joked that her home resembled a funeral parlor. Two months later, she died in a car crash in Paris.
Shortly before her death, Princess Diana made a joking remark about a funeral that took on a sinister undertone after her death. Her brother Charles Spencer recounted the episode in his new book, "A Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," E! News reports, writes UNN.
Details
For her 36th birthday, Diana received many flowers. In a thank-you letter to one of her relatives, she joked: "I’m so lucky! My house is so full of wonderful flowers that it looks like a funeral parlor!"
Two months later, on August 31, 1997, the princess died in a car crash in Paris. Spencer recalled her words while preparing a speech for his sister’s funeral.
The brother’s last meeting with Diana
Spencer also said that he last saw his sister approximately two months before her death. They happened to meet at the Tate Gallery in London and spoke only briefly.
Neither of us had any idea that the other would be at the event. We spoke only briefly, never to see each other again
In the book, Spencer also claims that after Diana’s death, then-Prince Charles told him: "Be assured, we will forget her soon."
Commenting on these claims, Buckingham Palace stated that prolonged grief can affect a person’s judgment and memories.

AMIA bombing: Why Argentina is charging Iran and Hezbollah suspects, 32 years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:03:41 UTC
06:03:41 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- Latin America
- AMIA bombing: Why Argentina is charging Iran and Hezbollah suspects 32 years later
AMIA bombing: Why Argentina is charging Iran and Hezbollah suspects 32 years later
A new Argentine indictment names seven Iranian officials and a Hezbollah operative accused of roles in the 1994 attack on Buenos Aires’ Jewish community center
More than three decades after a bombing destroyed Argentina’s Jewish community center and killed 85 people, an Argentine judge has formally charged seven Iranians and a Lebanese national over their alleged roles in the attack.
The decision on Monday brings the country one step closer to a potential trial in absentia in one of the world’s longest-running terrorism investigations.
But what happened at the AMIA Jewish community center, who does Argentina hold responsible, and why has it taken 32 years for the case to reach this point?
Argentina’s Jewish community
Argentina is home to Latin America’s largest Jewish community, with an estimated 170,000 to 180,000 Jews, most of them living in Buenos Aires. The community has roots in waves of Jewish immigration from Europe, as well as longstanding Sephardic communities from the Middle East and Mediterranean.
Over generations, Argentine Jews built a strong network of synagogues, schools and community organizations. AMIA was one of its central institutions, making the 1994 bombing not only a mass-casualty attack, but a devastating strike at the heart of Jewish life in Argentina.
What happened in the AMIA bombing?
On July 18, 1994, a suicide bomber drove a van packed with explosives into the Argentine Israelite Mutual Association, known by its Spanish acronym AMIA, in Buenos Aires.
The blast killed 85 people and injured 151, destroying much of the seven-story Jewish community center.
The attack was the deadliest antisemitic attack outside Israel since the Holocaust.
It came just two years after another major bombing in Buenos Aires: the 1992 attack on the Israeli Embassy, which killed 29 people.
No one has ever been convicted of carrying out the AMIA bombing.
Who does Argentina say was behind the attack?
Argentina has long accused Iran and Hezbollah of orchestrating the bombing.
According to Argentine prosecutors and courts, the decision to attack AMIA was made by senior Iranian officials and was then carried out by Hezbollah, Iran’s Lebanese proxy group.
In 2024, an Argentine court formally ruled that Iran and Hezbollah were responsible for the attack.
Judge Daniel Rafecas’s latest ruling says the decision to attack AMIA was made in August 1993 by the highest levels of the Iranian regime and entrusted to Hezbollah. The group then allegedly organized a regional and local support network to prepare and carry out the bombing.
Iran has denied responsibility for the bombing.
How was the attack carried out?
According to Rafecas’s reconstruction, the attackers purchased a Renault Trafic van on July 10, 1994, just eight days before the bombing.
The vehicle was then modified and loaded with approximately 300 kilograms of ammonal and TNT.
The van was eventually driven onto the sidewalk outside the AMIA building and detonated, causing the massive explosion that killed 85 people and injured 151.
Who has now been charged?
Monday’s decision formally charged seven Iranian nationals and one Lebanese national, all of whom are outside Argentina and could face trial in absentia.
Judge Daniel Rafecas divided the defendants according to their alleged roles in the attack.
Four senior Iranian officials were charged as “indirect authors” of the bombing: Ali Fallahijan, who was Iran’s intelligence minister at the time; Ali Velayati, then foreign minister; Mohsen Rezai, then commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard; and Ahmad Vahidi, who commanded the Quds Force.
Rafecas also charged three other Iranian nationals as necessary accomplices: Hadi Soleimanpour, Iran’s ambassador to Argentina at the time; Mohsen Rabbani, the Iranian Embassy’s cultural attaché; and Ahmad Asghari, identified in the ruling as a Revolutionary Guard intelligence agent.
The eighth defendant is Salman Raouf Salman, also known as “Samuel El Reda,” a Lebanese Hezbollah operative whom Rafecas says coordinated the final stages of the attack.
The eight charged suspects are not in Argentine custody.
Why is there a trial in absentia?
The AMIA investigation has faced a fundamental problem for decades: the people Argentina accuses of organizing the attack have remained outside the country.
In June, Rafecas ruled that the Iranian and Lebanese suspects could be tried in absentia.
Argentina introduced a legal framework for trials in absentia in 2025. Under the system, defendants accused of certain serious crimes can be tried without being physically present, provided their rights to a defense and other due-process guarantees are protected.
The decision does not mean a trial will begin immediately.
The indictments can still be appealed, and additional procedural steps must be completed before a trial can move forward.
Why has the investigation taken so long?
The AMIA case has been plagued by allegations of political interference, corruption and obstruction of justice.
In 2004, prosecutor Alberto Nisman was appointed to investigate the bombing. He spent years building a case that Iran and Hezbollah were responsible.
But in January 2015, Nisman was found dead in his Buenos Aires apartment, just hours before he was due to present allegations that then-President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner and other senior officials had participated in an alleged cover-up of Iran’s role in the AMIA attack.
His death was initially ruled a suicide.
Argentine authorities later determined that Nisman had been murdered.
His death became another major controversy surrounding an investigation that had already deeply divided Argentine politics and society.
What happened to officials accused of obstructing the investigation?
The AMIA case has also led to criminal proceedings against Argentine officials accused of interfering with the investigation.
Former President Carlos Menem, who was in office during both the 1992 Israeli Embassy bombing and the 1994 AMIA attack, was tried over allegations that he helped cover up aspects of the investigation. He was ultimately acquitted and died in 2021.
Former intelligence chief Hugo Anzorreguy was sentenced to four and a half years in prison for obstructing the investigation.
Former AMIA investigating judge Juan José Galeano was also convicted. In 2019, he was sentenced to six years in prison for concealing evidence and violating his duties.
In 2024, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights also held the Argentine state responsible for failing in its duty to properly investigate the AMIA bombing.
Could the AMIA and Israeli Embassy bombings be connected?
Monday’s ruling also raised the possibility of formally connecting the two Buenos Aires attacks.
The Israeli Embassy bombing in March 1992 killed 29 people, while the AMIA attack two years later killed 85.
Both attacks have been linked by Argentine investigators to Hezbollah and Iran.
Rafecas has asked Argentina’s Supreme Court to weigh in on whether the two cases should be connected, potentially allowing investigators to examine the attacks as part of a broader campaign. (infobae)
What does this mean for Argentina’s Jewish community?
The AMIA bombing remains one of the defining tragedies in the history of Argentina’s Jewish community.
For decades, relatives of the victims have demanded accountability, while successive Argentine governments and courts have struggled to bring those accused of orchestrating the attack before a courtroom.
Monday’s indictment does not resolve the case.
But it represents a significant new legal step toward a trial, potentially one that could take place even if the accused never appear in Argentina.
President Javier Milei, a strong supporter of Israel who has made the AMIA investigation a prominent issue, welcomed the decision.
“Morality as state policy,” Milei wrote on X.
For the families of the 85 people killed in 1994, however, the central question remains the same: after more than three decades, will anyone ultimately be held accountable for the attack?

Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:02:47 UTC
06:02:47 KST

Guterres pleads for 'world built on interdependence' in final General Assembly address
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pleaded for “a world built on interdependence” Tuesday as he made his final address to the annual gathering of world leaders convening to face a formidable menu of challenges, from climate change and war to inequality and the rise of artificial intelligence.
In a no-nonsense farewell speech, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged global leaders Tuesday to respond to the defining challenge today: Will the world continue on its path to fragmentation, or cooperate to tackle the existential threats from climate crisis, runaway artificial intelligence and intensifying inequalities?
Read more'No peace without justice,' Macron tells UN General Assembly
The UN leader has long implored leaders not to give up on cooperation and shared decision-making in the face of accelerating global challenges and increasing great-powers competition. Tuesday’s message at the UN General Assembly took on additional urgency because he leaves office at the end of this year.
“The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing raging wars, rising temperatures and artificial intelligence, among other matters. Instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections”.
His speech opened the main portion of the world's biggest diplomatic meeting of the year. Leaders from the UN's 193 member countries address each other and the international community and air their hopes, plans and grievances.
Guterres also rebuked might-makes-right thinking, telling superpowers to recognise “that their power isn’t so super”. Recent years have made it clear that “military power alone cannot secure peace,” he said.
Yet about an hour after Guterres spoke, US President Donald Trump offered a different and equally frank view of power.
Read moreIran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
“While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said, touting his country's economic, technological and military footprint.
He reiterated his view that the UN has “great potential” but rebuked it for what he called “imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”. He went on to criticise such bodies as the International Criminal Court, to which the US is not a party.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will be consumed with wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living?
The future of the United Nations itself will also be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. Member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the UN next. Guterres’ second five-year term ends on December 31, and no clear successor has emerged. Guterres closed his speech by acknowledging the forthcoming departure and vowing to “never, ever give up” on the values for which the UN stands.
“Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible,” he said, before leaving the rostrum amid a sustained, standing ovation. He put his hand on his heart.
There is still no question that the UN remains the key gathering place for its member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly, along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners Tuesday: Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the UN because the US refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
Read moreUS again denies Palestinian leader visa for UN General Assembly
The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's UN ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said ahead of the gathering that it is “extremely critical” for world leaders to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet – especially at a time of such polarisation.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation”.
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organisation’s finances in rocky shape.
“While the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change," said former UN deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member.
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax”, and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.
Read moreTrump calls concerns over rogue AI a 'hoax' promoted by a ‘sick conspiracy’
The UN Security Council added a meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.
(FRANCE24 with AP)
