Jorge Palma (1950-2026): the songs that will never die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:05:26 UTC
04:05:26 KST

On Tuesday, Portugal woke up in mourning: Jorge Palma died at 76 following a cardiorespiratory arrest. His songs remain. Euronews asked artists from Herman José to António Zambujo for their favourite song.
Jorge Palma, one of the most influential singers, songwriters and composers in contemporary Portuguese music, died on Monday at the age of 76 in physical years, even if metaphorically he had lived more than a hundred thousand, as he sang on Encosta-te a mim, a track from the 2007 album Voo Nocturno. The music video, in which Palma appears surrounded by lifelong friends and recent companions, will live on. Palma may have left us, but his songs will forever be part of Portuguese culture and soul.
On Estróina, a track on his most recent album, Vida (2023), he sings: "Whoever my undertaker may be, make sure I am properly dressed." There could be no finer attire than the many farewell words already dedicated to him, alongside the many he himself wrote.
And, as he went on singing, "and since life is meant to be lived live and in full colour, let us raise a glass to pleasure, with no false modesty." That is exactly what we will do. Euronews spoke to several people close to the singer, to Portuguese culture and to his work, all unconditional admirers of his legacy, to understand what remains after his passing and which songs they will never forget.
Herman José - Actor and comedian
For Herman José, who crossed paths with Jorge Palma many times and in many different settings, his death "leaves a silence that will be hard to fill".
One of his most cherished memories with the singer goes back to 1974. "I was one of his musicians, alongside the great Pedro Osório. It is one of those memories that time does not erase and that today returns with particular strength. We were all much younger, in a Portugal that itself was embarking on a new life, and even then Jorge's extraordinary musical personality was already there – restless, free, unpredictable, fascinating," he recalls.
The comedian says Jorge Palma was an "utterly unique musician", one of those who "never needed to resemble anyone else to be recognised from the very first chord, the first word, the first inflection of that voice".
From all the work Jorge Palma leaves behind, Herman José chooses Deixa-me Rir (from O Lado Errado da Noite, 1985), "perhaps because in it I find so much of Jorge: the intelligence, the irony, the mistrust of certainties, a certain melancholy hidden behind the smile. And that rare ability to say serious things without ever losing his irreverence," he concludes.
António Zambujo - Singer and songwriter
For the singer from Beja, choosing just one Jorge Palma song is "unfair" because "his body of work is immensely rich". Even so, he accepted Euronews' challenge and picked the song O Meu amor Existe, from the voice-and-piano album Só, released in 1991.
"I consider this record the best in the history of Portuguese music, and whatever I might say about Jorge Palma would never be enough, given the dimension I believe he has," he said.
Gabriel Gomes - Musician and composer
"I have lost a friend, a hero," Gabriel Gomes, accordionist and former member of Madredeus and Sétima Legião, tells us to begin with. He quickly adds: "But I gained so much from his presence in my life."
Earlier this year he shared the stage with Jorge Palma and, at the Artes à Vila festival in the Batalha Monastery, presented his first solo project.
"The emptiness hurts, but his memory and his work will eventually fill it. It was quick, as he deserved," he sums up.
Gabriel Gomes chose the song Passos em Volta, from the album Bairro do Amor, which they played together on stage so many times and in which, just as in the lyrics, Jorge Palma "opened the window and flew away".
Tiago Cação - artistic agent
With a long career in the music, live entertainment and artist management industries, he confided that he had never wanted to meet Jorge Palma.
"I never wanted to meet Jorge. I never wanted to get close to him. I always wanted to keep Jorge in an intangible place, alongside the great poets and great musicians I have always admired. On Friday, my father (much younger than Jorge), whom I thought knew nothing about music, said: 'I would not like to die without seeing a Jorge Palma concert. Because with artists like Jorge, we always think they do not die. And they do not'," he shared.
For Tiago, the song he will never forget is Sonhadores inatos. "I identify with the simple idea of never stopping dreaming, despite the inevitabilities that come with being alive."
Fernando Vendrell - Film director
The filmmaker admits that today he can only think of Frágil (Bairro do Amor, 1989). "Tonight I feel so fragile," he paraphrases.
Director of films such as "Aparição" and "Sombras Brancas", Fernando Vendrell remembers Jorge Palma as "an extraordinary writer of songs".
"In my view, they are among the most perfect songs ever written in Portugal. His gaze and his writing were agile, his melodies graceful and unique. They brought with them a world we belonged to or wanted to be part of," he says.
Ana Margarida de Carvalho - Journalist and writer
When she heard the news of the singer's death, the song that came to her mind was Na Terra dos Sonhos, for its melody and because it was written by a "sceptical optimist".
Ana Margarida de Carvalho says she knows all the albums, songs, acoustic versions and live recordings, where his "virtuosity on piano, acoustic guitar or electric guitar" always stood out: "He had enormous versatility, a powerful voice that stood the test of time," she recalls, referring to the many concerts she attended. Jorge Palma's voice also became part of her everyday life. "He is always on my car playlist..." she says.
Among the many songs by Jorge Palma, the journalist also highlights Portugal, Portugal, which she considers "an anthem", and Estrela do Mar, whose chords "sound like waves, or the string quartet, in which he pays tribute to Durrell's Alexandria Quartet".
However, she told Euronews she was choosing Eu Fui um Lobo Malvado (Acto Contínuo, 1982). "With lyrics that are naïve, perhaps, but which in my view make it a song that turns back on itself and becomes the most beautiful declaration of welcome, a song about friendship and reconciliation, ultimately – and I know it by heart, and so do my children."
"I have not yet wielded a weapon that did not ricochet / and the scar always outlives even the neatest bandage / but whenever you want you are welcome in my castle / which perhaps because it is old and wrinkled / does not need painting," she quotes.
Luiz Carvalho - Photographer
The author of the cover photo for this article (kindly made available for publication) recalls his first encounter with the singer: "I have known you since that afternoon in 1980 in Paris when I photographed you singing in the Saint-Michel metro station. Afterwards we went for a drink, I think Graça Lamy was there too. The damned negative exists but I just cannot find it. I love your work and, above all, your attitude to life: free, non-conformist, polite, a musician with classical roots, at times too wild for the body to be able to keep up. I would have loved to make a documentary about you, something alive, handheld camera, direct sound... You will always be in my heart and in my ears, for as long as I still have road ahead of me."
The song he has chosen is O Lado Errado da Noite, "a striking melody, very much in tune with part of his own journey".
Finally... the choices of the authors of this piece
Ana Filipa Palma: A Gente Vai Continuar is not only one of his greatest songs, it is also one of the most listened to today and, above all, a promise that his voice will remain "for as long as there are winds and sea".
The tribute to Palma at the latest edition of the Play awards ended with the whole audience singing A Gente Vai Continuar.
Ricardo Figueira: I choose Bairro do Amor because it is comforting to believe there is a place drawn in coloured pencil by people who have suffered for not having anyone, a country with no prisons and no hospitals, where the sun seems bigger and there are waves of tenderness in every look. Even if that place exists only in songs.

How is the US trying to ground Iranian airlines worldwide?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:04:59 UTC
04:04:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside Trump's bid to shut Iran out of global aviation
The US has issued an ultimatum to countries and companies continuing to provide services to Iranian airlines.
In the latest salvo under the Trump administration's "Operation Economic Outcast", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has announced that organisations that continue to have ties to the country's airlines after Wednesday risk being frozen out of the global financial system.
Here's what we know about Washington's bid to shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation.
What has the US done?
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that, from 23 September, the US will impose secondary sanctions on airports and aviation service companies that continue to work with Iranian airlines.
Companies that continue to deal with Iranian carriers after this date risk being locked out of the dollar-based financial system.
That includes airport operators, cargo service providers, ground handlers and fuel suppliers.
"On 23 September all Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world," Bessent told CNBC.
"How do we do that? That if they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he said.
This follows a decision by the Treasury on 8 September to slap sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines and another nine aviation service companies.
"Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran's remaining airlines: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system," Bessent said at the time.
How have countries responded?
Several countries have announced restrictions in the days since the sanctions were announced.
Mahan Air announced it had suspended flights to Istanbul and Ankara at the request of Turkish authorities on 21 September. A few days earlier, the carrier halted its Tehran-Muscat route.
Georgia has also introduced a blanket ban on Iranian carriers using the country's aviation sector.
Meanwhile, AFP reported that Iraq is expected to comply with the US measures, citing several sources, including a senior Iraqi government official.
However, Baghdad had not formally announced the restrictions as of Tuesday, while online flight data seen by The New Arab continued to show Iranian-operated flights available to Baghdad and Najaf.
The uncertainty has already caused disruption for Iraqi travel agencies, particularly in Najaf, where many businesses depend heavily on flights carrying pilgrims between Iraq and Iran.
Some agencies have stopped taking flight bookings or begun switching customers to land routes, while others have warned that the restrictions could cause major losses. Travelling overland can also significantly increase journey times, particularly for elderly passengers and Iraqis travelling to Iran for medical treatment. A journey to the holy city of Qom, for example, can take more than 12 hours from the border.
Mahan Air routes to key countries, including the United Arab Emirates, China, Russia, India, Pakistan and Thailand, also do not appear to have been affected so far.
Beijing sharply criticised the measures as "illegal".
"China consistently opposes illegal unilateral sanctions that lack a basis in international law or authorisation from the UN Security Council," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters.
How will this impact Iran's aviation industry?
Iran's aviation industry has already been severely degraded after years of US sanctions that have made it extremely difficult to modernise and maintain its ageing civilian aircraft fleet.
Airlines have struggled to obtain crucial spare parts and components needed for repairs and maintenance, raising longstanding concerns about the safety and reliability of the country's ageing aircraft.
The impact of the latest measures will depend largely on how many countries and aviation companies comply with Washington's threat of secondary sanctions.
The most immediate effects will be felt by carriers operating international routes. The bulk of Iran's overseas routes are handled by three airlines - state-owned flag carrier Iran Air, Mahan Air and Qeshm Air - while smaller carriers operate short-haul routes to Iraq and Gulf countries.
If airports, fuel suppliers, ground handlers and ticketing companies comply with the US measures, Iranian carriers could find it increasingly difficult to operate abroad even in countries that have not formally banned them.
Why is the US doing this?
The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's so-called "economic D-Day", which aims to further isolate Iran from the global economy.
Aviation was among five sectors the administration said Tehran was using to circumvent existing US sanctions, move money and provide military support to its allies in the region.
"Iran continues to use its supposed 'commercial' airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and the IRGC, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and hard cash to its proxies," the Treasury wrote.
The return to economic pressure comes amid continued deadlock after almost seven months of war.
Concerns about munitions stockpiles, souring public opinion and limited military options have left the White House hesitant to return to open conflict but unwilling to negotiate a peace deal.
The deadlock comes at a particularly sensitive time for Trump, less than two months before the crucial US midterm elections, with polls showing declining public support for both the war and his presidency.

====================================================================================================

Airlines have struggled to obtain crucial spare parts and components needed for repairs and maintenance, raising longstanding concerns about the safety and reliability of the country's ageing aircraft.
The impact of the latest measures will depend largely on how many countries and aviation companies comply with Washington's threat of secondary sanctions.
The most immediate effects will be felt by carriers operating international routes. The bulk of Iran's overseas routes are handled by three airlines - state-owned flag carrier Iran Air, Mahan Air and Qeshm Air - while smaller carriers operate short-haul routes to Iraq and Gulf countries.
If airports, fuel suppliers, ground handlers and ticketing companies comply with the US measures, Iranian carriers could find it increasingly difficult to operate abroad even in countries that have not formally banned them.
Why is the US doing this?
The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's so-called "economic D-Day", which aims to further isolate Iran from the global economy.
Aviation was among five sectors the administration said Tehran was using to circumvent existing US sanctions, move money and provide military support to its allies in the region.
"Iran continues to use its supposed 'commercial' airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and the IRGC, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and hard cash to its proxies," the Treasury wrote.
The return to economic pressure comes amid continued deadlock after almost seven months of war.
Concerns about munitions stockpiles, souring public opinion and limited military options have left the White House hesitant to return to open conflict but unwilling to negotiate a peace deal.
The deadlock comes at a particularly sensitive time for Trump, less than two months before the crucial US midterm elections, with polls showing declining public support for both the war and his presidency.

Should alcohol have more explicit health warnings? These experts think so
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Push for more detailed alcohol labelling, after low uptake of voluntary system
In short:
An analysis of labels from 6,037 different alcoholic drinks sold in Australia has found just one in four included a voluntary warning label.
The study's lead author says this indicates harms are not being communicated clearly and wants labels to be more specific, warning consumers about the risk of cancer and liver disease.
What's next?
The UK and Ireland have committed to introducing mandatory health warning messages on alcohol labels to include conditions such as cancer, but there are no plans to upgrade current mandatory labelling requirements in Australia beyond pregnancy warnings.
Alcohol use is widespread in Australia, with about three in four people aged 14 and older consuming it over the course of a year.
But public health experts say harms associated with drinking, even at low levels, are not being communicated clearly enough to consumers.
Drinking alcohol is one of the leading risk factors for the burden of disease in Australia, and is linked to several types of cancer as well as liver disease, heart disease and stroke.
While it's mandatory in Australia to include a pregnancy warning on drinks containing 1.15 per cent alcohol by volume, additional warnings about alcohol-related harm are voluntary.
Australian research published today in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health analysed labels of 6,037 alcoholic drinks sold in Sydney stores to determine how many products included one.
The researchers found just one in four products included a voluntary warning label, most of which targeted specific groups, such as drivers or underage drinkers.
Two in three products included a responsible consumption message such as "drink responsibly".
But study lead author Asad Yusoff, of the George Institute for Global Health, said separate research suggested responsible consumption messages were "ineffective" and often "confusing" to consumers.
"There's no real definition around what it means to drink responsibly,"
Australian guidelines recommend healthy adults drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than four standard drinks on any one day.
Although the percentage of Australians consuming more than this amount was decreasing, Mr Yusoff said many people did not realise that even low-level drinking could cause harm.
"One to two standard drinks per day significantly increases your risk of developing both breast and colon cancer," he said.
There is no safe level of alcohol consumption, according to the World Health Organization.
Warnings need to be prominent and explicit
Mr Yusoff said there needed to be clear and prominently placed warning labels on all alcoholic drinks sold in Australia, explicitly telling people about specific harms associated with drinking, such as cancer or liver disease.
Current warnings were mostly small, dull in colour and tucked away where people were "unlikely to view them", he said
"For a warning label to be effective it really needs to be on the front of the package."
Eric Hadinata, an addiction medicine specialist who did not contribute to the study, noted that government-mandated pregnancy warning labels typically included the words "alcohol can cause lifelong harm to your baby" next to a pictogram.
Dr Hadinata wanted this warning to be more prominent and placed on the front label.
Terry Slevin, chief executive of the Public Health Association of Australia, who did not contribute to the study, said the low uptake of these voluntary labels was "not a surprise".
Like Mr Yusoff, Mr Slevin said warnings on alcohol packaging needed to be more detailed about the exact harms drinking could cause to have an impact.
This, he said, would give people "full, informed consent" about what they were consuming.
"We have that expectation for all the products we use and all the products that we buy; I think it's fair that we have that expectation of alcohol,"
Australia's Food Standards Code outlines what information manufacturers need to include on their packaging, which varies depending on alcohol content.
UK, Ireland mandate health warning labels
The United Kingdom and Ireland have both committed to introducing mandatory health warning messages on alcohol labels.
The Irish laws, to be implemented in late 2028, will require labels to include calorie content as well as warning consumers about the dangers of drinking while pregnant and warnings about liver disease and cancer.
Both Mr Yusoff and Mr Slevin would like the Australian government to introduce similar legislation.
Dr Hadinata, who co-chairs the Alcohol and Other Drugs Committee at the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, also wants more detailed warnings, but suggests plain packaging similar to tobacco products will also improve health outcomes.
Alistair Coe, executive director of Alcohol Beverages Australia, said labelling in Australia already contained useful information and guidance, including alcohol content, the number of standard drinks and pregnancy warnings.
"Australia has one of the world's most comprehensive and transparent alcohol regulatory systems, supported by clear government guidance that considers all the evidence," he said.
"Policy efforts should remain targeted at the minority of people who need support, not the vast majority of responsible drinkers."
A spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said alcohol labels were part of a "multi-pronged response" to increase awareness about and respond to alcohol-related harm, alongside other initiatives.
They did not comment on whether the department would seek to introduce additional mandatory health warning labels.

Iraq to launch platform to report sectarian hate speech online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:55:24 UTC
03:55:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq to launch platform to report sectarian hate speech online
Iraq is set to launch a platform allowing members of the public to report sectarian hate speech and incitement online, a senior security official said on Monday.
Once launched, the platform will enable citizens to report sectarian content disseminated through social media and other online platforms, Security Media Cell chief Saad Maan told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).
Maan said those found to be promoting sectarian incitement and hate speech could face legal penalties, with prison sentences of up to 10 years depending on the offence and the relevant provision of Iraqi law.
He said Iraqi law determines what constitutes hate speech and sectarian rhetoric on social media, stressing the importance of distinguishing between freedom of opinion and expression and conduct that infringes on others' privacy or reputation or threatens national security.
Maan pointed to Article 200(2) of the Iraqi Penal Code, which he said is the provision most directly applicable to the work of an Interior Ministry committee dealing with such offences. The article punishes those who promote sectarian or ethnic incitement, encourage conflict between groups or stir hatred and hostility among Iraq's population.
The provision carries a sentence of up to seven years in prison or detention, Maan said, adding that it also applies to hate speech posted on social media.
He also cited Article 202, which covers publicly insulting the Iraqi people or a section of the population and carries a sentence of up to 10 years in prison or detention.
Other provisions cover the deliberate dissemination of false or malicious news, statements or inflammatory propaganda that could disturb public order, spread fear among the population or harm the public interest, as well as the publication of false reports or fabricated incidents falsely attributed to others, he said.
Maan said the issue extends beyond sectarian and ethnic rhetoric to content that could disrupt public order, adding that sectarian speech targeting a particular group could affect internal security.
He stressed that the competent court would determine which legal provision applies following an initial investigation by an investigating judge.
Regarding the planned reporting platform, Maan said the Interior Ministry has specialised security, technical and cyber teams capable of screening and analysing reports in coordination with the intelligence service and National Security Service.
He said citizens would be able to use the platform once it is launched, adding that authorities have the technical capabilities to distinguish between individual violations and organised activity on social media and identify those behind such campaigns.
Iraq has long faced sectarian tensions, particularly following the 2003 US-led invasion and the emergence of Sunni and Shia militant groups that contributed to the civil war in the years that followed. The Islamic State group's takeover of large parts of the country between 2014 and 2019 further exacerbated sectarian divisions.
The country operates under an informal power-sharing system in which the presidency is traditionally held by a Kurd, the premiership by a Shia Muslim and the parliamentary speakership by a Sunni Muslim. The presidency is largely ceremonial, while most executive powers are held by the prime minister.
Iraq is also home to a number of religious and ethnic minorities, though many of these communities have declined significantly in size in recent decades.

US, Greenland and Denmark sign agreement in bid to end Arctic standoff
Unknown

US, Greenland and Denmark sign agreement in bid to end Arctic standoff

====================================================================================================

Explainer-What is in the US-Greenland-Denmark security deal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:54:24 UTC
03:54:24 KST

Explainer-What is in the US-Greenland-Denmark security deal?
COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 - The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement on Tuesday aimed at ending months of tension over the Danish self-governing territory after US President Donald Trump's repeated threats to take control of the vast Arctic island.
Here are some key components of the deal, which adds to a 1951 US-Danish pact on Greenland's defence, according to a text published by the Danish government.
WHAT ARE THE MILITARY ASPECTS OF THE DEAL?
The agreement allows the United States to establish two new military bases — one at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and the other at Mestersvig on the east coast — and to expand Pituffik Space Base, currently its only active base on the island.
US craft including planes and vessels get flyover, landing and undersea rights in all of Greenland, including territorial waters.
The agreement does not specify troop numbers or timelines.
HOW DOES THE PACT WORK WITH NATO?
The agreement expresses support for a stronger NATO presence in the Arctic, and Denmark commits to further strengthen its own security posture in the region.
If Greenland ever become independent, Denmark and Greenland must ensure the new state remains in NATO, applying for membership if necessary.
Non-NATO members are barred from having an ongoing military presence in Greenland.
WHAT RIGHTS DOES GREENLAND HAVE?
The agreement says it respects Greenland's right to self-determination. Under the accord, the US must act in a way that respects Greenlandic society and the Greenlandic way of life.
WHAT ARE ECONOMIC ASPECTS OF THE PACT?
The agreement does not address US interests or investments into Greenland's mining and resources sector.
The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland.
Greenland will screen investments to enforce those rules.
WHAT HAPPENS NOW?
The parliaments of Greenland and Denmark must approve the agreement before it goes into effect.
The pact has no end date and can be amended only by mutual consent. REUTERS

Queensland yet to sign on to Thriving Kids a week from launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:50:36 UTC
03:50:36 KST

Queensland lashed over Thriving Kids holdout, days out from launch
In short:
A week out from the launch of Thriving Kids, the minister who announced the program to shift some children under nine off the NDIS has lashed out at the last state yet to formally sign its side of the deal.
The Queensland government says it remains concerned the Commonwealth is walking away from vulnerable Australians.
What's next?
The first phase of Thriving Kids is set to begin October 1.
A frustrated federal Health Minister Mark Butler has denounced the Queensland government over its refusal to sign up for the Thriving Kids program, a week before the first phase of the NDIS alternative for some children is set to begin.
Announced last August, Thriving Kids is a pillar of the federal government's efforts to curb spending on the $51 billion NDIS, and will see states and territories provide services for children under nine with developmental delay or autism who have "low to moderate" support needs.
Queensland's Liberal National government has held out on signing up, accusing the Albanese government of cost shifting and failing to explain important information about the program, including how "low to moderate" support needs would be defined.
But with the first phase of the program set to begin on October 1, Mr Butler said time was running out.
"All other states and territories, Liberal and Labor alike, [are] just getting on with the business of developing their programs. So I'm frustrated with Queensland; it's a big state with a dispersed community," he told the ABC.
"We're losing time, frankly, for Queensland parents and children."
Earlier this year, the premiers and chief ministers of all states and territories, including Queensland, agreed to set up "foundational supports" outside the NDIS, such as Thriving Kids, in exchange for $25 billion in hospital funding from the Commonwealth.
Most of those jurisdictions have started tender processes and set aside money in their most recent state budgets.
"[Queensland] signed the grand bargain," Mr Butler said.
"They're receiving substantial additional hospital funding … money is available for parents to receive these services in Queensland, as very soon they will be just south of the border in New South Wales and in every other state and territory."
Autism Association of Australia CEO Nicole Rogerson said it was "not OK" that Queensland was yet to formally commit to Thriving Kids.
"The sheer audacity of Queensland just saying 'I'm not prepared to be involved' is sort of shocking. I understand they're trying to make a political point, but there are families, real children at the end of this that won't have services in the state of Queensland," she said.
"I'm sorry, but the grown-ups have to come to the table and work this out."
A spokesperson for Queensland's Acting Disability Minister Ros Bates said the state government's concerns remained.
"Not only for young people who may fall through cracks in the system, but also for those vulnerable Queenslanders who have relied on the NDIS since it was established more than a decade ago to provide support for those in need," they said.
Ms Bates then told a press conference this morning the Queensland government was "not being belligerent" by not signing on, but rather doing its "due diligence" for state taxpayers.
"We want to see the detail. We want to know what it means for kids who are under nine years of age, what happens after?" she said.
"Mark Butler knows full well that the deal that they are trying to give Queensland is substandard."
Major questions remain
The first phase of Thriving Kids will focus on "general supports" such as online parenting courses and information resources including phone lines.
"Targeted supports", such as therapies in schools, will then gradually roll out, with full implementation set to be complete by January 2028, when the government intends for new NDIS eligibility rules to be in place.
Many in the disability community fear Thriving Kids will not adequately support children with moderate needs, that parenting courses will not be effective, and that already exhausted parents will be shouldering additional responsibilities.
Mr Butler told the ABC talks were starting with the states over the development of non-NDIS supports for other groups.
"We've started that process with states at an official level … we've got to develop foundational support programs for children over the age of nine and for adult cohorts who might not end up being on the NDIS, for example, adults with psychosocial disability," he said.
"When [Education Minister] Jason Clare and I meet with school principals to talk about these issues, a message that comes to me from them, using their words, is we need a 'Thriving Teens' program."
Ms Rogerson said it was too early to be thinking about something like that when Thriving Kids was still so far away from being fully operational.
"The kinds of supports we give very small children with autism are very different when children are above age nine," she said.
"If we don't get [Thriving Kids] right, I promise you it's going to cost a lot more money, because children are adults for many more years than children."

Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran at UN, then confirms direct talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:50:18 UTC
03:50:18 KST

Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump asked whether he should "annihilate the Islamic Republic" or offer it a deal to rebuild before telling reporters that US and Iranian officials had met on the sidelines. Most of Iran's delegation walked out during his speech.
US President Donald Trump first threatened to "annihilate" Iran in an address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, but then said US and Iranian officials had met on the sidelines hours later, in what is the first confirmed direct contact between the two sides since the war began in February.
At a tumultuous moment for the world — and for his presidency — Trump lauded his own fortitude compared to other leaders as he defended his decision to start a war with Iran in his speech at the UN headquarters in New York.
Trump then suggested that he could be facing "a big decision" in the ongoing war with Iran as he called on Tehran to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to the negotiating table to find a settlement.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world," Trump said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" he asked.
Trump further pushed back on the notion that Iran has shown any resilience.
"The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate," Trump said.
Trump also accused Tehran of stalling to make a deal to fully reopen Hormuz and negotiate an endgame to the war until after the midterm elections in the US. He insisted the tactic would not affect his approach to the war.
Most of Iran's delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump railed against the Islamic Republic.
Yet after his blustering speech and fulsome defence of the war, the US president told reporters about the meeting between the two sides but offered few details.
"It was a very good meeting," Trump said.
Venezuela, Ukraine, Yemen
After his speech, Trump gathered with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the General Assembly to sign a new security agreement.
The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to "take over" Greenland, a territory of NATO ally Denmark, by military force if necessary.
Trump said Tuesday the US will immediately begin developing a larger military presence in Greenland, including "building two very major military bases."
Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark's territory.
Trump also held talks with new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The leaders said they discussed migration, the conflict in Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war and more.
Trump also met with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and will hold a more informal meeting with Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez, the White House said.
He's also scheduled to meet with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia — to discuss the way ahead with the Iran war and growing concern about recent Tehran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Trump also plans to take part in an event on the Shield of Americas, an initiative Trump launched with Latin American countries earlier this year focused on combating violent cartels.
Iran war looms large at General Assembly
Trump returned to the UN General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Tehran.
Nevertheless, Trump argued in his speech that the world was better off under his auspices.
"As president of the most extraordinary nation in history," Trump said. "I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester."
The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the US and Israel have killed much of Iran's top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a US blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles.
The energy market remains spooked by the war, and oil prices spiked further after Saudi Arabia last week shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf.
The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq while mired in an exchange of fire with Yemen's Houthis.
At the same time, Houthi territorial advances and their takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb strait have now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane.
But Trump insisted anew that the elevated oil prices are a transitory problem that will fade once the war ends.
"Oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict," Trump said. "And they were very low in the United States. They were really low."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Trump is open to meeting with Iran's president Masoud Pezeshkian while he is in New York for the General Assembly.
"This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems," Rubio told NBC. "It doesn't mean you're going to end up agreeing with them, but it's important."

Investigators Blame F-16 Thunderbird Crash on Turned Fan Blade Deep in Engine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:50:11 UTC
03:50:11 KST

A misaligned vane in an F-16 engine that field-level maintainers cannot see to inspect caused one of the U.S. Air Force’s Thunderbird jets to crash last December, a new report concludes. The same problem led another F-16 to crash 20 months earlier.
The pilots ejected in both cases, escaping with minor injuries, while both jets were total losses. Separate Air Force Accident Investigation Boards came to similar conclusions.
The report on the Dec. 3, 2025, Thunderbird crash in the California desert was released Sept. 21. The report on the prior crash, on April 30, 2024, near Holloman Air Force Base, N.M., was released months before the Thunderbird crash, in February 2025.
The latest investigation report valued the loss of the Thunderbird F-16 at $33.5 million.
Both accidents were blamed on turned variable vanes deep in the Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-220 engine’s high-pressure compressor. Investigators determined that one or more vanes were turned and misaligned, creating “abnormal aerodynamic forces” and “irregular wake patterns” as air flowed through the engines. The resulting stress on compressor blades caused vanes to break or crack, casuing the engines to “catastrophically” fail.
The Thunderbird investigation report cited three known instances where compressor blades fractured due to turned vanes, but it did not specify a third instance. Besides the Holloman crash in 2024 and the Thunderbird crash in 2025, no publicly released Accident Investigation Board reports from the last decade mention fractured compressor blades in the F100-PW-220.
In both the Holloman and Thunderbird cases, field maintainers failed to catch the misaligned vanes. While some stages can be inspected with a borescope, the fifth stage of the engine core cannot be seen in the F100-PW-220 without completely disassembling the engine core.
Notably, both F-16 engines in question had experienced foreign object debris, or FOD, events in the years prior to the crashes. The Thunderbird jet engine’s FOD event occurred in October 2021, and the Holloman F-16’s FOD event happened in August 2022. In both cases, maintainers noted damage to early stages of the inlet fan but found no issues with the fourth, seventh, or eighth stages, which they could inspect using a borescope.
The Air Force’s technical orders for the F-16 do not require maintainers to remove and disassemble the engine core to inspect those stages after a FOD event if no damage is found in the surrounding stages. It’s unclear if the FOD events caused the vanes to turn, however, so cannot be clearly blamed for triggering the events.
The accident investigation board for the Holloman F-16 crash noted that Pratt & Whitney’s analysis determined the FOD event was the probable cause of the vane turning, but expert opinions varied when asked if it was possible for damage to occur to a later stage if no damage was observed in the ones before it. That left the cause inconclusive.
Similarly, the board for the Thunderbird crash noted that it was “impossible to conclusively determine” what caused the turned vanes. It did, however, note that the lack of inspection for the fifth and sixth stages after a FOD event “substantially contributed to the mishap.”
“The post-FOD event guidance contains an inherent inability to inspect these specific sections of the engine core. Additionally, the core of the engine is only inspected during scheduled maintenance when a core component reaches its overhaul threshold, leaving time for potential damage to progress undetected,” the report states.
A spokesperson for the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately comment on whether the technical guidance might be changed to require complete inspections following a FOD event or to trigger other steps to prevent similar mishaps. In February 2025, after the report for the Holloman crash was released, the spokesperson said the center’s F-16 program office “is looking at this issue and is working closely with the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Propulsion Directorate, the engineering authority for the engine, to correct any deficiencies.”
‘Ejecting Was Ultimately the Only Option’
In addition to detailing the engine issues, the Thunderbird report detailed how the pilot did everything possible to save the jet.
An experienced instructor pilot with nearly 1,400 flight hours, the pilot was on a routine training flight working on loops and rolls and flying from the Thunderbirds’ famed “delta formation.” The mishap pilot had planned to peel off from the formation during the loops to avoid exacerbating a stiff neck, then rejoin the formation for the rolls. But as the pilot waited to rejoin, the engine stalled. It felt “like the jet just … stopped midair,” the pilot told investigators.
Seeking to recover, the pilot sacrificed speed to gain altitude, then tried a secondary engine control. When that didn’t work, the pilot attempted an engine restart. “It sounded like things were grinding,” the pilot reported later. Finally, more than four minutes after the engine stalled, the pilot chose to eject.
The Accident Investigation Board concluded that “ejecting was ultimately the only option which provided a favorable outcome.”
Yet the ejection wasn’t flawless—the F-16’s ACES II ejection seat has two hoses that transfer hot gas from the ejection initiators to the sequence valves, and they’re supposed to disconnect automatically during an ejection. One of the hoses in the Thunderbird F-16 didn’t disconnect properly but ripped from the violence of the ejection.
The plane went down near Trone, Calif., a small desert community near Death Valley. Upon impact, debris scattered up to 750 feet away. A local civilian who saw the crash got to the pilot first, and Navy search and rescue responded within minutes to transport for medical care. The pilot was discharged the same day.

Has Queen Nefertiti's long-lost tomb finally been found?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:49:43 UTC
03:49:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Has Queen Nefertiti's long-lost tomb finally been found?
New evidence pointing to hidden chambers near the tomb of Tutankhamun has revived hopes that the long-lost tomb of Queen Nefertiti, one of ancient Egypt's most celebrated figures, may finally be within reach.
Researchers using ground-penetrating radar and microgravity surveys say they have detected signs of previously unknown corridors and chambers extending beyond the famous pharaoh's tomb, known as KV62, in Egypt's Valley of the Kings.
The findings have breathed new life into a controversial theory first proposed by British Egyptologist Nicholas Reeves in 2015: that Tutankhamun's surprisingly small tomb is actually only the outer section of a much larger royal burial complex, and that Nefertiti could lie within its still-sealed chambers.
Though her tomb has not yet been found, researchers believe they may finally have identified a promising new place to look.
The team, led by former Egyptian antiquities minister and Ain Shams University archaeologist Mamdouh Eldamaty, combined radar surveys from inside Tutankhamun's tomb with more than 1,200 microgravity measurements of the surrounding ground.
The results indicate what researchers believe could be a rubble-filled corridor around two metres wide leading away from Tutankhamun's burial chamber, along with several low-density structures with right angles that could represent artificial rooms.
One particularly intriguing feature, dubbed "anomaly 7", appears as a roughly square high-density area surrounded by a lower-density zone.
Structural engineer George Ballard, one of the researchers, suggested it could potentially represent a chamber containing objects, although he cautioned that the measurements were approaching the limits of what the technology can reliably detect.
Who was Queen Nefertiti?
Nefertiti was the Great Royal Wife of Pharaoh Akhenaten, one of the most controversial rulers of ancient Egypt, who radically transformed Egyptian religion during the 14th century BC by elevating the worship of the sun disc Aten and introducing a form of worship sometimes described as an early form of monotheism.
She occupied an unusually prominent position alongside her husband, appearing in surviving images performing religious and royal functions normally associated with the pharaoh himself.
Nefertiti was also closely connected to Tutankhamun. Genetic evidence indicates Akhenaten was Tutankhamun's father, while his mother was another close relative of Akhenaten rather than Nefertiti, according to the prevailing interpretation of DNA studies.
Nefertiti was therefore likely Tutankhamun's stepmother, but she was also his mother-in-law: Tutankhamun married Ankhesenamun, one of the daughters of Akhenaten and Nefertiti.
Towards the end of Akhenaten's reign, Nefertiti largely disappears from the historical record. Some Egyptologists believe she may subsequently have ruled Egypt herself, potentially under another royal name, although the theory remains disputed.
Her fate, death and burial place have never been conclusively established.
Famous today for the painted limestone bust discovered at Amarna in 1912, Nefertiti has consequently become one of the most recognisable figures from ancient Egypt despite the mystery surrounding her final years.
What could be behind Tutankhamun's walls?
That mystery is central to Reeves's theory about Tutankhamun's tomb.
Despite the extraordinary treasures Howard Carter discovered there in 1922, KV62 itself is unusually small for a royal burial. Reeves proposed that it had originally been constructed for another royal figure and was hurriedly adapted after Tutankhamun died unexpectedly while still young.
He identified lines and cracks beneath the tomb's decorated walls that he argued could mark concealed doorways leading to the remainder of an older royal burial.
Attempts to prove the theory have produced conflicting results, however. Previous radar surveys have variously suggested hidden spaces or found no evidence of them, and the idea that Nefertiti lies nearby remains disputed among Egyptologists.
The researchers may soon have an opportunity to test what is actually there.
They are seeking permission from Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities to drill small exploratory holes towards one of the suspected spaces and potentially send miniature camera-equipped vehicles inside.
If approval is granted, the investigation could begin as early as November.

Quest tells customers to replace passports after security breach

Quest Apartment Hotels tells customers to replace passports and licences after security breach
In short:
Quest Apartment Hotels has issued warnings to affected customers to reissue their passports and replace their driver's licences after personal data was exposed.
The company initially advised customers that their information had leaked in August this year but did not detail the extent.
Customers told the ABC they had to reissue credit cards and licences.
Quest Apartments has advised customers affected by a data breach in August to replace their passports and driver's licences after its investigation revealed additional information had been leaked.
In August, Quest said that it had identified unauthorised access to a database system "from a vulnerability through a third-party service provider".
It advised affected customers that their data from before June 2025, including full names, email addresses and other contact details, had been exposed.
But in new emails and text messages seen by the ABC, Quest told customers an investigation found additional information, including passports, driver's licences, credit card numbers including CVV numbers, and other personal information, had been leaked.
Quest advises reissuing documents
In an email to a concerned customer seen by the ABC, Quest wrote:
"If your driver's licence number was affected, consider contacting your local road authority about obtaining a replacement licence," it said.
"If your passport number was affected, contact the Australian Passport Office (or the relevant issuing authority for non-Australian passports) to discuss whether your passport should be flagged or reissued."
Quest contacted Steven Cooper from NSW via text message.
The text seen by the ABC said: "Our forensic data analysis has confirmed that some additional categories of your personal information were involved in the data security incident we previously notified you about."
Mr Cooper had been a victim of multiple data breaches, including the Origin, Optus and Medibank security leaks, which he said had been frustrating.
"It's pretty annoying to be listed, you know, three or four times," Mr Cooper said.
"The Origin one came, and then the Quest one came quite quickly after,"
In this breach, he said he was told his information, credit cards, including CVV numbers, car registration and date of birth had been leaked.
Mr Cooper said he stayed with Quest quite often, so he had to change multiple credit card passwords on his joint accounts.
"They said that it's happening even with expired cards. So I guess that's the kind of currency that the hackers are interested in so they can defraud people," he said.
Another customer, who chose to remain anonymous, said Quest emailed them to say their credit cards and personal information had been leaked.
They had stayed at Quest Apartments several times and used multiple credit cards, and had to cancel them and have their licence reissued.
They said the whole process was time-consuming and inconvenient.
Currently, the waiting time to have your licence reissued and mailed to you, depending on the state, can be up to 14 days.
Getting a passport reissued can take up to six weeks to process according to the Australian Passport Office website.
Information leaked from COVID period
Lizzy, who asked to use only her first name to protect her identity, said she was also advised via text that her information, including her credit card details, was leaked six years ago during the COVID-19 pandemic.
At the time, she couldn't stay at the Quest apartments because of COVID restrictions, but she said she booked and paid for the apartment with her credit card.
"It just seems strange that they've still got my credit card details on file, when really, all I did was pay for it online … even though I never ended up staying there and it's been six years," she said.
When she got the first text in August advising that her name and other details had been leaked, she said she didn't "really bother" to worry about it.
"I really just thought that text was a scam, so I didn't really think much of it. I didn't get a follow-up email about it," she said.
It was only when she got a follow-up text last week letting her know her credit card details were also leaked that she started to worry.
David Mansfield, managing director for Australasia at The Ascott Limited, said in a statement that earlier updates advised that: "For the overwhelming majority of impacted individuals, the information identified at that preliminary stage was limited to a combination of name and contact information.
"Our forensic data analysis has now enabled us to determine the specific types of personal information affected.
"I recognise the concern this incident has caused. On behalf of Quest, I sincerely apologise to those who have been affected."
In a statement, Quest said the investigation found information relating to 1,991,613 customers was affected.
It outlined that the following additional information was compromised.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was aware of a "cyber incident" affecting Quest Apartments and Hotels.
"If your Australian passport number was compromised in this data breach, your passport is still safe to use for international travel. Your passport number cannot be used to obtain a new passport," the department said in a recent statement.
"Robust controls are used to protect passports from identity takeover, including sophisticated facial-recognition technology."

US signs ‘tremendous’ Arctic security deal with Denmark, Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:46:32 UTC
03:46:32 KST

Trump signs ‘tremendous’ Arctic security deal with Denmark, Greenland
NATO and the European Union welcome accord that ends a months-long standoff after Trump threatened to seize Greenland.
The United States, Denmark and Greenland have signed a deal on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, granting Washington a greater military presence on the continent-sized Arctic island.
After years of tensions between the US and Denmark, which holds sovereignty over the autonomous and resource-rich territory of Greenland, Tuesday’s agreement resolves a key point of contention among Western transatlantic allies. It is set to expand a longstanding US presence just as great-power competition with Russia and China heats up.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump says Denmark deal gives US security ‘control’ over Greenland
- list 2 of 3Trump’s Greenland deal: A triumph of optics?
- list 3 of 3Where is the US opening new military bases in Greenland?
“This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States and for everybody,” US President Donald Trump said before signing the agreement. “And for Greenland, it’s going to be incredible.”
Addressing the UNGA earlier on Tuesday, Trump said the US would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations”, including “building two very major military bases”.
Agreement details
The agreement allows Washington to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base in northwest Greenland. Bases will be established at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east with the option to “establish additional defense areas” and expand operations.
It also permits US aircraft to fly over and land anywhere in Greenland, including its territorial waters while also granting “undersea access”.
No non-NATO country will be allowed to set up military installations or a “persistent” military presence in Greenland without unanimous approval by Denmark, Greenland and the US. The agreement also bars investors from “sensitive sectors” outside NATO and the European Union.
The accord does not have an end date. If Greenland becomes independent, it will remain in NATO and assume Denmark’s obligations under the deal.
“The Danish government and the Greenland government will maintain sovereignty over Greenland’s territory, but the US will have essentially veto power over what other countries are able to come to the island,” said Al Jazeera correspondent Rosiland Jordan reporting from UN Headquarters in New York.
“It does give Washington a great deal of what it wants: a military presence and the ability to keep rival nations, notably China and Russia, off,” she added.
Months of standoff
The deal follows a months-long standoff after Trump threatened to seize Greenland, prompting warnings from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen that a US takeover would end the NATO alliance.
Since 1945, the US military presence in Greenland shrank from thousands of troops across 17 bases to about 200 stationed at the remote Pituffik base.
Frederiksen called the new agreement “a deal that can last forever”, while Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described it as “a win-win-win”, saying: “Your security is our security, and our security is your security.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European Council President Antonio Costa both welcomed the deal, with the latter calling it “a positive step for transatlantic cooperation and Arctic security”, grounded in “respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.

Space Force Seeks Maneuverable Spacecraft for On-Demand Launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:43:40 UTC
03:43:40 KST

The Space Force may invest in a maneuverable space vehicle that can be available for an on-demand launch in response to “emerging threats,” according to a new industry notice.
In a Sept. 18 request for information, Space Systems Command’s Space Safari program office—which leads the service’s Tactically Responsive Space program—said they’re interested in buying a commercial spacecraft that can perform what are known as rendezvous proximity operations and dock to other satellites. The notice specifies a potential need for the capability as soon as fiscal 2029.
“[The] Space Safari program rapidly acquires, integrates, and deployed space systems to address urgent combatant commander needs and emerging threats outside traditional programs of record,” the notice states. “To achieve this, the office seeks innovative, cost-efficient solutions for unpredictable mission requirements.”
The notice doesn’t spell out how many of these vehicles the Space Force might buy but identifies a target “tasking-to-launch” timeline of 14 days. It also stresses the need for modular systems that can integrate a variety of payloads should the service need to swap a system at the last minute.
The Space Force defines Tactically Responsive Space, or TacRS, as the ability to quickly respond to on-orbit threats in any number of ways—from launching a rocket on demand to maneuvering an at-the-ready satellite to replace or augment another to buying commercial space capabilities during a conflict.
Space Safari has been demonstrating and progressing new TacRS capabilities over the last few years. In 2023, Firefly’s Alpha rocket launched a Millennium Space Systems payload just 27 hours after receiving launch orders as part of the service’s Victus Nox mission. Then in late 2025 and early 2026, it conducted a tabletop effort and field exercise called Victus Diem aimed at refining its processes for repeatable rapid launch.
In June, the service launched Victus Haze, which focused on validating multiple TacRS concepts, including dynamic space operations between two satellites. In this case, a Rocket Lab satellite launched on demand and a True Anomaly spacecraft prepositioned on orbit took turns playing the role of adversary and conducting “dynamic engagements” including pursuits between the two satellites.
Those demonstrations have put the service on a path toward operationalizing TacRS concepts. The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget request, which includes $86 million for TacRS demonstrations, says Space Safari plans to use funding to support “operational missions requiring both rapid launch and maneuverable, prepositioned capabilities.”
The documents also note that the Space Force plans to establish a “rapid reaction force structure” that would involve having satellites in production and on hand, ready for rapid launch as needed. The Sept. 18 notice appears to be an early step in that direction.
In a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space combat power Col. Bryon McClain told reporters the service is in the process of transitioning TacRS into an “operational system.” He noted that while the Space Force has additional missions planned, it would likely be saying “less and less” about them.
“You’re probably going to hear a lot less about that overall because we see this as an important warfighting capability, and the last thing you want to do is make that too public,” he said Sept. 16.
For now, the five known TacRS missions expected to launch in the next few years are:
- Victus Surgo, a mission cosponsored by the Defense Innovation Unit that will feature a SpaceX Falcon 9 launching a highly maneuverable spacecraft built by Impulse Space
- Victus Salo 1, set to launch in 2027 on a Falcon 9 rocket that will carry a payload built by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Victus Salo 2 and 3, which don’t yet have a public timeline but will involve Impulse Space’s pre-positioned Mira orbital maneuver vehicle
- Victus Sol, launched by Firefly’s Alpha, which will carry an operational payload

AI data centre funding surges to record $35 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:43:10 UTC
03:43:10 KST

Data centre funding surges to record $35b this year despite AI 'bubble' risks
In short:
A Reserve Bank staff note reveals Australian data centre operators have raised a record sum of at least $35 billion so far this year.
Funding obtained by Australian-focused operators has increased 46 per cent from 2025.
What's next?
The amount of capital being raised can provide early indications of how much more construction is coming.
Australian data centre operators have raised record capital of at least $35 billion so far this year, as the rapid construction of AI infrastructure has become an increasingly important part of the country's business investment growth.
A new Reserve Bank staff note obtained exclusively by the ABC shows funding obtained by Australian-focused operators had already surpassed the $24 billion raised across all of 2025, an increase of 46 per cent.
The research marks the first time an analyst from the RBA has estimated how much money has been raised to build Australian data centres.
The analysis covers Airtrunk, CDC, Firmus, Goodman, Macquarie Technology and subsidiaries of Stack Infrastructure and Equinix. It draws on financing across syndicated lending, bonds, public and private equity as well as some private transactions.
This year's funding is also more than seven times the annual average recorded between 2020 and 2024, highlighting the breakneck speed at which financing for the sector has accelerated.
However, the rapid growth is coming off a low base.
Data centre operators still account for only 16 per cent of funding raised by Australian "non-financial corporates" across the markets captured by the analysis.
The author of the note, RBA analyst Bradley Speed, states the $35 billion figure was conservative because the data does not capture all single-bank loans and may also miss some private transactions.
Why the RBA is watching
One reason the note examines data centre financing is because the amount of capital being raised can provide early indications of how much more construction is coming.
Mr Speed said funding could provide a "useful leading indicator for data centre investment in Australia", because local operators tend to rely on external capital to fund large construction programs.
This comes as the RBA grapples with how to respond to the AI investment boom, which is contributing to Australia's high inflation problem.
Building data centres requires huge amounts of spending on construction, electrical infrastructure and skilled labour, as well as imported equipment such as advanced chips and servers.
As the data centre boom increases demand for workers and resources in an already stretched construction sector, it means those resources could, relatively speaking, become more expensive and add to inflationary pressures elsewhere in the economy.
Governor Michele Bullock said on Tuesday that while AI investment was already adding to demand, there were "very few signs yet" that it was boosting the economy's supply capacity.
"So we've got this sort of awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand and the AI boom is adding to that demand ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forward," she said.
The governor also said central banks globally were watching the risk of an AI investment bubble and the potential consequences if it unwound in a disorderly way.
"You know, it might not be a bubble, but it might be."
The RBA's August meeting minutes showed the board had discussed the possibility of the AI and data centre investment boom becoming larger than anticipated, which runs the risk of driving inflation higher.
Mostly borrowed money
The RBA analyst note shows the boom is being financed overwhelmingly through borrowing money.
Debt accounted for 85 per cent of new funding obtained by Australian data centre operators so far in 2026, slightly above estimates of 60 to 80 per cent in the United States.
The biggest source has been syndicated lending, in which a group of lenders combines to provide a single, often large, loan.
Syndicated loans can be attractive for data centre build out because it "allows for greater loan sizes than with a single bank" and is generally "more accessible than the corporate bond market for firms without an investment grade rating".
About $25 billion has been raised through this method this year, accounting for about three-quarters of data centre financing in both 2025 and 2026 to date.
Mr Speed also says the sector is particularly suited to debt financing because operators often secure long-term customer leases, providing relatively predictable cash flows, while real estate can be used as collateral.
Australian operators have made less use of bonds than their US counterparts, although the note says funding sources could become more diverse as the sector expands.
Is the boom squeezing out other borrowers?
The second issue examined in the note is whether the rapid growth in AI-related fundraising could begin to crowd out financing for other Australian companies.
That concern has become more prominent overseas, particularly in the United States, where the scale of investment in AI infrastructure has prompted concerns that heavy borrowing by tech firms could crowd out other borrowers.
That is happening against a broader backdrop of rising borrowing costs globally.
The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 5 per cent recently, reaching its highest level since 2007.
Heavy AI-related borrowing is increasing demand for capital, but it is only one factor, among a number, behind higher long-term borrowing costs.
But the note finds little evidence that similar pressures are emerging in Australia so far.
Despite the rapid growth in data centre financing, it remains small relative to Australia's broader funding markets.
The note says there is little evidence the sector has materially affected financing conditions for other Australian borrowers.
